questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: In the Schopenhauer epigraph that opens the Introduction, what attitude should you take when you meet meanness or stupidity in someone?
options: That of a mineralogist who finds a very characteristic specimen of a mineral
That of a priest who listens to a confession without condemning it
That of a doctor who calmly diagnoses an illness in a patient
That of a judge who weighs the evidence before passing sentence
questions.explain: Schopenhauer advises treating such traits as an addition to your knowledge, the way a mineralogist treats a characteristic specimen. The point is detached study, not judging, treating or forgiving.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: According to Greene, what does human nature stem from?
options: Our brain wiring, nervous system and way of processing emotions, formed over about five million years of evolution
The modern technologies and institutions that shape how people now communicate and behave
The personal habits and choices each of us builds up through adulthood and working life
The particular culture, upbringing and moral teachings of the society each of us grows up in
questions.explain: Greene roots human nature in the wiring of the brain, the nervous system and how we process emotions, all of which emerged over roughly five million years of evolution. Culture and technology are shaped by this nature, not its source.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did our earliest ancestors evolve complex emotions whose signs could be read on their faces?
options: To hide their real intentions from rival groups competing for the same territory
To display their rank within the group and so avoid costly fights over status
To attract mates by signalling health and strength to the rest of the tribe
To communicate moods quickly and bind the group together, well before language existed
questions.explain: Survival depended on communicating before language was invented, so emotions such as joy, shame and jealousy showed on the face and spread through the group, uniting it.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why does Greene call the forces he describes laws?
options: They hold for every individual in every situation without exception
They were first discovered and named by experimental psychologists
They are moral rules that every decent person ought to obey
Under their influence humans tend to react in relatively predictable ways
questions.explain: Greene uses the word laws because under these elemental forces people react in relatively predictable ways. He presents the book as based on evidence, not moral rules, and claims tendencies rather than exceptionless rules.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: How does Greene answer the objection that knowledge of our primitive nature is old-fashioned in a technologically advanced age?
options: Our nature is being rewritten by progress, so the laws matter mainly for understanding history
Modern institutions now restrain our nature, so the laws apply mostly to private life
We have never been more in the thrall of human nature and its destructive potential than now
Technology has largely tamed our nature, but a few primitive traits still linger in us
questions.explain: Greene says the truth is the opposite of the objection: “we have never been more in the thrall of human nature and its destructive potential than now.” Ignoring this, he warns, is playing with fire.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: In Greene's account, what has social media done to the permeability of our emotions?
options: Turned it into a mainly positive force that spreads empathy between distant groups
Left it unchanged, since emotional contagion depends only on face-to-face contact
Reduced it, because screens filter out the faces that once spread emotion between people
Heightened it, so viral feelings sweep through us and manipulative leaders can exploit us
questions.explain: Greene says the permeability of our emotions has only been heightened through social media, where viral effects keep sweeping through us and manipulative leaders can exploit and control us.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: According to Greene's first benefit of the Laws, why should you not take personally someone's coldness or irritation toward you?
options: Their behavior is usually a deliberate test of your loyalty that you can pass by staying silent
Most people are simply rude by temperament and treat everyone around them in exactly the same way
Their emotions have deep roots that predate you, and they are rarely relating to you as an individual
Showing that you are hurt gives them power over you, so you must hide your feelings from them
questions.explain: Greene explains that people carry desires and disappointments that predate you by years; you become a convenient target of their anger or a screen for their projections. Seeing this should liberate you rather than upset you.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene advises thinking in opposites when reading people. If someone makes an overt display of confidence or hypermasculinity, what is most often true?
options: They genuinely have that trait in abundance
They are trying to provoke you into a fight
They are imitating a leader they admire
They are concealing the contrary reality
questions.explain: Greene says that when people overtly display a trait such as confidence or hypermasculinity, they are most often concealing the contrary reality; the show is a cover, not a sign of abundance.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: When someone takes an action that seems out of character, what does Greene say you should conclude?
options: It shows outside pressure forced their hand
It is a rare lapse that is best overlooked
It means your first impression was correct
It often reveals more of their true character
questions.explain: Greene writes that “what often appears out of character is actually more of their true character.” Such moments are signs of the shadow leaking out, not lapses to dismiss.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: According to Greene, what is your greatest defense against aggressive, envious and manipulative people?
options: Appealing to their better instincts
Confronting them openly at once
Identifying these types in advance
Matching their pressure with your own
questions.explain: Greene says the Laws teach you to identify toxic types in advance, which is your greatest defense: you can steer clear of them or foresee their maneuvers and keep your emotional balance.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Given the permeability of emotions, what does Greene say is the most effective means of influencing people?
options: Offering rewards and incentives that make agreement more attractive than resistance
Presenting stronger arguments and evidence until the other person runs out of objections
Lecturing people firmly on why their current position is mistaken and harmful to them
Altering your own moods and attitude, since people respond to your energy more than your words
questions.explain: Because emotions are permeable, people respond to your energy and demeanor even more than to your words, so the most effective influence comes from altering your moods and attitude. Arguing and lecturing only make people more defensive.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, does trying to change people's minds by arguing, lecturing or cajoling usually fail?
options: It bores them, because people pay attention only to stories and never to arguments
It makes them more defensive, and people are naturally stubborn and resistant to influence
It makes you look weak, and people only follow those who seem completely indifferent
It confuses them, because most people cannot follow a complicated line of reasoning
questions.explain: Greene says direct attempts to change minds make people more defensive, since they are naturally stubborn and resistant. Influence must begin by lowering their resistance.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: What does Greene describe as our natural response to reading or hearing about the darker qualities in human nature?
options: To exclude ourselves, assuming it is always the other person who has them
To become fascinated by them and wish to imitate the people who show them
To feel guilty and immediately recognize those qualities in our own behavior
To dismiss the descriptions as exaggerated and deny that anyone has them
questions.explain: Greene says we naturally exclude ourselves: it is always the other person who is narcissistic, envious or aggressive, while we see ourselves as having the best intentions. The Laws aim to end this self-deluding process.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: In Greene's picture of our two contrary selves, which one tends to be stronger?
options: Whichever self was strongest in early childhood
Neither, since the two are always equally balanced
The lower self, which is more animal and reactive
The higher self, because it is more truly human
questions.explain: Greene says the lower self tends to be stronger and is easy to slip into; because the higher impulse is weaker, connecting to it requires effort and insight. Being more truly human does not make the higher self stronger.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: To what does Greene compare the practice of empathy as you keep doing it?
options: A muscle that gets stronger the more you exercise it
A tool that wears out the more often it is used
A talent some people are born with and others lack
A language that must be learned before the age of ten
questions.explain: Greene says that as you practice empathy it becomes like a muscle that strengthens with exercise; it is a latent power everyone is born with, not a gift for a few.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: According to Greene, letting go of preconceptions and continually adapting your ideas about people through empathy leads to what in your thinking generally?
options: A loss of firm principles
Greater suspicion of others
The essence of creative thinking
Faster snap judgments
questions.explain: Greene says the fluidity gained from empathy carries over into how you attack problems, entertaining other possibilities and taking alternative perspectives, which he calls the essence of creative thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: What idea does the Anton Chekhov line that closes the Introduction express?
options: People cannot change their nature, so it is wiser to accept them as they are
People improve only when they are made to see what they are really like
People become better mainly by obeying the rules of the society around them
People improve fastest when they are praised rather than criticized
questions.explain: Chekhov's line says man will only become better when you make him see what he is like, matching Greene's aim of a brutally realistic appraisal that helps readers change.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: How does Greene ask readers to think of themselves as they begin the book?
options: As judges of human nature who will learn to sort people into good and bad characters
As scientists running experiments on the people they meet in their daily lives
As patients in therapy who will be cured of their darker impulses by reading
As apprentices in human nature who will develop skills and, through practice, become masters
questions.explain: Greene says you are about to become an apprentice in human nature, developing skills of observation and self-insight and, through practice, emerging a master of the art.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why does Greene think pat explanations such as calling someone evil, or saying something came over me, are not good enough?
questions.a: Such simple labels let us settle for the easiest and most convenient story while we stay on the surface, reacting emotionally. They give no real understanding of the roots of behavior, so they do nothing to stop the same patterns from recurring. Greene wants us to dive below the surface to the actual causes.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: What common misconception about our behavior does Greene say we must clear up first, and what is the reality?
questions.a: We tend to think our behavior is largely conscious and willed. In reality we are subject to forces from deep within that operate below the level of awareness; we see the results in our thoughts, moods and actions but have little conscious access to what moves our emotions. Greene admits this is a frightening thought, but it is the reality.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: How does Greene use our evolution as a social animal to explain human nature?
questions.a: Greene says human nature stems from brain wiring, the nervous system and how we process emotions, developed over about five million years. Many of its details come from how we evolved as a social animal to survive: cooperating, coordinating with the group, creating new forms of communication and maintaining group discipline. That early development still determines our behavior in the modern world.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Explain what Greene means by the permeability of emotions, where it came from, and how it shows up today.
questions.a: Before language, our ancestors evolved emotions readable on their faces and became highly permeable to each other's moods so the group could feel joy or grief as one and stay united in danger. Today we remain highly susceptible to the moods of those around us, unconsciously imitating others, wanting what they have and getting swept up in viral anger. We imagine we act freely, unaware of how much this affects us.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: According to Greene, how does a shadow personality form, and how have people explained it?
questions.a: We have a primitive need to wear masks to disguise behavior the tribe frowns upon. The dark desires we repress in doing so form a shadow personality. Our ancestors sensed its danger and blamed spirits and demons that had to be exorcised; we rely on a different myth, saying that something came over me.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why does Greene insist that knowledge of our primitive nature is more urgent now, not less, in a technologically advanced age?
questions.a: Greene argues that modern technology has intensified our primal traits: social media heightens emotional contagion, makes open aggression easy, intensifies envy and status-seeking through comparison, and gives tribalism echo chambers and mobs. Human nature is stronger than any individual, institution or invention and shapes what we create in its own image. Ignoring the laws dooms us to patterns we cannot control.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: How do the Laws help you stop taking people's coldness or insinuating comments personally, and what follows from that?
questions.a: The Laws show that people are dealing with emotions and issues with deep roots that predate you by years; you are often just a convenient target or a screen for their projections, so they are rarely relating to you as an individual. Grasping this lets you respond with a desire to understand rather than with emotion, making you calmer. You become less prone to moralize, accept people's flaws as part of human nature, and people like you more for this tolerance.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why does Greene say that identifying toxic types in advance is so valuable, and how should you treat them once you see them?
questions.a: Aggressive, envious and manipulative people do not announce themselves; they appear charming and use flattery, then blindside us and create pressure that makes it hard to think. Spotting them in advance lets you steer clear or foresee their moves, keeping your emotional balance. You cut them down to size, see the insecurities behind their bluster, scoff at their cover stories, and even treat the encounter as a chance to hone self-mastery.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Why does Greene think recognizing the dark tendencies of human nature in yourself is liberating rather than burdensome?
questions.a: We all share the same tendencies, so excluding ourselves is self-deception. Examining your own motives and shadow makes you humbler and better at spotting such traits in others. Greene says this does not bring guilt: you accept yourself as a complete individual, good and bad, drop the falsified self-image as a saint, and feel relieved of hypocrisy and freer to be yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Describe the practice of empathy Greene says the Laws will teach.
questions.a: Empathy is a latent power from our ancestors, who learned to intuit others' moods by placing themselves in their perspective. You quiet your interior monologue, listen closely, assume the other's viewpoint and draw on your own experiences as analogues, then analyze what you glean, cycling between empathy and analysis. It requires humility, since you can never know exactly what people think, and it strengthens like a muscle with exercise.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Contrast the lower and higher selves Greene describes, and explain why the higher self takes effort to reach.
questions.a: The lower self is the more animal and reactive side: it pulls us into emotional reactions, defensiveness and self-righteousness, grabs immediate pleasures and loses itself in the group. The higher self is the more truly human side, drawn to connect with others, absorb itself in work, think instead of react and follow its own path. Because the lower self tends to be stronger, connecting to the higher requires effort and insight, yet only developing it brings real fulfillment.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: How does Greene say each chapter of The Laws of Human Nature is built, and how does that structure serve his aim?
questions.a: Each chapter treats one law, opens with the story of an iconic individual who illustrates it negatively or positively, and gives ideas and strategies for dealing with yourself and others under its influence. Each chapter ends with a section on transforming that force into something positive and productive. This matches his aim that readers stop being passive slaves to human nature and instead actively transform it toward their higher self.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene calls the collection of forces that push and pull at us from deep within ____.
questions.explain: Greene names this collection of deep forces human nature, which he traces to the wiring of the brain and our evolution as a species.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene writes that in our self-destructive patterns it is as if we harbor a ____ within us, a little demon working independently of our willpower.
questions.explain: Greene describes a stranger within us; he later argues that understanding it shows it is not a stranger at all but part of ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Our need to wear masks to hide behavior the tribe frowns on leads, Greene says, to the formation of a ____ personality made of repressed dark desires.
questions.explain: The repressed dark desires form a shadow personality, which our ancestors blamed on spirits and demons.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: To bind the group together, our ancestors became extremely ____ to the emotions of others.
questions.explain: Greene says early humans became extremely permeable to others' emotions, a trait he calls the permeability of emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene asks readers to consider the book a kind of ____ for deciphering people's behavior.
questions.explain: He calls The Laws of Human Nature a kind of codebook for deciphering behavior, from ordinary to destructive.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene says the book bases itself on the ____, not on particular viewpoints or moral judgments.
questions.explain: Greene presents the book as a guide grounded in evidence drawn from many fields, rather than in viewpoints or moral judgments.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene describes the book as a brutally ____ appraisal of our species.
questions.explain: He calls it a brutally realistic appraisal, dissecting who we are so we can operate with more awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Each chapter of the book ends with a section on how to ____ the basic human force it describes into something more positive and productive.
questions.explain: Greene says each chapter closes by showing how to transform the force, so we are no longer passive slaves to human nature.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: In practicing empathy, Greene says you will continually cycle between empathy and ____.
questions.explain: Greene stresses that empathy should not be simply intuitive; you analyze what you glean and keep cycling between empathy and analysis.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene says the higher self is the more truly ____ side of our nature, the side that makes us thoughtful and self-aware.
questions.explain: The lower self is the more animal and reactive side; the higher is the more truly human side.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Greene tells readers that they are about to become an ____ in human nature.
questions.explain: He frames reading the book as an apprenticeship that, through practice, leads to mastery of the art.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these primitive traits does Greene say emerged from our deep past and still mold our behavior?
options: An inborn preference for living apart from any group
A natural immunity to the moods of the people around us
A need to wear masks to disguise behavior the tribe frowns on
A need to rank ourselves and measure self-worth through status
Tribal instincts that divide people into insiders and outsiders
questions.explain: Greene names status ranking, tribal instincts and wearing masks as primitive traits. He says the opposite of immunity to others' moods, and stresses we evolved as a social animal, not a solitary one.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say social media and fast communication have intensified?
options: Comparing ourselves with others, envy and status-seeking
Viral emotional effects that sweep through us
Open aggression and acting out our shadow sides
Patience and careful reflection before reacting
Respect for those outside our own group
questions.explain: Greene lists heightened emotional contagion, open aggression online, and intensified envy and status-seeking. He says tribalism now demonizes outsiders, the opposite of greater respect.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these impulses does Greene attribute to the lower self?
options: Adopting what other people think and losing ourselves in the group
Following our own path in life
Reacting emotionally and feeling self-righteous and superior
Grabbing for immediate pleasures and distractions
Absorbing our minds deeply in our work
questions.explain: Greene assigns emotional reaction, immediate pleasure and losing oneself in the group to the lower self; absorption in work and following one's own path are impulses of the higher self.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these sources does Greene say he draws on to build his guide to human nature?
options: A century of psychological literature
Scientific studies of the brain, primates and hunter-gatherers
Surveys of public opinion on moral questions
Insights of novelists sensitive to unseen behavior
Astrological traditions about personality types
questions.explain: Greene cites psychology, the sciences, philosophers, novelists and biographies. He bases the book on evidence, not on belief systems or opinion about moral questions.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as part of the empathy the Laws will teach?
options: Cutting off your incessant interior monologue and listening closely
Drawing on your own painful moments as analogues for another's pain
Reaching a firm judgment of the person as early as possible
Relying purely on intuition and never analyzing what you sense
questions.explain: Greene asks you to quiet your inner monologue and use your own experiences as analogues. He rejects pure intuition in favor of cycling with analysis, and warns against rushing to judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these tactics does Greene say toxic types typically use?
options: Creating constant pressure that makes it hard to think straight
Appearing charming in initial encounters
Using flattery to disarm us
Announcing their aggressive intentions openly at the start
questions.explain: Greene says aggressive, envious and manipulative people do not announce themselves; they appear charming, use flattery and create constant pressure.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Which of these are the simple, pat explanations Greene says we latch onto for troubling behavior?
options: Deep evolved forces operate below my awareness
That person is evil, a sociopath
Something came over me; I was not myself
Early childhood circumstances trigger this emotion in me
questions.explain: Greene cites labeling someone evil and saying something came over me as pat descriptions. Tracing triggers to childhood and to deep evolved forces is the deeper understanding he advocates.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene says we have clear conscious access to what moves our emotions, even if we often ignore it.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: we see the results in our thoughts, moods and actions but have little conscious access to what actually moves our emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the need to rank ourselves through status is noticeable among all hunter-gatherer cultures and even among chimpanzees.
questions.explain: Greene points to status ranking, along with tribal instincts, as traits found across hunter-gatherer cultures and even in chimpanzees.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Because of the open-ended way we evolved, Greene says the forces of human nature are unlimited in number.
questions.explain: Greene says that because of the precise way we evolved, there are a limited number of these forces.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the forces of human nature lead not only to envy and aggression but also to empathy and other positive behavior.
questions.explain: After listing envy, grandiosity and similar traits, Greene notes the same forces also lead to empathy and other positive forms of behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the higher self is stronger than the lower self, so connecting to it comes naturally.
questions.explain: Greene says the lower self tends to be stronger; because the higher impulse is weaker, connecting to it requires effort and insight.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene warns that looking at your own shadow will leave you feeling guilty and weighed down.
questions.explain: Greene says self-awareness will not make you feel guilty or weighed down but quite the opposite: you accept yourself as a complete individual and feel relieved of hypocrisy.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: True or false: Greene says each chapter tells the story of an iconic individual who illustrates the law either negatively or positively.
questions.explain: Greene explains that every chapter has the story of some iconic individual or individuals illustrating its law, negatively or positively, alongside ideas and strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put these benefits of the Laws in the order Greene presents them.
items: Becoming a calmer, more strategic observer of people
Becoming a master interpreter of people's cues
Outthinking the toxic types who cross your path
Learning the true levers for motivating and influencing people
Seeing the forces of human nature within yourself
Becoming a more empathetic individual
questions.explain: Greene lists the benefits in this sequence, moving from observing others calmly, through reading and handling them, to self-knowledge and empathy; a final benefit about the higher self follows.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put the parts of a typical chapter of the book in the order Greene describes them.
items: The story of an iconic individual illustrating the law
Ideas and strategies for dealing with the law
A closing section on transforming the force positively
questions.explain: Greene says each chapter has the story of an iconic figure, ideas and strategies, and ends with a section on transforming the basic force into something productive.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put these stages of the Introduction's argument in the order Greene presents them.
items: Troubling people and our own surprising behavior catch us off guard
We wrongly assume our behavior is conscious and willed
Human nature is defined and traced to our evolution
Decades of research now let us see that nature clearly
The book is offered as a codebook of laws
The ways the Laws will change how you see people and yourself
questions.explain: Greene opens with the problem, corrects the misconception, defines human nature, surveys the knowledge now available, introduces the book as a codebook, then lists its benefits.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put these steps in Greene's account of how emotional permeability developed in the order they occurred.
items: Ancestors had to communicate before language existed
They evolved complex emotions readable on their faces
They became highly permeable to each other's emotions
Modern people get swept up in viral anger and outrage
questions.explain: Greene traces the need to communicate before language, to emotions shown on the face, to permeability that bound the group, to today's susceptibility to viral feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put these events in the order Greene describes for a typical encounter with a troublesome type in the Introduction's opening.
items: They appear charming and confident, and we fall under their spell
Their ugly behavior catches us off guard
They offer cover stories or blame scapegoats
We feel helpless, and then another such type enters our life
questions.explain: Greene describes falling under a charming person's spell, being caught off guard, being confused by cover stories, and ending helpless before the story repeats with someone new.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Put these stages of the reader's journey in the order Greene sets out at the end of the Introduction.
items: Becoming an apprentice in human nature
Developing skills of observing and measuring character
Working on bringing out your higher self
Emerging, through practice, as a master of the art
questions.explain: Greene closes by casting the reader as an apprentice who develops skills, works on the higher self, and through practice emerges a master.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each researcher Greene cites to the area of human nature he links them with.
pairs: Childhood and the impact of early development
The shadow sides of our personality
questions.explain: Greene lists these psychologists with these topics in his survey of the knowledge now available about human nature.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each scientist Greene cites to the field of study he links them with.
questions.explain: Greene draws on these scientists for the brain, primates, hunter-gatherers, economic behavior and group behavior respectively.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each chapter Greene previews in the Introduction to the positive use he says it teaches.
pairs: Subtracting emotions from thinking to become truly rational
Forging an attitude that is expansive and fearless
Using comparison as a spur to excel and to emulate others
questions.explain: Greene gives these three examples of how each law contains a positive element that can resist the downward pull of our lower nature.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each trait the Introduction warns about to the later chapter law that treats it.
pairs: Colleagues who sabotage us out of secret envy
Misplaced confidence that makes people feel godlike
Losing ourselves in the group and its tribal opinions
Repressed dark desires forming a shadow
Wearing masks to disguise frowned-on behavior
questions.explain: The Introduction previews traits that later chapters each develop as a law: envy, grandiosity, conformity, repression and role-playing.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each common belief Greene challenges to his correction.
pairs: Our behavior is largely conscious and willed
Forces below our awareness drive much of what we do
Technology has moved us beyond our primitive roots
We have never been more in the thrall of human nature
Dark traits belong to other people
We are all cut from the same cloth
They are rarely relating to you as an individual
First impressions can be very deceptive
questions.explain: Each belief is one Greene names and overturns in the Introduction, from the illusion of conscious control to the trust in first impressions.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Match each online phenomenon Greene describes to the primal trait he says it amplifies.
pairs: Virtual echo chambers and mob intimidation
questions.explain: Greene argues each feature of online life gives an old trait a new and more powerful outlet.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Sort these impulses into Greene's lower self and higher self.

items.t: Reacting emotionally and defensively
Taking the path of least resistance
Losing ourselves in the group
Feeling superior to others
Connecting more deeply with others
Thinking instead of reacting
Discovering what makes us unique
Absorbing our minds in our work

questions.explain: Greene describes the lower self as animal and reactive and the higher self as thoughtful, self-aware and drawn out of itself.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Sort these figures Greene cites into philosophers and novelists.

items.t: Arthur Schopenhauer
Friedrich Nietzsche
José Ortega y Gasset
George Eliot
Henry James
Ralph Ellison

questions.explain: Greene names Schopenhauer, Nietzsche and Ortega y Gasset as philosophers, and Eliot, James and Ellison as novelists most sensitive to unseen behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Sort these figures Greene cites into psychologists and scientists of the brain, biology or evolution.

items.t: John Bowlby
Donald Winnicott
Heinz Kohut
Carl Jung
Joseph E. LeDoux
Edward O. Wilson
V. S. Ramachandran
Frans de Waal

questions.explain: Greene groups the first set under the literature of psychology and the second under advances in the sciences of the brain, biology, body and mind, and primates.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Sort these habits of reading people into what Greene recommends and what he warns against.

items.t: Slowing down and mistrusting your initial judgment
Thinking in terms of opposites
Noting actions that seem out of character
Watching small details for clues
Hurrying to fit actions into categories
Accepting people's self-serving explanations
Settling for judgments that suit your preconceptions

questions.explain: Greene says we normally rush to conclusions and accept self-serving stories; the Laws teach slowing down, thinking in opposites and attending to telling details.

questions.unitTitle: Introduction
questions.q: Sort these approaches to influencing people into what Greene says works and what backfires.

items.t: Lowering their resistance first
Validating the self-opinion they need
Altering your own moods and attitude
Being relaxed and genuinely interested
Arguing with them
Lecturing them
Cajoling them

questions.explain: Greene says arguing, lecturing and cajoling make people more defensive, while lowering resistance and working through mood and attitude actually move them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How does Greene define rationality at the start of Chapter 1, The Law of Irrationality?
options: A natural gift that intelligent people are simply born with
The habit of suppressing every feeling before making a choice
The skill of winning arguments through careful logical debate
The ability to counteract emotional effects and think instead of react
questions.explain: Greene calls rationality the ability to counteract the effects of emotion and open the mind to what is really happening. He stresses it is not innate but must be cultivated, and it does not mean wiping out feeling.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of Pericles, what did the Spartan representatives present to Athens toward the end of 432 BC?
options: An offer to join Athens in a league of democracies
A formal declaration that war had already begun
New terms of peace, with war threatened if Athens refused
A demand that Athens hand over its navy to Sparta
questions.explain: Sparta brought new peace terms and said it would declare war if Athens did not accept them. This ultimatum is what the Assembly gathered on the Pnyx Hill to debate.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of Pericles, what kind of leader had Athenians preferred in the early years of their democracy, before Pericles?
options: Quiet philosophers who avoided public speeches
Generals who refused to take any military risks
Aristocrats who ruled for decades without opposition
Dramatic, persuasive speakers who championed one faction
questions.explain: Earlier leaders were inspiring orators with a flair for drama who took risks in war for glory and pushed the interests of a single faction. This made politics divisive, and such leaders rose and fell within a few years.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene, what was Pericles's first and most unusual political move?
options: He led an attack on Sparta to win early glory
He allied with the aristocrats to secure his family's power
He refused to speak in the Assembly for several years
He allied with the lower and middle classes despite his aristocratic birth
questions.explain: Although from an illustrious aristocratic family, Pericles sided with farmers, oarsmen and craftsmen and worked to increase their voice. He thus represented the majority of citizens rather than a small faction.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of Pericles, what did he do with the growing surplus of money that his policies produced?
options: Used it to buy political favors from rival factions
Launched a massive public building project that employed the city's craftsmen
Spent it on a larger army to rival Sparta's on land
Returned it to the wealthy families who had funded the navy
questions.explain: Instead of buying political favors, Pericles commissioned temples, theaters and concert halls, putting Athenian craftsmen to work. The greatest of these was the Parthenon.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How does Greene describe Pericles's speaking style?
options: Fiery and theatrical, stirring the crowd's passions
Humorous and flattering, winning people over with charm
Restrained and dignified, persuading through airtight arguments
Brief and vague, leaving the Assembly to decide alone
questions.explain: Pericles avoided the usual flights of rhetoric and convinced audiences through careful logic. Greene says this made people listen closely and found the style compelling and calming.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What strategy did Pericles propose to the Assembly for the war with Sparta?
options: An alliance with Syracuse to attack Sparta from two sides
A limited, defensive war: shelter within the walls, refuse land battle, use the navy
Accepting Sparta's peace terms to buy time to rebuild
A swift land invasion of Sparta before its army could grow
questions.explain: Pericles proposed bringing people inside the walls, refusing to fight on land, supplying the city by sea and raiding coastal towns. He expected Sparta to grow frustrated, run out of money and agree to a lasting peace.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of Pericles, what disaster upended his strategy in the second year of the war?
options: The defection of Athens's main allies to Sparta
A revolt by the lower classes he had championed
A Spartan victory at sea that cut off Athens's supplies
A plague that spread through the crowded city and killed over a third of citizens
questions.explain: With so many people packed within the walls, a plague spread quickly, killing over one third of the citizenry and Pericles himself. His careful plan depended on patience that the disaster destroyed.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of the Sicilian expedition, what was the effect of Nicias's argument that only a much larger force could win?
options: The Assembly replaced Nicias with a more confident commander
The Assembly cancelled the expedition and sought peace with Sparta
The Assembly enlarged the expedition to one hundred ships and double the soldiers
The Assembly delayed the expedition for several years to prepare
questions.explain: Nicias wanted to kill the plan, but his argument had the opposite effect: if a bigger force was needed, the Athenians would send one. Their emotional excitement turned a warning into a reason to raise the stakes.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the story of the Sicilian expedition, how did news of the disaster first reach Athens?
options: Spartan envoys arrived to demand surrender
Nicias sent a letter to the Assembly announcing the defeat
A barber in Piraeus heard a rumor from a customer
A surviving ship sailed into the harbor with the news
questions.explain: A barber in the port of Piraeus heard from a customer that the whole expedition had been wiped out, and the rumor spread to Athens. It was confirmed a week later. Nicias's letter had come earlier and only reported a negative turn.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's interpretation, what did Pericles conclude about the other Athenian politicians who believed themselves rational?
options: They were rational but unlucky in war
They were rational but lacked the money to succeed
They were not rational at all, merely selfish and shrewd
They were too cautious to achieve lasting results
questions.explain: Greene writes: “The answer was simple: his fellow Athenians were not rational at all, merely selfish and shrewd.” Their tactics served base desires for power, attention and money and led to nothing lasting.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's account, what is nous, the thing Pericles chose to worship?
options: The ancient Greek name for the goddess of war
The Greek word for courage in battle
The ancient Greek word for mind or intelligence, a force creating order
The spirit of the Athenian democracy
questions.explain: Nous means mind or intelligence, a force that permeates the universe and creates meaning and order. Pericles saw it embodied in Athena.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Chapter 1 open with the story of Pericles before the Keys to Human Nature section?
options: To show that rationality depends on political power
To argue that ancient Athens was more rational than modern society
To prove that war is always the result of irrationality
To give a concrete model of the rational ideal that the Keys then explain
questions.explain: The Pericles story shows what rationality looks like in action and what happens when it is lost; Greene says his solution should serve as our ideal. The Keys section then explains why irrationality is so ingrained and how to work toward that ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Pericles based all his political decisions on one standard. What was it?
options: What actually served the greater good of Athens
What would most weaken Sparta in the short term
What the majority in the Assembly wanted that day
What would bring him the most personal glory
questions.explain: Pericles decided to judge every decision by what truly served the greater good of Athens. This standard helped him avoid the ego trap, even when it cost him personal glory.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: A manager reads an insulting email and feels a surge of fury. Following Pericles's practice, what should she do?
options: Ignore the feeling entirely and pretend the email never arrived
Make no decision while the emotion is strong, step away and examine the feeling
Reply immediately while the facts are fresh in her mind
Forward the email to colleagues to gather support
questions.explain: Pericles trained himself never to react in the moment or decide under a strong emotion; he analyzed his feelings, often found them unjustified, and sometimes withdrew home to calm down. Pretending the feeling is absent is not the same as examining it.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene in Keys to Human Nature, what is our first reaction when something goes wrong in our life?
options: To examine our own emotions for the cause
To accept the loss calmly and move on
To look outward for the cause, at people or forces that tripped us up
To ask others for honest feedback
questions.explain: Greene says we typically blame sabotage, hostile larger forces, bad advice or bad luck. This outward-looking reaction is deeply ingrained and hides our own irrationality from us.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's analysis of the crash of 2008, what do the common media explanations ignore?
options: The complexity of derivatives that no one could value
The influence of corrupt insiders seeking quick profits
The basic irrationality that drove millions of buyers and sellers
The role of cheap credit and excess leverage
questions.explain: The media pointed to credit, derivatives, insiders, regulation and computer models. Greene says all of this denies the basic reality that millions of people, infected by the lure of easy money, chose risky investments.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do bubbles and crashes keep repeating throughout history?
options: Because their emotional pull overwhelms reason and we do not confront that source
Because regulators always arrive too late to stop them
Because economic cycles follow fixed natural laws
Because only a few corrupt insiders profit from them
questions.explain: Bubbles stir our tendencies toward greed, easy money and quick results. Greene says “There is no regulatory force on the planet that can control human nature,” so blaming outside factors leaves the real cause untouched.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's description of the three-part brain, what does the old mammalian or limbic brain govern?
options: Feeling and emotion
Automatic responses that regulate the body
Memory of historical events
Language and abstract thought
questions.explain: The reptilian brain handles automatic bodily responses, the limbic brain governs feeling and emotion, and the neocortex controls cognition and language.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Greene say our translation of emotions into words is often slippery and inaccurate?
options: Because emotions are processed in a different part of the brain from language and thinking
Because other people tell us what we are feeling
Because language was invented before emotions evolved
Because emotions last only a few seconds
questions.explain: Emotions begin as chemical reactions and sensations that we must interpret in words, but they arise in a different part of the brain from language. So we often latch onto simple interpretations that suit us.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's example of person X, what might really lie behind the anger we feel toward X?
options: Simple tiredness from a long day
A rational judgment of X's bad behavior
Envy, felt below awareness and translated into something more palatable
Love that we are afraid to admit
questions.explain: Greene suggests we may feel inferior to X and want something X has, but envy is uncomfortable, so we translate it into anger, dislike or resentment. A passing mood is his separate example of person Y.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene, what effect have progress and technology had on our Emotional Self?
options: They have made us more violent and superstitious
They have tamed it, making us calmer than our ancestors
They have altered the forms of our emotions but not rewired us
They have given us more mental space for reflection
questions.explain: Greene says the idea that we have tamed our emotions is an illusion: “Progress and technology have not rewired us.” New media, advertising and social media in fact leave less space to step back and think.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: When hiring an assistant or partner, what does Greene say a rational person uses as the barometer?
options: Competence: can this person do the job?
Charm and ease of conversation
How much the person flatters their ideas
How little challenge the person poses
questions.explain: Rational people ask whether the candidate can do the job. Irrational people fall for charm, for those who feed their insecurities, or for those who pose no threat, and then blame others for the result.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Chapter 1, which later section takes up the low-grade irrationality that Keys to Human Nature names as the first thing to become aware of?
options: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
Step One: Recognize the Biases
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
The Inner Athena
questions.explain: The Keys section says low-grade irrationality creates ingrained biases, and Step One: Recognize the Biases addresses them. Step Two deals with high-grade irrationality and Step Three with strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene says rationality does not come naturally but is a power we must cultivate.
questions.explain: The opening states that rationality does not come naturally; it is a power to be cultivated, and in cultivating it we realize our greatest potential.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Pericles argued for expanding Athens's democratic empire as his influence grew.
questions.explain: Pericles argued against expanding the empire, fearing the Athenians would overreach; he worked instead to consolidate it and strengthen existing alliances.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Pericles's greatest building commission was the Parthenon, with its enormous forty-foot statue of Athena.
questions.explain: Greene names the Parthenon as Pericles's greatest commission and notes its forty-foot statue of Athena, the guiding spirit of Athens.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: After Pericles died of the plague, the Athenians mourned him deeply and held firm to his defensive strategy.
questions.explain: The Athenians did not mourn him; they blamed him for the plague and attacked his strategy. Their love turned to hate and the war party took over.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: After Pericles was gone, Athens attacked Melos and, after the Melians surrendered, killed all the men and sold the women and children into slavery.
questions.explain: Greene describes this atrocity against Melos, a Spartan ally, and says nothing remotely like it had happened under Pericles.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene says animals, like humans, dwell on their fears long after the danger has passed.
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the two: animals feel fear briefly and then it is gone, while humans dwell on their fears, intensifying them into constant anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene notes that chimpanzees have been shown to feel envy and the desire for vengeance.
questions.explain: In tracing the evolution of emotions, Greene says that with primates emotions became more complex, and chimpanzees can feel envy and the desire for vengeance.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene says we can reliably judge whether a person is rational from a single decision they make.
questions.explain: Greene says everyone makes some irrational decisions and even emotional types can succeed momentarily, so it is important to judge over time, by sustained success and learning from failure.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene points ahead to the discussion of trigger points from early childhood that comes later in Chapter 1.
questions.explain: When explaining that children who felt abandoned recreate patterns of abandonment, Greene refers the reader to Trigger Points from Early Childhood, which appears in Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene's vision of rationality, modeled on Pericles, means transcending emotion altogether.
questions.explain: Greene writes: “It is important to understand that rationality is not some means of transcending emotion.” Pericles sought balance, with the energy of emotions serving the thinking self.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Pericles chose to worship ____, the ancient Greek word for mind or intelligence.
questions.explain: Pericles's object of worship was nous, a force that permeates the universe creating meaning and order, which he saw embodied in Athena.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Pericles's greatest building commission, with a forty-foot statue of Athena, was the ____.
questions.explain: Among the temples, theaters and concert halls Pericles commissioned, the Parthenon was the greatest.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In 415 BC, Athenian leaders planned an expedition against ____, the rising power on Sicily that supplied Sparta.
questions.explain: Taking Syracuse would add to the empire and deprive Sparta of resources, which is why the Athenians sent their armada to Sicily.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: The commander who had great doubts about the Sicilian expedition and feared Athens was underestimating its enemy was ____.
questions.explain: Nicias laid out the negative scenarios and said only a much larger force could win, which backfired by making the Assembly enlarge the expedition.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's account, Athena was the goddess of wisdom and practical ____.
questions.explain: Athena, the guiding spirit of Athens, stood for wisdom and practical intelligence and represented the values Pericles wanted to promote.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene urges the reader to make a simple decision to cultivate their inner ____.
questions.explain: The voice of Athena stands for a higher rational power within us; Greene says cultivating the inner Athena makes rationality our guiding value.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Pericles told the Assembly that what he feared was not the enemy's strategy but Athens's own ____.
questions.explain: Pericles said: “What I fear is not the enemy’s strategy but our own mistakes.” He warned against adding to the empire or courting new perils during the war.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's three-part brain, the oldest part, which controls automatic responses that regulate the body, is the ____ brain.
questions.explain: The reptilian brain is the instinctive part, beneath the limbic brain and the neocortex.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's three-part brain, the ____ is the newest part, controlling cognition and, for humans, language.
questions.explain: The neocortex evolved on top of the reptilian and limbic brains and handles thinking and language.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene says the split between our emotions and our cognition forms a second ____ Self within us that operates beyond our will.
questions.explain: Because emotions and cognition evolved separately and are not seamlessly connected, Greene describes an Emotional Self that causes constant internal friction.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: The first step toward rationality is to become aware of ____ irrationality, the continual moods and feelings below the level of consciousness.
questions.explain: Low-grade irrationality skews thinking through ingrained biases that appear in all cultures and periods of history.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene calls the irrationality that occurs when emotions become inflamed, generally under pressure, ____ irrationality.
questions.explain: High-grade irrationality turns emotion into a reactive state and is the source of crises, conflicts and disastrous decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene calls our deep-rooted irrationality our ____ spot, and offers the crash of 2008 as exhibit A of it.
questions.explain: We cannot see how far emotion governs our minds; Greene uses the 2008 crash as a compendium of all varieties of human irrationality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Chapter 1, Master Your Emotional Self, is subtitled the Law of ____.
questions.explain: The chapter's law names the problem it addresses: our minds are governed by emotion far more than we realize.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene says the old mammalian part of the brain, which governs feeling and emotion, is also called the ____ brain.
questions.explain: The limbic brain sits between the reptilian brain and the neocortex and governs feeling and emotion.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these were features of Pericles's leadership of Athens?
options: Pushing to expand Athens's empire
A public building project that transformed the city
Championing a small faction of aristocrats
A restrained, dignified speaking style
Limiting military campaigns and winning through maneuvers
questions.explain: Pericles limited wars, funded temples and theaters, and spoke through careful argument. He represented the majority, not a faction, and argued against expanding the empire.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these did Pericles do to master his emotions and decide well?
options: Opened his mind to many options, even his opponents' ideas
Consulted the mood of the crowd before deciding
Retired alone to his house for days to calm down
Acted quickly to seize the initiative before doubts arose
Never made a decision while under a strong emotion
questions.explain: Pericles refused to react in the moment, sometimes withdrew home for days, and weighed many ideas and consequences before committing. Following the crowd's mood or rushing to act is what he avoided.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these accusations did Pericles's enemies make against him?
options: That he was a secret dictator
That he was a coward who fled battle
That he took bribes from Sparta
That he was an atheist who scoffed at traditions
questions.explain: Because he stayed in power so long, many called him a secret dictator, and he was suspected of being an atheist. Greene mentions no charges of cowardice or bribery.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these dangerous emotions does Greene say Pericles had curbed in the Athenians?
options: Boredom
Grief
Aggression
Greed
Hubris
questions.explain: Greene names aggression, greed, hubris and selfishness as the emotions Pericles had curbed, whose return led Athens to ruin.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene, which of these may people make the main object their mind worships, in place of nous?
options: The law
Their family or clan
Their ego
Beauty
Their nation
questions.explain: Greene says the mind must worship something: for most it is the ego, for some their family, clan, god or nation. Pericles chose nous instead.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these are typical explanations Greene says we give when our plans go wrong?
options: My impatience led me to a poor decision
Someone sabotaged me, perhaps out of dislike
Large antagonistic forces such as the government hindered me
My own emotions skewed my thinking
It was all bad luck and unfortunate circumstances
questions.explain: We tend to look outward: to saboteurs, hostile larger forces, bad advice or bad luck. Looking inward at our own emotions is exactly what these explanations avoid.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these warnings or precedents does Greene say were available to people before the crash of 2008?
options: The stock market bubble and crash of 1929
The bubble of 1987
A law that banned no-money-down mortgages
The crash of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management
questions.explain: Greene cites Long-Term Capital Management, the 1987 bubble and the 1929 crash as lessons available to anyone with a long memory or knowledge of history. No such law is mentioned; he says no-money-down mortgages were plainly risky.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as negative patterns that reveal irrational people over time?
options: Dreams and projects that are never realized
Finishing projects that last
Unnecessary conflicts that follow them wherever they go
The ability to work effectively with a team
Mistakes that keep repeating
questions.explain: Irrational people show repeated mistakes, needless conflicts and unrealized projects. Working well with a team and creating something lasting are signs of rational people.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say modern media and technology do to our emotions?
options: Let advertisers bombard us with subliminal messages
Make us prone to viral emotional effects through social media
Rewire our brains to be calmer than our ancestors
Give us more space for calm reflection
Help politicians play on our emotions in subtler ways
questions.explain: Greene says new media enhance politicians' power over our emotions, advertisers use subliminal messages and social media spreads viral emotions. These media are not designed for calm reflection and have not rewired us.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these Chapter 1 sections carry out the three-step path to rationality that Keys to Human Nature lays out at its end?
options: Step One: Recognize the Biases
Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
The opening statement of the Law of Irrationality
The Inner Athena
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.explain: The Keys section ends by naming three steps: awareness of low-grade irrationality, understanding high-grade irrationality, and strategies to strengthen thinking. The three Step sections follow in that order; the Pericles story comes before.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these events of Athens's war with Sparta in the order Greene tells them.
items: Sparta's ultimatum is debated in the Assembly
A plague kills over a third of the citizens
Pericles dies of the plague
Athens attacks Melos
The Sicilian expedition sets sail
Athens accepts Sparta's harsh terms in 405 BC
questions.explain: The war began after the ultimatum debate; the plague came in its second year and killed Pericles. Later came the Melos atrocity, the 415 BC Sicilian plan, and final defeat in 405 BC.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these stages of the Sicilian expedition in order.
items: Nicias warns that only a much larger force could win
A huge armada of one hundred ships launches amid celebration
Athens lays siege to Syracuse
Spartan reinforcements put Athens on the defensive
A second armada is sent as reinforcement
A barber in Piraeus hears that the expedition was wiped out
questions.explain: Nicias's warning enlarged the fleet; the siege looked promising until Spartan reinforcements arrived. Nicias's letter led to a second armada, and then the rumor of total destruction reached Piraeus.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these stages of Pericles's career in the order Greene describes them.
items: He enters public life around 463 BC
He allies with the lower and middle classes
He argues against expanding the empire and limits wars
Prosperity creates a growing surplus of money
He launches the public building project, including the Parthenon
questions.explain: Pericles first built a base among the majority, then used his influence to change policy. Fewer wars brought prosperity, and the surplus funded the building project.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these steps in Pericles's way of handling a strong emotion in order.
items: He refuses to react or decide in the moment
He analyzes the feeling closely
He sees it is not really justified and it loses significance
The voice of Athena slowly comes to him
questions.explain: Pericles trained himself not to react, then examined his insecurities or anger. Under scrutiny they lost their hold, and slowly the voice of Athena came to him.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these stages in the evolution of emotions in the order Greene describes.
items: Instant instinctive flight with no gap between impulse and action
Fear as a longer arousal that widens the animal's options
Feelings as a form of communication among social animals
Cognitive powers, language and abstract thinking
questions.explain: Greene traces a path from reptile-like instinct, to fear as arousal, to emotions as social signals, and only much more recently to cognition and language.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Order Greene's three parts of the brain from oldest to newest.
items: Reptilian brain
Limbic brain
Neocortex
questions.explain: The reptilian brain is the oldest, the old mammalian or limbic brain sits above it, and the neocortex evolved on top.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put the three steps of Greene's process for acquiring rationality in order.
items: Become aware of low-grade irrationality and its biases
Understand high-grade irrationality, when emotions are inflamed
Practice strategies that strengthen the thinking part of the brain
questions.explain: Greene says acquiring rationality requires these three steps in this order; the chapter's Step One, Step Two and Step Three sections follow them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put these sections of Chapter 1 in the order they appear.
items: The Inner Athena
Keys to Human Nature
Step One: Recognize the Biases
Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the Pericles story, to an explanation of irrationality, to the three practical steps it announces.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each figure in the Athenian story to their role.
pairs: Elder statesman who proposed a limited, defensive war
Commander who doubted the Sicilian expedition
Goddess of wisdom and practical intelligence
First heard the rumor of the Sicilian disaster
questions.explain: Pericles led Athens with restraint; Nicias warned against Sicily; Athena embodied the nous Pericles worshipped; the barber heard the rumor that spread to Athens.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each place in the Athenian story to Greene's description.
pairs: A total military state that relied on its army
Preeminent commercial power, relying on its navy and wealth
Rising power on Sicily that supplied Sparta
Spartan ally whose men Athens killed after surrender
Where the Assembly met to debate the ultimatum
questions.explain: Greene sets Athens and Sparta up as opposites, then follows the war to Melos and Syracuse; the Assembly gathered on the Pnyx Hill overlooking the Acropolis.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each date to the event in the Athenian story.
pairs: Leaders propose the expedition to Sicily
questions.explain: Pericles's career began around 463 BC; the ultimatum came at the end of 432 BC; the Sicilian plan arose in 415 BC; Athens was defeated in 405 BC.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each part of the brain to what it controls, according to Greene.
pairs: Automatic responses that regulate the body
questions.explain: Greene describes three evolutionary layers: instinct at the base, emotion above it, and thinking and language on top.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each of Greene's example persons to what is really behind our reaction to them.
pairs: Anger that masks envy we are uncomfortable feeling
An unrelated mood of frustration that makes us lash out
Anger caused by someone in our past, perhaps a parent
questions.explain: Each example shows that we lack conscious access to the origins of our emotions and so misread them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each situation to how Greene says a rational person handles it.
pairs: A divorce with child custody issues
Lets go of bitterness and reasons about the child's long-term interests
Seeks positions that fit long-term goals
questions.explain: In each case the irrational person is driven by vengeance, charm or immediate rewards, while the rational person weighs long-term effects.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each term to Greene's description.
pairs: Continual moods below awareness that create ingrained biases
Emotions inflamed by pressure into a reactive state
Second self from the split between emotion and cognition
Greek word for mind, a force that creates order
questions.explain: Low- and high-grade irrationality are the two forms of irrationality Greene's steps address; the Emotional Self operates beyond our will; nous is what Pericles worshipped.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 1 to its role in the chapter.
pairs: Story of Pericles as a model of rationality
Explains why we are irrational and defines rationality
Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
Gives practices to strengthen the thinking self
questions.explain: The chapter moves from example, to explanation, to the three steps announced at the end of the Keys section.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these traits: Pericles, or the typical Athenian leaders before him?

items.t: Restrained, dignified speeches built on argument
Limited campaigns with minimal loss of life
Remained in power decade after decade
Represented the majority of citizens
Flair for drama in speeches
Risk takers seeking glory in battle
Advanced by serving a single faction
Rose and fell in cycles of a few years

questions.explain: Greene contrasts Pericles's calm, unifying leadership with the dramatic, factional, glory-seeking leaders Athens had preferred before.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these positions from the Assembly's debate on Sparta's ultimatum: hawks or doves?

items.t: Wanted Athens to attack Sparta first
Wanted to seize the initiative
Were reminded that Spartan land forces were nearly unbeatable
Favored accepting Sparta's peace terms
Were told their plan would show fear and embolden Sparta

questions.explain: The hawks pressed for a first strike, but others noted Sparta's strength on land; the doves wanted peace, but critics said it would embolden Sparta and buy it time.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these: Athens under Pericles, or Athens after he was gone?

items.t: A golden age in the arts and sciences
A public building project employing craftsmen
Wars limited to save lives and money
Factions returning with a vengeance
Killing the men of Melos
The expedition to Sicily

questions.explain: Pericles's restraint brought prosperity and beauty; after him, factions, aggression and greed led to atrocities and the Sicilian disaster.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these traits: rational people or irrational people, in Greene's account?

items.t: Finish projects and realize their goals
Readily admit their irrational tendencies
Work effectively with a team
Create something that lasts
Grow defensive when challenged about their motives
Repeat the same mistakes
Never turn anger and wishes for change into action
Rush into action without weighing consequences

questions.explain: Greene says the difference shows in results over time and in awareness: rational people can admit their emotional tendencies, while irrational people cannot introspect.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these features: low-grade or high-grade irrationality?

items.t: Comes from continual moods below consciousness
Creates biases found in all cultures and periods
Skews ordinary planning without our noticing
Arises when emotions are inflamed by pressure
Can lead to violence and manic obsessions
Source of acute crises and disastrous decisions

questions.explain: Low-grade irrationality quietly biases everyday thinking; high-grade irrationality is an inflamed, reactive state behind more acute problems.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these: how emotions work in animals, or in humans, according to Greene?

items.t: Fear lasts a brief time, then is gone
Emotions function smoothly, as they were meant to
No need to translate sensations into abstract language
Dwell on fears until they become constant anxiety
Often misinterpret the source of their feelings
Experience constant friction between emotion and cognition

questions.explain: For animals emotions work as designed; for humans, the split between emotion and cognition creates an Emotional Self that misreads and prolongs feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort these explanations of the crash of 2008: the common media explanations, or Greene's own view?

items.t: Cheap credit led to excess leverage
A corrupt cabal of insiders manipulated the system
Computer models and trading systems ran amok
Too much or too little government regulation
Millions were infected by the lure of easy money
A wave of unbridled optimism swept through people
People ignored warnings and the lessons of history

questions.explain: Greene lists the media's outward-looking causes and argues they deny the basic irrationality of the millions of buyers and sellers who chose risk.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to the opening of Chapter 1, how do emotions affect our thinking, and why does this matter?
questions.a: Greene says we imagine we are in control, but emotions dominate us: they push us toward ideas that soothe the ego and evidence that confirms what we want to believe. This disconnect from reality is the source of bad decisions and negative patterns. Rationality is the cultivated ability to counteract these effects and see what is really happening.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why did Pericles's policy of limiting wars seem unheroic to many Athenians, and what did it achieve?
questions.a: Earlier leaders sought glory through risky campaigns, so Pericles's preference for maneuvers and minimal loss of life looked unheroic. Yet without needless wars draining the treasury, the empire ran smoothly and Athens entered unprecedented prosperity, which funded the public building project and a golden age.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Explain Pericles's proposed strategy for the war with Sparta and how he expected it to end.
questions.a: He proposed a limited, defensive war: bring everyone inside the city walls, refuse to fight Sparta on land, keep Athens supplied by sea and raid Spartan coastal towns with the navy. He expected the Spartans to grow frustrated, run out of money feeding their army, and quarrel with their allies, so that the war party would be discredited and a lasting peace agreed at little cost to Athens.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why did the Athenians turn against Pericles after the plague, and what followed?
questions.a: Suffering and frightened, they blamed Pericles for the plague and attacked his strategy as ineffective; they were no longer in the mood for patience or restraint. Their love turned to hate, factions returned, and the war party offered an aggressive strategy that released pent-up emotions, leading to escalating violence such as the attack on Melos.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In the Sicilian expedition story, how did Nicias's warning backfire, and what does it show about the Athenians?
questions.a: Nicias argued that only a much larger expedition could ensure victory, hoping to kill the plan. The excited Athenians instead doubled the force to one hundred ships and twice the soldiers. It shows how people in the grip of emotion, here greed and the smell of victory, turn even warnings into reasons to raise the stakes.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What did Pericles conclude about Athenian politicians who all believed themselves rational?
questions.a: He saw that they had plans and good excuses, yet their policies added up to chaos, corruption and a fragile democracy. He concluded they were not rational at all, merely selfish and shrewd: tactical and clever in serving base emotions such as hunger for power, attention and money, but producing nothing lasting for the democracy.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What did Athena represent for Pericles?
