questions.a: Athena embodied nous, mind or intelligence, but in a practical, earthy form: the voice that comes to heroes in need, calming them and orienting them toward the right idea and giving them energy to act. Under her influence one could see the world with clarity and hit on the action right for the moment. In essence she stood for rationality, the greatest gift of the gods.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How did basing every decision on the greater good of Athens help Pericles avoid the ego trap?
questions.a: A single standard outside himself kept his personal desires from steering policy. It led him to empower the lower and middle classes even though this could turn against him, to limit wars despite the loss of personal glory, and to launch the public works project. With a calm spirit and an open mind he could weigh options and consequences rather than react.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Greene say the Sicilian expedition represented everything Pericles had opposed?
questions.a: Pericles had warned against adding to the empire during the war and against needless new perils. The Sicilian expedition was a decision secretly driven by the desire to grab more land and blind to its possible consequences, the opposite of his calm weighing of outcomes. Its failure showed what happened to Athens once his rational spirit was gone.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What does Greene say happens when you decide to cultivate your inner Athena?
questions.a: Rationality becomes your highest value and guide. You question your emotions, asking why you feel anger or a need for attention, and under scrutiny they lose their hold, so you think for yourself instead of reacting to others' dramas. With a calm spirit you weigh more options, deliberate longer, and like an athlete in training your mind grows more flexible and resilient.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do our explanations for failure tend to look outward, and what is wrong with them?
questions.a: Not finding a cause would intensify our pain, so we reach for familiar explanations: sabotage, hostile forces, bad advice or bad luck. These stress our helplessness, are vague, and feed emotions like anger and self-pity. Above all they hide the real cause of most bad decisions, our own deep-rooted irrationality, which is our blind spot.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Greene argue that regulation cannot prevent financial bubbles?
questions.a: Bubbles arise from their intense emotional pull, which stimulates greed and the wish for easy money and quick results and overwhelms individual reasoning. Reforms and laws after past crashes did not work, because no regulatory force can control human nature. Since people blame outside forces instead of confronting this source, bubbles keep repeating, much as the same mistakes recur in our own lives.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene, how did emotions evolve, and what role did they come to play in social animals?
questions.a: Instinctive reactions gave way to fear as a longer state of arousal that captured attention and widened an animal's options, improving survival. In social animals, arousals and feelings became a critical form of communication: displays of anger warded off enemies, postures signaled sexual readiness or play, and calls from the young signaled anxiety. In primates these grew more complex, including envy and vengeance.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is so hard for us to understand and learn from our own emotions?
questions.a: Emotions start as physical arousal processed in a different part of the brain from language, so we must translate them into words and often do so wrongly, latching onto simple interpretations that suit us. We have no conscious access to their origins, such as envy disguised as anger or an old hurt from a parent. Because this is unconscious, we repeat compulsive patterns without seeing why.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What barometer does Greene offer for telling rational from irrational people?
questions.a: Everyone's thinking is infected by emotion; rational people are aware of this and, through introspection and effort, can partly subtract emotion from their thinking, while irrational people lack this awareness and rush to act. The difference shows over time in results: rational people finish projects and create lasting things, while irrational people show negative patterns like repeated mistakes and needless conflicts.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What was Pericles's vision of rationality, according to Greene, and why is it not the elimination of emotion?
questions.a: Pericles valued bold action, loved the inspiration of Athena, and wanted Athenians to feel love for their city and empathy for each other. His ideal was balance: understanding why we feel as we do and being conscious of our impulses, so that we think without being secretly compelled by emotion. He wanted the energy of emotions to serve the thinking self.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How does the first half of Chapter 1 prepare the ground for the three steps that follow it?
questions.a: The Pericles story presents rationality as an ideal and shows its loss, and the Keys section explains why irrationality is wired into us, defines rationality, and argues that “The first step toward becoming rational is to understand our  fundamental irrationality.” It then announces a three-step process: recognize low-grade irrationality and its biases, beware the inflaming factors of high-grade irrationality, and practice strategies to strengthen the thinking self, which the rest of the chapter develops.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's Step One on recognizing the biases, what does he name as the source of all our mental biases?
options: The halo effect in judging others
Trigger points from early childhood
The pleasure principle in thinking
The group effect in large crowds
questions.explain: Greene says our thoughts revolve around the desire for pleasure and the avoidance of pain, and calls this “pleasure principle in thinking” the source of all our biases. The group effect and trigger points belong to high-grade irrationality, and the halo effect is only one part of the appearance bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene's account of confirmation bias, which people are most subject to it when they ask for advice?
options: The least experienced people
The most anxious people
The most powerful people
The youngest people
questions.explain: Greene writes that people asking advice mainly want their own ideas confirmed by an expert, and “The more powerful the person, the more they are subject to this form of the confirmation bias.”

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene says the conviction bias makes us especially susceptible to which kind of people?
options: Salesmen and demagogues who display conviction
Friends who share our political party
Consultants who flatter our existing plans
Experts who present careful statistics
questions.explain: Because we assume an idea expressed with heated certainty must have been carefully examined, salesmen and demagogues can use a show of conviction to convince and deceive us, cloaking half-truths with dramatic effects.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Greene's list of biases, the halo effect is presented as part of which bias?
options: The appearance bias
The superiority bias
The conviction bias
The confirmation bias
questions.explain: The appearance bias says we see people as they appear, not as they are; the halo effect is its second aspect, where one quality we notice implies others that fit with it, as when good-looking people seem more trustworthy.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why, according to Greene's blame bias, do we avoid looking closely at our own part in a mistake?
options: It is too painful and pokes at our feelings of superiority
Others usually really are responsible for our failures
Reflection takes more time than most people can spare
We lack the information needed to judge what went wrong
questions.explain: Greene says it is often too painful to look at our mistakes because it calls into question our sense of superiority and pokes at the ego, so we blame others or circumstances and later forget our own small share.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: To what does Greene compare the superiority bias, in which we see others' faults but not our own?
options: A mirror that flatters
A mask worn in society
An optical illusion
A contagious disease
questions.explain: Greene calls the superiority bias the equivalent of an optical illusion: we cannot seem to see our own faults and irrationalities, only those of others. Masks belong to the appearance bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene's group bias, why do we take up many of our ideas and opinions?
options: Because they bring relief from feeling isolated
Because a leader has openly pressured us
Because we have tested them against evidence
Because they flatter our sense of being unique
questions.explain: Greene says isolation from the group is depressing and terrifying, so we feel relief when others think as we do and are motivated to take up ideas because they bring this relief, while imagining we reached them on our own. No overt pressure is needed.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: A company head hires a consultant, then dismisses every recommendation that contradicts the expansion plan he already favors. Which of Greene's biases best explains this?
options: The appearance bias
The blame bias
The group bias
The confirmation bias
questions.explain: Greene says this is the bane of most consultants: people asking advice want their own ideas confirmed by an expert and find ways to dismiss advice that runs counter to their desires, which is confirmation bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: In Greene's Step Two, how does high-grade emotion differ from the low-grade emotions behind the biases?
options: It works quietly below awareness and shapes all our planning
It affects only people who were wounded in childhood
It is generally sparked by something external and reaches an explosive pitch
It arises only from the desire for comforting thoughts
questions.explain: Low-grade emotions continually affect our thinking and come from our own impulses, such as the wish for comforting thoughts; high-grade emotion comes at certain moments, reaches an explosive pitch and is generally sparked by a person or circumstance outside us.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: According to Greene, how can you recognize a trigger point from early childhood at work in yourself or others?
options: A steady rise in confidence after repeated success
A calm refusal to discuss the past with anyone
Behavior that slowly hardens into a habit over years
Behavior suddenly childish in its intensity and out of character
questions.explain: Greene says the way to recognize trigger points is by noticing behavior that is suddenly childish in its intensity and seemingly out of character, often with unusually primal emotions and a changed tone of voice and body language.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: In Greene's discussion of trigger points, what does extreme mistrust originating from a disappointing early authority figure often trigger?
options: A sudden illness that removes us from the scene
A search to re-create a lost close relationship
A sudden rebellious attitude
A desire to please everyone present
questions.explain: Greene traces extreme mistrust to an authority figure in early childhood who disappointed or betrayed us, generally the father, and says it often triggers a sudden rebellious attitude. Sudden illness goes with fear, and re-creating a relationship goes with love.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: When gains come suddenly, which basic wisdom does Greene say we tend to lose sight of?
options: That money matters less than attention
That success brings envy from those around us
That the group will turn against a winner
That true success, to last, must come through hard work
questions.explain: Greene writes that when gains come quickly we forget that lasting success must come through hard work, ignore the role of luck, and try again and again to recapture the high.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: According to Greene, what can a string of previous losses and misses induce in sports?
options: Tunneling
Group euphoria
Grandiosity
Choking
questions.explain: Greene says unexpected losses make us fearful and hesitant, and in sports previous losses and misses weigh on the mind and tighten it, inducing what is known as choking. Grandiosity belongs to sudden gains.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: What does Greene recommend whenever you experience unusual gains or losses?
options: Step back and counterbalance them with some pessimism or optimism
Act quickly before the streak changes
Repeat exactly what led to the result
Seek the advice of the group to steady yourself
questions.explain: Greene calls the solution simple: unusual gains or losses are precisely the time to step back and counterbalance them with some necessary pessimism or optimism, being extra wary of sudden success because of its addictive pull.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is often wise to observe people under rising pressure?
options: Stress lets you see who will make the boldest decisions
Stress shows who is most loyal to the group
Stress can reveal flaws they have carefully concealed, showing their true character
Stress makes them more open to persuasion
questions.explain: Greene says that under stress the cool mask of self-control comes off and primitive parts of the brain take over, so tension can reveal concealed flaws; observing people then is a way to judge their true character.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: What strategy does Greene recommend for dealing with inflaming individuals such as Alcibiades or Julius Caesar?
options: Become a devoted follower so as to share their energy
See through their mythic front and recognize their very human weaknesses
Judge them only by how they make you personally feel
Oppose them openly before others fall under their spell
questions.explain: Greene says inflamers cast a larger-than-life, mythic image, but are full of the same insecurities as everyone; you should recognize these human traits and demythologize them. He also says to judge them by how they affect others, not just yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: According to Greene, how can the group effect operate without the physical presence of others?
options: Through memories of childhood family gatherings
Virally, as a strong opinion such as outrage spreads over social media
Only through dreams of belonging to a crowd
Through a leader's private letters to followers
questions.explain: Greene says the group effect does not necessarily require others to be present; it can occur virally as an opinion, generally a strong one such as outrage, spreads over social media and infects us with the desire to share it.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: According to Greene, what kind of words do demagogues rely on when exploiting the group effect?
options: Gentle words that admit doubt and nuance
Humorous words that defuse tension in the crowd
Vague but loaded words such as justice, truth or patriotism
Precise technical terms that sound expert
questions.explain: Greene says demagogues warm up the crowd with shared values and rely on vague but emotive words such as justice, truth or patriotism, speaking of abstract, noble goals rather than concrete solutions to specific problems.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: In Greene's final word on irrationality, what happened after the golden age of Pericles?
options: A return to democratic debate on the Pnyx
An age of superstition, cults and intolerance
A lasting age of science and tolerance
An age of commercial expansion in the Mediterranean
questions.explain: Greene uses this to show that history moves in cycles of rising and falling irrationality: Pericles' age of philosophers and early scientific spirit was followed by superstition, cults and intolerance, as happened again after the Italian Renaissance.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: When his girlfriend mildly criticizes one of his habits, a man feels a rush of betrayal, accuses her and withdraws, though nothing serious happened. Which inflaming factor in Greene's account best fits this?
options: The group effect
A trigger point from early childhood
Sudden gains or losses
Rising pressure
questions.explain: This mirrors Greene's example of a young man whose cold mother left a sense of abandonment; a partner's healthy disapproval hits that trigger point, and his overreaction leads to the very abandonment he feared.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In Greene's maker's mind-set, which emotion is the only one we can afford while getting a project done?
options: Resentment of interruptions
Fear of failure
Pride in our talent
Excitement and energy
questions.explain: Greene says that with a project and a deadline, the only emotion we can afford is excitement and energy; other emotions make it impossible to concentrate, so we become practical, calm and free of ego.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In Greene's rider-and-horse metaphor, what goes wrong in people whose rider is too strong?
options: The rider holds the reins too tightly and fears letting the horse gallop
The horse runs wild and heads into trouble
The horse loses all its energy and dies
The rider and horse share control equally
questions.explain: Greene says in most people the horse dominates, but in some the rider is too strong, holds the reins too tightly and is afraid to occasionally let the animal gallop; the ideal is for horse and rider to work together.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: How did Anton Chekhov, as Greene describes him, come to forgive even the worst people, including his father?
options: By treating every person with constant suspicion
By cutting off contact and focusing on his medical work
By confronting them until they admitted their faults
By imagining each person's story from the inside, as a logic that made sense to them
questions.explain: Greene says Chekhov imagined that each person, however twisted, has a reason for what they have become and is striving for fulfillment in their own irrational way; this cut brutes down to human size so they elicited pity rather than hatred.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: In Chapter 1's three-step process toward rationality, what does the second step add after the reader learns to recognize the everyday biases?
options: Understanding high-grade irrationality and its inflaming factors
Strategies that strengthen the thinking self
A historical story about Pericles and Athens
A list of narcissistic types to avoid
questions.explain: The Keys to Human Nature section lays out the process: first become aware of low-grade irrationality (the biases), second understand high-grade irrationality when emotions become inflamed, and third enact strategies. Narcissistic types belong to Chapter 2.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Why does Greene say that believing yourself immune to the mental biases is itself an example of the pleasure principle?
questions.a: Greene argues that our thinking revolves around the desire for pleasure and the avoidance of pain, so we hold on to ideas that soothe our egos and make us feel superior. Believing we are free of bias is exactly such a comforting idea. Instead, he advises searching for how the biases continually operate inside us and learning to spot them in others.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How does confirmation bias show itself when people make high-stakes plans, and what does Greene say your first impulse should be?
questions.a: A plan is designed to reach a desired positive result, so people inevitably veer toward information confirming the rosy scenario without realizing it. Evidence for almost any view is easy to find once we are convinced. Greene says your first impulse should be to look for the evidence that disconfirms your most cherished beliefs and those of others, which he calls true science.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: What is the conviction bias, and how does it distort the way we judge leaders?
questions.a: When we secretly doubt a pleasing idea, we go an extra mile to believe it vehemently and loudly contradict challengers, taking our own energy as proof it is true. With leaders, we assume that heated words, colorful metaphors and deep conviction mean the idea has been carefully examined, while those who speak with nuance and hesitation seem weak or even dishonest. This leaves us open to salesmen and demagogues who display conviction to deceive.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: According to Greene's blame bias, why do people keep repeating the same mistakes?
questions.a: Mistakes create a need to explain, but looking closely at what we did is painful and threatens our sense of superiority, so we blame others, circumstances or a momentary lapse. We go through the motions of reflecting, then the pleasure principle returns and we forget the small part we admitted. Desire and emotion blind us again and we repeat the same mistake, which is why few people truly learn from experience.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: How does high-grade emotion take over, and what does Greene mean when he says the mind tunnels into it?
questions.a: High-grade emotion is usually sparked by something external and reaches an explosive pitch, capturing our attention completely. The more we think about it the stronger it gets, so the mind tunnels into the emotion and everything reminds us of our anger or excitement. Unable to bear the tension, we often release it in a rash action we regret, feeling as if a second, limbic self had taken over.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Using Greene's example of the young man with a distant, narcissistic mother, explain how a childhood trigger point produces irrational behavior.
questions.a: As a child he experienced his mother's coldness as abandonment and concluded he was unworthy of love. Later, when a partner hints at healthy disapproval, it hits this trigger point and he feels imminent betrayal without seeing its source. He overreacts, accuses and withdraws, bringing about the very abandonment he feared, because he is reacting to a reflection in his mind rather than to reality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Why does Greene consider sudden success or winnings dangerous?
questions.a: Sudden gains release chemicals that give a powerful jolt of arousal and a desire to repeat the experience, which can start addiction and manic behavior. We forget that lasting success requires hard work and ignore luck, grow grandiose and resist anyone who warns us. Because this cannot be sustained, an inevitable and painful fall follows, as with gamblers, businesspeople in bubbles and people who gain sudden public attention.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: What does Greene say happens to people under rising pressure, and how should you watch yourself when your own stress rises?
questions.a: Under stress the most primitive parts of the brain overwhelm reasoning, so the cool mask comes off and people lash out, become paranoid, hypersensitive and petty, revealing hidden flaws. When your own stress rises, monitor yourself for unusual brittleness, sudden suspicions and disproportionate fears, and find time and space alone for perspective. Greene insists no one withstands rising stress without emotional leakage, but self-awareness can prevent regrettable decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: In his final word on the irrational, why does Greene say progress and enlightenment have not overcome irrationality?
questions.a: History shows continual cycles of rising and falling irrationality, as when the golden age of Pericles gave way to superstition and cults, and the same after the Renaissance. The irrational simply changes its look: instead of witch hunts we have had show trials, the McCarthy hearings and cults of personality and celebrity. Greene concludes that rationality must be acquired by individuals, not by mass movements or technology, and that feeling superior to irrationality is a sure sign of it.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In the strategy Know yourself thoroughly, why does Greene say the first step toward the rational is always inward?
questions.a: The Emotional Self thrives on ignorance, and the moment you see how it operates and dominates you, it loses its hold and can be tamed. So you must catch it in action by reflecting on how you behave under stress and looking for patterns and insecurities behind ineffective decisions. Knowing your strengths and what makes you different also helps you choose fitting goals and resist the pull of the group.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In the strategy Examine your emotions to their roots, what should it tell you when your anger is triggered by something trivial, and what should you do?
questions.a: Anger over something seemingly trivial or petty is a sure sign that something or someone else lies behind it, perhaps a more uncomfortable emotion such as envy or paranoia. You must look at this directly and dig below trigger points to where they began, perhaps recording self-assessments in a journal with ruthless objectivity. The aim is a neutral position from which you observe yourself with detachment and even humor, despite the ego's comforting illusions.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Why does Greene compare increasing your reaction time to resistance training?
questions.a: Greene says this power comes through practice and repetition: you train yourself to step back, by being alone, by not sending the angry email, or by waiting a day before committing to people. Perspective comes with time, so the longer you resist reacting, the more mental space you have for real reflection. Like resistance training, each act of holding back makes the mind stronger.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: What does Greene mean by accepting people as facts, and how does it help us become more rational?
questions.a: People are the main source of emotional turmoil because we keep judging them and wanting them to think and act as we do. Greene advises seeing them as phenomena, as neutral as comets or plants, working with what they give us and treating understanding them as a game of solving puzzles. Accepting human nature as radically as possible calms us, stops us projecting our emotions onto others and gives us more mental space to think.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Explain Greene's use of the ancient Greek metaphor of the rider and the horse.
questions.a: The horse is our emotional nature, full of energy and power but wild and headed for trouble without guidance; the rider is our thinking self, which through training holds the reins and turns that energy into something productive. Neither works alone: without the rider there is no direction, without the horse no power. We should think as much as possible before deciding, then loosen the reins and act boldly, channeling the energy rather than being its slave.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Why does Greene insist that the path to rationality should not be seen as painful or ascetic?
questions.a: He says rationality brings powers that are deeply satisfying, more so than the manic pleasures the world offers, as we feel when absorbed in a project and making discoveries. Taming the Emotional Self brings calmness and clarity, fewer petty conflicts, more effective action, more room for creativity and the satisfaction of mastering oneself. Knowing this makes it easier to motivate ourselves, following Pericles, who loved the goddess Athena as the embodiment of rationality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: How does the closing step of Chapter 1 tie the practical strategies back to the figure of Pericles from the chapter's opening story?
questions.a: The chapter opens with Pericles guiding Athens, and Step Three presents its strategies as ways to bring out the reader's inner Pericles or Athena. Pericles is named among the people of high rationality who serve as ideals, and the final strategy, Love the rational, describes following his path: he envisioned Athena as embodying the practical powers of rationality and loved her above all gods. The reader is asked to internalize that same love of rationality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene calls the source of all our mental biases the ____ in thinking: the desire for pleasure and the avoidance of pain.
questions.explain: Greene says our thoughts revolve around seeking pleasure and avoiding pain, so we hold on to ideas that soothe our egos; this is the root of every bias he lists.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: When we see one quality in a person, such as good looks, and assume other fitting qualities, such as trustworthiness, we fall for the ____.
questions.explain: Greene presents the halo effect as the second part of the appearance bias: certain positive or negative qualities lead us to imply others that fit with them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene sums up the ____ bias with the inner statement: I am different, more rational and more ethical than others.
questions.explain: In the superiority bias we cannot see our own faults, only others', and we readily ascribe Machiavellian tactics to other people while crediting our own success to talent and hard work.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Greene says rationality and ethical qualities do not come naturally but are achieved through awareness and effort in a ____ process.
questions.explain: Closing the superiority bias, Greene says rationality and ethics must be achieved through awareness and effort; they come through a maturation process, not by nature.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: In high-grade emotion, the more we think about the emotion the stronger it gets, until our minds ____ into it and everything reminds us of our anger.
questions.explain: Greene describes the mind tunneling into the emotion so that we become reactive; being aware of this lets you stop the tunneling before a regrettable releasing action.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Greene says a string of previous losses and misses can weigh on an athlete's mind and induce what is known as ____.
questions.explain: Unexpected losses make us feel cursed and hesitant, which leads to more mistakes; in sports this tightening of the mind is called choking.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Greene describes the ____ as the high-grade variety of the group bias, felt at sporting events, concerts and political gatherings.
questions.explain: In a large enough group we become different and are caught up in collective emotions; Greene calls this the group effect, the inflamed form of the everyday group bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Faced with inflaming individuals, Greene advises recognizing their very human insecurities and weaknesses so that you can ____ them.
questions.explain: Inflamers project a larger-than-life, mythic image; seeing their ordinary human traits lets you demythologize them and keep your distance.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Greene warns that a ____ exploits the group effect by warming up the crowd and stirring a continual sense of panic, urgency and outrage.
questions.explain: Greene says demagogues in politics or the media must keep emotional levels high; when you sense one, become doubly wary and analytical.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Greene calls the calm, practical focus we feel when we have a project to finish, perhaps with a deadline, the ____ mind-set.
questions.explain: In the maker's mind-set the only emotion we can afford is excitement and energy, our ego does not intrude, and these moments reveal the rational self waiting to come out.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Instead of judging people and trying to change them, Greene advises seeing them as ____, as neutral as comets or plants.
questions.explain: Under the strategy of accepting people as facts, Greene says to see others as phenomena that simply exist, and to work with what they give you.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In the ancient Greek metaphor Greene uses, the ____ is our thinking self, which holds the reins and guides our emotional energy.
questions.explain: The horse is our emotional nature, full of energy; the rider is the thinking self that, through training and practice, guides that energy into something productive.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: To examine your emotions to their roots, Greene suggests keeping a ____ in which you record your self-assessments with ruthless objectivity.
questions.explain: Greene says it might be wise to use a journal for self-assessments, because the ego otherwise makes us maintain comforting illusions about ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: As an example of balancing rider and horse, Greene suggests keeping a perfect balance between skepticism and ____.
questions.explain: Skepticism plays the rider and curiosity the horse: you scrutinize ideas yourself while keeping a child's interest in everything. Greene says this balance is one all geniuses possess.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these are biases that Greene lists in Step One: Recognize the Biases?
options: Sunk-cost bias
Blame bias
Anchoring bias
Conviction bias
Confirmation bias
questions.explain: Greene's list is confirmation, conviction, appearance, group, blame and superiority biases. Anchoring and sunk-cost biases are not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as part of the appearance bias?
options: Assuming good-looking people are more trustworthy
Distrusting speakers whose tone is hesitant
Imagining successful people are probably ethical and deserving
Following a party line on dozens of issues
Taking people's carefully trained social fronts for reality
questions.explain: The appearance bias covers mistaking social masks for reality and the halo effect, such as trusting good-looking politicians or assuming success means virtue. Distrusting hesitant speakers belongs to conviction bias, and following a party line to group bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list among the inflaming factors in Step Two?
options: Inflaming individuals
The maker's mind-set
The group effect
Confirmation bias
Rising pressure
questions.explain: The inflaming factors are trigger points from early childhood, sudden gains or losses, rising pressure, inflaming individuals and the group effect. Confirmation bias is a low-grade bias from Step One, and the maker's mind-set is a source of rationality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Which of these are key emotions that Greene says childhood trigger points can center on?
options: Fear of losing control or of failure
Extreme mistrust of authority
Love that seeks to re-create a close parental or sibling bond
Boredom with routine work
Envy of a successful rival
questions.explain: Greene names fear, love and extreme mistrust as emotions trigger points can center on. Boredom is not mentioned, and envy appears instead as a possible hidden root of anger in Step Three.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Which of these are devices Greene says demagogues use to exploit the group effect?
options: Speaking of abstract, noble goals
Proposing concrete actions to solve specific problems
Using vague but emotive words such as justice or truth
Warming up the crowd with ideas and values everyone shares
Expressing nuance and hesitation to seem honest
questions.explain: Greene says demagogues create a pleasant feeling of agreement, rely on loaded words and talk of abstract noble goals rather than concrete solutions. Nuance and hesitation are what the conviction bias makes audiences distrust.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Which of these are qualities Greene says highly rational people such as Darwin, Lincoln and Warren Buffett share?
options: A realistic appraisal of themselves and their weaknesses
The ability to reach goals they have set
A tolerant attitude toward people
Complete freedom from emotion
Unwavering conviction in their own ideas
questions.explain: Greene lists a realistic self-appraisal, devotion to truth and reality, tolerance toward people and the ability to reach set goals. He insists rationality is not freedom from emotion, and vehement conviction is a bias.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Which of these are ways Greene suggests to increase your reaction time?
options: Deciding quickly so the emotion does not linger
Calling the person at once to clear the air
Physically removing yourself to be alone
Writing the angry email but not sending it
Waiting a day before committing to hire or be hired
questions.explain: Greene says to step back, be alone, sleep on angry emails for a day or two and give commitments a day, because perspective comes with time. He warns against communicating while feeling a sudden emotion.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Which of these pleasures does Greene say come from taming the Emotional Self and loving the rational?
options: An overall calmness and clarity
The satisfaction of mastering yourself
The jolt of sudden winnings
More mental space to be creative
The relief of agreeing with the group
questions.explain: Greene says rationality brings calmness, clarity, more effective action, room for creativity and self-mastery, pleasures deeper than the manic ones the world offers. Sudden winnings and group relief are sources of irrationality in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Which of these sections belong to the second half of Chapter 1, after Keys to Human Nature?
options: The Narcissistic Spectrum
The Inner Athena
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
Step One: Recognize the Biases
Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.explain: After the opening story (The Inner Athena) and Keys to Human Nature, the chapter's three steps follow in order. The Narcissistic Spectrum opens Chapter 2.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the more powerful a person is, the less subject they are to confirmation bias when asking for advice.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: the more powerful the person, the more they are subject to this form of confirmation bias, wanting experts only to confirm their own ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene notes that on the internet it is easy to find studies supporting both sides of an argument.
questions.explain: This is why Greene says never to accept people's ideas just because they supply evidence, but to examine it yourself with as much skepticism as you can muster.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: True or false: Greene says high-grade emotion generally comes from our own inner impulses, while low-grade emotion is usually sparked by something external.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: low-grade emotions originate from our own impulses, such as the desire for comforting thoughts, while high-grade emotion is generally sparked by something external.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that with enough discipline a person can withstand rising stress without any emotional leakage.
questions.explain: Greene tells readers never to imagine they can withstand rising stress without emotional leakage, saying it is not possible; self-awareness and reflection only prevent regrettable decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: True or false: Greene acknowledges an exhilarating, positive aspect to group emotions, since this is how people can be rallied for the collective good.
questions.explain: Greene grants the positive side of the group effect but warns to inoculate yourself when the appeal is to darker emotions such as hatred of the other or rabid patriotism.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Chekhov's father was an alcoholic who beat his children, yet through his writing Chekhov came to forgive him.
questions.explain: Greene says that by getting inside even the worst characters in his stories and plays, Chekhov could forgive anybody, even his father.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: True or false: Greene describes the path to rationality as necessarily painful and ascetic.
questions.explain: Under Love the rational, Greene says it is important not to see the path as painful and ascetic; it brings powers more satisfying than the manic pleasures the world offers.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's rider-and-horse metaphor, in most people the rider dominates and the horse is weak.
questions.explain: Greene says that in most people the horse dominates and the rider is weak; only in some is the rider too strong, holding the reins too tightly.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: True or false: Step One of Chapter 1 deals with low-grade irrationality, which the Keys to Human Nature section describes as continual moods and feelings below the level of consciousness.
questions.explain: The Keys section introduces low-grade irrationality as moods and feelings below awareness that skew our thinking into biases; Step One then lists those biases.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Put the biases in the order Greene presents them in Step One.
items: Confirmation bias
Conviction bias
Appearance bias
Group bias
Blame bias
Superiority bias
questions.explain: Greene moves from how we gather evidence (confirmation, conviction) to how we judge others (appearance), how the group shapes us, and finally how we see ourselves (blame, superiority).

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Put the inflaming factors in the order Greene presents them in Step Two.
items: Trigger points from early childhood
Sudden gains or losses
Rising pressure
Inflaming individuals
The group effect
questions.explain: Greene starts with wounds buried deep inside us, moves through circumstances such as gains, losses and stress, then to the people and crowds that inflame us, and ends with a final word on historical cycles of irrationality.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene's example of the young man with a distant mother in order.
items: As a child he feels his mother's coldness as abandonment
Later a partner hints at disapproval of some trait
He feels a powerful rush of imminent betrayal
He overreacts, accuses and withdraws
His behavior brings about the abandonment he feared
questions.explain: Greene uses the story to show how a childhood wound programs us to repeat the early experience: reacting to a reflection in the mind rather than reality produces the very outcome feared.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene's cycle of sudden gains in order.
items: Sudden winnings give a powerful chemical jolt
We try again and again to recapture the high
We grow grandiose and resist anyone who warns us
An inevitable fall leads to depression
questions.explain: Greene says sudden success creates a desire to repeat it and feelings of grandiosity; because this cannot be sustained, the fall comes and is all the more painful.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Put the strategies for bringing out the rational self in the order Greene presents them.
items: Know yourself thoroughly
Examine your emotions to their roots
Increase your reaction time
Accept people as facts
Find the optimal balance of thinking and emotion
Love the rational
questions.explain: Greene begins inward, with self-knowledge and examining emotions, moves to restraint and to how we view others, then to balancing thought and emotion, and ends by making rationality something we love.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Put the stages of Anton Chekhov's path, as Greene tells it, in order.
items: Beaten as a child by his alcoholic father
Trained and worked as a doctor
Took up writing as a side career
Got inside his characters to understand even the worst types
Came to forgive anybody, even his father
questions.explain: Greene presents Chekhov as a model for accepting people as facts: he applied a doctor's eye to the human animal and, by imagining others from the inside, turned hatred into pity.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each bias in Greene's Step One to the inner statement he uses to sum it up.
pairs: I look at the evidence and decide through rational processes
I believe in this idea so strongly. It must be true
My ideas are my own. I am not a conformist
I learn from my experience and mistakes
I’m different, more rational and ethical than others
questions.explain: Greene opens each bias with the flattering belief it hides behind, then shows how the pleasure principle makes that belief false.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each bias to Greene's example of it.
pairs: A planner veering toward information that confirms the rosy scenario
Trusting a leader because he speaks with heated words and colorful anecdotes
Assuming a successful person must be ethical and deserving
Party supporters whose opinions follow the same direction on dozens of issues
questions.explain: Each example shows the bias at work in ordinary life: in plans, in judging leaders, in judging the successful, and in political orthodoxy that arises without overt pressure.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Match each inflaming factor to the response Greene recommends.
pairs: Detach and contemplate the possible source, the early wound
Counterbalance with some necessary pessimism or optimism
Observe yourself with detachment, finding time and space alone
See through their mythic front and demythologize them
Avoid the group setting or enter it with maximum skepticism
questions.explain: For each source of high-grade irrationality Greene offers a way to step back from the inflamed state before it drives a regrettable action.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Match each key emotion behind a childhood trigger point to the reaction Greene associates with it.
pairs: Fear of losing control or failing
Withdrawing like a child curling into a ball, or a sudden illness
Desperately trying to re-create a close parental or sibling bond
questions.explain: Greene says trigger points can center on any key emotion, and each produces behavior that is childish in intensity and seemingly out of character.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Match each of Greene's strategies to a practice he recommends under it.
pairs: Reflect on what weaknesses come out under stress
Examine your emotions to their roots
Sleep on an angry email for a day or two
Think like a writer, as Chekhov did
Recall the pleasure of being absorbed in a project
questions.explain: Each strategy has a concrete practice: inward reflection, honest journaling, delaying responses, imagining others from the inside, and recognizing the deep pleasures rationality brings.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Match each element of Greene's rider-and-horse metaphor to its meaning.
pairs: Our emotional nature, full of energy and power
Our thinking self, which holds the reins through training
Wild, unguided and continually heading into trouble
A rider who is too strong
Holds the reins too tightly and fears letting the animal gallop
questions.explain: Greene says the one without the other is useless: without the rider there is no direction, without the horse no energy; they must work together.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 1 to what it mainly does.
pairs: Tells the story of Pericles and his ideal of rationality
Explains the law of irrationality and outlines a three-step process
Lists low-grade biases rooted in the pleasure principle
Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
Describes what drives emotion to a high-grade, reactive state
Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
Offers practices to strengthen the thinking self
questions.explain: The chapter moves from an exemplary story to the general law and then through three steps, from awareness of everyday biases to inflamed states to practical strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort each example into the conviction bias or the appearance bias.

items.t: Trusting a leader who speaks with heated certainty
Suspecting a speaker who expresses nuance of weakness
Defending a doubtful idea more loudly to quiet our doubts
Assuming a good-looking politician is trustworthy
Taking someone’s noble, hardworking front for reality
Imagining that a successful person is deserving

questions.explain: Conviction bias treats the force of belief as proof of truth; appearance bias mistakes people's fronts and halo qualities for who they really are.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort each example into the group bias or the superiority bias.

items.t: Taking up opinions for the relief of thinking like others
Holding views that follow one party’s line on many issues
Believing our ideas came to us completely on our own
Believing the other party is irrational but ours is not
Seeing Machiavellian tactics in others but never in ourselves
Crediting all our success to talent and hard work

questions.explain: The group bias hides the pull of belonging behind a belief in independent thinking; the superiority bias is the optical illusion of seeing irrationality and manipulation only in others.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Sort each reaction into what Greene links to sudden gains or to sudden losses.

items.t: Feelings of grandiosity
Resisting anyone who tries to warn us
Forgetting that lasting success needs hard work
Imagining we are cursed with bad luck
Becoming fearful and hesitant
Choking in sports

questions.explain: Greene says gains bring a manic, addictive high and grandiosity, while losses make us feel cursed and hesitant, breeding further failures.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Two: Beware the Inflaming Factors
questions.q: Sort each item into what inflaming individuals do or how Greene advises handling them.

items.t: Express their emotions eloquently, stirring parallel feelings
Project their internal drama outward onto others
Cast a larger-than-life, mythic image
Make you think of them continually
Recognize them by how they affect others
Distance yourself from them
See their very human insecurities

questions.explain: Inflamers provoke extreme attraction or repulsion; Greene's defense is to spot their effect on others, keep distance and demythologize them.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: In Greene's balance of skepticism and curiosity, sort each trait into the rider or the horse.

items.t: Refusing to accept explanations at face value
Looking at results rather than stated motives
Verifying and scrutinizing ideas for yourself
A childlike interest in everything
Openness to wild ideas
Enjoying exciting speculations

questions.explain: Greene casts skepticism as the rider and curiosity as the horse; the rational mind keeps both, with the elasticity of a child and the hard-nosed need to verify.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.section: Step Three: Strategies Toward Bringing Out the Rational Self
questions.q: Sort each attitude into what Greene recommends or rejects under the strategy Accept people as facts.

items.t: Seeing people as phenomena, like comets or plants
Working with what people give you
Treating understanding people as a game of puzzles
Imagining a person’s story from the inside
Wishing people were something they are not
Trying to make others think and act as you do
Projecting your own emotions onto others

questions.explain: Greene says constant judging and wanting to change people keeps us frustrated, while radical acceptance calms us and lets us observe people dispassionately.

questions.unitTitle: Master Your Emotional Self
questions.q: Sort each item into low-grade irrationality (Step One) or high-grade irrationality (Step Two) as Chapter 1 organizes them.

items.t: Confirmation bias
Blame bias
Appearance bias
Superiority bias
Rising pressure
The group effect
Sudden gains or losses
Trigger points from early childhood

questions.explain: The chapter's process splits irrationality into everyday biases below awareness (Step One) and inflamed reactive states usually sparked from outside (Step Two).

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: In the statement of the Law of Narcissism, Greene calls ____ the most remarkable tool we all naturally possess for connecting to people and attaining social power.
questions.explain: The law opens by naming empathy as our natural instrument for seeing into others’ moods and minds, anticipating their actions and lowering their resistance.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to the Law of Narcissism, our natural instrument of empathy is blunted by our habitual ____.
questions.explain: Greene says the instrument is “blunted by our habitual self-absorption”, which is why the chapter treats narcissism as the obstacle to empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Put the ideas of the Law of Narcissism statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: Empathy is our most remarkable tool for connecting to people
This tool is blunted by habitual self-absorption
We are all narcissists, some deeper on the spectrum
Our mission is to turn our sensitivity outward
We must also recognize the toxic narcissists among us
questions.explain: The statement moves from the power of empathy, to what blunts it, to the claim that everyone is on the narcissistic spectrum, and ends with the twofold mission of turning outward and spotting toxic narcissists.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Narcissism says we must recognize the toxic narcissists among us before getting enmeshed in their dramas and poisoned by their envy.
questions.explain: This is the closing sentence of the law’s statement: alongside turning our own sensitivity outward, we must spot toxic narcissists early.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Narcissism say empathy, when cultivated and properly used, allows us to do?
options: Win every argument by force of reason
Anticipate people’s actions
Stop needing attention from others
Gently lower people’s resistance
See into the moods and minds of others
questions.explain: The law credits empathy with letting us see into others’ moods and minds, anticipate their actions and gently lower their resistance. It never claims empathy removes our own need for attention or wins arguments by logic.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: In Greene’s account of the human need for attention, what happens to people who go through long periods of isolation without eye contact?
options: They begin to doubt their existence and fall into deep depression
They grow more self-reliant and stop craving recognition
They become calmer once the competition for attention ends
They develop sharper empathy for others’ hidden moods
questions.explain: Greene uses isolation to show that part of the need for attention is purely physical: without people looking at us, we begin to doubt our existence and descend into depression.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, why does doubling our efforts to win attention often backfire?
options: Others resent anyone who openly competes with siblings or colleagues
People who try too hard seem desperate and repel the attention they want
It builds a self-image too divorced from reality to survive
It turns us into self-objects that others control at will
questions.explain: Greene notes that extra effort exhausts our energy and that people who try too hard “seem desperate and repulse the attention they want”.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: In building a self-image, why can we not go too far in accentuating our positive qualities and explaining away our flaws?
options: We will become enmeshed in other people’s dramas
We will stop needing other people and lose our social bonds
Our parents will no longer validate our early independence
Others will point out the gap with reality and we will doubt ourselves
questions.explain: Greene says that if our self-image is too divorced from reality, other people will make us aware of the discrepancy and self-doubt follows; done properly, it gives us a self we can love.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Greene says the self-image we build operates as a ____, helping us regulate our doubts and insecurities.
questions.explain: He writes that “This self-image operates as a thermostat”, quietly raising us up when we feel unappreciated so we are not wholly dependent on others.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say the self-image, working as a thermostat, does for a functional person?
options: Makes us constantly conscious of how it is working
Removes our need for attention from others altogether
Makes us less completely dependent on others for attention
Lets us retreat to it and soothe ourselves when we feel unappreciated
Raises us up in moments of doubt and depression
questions.explain: The thermostat soothes us, lifts us in doubt and reduces our dependence on others. Greene stresses that it works largely unconsciously and does not abolish our need for attention.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, what problem leads most of us, from early childhood, to create a self, and what does that self give us?
questions.a: We crave attention and validation, but attention is limited: we compete with siblings, classmates and colleagues, people are often indifferent, and trying too hard repels them. Our solution is to create a self, an image of our tastes, opinions and values that we can love. This self lets our energy turn inward, so we can soothe ourselves when alone or unappreciated; in Greene’s words, “We have self-esteem.”

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Explain Greene’s comparison of the self-image to a thermostat, and why he says we rarely notice it.
questions.a: Like a thermostat regulating temperature, the self-image regulates our doubts and insecurities: when we feel alone or unappreciated, we retreat to it and our self-love raises us up, even making us feel superior. We take it for granted like the air we breathe because it operates largely unconsciously. The best way to see it is to look at deep narcissists, who lack this device.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the key moment in building a self we can love occurs between the ages of two and five.
questions.explain: He places the key moment between two and five, when we separate from our mother, cannot get instant gratification, and must incorporate our parents’ strengths into ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, how does a child between two and five years old answer the discovery that it is alone yet dependent on its parents?
options: By mimicking the facial expressions of all its caregivers
By retreating into a fantasy self far superior to others
By identifying with its parents’ best qualities and making them its own
By competing with its siblings for every scrap of attention
questions.explain: Greene says our answer is to identify with our parents’ strength and ability to soothe us and incorporate these qualities; if parents encourage early independence, the self-image takes root.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Put these steps in how Greene says we come to have self-esteem in the order he describes them.
items: We feel a never-ending need for attention from birth
We find there is only so much attention to go around
We create a self-image that we can love
That self-image regulates our doubts and insecurities
questions.explain: Greene starts from the need for attention, shows that attention is scarce and fleeting, and presents the self-image as our solution, a thermostat that gives us self-esteem.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Sort these into the physical and the psychological sides of the human need for attention, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Needing people looking at us to feel alive
Doubting our existence without eye contact
Feeling recognized for who we are
Feeling appreciated through the quality of attention
Self-worth that depends on others’ regard

questions.explain: Greene says part of the need is purely physical, as isolation without eye contact shows, but it is also deeply psychological, since our sense of self-worth depends on being recognized and appreciated.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Greene calls parents who are overinvolved in a child’s life, suffocating it with attention and living through its advancement, ____.
questions.explain: Enmeshers isolate the child and use its success to validate their own self-worth, leaving it no room to establish a self.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Sort these parental patterns into the two backgrounds Greene finds behind almost all deep narcissists.

items.t: A parent too self-absorbed to acknowledge the child
No encouragement of the child’s first efforts at independence
Suffocating the child with attention
Isolating the child from others
Living through the child’s advancement to feel worthy
A parent who is a deep narcissist and ignores the child

questions.explain: Greene writes that “In the backgrounds of almost all deep narcissists we find either abandonment or enmeshment”: either parents too self-absorbed to notice the child, or parents so overinvolved that the child has no room for a self.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: What goes wrong in the early development of deep narcissists, and what is the result?
questions.a: Deep narcissists suffer a sharp break between about two and five, so they never build a consistent, realistic self. Their parents either abandon them emotionally, being too self-absorbed to acknowledge and encourage them, or enmesh them, suffocating them with attention and living through them. The result is that they have no self to retreat to and no foundation for self-esteem, so they depend completely on attention from others to feel alive and worthy.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Greene says introverted deep narcissists swing between a fantasy of superiority and self-loathing, so that they are either a god or a ____.
questions.explain: Because their unrealistic fantasy self gets no validation from others, they veer between superiority and great doubt: “They are either a god or a worm.”

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Sort these descriptions into extroverted and introverted deep narcissists, as Greene describes them.

items.t: As a child, masters attracting notice and monopolizing attention
As a child, retreats into a fantasy of a superior self
Later becomes more dramatic, exhibitionistic and grandiose
Changes friends and scenes to find a fresh audience
Socially awkward yet radiating superiority
Keeps trying on new personalities in fantasy

questions.explain: Extroverts feed on stimulated attention and need ever-new audiences; introverts live in a shifting fantasy self and alienate people with their awkward superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: How do extroverted and introverted deep narcissists differ in childhood, and what happens to both later in life?
questions.a: Extroverted deep narcissists can thrive as children, becoming masters at attracting notice and seeming vivacious, while secretly growing addicted to hits of attention. Introverts retreat into a fantasy of a superior self, swinging between grandeur and self-loathing. In their twenties and thirties extroverts become more dramatic and need fresh audiences, while introverts sink further into fantasy and isolation; both may lean on drugs, alcohol or other addictions to soothe their doubts.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the nightmare for deep narcissists generally arrives in their teenage years.
questions.explain: Greene places the nightmare in their twenties and thirties, when the lack of an inner thermostat catches up with them and extroverts grow more exhibitionistic while introverts sink further into fantasy.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Put these stages in the life of a deep narcissist in the order Greene describes them.
items: A sharp break in development between two and five
Childhood functioning by monopolizing attention or by fantasy
A nightmare arriving in the twenties and thirties
Reliance on drugs, alcohol or other addiction as a crutch
questions.explain: The early break leaves no self; childhood coping can look like success; the lack of a thermostat bites in the twenties and thirties; and addiction becomes a crutch for the inevitable doubt.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, how do deep narcissists generally react when they are insulted or challenged?
options: By quietly withdrawing to soothe themselves with their self-image
With great rage and a thirst for vengeance, full of righteousness
By asking for direct feedback on how they were misread
By laughing at the slight and letting it wash over them
questions.explain: Having nothing internal to soothe them, deep narcissists answer insults with rage and vengeance; laughing off slights is the mark of the healthy narcissist instead.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Which of these are behavior patterns by which Greene says you can recognize deep narcissists?
options: Casting themselves as the wounded victim in conflicts
Turning the conversation back to themselves
Recovering quickly from insults
Vicious envy when others get the attention they feel they deserve
Freely admitting and laughing at their flaws
questions.explain: Greene lists playing the victim, steering talk back to themselves and bouts of envy among the signs. Quick recovery and laughing at one’s flaws describe the healthy narcissist.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do deep narcissists so often display extreme self-confidence?
options: It comes from genuine recognition earned through their work
It shows they no longer depend on others’ opinions
It reflects the strong self they built between two and five
It gains attention and covers up their inner emptiness
questions.explain: Greene says the confidence helps attract attention and hides “their gaping inner emptiness” and fragmented self, which is why it collapses if it is truly tested.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Greene says deep narcissists see other people as extensions of themselves, known as ____.
questions.explain: Self-objects exist only as instruments for attention and validation, to be controlled like one’s own arm or leg.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, why does a deep narcissist in a relationship slowly make the partner cut off contact with friends?
options: The narcissist fears the friends will expose their past
There must be no competition for the partner’s attention
The narcissist wants to spare the partner others’ envy
The narcissist is too introverted to tolerate social events
questions.explain: Since others are self-objects meant to supply attention, any friend competes for that attention, so the narcissist isolates the partner.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, why do most deep narcissists find it hard to concentrate on their work?
options: They prefer stable careers but are always pushed out
They keep worrying about what others think and cannot focus outward
They are too absorbed in empathy for their colleagues
Their work brings them too much genuine recognition
questions.explain: Lacking the thermostat, they worry constantly about others’ opinions, find it hard to bear the impatience and anxiety of work, and change jobs often, which leaves them forever needing to stimulate attention artificially.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: What does Greene say is the best solution once we identify someone close to us as a deep narcissist?
options: To confront their insecurity openly and firmly
To mirror their moods until they calm down
To get out of their way
To give them the constant attention they need
questions.explain: Because deep narcissists entangle us in their dramas and make us feel guilty for withholding attention, Greene advises: “The best solution in such cases is to get out of their way”.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as examples of the narcissistic leader from the Bible and ancient literature?
options: Abraham Lincoln
Alcibiades
Emperor Nero
Absalom
Alex Haley
questions.explain: Greene calls Absalom perhaps the first recorded example and cites Alcibiades, Cicero and Nero. Lincoln and Haley appear later in the chapter as models of empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, why do narcissistic leaders like to stir up constant drama?
options: It tests which followers are loyal enough to keep
It helps the organization build a coherent structure
It distracts followers from the leader’s genuine creative vision
It justifies their power, since only they can solve the problems they create
questions.explain: Greene says the drama makes them indispensable, since “they are the only ones who can solve the problems they create”, and keeps them at the center of attention.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: What do narcissistic leaders proclaim as a virtue, according to Greene, when in fact they lack the ability to focus and build something solid?
options: Being empathic and attuned
Being authentic and spontaneous
Being patient and methodical
Being humble and self-critical
questions.explain: Because everything must flow through them, they cannot forge a coherent structure, and they dress this chaos up as authenticity and spontaneity.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say narcissistic leaders typically do?
options: Say and do things other people do not dare to
Insist that everything flow through them
Use people as experts at exploiting them
Forge a coherent, lasting structure for the group
Calmly welcome challenges to their ideas
questions.explain: Greene describes their daring that seems authentic, their skill at using people and their need to control everything. They cannot forge coherent structure and react to challenges with narcissistic rage.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Put these stages in the career of a narcissistic leader in the order Greene describes them.
items: Radiating confidence that attracts followers
Early success that draws still more followers
Grandiose tendencies inflated by the attention
Inner chaos mirrored in the group they lead
Burning and destroying what they created
questions.explain: Success sets a terrible momentum in place: followers inflate grandiosity, the leader’s inner instability spreads to the organization, and in the end “They tend to burn and destroy whatever they create.”

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Why does Greene consider the narcissistic leader more dangerous than the ordinary deep narcissist?
questions.a: The narcissistic leader has more ambition and can channel it into work, and their confidence and daring attract followers, so they reach far higher levels of power. Success creates a momentum that inflates their grandiosity, and they stir up drama to justify their power while reacting to any challenge with rage. Their inner instability is eventually mirrored in the group they lead, and they tend to burn and destroy whatever they create.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: According to Greene, why do organizations run by narcissistic leaders become unstable?
questions.a: Such leaders cannot forge a coherent structure because everything must flow through them and they must control everyone as self-objects. They stir up constant drama to justify their power, so the workplace is never stable. Their own inner instability and chaos come to be mirrored in the company, though they proclaim it as being authentic and spontaneous.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: On Greene’s scale of self-absorption, people above the halfway mark, where most of us reside, are ____ narcissists.
