Sonya, instead of focusing on his hypocrisy, could have seen an unhappy man who had never felt loved enough since childhood and offered support while gently declining to follow him all the way. Either way, empathy would have broken the mutual narcissism.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Why does Greene think empathy from just one partner can transform a narcissistic relationship?
questions.a: Empathy coming from one side tends to soften the other and invite empathy in return, because it is hard to stay defensive when someone is seeing and expressing your side. Secretly people yearn to let go of their resistance, since constant suspicion is exhausting. By keeping in mind the other's value system, you can enter their perspective at the moment you would normally turn defensive.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Why did Shackleton treat his men's morale as the decisive factor for survival on the ice?
questions.a: Morale was invisible and rarely discussed, yet a slight dip in spirit or crack in unity could make it too hard to decide well under duress. A few malcontents could spread negativity until it became every man for himself, and one impatient attempt to escape the floe would mean death. He was thrown back into the primal condition of a group in danger, dependent on one another.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: What does Shackleton's outburst at the bird near South Georgia show about his leadership?
questions.a: For fifteen months he had kept his frustrations in check because the leader infects the group with his mind-set. When he lost his composure and swung at the bird, he felt embarrassed at once. Minutes later he made a joke at his own expense and vowed never to repeat such a display, knowing he had set the tone and could not go back on it.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: Drawing on Shackleton's story, why does Greene say most of us fail to develop our empathic powers, and what is the first step?
questions.a: Normally we do not feel the need: we assume we understand people, have other tasks, and lazily rely on predigested judgments. We fail to see the link between our problems and our constant misreading of people's moods and intentions. The first step is to realize that you have a remarkable social tool you are not cultivating, then try it by stopping your interior monologue and paying deeper attention to people.

questions.unitTitle: Transform Self-love into Empathy
questions.q: How do Chapter 2's four examples carry out the threefold task Greene sets in The Narcissistic Spectrum?
questions.a: Greene's task is to understand deep narcissists, to be honest about our own narcissism, and to become healthy narcissists. Stalin and Jeanne de Belciel show the toxic deep narcissists we must recognize and resist, the Tolstoys show how ordinary self-absorption in a relationship needs honest correction through empathy, and Shackleton shows the healthy narcissist turning attention outward. The section thus moves from warning to model, matching the chapter title's call to transform self-love into empathy.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In the opening of the Law of Role-playing, Greene says people’s masks have cracks in them. What are those cracks?
options: Inconsistencies in the stories people tell about themselves over time
Moments when people openly confess their envy to close friends
Slips of the tongue that reveal unconscious wishes in their words
Nonverbal cues people cannot fully control, such as facial expressions and vocal inflections
questions.explain: People continually leak their true feelings through facial expressions, vocal inflections, bodily tension and nervous gestures. The cracks are nonverbal, not verbal slips or confessions.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to the opening of the Law of Role-playing, what two things must you learn to do because people wear masks?
questions.a: First, you must become a superior reader of men and women, mastering the nonverbal language people leak so you can take proper defensive measures against hidden hostility or manipulation. Second, since appearances are what people judge you by, you must learn to present the best front and play your own role to maximum effect.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In the opening of the Law of Role-playing, Greene warns that if we take people’s masks for reality, we will sometimes be blindsided by their sudden resistance, hostility and manipulative actions.
questions.explain: Greene says that taking appearance for reality means we never know people’s true feelings and are occasionally blindsided by their hostility.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In 1919, what illness left the seventeen-year-old Milton Erickson paralyzed, at one point able to move only his eyeballs?
options: A spinal injury from heavy farm work
Tuberculosis caught from a farmhand
A stroke suffered after a fall on the farm
Polio, a near epidemic at the time
questions.explain: Erickson was diagnosed with polio, and the paralysis spread until even his lips could not move; only his eyeballs could.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why did the paralyzed young Milton Erickson keep asking his mother to move the chest of drawers near his bed?
options: He was testing whether she would obey a dying son
He wanted to distract her from her grief and set its mirror just right
He was delirious from fever and confused about the room
He wanted his belongings within reach of his hands
questions.explain: His mother thought he was delusional, but he wanted to ease her anguish and angle the mirror so he could hold on to the reflected sunset.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Fearing he might lose consciousness, the young Milton Erickson positioned a mirror so he could focus on the reflected ____, hoping that, like the sun, he too would return.
questions.explain: The sun always returned, and Erickson hoped he would as well, proving the doctors wrong.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Listening to his sisters for a day, the paralyzed Milton Erickson counted sixteen different forms of the word ____, each showing a different degree of hardness.
questions.explain: He noticed that a yes could really mean no, and that the many forms of no came with different facial expressions.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: When one of Milton Erickson’s sisters offered another an apple, Erickson read from the tension in her face and arms that she really wanted to keep it for herself.
questions.explain: Erickson saw that she was just being polite; the signal went unnoticed by the others but seemed clear to him.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each cue Milton Erickson noticed in his sisters to what it indicated.
pairs: A deliberate brushing back of hair
A quicker, unconscious stroke of the hair
Pulsing neck veins as they stood over his bed
Boredom, usually followed by a yawn
Saying yes in a monotone with a smirk
Really thinking the idea was bad
questions.explain: Erickson learned to read hair, breathing, neck veins and tone of voice as a second channel that often contradicted his sisters’ words.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What pattern did the paralyzed Milton Erickson notice in his sisters’ conversations in the next room, and what game did he make of it?
questions.a: He noticed that people were rarely direct: a sister would spend minutes beating around the bush, hinting at what she wanted, such as borrowing clothing or getting an apology, with her tone stressing certain words. Often the hints were ignored and she had to say it outright. Erickson made a game of guessing, within as few seconds as possible, what she was hinting at.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene calls the channel Milton Erickson discovered while paralyzed, in which people express something from deep within themselves, sometimes without being aware of it, a second ____.
questions.explain: Erickson became aware of a second channel of communication, which Greene names the second language.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put the events of Milton Erickson’s polio ordeal in the order they happened.
items: Overhears a doctor say he will be dead by morning
Falls into a coma
Wakes able to move only his eyeballs
Starts reading his sisters’ nonverbal cues
Feels a leg muscle twitch while imagining standing up
questions.explain: He overheard the doctor, fell into a coma for three days, woke fully paralyzed, discovered the second language while bedridden, and months later felt the twitch that began his recovery.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put the stages of Milton Erickson’s recovery of movement in order.
items: Feels a twitch in a leg muscle while imagining standing
Focuses on single muscles as his nurse massages them
Teaches himself to stand
Walks around his room
Walks outside over increasing distances
questions.explain: Starting from one twitch, he worked muscle by muscle with his nurse, then stood, walked his room, and finally walked outside for longer and longer distances.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What lesson did Milton Erickson draw from regaining movement through willpower and imagination?
options: Childhood experiences decide what the adult body can do
Doctors’ predictions are usually wrong and should be ignored
The mind and the body operate together in ways we are hardly aware of
Physical therapy works only when combined with hypnosis
questions.explain: Erickson realized that mind and body work together, which led him to study medicine and psychology.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: As a psychiatrist, Milton Erickson, like most of his colleagues, focused mainly on getting patients to talk about their early childhood.
questions.explain: That was the method of almost all other psychiatrists. Erickson focused on patients’ physical presence, since words are often a cover-up.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these practices by whether they belonged to most psychiatrists of Erickson’s time or to Milton Erickson himself.

items.t: Getting patients to talk at length
Going over patients’ early childhood
Treating words as the route to the unconscious
Treating physical presence as the route to the unconscious
Regarding words as often a cover-up
Reading tension in face, voice and posture

questions.explain: Most psychiatrists relied on talk about childhood; Erickson’s method was diametrically opposed, reading hidden tension in the body and seeing words as a way to conceal.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each walking style Milton Erickson observed to what he took it to reveal.
pairs: Swaying hips or a strut that lifts the head
questions.explain: Erickson watched people walk all over the city and found that the heaviness and style of the step supplied endless information about mood and self-confidence.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why did Milton Erickson place his desk at the far end of his office?
options: To give patients a feeling of privacy and space
To stay out of patients’ direct line of sight
To make patients walk toward him so he could study their walk
To make the room feel larger and calmer
questions.explain: Erickson wanted to watch patients walk toward him and compare their walk before and after the session.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How did Milton Erickson cure the ruined businessman who could only cry and move his hands back and forth from his chest?
questions.a: Erickson saw that the gesture expressed the man’s futile efforts to get ahead and his despair. Saying “Your life has had many ups and downs,” he shifted the motion to up and down, then, with an occupational therapist, gave the man sandpaper and lumber so the motion became sanding wood. The man stopped crying, took woodworking classes and sold the chess sets he carved: changing his physical motion unlocked his mind.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these clues did Milton Erickson use to see that the young patient in women’s clothes was a man?
options: An assertive, staccato vocal rhythm when demanding to test Erickson first
Legs locked with one foot tucked around the ankle
A noticeably deep voice
Picking lint off the sleeve without a natural detour around the breast area
Unusually large, rough hands
questions.explain: Erickson relied on the lint-picking motion and the masculine staccato rhythm; the patient’s voice had been carefully worked on to sound feminine, and the locked legs belong to a different case.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these signs led Milton Erickson to conclude that the woman with a fear of flying was having an affair?
options: Avoiding eye contact when she mentioned her husband
Nervous laughter whenever airplanes came up
Saying a-broad hesitantly, as if ashamed
A walk suggesting she felt trapped in complicated relationships
Legs crossed tightly with one foot tucked around the ankle
questions.explain: Erickson pointed to her locked legs, her hesitant a-broad and her trapped-looking walk; he did not cite eye contact or laughter.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: By mirroring a patient’s ____ patterns, Milton Erickson could lead them into a hypnotic trance and create a feeling of deep rapport.
questions.explain: Erickson could read states of mind from breathing and use mirrored breathing to build rapport.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each case from Milton Erickson’s practice to the nonverbal clue he read.
pairs: Hands moving back and forth from the chest
Picking lint without a detour around the breast
Legs locked with a foot tucked around the ankle
The quality of their hands and heaviness of step
questions.explain: In each case Erickson read the body rather than the words, which is why people thought he had psychic powers.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did patients and friends think Milton Erickson had psychic powers?
options: He used hypnosis to read their private thoughts
They did not see how long and hard he had studied the second language
He secretly gathered information about them in advance
He was born with an unusual gift for intuition
questions.explain: Greene says Erickson’s apparent psychic powers came from years of hard study; his reading skill was learned, not innate.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What did Milton Erickson discover about how nonverbal communication must be experienced, according to Greene’s interpretation?
questions.a: It cannot be grasped simply by thinking and translating thoughts into words; it must be felt physically, registering another person’s tension or expression as something within oneself. It is a different form of knowledge connected to the animal part of our nature and our mirror neurons. To master it, Erickson had to relax, curb the urge to categorize with words, and tamp down his ego, directing his attention outward.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: Milton Erickson observed that most people grow more observant of others with each passing year as they gain experience of life.
questions.explain: Erickson saw the opposite: most people become more self-absorbed and unobservant each year, because the harshness of life turns them inward.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: People at Milton Erickson’s lectures asked why he never used the strange pointer he carried, having failed to notice his limp and his need for a ____.
questions.explain: The pointer was his cane; the anecdote shows how unobservant most people are.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What figures does Greene give for nonverbal communication?
options: About half of communication is nonverbal, and people take in about a fifth of it
About a third of communication is nonverbal, and people take in nearly all of it
Over 65 percent of communication is nonverbal, but people take in only about 5 percent of it
Over 90 percent of communication is nonverbal, and people take in about half of it
questions.explain: Greene says over 65 percent of human communication is nonverbal, yet people internalize only about 5 percent, because their attention is absorbed by words.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say nonverbal cues tell us about people?
options: What they are actively hiding, their real desires
Their emotions and moods, in an immediate way
Their exact thoughts, word for word
What they are trying to emphasize and the subtext of their message
The details of their childhood history
questions.explain: Greene lists emphasis and subtext, hidden desires, and immediate emotions and moods. Cues are suggestive, not a word-for-word transcript of thought or a life history.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put in order the steps Greene sets out, after the Erickson story, for learning the second language.
items: Recognize your self-absorption and how little you observe
Understand the physical, felt nature of this communication
Build a vocabulary correlating gestures with emotions
Discover a deeper way of relating to people
questions.explain: Greene says recognizing your self-absorption motivates you; then you grasp the different nature of the language, your vocabulary grows, and a deeper way of relating follows.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In the Schopenhauer passage that closes the Erickson story, what does Schopenhauer compare people to, and what is his point about their masks?
questions.a: He says people are like the moon: they show you only one of their sides. Everyone has an innate talent for making a mask of their face so they look like what they pretend to be, and if you expect devils and fools to come with horns or jangling bells you will be their prey. You should treat such a mask as if it were made of wax or cardboard.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene say a person who never developed acting skills, who grimaces when displeased and always speaks his mind, would fare badly?
options: He would become a constant target of envy
He would be shunned, ridiculed and despised
He would be easily manipulated by better actors
He would never discover his true calling
questions.explain: Greene asks us to imagine such a person and concludes he would be shunned, ridiculed and despised, showing how essential acting is to social life.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene says we imagine we are almost always being ____ in our social encounters, which any good actor will tell you is the secret behind believable acting.
questions.explain: We are such good actors that we are not aware of it; believing in our own sincerity is what makes the performance convincing.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each stage of life to the acting skill Greene says we learn in it.
pairs: Putting on looks that elicit sympathy or affection from parents
Wearing the same clothes and speaking the same language as the group
Creating the proper front to be hired and fit the group culture
Acting the part of an executive, professor or bartender
questions.explain: Greene traces how we become consummate actors from childhood onward, until we are so good at it that we no longer notice.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, can we never completely control what we communicate nonverbally?
questions.a: For hundreds of thousands of years before language, our hunter-gatherer ancestors survived by communicating through nonverbal cues, which is why the face became so expressive and gestures so elaborate; this is bred deep within us. We also need to conceal our feelings for proper social functioning. With the desire to communicate and the need to conceal battling inside us, real feelings continually leak out in gestures, tone of voice, facial expressions and posture.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say you can gain by paying extra-close attention to the nonverbal cues of people you have recently met?
options: Mirroring their moods so they relax and you build rapport
Guaranteeing that they will always be honest with you
Saving yourself from an unnecessary battle or an act of sabotage
Changing their basic character over time
Seeing through fake, tight smiles and politely disengaging from hostile people
questions.explain: Greene describes winning over allies through mirroring and avoiding hostile people before they sabotage you; reading cues does not make others honest or change who they are.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these attitudes by whether Greene’s student of human nature adopts or rejects them toward role-playing.

items.t: Accepting the theatrical quality of life
Playing your own part with consummate skill
Becoming a master decoder of true feelings
Moralizing against the wearing of masks
Mistaking appearances for reality
Being blinded by people’s acting skills

questions.explain: Greene’s twofold task is to accept and master the theater of social life while never being naive about others’ appearances.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: At a new job, Priya notices that, without planning it, she speaks more formally and holds a straighter posture with her manager than with her teammates. How would Greene explain this?
options: Like everyone, she is a consummate actor adjusting her role almost without thinking
She has an unusually anxious personality
She is deliberately trying to manipulate her manager
She is being insincere and should drop the act
questions.explain: Greene says we all subtly change our words, tone and body language to suit each person and situation, almost without thinking; he does not treat this as a moral failing.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene say children are the bane of liars, con artists and magicians?
options: They mock adults and expose them by imitation
They do not care whether adults approve of them
Small and weak, they depend on decoding people, so they quickly see through a front
They ask blunt questions that adults politely avoid
questions.explain: Because a child’s survival depended on reading smiles and tones of voice, children are great observers and see through pretenders.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: Greene says nonverbal cues are less ambiguous than words, because there is a fairly fixed meaning for each gesture.
questions.explain: Greene says the reverse: words express direct information, while nonverbal cues are more ambiguous and indirect, with no dictionary; their meaning depends on the individual and context.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put in order the progression of observation exercises Greene recommends for a beginner.
items: Notice one or two facial expressions that contradict someone’s words
Repeat the exercise with another person, still focusing on the face
Note changes in a person’s voice, such as pitch and pace
Graduate to body language such as posture, hand gestures and legs
questions.explain: Greene advises baby steps: start with the face, extend to other people, then voice, and only later the body.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise while observing someone during a conversation?
options: Mirror them with comments that play off what they have said
Put each cue into words as soon as you see it
Talk less and get them to talk more
Hold steady, direct eye contact to catch every change
Use quick peripheral glances rather than direct stares
questions.explain: Getting people to talk makes them leak more cues, and observing must never be obvious; too much eye contact betrays you, and you should not rush to interpret in words.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Before you can read changes in someone, Greene says, you need to establish their ____ expression and mood, so that deviations stand out.
questions.explain: Knowing a person’s usual demeanor, such as reserved or anxious, lets you notice sudden departures from it.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How did Octavius realize that Mark Antony had hostile intentions after the assassination of Julius Caesar?
options: Antony’s letters to him suddenly turned cold and formal
Antony began laughing too loudly at Octavius’s jokes
Antony stopped attending their meetings altogether
The normally jovial Antony became silent and sullen in their meetings
questions.explain: Antony’s baseline was jovial and teasing, so his sudden silence was a telling deviation.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Dan is normally anxious and fidgety in meetings, but today he looks unusually relaxed just before a big decision is announced. Following Greene, what should you do?
options: Treat it as a deviation from his baseline that deserves closer attention
Ask him directly in front of others why he is so relaxed
Ignore it, since one day’s mood never means anything
Conclude at once that he is lying to the team
questions.explain: Greene gives a relaxed look from the habitually nervous as an example of a deviation worth noticing; it calls for attention, not an instant verdict or an obvious confrontation.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: When someone gives you mixed signals, which signal does Greene say to weigh more heavily, and why?
questions.a: Give greater weight to the negative cue as indicating the person’s true feelings, because a greater part of nonverbal communication involves the leakage of negative emotions. For example, someone may say they love your idea while their face is tense and their voice strained. You can then ask yourself why they might feel sadness or antipathy.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In Henry James’s The Ambassadors, what reveals to the narrator the discomfort of the woman visiting him?
options: Her forced laugh at his jokes
The tension with which she holds her parasol while smiling
Her refusal to take a seat
Her repeated glances toward the door
questions.explain: She smiles through most of the conversation, but her tight grip on the parasol is a mixed signal from a different part of the body.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What is Othello’s error, and where exactly does the mistake lie?
questions.a: In Shakespeare’s play, Othello takes Desdemona’s nervousness under questioning as a sign of guilt, when in fact his own aggressive, paranoid questioning caused it. More generally, we pick up an emotional cue such as nervousness and rush to the first explanation that fits what we want to see, though it could have several causes. The error is not in the observing but in the decoding.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why did much of the French public take Alfred Dreyfus’s demeanor in 1894 as a sign of guilt?
options: He answered calmly and efficiently, while they assumed an innocent man would protest loudly
He was visibly sweating and stammering
He refused to answer any questions
He smiled during his questioning
questions.explain: Dreyfus’s calm tone came from his bureaucratic training and his effort to contain nervousness, but a public with anti-Semitic feelings decoded it as guilt.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene calls the different forms of behavior that cultures consider acceptable, such as how much people smile or touch, ____ rules.
questions.explain: Because of display rules, Greene says you must always consider people’s cultural background when interpreting cues.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each figure to the reading of nonverbal cues Greene describes.
pairs: Took his wife’s nervousness under questioning as guilt
Took Dreyfus’s calm, efficient tone as guilt
Read hostility in Antony’s sudden silence
Saw discomfort in a tightly held parasol
questions.explain: Octavius and James’s narrator read deviations and mixed signals correctly; Othello and the French public decoded cues through their own suspicions or prejudice.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these into practice habits Greene recommends and pitfalls he warns against.

items.t: Watching people in a café and guessing their professions
Noticing your own fake smiles and nervous habits
Writing down observations and patterns
Reading any cue from someone you dislike as hostile
Staring directly so as to catch every change
Ignoring a person’s cultural background

questions.explain: Greene recommends public-space practice, self-observation and note-taking, and warns against personal bias, obvious scrutiny and ignoring display rules.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene’s three most important categories of cues to decode are dislike/like, dominance/submission, and ____.
questions.explain: These three categories organize the decoding keys: dislike and like cues, dominance and submission cues, and deception cues.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do we tend to miss the signs before someone turns openly hostile?
questions.a: Hostile actions never come out of the blue, but we are not paying attention, and we inherently dislike the thought of conflict, preferring to assume people are on our side or at least neutral. Often we feel something is not quite right but ignore the feeling. Greene says we must trust such intuitive responses and look more closely at the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as body-language signs of active dislike or hostility?
options: A torso or feet turned away while still in conversation
Frequent head nods
Sudden squinting of the eyes at something you have said
Pursing the lips until they nearly disappear
Dilated pupils
Relaxed lines on the forehead
questions.explain: Squinting, pursed lips and a body turned away signal dislike; dilated pupils, nodding and a relaxed forehead are signs of comfort and liking.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How long does Greene say a microexpression lasts?
options: Several seconds, long enough to notice consciously
Until the person notices that they are being watched
Less than a second
About as long as a genuine smile
questions.explain: Psychologists documented the microexpression on film; it lasts less than a second, which is why you must catch it out of the corner of your eye.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What are the two varieties of microexpression Greene describes?
questions.a: In the first, people are aware of a negative feeling and try to suppress it, but it leaks out in a fraction of a second. In the second, the person is not aware of the hostility, yet it shows itself in quick flashes on the face or in the body. Typical forms are a momentary glare, tensing facial muscles, pursed lips, or the beginnings of a frown, sneer or look of contempt.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: You approach a colleague from an unexpected angle, and for a second he looks displeased before breaking into a warm smile. What does Greene suggest this may mean?
options: He was simply startled, so it tells you nothing
He harbors negative feelings that showed before his affable mask was in place
He is hiding a mistake he made at work
He is shy and uncomfortable with everyone
questions.explain: Greene says surprising someone from an angle can reveal displeasure at your approach for a second or two, before they fit on their mask.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: When someone repeatedly aims sarcastic, pointed remarks at you with a smile and a jokey tone, Greene says to pay attention to the words rather than the body language.
questions.explain: In this reverse mixed signal, especially if it recurs, the joking manner is cover and the words are a repressed way of expressing hostility.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In Stendhal’s The Charterhouse of Parma, how does Count Mosca work out that the Prince sent the anonymous letter?
options: The Prince avoids him for the rest of the day
He recognizes the Prince’s handwriting
A courtier confesses the Prince’s role to him
He recalls a malicious glint and ambiguous smile as the Prince spoke of love
questions.explain: The Prince spoke of love in general, but the look was aimed at Mosca: his venomous glee leaked out in a variation on the mixed signal.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene says people who praise or flatter you without their eyes lighting up could be showing a sign of hidden ____.
questions.explain: Praise without lit-up eyes is a mixed signal that may conceal envy.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these states does Greene say make people leak more of their true, and especially hostile, feelings?
options: Being under stress
Being well rested and calm
Being sleepy
Being drunk
Being in a formal setting
questions.explain: Greene lists being drunk, sleepy, frustrated, angry or stressed; people excuse it later, but in those moments they were more themselves than ever.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How did Louis XIV test the nobles at Versailles for hidden hostility?
questions.a: He would suddenly appear without warning and look for the immediate expressions on their faces. He would ask a nobleman to move his family to Versailles, knowing it was costly and unpleasant, and watch for annoyance in face or voice. He would also say something negative about a courtier’s ally and watch the reaction; enough signs of discomfort revealed secret hostility.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: You suspect a friend secretly envies you. Which test follows Greene’s advice?
options: Stop contacting them and see whether they notice
Mention your latest good news without bragging and watch for flashes of disappointment
Ask them directly whether they envy you
Praise them lavishly and see whether they relax
questions.explain: Greene suggests probing envy by sharing good news without appearing to brag and watching for microexpressions of disappointment, eliciting responses people cannot suppress quickly.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What strategic options does Greene say you gain by detecting someone’s hostility early?
questions.a: You can lay a trap, deliberately stirring their hostility so they commit an aggressive act that embarrasses them in the long run. You can work doubly hard to neutralize their dislike and win them over with a charm offensive. Or you can simply create distance, by not hiring them, firing them or refusing to interact. Either way you avoid surprise battles and acts of sabotage.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to the research Greene cites from Paul Ekman, E. H. Hess and others, which of these signs show that someone feels positively toward you?
options: Relaxation in the forehead lines and around the mouth
Dilated pupils
Pursing of the lips
Widening of the whole area around the eyes
A stiff neck
questions.explain: Relaxed facial muscles, widened eyes and dilated pupils are involuntary signs of comfort and liking; pursed lips and a stiff neck signal dislike.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to Greene, what physical sign marks a genuine smile?
options: It is perfectly symmetrical on both sides of the face
It shows more teeth than a fake smile does
It affects the muscles around the eyes, often with crow’s-feet, and pulls the cheeks up
It lasts noticeably longer than a fake smile
questions.explain: Greene says there is no genuine smile without a definite change in the eyes and cheeks.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the genuine smile is more common than the fake one, so it rarely needs special attention.
questions.explain: The fake smile is the one we most often resort to, because it is easy; since the genuine variety is less common, you must learn to recognize it.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Beyond the physical signs, what context does Greene say to check when judging whether a smile is genuine?
questions.a: Because some people fake a genuine smile with a very broad one that partly alters the eyes, you must look at context. A genuine smile is spontaneous, elicited by some action or words. Ask whether the smile is unrelated to or unwarranted by what was said, whether the person is straining to impress or has strategic goals, and whether the timing is slightly off.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene call the voice perhaps the most telling indicator of positive emotions?
options: The voice carries further than facial expressions do
The voice changes before any other part of the body
Unlike the face, which we can practice in a mirror, the voice is very hard to modulate consciously
People speak far more often than they gesture
questions.explain: Greene says it is much easier to control the face, but unless we are professional actors the voice resists conscious control.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene says the warm, almost purring quality of a voice that shows real engagement has been likened to a vocal ____.
questions.explain: This warmth, with a rising pitch and no tension, contrasts with the simulated warmth of a salesman.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene calls the best and most exciting sign that someone is falling under your spell ____, the other person unconsciously mirroring you.
questions.explain: In synchrony, legs cross the same way, heads tilt alike and one smile induces another.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put these signs of synchrony in order from the surface level to the deepest level Greene describes.
items: Postures mirrored, such as legs crossing the same way
Breathing patterns falling into the same rhythm
The complete synchrony of a kiss
questions.explain: Greene says that at the deepest level of synchrony, as Erickson discovered, breathing falls into the same rhythm, which can end in a kiss.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: Greene notes that very few people naturally reveal much emotion early on, so a show of falling for you that seems rushed may be contrived.
questions.explain: Expert seducers mimic the positive cues; Greene advises telling them to slow down and watching for microexpressions of frustration.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these cues by whether Greene links them to liking or to dislike.

items.t: Standing closer or leaning in
Frequent head nods and attentive gazes
Rising vocal pitch and quickening banter
Eyebrows rising as the eyes widen
Eyes rolling, quickly covered by a smile
A glare
Arms folded as you make a point
Brooding silence after your remark

questions.explain: Closeness, nods, an animated voice and widened eyes signal comfort; eye-rolling, glares, folded arms and sullen silence leak dislike.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these cues by whether Greene links them to confident power or to an insecure leader.

items.t: Eyelids more closed
Smiling less
Friendly pats on others’ backs or arms
Taking up more space in a meeting
Halting speech with long pauses
A voice that rises in pitch and stays there
Touching one’s own hair, neck or forehead
Blinking more

questions.explain: The powerful are relaxed, smile less and feel entitled to touch others; insecure leaders hesitate, rise in pitch, blink and soothe themselves.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Touching your own hair, neck or forehead in an attempt to soothe your nerves is what Greene calls ____ behavior.
questions.explain: Insecure leaders, instead of feeling entitled to touch others, touch themselves in pacifying behavior.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as ways alpha males signal their superior rank?
options: An extra vigorous, almost crushing handshake
Speaking faster and interrupting to control the conversation
Always arriving early to meetings
Smiling frequently to reassure others
A taller stance and purposeful stride, with inferiors walking behind
questions.explain: Greene describes fast talk, crushing handshakes and a purposeful stride; frequent smiling signals insecurity, and showing up late, not early, is a cue of superiority.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How does Greene describe Angela Merkel’s style of nonverbal authority?
questions.a: It is calm, confident, warm yet businesslike. She smiles rarely but meaningfully, listens with complete absorption and a still face, gets others to do most of the talking while controlling the conversation, and never needs to interrupt. She attacks with looks of boredom, iciness or contempt rather than blustery words; quieter than alpha male posturing, it is powerful in its own way.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each figure to the behavior Greene describes.
pairs: Met Putin’s dog ploy with a calm look in the eye
Cornered senators with jokes, touches and big smiles
Lulled victims with a dull professional patter
Appeared without warning to catch courtiers’ faces
Acted harmless, then sprang an uncomfortable question
questions.explain: Merkel shows quiet dominance, Johnson and Lustig show the animated and the dull fronts of deception, and Louis XIV and Columbo show ways of testing people.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What does Greene mean by the symptom as a subtle means of asserting dominance in a relationship?
options: Signs of age that make others defer to a partner
A recurring argument that one partner always starts
A visible nervous tic that betrays insecurity
A partner suddenly falling ill, drinking or turning negative, forcing the other to tend to them
questions.explain: Greene calls it the willful use of sympathy to gain power: the other side must play by the sufferer’s rules.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In the couples Greene describes, the dominant partner makes eye contact with their partner while only half listening to you.
questions.explain: It is the reverse: the dominant one makes eye contact with you, not with the partner, and seems to only half listen to what the partner says.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: When an argument turns personal, dominant people resort to what is known as ____, finding an action on the other side that supposedly started it all.
questions.explain: Through punctuation they assert who is to blame, even though the action is clearly part of the relationship pattern.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each type of would-be leader to Greene’s advice on how to respond.
pairs: A leader whose insecurities poke through
Usually best not to attach yourself too closely
A rising star full of self-belief
It might be wise to rise along with them
questions.explain: Insecure leaders tend to do poorly and drag others down, rising stars radiate positive energy, and petty despots take lip service without giving anything back.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene say we humans are easy prey for deceivers?
questions.a: We are by nature gullible: we want to believe that we can get something for nothing, that some new trick can restore our health or even cheat death, and that most people are good and can be trusted. Deceivers and manipulators thrive on this. Since we cannot change human nature, the best we can do is learn the telltale signs of deception and keep our skepticism while we examine the evidence.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: What does Greene call the most clear and common sign of an attempt at deception?
options: An extra-animated front: smiling a lot, seeming more than friendly
A quiet, flat tone of voice
Avoiding eye contact while speaking
Long pauses before every answer
questions.explain: Deceivers often put on an extra-animated front, like Lyndon Johnson’s jokes and big smiles, which lowers our resistance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to Greene, which part of the body do animated deceivers most often use to draw your attention?
options: The voice, by dropping it almost to a whisper
The area around the mouth, with large smiles and changing expressions
The posture, by standing unusually upright
The eyes, through long and steady gazes
questions.explain: The mouth is the easiest area to manipulate; the giveaway is tension elsewhere, such as tense eyes or an unusually still body.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these behaviors by the type of deceptive front Greene describes.

items.t: Big smiles and an entertaining manner
Loud, righteous denials
Telling off-color jokes and touching your arm
An unusually still face and competent exterior
A highly plausible, nearly seamless account of events
A boring patter full of numbers and statistics

questions.explain: Some deceivers distract with exuberance and vehemence; cleverer ones, like Victor Lustig or Bernie Madoff, seem bland, competent and seamless.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene say an explanation that is too slick and seamless should make you skeptical?
questions.a: Clever deceivers hide behind a serious, competent exterior and a nearly seamless account, as con artists such as Victor Lustig and Bernie Madoff did. But reality is messy: real events involve sudden random intrusions and accidents, and the pieces rarely fit perfectly, which is what raised suspicions about the Watergate cover-up. When an explanation or come-on is a little too slick or professional, that should trigger your skepticism.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put in order the approach Greene recommends, like detective Columbo’s, when you suspect someone is deceiving you.
items: Show interest and encourage them to keep talking
Let them reveal more signs of tension and contrivance
Surprise them with an uncomfortable question or remark
Watch for a freeze response and microexpressions
questions.explain: Greene advises not confronting at once but drawing deceivers out, then springing a surprise and watching their face and body as they try to mask their anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises simply ignoring little white lies such as everyday flattery, and saving your alertness for situations where the stakes are higher.
questions.explain: Polite society depends on saying things that are not always sincere, so constant awareness of this low end of the deception scale would be socially damaging.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene’s scale of deception suggests ignoring them or saving your alertness for them.

items.t: A friend saying you look great today
Someone claiming to love your screenplay
A colleague not saying exactly what they did all day
A stranger’s slick, seamless investment pitch
Loud, righteous denials about missing money
A new acquaintance rushing to seem in love with you

questions.explain: White lies and small privacies are harmless; high-stakes situations where people may be angling for something valuable deserve your skepticism.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Chapter 3, See Through People’s Masks, is subtitled with which law?
options: The Law of Narcissism
The Law of Compulsive Behavior
The Law of Irrationality
The Law of Role-playing
questions.explain: Chapter 3 is the Law of Role-playing; narcissism and irrationality belong to chapters 2 and 1, and compulsive behavior to chapter 4.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put in order the three aspects of the Law of Role-playing, as Greene lists them at the end of the Keys to Human Nature.
items: Understanding how to observe people
Learning basic keys for decoding nonverbal communication
Mastering the art of impression management
questions.explain: These three aspects set out the plan of the chapter: observational skills, decoding keys, and the art of impression management.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 3 in the order they appear.
items: The Second Language
Keys to Human Nature
Observational Skills
Decoding Keys
The Art of Impression Management
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Erickson’s story to the general law, then to how to observe, how to decode, and finally how to play your own role.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 3 to the job it does in the argument.
pairs: Shows through Erickson that nonverbal reading can be mastered
Argues that all humans are actors and sets out three aspects
Trains you to notice cues and avoid decoding errors
Explains dislike, dominance and deception cues
Teaches how to play your own role to maximum effect
questions.explain: The chapter builds from a model case to the general law, then to the three practical aspects in turn.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does Greene open Chapter 3 with the story of Milton Erickson?
options: To show that paralysis sharpens the hearing
To show that the second language can be mastered through long, patient observation
To argue that psychiatry should abandon talk therapy
To introduce hypnosis as the main tool of the chapter
questions.explain: Erickson’s apparent psychic powers came from long, hard study, which models the skill the chapter asks readers to develop.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How does the title See Through People’s Masks relate to the two-sided task Greene sets in Chapter 3?
questions.a: The title stresses decoding: not mistaking people’s appearances for reality and becoming a master reader of their true feelings, the subject of the observation and decoding sections. But the Law of Role-playing also asks you to accept the theatrical quality of life and play your own part with consummate skill, which the closing section on impression management addresses. Masks are both something to see through and something to wear well.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these later chapters, judging by their titles, take up concerns raised in Chapter 3 about what hides behind people’s friendly fronts?
options: Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego (The Law of Envy)
Chapter 16, See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality
Chapter 6, Elevate Your Perspective
Chapter 17, Seize the Historical Moment
questions.explain: Chapter 3 warns that hostility hides behind friendly smiles and that flattery without lit-up eyes may hide envy, the subjects of Chapters 16 and 10.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: When Greene says deceivers’ vehement denials play on the conviction bias, he refers back to Chapter ____, Master Your Emotional Self.
questions.explain: The conviction bias is one of the biases described in Chapter 1, the Law of Irrationality, which Greene cross-references in the deception cues.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says the word role-playing generally has negative connotations. What do we usually contrast it with?
options: Humility
Authenticity
Empathy
Rationality
questions.explain: We contrast role-playing with authenticity, imagining that a truly authentic person can simply be him- or herself without playing a role.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene notes that we usually contrast role-playing with ____: the idea that a person can simply be him- or herself.
questions.explain: Role-playing has negative connotations because we set it against authenticity, though Greene argues the contrast breaks down in professional and public life.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene grants that the concept of authenticity has value in friendships and intimate relationships, where we can hopefully drop our masks.
questions.explain: Greene allows that in friendships and intimate relationships we can feel comfortable displaying our unique qualities; it is professional life that is more complicated.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, why does Greene say the ideal of authenticity becomes complicated in professional life?
questions.a: In friendships and intimate relationships we can hopefully drop our masks, but in a job or social role we carry expectations about what is professional. If people in those roles acted completely like themselves and refused to play their parts, we would feel uncomfortable and question their competence. So in professional life playing the expected role is part of doing the job.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene imagines an airplane pilot who suddenly starts to act like a car salesman. What does he say our reaction would be?
options: We would assume the pilot was secretly trying to sell us something
We would feel uncomfortable and question the pilot's competence
We would find the pilot more relatable and trust him more
We would admire the pilot's refusal to hide behind a mask
questions.explain: Greene says that if such people dropped their masks and refused to play their roles, we would question their competence. Professional roles carry expectations, so authenticity here does not win trust.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these mismatches does Greene give in The Art of Impression Management as examples of people abandoning their expected professional role?
options: A doctor acting like a comedian
A lawyer acting like a poet
A mechanic acting like a therapist
A professor acting like a rock musician
A pilot acting like a car salesman
questions.explain: Greene lists the pilot as car salesman, the mechanic as therapist and the professor as rock musician. The doctor and lawyer examples are not in the book.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each professional to the role Greene imagines them wrongly adopting.
questions.explain: Greene uses these three mismatches to show that we expect people to play their professional roles, and would question their competence if they did not.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, why do some politicians or public figures strike us as more authentic than others?
options: They are genuinely less guarded in public than their rivals
They refuse to play any role in public life
Their careers are secure, so they no longer need a mask
They are better at projecting the quality of authenticity
questions.explain: Greene says the more authentic-seeming public figure is generally better at projecting that quality; we are not seeing them as they are at home. In his words, “Life in the public sphere means wearing a mask”.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say, in The Art of Impression Management, public figures use to produce an authentic effect?
options: Displaying anger openly when criticized
Telling an anecdote that reveals some vulnerability
Appearing humble
Refusing to answer reporters' questions
Discussing their private life
questions.explain: Greene says such figures know that appearing humble, discussing their private life or telling a revealing anecdote will have the authentic effect. Refusing questions or showing anger are not among his examples.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene mean when he says some people wear the mask of authenticity?
questions.a: A public figure who seems more authentic than others is usually just better at projecting that quality. They know that appearing humble, discussing their private life or telling an anecdote that reveals vulnerability will have the authentic effect, but we are not seeing them as they are in private. Since life in the public sphere means wearing a mask, authenticity itself becomes one of the masks.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, why can't the hipster or the rebel suddenly start wearing a business suit?
options: Employers would stop trusting the rebel's competence
It would send dominance cues that alienate their peers
Others in their circle would question their sincerity, which depends on the right appearance
It would betray values the rebel genuinely and privately holds
questions.explain: Greene says “Even the hipster or the rebel is playing a role, with prescribed poses and tattoos.” Their sincerity depends on displaying the right appearance, so they lack the freedom to change costume.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that even the hipster or the ____ is playing a role, with prescribed poses and tattoos.
questions.explain: Greene's point is that even figures who seem to reject convention follow a script; their sincerity depends on the right appearance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, when do people gain more freedom to bring their personal qualities into the role they play?
options: When they are young and still exploring who they are
When they refuse to conform to what is expected of their role
Whenever they are speaking to people of lower status
Once they have established themselves and their competence is no longer in question
questions.explain: Greene says people have more freedom once their competence is no longer in question, though always within limits. Refusing the role leads to marginalization, not freedom.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that once people have established their competence, they can bring their personal qualities into their role without any limits.
questions.explain: Greene says established people have more freedom to bring in personal qualities, but adds that this is always within limits.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order the stages by which, according to Greene, a person earns the freedom to be more themselves in a role.
items: Adhere to what is expected of the role
Establish yourself so your competence is no longer in question
Bring more of your personal qualities into the role, within limits
questions.explain: Greene says people gain freedom to show personal qualities only once they have established themselves and their competence is not in question, and even then within limits.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that, consciously or unconsciously, most of us adhere to what is expected of our role because we realize our social success depends on it.
questions.explain: This is Greene's claim: adherence to the role's expectations is driven by the recognition that social success depends on it.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene say eventually happens to people who refuse to play the role-playing game?
options: They gain more freedom with age as others stop expecting a role from them
They become master decoders because they stand outside the game
They are marginalized into the outsider role, with fewer options and less freedom as they age
They gradually win respect for their authenticity and become leaders
questions.explain: Greene says refusers are marginalized and forced to play the outsider role, with limited options and decreasing freedom as they get older. Refusal brings less freedom, not more.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene warns that people who refuse to play the game are marginalized and forced to play the ____ role.
questions.explain: Even refusal becomes a role: the outsider, with limited options and decreasing freedom as the person gets older.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order what Greene says happens to someone who refuses to play the role-playing game.
items: They refuse to adhere to what their role requires
They are marginalized and pushed into the outsider role
Their options become limited and their freedom shrinks as they age
questions.explain: Greene traces refusal to marginalization, then to the outsider role with limited options and decreasing freedom with age.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene say happens to those who refuse to play the social role-playing game, and what attitude does he recommend instead?
questions.a: Those who refuse are marginalized and forced to play the outsider role, with limited options and decreasing freedom as they get older. Greene recommends instead that we simply accept the dynamic and derive some pleasure from it. Knowing which appearances to present and how to shape them, we can become superior actors on the stage of life and enjoy our moment in the limelight.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what attitude does Greene recommend toward the dynamic of social role-playing?
options: Expose other people's roles so the game loses its power
Resist it quietly and keep your true self for intimate friends alone
Tolerate it reluctantly as a burden imposed by society
Accept it and derive some pleasure from it, becoming a superior actor
questions.explain: Greene writes, “In general, it is best to simply accept this dynamic and derive some pleasure from it.” He wants you to enjoy your moment in the limelight, not merely endure or expose the game.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these settings by whether Greene treats them as places where we can hope to drop our masks or where a role is expected.
groups: We can hope to drop our masks

items.t: Friendships
Intimate relationships
Flying a passenger plane
Life in the public sphere
Teaching as a professor
A job interview

questions.explain: Greene says authenticity has value in friendships and intimate relationships, but in professional and public life we expect people to play their roles.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each role to what Greene says about it.
pairs: Plays a role with prescribed poses and tattoos
Role forced on those who refuse to play the game
Enjoys a moment in the limelight on the stage of life
questions.explain: Each figure shows that role-playing is inescapable: even rebels and outsiders are playing parts, so Greene urges becoming a superior actor.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, when does Greene say people pay greater attention to the nonverbal cues we emit?
options: When they want to get a fix on who we are, as in a job interview
When they are relaxed among close friends and family
When they read what we have written about ourselves
When they already know us well and trust us
questions.explain: Greene says in certain settings, such as a job interview, a group meeting or a public appearance, people trying to get a fix on us watch our nonverbal cues more closely.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say, in The Art of Impression Management, smart social performers know how to do when they master the nonverbal cues?
options: Always speak their mind so their words match their faces
Keep a constantly blank face so nothing leaks
Seem likable and flash genuine smiles
Radiate confidence using dominance cues
Mirror the people they deal with
questions.explain: Smart performers consciously emit suitable, positive signs: likability, genuine smiles, welcoming body language, mirroring and dominance cues. Greene does not advise a blank face or always speaking one's mind.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says smart social performers know how to seem likable, use welcoming body language, and ____ the people they deal with.
questions.explain: Mirroring others is one of the positive nonverbal signs that smart performers emit consciously.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene mean by the advice to master the nonverbal cues?
questions.a: In settings such as job interviews, group meetings or public appearances, people watch our nonverbal cues to get a fix on who we are. Smart social performers therefore control these cues to some degree and consciously emit suitable, positive signs: seeming likable, flashing genuine smiles, using welcoming body language, mirroring people and radiating confidence through dominance cues. The aim is to be aware of your own nonverbal style so you can consciously alter parts of it for better effect.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how does Greene say a method actor manages to feel sad when the part calls for it?
options: By copying the facial expressions of people who are genuinely sad
By suppressing every other emotion until only sadness remains
By recalling their own experiences that caused such emotions, or imagining them
By watching how the audience responds and adjusting to it
questions.explain: In method acting you recall your own experiences that caused the emotion or, if necessary, imagine such experiences. Greene adds, “The point is that you have control.”

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene advises you to be a ____ actor, training yourself to display the proper emotions on command.
questions.explain: Method acting trains you to display emotions on command by recalling or imagining experiences; the point is control.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, what do you subtly signal if you continually emote whatever comes to you in the moment?
options: Dominance and a readiness to take charge
Weakness and an overall lack of self-mastery
Hidden hostility toward the people around you
An authenticity that makes people trust you more
questions.explain: Greene says that without control over your emotions you signal weakness and a lack of self-mastery; uncontrolled emoting does not read as authenticity.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how does Greene suggest you can act like a method actor in daily life, and why?
questions.a: Greene admits we cannot train ourselves as fully as actors, but having no control and emoting whatever comes in the moment signals weakness and a lack of self-mastery. So you should consciously put yourself in the right emotional mood by imagining how and why you should feel the emotion suited to the occasion, then surrender to it so your face and body are naturally animated. Just as important, you should return to a more neutral expression at a natural moment, careful not to go too far.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order the steps Greene gives for being a method actor in daily life.
items: Imagine how and why you should feel the emotion suited to the occasion
Surrender to the feeling so your face and body are naturally animated
Return to a more neutral expression at a natural moment
questions.explain: Greene first has you put yourself in the right mood by imagining, then surrender to the feeling, and finally return to neutral so you do not go too far.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that deliberately making yourself smile or frown cannot produce any of the emotions that go with those expressions.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: sometimes by actually making yourself smile or frown, you will experience some of the emotions that go with these expressions.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, besides putting yourself into the right emotional mood, what further discipline does Greene ask of the everyday method actor?
questions.a: He asks you to train yourself to return to a more neutral expression at a natural moment, being careful not to go too far with your emoting. The goal of method acting is control, so knowing when to stop displaying an emotion matters as much as summoning it. Greene calls this just as important as getting into the mood.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these tips into Be a method actor or Use dramatic effects.

items.t: Recall or imagine experiences to summon an emotion
Return to a neutral expression at a natural moment
Make yourself smile to feel some of the matching emotion
Regulate how often and when you appear
Cloak yourself in some mystery
Withhold information about yourself

questions.explain: Method acting is about controlling and displaying emotion; dramatic effects are about presence and absence, mystery and unpredictability.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene's example of Bill Clinton in The Art of Impression Management illustrates which basic of impression management?
options: Adapt to your audience
Use dramatic effects
Be a method actor
Create the proper first impression
questions.explain: Clinton adjusted his accent and words for autoworkers and for executives, which is Greene's illustration of adapting to your audience while staying within your role.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that when Bill Clinton spoke to a group of autoworkers he would adjust his ____ and his words to fit the audience.
questions.explain: Clinton changed his accent and words for different audiences while still projecting the confidence and power of a president.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says Bill Clinton, while adjusting to different audiences, never lost sight of the fact that as president he had to project confidence and power.
questions.explain: Greene uses Clinton to show flexibility within a role's parameters: the presidential confidence stayed fixed while accent and words changed.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how does the example of Bill Clinton show what Greene means by adapting to your audience?
questions.a: Greene says that although you conform to parameters set by your role, you must be flexible. Clinton never forgot that as president he had to project confidence and power, yet he adjusted his accent and words for a group of autoworkers and did the same for executives. The lesson is to know your audience and shape your nonverbal cues to their style and taste.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these features of Bill Clinton's performances by whether, in Greene's account, they stayed fixed or were adjusted to each audience.

items.t: Projecting confidence
Projecting power
The parameters of the presidential role
His accent
His words
His cues to suit the audience's style

questions.explain: Clinton illustrates flexibility within a role: the presidential confidence and power remained constant, while accent and words were shaped to autoworkers or executives.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene advise as the general approach when making a first impression?
options: Confess a weakness early so people see you as authentic
Tone down your nonverbal cues and present a more neutral front
Show as much excitement as you can to seem enthusiastic
Display strong dominance cues to establish your rank at once
questions.explain: Greene says it is best to tone down your cues in first encounters. He warns, “Too much excitement will signal insecurity and might make people suspicious.”

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, why is showing too much excitement in a first encounter a mistake?
options: It stirs envy in those who feel less enthusiastic
It makes you look like a Machiavellian manipulator
It makes people bored because you seem too predictable
It signals insecurity and might make people suspicious
questions.explain: Greene says too much excitement signals insecurity and may arouse suspicion. Boredom from predictability belongs to his advice on presence and absence, not first impressions.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene warns that too much excitement in a first encounter will signal ____ and might make people suspicious.
questions.explain: This is why Greene advises toning down your nonverbal cues and presenting a more neutral front at first.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene recommend in The Art of Impression Management for creating the proper first impression?
options: A more neutral front with toned-down nonverbal cues
Maximum excitement to show enthusiasm
Looking people in the eye
Avoiding eye contact to seem mysterious
A relaxed smile
questions.explain: Greene says a neutral front, a relaxed smile and eye contact can do wonders for lowering people's natural resistance; too much excitement signals insecurity.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says people readily reassess the judgments they form from first impressions.
questions.explain: Greene says the reverse: people tend to judge on first impressions and have difficulty reassessing those judgments, which is why the first appearance deserves extra attention.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, why does Greene say you must give extra attention to your first appearance, and what does he recommend?
questions.a: People tend to judge based on first impressions and have difficulty reassessing those judgments. So Greene recommends toning down your nonverbal cues and presenting a more neutral front, since too much excitement signals insecurity and may make people suspicious. A relaxed smile and looking people in the eye can do wonders for lowering their natural resistance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order Greene's reasoning about first impressions.
items: People tend to judge based on first impressions
They have difficulty reassessing these judgments
So you must give extra attention to your first appearance
So you tone down your cues and present a neutral front
questions.explain: Greene moves from the fact that first judgments stick to the practical advice of giving extra attention to a toned-down, neutral first appearance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says using dramatic effects mostly involves mastering the art of presence/____.
questions.explain: Presence and absence means selectively absenting yourself so people want to see more of you, not less.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, why must you know how to selectively absent yourself?
options: Being seen less protects you from people's envy
Absence makes people fear what you might be planning
Staying away hides the insecurities your face leaks
If people see you too often or can predict you, they grow bored
questions.explain: Greene says that if you are too present or too predictable, people quickly grow bored; regulating your appearances makes them want to see more of you.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these are part of using dramatic effects, according to The Art of Impression Management?
options: Selectively absenting yourself
Displaying some subtly contradictory qualities
Withholding information
Appearing as often as possible to stay on people's minds
Making your behavior consistent and predictable
questions.explain: Greene advises regulating your appearances, cloaking yourself in mystery with contradictory qualities and withholding information. Constant presence and predictability make people bored.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene advises that to use dramatic effects you should cloak yourself in some ____, displaying subtly contradictory qualities.
questions.explain: Greene writes, “People don’t need to know everything about you.” Mystery and less predictable behavior keep people interested.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene mean by the art of presence and absence?
questions.a: If you are too present, so that people see you too often or can predict exactly what you will do next, they quickly grow bored with you. So you must selectively absent yourself, regulating how often and when you appear, making people want to see more of you, not less. Along with this you cloak yourself in some mystery, display subtly contradictory qualities, withhold information and make your behavior less predictable.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
