questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how does Greene say you should use dominance cues and an air of destiny when projecting saintly qualities?
questions.a: Greene advises using the appropriate dominance cues to make people think you are powerful even before you reach the heights. You want to seem as if you were destined for success, which he calls a mystical effect that always works. At the same time you avoid overtly playing the Machiavellian leader and let others do any dirty work, so your hands stay clean.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order Greene's reasoning behind the art of presence and absence.
items: You are too present or too predictable
People quickly grow bored with you
So you selectively absent yourself and regulate your appearances
People want to see more of you, not less
questions.explain: Greene says overexposure and predictability breed boredom, so regulating how often and when you appear makes people want more of you.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene say remains the same about appearing saintly from the sixteenth century to today?
options: The essence: you embody what is considered good and above reproach
The content: devotion, poverty and self-denial
The method: performing public acts of religious penance
The audience: only religious authorities judge it
questions.explain: Greene says appearing saintly today differs in content from the sixteenth century, but the essence is the same: embodying what is considered good and above reproach.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says the appearance of ____ never goes out of fashion.
questions.explain: Greene writes that “the appearance of saintliness never goes out of fashion”, though its content changes with the period.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, what does appearing saintly mean in the modern world?
options: Showing yourself as progressive, supremely tolerant and open-minded
Showing yourself as devout, austere and self-denying
Showing yourself as reserved, private and aloof
Showing yourself as tough, decisive and unyielding
questions.explain: Greene says that in the modern world saintliness means being seen as progressive, supremely tolerant and open-minded, giving to causes and supporting them on social media.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list in The Art of Impression Management as ways to project saintly qualities?
options: Making a few public confessions of your weaknesses and vulnerabilities
Occasionally lowering your head and appearing humble
Being seen giving generously to causes and supporting them on social media
Openly playing the ruthless Machiavellian leader
Doing the dirty work yourself so no one else is blamed
questions.explain: Greene recommends visible generosity, public confessions and displays of humility. He warns never to play the Machiavellian leader overtly and to get others to do the dirty work.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene observes that people see signs of humility as authentic, even though those signs might very well be simulated.
questions.explain: Greene writes, “For some reason people see signs of humility as authentic, even though people might very well be simulating them.”

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how does Greene suggest you use humility and confession in projecting saintly qualities?
questions.a: Projecting sincerity and honesty always plays well, and Greene says a few public confessions of your weaknesses and vulnerabilities will do the trick. People see signs of humility as authentic even though they might well be simulated, so you should learn how to occasionally lower your head and appear humble. These displays help you seem good and above reproach.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what does Greene advise if dirty work must be done?
options: Refuse to do it so you remain above reproach
Do it openly to signal dominance and strength
Get others to do it, so your hands stay clean
Do it yourself quickly, then confess it publicly
questions.explain: Greene says, “If dirty work must be done, get others to do it. Your hands are clean.” Saintliness depends on appearing above reproach.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: According to The Art of Impression Management, why should you never overtly play the Machiavellian leader?
options: It reveals the insecurities hidden behind your mask
It provokes envy in rivals who want the same power
It makes you too predictable, so people grow bored
That only works well on television, not in real life
questions.explain: Greene writes, “Never overtly play the Machiavellian leader—that only works well on television.” Real-life saintly projection depends on keeping your hands clean.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says you want to seem like you were ____ for success, a mystical effect that always works.
questions.explain: Using dominance cues before you reach the heights makes people think you are powerful and that your success was destined.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each saintly technique Greene recommends to the effect he says it has.
pairs: Getting others to do the dirty work
Dominance cues before reaching the heights
Makes people think you are powerful
A mystical effect that always works
questions.explain: Each technique supports the image of someone good, above reproach and naturally powerful, which is the essence of saintliness for Greene.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these tips into Project saintly qualities or Create the proper first impression.

items.t: Give generously to causes and support them on social media
Make a few public confessions of weakness
Get others to do the dirty work
Tone down your nonverbal cues
Offer a relaxed smile
Look people in the eye

questions.explain: Saintly qualities concern appearing good and above reproach; first-impression advice is about a neutral, relaxed front that lowers people's natural resistance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how did Emperor Augustus use his early rival Mark Antony?
options: As a foil, a villain he could contrast himself with
As a mentor whose style he could imitate
As a scapegoat for Rome's military defeats
As a trusted ally to do his dirty work
questions.explain: Greene says Augustus understood the value of having a good enemy, and Antony was the perfect foil against whom he could show himself as the embodiment of Roman values.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says Emperor Augustus used his early rival Mark ____ as the perfect foil.
questions.explain: Augustus contrasted his traditional Roman image with Antony, who was dallying in Egypt with Cleopatra.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, where did Augustus place his home to ally himself with everything traditional in Roman society?
options: Among the military camps that guarded the city
Beside the Senate house in the heart of the Forum
In a luxurious villa outside Rome
Near the spot where the city had supposedly been founded
questions.explain: Augustus placed his home near Rome's supposed founding spot. The luxurious villa outside Rome is where he really spent most of his time, behind the show.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, how did Augustus use Mark Antony to shape his own image?
questions.a: Augustus understood the value of having a good enemy, a villain to contrast himself with, and Antony was the perfect foil. While Antony was in Egypt dallying with Cleopatra and giving in to luxury, Augustus allied himself with everything traditional in Roman society. He could continually point to their differences and show himself off as the embodiment of the Roman values Antony had betrayed.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these did Augustus do, according to The Art of Impression Management, as a public show of humility once he became supreme leader of Rome?
options: Moved to Egypt to live quietly
Gave up command of the military
Lived simply, like a man of the people
Spoke a more vernacular Latin
Gave powers back to the Senate and the people
questions.explain: Augustus seemed to give powers back, spoke vernacular Latin and lived simply, but he held tightly onto the military, the real reins of control.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, while seeming to give away power, what did Augustus actually hold on to tightly?
options: The Senate
The treasury
The military
The priesthood
questions.explain: Greene says that while appearing to give powers back to the Senate and the people, Augustus kept the real reins of control: the military.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says Augustus really did spend most of his time living simply in a modest home in Rome, like a man of the people.
questions.explain: Greene says the simplicity was all a show: in fact Augustus spent most of his time in a luxurious villa outside Rome.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these, according to The Art of Impression Management, reveal that Augustus's humble image was a show?
options: He placed his home near Rome's founding spot
He held tightly to control of the military
He had many mistresses, some from places as exotic as Egypt
He spent most of his time in a luxurious villa outside Rome
He spoke a more vernacular Latin
questions.explain: The villa, the mistresses and his grip on the military were the reality behind the mask. Vernacular Latin and the home near the founding spot were part of the show itself.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each part of Augustus's public show to the private reality Greene describes behind it.
pairs: Giving powers back to the Senate and people
Kept tight hold of the military
Living simply like a man of the people
Spent most of his time in a luxurious villa
Had many mistresses, some from Egypt
questions.explain: Greene says it was all a show: behind each public display of humility and tradition lay luxury, indulgence and firm control.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these details about Augustus into his public show and the private reality.

items.t: Speaking a more vernacular Latin
Giving powers back to the Senate
A home near Rome's founding spot
A luxurious villa outside Rome
Many mistresses from exotic places
Tight control of the military

questions.explain: Greene calls Augustus a master showman: the vernacular Latin, the returned powers and the traditional home were the mask; the villa, mistresses and military control were the reality.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each figure to their part in the story of Augustus.
pairs: Showed himself off as the embodiment of Roman values
The early rival used as a perfect foil
The Egyptian queen with whom Antony dallied
Body to which Augustus publicly gave back powers
questions.explain: Augustus contrasted himself with Antony, who was in Egypt with Cleopatra, and later made a public show of returning powers to the Senate and the people.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put these events from Greene's account of Augustus in order.
items: Augustus contrasts himself with Antony, who is in Egypt with Cleopatra
Augustus becomes the supreme leader of Rome
He makes a public show of giving powers back to the Senate
He asks on his deathbed whether he played his part well
questions.explain: Greene tells how Augustus used Antony as a foil in his rise, staged humility once supreme, and ended with his theatrical last words.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Augustus's last words were: Have I played my part in the ____ of life well enough?
questions.explain: His deathbed words, “Have I played my part in the farce of life well enough?”, suggest he knew he had been a master showman and wearer of masks.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, what do Augustus's last words reveal, according to Greene?
questions.a: On his deathbed Augustus asked, “Have I played my part in the farce of life well enough?” Greene takes this as a sign that Augustus realized he was a master showman and wearer of masks. Obsessed with the theater, he had played the role of humble, traditional Roman leader while privately living in luxury and holding on to the military.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene notes that the word personality comes from the Latin ____, which means mask.
questions.explain: The etymology supports Greene's claim that wearing a mask in public is natural and has a positive function.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: In The Art of Impression Management, Greene says that if we displayed exactly who we are and spoke our minds truthfully, we would win most people's respect.
questions.explain: Greene says we would offend almost everyone and reveal qualities that are best concealed; the mask has a positive function.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, why does Greene say wearing a mask in public has a positive function?
questions.a: If we displayed exactly who we are and spoke our minds truthfully, we would offend almost everyone and reveal qualities best concealed. “Having a persona, playing a role well, actually protects us from people looking too closely at us”, with all the insecurities that would churn up. Moreover, the better you play your role, the more power you accrue, and power gives you freedom to express more of your peculiarities.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these benefits of having a persona does Greene name in The Art of Impression Management?
options: It removes any need to observe other people's cues
It protects us from people looking too closely at us
It keeps us from offending almost everyone
It guarantees that intimate friends will trust us
Playing the role well brings power and the freedom to express our peculiarities
questions.explain: Greene says a persona protects us from scrutiny, spares us from offending people, and when played well brings power and freedom. He does not claim it replaces observation or guarantees trust.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put in order Greene's chain of reasoning about the persona.
items: The word personality comes from persona, meaning mask
A persona protects us from people looking too closely
The better you play your role, the more power you accrue
With power you have freedom to express your peculiarities
Your persona comes to match your unique traits, heightened for effect
questions.explain: Greene moves from the etymology to the protective function of the mask, then to power, freedom, and finally a persona that matches your own character heightened for effect.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each term to its meaning in Greene's account.
pairs: Latin word for mask, root of personality
Displaying the proper emotions on command
Regulating how often and when you appear
Playing your role to maximum effect
questions.explain: These terms name the tools Greene offers for playing your part on the stage of life with skill.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each mistake to what Greene says it signals or causes.
pairs: Signals weakness and lack of self-mastery
Too much excitement at a first meeting
Signals insecurity and may arouse suspicion
People quickly grow bored with you
questions.explain: Each basic of impression management guards against a specific way the performance fails.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, match each basic of impression management to a piece of advice Greene gives under it.
pairs: Mirror the people you deal with
Shape your cues to their style and taste
questions.explain: Each pairing comes from Greene's list of basics, from controlling cues to the timeless appeal of saintliness.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, put these basics in the order Greene presents them.
items: Master the nonverbal cues
Be a method actor
Adapt to your audience
Create the proper first impression
Use dramatic effects
Project saintly qualities
questions.explain: Greene moves from controlling your cues and emotions to fitting the audience, first impressions, dramatic effects and finally saintly qualities, illustrated by Augustus.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these by whether Greene treats them as advice to follow or as mistakes to avoid.

items.t: Presenting a neutral front at a first meeting
Selectively absenting yourself
Returning to a neutral expression at a natural moment
Showing too much excitement at first
Being entirely predictable
Continually emoting whatever you feel
Overtly playing the Machiavellian

questions.explain: Greene's basics favor control, restraint and mystery; uncontrolled emotion, overexcitement, predictability and open Machiavellianism undermine the performance.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: In The Art of Impression Management, sort these outcomes by whether Greene links them to playing your role well or to refusing to play the game.

items.t: Accruing more power
Freedom to express your peculiarities
Protection from people looking too closely
Being marginalized
Being forced into the outsider role
Decreasing freedom with age

questions.explain: Greene argues the better you play your role, the more power and freedom you gain, while refusers end up marginalized with shrinking options.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Why does The Art of Impression Management come last among the sections of Chapter 3, See Through People’s Masks?
options: It completes the twofold task: after learning to read others' masks, you learn to play your own role
It summarizes the Milton Erickson story that opens the chapter
It shifts from human nature to the history of the Roman Empire
It introduces the idea of masks before the chapter's examples of decoding
questions.explain: Greene lists three aspects of the law: observing people, decoding nonverbal cues and impression management. The last section turns from seeing through others' masks to presenting your own.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Greene's advice in The Art of Impression Management to master presence and absence, so people want more of you, anticipates the theme of which later chapter?
options: Chapter 8, Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
Chapter 11, Know Your Limits
Chapter 5, Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.explain: Selectively absenting yourself so that people want to see more of you is the idea of elusiveness that Chapter 5, the Law of Covetousness, develops.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Chapter 3 closes with Sherlock Holmes telling Watson that what he missed was not invisible but unnoticed. Which theme of the chapter does this quote reinforce?
options: That saintliness never goes out of fashion
That a persona protects us from people looking too closely
That first impressions are hard for people to reassess
That reading people is about learning where to look, not seeing hidden things
questions.explain: Holmes says Watson did not know where to look. This echoes the chapter's argument that people's cues leak out constantly and are simply unnoticed until we train our observation.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How does The Art of Impression Management relate to the twofold task Greene sets in the Keys to Human Nature of Chapter 3?
questions.a: Greene says the student of human nature must first understand and accept the theatrical quality of life and play his or her part with consummate skill, and second must not mistake people's appearances for reality. The Observational Skills and Decoding Keys sections serve the second task by teaching you to read masks. The Art of Impression Management serves the first, showing how to accept role-playing and play your own role to maximum effect.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: How does The Art of Impression Management turn the decoding skills of Chapter 3 back on yourself?
questions.a: The earlier sections teach you to read the nonverbal cues others leak, such as signs of like and dislike or dominance. Impression management asks you to apply the same knowledge to your own performance: since people watch your cues to get a fix on you, you consciously emit suitable signs such as genuine smiles, mirroring and dominance cues. In this way the reader of masks also becomes a superior actor on the stage of life.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: True or false: The Art of Impression Management is the final section of Chapter 3, and it comes directly after Decoding Keys.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 runs The Second Language, Keys to Human Nature, Observational Skills, Decoding Keys and finally The Art of Impression Management.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: The Art of Impression Management is the third and final aspect of the Law of ____, the law behind Chapter 3, See Through People’s Masks.
questions.explain: Chapter 3 presents the Law of Role-playing, whose three aspects are observing people, decoding nonverbal communication and impression management.

questions.unitTitle: See Through People’s Masks
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name, at the end of the Keys to Human Nature in Chapter 3, as aspects of the Law of Role-playing?
options: Recognizing the triggers of envy
Overcoming the narcissistic spectrum
Learning basic keys for decoding nonverbal communication
Understanding how to observe people
Mastering the art of impression management
questions.explain: Greene names observing people, decoding nonverbal communication and impression management. Envy and narcissism belong to other chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to the summary of the Law of Compulsive Behavior, by what should you gauge the relative strength of a person’s character?
options: How impressive their reputation and their list of past achievements are
How well they handle adversity, adapt, work with others, show patience and learn
How firmly they hold to a religion, a political creed or a moral code
How charming, confident and intelligent they seem at a first meeting
questions.explain: Greene lists handling adversity, adapting and working with others, patience and the ability to learn. Reputation and surface charm are exactly what he warns will mesmerize you.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: The Law of Compulsive Behavior says that people’s character is formed in their earliest years and by their daily ____.
questions.explain: Character, formed early and by daily habits, is what compels people to repeat certain actions and fall into negative patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Compulsive Behavior advises you to know your own character thoroughly so that you can break your compulsive patterns and take control of your destiny.
questions.explain: The summary ends by turning the law on the reader: know your own character so you can break your compulsive patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to the summary of the Law of Compulsive Behavior, how should you go about choosing the people you work and associate with?
questions.a: Do not be mesmerized by their reputation or the surface image they project; train yourself to look deep within them and see their character. Look closely at their patterns, remembering that people never do something just once and will inevitably repeat their behavior. Gravitate toward those who show signs of strength and avoid the many toxic types.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the story of Howard Hughes, why did his mother dote so completely on him as a boy?
options: She wanted to prepare him to take over the family business
His father had abandoned the family to run the tool company abroad
He had been born sickly and had nearly died as an infant
She had nearly died giving birth to him and could have no other children
questions.explain: Because she nearly died in childbirth and could have no more children, she poured her anxiety into her only son, watching his every move.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: In the story of Howard Hughes, his relatives were not surprised by his rebellion after his father’s death, because he had always been defiant as a boy.
questions.explain: As a boy and young man Hughes had been shy, polite, soft-spoken and obedient; his relatives were shocked by the abusive rebel who emerged, a mystery they never solved.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these events from Howard Hughes’s early life in the order they happened.
items: His mother suddenly dies
His father dies two years later
He buys out his relatives’ shares in the tool company
He settles in Los Angeles to pursue film and flying
Hell’s Angels premieres as a smash hit
questions.explain: His mother died in 1922 and his father two years later; Hughes then took control of the company, moved to Los Angeles, and Hell’s Angels premiered in 1930.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: To run his own life with no interference, the nineteen-year-old Howard Hughes befriended a local judge and had the courts declare him an ____.
questions.explain: Under Texas law he could petition the courts to declare him an adult if he proved himself competent, and he got the declaration he wanted.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the story of Howard Hughes, what did director Luther Reed say to Hughes when he quit Hell’s Angels?
options: If you know so much, why don’t you direct it yourself?
Either you leave the set or I do, permanently.
You will never finish this picture on budget.
No one man can possibly know everything about a film.
questions.explain: Reed was tired of Hughes’s constant interfering; Hughes took the parting shot as advice and named himself director. The line about no one man knowing everything was Hughes’s own later lesson.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why was Hell’s Angels seen as a triumph for Howard Hughes, and what did the reality of the production show?
questions.a: The film premiered in 1930 as a smash hit because its flying and action sequences thrilled audiences, and the legend was born of Hughes as the dashing maverick and rugged individualist who did everything himself. In reality the story was a mess, he had fired directors and department heads and run everything himself, three stunt pilots died, and the film cost $3.8 million and lost close to $2 million, which nobody paid attention to.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: After Hell’s Angels, Howard Hughes humbly claimed that trying to do the work of twelve men had been a mistake and that he had learned his lesson.
questions.explain: Hughes said, “Trying to do the work of twelve men was just dumbness on my part.” His later ventures showed he had not learned it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these impressed Defense Department officials into awarding Hughes Aircraft the contract for the Hercules flying boats?
options: The meticulous attention to detail he showed in interviews
The lowest price bid among competing firms
His tireless lobbying
A record of delivering military planes on time
His aviation feats
questions.explain: Officials were swayed by his aviation feats, his attention to detail in interviews and his lobbying. He had no record of delivering military planes, and the low-price bid belongs to the later helicopter contract.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: The one Hercules flying boat Howard Hughes completed after World War II later became known as the ____.
questions.explain: Hughes called it a marvel of engineering, but on its test flight it lacked the power for its weight and never flew again.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the story of Howard Hughes, what was the underlying organizational problem at Hughes Aircraft during the war?
options: Military auditors controlled spending and blocked every design change Hughes wanted
A powerful general manager ran the firm and kept Hughes out of all decisions
The company had too few departments to handle large orders at the same time
Departments barely communicated, and every decision, however small, had to flow through Hughes
questions.explain: The company began as a hobby staffed with Hollywood and aviation friends; everything went through Hughes, and the general manager he hired quit after two months because Hughes vetoed his decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these events in the history of Hughes Aircraft during World War II in the order they happened.
items: The Defense Department awards an $18 million grant for three Hercules planes
The air force orders one hundred photo-reconnaissance planes
Two-thirds of the money for the first Hercules is spent with the plane far from complete
Charles Perelle is hired as general manager
The air force cancels the reconnaissance contract
questions.explain: The Hercules grant came in 1942 and the reconnaissance order less than a year later; by late summer 1943 the money was running out, Perelle came in 1944, and the contract was canceled at the war’s end with no planes produced.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each person from the Howard Hughes story to their role.
pairs: Aviation-buff director who quit Hell’s Angels
Boy wonder of aircraft production hired to rescue the reconnaissance order
Head of RKO’s new regime who resigned once Hughes began phoning
Owner of RKO who sold his shares to Hughes
Director of Jet Pilot who quit after too many phone calls
questions.explain: Each of these people dealt with the same Hughes pattern: promises of freedom followed by meddling and control.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: How did Howard Hughes persuade Charles Perelle to take over Hughes Aircraft, and how did it turn out?
questions.a: Hughes went on a charm offensive: he seemed completely humble, said he had realized the error of his ways, made himself out to be the victim of unscrupulous executives, impressed Perelle with his technical knowledge, and promised him the authority he needed. Once in the job, Perelle found the planes further behind than he had been told, and nobody respected his authority because Hughes kept undermining his reforms. No reconnaissance plane was produced, the contract was canceled, and Perelle quit, broken by the experience.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: By the end of World War II, Hughes Aircraft had delivered only a handful of the one hundred photo-reconnaissance planes the air force had ordered.
questions.explain: Not a single reconnaissance plane had been produced by the end of the war, and the air force canceled the contract.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the story of Howard Hughes, what happened when he test-flew the Hercules flying boat himself?
options: It crashed into the ocean shortly after takeoff, injuring Hughes
It lacked the power for its weight, so after about a mile he set it down on the water
It flew triumphantly along the coast, and Hughes then sold it for scrap
It never left the water because the engines failed on the runway
questions.explain: He meant to prove the doubters wrong, but the plane clearly lacked power, and it was towed back and never flew again; Hughes refused to scrap it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these descriptions of Howard Hughes by whether they belong to his public image or to the reality Greene describes.

items.t: Rugged individualist
Consummate American maverick
Successful businessman leading a billion-dollar empire
Irrational micromanager
Terrible businessman whose ventures lost money
Isolated addict afraid of germs

questions.explain: Hughes carefully built a public image of the maverick and empire-builder that concealed the glaring weaknesses in his character, revealed fully only after his death.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these events of Howard Hughes’s time at RKO in the order they happened.
items: Hughes buys Floyd Odlum’s controlling shares
Hughes promises Dore Schary he will be left alone
Hughes phones asking Schary to replace an actress
Schary resigns, taking many of his staff
Hughes sells RKO to the General Tire Company
questions.explain: Hughes bought RKO in 1948, charmed Schary, then began meddling within weeks; Schary left, the studio lost money, and Hughes sold it in 1955.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these were true of Howard Hughes’s film Jet Pilot?
options: It was finished quickly and under budget
It became a smash hit like Hell’s Angels
It starred John Wayne
By the time it was ready, its jet scenes were out of date
Josef von Sternberg was to direct it but quit
questions.explain: Jet Pilot was a complete repeat of Hell’s Angels in its making but not its reception: it took six years and fell into complete obscurity.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the story of Howard Hughes, how did his company win the army’s light observation helicopter contract?
options: By bidding a price so low it would lose money, planning to raise prices on later orders
By offering the army its design for free in return for future orders
By teaming up with an experienced helicopter firm to share production
By promising much faster delivery than either rival manufacturer
questions.explain: After lobbying got his rejected design back into the running, Hughes won on price with a bid that seemed impossible to profit from; the bet was to recoup losses on the follow-on order.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why did Howard Hughes’s army helicopter contract end in a loss of $90 million?
questions.a: Hughes won by bidding so low he would lose money, betting he could raise the price on later orders. Production was chaotic, with no organized line, a plant too small, unprofessional drawings, poor tools and too few skilled workers, so helicopters only trickled in. The army held a new auction for 2,200 more helicopters; Hughes could not bid low enough and still profit, and he was underbid.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene calls it the ultimate ____ that Howard Hughes, who feared any loss of control, ended his life at the mercy of a handful of assistants and executives.
questions.explain: The man obsessed with control was isolated, drugged and dependent on those who oversaw his slow death and took control of his company.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these did the autopsy on Howard Hughes reveal to the public about his last decade?
options: He had reconciled with his relatives and lived with them
He had been running his companies energetically by phone
He had been addicted to pain pills and narcotics
He weighed a mere ninety-three pounds at his death
He had lived in sealed hotel rooms, afraid of germs
questions.explain: Hughes lived in near-total isolation attended by a few assistants, who wrested control of the company from him; he never reconciled with his relatives.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of Howard Hughes, how did the young Hughes really feel about his total dependence on his parents?
options: He bitterly resented it, though he hid this beneath politeness and obedience
He was grateful for it and saw it as the source of his success
He was indifferent to it, being absorbed in planes and films
He found it comforting and later tried to recreate it with his relatives
questions.explain: Out of fear of disappointing his parents he became polite and obedient, but he bitterly resented his dependence, and his true character emerged once they died.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what did flying mean for Howard Hughes’s character?
questions.a: Only in the air, alone and at the helm, could Hughes experience the exhilaration of control and release from his anxieties. He could soar high above the masses, whom he secretly despised. He could brave death, as he did many times, because it would be a death under his own power.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says the paradox of Howard Hughes’s leadership was that by trying to gain total ____ he tended to lose it.
questions.explain: One man could not keep on top of everything, so unforeseen problems arose wherever he insisted that all decisions flow through him.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did Howard Hughes keep a loose structure in his companies, with executives fighting for his attention?
questions.a: Any writer, director or executive who came forward with ideas seemed a personal challenge to his authority, stirring his old anxieties about being helpless and dependent on others. To combat that anxiety he had to control every aspect of the business, down to the spelling in publicity notices. Some internal chaos was better to him than anything not flowing through him.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation, what did Howard Hughes tend to do when his projects fell apart and the heat became intense?
options: Fire the whole management team and start over
Admit his mistakes publicly and hand over control
Disappear from the scene or conveniently fall ill
Take on still more of the work himself, day and night
questions.explain: Greene notes this as part of the pattern, seen when Hughes vanished with an apparent breakdown during the reconnaissance crisis.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene conclude that Howard Hughes was in fact a terrible businessman, despite his reputation?
questions.a: Hughes inherited a highly profitable tool business, and the only parts of his empire that made substantial profits, the tool company and an earlier version of Hughes Aircraft, were run completely independently of him. The businesses he personally ran, his later aircraft division, film ventures and Las Vegas hotels and real estate, all lost substantial amounts covered by the other two. The pattern of failure was plain for everyone to see.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these parts of Howard Hughes’s business empire by how Greene says they performed.

items.t: The tool company inherited from his father
The earlier version of Hughes Aircraft
His later aircraft division
His film ventures
His Las Vegas hotels and real estate

questions.explain: The two profitable businesses were run completely independently of Hughes; the ones he personally ran lost money that the other two covered.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says our poor ability to gauge the character of the people we deal with is the ____ in human nature.
questions.explain: Public image and reputation mesmerize us, and because of this blind spot we suffer under irresolute leaders, micromanaging bosses and conniving partners.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say we usually base our choice of whom to work with or hire on, instead of character?
options: How they handle adverse circumstances
Intelligence
A glittering résumé
Patterns revealed in their past
Charm
questions.explain: We choose by résumé, intelligence and charm; the patterns from the past and the response to adversity are exactly the signs of character Greene wants us to look at instead.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which positive trait does Greene single out as worthless if the person also has a weak or dubious character?
options: Loyalty
Intelligence
Patience
Humility
questions.explain: Greene says even intelligence is worthless if the person is of weak or dubious character. Patience, by contrast, is one of his signs of strength.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each Howard Hughes venture to the recurring behavior it showed.
pairs: Fired the director and ran every department himself
A general manager quit after Hughes vetoed his decisions
Promised Schary freedom, then began phoning with demands
A lowball bid followed by chaotic production
questions.explain: Each venture repeated the same compulsive need for control behind a charming public front, which is why Greene calls it a pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: At the end of the Howard Hughes interpretation, what does Greene tell you to look at instead of the front people display, and why?
questions.a: Look for signs of character in the patterns from their past, the quality of their decisions, how they have solved problems, and how they delegate authority and work with others. A person of strong character is rare but invaluable because they can adapt, learn and improve. Since your success depends on the people you work with and for, making character your primary object of attention spares you the misery of discovering it too late.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: The Pattern ends with a line from Heraclitus: Character is ____.
questions.explain: The epigraph sums up the law: the character stamped in us compels the patterns that shape our lives.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what did the ancient Greek word from which character comes originally refer to?
options: An engraving or stamping instrument
The fate allotted to each person by the gods
A mask worn by an actor on stage
The inner spirit or soul of a person
questions.explain: Character is something so deeply engraved or stamped in us that it compels us to act in certain ways beyond our awareness. The mask idea belongs to role-playing, and fate is what Greene says character replaces.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene argues that there is some truth to the concept of fate, but that what controls us is our character rather than spirits or gods.
questions.explain: We repeat the same decisions and ways of dealing with problems, so our lives show a pattern; Greene locates the force behind it in character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put the layers of character Greene describes in order, from the earliest and deepest to the last to form.
items: Genetics and the wiring of our brains
Attachments formed with mother and caregivers
Habits and experiences as we get older
A front that disguises our flaws
questions.explain: Genetics is the deepest layer, early attachment comes next, habits form above these, and a fourth layer, developed in late childhood and adolescence, covers up flaws.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: The psychoanalyst Melanie Klein, who studied infants, believed that the ____ and grasping type of child came into the world predisposed toward that trait.
questions.explain: Greene uses Klein to illustrate the genetic layer, which can incline some people toward greed for attention, privilege or possessions.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each of John Bowlby’s attachment schemas to the kind of mother that stamps it.
pairs: Gives freedom to explore, stays sensitive to needs and protects
Inconsistent: suffocating at times, then retreating
Sends highly conflicting signals that reflect her own inner chaos
questions.explain: Bowlby’s four schemas describe the quality of early attachment, which shapes how we later use relationships to handle stress.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In Greene’s account of attachment schemas, how can enmeshed-ambivalent mothers make their children feel?
options: As if nothing they do will ever be right
As if they have to take care of the person who should be taking care of them
As if they must always fend for themselves, abandoned and alone
Free to explore the world while knowing they are protected
questions.explain: Their inconsistent attention leaves the child caring for the parent. Feeling abandoned belongs to the dismissing schema, and nothing being right to the disorganized one.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these tendencies by whether Greene links them to children of dismissing parents or children of enmeshed parents.

items.t: Avoiding negative emotional situations
Walling themselves off from feelings of dependency
Finding it hard to commit and pushing people away
Great anxiety in relationships
Feeling ambivalent toward people
Pursuing people and then unconsciously retreating

questions.explain: Children of dismissing parents defend against dependency, while children of enmeshed parents swing between pursuit and retreat out of conflicting emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as tones of character that people display from their earliest years?
options: Needy and enmeshing
Hostile and aggressive
Idealistic and materialistic
Generous and empathetic
Anxious and avoidant
questions.explain: Greene names hostile and aggressive, secure and confident, anxious and avoidant, and needy and enmeshing. Idealistic and materialistic is his example of conflicting traits, not an early tone.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In Greene’s third layer of character, how does a single decision turn into part of our character?
questions.a: Based on the first two layers, we come to rely on certain strategies for dealing with stress, seeking pleasure or handling people, and these become habits set in our youth. A decision we make is engraved in our brains neurologically, so we are compelled to repeat it because the path is already laid. Our character is formed out of thousands of such habits, the earliest set before we could be conscious of them.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In Greene’s fourth layer of character, people who sense a flaw such as timidity learn to disguise it with a ____, appearing outgoing or even domineering.
questions.explain: Because the flaw is not socially acceptable, they compensate, which makes their real character harder for us to determine.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: A coworker who is deeply anxious and timid acts loud, carefree and domineering in meetings. Which part of Greene’s account of character best explains this?
options: The fourth layer, a front built to cover a flaw
The dismissing attachment schema from infancy
Conflicting traits that swing back and forth
The genetic layer that makes some people extroverts
questions.explain: Greene says people who sense they are anxious and timid often compensate by appearing outgoing, carefree or domineering, a front developed in late childhood and adolescence.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene say the weakest parts of our character are the ones that create habits and compulsive behavior?
questions.a: Strong qualities such as generosity, empathy and resilience usually require awareness and practice to become habits we can rely on, and life tends to weaken us as we get older. Without conscious effort these strengths wear down or turn into weaknesses, as confidence without self-awareness becomes grandiosity. Weaknesses need no effort or practice to maintain, so they become the compulsive patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene warns that confidence without self-awareness and control can turn into envy.
questions.explain: Greene says such confidence can become grandiosity, as one example of strengths turning into weaknesses without conscious effort.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, how does a person with conflicting character traits, such as being both idealistic and materialistic, reveal their character?
options: Through the stronger trait, which always wins out by adulthood
Through decisions that reflect their ambivalence or swing back and forth
Through no pattern at all, since the traits cancel each other out
Through random choices that cannot be predicted from their past
questions.explain: Greene says the law remains the same: the conflicted character, formed early, merely shows a different kind of pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these tasks by which half of the student of human nature’s twofold task they belong to.

items.t: Examine the elements in your past that formed you
Notice the negative patterns recurring in your life
Create new habits through practice
Treat character as a primary value when choosing a partner
Observe people’s actions and patterns
Recognize signs people emit in certain situations

questions.explain: First you study and reshape your own character; second you develop the skill of reading the character of those you deal with.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that through enough awareness you can get rid of the stamp that constitutes your character.
questions.explain: Greene says it is impossible to get rid of the stamp because it is too deep, but awareness lets you mitigate or stop certain negative patterns and transform weaknesses into strengths.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as illusions that lead us to misjudge people’s character?
options: Assuming a person’s religion or politics comes with a matching character
Weaknesses presented as positive qualities
Giving too much weight to people’s genetic makeup
Seeing only someone’s reputation and position rather than the individual
Paying too much attention to small everyday behavior
questions.explain: We base judgments on what is most apparent: disguised weaknesses, reputation and position, and professed beliefs. Small everyday behavior is, for Greene, a revealing sign worth watching.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each appealing first impression to the flaw Greene says it can turn out to hide.
pairs: Boorish and unable to consider others’ feelings
Timid at the core and afraid of criticism
questions.explain: People often cover weaknesses by presenting them as something positive, creating optical illusions we fall for.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says a person can be a progressive liberal or a loving Christian and still be an intolerant ____ at heart.
questions.explain: People bring the character they have to the position they occupy or the religion they practice; a belief system does not supply character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene say we must scrutinize successful people for signs of character too?
options: Successful people have just as many character flaws as anyone else
Successful people are usually introverts who hide their true selves
Success almost always corrupts a person’s character over time
Success comes mainly from luck, which says nothing about a person
questions.explain: We tend to believe success means a person is generous, intelligent and good, but some succeed by using others or masking incompetence, and some are completely manipulative.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Once we are aware of the illusions and façades around people, what three components of the skill of studying character does Greene say we can work on?
questions.a: First, recognizing certain signs that people emit in certain situations that clearly reveal their character. Second, understanding some general categories people fit into, such as strong versus weak character. Third, being aware of certain types of characters that are often the most toxic and should be avoided if possible.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: You must choose between two job candidates: one dazzles with charm and a glittering reputation, the other is plainer but has a record of finishing hard projects. What does Greene’s advice suggest?
options: Pick the charming candidate, since charm reflects inner strength
Treat them as equal, since character cannot be judged in advance
Pick whoever has the more prestigious past positions
Weigh character above charm and reputation, and favor the steadier record
questions.explain: Greene says to give character more value than charm, intelligence or reputation, and to judge it by actions and patterns, such as what people have actually completed.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene presents them as a common error in judging people or as his corrective.

items.t: Basing judgments on what is most apparent
Being blinded by our desire to like those who charm us
Assuming a successful person must be good and deserving
Scrutinizing everybody, whatever their position
Training ourselves to look through façades
Judging by actions and patterns rather than words

questions.explain: Greene says we are generally inept at reading character because we judge by appearances, so the skill must be consciously developed.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the most significant indicator of people’s character?
options: Their actions over time
What they say about the lessons they have learned
The impression they make at a first meeting
The opinions of those who recommend them
questions.explain: Despite what people say about how they have changed, as Hughes did, the same actions and decisions keep repeating, and in them they reveal their character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene calls it the primary corollary of the Law of Compulsive Behavior that people never do something just ____.
questions.explain: People may excuse themselves as having lost their heads, but compelled by character and habit they will repeat the behavior, even against their own interest.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put the steps Greene recommends for studying someone’s salient behavior in order.
items: Notice a salient form of behavior
Research their past for actions that fit the pattern
Pay close attention to what they do in the present
See their actions as parts of a compulsive pattern
questions.explain: Once a salient behavior is fixed in your mind, you look back for matching actions, watch the present, and treat incidents as parts of a pattern; ignoring the pattern is your own fault.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these events in the career of the Roman orator Cassius Severus in the order they happened.
items: Attacks high-ranking Romans for their extravagant lifestyles
His books are burned and he is banished to Crete
He insults local Cretan officials, who want him put to death
He is banished to the rock of Serifos
questions.explain: Severus was banished to Crete in AD 7, kept up his attacks there, and in AD 24 was sent to Serifos, where he spent his last eight years.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does the story of Cassius Severus illustrate about character, and what Biblical line does Greene use to sum it up?
questions.a: Severus kept escalating his insulting attacks despite warnings, book burning and two banishments, showing that people repeat their actions even when it is completely against their self-interest. We want to give such people the benefit of the doubt, as the Romans did, but should remember the Bible: “Like a dog that returns to his vomit is a fool that repeats his folly.”

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Following Greene, if a new colleague was fired from a previous job for insulting a client in a fit of temper, you should expect the behavior to recur.
questions.explain: People never do something just once; they may claim they lost their heads, but they will repeat the foolishness on another occasion.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene treat as everyday signs of a person’s character?
options: The prestige of the schools they attended
Being late in finishing simple assignments
How eloquently they describe their own goals
Becoming irritated by little inconveniences
Treating underlings differently from the persona they present
questions.explain: Small habits predict larger ones: lateness, irritation and inattention to details scale up, and treatment of underlings exposes the persona. Credentials and fine words are surface image.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: During Jeb Magruder’s 1969 job interview at San Clemente, what did Bob Haldeman do that revealed his character?
options: Lied about his own role in the Nixon campaign
Boasted about humiliating political rivals in the Senate
Became frantic and insulting toward staff when no golf carts were available
Kept Magruder waiting for hours to test his patience
questions.explain: Haldeman had seemed earnest, honest and sharp, but the golf cart incident showed control issues and a vicious streak; humiliating Senate rivals is the Lyndon Johnson story.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What should Jeb Magruder have learned from Bob Haldeman’s outburst over the golf carts, and why did he ignore it?
questions.a: The outburst was a sign that Haldeman was not what he appeared, that he had control issues and a vicious streak beneath his earnest, intelligent manner. Magruder ignored it because he was charmed by the aura of power at San Clemente and wanted the job, much to his later dismay.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene quotes Lincoln: If you want to test a man’s character, give him ____.
questions.explain: On the way up people play the courtier, but once at the top there are fewer restraints and they reveal things not noticed before.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene argues that power usually changes people, turning respectful individuals into tyrants.
questions.explain: Greene says we often think power has changed people, when in fact “it simply reveals more of who they are.”

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these did Lyndon Johnson do once he became Senate majority leader?
options: Spoke only to the assistant of a senator who had crossed him
Refused to let disliked senators’ bills come to a vote
Insulted the Senate in interviews with the press
Walked off the floor during a disliked senator’s important speech, making others follow
questions.explain: Tired of years as the perfect courtier, Johnson relished humiliating those who had crossed him, in the two ways Greene describes; the other actions are not in the book.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether Greene associates them with extroverts or introverts.

items.t: Dominated by the question of what others think of them
Crave stimulation and attention
Have a nose for trends
Value good clothes and great meals
Easily exhausted by too much outward activity
Find it distasteful to promote what they produce
Like to keep secrets and part of life separate
Feel more lost the bigger the crowd

questions.explain: Extroverts are governed by external criteria and seek stimulation; introverts conserve energy and draw on inner criteria.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, why might a person choose a partner who is noticeably inferior to them in looks or intelligence?
options: Out of a fear of abandonment from infancy, knowing that person will cling to them
Out of a desire to be pampered as a parent would pamper them
Out of an intellectual calculation about long-term compatibility
Out of a wish to play the savior and rescue someone in trouble
questions.explain: Greene gives this as an example of the internal logic of surprising choices. Rescuing and seeking a mommy or daddy figure are other patterns, and such choices are rarely intellectual.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene say a person’s choice of spouse or partner says a lot about them?
questions.a: Such choices are rarely intellectual; they reflect people’s earliest years and attachment schemas. Some seek a partner they can dominate and control, some a person they can rescue in the savior role, and some someone to fill the mommy or daddy role. Even surprising, outwardly incompatible choices have an internal logic.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: A friend cannot bear to be overtaken even when driving and sulks or bends the rules when losing at board games. What does Greene say such off-hours behavior reveals?
options: Deep layers of insecurities behind a competitive nature that cannot be turned off
A sign of introversion and a need to conserve energy
A healthy drive that will make them reliable under pressure at work
Simple boredom with games that has no bearing on character
questions.explain: Greene says competitiveness that cannot switch off, even when driving, reveals deep layers of insecurities, though it can be channeled into work.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says extroverts are largely governed by ____ criteria, liking what others like.
questions.explain: The groups extroverts belong to often determine their opinions; introverts, by contrast, draw on inner criteria.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene notes that there are generally more introverts than extroverts in the world.
questions.explain: Greene says there are generally more extroverts than introverts.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is important to gauge whether someone is an introvert or an extrovert?
options: The type changes with circumstances and predicts what people will do next
The two types do not naturally understand each other, so you must not foist your own preferences on them
Extroverts are always stronger characters and make better partners
Introverts are hiding a front that must be seen through
questions.explain: Each type misreads the other, and being one or the other is generally genetic, so you must reassess the person’s character on its own terms.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each half-statement about introverts and extroverts to its completion in Greene’s account.
pairs: To the extrovert, the introvert seems
To the introvert, the extrovert seems
Shallow, flighty and overly concerned with what people think
Bold introverts show their boldness in
questions.explain: The two types see the same thing in totally different lights, and even their boldness takes different forms.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says strong character has a ____ quality like a good piece of metal: it can give and bend but never breaks.
questions.explain: Strength shows not as bluster or aggression but as resilience and adaptability rooted in personal security and self-worth.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as qualities of people with strong character?
options: They display their strength through bluster and aggression
They can take criticism and learn from experience
They avoid chaotic or unpredictable situations
They can subsume their personal interests to the good of the group
They are open to new ideas without compromising their basic principles
questions.explain: Strength is not outward bluster, and strong characters handle chaos and the unpredictable without succumbing to anxiety rather than avoiding it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, why are people of weak character so hard to work with?
questions.a: They are easily overwhelmed by circumstances, which makes them hard to rely on, and they are slippery and evasive. Worst of all, they cannot be taught, because learning from others implies criticism. They may seem to listen to your instructions but simply revert to what they think is best, so you continually hit a wall.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what does Warren Buffett look for above all in the CEOs he will deal with?
options: Their charisma, vision and public profile
Their ambition, competitiveness and drive
Their resilience, dependability and self-reliance
Their intelligence, education and technical knowledge
questions.explain: Buffett looks beyond the numbers to strength of character; Greene wishes we used such measures for hires, partners and politicians.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each figure in the Character Signs section to what Greene uses them to show.
pairs: Raged at staff over missing golf carts
Humiliated senators who had once crossed him
Kept insulting officials even in exile
Judges CEOs by resilience and dependability
Chose a wife for her openness and determination
questions.explain: Greene draws on these figures for everyday signs, power revealing character, repeated folly, and strength of character as a basis for choices.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each test Greene suggests to what it reveals about a person.
pairs: A good-natured joke at their expense
Whether they respond graciously or with resentment
Sharing strategic information or a rumor
Their trustworthiness as a team player
Whether they learn and improve or resent it
An open-ended assignment with little direction
How they organize their thoughts and time
questions.explain: Greene suggests actively testing people, since strength or weakness shows in how they handle stress, criticism and responsibility.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: A brilliant analyst produces excellent ideas but bristles at every criticism, and his arrogance is driving teammates to quit. What would Greene conclude?
options: He simply needs more power, which will bring out his best side
His intelligence outweighs his flaws, so he is worth keeping at any cost
His weak character neutralizes his intelligence, bringing hidden costs to the whole team
His behavior shows a strong character with a tensile quality
questions.explain: Greene says weak character neutralizes all other good qualities; someone less brilliant but of strong character will prove more reliable over the long run.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says people of real strength are as rare as ____, and finding one is like discovering a treasure.
questions.explain: Because strong character is rare, Greene urges you to treat such people as a treasure when you find them.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene say people reveal in times of stress or crisis, and how should you respond?
questions.a: In everyday life people can disguise their flaws, but under stress they lose their normal self-control and reveal insecurities about their reputation, their fear of failure and their lack of inner resilience. Some, on the other hand, rise to the occasion and show strength under fire. There is no way to tell until the heat is on, so you must pay extra attention to such moments.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does it make sense that Determine the Strength of People’s Character comes right after See Through People’s Masks?
options: Having learned to read the masks people wear, the reader goes deeper to the character those fronts conceal
It shifts from reading individuals to reading the moods of whole groups
It abandons observation of others to focus only on one’s own emotions
It moves from the topic of desire to the topic of envy among friends
questions.explain: Chapter 3 teaches decoding the masks people present; chapter 4 looks beneath them to the stamped character that compels people’s patterns, noting that people even build a front to hide their flaws.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does the subtitle The Law of Compulsive Behavior signal about chapter 4’s argument?
options: People act compulsively only in rare moments of crisis
Compulsive behavior comes from following the group
Character compels people to repeat the same actions, often beyond their awareness
Behavior is random, so character cannot be read
questions.explain: Greene argues that character is engraved so deeply that it compels repetition; hence people never do something just once.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put the sections of chapter 4, Determine the Strength of People’s Character, in order.
items: The Pattern
Keys to Human Nature
Character Signs
Toxic Types
The Superior Character
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the Hughes story, to how character forms, to signs that reveal it, to types to avoid, and finally to shaping one’s own character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these chapters of The Laws of Human Nature in order.
items: See Through People’s Masks
Determine the Strength of People’s Character
Become an Elusive Object of Desire
Elevate Your Perspective
questions.explain: Chapter 4 sits between the law of role-playing (chapter 3) and the law of covetousness (chapter 5), followed by the law of shortsightedness (chapter 6).

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these topics by whether chapter 4 covers them in its first half or defers them to its later sections.

items.t: The life of Howard Hughes
The layers that stamp a person’s character
Tests for the strength of someone’s character
The most toxic types of character to avoid
Shaping your own character through new habits

questions.explain: Keys to Human Nature promises a discussion of toxic types and sends readers to the last section for transforming one’s own character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each section of chapter 4 to its role in the chapter.
pairs: A life story of a hidden character pattern
How character is stamped in layers
Behaviors and tests that reveal character
How to shape your own character
questions.explain: The chapter moves from example, to theory, to practical signs, and finally to the reader’s own character, as Keys to Human Nature promises.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: How does Greene link chapter 4’s account of character to chapter 2 on empathy?
questions.a: When explaining why strengths fade, Greene notes that as we get older life tends to weaken us and our empathy is harder to hold on to, pointing back to chapter 2. Like generosity or resilience, empathy needs awareness and practice; without conscious effort such strengths wear down or turn into weaknesses, which is why weak traits become our compulsive habits.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these ideas raised in the first half of chapter 4 does Greene say he will develop later in the chapter?
options: Constant improvement as a source of strong character
Transforming the weak aspects of your character into strengths
The story of Howard Hughes’s business failures
Types of characters that are most toxic and should be avoided
John Bowlby’s four attachment schemas
questions.explain: Greene points ahead to toxic types and twice refers readers to the final section for self-transformation and constant improvement; the Hughes story and Bowlby’s schemas are dealt with already.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the Law of Compulsive Behavior, why does Greene say the toxic types are trickier to deal with than obviously evil or manipulative characters?
options: They lure you in with an appearance that presents their weaknesses as something positive
They are fully aware of their compulsions and hide them deliberately
They are far more intelligent and plan their manipulations years in advance
They usually hold positions of power that make them impossible to avoid
questions.explain: Greene says these types present their weaknesses as positives, so their toxic nature shows only over time, often too late. The point is the misleading appearance, not superior cunning or power.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what is your best defense against the toxic types described in the Law of Compulsive Behavior?
questions.a: Your best defense is knowledge of the types themselves, so you can notice their signs early on. Then you either avoid getting involved with them or disengage as quickly as possible, before their toxic nature, hidden beneath an attractive appearance, surfaces when it is too late.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what really lies behind the Hyperperfectionist’s long hours and insistence on doing everything right?
options: A wish to be admired as the hardest worker in the company
Power and control, rooted in dependency issues from their family background
A genuine dedication to the group and its highest standards
A fear of being found out as less talented than others
questions.explain: Greene says it is less about high standards and dedication than about power and control; any feeling of having to depend on someone opens old wounds and anxieties.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the Hyperperfectionist’s compulsive micromanaging makes people feel resentful and secretly resistant, which is precisely what the Hyperperfectionist fears most.
questions.explain: Because they cannot trust anyone and imagine everyone slacking off, they micromanage, and the resulting resentment and secret resistance is the very thing they dread.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, is a group led by a Hyperperfectionist poorly organized?
options: The leader sets standards so vague that nobody knows what to do
Everything must flow through the leader, producing chaos and political infighting
The leader hires only inexperienced people who will not question them
The leader is so often absent with health problems that nobody is in charge
questions.explain: Since everything must pass through the controlling leader, the result is chaos and infighting as the courtiers struggle to get closer to the king who controls everything.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene compares the Hyperperfectionist to Howard Hughes, saying such people often have ____ issues stemming from their family background.
questions.explain: Any feeling that they might have to depend on someone opens up old wounds and anxieties, which is why they cannot delegate.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put in order the way a career with a Hyperperfectionist typically unfolds, as Greene describes it.
items: You are drawn in by their dedication and long hours
You discover they cannot delegate and must oversee everything
Micromanaging breeds resentment, chaos and infighting
Initial success gives way to burnout and spectacular failure
questions.explain: Greene describes the lure of dedication, the slow discovery of the need for control, the resulting resentment and chaos, and a pattern of initial success followed by burnout and failure.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
