questions.q: Why, according to Greene, are almost all of us secretly attracted to the Relentless Rebel?
options: Their attitude appeals to the adolescent within us who wants to snub the teacher
They seem to offer protection against the authorities we fear
Their moral convictions make us feel that we are on the right side
Their biting humor is always directed at our enemies, never at us
questions.explain: Greene says hating authority and loving the underdog appeals to the adolescent within us, the desire to snub our nose at the teacher.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene say really drives the Relentless Rebel’s contempt for rules and authority, and where does it come from?
questions.a: Their rebellion is not a higher moral quality but a compulsion to feel superior that they cannot control. In childhood a parent or father figure probably disappointed them, so they came to mistrust and hate all those in power. In the end it is all about power: no one shall be above them, and they cannot accept any criticism because it reeks of authority.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the Relentless Rebel takes criticism well as long as it comes from a peer rather than from a boss.
questions.explain: Greene says Rebels cannot accept any criticism from others because it reeks of authority; they can never be told what to do, and everything must be on their terms.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as signs or consequences of dealing with the Relentless Rebel?
options: They tend to split with people on very bad terms
They brood for days over comments others have forgotten
If you cross them, you will be painted as the oppressor
They become addicted to the attention their rebel pose earns them
They quietly defer to whoever holds power while mocking them in private
questions.explain: Greene says crossing a Rebel makes you the oppressor and the brunt of their humor, that their past shows bitter splits, and that they become addicted to attention. Quiet deference belongs to the Pleaser and brooding to the Personalizer.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says Relentless Rebels are eternally locked in ____, so working with them is like locking horns with a sullen teenager.
questions.explain: Greene ends the portrait by saying such types are eternally locked in adolescence; their rebellion is a pose, not maturity.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, in which direction does the Personalizer’s sensitivity really go?
options: Inward, so that they take everything personally
Outward, toward the needs of those who are suffering
Toward ideas and art rather than toward people
Upward, toward those who can advance their career
questions.explain: The Personalizer seems sensitive and thoughtful, but their sensitivity goes in only one direction, inward; they take what people say or do as personal and brood for days.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what childhood experience shapes the Personalizer, and how does it play out in their adult life?
questions.a: As children, Personalizers had a gnawing feeling that they never got enough from their parents: love, attention or material possessions. As adults everything reminds them of what they did not get, so they resent it and want others to give them things without having to ask. Irritable and touchy, they push people away, which makes them even more sensitive, until they wear a look of perpetual disappointment.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says that over time the Personalizer starts to have a look of perpetual ____.
questions.explain: Being irritable and touchy, Personalizers push people away, which makes them more sensitive, and at some point they wear a look of perpetual disappointment.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put in order the self-reinforcing cycle of the Personalizer, as Greene describes it.
items: As children they feel they never got enough from their parents
As adults everything reminds them of what they did not get
Being irritable and touchy, they push people away
Pushed-away people make them even more sensitive
questions.explain: Greene traces the Personalizer from childhood deprivation to adult resentment, and shows how their touchiness drives people off, deepening the sensitivity in a loop.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene warn will happen if you inadvertently insult a Personalizer?
options: They will turn the insult into one of their dramatic stories
They will try to make you their savior and caretaker
They have a long memory and can spend years getting back at you
They will confront you openly and then forget it
questions.explain: Greene says never to insult such a type even by accident: they have a long memory and can spend years getting back at you.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what did the Drama Magnet learn as a child?
options: That being calm and helpless would get their parents to pamper them
That smiling and deferring would deflect their parents’ hostility
That caring for a needy parent gave them a feeling of power
That only by enmeshing their parents in large troubles could they get lasting love and attention
questions.explain: Drama Magnets learned that troubles large enough to engage their parents emotionally over time were the only way to get love and attention that lasted. The other options describe the Pampered Prince, the Pleaser and the Savior.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that while most people shrink from confrontation, the Drama Magnet seems to live for it, yet always positions themselves as the victim in their stories.
questions.explain: Greene says the Drama Magnet lives for confrontation, and as you hear more of their stories of battles, they manage always to position themselves as the victim.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene say is the Drama Magnet’s greatest need, and what does he advise you to do about it?
questions.a: Their greatest need is to get their hooks into you by any means possible, embroiling you in their drama until you feel guilty for disengaging. Greene advises recognizing them as early as possible, before you are enmeshed and dragged down, by examining their past for the pattern, and to run for the hills if you suspect you are dealing with such a type.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what inner conflict makes the Big Talker slip away at the last moment?
options: A clash between their loyalty to old partners and their wish for new ones
A clash between fear of the effort and responsibility of action and a craving for attention and power
A clash between their need for control and their dislike of details
A clash between their idealism and their fear of being seen as greedy
questions.explain: Greene calls Big Talkers ambivalent: secretly afraid of the effort and responsibility of turning ideas into action, yet craving attention and power. The anxious part wins, so they pull out after you have committed.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says the Big Talker is not overtly dangerous but can prove maddening and waste your valuable ____.
questions.explain: Greene presents the Big Talker as less dangerous than other types but a drain on your time, since they never finish anything.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does the Big Talker talk well but never follow through, according to Greene’s account of their childhood, and how should you respond to one?
questions.a: Big Talkers often had inconsistent parents who would turn on them suddenly for the smallest misdeed, so their goal in life became avoiding situations that open them up to criticism and judgment. They learned to talk well and impress people with stories but run away, always with an excuse, when called to account. Greene advises checking their past for this pattern and, if they fit, being amused by their stories but taking it no further.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say the Big Talker does when their projects fail to materialize?
options: Admits openly that they lost their nerve
Turns to moral outrage against those who succeeded
Finds a sucker to do the hard work and take the blame if it goes wrong
Blames society, nebulous antagonistic forces or bad luck
Works themselves to the bone trying to finish alone
questions.explain: Greene says Big Talkers blame others for their unrealized visions or find a sucker to do the work and take the blame. They never finish anything themselves and never own up to their anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what happens to the Sexualizer as they get older?
options: They turn into Easy Moralizers who condemn what they once did
Long periods without sexual validation can lead to depression, so they grow more desperate
They gradually outgrow the pattern and settle into stable relationships
They redirect their energy into creative work and become calmer
questions.explain: Sex becomes their means of self-validation; as they age, long periods without it can lead to depression, so they become more desperate, and the pattern grows more pathetic and frightening.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that with patience and understanding you can help a Sexualizer overcome their compulsion.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: you cannot help or save them from their compulsion, only save yourself from entanglement with them on any level.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: For the Sexualizer, Greene says sex becomes a means of self-____.
questions.explain: The Sexualizer sees every relationship as potentially sexual because sex has become their way of validating themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, how do you typically get drawn into serving a Pampered Prince or Princess?
options: Their calm, regal air draws you in, and slowly you find yourself doing favors and working extra hard for no pay
They flatter you excessively until you feel obliged to repay them
They offer to rescue you from your troubles and then ask for favors in return
They openly demand favors and threaten you if you refuse
questions.explain: Greene says they draw you in with a regal air and confidence; without understanding how, you end up doing favors and extra work, since they are masters at getting others to pamper them.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says the early pampering that the Pampered Prince or Princess wants to replicate as an adult remains their lost ____.
questions.explain: As adults their greatest desire is to recreate the indulgence of childhood, which Greene calls their lost paradise.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as part of the Pampered Prince or Princess pattern?
options: Blaming society and bad luck when their visions fail
Parents who indulged their slightest whim and shielded them from the harsh outside world
Parents who scrutinized and punished their every action
Pouting or tantrums when they do not get what they want
Turning to drinking and drugs to soothe themselves when no one pampers them
questions.explain: Greene names indulgent parents, baby-like pouting and tantrums, and resort to drink and drugs. Blaming society for unrealized visions belongs to the Big Talker, and harsh scrutinizing parents to the Pleaser.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, why has the Pleaser developed such niceness and charm?
options: As a strategy to win promotions quickly
Because they were pampered and expect the same from others
Out of genuine affection for their fellow humans
As a defense mechanism against harsh, punishing parents who scrutinized them
questions.explain: Greene says Pleasers developed niceness not out of genuine affection but as a defense; smiling and deferring was how they deflected hostility from harsh parents.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene say lies behind the Pleaser’s smiles and flattery, and how does it eventually show?
questions.a: Behind the smiles is a great deal of resentment at the role they have to play; they secretly yearn to harm or steal from the person they serve or defer to. It shows subtly at first, as they fail to show up as promised or do a job poorly, and then it seems they are sabotaging you or talking behind your back. They can turn out to be passive-aggressive, hitting you when your guard is down.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene calls Pleasers consummate ____, whose niceness is a defense rather than genuine affection.
questions.explain: Pleasers are consummate courtiers who smile and defer to deflect hostility, a pattern formed with harsh parents.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, when do your doubts about a Savior typically begin?
options: The moment you want to assert your independence and do things on your own
When they fail to show up as they promised
When they ask you for money in return for their help
When you discover their secret life or vice
questions.explain: In the beginning the Savior’s help is seductive, but doubts start when you want to stand on your own, since their compulsion shows in their need to control you.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: How does Greene explain the origins of the Savior’s need to rescue people, and how can you tell whether a particular Savior is genuinely noble?
questions.a: As children, Saviors often had to become caregivers to their own mother, father or siblings, and they compensated for the lack of care with the feeling of power from that inverted relationship. This set a pattern of gaining satisfaction from rescuing people. If they let you stand on your own two feet after some initial help, they are truly noble; if not, it is really about the power they exercise over you.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that, when dealing with a Savior, it is always best to accept their help gratefully and let them guide you.
questions.explain: Greene advises the opposite: it is always best to cultivate self-reliance and tell saviors to save themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what cracks in the Easy Moralizer’s righteous veneer might you detect?
options: They treat their employees poorly, are condescending to their spouse, and may have a secret life
They work themselves to the bone and blame others for failures
They talk grandly about projects but never finish them
They take every comment personally and brood for days
questions.explain: Greene says that behind the eloquent outrage you may glimpse poor treatment of employees, condescension to a spouse, and a secret life or vice. The other options describe other toxic types.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, why are Easy Moralizers so quick to judge and condemn others?
questions.a: As children they were made to feel guilty for their strong impulses and desires for pleasure, were punished, and tried to repress them. This leaves them with some self-loathing, so they project negative qualities onto others and look enviously at people who are not so repressed. Instead of expressing that envy, they judge and condemn, though in truth they are secretly drawn toward what they condemn.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says the adult Easy Moralizer shows a complete lack of ____: people are good or evil, with no middle ground.
questions.explain: The Easy Moralizer sees the world in black and white and is at war with human nature, unable to accept our less-than-perfect traits.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene call the Easy Moralizer’s morality “easy”?
options: It is shared by most people in their culture, so it is never challenged
It is based on simple rules that anyone can follow
It is as compulsive as drinking or gambling and requires no sacrifices, just noble words
It comes naturally to them because they were raised by kind parents
questions.explain: Greene says their morality is as easy and compulsive as drinking or gambling and costs them nothing but a lot of noble words.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each toxic type to the childhood origin Greene gives for it.
pairs: A parent or father figure disappointed them
Inconsistent parents turned on them for the smallest misdeed
They had to become caregivers of a parent or siblings
They were made to feel guilty for strong impulses and desires
Harsh, punishing parents scrutinized their every action
questions.explain: Greene traces each type to a childhood pattern: disappointment by authority, inconsistency, an inverted caring relationship, guilt over desire, and harsh scrutiny.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each toxic type to the attractive appearance that, according to Greene, first lures you in.
pairs: How hard they work and how dedicated they are
They seem sensitive, thoughtful and a little sad
Exciting presence, unusual energy and stories to tell
A calm, regal air of confidence
questions.explain: Each type presents a weakness as a virtue: control as dedication, self-absorption as sensitivity, need for drama as excitement, entitlement as regal calm, and repression as moral passion.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each toxic type to Greene’s advice for handling it.
pairs: Be amused by their stories but take it no further
Run for the hills if you suspect the type
Cultivate self-reliance and tell them to save themselves
Save yourself from entanglement on any level
Notice their lack of empathy early and keep your distance
questions.explain: Greene ends each portrait with practical advice; in every case the emphasis is on recognizing the type early and limiting your involvement.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these childhood origins by toxic type, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Parents indulged their slightest whim
Parents shielded them from the harsh outside world
Some acted especially helpless to incite care
Only large troubles kept their parents engaged
Problems became their way of feeling alive and wanted
They enmeshed their parents in their troubles

questions.explain: The Pampered Prince or Princess was indulged and protected, while the Drama Magnet learned that only troubles big enough to engage parents emotionally brought lasting attention.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether Greene attributes them to the Pleaser or to the Savior.

items.t: Niceness developed as a defense mechanism
Practiced and expert liar
Secretly yearns to harm the person they serve
Has a nose for those in need of salvation
Gains a feeling of power from an inverted relationship
Reveals the compulsion through a need to control you

questions.explain: Pleasers hide resentment behind defensive charm and lies; Saviors, former child caregivers, gain power from rescuing others and show it by controlling them.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether Greene presents them as the toxic type’s alluring surface or its hidden reality.

items.t: The Hyperperfectionist’s high standards
The Rebel’s love of the underdog
The Sexualizer’s refreshing lack of repression
The Hyperperfectionist’s need for power and control
The Rebel’s compulsion to feel superior
The Sexualizer’s compulsion from a dark place

questions.explain: Greene’s pattern for every toxic type is a weakness disguised as a virtue: standards hide control, rebellion hides superiority, and unrepressed sexuality hides a compulsion from early abuse.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether Greene attributes them to the Hyperperfectionist or to the Relentless Rebel.

items.t: Cannot trust anyone and imagines everyone slacking off
Often has health problems from overwork
Shows initial success followed by burnout
Cannot ever be told what to do
Has a biting sense of humor turned on others
Becomes addicted to the attention of their pose

questions.explain: The Hyperperfectionist’s compulsion is control and overwork; the Rebel’s is a need to feel superior to any authority, expressed in mockery and attention-seeking.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these toxic types does Greene say leave a history of falling-outs in which they cast themselves as the wronged party or victim?
options: The Drama Magnet
The Big Talker
The Savior
The Personalizer
The Pampered Prince or Princess
questions.explain: The Personalizer has many falling-outs but always sees themselves as wronged, and the Drama Magnet tells of battles in which they are always the victim.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these toxic types in the order Greene presents them in the Law of Compulsive Behavior.
items: The Hyperperfectionist
The Personalizer
The Sexualizer
The Pleaser
The Easy Moralizer
questions.explain: Greene begins with the Hyperperfectionist and Relentless Rebel, moves through the Personalizer, Drama Magnet, Big Talker and Sexualizer, then the Pampered Prince, Pleaser and Savior, and ends with the Easy Moralizer.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: A new colleague volunteers to reorganize your diet, schedule and reading list, but becomes cold and insistent when you say you would like to manage on your own. Which toxic type from Greene does this most resemble?
options: The Pampered Prince or Princess
The Personalizer
The Pleaser
The Savior
questions.explain: The Savior arrives with books, strategies and the right foods, and the compulsion shows when you assert independence, revealing a need to control.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: A charismatic acquaintance pitches you an exciting startup idea and asks you to invest; you find no finished projects in their past, only stories. Which toxic type does Greene’s description fit, and what does he advise?
options: The Drama Magnet; run for the hills immediately
The Big Talker; enjoy their stories but take it no further
The Relentless Rebel; avoid crossing them in public
The Hyperperfectionist; let them control the project and stay out of the way
questions.explain: Greene says to check a Big Talker’s record for tangible achievements and, if they fit the type, be amused by their stories but go no further.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these toxic types does Greene say will make you feel guilty, either for disengaging or for not helping them?
options: The Drama Magnet
The Hyperperfectionist
The Personalizer
The Pampered Prince or Princess
The Big Talker
questions.explain: Greene says the Personalizer will make you feel guilty for something, the Drama Magnet makes you feel guilty for disengaging, and guilt at not helping the Pampered Prince shows you are hooked.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, does the Hyperperfectionist end up producing the very resistance and failure they fear?
questions.a: Because of dependency issues from their family background, Hyperperfectionists cannot trust anyone or delegate, and imagine everyone slacking once their back is turned. Their compulsive micromanaging makes people resentful and secretly resistant, and since everything must flow through them, the group falls into chaos and infighting. Working themselves to the bone and blaming others, they show a pattern of initial success followed by burnout and spectacular failures.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the Superior Character, how does Greene say the brain helps a set character compel us to repeat ourselves?
options: Memories of early punishment block the formation of new habits
The brain stores only our first decisions and discards later ones
Hormones released in childhood fix our moods for life
Once we think and take an action, a neural pathway forms that leads us to do it again
questions.explain: Greene says the brain is structured to facilitate repetition: an action taken once forms a neural pathway that leads us to repeat it again and again.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the Superior Character, Greene says that one direction you can take in relation to the law is ignorance and ____.
questions.explain: The first of the two directions is ignorance and denial: not noticing your patterns and imagining your character is completely plastic.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Describe the first direction, ignorance and denial, that Greene says people take in relation to the Law of Compulsive Behavior, and its result.
questions.a: People in denial do not notice the patterns in their lives or accept that their earliest years left a lasting imprint; they imagine their character is completely plastic and that they can re-create themselves at will, even following someone else’s path to power. Because a set character feels like a prison, many secretly want to escape themselves through drugs, alcohol or video games. The result is that their compulsive behavior and patterns become even more set into place.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that people who deny their set character often secretly want to be taken outside themselves through drugs, alcohol, or video games.
questions.explain: Greene says the concept of a set character can seem like a prison, so many people seek to escape themselves in these ways.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene in the Superior Character, what was Howard Hughes’s real strength, which he failed to accept?
options: Managing large teams of people
Raising money and negotiating with investors
The design and engineering aspects of airplane production
Promoting films and handling publicity
questions.explain: Greene says Hughes was not by nature a good manager of people; his real strength was technical, a great feel for design and engineering of airplanes.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What does Greene say Howard Hughes could have done had he known and accepted his character, and why did he fail instead?
questions.a: Had he accepted that his strength was technical, Hughes could have had a brilliant career as the visionary behind his own aircraft company, leaving day-to-day operations to someone truly capable. Instead he imagined himself a great businessman whose empire would outdo his father’s, living with an image of himself that did not correlate with his character. This led to a pattern of failures and a miserable life.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as things you examine in yourself when taking the second, harder direction?
options: The quality of attachments you formed with your parents, as shown by your current relationships
Whether you are an introvert or an extrovert
Which famous person’s path to power you could copy
Your primal inclinations, the subjects and activities you are naturally drawn to
How quickly you could re-create yourself into someone else
questions.explain: Greene lists temperament, primal inclinations and attachment quality among the deep layers to examine. Copying another’s path or re-creating yourself belongs to the first direction, denial.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says you should look at your current ____ as the best sign of the quality of the attachments you formed with your parents.
questions.explain: When examining your attachment schema, Greene says your current relationships are the best sign of it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what does self-awareness allow you to do when you see yourself falling into one of your usual patterns?
options: Replace your whole character with a new one
Catch yourself in time and step back, mitigating its effects with practice
Blame the pattern on your parents and move on
Eliminate the pattern completely after one effort
questions.explain: Greene says you may not completely eliminate such patterns, but you can catch yourself, step back, and with practice mitigate their effects.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that with enough self-awareness you can completely eliminate your compulsive patterns.
questions.explain: Greene says you may not be able to completely eliminate such patterns, but with practice you can mitigate their effects.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says you should see your character as the ____ that you will work with, slowly transforming your weaknesses into strengths.
questions.explain: Rather than trying to become someone else, you work with your character as a sculptor works clay, turning flaws into sources of power.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put the events of Joan Crawford’s early life in order, as Greene recounts them.
items: Her father abandons the family shortly after her birth
She grows up in poverty, beaten by her mother
She learns her adored stepfather is not her father, and he leaves
She begins her film career and examines her flaws
She builds a career spanning over forty years
questions.explain: Greene describes the abandonment by her father, a childhood of poverty and beatings, the stepfather’s revelation and departure, then her self-examination as a young actress and her forty-year career.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each of Joan Crawford’s weaknesses to the strength she turned it into, according to Greene.
pairs: Pain and sadness she could not disguise
Sadness and betrayal brought into her roles
A desperate need to be loved
Directed her need for love toward the camera
A continual need for a father figure
Treated directors as adored father figures
Fine antennae tuned to directors’ likes and dislikes
questions.explain: Greene presents Crawford as an example of alchemy: each insecurity became a pillar of her career, from sadness on screen to sensitivity turned outward toward directors.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did women around the world identify with Joan Crawford?
options: She brought her own sadness and betrayal into her roles, unlike falsely cheerful actresses
She played glamorous, cheerful heroines they wanted to be
She spoke openly in interviews about her abusive childhood
She chose only roles of strong, independent businesswomen
questions.explain: Greene says she brought her feelings of sadness and betrayal into all her roles, unlike the many falsely cheerful and superficial actresses of her time.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: How did Joan Crawford turn her hypersensitivity outward rather than inward, according to Greene, and what was the result?
questions.a: Instead of letting hypersensitivity wound her, Crawford developed intensely fine antennae tuned to the likes and dislikes of her directors. Without looking at them or hearing a word, she could sense their displeasure with her acting, ask the right questions, and quickly incorporate their criticisms. She became a director’s dream, and with her fierce willpower she forged a career of over forty years, unheard of for a Hollywood actress.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene calls the process by which Joan Crawford turned her weaknesses into strengths the ____ that you must use on yourself.
questions.explain: After the Crawford story Greene says this is the alchemy you must use on yourself, transforming each flaw into a corresponding strength.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each compulsive trait to the strength Greene says it can be redirected into.
pairs: Productive work with attention to detail and high standards
Charm used as a genuine social skill
Active empathy for positive social purposes
Innovative work that breaks with convention
questions.explain: Greene says for each weakness there is a corresponding strength: control into productive work, courtier charm into social skill, sensitivity into active empathy, and rebellion into innovation.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that a rebellious character should channel their natural dislike of conventions into some kind of innovative work.
questions.explain: Rather than compulsively insulting and alienating people, the rebel can turn their dislike of the usual ways of doing things into innovation.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, how should a hyperperfectionist who likes to control everything handle that trait?
options: Find a team that enjoys being closely supervised
Accept it as fixed and avoid leadership roles altogether
Redirect the energy into productive work instead of using it on people
Suppress it entirely and delegate every task
questions.explain: Greene says the hyperperfectionist must redirect this energy into productive work rather than people; attention to detail and high standards are positives if channeled correctly.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as traits that go into a strong character and should be refined or cultivated?
options: Skill at impressing people with stories
Tolerance of people’s differences
Resilience under pressure
An unwavering refusal to change your strategies
The ability to complete things
questions.explain: Greene lists resilience, attention to detail, the ability to complete things, teamwork and tolerance. He values flexibility, not rigid refusal to change, and impressive talk without follow-through is the Big Talker’s weakness.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Greene says the only way to cultivate the traits of a strong character is to work on your ____, which go into the slow formation of character.
questions.explain: Character is formed partly by daily habits, so Greene says strengthening it means deliberately training new habits.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each habit-training practice to the quality Greene says it builds.
pairs: Repeatedly placing yourself in stressful situations
Taking on tasks slightly above your level
Occasionally doing the opposite of what you normally would
questions.explain: Greene gives each practice a purpose: exposure to stress for composure, routine for patience, stretch tasks for discipline, and shaking yourself up for flexibility.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does Greene recommend seeking out people who display a strong character, and why does he advise occasionally shaking yourself up?
questions.a: Associating as much as possible with people of strong character lets you assimilate their energy and their habits, which slowly shape your own character. Shaking yourself up, by trying a new strategy or way of thinking and doing the opposite of what you would normally do, develops flexibility in your character, which Greene calls always a sign of strength.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these by which of the two directions Greene says people take in relation to the Law of Compulsive Behavior.

items.t: Imagining your character is completely plastic
Following someone else’s path to power
Escaping yourself through drugs or video games
Knowing your limitations and choosing a suitable career
Looking honestly at your mistakes and patterns
Seeing flaws as a source of power

questions.explain: Denial pretends character can be remade at will or escaped; the harder direction studies character honestly and works with it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these by whether they were Joan Crawford’s flaws or the uses she made of them, according to Greene.

items.t: Hypersensitive and fragile
Wanted desperately to be loved
A continual need for a father figure
Sensing directors’ displeasure without a word
Directing her need for love toward the camera
Treating directors with extreme respect

questions.explain: Crawford examined her flaws with ruthless objectivity and then transformed each into a professional strength.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they match Greene’s account of character in the Superior Character or contradict it.

items.t: Character was formed from elements that predate conscious awareness
For each weakness there is a corresponding strength
Flexibility of character is always a sign of strength
You can re-create yourself at will
Self-awareness completely eliminates compulsive patterns
The goal is to become someone else

questions.explain: Greene holds that character is set early, that weaknesses can be turned into strengths, and that flexibility is strength, while denying that character is plastic, that patterns vanish entirely, or that you should become someone else.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put in order the scenario in the Cesare Pavese passage that closes the Law of Compulsive Behavior.
items: People resolve to slave away and save every penny till thirty
At thirty they have a bent for avarice and hard work
They never enjoy themselves any more
questions.explain: Pavese’s example shows that what one does, one will do again: years of saving create a lasting habit of avarice that rules out the planned enjoyment.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: In the Cesare Pavese passage that closes the Law of Compulsive Behavior, why are our decisions and actions omens of what we will do another time?
options: Because other people expect us to behave consistently
Because we remember and regret our past mistakes
Because they result from an automatic reaction that will repeat itself
Because fate and the stars have fixed our course in advance
questions.explain: Pavese says decisions are infallible omens not for any mystic or astrological reason but “because they result from an automatic reaction that will repeat itself.”

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: According to Greene, what does the second, harder direction finally give you that the first direction cannot?
questions.a: It is the only path that leads to true power and the formation of a superior character. Knowing yourself deeply, you are no longer the captive of your character compelled to repeat the same mistakes; you choose paths that suit you and turn weaknesses into strengths. With work on your habits you are no longer a slave to the character created by your earliest years, and can actively shape your character and the fate that goes with it.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Maya knows she takes criticism personally and broods. Following Greene’s advice in the Superior Character, what should she do with this trait?
options: Avoid all feedback so she cannot be hurt
Accept that the trait will ruin her career and lower her ambitions
Work to redirect her sensitivity into active empathy toward others
Pretend to be thick-skinned until it becomes true
questions.explain: Greene says that if you are highly sensitive and take things personally, you can redirect this into active empathy, turning the flaw into an asset.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say knowing your limitations allows you to do?
options: Stop examining yourself once you know your weaknesses
Copy any successful person’s career regardless of background
Choose career paths that suit you and mesh with your character
Avoid trying your hand at things for which you have no capacity or inclination
questions.explain: Greene says knowing your limitations keeps you from attempting what you have no capacity for and leads you to careers that suit your character, unlike the denier who copies others.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put in order the steps of the harder direction toward a superior character, as Greene describes them.
items: Examine the deepest layers of your character honestly
Recognize your usual patterns as they begin
Catch yourself and step back to mitigate them
Transform your weaknesses into strengths
questions.explain: Greene says you first examine yourself thoroughly, which lets you see patterns forming, catch yourself in time, and then work your character like clay into strengths.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: What point about compulsive behavior does the Cesare Pavese passage at the end of the chapter make?
questions.a: Pavese says it is a mistake to think one can act a certain way just once: what one does, one will do again, and has probably already done before. His example is people who plan to slave and save until thirty and then enjoy themselves, but by thirty have a bent for avarice and hard work. Our decisions are omens of future behavior not for mystic reasons but because they come from an automatic reaction that repeats itself.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Why does the Law of Compulsive Behavior end with the Superior Character after the Toxic Types?
options: To introduce the subject of envy that the next chapter covers
To show that toxic types can be cured if you are patient with them
To prove that character is completely plastic after all
To turn from judging others’ character to knowing and shaping your own
questions.explain: After teaching how to read and avoid others’ compulsive patterns, Greene turns the lens inward, matching the law’s instruction to know thoroughly your own character and take control of your destiny.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Match each kind of toxic person to the later chapter that Greene says describes more of them.
pairs: Chapter 16, See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.explain: Greene closes Toxic Types by pointing to the chapters on envy (10), grandiosity (11) and aggression (16) for more toxic types.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: When Greene advises highly sensitive people to redirect their touchiness into active empathy, he refers back to Chapter ____, Transform Self-love into Empathy.
questions.explain: The Superior Character cross-references chapter 2, the Law of Narcissism, where active empathy is developed.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: True or false: Howard Hughes, the subject of the chapter’s opening story, The Pattern, is referred to again in both Toxic Types and the Superior Character.
questions.explain: Greene compares the Hyperperfectionist’s dependency issues to Hughes in Toxic Types, and in the Superior Character uses Hughes as the example of denying one’s character.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Put these sections of the Law of Compulsive Behavior in the order they appear.
items: The Pattern
Keys to Human Nature
Character Signs
Toxic Types
The Superior Character
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the Hughes story to the theory of character, then to signs for judging others, the toxic types to avoid, and finally the superior character you can build in yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: How does the chapter title, Determine the Strength of People’s Character, fit the two halves of the chapter that cover Toxic Types and the Superior Character?
questions.a: The title asks you to judge how strong or weak people’s character is. Toxic Types shows what weak character looks like in practice: compulsions formed in childhood and disguised as virtues, which you should recognize early and avoid. The Superior Character then applies the same standard to yourself, showing how to know your own character, work on your habits, and build the strength the title asks you to look for in others.

questions.unitTitle: Determine the Strength of People’s Character
questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in the Law of Compulsive Behavior does the Superior Character section build on?
options: Howard Hughes’s life as an example of a pattern of failures
People never do something just once
Toxic types are best handled by trying to save them
Character is formed in our earliest years and compels us to repeat patterns
Character is completely plastic and can be remade at will
questions.explain: The Superior Character restates that character is set early and compels repetition, returns to Hughes, and closes with Pavese’s point that what one does one will do again. It rejects the idea that character is plastic and that toxic types can be saved.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the opening of the Law of Covetousness, what effect does Greene say a degree of absence has on us?
options: It signals weakness and a need for reassurance
It spurs our interest in the person who is absent
It breeds resentment and slowly makes us forget
It suffocates the relationship with too much doubt
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the two: too much presence suffocates, while a degree of absence spurs our interest. Suffocation is what he attributes to presence, not absence.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: The opening of the Law of Covetousness sums up our restless desire with a proverb: the ____ is always greener on the other side of the fence.
questions.explain: Greene cites the proverb that the grass is always greener on the other side of the fence, the root of what he later calls the grass-is-always-greener syndrome.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the opening of the Law of Covetousness, Greene says you should overcome covetousness in yourself by embracing your circumstances, your fate.
questions.explain: The opening ends by telling you to overcome this weakness in yourself by embracing your circumstances, your fate. The law has an outward use (stirring desire in others) and an inward one (calming your own).

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: According to the opening of the Law of Covetousness, what should you do to make people desire you, and why does it work?
questions.a: Learn to create some mystery around you, use strategic absence so people want your return and want to possess you, and dangle in front of them what they are missing most or are forbidden to have. It works because we are marked by the continual desire to possess what we do not have, the object projected by our fantasies.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story in the Law of Covetousness, what happened to eleven-year-old Gabrielle Chanel after her mother died?
options: She was sent to live with a wealthy aunt in Paris
She went on the road with her father selling goods
Her father left her at a convent, promising to return, and never came back
She was apprenticed to a seamstress in a small town
questions.explain: A few days after the mother’s death her father deposited Gabrielle and two sisters at a convent in central France; he promised to return soon, but they never saw him again. Seamstress training came later, at a boarding school.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, the smuggled romance novels by Pierre Decourcelle that Gabrielle read in the convent almost all told a ____-like story of a poor, shunned girl suddenly whisked into wealth.
questions.explain: The novels involved a Cinderella-like plot, and Gabrielle identified with the heroines, especially loving the descriptions of their dresses.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, match each period of Coco’s life to what she longed for then.
pairs: The palaces and dresses of romance-novel heroines
Fame as an actress in the theater
The wardrobe and freedom of a great courtesan
The power and freedom that men possessed
Her fashions copied by women of all classes and nations
questions.explain: Her desires kept moving to something beyond reach until she understood her longing for men’s power and freedom and turned it into objects others coveted.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why did Coco give up her dream of a career in the theater?
options: The nuns at her boarding school forbade it
Etienne Balsan insisted she leave the stage
She found the world of costumes and makeup dull
She realized she lacked the talent for the success she wanted
questions.explain: She had energy and charisma but quickly realized she lacked the talent for the kind of success she desired. She actually loved the costumes, sets and makeup of the theater.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why did the life of a courtesan appeal to Coco after the theater failed her?
questions.a: Many actresses who could not live from their work became courtesans supported by wealthy lovers. Such women had enormous wardrobes and could go where they pleased, and although shunned by good society they were not shackled to some despotic husband. It was another forbidden, seemingly out-of-reach life of the kind she always coveted.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why did Coco judge her dream of becoming a great courtesan to be absurd?
options: Courtesans were banned from the château she lived in
She had no money to buy the wardrobe a courtesan needed
Balsan refused to introduce her to wealthy men
The great courtesans were voluptuous beauties, and she looked more like a boy
questions.explain: The great courtesans were all voluptuous, beautiful women, while Coco had no curves and was not a classic beauty; it was her presence and energy that charmed men, and she feared that would not last.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Chanel story, Greene says that whenever Coco got what she wanted, such as a boyfriend or the life in a château, she felt disappointed by the reality.
questions.explain: She always wanted what others had, imagining it held some hidden treasure, but once she got it she inevitably felt disappointed, an early picture of the grass-is-always-greener syndrome.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these did Coco notice when she first wore outfits made from Etienne Balsan’s clothes?
options: Immediate orders from Paris boutiques
A sense of freedom after leaving behind corsets and constricting gowns
A new kind of attention, including envy from the other courtesans
Mockery from the courtesans, who found the style ridiculous
Anger from Balsan, who demanded his clothes back
questions.explain: She noticed two things: an incredible sense of freedom and a new kind of attention, as the other courtesans watched her with envy. Balsan was charmed, not angry, and introduced her to his tailor.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, as her new persona developed, Coco realized her vague longings were for the power and ____ that men possessed, reflected in their less constricting clothes.
questions.explain: It became clear that what she wanted was the power and freedom men had, and she sensed the other women shared this repressed desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, what was the first Chanel creation that other women began asking to buy?
options: Jersey swimming costumes she made for herself
A boy’s riding costume with jodhpurs
A cardigan cut from a man’s sweater
Simple straw hats she decorated with ribbons and feathers
questions.explain: Courtesans tried on her decorated straw hats, which were simpler than the elaborate pinned hats of the day, and soon other women in the area were asking where to buy them. The swimming costumes and cardigan came later in Deauville.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, match each person to their role in her life.
pairs: Wealthy heir who invited her to his château and lent her his Paris apartment
English lover who sent aristocratic lady friends to her studio
Author of the romance novels she read in the convent
The stage star Coco once dreamed of becoming
Wore her suits, a symbol of her reclaimed power
questions.explain: Balsan gave her the château life and the Paris apartment; Capel promoted her hats among aristocrats; Decourcelle wrote the novels; Bernhardt was her theatrical ideal; Kennedy’s wearing of her suits marked the comeback’s success.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, match each Chanel creation to how she made it.
pairs: Cut open one of Capel’s sweaters and added buttons
Made from jersey fabric because women’s versions barely existed
Had Balsan’s tailor make a boy’s costume with jodhpurs
Decorated simple straw hats with ribbons and feathers
Cut her own hair to suit her face
questions.explain: Each look came from improvising with men’s clothing or simple materials and then letting others see her wear it, which turned it into a trend.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, Coco created a modern women’s cardigan by cutting open one of Arthur Capel’s ____ and adding buttons.
questions.explain: She kept improvising with men’s clothing; cutting open Capel’s sweater and adding buttons produced a cardigan that became the rage.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put these stages of Coco Chanel’s rise in the order Greene tells them.
items: Reads romance novels in the convent
Takes the stage name Coco in the theater
Lives at Balsan’s château and wears his clothes
Makes hats in Balsan’s Paris apartment
Opens a shop in Deauville
Launches Chanel No. 5
questions.explain: Each stage grew out of the last: forbidden dreams in the convent, the theater, the château where she found her look, hats in Paris, the Deauville shop, and then the perfume around 1920.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, how did Chanel No. 5 differ in scent from the other perfumes of the time?
options: It was not identifiable as any particular flower
It was designed to smell exactly the same on every woman
It used a single rare flower no one else could obtain
It copied the most popular floral scent at a lower price
questions.explain: Other perfumes were tied to a natural floral scent; she wanted something pleasant but novel that no one could identify as a particular flower, which would smell different on each woman.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, Chanel wanted her perfume to smell like a bouquet of ____ flowers, pleasant but completely novel.
questions.explain: She wanted “a bouquet of abstract flowers,” going in the opposite direction from perfumes tied to a single natural flower.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, sort these features into typical perfumes of the time and Chanel No. 5.

items.t: Associated with a natural floral scent
Very poetic, romantic names
Named after its maker with a simple number
Sleek modernist bottle with interlocking C’s
Smelled different on each woman
Scent impossible to identify as a known flower

questions.explain: Chanel went the opposite way from the industry: an abstract scent, a name like a scientific concoction and modernist packaging, where others relied on floral scents and romantic titles.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, put the steps of Chanel’s subliminal launch of her perfume in order.
items: Sprays the scent everywhere in her Paris store
Feigns ignorance when women ask what it is
Slips unlabeled bottles into the bags of top clients
Women talk about the strange new scent
Places the perfume discreetly on her shelves
questions.explain: She built mystery and word of mouth first, and only when women were begging to buy it did she put it on the shelves, where it sold out in the first weeks.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Chanel story, Greene says the perfume was in truth a mix of rare, exotic ingredients that no competitor could match.
questions.explain: Greene says the perfume was a mix of ordinary flowers, such as jasmine, and chemicals, nothing exotic. Its power came from psychological magic, not its ingredients.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why does Greene call her 1953 return to fashion the ultimate challenge for her?
questions.a: She was seventy and had been out of business for some fourteen years, largely forgotten and no longer seen as a trendsetter, and she was disgraced in France by her wartime Nazi sympathies. She had to start almost completely over, driven by disgust that fashion had returned to the old constrictions and fussiness she had sought to destroy.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why was the Paris audience disappointed by her 1954 comeback show?
options: The clothes were too shocking and transgressive
She refused to let anyone into the store to watch
The clothes were mostly a rehash of her 1930s styles
The show copied the latest constrictive trends
questions.explain: The clothes were mostly a rehash of her 1930s styles with a few new touches, so she seemed locked in the past; the press also dredged up her Nazi associations.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these were reasons Chanel targeted the United States with her 1954 line?
options: American women had more money to spend than anyone else
She had lived in America during her exile
The American press had praised her Paris debut
American women were athletic and liked ease of movement and unfussy silhouettes
American women were eminently practical
questions.explain: American women reflected her sensibility best and had the most money to spend. The Paris press had pilloried the debut, and her exile was in Switzerland.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Chanel story, after her comeback Chanel fought all imitations of her designs through the courts, as other designers did.
questions.explain: Chanel did the opposite of other designers: she let people photograph her shows and even invited wealthy women to bring seamstresses to sketch and copy the designs.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, why did Chanel welcome the copying of her designs when other designers fought piracy?
questions.a: More than money, she wanted her fashions spread everywhere, so that she and her work would be objects of desire for women of all classes and nations. It was the ultimate revenge for the girl who had grown up ignored, unloved and shunned, and copies also kept her look seen everywhere, feeding others’ desire for it.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chanel story, what changed for her the moment she wore Balsan’s clothes and drew a new kind of attention?
questions.a: Until then she had always coveted something transgressive that stirred her fantasies. Now she was the object others coveted, drawn by the transgressive flouting of gender roles in her clothes. She only had to reverse her perspective, thinking of the audience first and playing on their imagination, building into her creations the vague, elusive and taboo qualities that had drawn her own desires.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Chanel story, sort these moments into Coco coveting something and Coco being coveted.

items.t: Dreaming of palaces from romance novels
Wanting to be another Sarah Bernhardt
Stealing other women’s boyfriends
Courtesans envying her riding costume
Women clamoring for her swimming costumes
Women begging to buy her new scent

questions.explain: Greene’s interpretation turns on this reversal: she moved from being locked in fantasies of what she lacked to stimulating such fantasies in other people.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chanel story, put the three elements of her magic in the order he presents them.
items: An aura of mystery around herself and her work
Association with something vaguely transgressive
Making sure her clothes were seen everywhere
questions.explain: Greene lists them as first, second and finally: mystery, then the transgressive edge, then ubiquity that stirs competitive desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chanel story, sort these tactics into creating mystery and creating a transgressive edge.

items.t: Invented contradictory stories about her past
Never revealed the recipe for her perfume
Controlled the number of her public appearances
A logo designed to stimulate interpretations
A masculine edge on decidedly feminine clothes
Clothes that hugged the body, mixing freedom and sex
Not your mother’s clothes: youth and modernity

questions.explain: Mystery left space for the public to imagine the Coco myth; the transgressive edge gave women the sense of crossing gender boundaries and loosening constrictions.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chanel story, why did making sure her clothes were seen everywhere stimulate desire?
options: It proved the clothes were well made and durable
Seeing others wear them stirred competitive desires not to be left out
It reassured buyers that the style was respectable
It made the clothes cheaper to produce in bulk
questions.explain: Observing other women in the clothes stimulated competitive desires to have the same. Coco remembered desiring men who were already taken: they were desirable because someone else desired them.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say were, in truth, quite ordinary about Chanel’s creations?
options: The perfume was ordinary flowers like jasmine plus chemicals
Her first clothes were made of the cheapest materials
The boater hats were common objects sold in department stores
The clothes were hand-embroidered from imported silk
The perfume was distilled from a rare orchid
questions.explain: Greene stresses that the hats, the cheap jersey clothes and the perfume were ordinary; it was “pure psychological magic” that turned them into objects of intense desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: After the Chanel story, what does Greene mean when he says you must reverse your perspective?
questions.a: Instead of focusing on what you want and covet, train yourself to focus on others, on their repressed desires and unmet fantasies. Learn to see how they perceive you and the things you make, as if looking at yourself from the outside. This gives you the power to shape their perceptions and excite their desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise after the Chanel story to make you and your work objects of desire?
options: Create an air of mystery around you and your work
Leave your message vague rather than defining it
Create an illusion that your object is seen everywhere
Reveal as much as possible so people trust you
Make your message as clear and complete as possible
questions.explain: Greene advises mystery, a vague message and an illusion of ubiquity, plus association with the new and taboo. Full disclosure and a clearly defined message are what he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: After the Chanel story, Greene advises creating an illusion of ____: your object seems to be seen everywhere and desired by others.
questions.explain: An illusion of ubiquity lets latent covetousness set off a chain reaction of desire, as Chanel’s clones did across Deauville and Paris.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: A small bakery owner wants her new pastry to become the talk of the neighborhood. Which move best follows Greene’s lesson from the Chanel story?
options: Explain at length how much effort went into developing it
Post the full recipe online so customers trust its quality
Hand a few unlabeled samples to well-connected regulars and keep the recipe secret
Put up large posters listing every ingredient and its price
questions.explain: Like Chanel slipping unlabeled perfume into top clients’ bags and never revealing her recipe, this builds mystery and word of mouth. Full disclosure and stressing your own effort leave no room for the imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: The Beaumarchais epigraph after the Chanel story says that pleasure isn’t in the fulfillment, but in the ____.
questions.explain: The speaker has what he wanted yet is not happy, because his soul has lost the activity that desire conferred: “pleasure isn’t in the fulfillment, but in the pursuit.”

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene names our habit of wanting what is distant and unattainable the grass-is-always-greener ____.
questions.explain: He calls it the grass-is-always-greener syndrome: the more distant the new object, the greater our desire for it.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, what does Greene compare the grass-is-always-greener syndrome to?
options: A fever that passes once the object is possessed
A habit learned only in modern consumer culture
A psychological equivalent of an optical illusion
A mirror that shows us our own flaws
questions.explain: He calls it the psychological equivalent of an optical illusion: get too close to the grass and it is not so green after all. He also says the syndrome has very deep roots, not modern ones.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How does the story of the Hebrews in the wilderness illustrate the grass-is-always-greener syndrome in the Law of Covetousness?
questions.a: Though they had been slaves in Egypt, once they suffered hardships in the desert they grew nostalgic for their old life, comparing God’s manna unfavorably with Egypt’s melons, cucumbers and meats. Unmoved by miracles, they turned to a golden calf, lusted after foreign women and kept looking for new cults. Even after the next generation reached the Promised Land, the grumbling continued: whatever they had, they dreamed of something better.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene says God was so irritated by the Hebrews’ discontent that he barred their whole generation, Moses included, from entering the Promised Land.
questions.explain: Greene recounts that God barred that entire generation, including Moses, and notes the grumbling continued even after the next generation settled there.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give in the Law of Covetousness as everyday examples of the grass-is-always-greener syndrome?
options: Dreaming of a utopia that a revolution would bring
Making the most of the job we already have
Finding some charm in a partner’s weaknesses
Letting our minds wander from a satisfying partner to someone without their flaws
Imagining other people’s parents were more loving
questions.explain: Envying others’ families, idealizing a new partner and dreaming of utopia all imagine something better at a distance. Accepting a partner’s flaws and making the most of what you have are Greene’s remedies, not symptoms.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, why does Greene say we remember childhood as a golden time?
options: Our parents shaped our memories with stories
Childhood really was free of anxieties and hurts
Children feel pleasure more intensely than adults
Youth grows more distant as we age, so we can idealize it
questions.explain: Because youth is an object that recedes as we age, we idealize it and forget the anxieties, insecurities and hurts that likely took up more of our mental space than its pleasures.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, put the three qualities of the brain that explain the grass-is-always-greener syndrome in the order Greene gives them.
items: Induction: the mind works by contrasts
Complacency would be a dangerous evolutionary trait
The real and the imagined are experienced similarly
questions.explain: Greene first explains induction, second the survival value of alertness over complacency, and finally that imagination has almost the force of real experience.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, the first quality of the brain behind the syndrome, how something positive generates a contrasting negative image in our mind, is known as ____.
questions.explain: Induction is clearest in vision: looking at a red object can make a green halo appear around it, and generally the mind forms concepts through their opposites.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene says a taboo instantly brings to mind the very thing forbidden: every no sparks a corresponding ____.
questions.explain: Because the mind moves between contrasts, a forbidden desire brings that desire to mind; Greene cites the outlawing of pornography in Victorian times creating the first pornographic industry.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene says our early ancestors survived because they tended to feel content with their present circumstances.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: complacency would have been dangerous, and we survived through continual alertness to possible dangers, which leaves us with a negative bias expressed in complaining and griping.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, match each illustration to the point Greene uses it to make.
pairs: Hebrews comparing manna to Egypt’s melons
What recedes into the distance gets idealized
Green halo around a red object
A taboo sparks desire for what is forbidden
Imagining something resembles living it in the brain
questions.explain: Each example supports one strand of the argument: the syndrome’s ancient roots, the role of distance, induction, the pull of taboo, and the near-equal force of imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list in the Law of Covetousness as harsh limits of reality that our imagination lets us escape?
options: We all must die
Every day we get older and less strong
Success requires sacrifice and hard work
Our memories are perfectly accurate
Other people always envy what we have
questions.explain: Reality is full of limits like death, aging and the sacrifice success demands; in imagination we can voyage beyond them, which makes imagining something better so pleasurable.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, how does the brain’s handling of the real and the imagined make the grass-is-always-greener syndrome inevitable?
questions.a: Experiments using fMRI show that imagining something produces brain activity remarkably similar to actually living it. Reality is harsh and limited, while imagination is essentially limitless and has almost the force of real experience. So we are continually prone to imagining something better than our present circumstances and enjoying the release from reality that imagination brings.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Why does Greene say in the Law of Covetousness that we should not moralize or complain about the grass-is-always-greener syndrome?
questions.a: It is part of everyone’s mental life and has many benefits. It is the source of our ability to think of new possibilities and innovate and has made our imagination a powerful instrument. It is also the material from which we can move, excite and seduce people, the basis of all forms of persuasion.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, sort these into illusions of the grass-is-always-greener syndrome and benefits Greene sees in it.

items.t: Another family seems happier than ours
A new person seems free of our partner’s flaws
A revolution will bring a utopia
Thinking of new possibilities and innovating
Making imagination a powerful instrument
Material for moving, exciting and seducing people

questions.explain: Up close the envied family, partner or utopia loses its glow, yet the same restless imagination drives innovation and persuasion.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, what does Greene say is the real problem with desire today?
options: People covet only what their friends already own
We are losing our connection to the art of working on covetousness
Advertisers have become too subtle to notice
People have suddenly stopped coveting things
questions.explain: The problem is not that people have stopped coveting but the opposite: we are losing touch with the art of stirring desire, and the power that goes with it.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene cite in the Law of Covetousness as signs of our age of bombardment and saturation?
options: Advertisers rely on subtle hints and strategic absence
Movies bludgeon us over the head, attacking our senses
Politicians are masters at stirring our imagination about the future
Politicians exploit our discontent but cannot spark imagination about the future
Advertisers blanket us with messages and brand presence
questions.explain: In each case subtlety is sacrificed, hardening our imaginations. Greene says politicians stir discontent but have no sense of how to spark imagination, and advertising is the opposite of subtle.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, sort these into what Greene says deadens desire and what stimulates it.

items.t: Blanketing people with your message
Revealing all your likes and dislikes
Making yourself as familiar as possible
An air of mystery
Strategic absence
A vague, undefined message

questions.explain: Saturation and full self-exposure leave no room for imagination or fantasy; mystery, absence and vagueness give people space to project their desires.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, what mistake does Greene see people making in personal relationships today, and what is the result?
questions.a: Many believe others should simply desire them for who they are, so they reveal as much as they can about themselves and make themselves as familiar as possible. This leaves no room for imagination or fantasy, so the person they want loses interest, and they then rant online about the superficiality of men or the fecklessness of women.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, why does Greene say people have become more obvious and forthright?
options: Because human nature has changed in recent generations
Out of a deep moral calling to honesty
Out of increasing self-absorption and overall laziness
Because modern audiences reward modesty
questions.explain: Greene rejects the moral explanation: human nature does not change in a few generations, and simply being oneself takes no effort, so it has little effect on others.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Someone fills their dating profile with every detail of their life, tastes and needs, and matches soon lose interest. According to the Law of Covetousness, what best explains this?
options: They were not honest enough about their flaws
They chose people who were too self-absorbed
They left no room for imagination or fantasy
They seemed too mysterious and cold
questions.explain: Making yourself as familiar as possible leaves nothing to imagine, so interest stays paper thin. Greene urges going in the opposite direction from easy honesty toward desirability.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene urges readers to accept the moralism of the day that puts honesty ahead of desirability.
