questions.explain: Greene says not to swallow the easy moralism that urges honesty at the expense of desirability; with so few people mastering desirability, going the opposite way offers endless chances to shine.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: What does the title Become an Elusive Object of Desire signal about the Law of Covetousness?
options: That you should become the coveted one, using distance and mystery
That honesty is the surest way to be wanted
That you should learn to get whatever you covet from others
That desire is a weakness you must eliminate entirely
questions.explain: The title reverses the usual stance, as Chanel did: instead of coveting, you make yourself the object others desire, and elusive points to the strategic absence and mystery the chapter recommends.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, Greene says we are increasingly self-absorbed and points back to which earlier chapter?
options: Chapter 1, the Law of Irrationality
Chapter 3, the Law of Role-playing
Chapter 2, the Law of Narcissism
Chapter 4, the Law of Compulsive Behavior
questions.explain: He refers the reader to chapter 2 on narcissism: self-absorption makes it harder to get into the other person’s psychology and imagine what they want from us.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How do the Chanel story and the Keys to Human Nature section work together in the first half of the Law of Covetousness?
questions.a: The Chanel story shows the law in action: a restless coveter who reverses her perspective and becomes an object of desire through mystery, transgression and ubiquity. The Keys section then explains why this works, tracing the grass-is-always-greener syndrome to how the brain handles contrasts, danger and imagination, and argues that today’s culture of saturation and self-exposure has lost this art. That prepares the practical strategies that follow.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put the sections of the Law of Covetousness in the order they appear.
items: The Object of Desire
Keys to Human Nature
Strategies for Stimulating Desire
The Supreme Desire
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the Chanel story, to the explanation of covetousness, to practical strategies, and ends by turning the law inward on your own covetous desires.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each part of the Law of Covetousness to its role in the chapter.
pairs: States the law in brief: absence spurs desire
Tells how Coco Chanel became an object of desire
Explains the roots of the grass-is-always-greener syndrome
Gives practical ways to create objects of desire
Turns awareness on your own covetousness and reality
questions.explain: The chapter follows Greene’s usual pattern: a summary, a story, an explanation of human nature, strategies, and a closing ideal for the reader’s own life.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, what does Greene call the key to making the law work for you?
options: Reveal your true self fully so that people love you for who you are
Stay constantly visible so that people never have a chance to forget you
See yourself and your work as objects that others perceive in their own manner
Imitate whatever the public currently desires most and offer more of it
questions.explain: Greene says you must objectify yourself and what you produce: others project their own fantasies onto you, so seeing yourself as an object they perceive gives you power to alter those perceptions. Expecting to be loved for who you are is the mistake he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In Greene's strategy of knowing how and when to withdraw, what is the first form of withdrawal you must practice?
options: Long physical absences of several weeks from the very first meeting
A touch of coldness, as if you feel you could do without others
Leaking rumors about yourself that you neither confirm nor deny
Refusing ever to speak about your work or your opinions in public
questions.explain: Greene calls this touch of coldness the first form of withdrawal; it signals that you consider yourself worthy of respect. Physical absence comes later, only once you have engaged people's imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Why does Greene hold up movie stars as masters of withdrawal?
options: They turn their faces and presence into screens for others' fantasies
They surround themselves with rival admirers wherever they appear
They always reveal secrets about their private lives to the press
They avoid public appearances almost entirely for most of their careers
questions.explain: Movie stars keep their opinions and tastes ambiguous, so their faces and presence become screens upon which people project their own fantasies. The point is blankness that invites interpretation, not total absence.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How did Michael Jackson handle stories his publicists leaked to the press, such as his use of hyperbaric chambers to stay young?
options: He explained them in long interviews to control the message
He confirmed them to prove his openness with his fans
He neither confirmed nor denied them, and the press ran wild
He denied them firmly to protect his serious artistic image
questions.explain: Jackson would neither confirm nor deny such stories, so he sparked rumors without anything concrete. This strategic elusiveness made him an object of continual desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: According to Greene, why has the work of Shakespeare and Chekhov lasted so long and still seems fresh?
options: They limited how often their plays could be staged, keeping them scarce
They wrote explicit morals that every new generation still finds useful
They never judged or directed the audience, so each generation reads in what it wants
They wrote about forbidden subjects that were taboo in their own time
questions.explain: These dramatists described timeless elements of human nature without telling the audience what to feel or think, leaving their work open to each generation's interpretation. Greene offers this as the model for anything you produce.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: What does Greene's example of children losing interest in games with explicit rules illustrate?
options: The more active our imagination becomes, the greater the pleasure we get
People desire most what their siblings and friends already have
Physical absence creates a feeling of emptiness that deepens desire
Forbidden things become attractive the moment they are banned
questions.explain: Loosely structured games let children inject their own fantasies and so held their interest longer. Greene uses this to show that open-ended work gives pleasure by letting people do the interpreting.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Where does Greene trace the root of rivalries of desire?
options: In childhood, when parental attention seemed a zero-sum game among siblings
In modern advertising, which teaches us to want what others buy
In adolescence, when we first compete for romantic partners
In our evolutionary need to stay alert to hidden dangers
questions.explain: Greene says we first coveted our parents' attention and saw it as zero-sum: more for a sibling meant less for us. This competitive pattern of wanting what others want becomes lifelong.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In any negotiating situation, what does Greene advise as a way to create a rivalry of desire?
options: Tell the other side openly how many offers you have already received
Lower your price so that you seem more attractive than competitors
Bring in a third or fourth party to vie for your services
Withdraw from the talks entirely until the other side begs you to return
questions.explain: Bringing in other parties creates a bidding war and also lets people see that others covet you, which enhances your value. Openly boasting of offers would be the explicit signaling Greene says neutralizes the effect.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the strategy of using induction, what does Greene say John F. Kennedy did?
options: He leaked rumors about his private life that he never confirmed
He brought rival parties into his campaign to bid for his support
He set himself off against the conformity of the Eisenhower era
He kept his opinions blank so voters could project their fantasies
questions.explain: Kennedy contrasted himself with the stodgy 1950s, so voting for him meant youth and vigor. Greene says he played to the young's secret, slightly taboo desire to get rid of the father figure.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: What illicit desire does Greene say almost all people share, one that theater and film depend upon?
options: Rebellion against parents
Envy of the rich
Revenge
Voyeurism
questions.explain: Peeking into others' private lives violates taboos on privacy, yet everyone feels its pull. Greene suggests giving the impression that you are revealing secrets that should not really be shared.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: What does Greene mean by objectifying yourself and what you produce, and why does it give you power?
questions.a: Normally we are locked in our own thoughts and assume people should love us, and our work, for who we are and the effort we invested. But others see none of this; they project their own fantasies and preconceptions onto us, and our public work is an object divorced from our hopes. Seeing ourselves and our work as objects people perceive in their own way gives us the power to alter their perceptions and create objects of desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: According to Greene, what happens if people can read you too easily or you show your needs too visibly, and what should you do instead?
questions.a: If you are too obvious and show your needs too visibly, people unconsciously begin to disrespect you and over time lose interest. Instead your presence should have a touch of coldness, as if you could do without others, which signals that you consider yourself worthy of respect and heightens your value. You should also keep your opinions, values and tastes somewhat blank and ambiguous so people can read into you what they want.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Once you have engaged people's imagination, how does Greene say physical absence works on them?
questions.a: Once you have your hooks in people, you make yourself less available, letting a day or a week pass without your presence. This creates a feeling of emptiness and a touch of pain inside them. In your absence you occupy more and more of their mental space, so they come to want more of you, not less.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How does Greene advise presenting the work you produce, and why does this excite people?
questions.a: Leave the presentation and message relatively open-ended, allowing several interpretations, and never define exactly how people should take or use the work. When we interpret an ambiguous painting, film, joke or advertisement ourselves, we exercise our imagination, and the more active our imagination is, the greater the pleasure we derive. Your work should stimulate this pleasure to the maximum degree.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How should an individual signal that others have found them desirable, according to Greene's strategy of creating rivalries of desire?
questions.a: You should make it clear that you have a past, not so much of one that it inspires mistrust but enough to show that others have desired you. This must be indirect: people should hear stories of your past and see the attention you receive from others without your saying a word. Any bragging or explicit signaling neutralizes the effect.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Why does Greene say people grasp so greedily at objects that promise the unattainable, such as quick wealth or lost youth?
questions.a: Life is full of limits: success takes great effort, we are locked inside our own character, we cannot recover our youth, and every day brings us closer to death. An object offering a shortcut past these limits is coveted precisely because the goal is considered impossible. By the law of induction we can imagine these fantasies, and imagining them is almost like experiencing them, which sparks the desire to reach them.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene concludes his strategies by saying that it is not possession but desire that secretly impels people. What follows from this for anyone who wants to stay desirable?
questions.a: Possessing something always brings some disappointment and sparks the desire for something new, so people are really driven by fantasy and the pleasure of the chase. Once people get what they want or possess you, your value and their respect immediately begin to fall. You must therefore keep renewing your efforts: keep withdrawing, surprising and stimulating the chase, because as long as you do, you have the power.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene's first strategy for creating objects of desire, which he calls the essence of the art, is: Know how and when to ____.
questions.explain: Withdrawal covers a touch of coldness, ambiguity about who you are, and physical absence once people are hooked.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene says movie stars turn their faces and their presence into ____ upon which people can project their own fantasies.
questions.explain: By keeping their opinions and tastes ambiguous, stars let others read into them whatever they want.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene's second strategy for creating objects of desire is: Create ____ of desire.
questions.explain: Because human desire is social, showing that others want you or your work drives up its value.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: To get her object seen everywhere, Chanel even encouraged ____, which Greene cites as a way to spark a viral pull.
questions.explain: Greene says you can manage it so your object is seen or heard everywhere, even encouraging piracy if necessary, as Chanel did.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene's third strategy for creating objects of desire is: Use ____.
questions.explain: Induction is the mind's tendency to conjure the opposite of what it sees, so every no sparks a yes; you link your object to something slightly illicit or forbidden.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: When tastemakers call what you offer new and revolutionary, Greene says you are trafficking in the future, in ____.
questions.explain: Having important people talk up your object fans the flames until others do not want to be left out.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene says Chanel associated her object with something slightly illicit through her overt ____ appeal and flouting of gender roles.
questions.explain: Her androgynous appeal gave her work the transgressive edge that the strategy of induction calls for.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene suggest as ways to create the impression that others desire your object?
options: Explain in detail exactly how people should use the object
Keep the object rare and hidden from public view
Feed rumors or stories about the object through various media
Openly brag about how many people want it
Get important people or tastemakers to talk about it
questions.explain: Greene recommends spreading the object everywhere, feeding rumors and recruiting tastemakers so that word of mouth does the work. Explicit direction or bragging kills the effect, and hiding it works against the viral pull he wants.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these did Michael Jackson do, according to Greene, to make himself an object of continual desire?
options: He carefully managed how often he gave interviews and performances
He published statements explaining his message to fans
He appeared constantly on television to stay in the public eye
He never talked about the meaning of his lyrics
He spread out the releases of his albums
questions.explain: Jackson was aware of the danger of saturating the market, so he made the public hungry by spacing releases and appearances and leaving his lyrics unexplained. Constant exposure or explaining his message would have been the opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene cite as constraints that make people today yearn for the transgressive?
options: There are more laws than ever governing behavior
Political correctness intensified by our visibility on social media
Our every move is followed digitally
The disappearance of strict parents from family life
A decline in the number of people who travel abroad
questions.explain: Greene says we live in a world more regulated than ever, with digital tracking, more laws and intensified political correctness, and so we secretly yearn for what lies beyond these limits. The other two are not in his argument.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these belong to Greene's strategy of knowing how and when to withdraw?
options: Bringing a third party into a negotiation
A touch of coldness in your presence
Letting days or a week pass without your presence
Feeding stories about your object to the media
Blankness and ambiguity about your opinions and tastes
questions.explain: Coldness, ambiguity and physical absence are the forms of withdrawal. Bringing in third parties and feeding stories to the media belong to creating rivalries of desire.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that any bragging or explicit signaling that others desire you will neutralize the effect.
questions.explain: Greene wants people to hear stories of your past and see the attention you receive without your saying a word; explicit signaling neutralizes the effect.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: Greene says negative comments and controversy always damage an object's appeal, so they must be suppressed.
questions.explain: Greene says even negative comments or controversy will do the trick, sometimes better than praise, because they give the object a provocative and transgressive edge.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that once people get what they want or possess you, your value and their respect for you begin to rise.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: once people possess you, your value and their respect immediately begin to lower, so you must keep withdrawing and stimulating the chase.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put Greene's three main strategies for creating objects of desire in the order he presents them.
items: Know how and when to withdraw
Create rivalries of desire
Use induction
questions.explain: Greene starts with withdrawal, the essence of the art, then the social side of desire, and ends with induction and the pull of the forbidden and the unattainable.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put the forms of withdrawal in the order Greene says to use them.
items: A touch of coldness in your presence
Blankness and ambiguity about who you are
Physical absence once people are hooked
questions.explain: Coldness is the first form of withdrawal, ambiguity is added to it, and physical absence comes only once you sense you have engaged people's imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene's viral process for making an object seem desired in the order he describes them.
items: Let the object be seen or heard everywhere
Feed rumors or stories through various media
Get tastemakers to call it new and revolutionary
Enough people do not want to be left out
questions.explain: Wide exposure sparks a viral pull, rumors speed it up, tastemakers fan the flames, and finally the fear of being left out pulls in still more people.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each figure to the point Greene uses them to illustrate in his strategies for stimulating desire.
pairs: Strategic elusiveness: spaced releases, unexplained lyrics, rumors
Open-ended work that each generation can reinterpret
Bold contrast with a stodgy previous generation
Androgynous appeal and flouting of gender roles
questions.explain: Each figure illustrates one tactic: Jackson and the dramatists show withdrawal and open-endedness, while Kennedy and Chanel show the transgressive pull of induction.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each of Greene's strategies for stimulating desire to its core idea.
pairs: Know how and when to withdraw
Coldness, ambiguity and absence make people chase you
Seeing others desire something drives up its value
Link your object to the slightly illicit or the impossible
questions.explain: Withdrawal works on the imagination, rivalry on our social nature, and induction on our pull toward what is forbidden or unattainable.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each form of rivalry of desire to Greene's description.
pairs: Parents’ attention seen as a zero-sum game among siblings
Wants only partners already desired by a third party
Wants not just to join a new gimmick but to corner the market
Wants to share and participate in what others enjoy
questions.explain: Greene traces rivalry to competition for parental attention; in some adults it becomes an overt wish to take and triumph, in others a subtler wish to share the experience.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each limit of life to the fantasy Greene says a desired object can offer.
pairs: A quick path to wealth and success
Our youth and health are lost
We are locked inside our own character
Every day brings us closer to death
questions.explain: Greene advises dangling the prospect of grasping the unattainable; people grasp greedily at such things because they are considered impossible.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Sort these tactics into the two strategies Greene describes.
groups: Know how and when to withdraw

items.t: Keep a touch of coldness in your presence
Keep your tastes ambiguous
Let a week pass without your presence
Bring a third party into a negotiation
Let people see the attention you receive
Encourage piracy so the object is everywhere

questions.explain: Withdrawal tactics stir the imagination through distance and mystery; rivalry tactics show that others already want you or your object.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Sort these tactics into the strategy each belongs to.
groups: Know how and when to withdraw

items.t: Reveal secrets that should not really be shared
Contrast yourself with a stodgy older generation
Present your object as new, unfamiliar and exotic
Never define how people should use your work
Space out releases to keep the public hungry
Never explain the meaning of your lyrics

questions.explain: Induction plays on the pull of the forbidden and unconventional, while withdrawal leaves gaps that people fill with their own imagination.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In the Law of Covetousness, what does Greene say we really must covet in the end?
options: The admiration and desire of as many people as possible
A deeper relationship to reality
Freedom from every kind of restlessness and discontent
The most distant and exotic experiences life can offer
questions.explain: Greene says what we must covet is a deeper relationship to reality, which brings calmness, focus and practical powers. Restlessness itself is not condemned; it has a productive side when consciously controlled.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In The Supreme Desire, what does Greene say we should have done instead of a big career change driven by vague discontent?
options: Made an even bolder change to a completely unrelated field
Followed whichever new career others found most exciting
A gentler change to related work that adapts our existing skills
Stayed in the same job and suppressed all feelings of discontent
questions.explain: Greene says we would have done better to think more deeply about what did not click in the previous career and try a more gentle change, choosing related work that requires adapting our skills.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: According to Greene, why do dreams of exotic places, new entertainments and speculative books never lead to fulfillment?
options: They stir up more chimeras, and we cannot escape from ourselves
Other people will envy us for pursuing them
They are too expensive to sustain for very long
They are forbidden by society and so bring guilt
questions.explain: Greene says this ceaseless desire for what is most distant only stirs up more chimeras to pursue; if we travel, we merely drag our discontented frame of mind along with us.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: What does Greene say about spending life searching for the perfect partner, and what should we do instead?
questions.a: Greene says we can spend our life searching for the perfect man or woman and end up largely alone, because nobody is perfect. It is better to come to terms with the other person's flaws, accept them, or even find some charm in their weaknesses. Calming our covetous desires, we can then learn the arts of compromise and how to make a relationship work, which never come easily or naturally.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: In The Supreme Desire, what does Greene say we gain by turning our attention to ourselves and our work rather than to distant things?
questions.a: Greene says we have mysterious corners we can never fully understand, and by trying to know ourselves better we can take charge of our own nature instead of being a slave to it. Our work also has endless possibilities for improvement and innovation and endless challenges for the imagination. These nearest things make up our real, not virtual, world.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene says we must see within ourselves the grass-is-always-greener ____ at work and how it continually impels us to certain actions.
questions.explain: Greene's path toward awareness starts with recognizing this syndrome in ourselves, not just exploiting it in others.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Greene warns that our discontent is often merely ____: our desire for change is vague and a reflection of our boredom.
questions.explain: Chronic, vague discontent leads to a waste of precious time, unlike restlessness that is under conscious control.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as positive sides of feeling restless and discontented?
options: It frees us from the need to compromise in relationships
It enlarges our imagination as we consider other possibilities
It can motivate us to search for something better
It guarantees that each change we make will be the right one
questions.explain: Greene says restlessness can push us not to settle and can enlarge our imagination, and renewing it can keep us youthful. But it must be under conscious control; it guarantees nothing, and relationships still require compromise.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say a deeper relationship to reality will bring you?
options: Practical powers to alter what can be altered
Focus
Calmness
The endless thrill of novelty
Freedom from all of life's limits
questions.explain: Greene says coveting a deeper relationship to reality brings calmness, focus and practical powers to alter what it is possible to alter. Escaping all limits and chasing novelty are the fantasies he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if you travel to exotic places, you merely drag with you your own discontented frame of mind.
questions.explain: Greene uses this to show that the desire for what is most distant never leads to fulfillment, since in the end you cannot escape from yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: In The Supreme Desire, Greene advises modeling your desires on what others find exciting, since following trends keeps you youthful.
questions.explain: Greene advises the opposite: instead of chasing the latest trends and modeling our desires on others, we should get to know our own tastes and tell true needs from desires manufactured by advertisers or viral effects.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene's example of a career change driven by chronic discontent in order.
items: Feel unhappy with how your career is going
Make a big change requiring new skills and contacts
Enjoy the newness of it all
Feel discontent stirring again years later
questions.explain: Greene uses this cycle to show how vague, chronic discontent wastes precious time; the new path turns out not to be right either.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Match each covetous habit to the better approach Greene recommends in The Supreme Desire.
pairs: A gentle change to related work adapting your skills
Accepting their flaws and finding charm in weaknesses
Learning your own tastes and true wants
Waiting and hoping for something better
Making the most of what you have
questions.explain: In each case Greene urges calming covetous desires and turning toward the reality in front of us instead of an imagined better alternative.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene treats as productive or counterproductive covetousness.

items.t: Restlessness that pushes you not to settle
Considering other possibilities to enlarge imagination
Renewing youthful restlessness to keep the mind active
Chronic, vague discontent born of boredom
A lifelong search for the perfect partner
Modeling desires on viral trends

questions.explain: Greene says restlessness under conscious control is productive, while chronic discontent and borrowed desires waste precious time.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene calls distant objects that feed fantasies and the nearest reality worth coveting.

items.t: Dreams of traveling to exotic places
Entertainment that brings new fantasies
Books of empty speculation unrelated to daily life
The people in your own circle
The history of the place where you live
Your own work and its possibilities

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the turmoil of desiring what is most distant with absorbing the mind in what is nearest, which brings a deeper connection and real opportunities.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: When Greene's strategy of dangling the unattainable says we are locked inside our own character, which earlier chapter does he point the reader to?
options: See Through People's Masks (The Law of Role-playing)
Transform Self-love into Empathy (The Law of Narcissism)
Master Your Emotional Self (The Law of Irrationality)
Determine the Strength of People's Character (The Law of Compulsive Behavior)
questions.explain: The text refers the reader to chapter 4, the Law of Compulsive Behavior, which deals with character. That earlier chapter explains why we cannot simply become someone else, a limit the desired object promises to overcome.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How does The Supreme Desire change the direction of the Law of Covetousness after the Strategies for Stimulating Desire?
options: It retells the Chanel story from the opening in greater detail
It adds a fourth strategy for making others covet you
It turns from exploiting covetousness in others to controlling it in yourself
It argues that covetousness is a flaw we must eliminate completely
questions.explain: The strategies teach how to stimulate desire in others; the final section asks us to see the grass-is-always-greener syndrome in ourselves and covet a deeper relationship to reality. Greene keeps the positive side of restlessness, so he does not call for eliminating it.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: How does Greene's strategy Use induction build on the Keys to Human Nature section of the Law of Covetousness?
questions.a: The Keys section explains induction as the mind's habit of conjuring the opposite of what it sees, so that every taboo sparks a desire for the forbidden thing, and notes that what we imagine is experienced almost like reality. The strategy turns this into practice: associate your object with something slightly illicit, unconventional or impossible. Because constraints make us yearn for what lies beyond them, and imagining a shortcut is almost like experiencing it, people are pulled toward the object.

questions.unitTitle: Become an Elusive Object of Desire
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Covetousness closes with a passage from Arthur Schopenhauer advising that you let acquaintances feel now and then that you could dispense with their company, which echoes the strategy of withdrawal.
questions.explain: Schopenhauer says that occasionally mixing a grain of disdain into your treatment of people makes them value your friendship more, the same logic as Greene's touch of coldness.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In the statement of the Law of Shortsightedness, Greene says it is in the ____ part of your nature to be most impressed by what you can see and hear in the present.
questions.explain: The law opens by tying our fixation on the present (news, trends, the opinions of those around us) to our animal nature, the theme the whole chapter develops.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to the Law of Shortsightedness, what does our fixation on the present make us fall for?
options: Pessimistic forecasts that keep us from acting at all
Old traditions that no longer fit the present
Slow, patient plans that hide their true costs
Alluring schemes that promise quick results and easy money
questions.explain: The law says being most impressed by the present is what makes us fall for schemes promising quick results and easy money, which the South Sea story then illustrates.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Shortsightedness advise?
options: Never lose sight of your long-term goals
Copy the actions of the people around you
Avoid entangling yourself with people in a continual reactive mode
Measure people by the narrowness or breadth of their vision
Follow the latest news closely so you can react first
questions.explain: The law tells us to judge people by the breadth of their vision, avoid reactive people who will infect us with their energy, and keep our long-term goals in view. Chasing the latest news and copying others are the very habits it warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Shortsightedness warns that people who cannot see the consequences of their actions will infect you with their reactive energy.
questions.explain: The law says to avoid those in a continual reactive mode because “They will infect you with this energy.”

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In the Law of Shortsightedness, what does Greene say an elevated perspective gives you, and where must your eyes be?
questions.a: Your eyes must be on the larger trends that govern events, on what is not immediately visible, and never off your long-term goals. With an elevated perspective, Greene says, you will have the patience and clarity to reach almost any objective, rather than overreacting with exhilaration or panic as events swing one way or another.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put the ideas of the Law of Shortsightedness statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: We are most impressed by what we see and hear in the present
This makes us fall for quick-result schemes and overreact
Measure people by the narrowness or breadth of their vision
Keep your eyes on larger trends and long-term goals
An elevated perspective brings patience and clarity
questions.explain: The statement moves from the animal pull of the present, to its costs, to judging others by their vision, and ends with the remedy and its reward.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How does the order of the first two sections of Chapter 6 (Moments of Madness, then Keys to Human Nature) build the argument?
options: A list of warning signs comes first, then the story of the South Sea crash
A historical case of collective madness comes first, then the general explanation of why we are shortsighted
A theory of time is stated first and then tested on John Law
The ideal farsighted human is described first, then contrasted with Blunt
questions.explain: The chapter follows the book’s usual pattern: the South Sea story dramatizes shortsightedness, and the Keys section then explains the human nature behind it. The signs and the farsighted ideal come only in the later sections.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In the story of the South Sea Company, what news from Paris made John Blunt angry and envious in 1719?
options: The Bank of Paris had refused to lend money to England
The Mississippi Company of John Law was making Frenchmen of all classes fabulously wealthy
France had defeated England’s navy in a new war
The French king had seized the trade routes to South America
questions.explain: Blunt followed the boom fueled by John Law’s Mississippi Company, which was drawing investment capital from all over Europe and making ordinary Frenchmen rich.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: During the Mississippi Company boom in France, the word ____ was coined to refer to the newly rich.
questions.explain: Greene notes that the word millionaire was coined in these months for the nouveaux riches of the French boom.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why did John Blunt fear the success of the Mississippi Company for England?
options: It would drive up the price of English land
It would make Paris the finance capital of the world, a danger to England if war broke out again
It would end the South Sea Company’s monopoly on trade with India
It would force the English king to pay France’s war debts
questions.explain: Blunt reasoned that France would surpass Amsterdam and London as the finance capital of the world, newfound power that could only spell disaster for England, especially in another war.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each figure in the South Sea story to their role.
pairs: Lead director of the South Sea Company who devised the debt scheme
Scotsman who started the Mississippi Company in France
Investor and governor of the South Sea Company
Chancellor of the exchequer who presented the proposal to Parliament
Nephew of Blunt who took his own life after the crash
questions.explain: Each person is named in Greene’s account: Blunt designed the scheme, Law ran the French model, George I backed it, Aislabie carried it to Parliament, and Charles Blunt was among the suicides after the collapse.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Sort these into the traditional way of building wealth and the new joint-stock way, as Greene describes them in the South Sea story.

items.t: Expensive to manage
Highly taxable
Relatively easy to earn money
Profits were tax free
All the rage in London

questions.explain: Greene contrasts land, which was costly to manage and heavily taxed, with stock in joint-stock corporations, which earned money easily, tax free, and was all the rage in London.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: in its early years, the South Sea Company did a great deal of trading in South America before it became involved in government debt.
questions.explain: It was the reverse: the company was formed to manage part of the government’s debt in exchange for a trade monopoly, but over the years it did almost no trading and served as an informal bank for the government.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: John Blunt’s motto in life, which he felt his debt scheme lived up to, was “Think ____.”
questions.explain: Greene says Blunt’s motto had always been “Think big,” and that his October 1719 scheme seemed worthy of it.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Explain the basic mechanics of John Blunt’s South Sea scheme as he proposed it in 1719.
questions.a: The South Sea Company would pay the government a fee to take over its entire debt of £31 million, receiving an annual interest payment in exchange. It would then sell this debt as shares, one share equaling £100 of debt: government creditors could convert their IOUs into shares, and leftover shares would be sold to the public, starting at £100. If the price rose, buyers could cash out for a profit and the company could pay dividends, so that debt seemed to be transformed into wealth.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What was the value of the government debt that the South Sea Company proposed to take over?
options: £7 million
£1,000 million
£31 million
questions.explain: Blunt proposed to take over the whole debt from thirty years of wars with France and Spain, valued at £31 million.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these reasons made Blunt’s scheme attractive to English creditors and the public, according to Greene?
options: Parliament guaranteed that the price would never fall
The shares were backed by gold held in the Bank of England
It was a patriotic duty that would help cancel the debt
The company had an intriguing name and might begin trading in South American wealth
Shares could earn more than the government’s interest payments if the price rose
questions.explain: Greene lists the intriguing name and promise of South American trade, patriotic duty, and the chance of making more than the annual interest. Nothing backed the shares except the interest the government paid, which is why the scheme collapsed.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why was King George I so ready to throw his weight behind Blunt’s proposal despite not understanding it?
questions.a: George was one of the most unpopular English kings: a German by birth with a horrific accent and coarse manners, facing several coup attempts, and he desperately wanted to prove he could be a great king. He also had an almost allergic reaction to debt and hated the crushing debts incurred before his reign. Blunt promised to cancel the debt and bring prosperity, solving his two greatest problems at once, which seemed almost too good to be true.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why did opposition to the South Sea bill in Parliament slowly wither away in 1720?
options: The opponents were arrested for plotting a coup
Isaac Newton publicly endorsed the scheme
Advance shares had been virtually gifted to the wealthiest and most powerful men, including MPs
The king threatened to dissolve Parliament
questions.explain: Prominent members of Parliament had received advance shares and, sensing their own sure profits, gave their approval to the bill.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: The center of activity in the South Sea mania was an area of London known as ____ Alley, where almost all stocks were sold.
questions.explain: Greene describes the narrow streets around Exchange Alley clogged with traffic as the public rushed to buy South Sea shares.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put these events of the South Sea scheme in the order they happened.
items: Blunt hits on his debt scheme
Aislabie presents the proposal to Parliament
The bill passes and the king buys £100,000 of shares
Blunt is knighted
The Bubble Act is passed
Panic selling nearly brings down the Bank of England
questions.explain: The scheme was devised in October 1719, presented in January 1720, passed in April, Blunt was knighted in June, the Bubble Act came that summer, and the panic struck in September.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How did Sir Isaac Newton’s dealings in South Sea shares show the pull of shortsightedness, according to Greene?
questions.a: Newton invested £7,000 early, but after a few weeks his logical mind saw the holes in the scheme and he sold, doubling his money. Then he watched others making far larger sums and it bothered him, so he got back in around August, the worst possible time, and lost some £20,000. Greene concludes that even this paragon of rationality had lost the ability to think past the day.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How much did Sir Isaac Newton lose in the South Sea crash, according to Greene?
options: About £1,000
About £7,000
About £20,000
questions.explain: Newton lost some £20,000 after re-entering the scheme, and from then on the mere mention of finance or banks would make him ill.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these signs of the South Sea boom does Greene describe?
options: Farmers sending relatives to London with their life savings
Porters and footmen quitting and hiring porters and footmen of their own
A former maid sitting in a more expensive opera box than her old mistress
The king refusing to celebrate his birthday out of frugality
Merchants returning rich from South American mines
questions.explain: Greene describes servants hiring servants, a maid outspending her mistress at the opera, and farmers emptying their savings. The king in fact threw the most lavish party anyone had seen, and the company never traded in South America.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What was John Blunt trying to do by offering ever more generous credit terms on South Sea subscriptions?
options: Reduce the number of shares so the company could close quietly
Make sure only the wealthy could afford shares
Keep up demand and make people feel they might miss their one chance for wealth
Repay the government’s debt before the price rose
questions.explain: Greene says Blunt wanted to keep demand up and make people feel they might be missing out on their one chance for wealth, so he lent heavily and asked for small advances.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: By June 15, Blunt had set the South Sea subscription price at £____, with only 10 percent down.
questions.explain: The astronomical £1,000 price came with only 10 percent down and installments spread over four years, terms few could resist.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these problems did Blunt fail to foresee as the South Sea boom went on?
options: A rash of new speculative ventures competing for limited cash
People cashing out to buy land as a safe investment
Parliament refusing to pass the bill
King George selling all his shares in May
The French losing faith in the Mississippi venture
questions.explain: Greene lists the flood of new joint-stock ventures, the move into land (which Blunt himself was secretly making) and the collapse of confidence in France. The king and Parliament both backed the scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each of John Blunt’s South Sea share offers to its terms.
pairs: Sometimes only a 20 percent advance required
£1,000 a share with only 10 percent down
£1,000 again, with a 30 percent Christmas dividend promised
questions.explain: Greene shows Blunt using ever more generous credit to keep demand rising, ending with a desperate promise of huge dividends the company could not afford.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: To stop rampant speculation, Blunt worked with Parliament to pass the ____ Act of 1720, which banned joint stocks not authorized by royal charter.
questions.explain: The Bubble Act was meant to end competing speculation, but it trapped people’s money in outlawed ventures and forced them to sell South Sea shares.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How did the Bubble Act backfire on John Blunt?
questions.a: The act banned all joint stocks not authorized by royal charter, but thousands had poured their savings into these new businesses and now had no way of getting their money back. Their only recourse was to sell South Sea shares, while many who had bought on credit could no longer afford their installments and also tried to cash out. The share price began to fall, which was exactly what the scheme could not survive.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In late August, what did Blunt promise in his fourth money subscription in a desperate attempt to keep the scheme going?
options: A Christmas dividend of 30 percent followed by an annual dividend of 50 percent
A royal title for every large investor
Free land in the Louisiana territories
A refund of all money invested since June
questions.explain: Blunt offered even more generous terms plus a 30 percent Christmas dividend and a 50 percent annual dividend, which made some people wonder how a company with no trade could pay so much.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: by Greene’s account, the only tangible asset of the South Sea Company was its rich trade with South America.
questions.explain: The company had not traded for anything in South America; its only tangible asset was the interest the government paid it on its debt.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What is the irony Greene sees in John Blunt’s fate?
questions.a: Blunt had wanted to change the course of history and assure his fame for all time, and he did both. But he is remembered as the man who conjured up one of the most absurd and destructive schemes ever devised in the history of business, rather than as the savior of English finance he hoped to be.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the South Sea story, what obvious question never seemed to cross Blunt’s mind?
options: Whether the king would agree to the plan
How to persuade the public to buy shares
Whether the French would copy his scheme
How the price could keep rising if it was not based on any real assets
questions.explain: Everyone would win only while the price rose, yet nothing such as real trade supported it; once it fell, panic and a chain reaction of selling were inevitable.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Greene explains Blunt’s blindness by saying his mental ____ had shrunk until he could no longer look months down the road and consider consequences.
questions.explain: Mesmerized by France and by imagined wealth, Blunt focused only on the present; by the end his time frame had shrunk to a matter of days.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put the stages of John Blunt’s shrinking time frame in the order Greene traces them.
items: Struck by vivid stories of quick fortunes in France
Focused only on launching the scheme successfully
Luring more investors with generous credit to make the price rise faster
Hoping to keep the ship afloat another week
questions.explain: Greene shows Blunt’s horizon narrowing step by step, from fascination with France, to the launch, to ever riskier credit, and finally to a time frame of days.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What pattern does Greene see in Blunt’s attempts to fix the scheme as it progressed?
options: Each decision was left entirely to Parliament
Each fix slowly restored public trust
Each step was planned months in advance
Each solution incurred several new dangers
questions.explain: Greene notes that luring investors with credit made the scheme more precarious, “one solution incurring several new dangers,” and the Bubble Act and dividends carried even greater risks.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when people lose the connection between their actions and their consequences, they lose their hold on reality, and the further this goes the more it looks like madness.
questions.explain: This is Greene’s central diagnosis of the South Sea episode: the madness spread from Blunt to the king, Parliament and the nation.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Sort these into the two phases of Isaac Newton’s involvement in the South Sea scheme.

items.t: Saw the holes in the scheme after a week
Sold and doubled his money
Bothered by others making larger sums
Got back in by August
Lost some £20,000

questions.explain: Newton first used his logic to exit with a profit, then envy of others’ gains pulled him back in at the worst time, and he lost heavily.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why does Greene stress that the South Sea madness infected a nation renowned for its common sense?
options: To show that shortsightedness is contagious and can overcome even sensible people
To prove that Parliament planned the fraud from the start
To show that the English were less rational than the French
To argue that only kings are prone to financial madness
questions.explain: Once the English saw compatriots making money, the scheme had to be a success, and they too lost the ability to think a few months ahead, showing how contagious short-term thinking is.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to Greene, how does human reality differ from the present-bound world of animals, and what happens when we forget this?
questions.a: Human reality encompasses the past, since every event belongs to an endless chain of historical causation and any present problem has deep roots in it, and the future, since whatever we do has consequences stretching far ahead. When we limit our thinking to what our senses provide, we descend to the animal level and our reasoning is neutralized. We no longer see why things happen, imagine a successful scheme can only get better, and set off unintended consequences or disasters like the South Sea crash or the crash of 2008.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as part of the antidote to shortsightedness at the end of the South Sea story?
options: Detaching from the immediate rush of events
Looking at the wider context and possible ramifications of our actions
Acting quickly before opportunities disappear
Keeping our long-term goals in mind
Trusting the judgment of the crowd around us
questions.explain: Greene’s antidote is to step back, consider the wider context and ramifications, and keep long-term goals in mind. Rushing to act and following the crowd are what fed the South Sea mania.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Greene says that in raising our perspective we will often decide it is better to do ____, letting time go by to see what it reveals.
questions.explain: Elevating our perspective often means not reacting at all; if Blunt had waited a few months he would have seen Law’s scheme fall apart.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What does Greene say would have happened if John Blunt had simply waited a few months before launching his scheme?
options: He would have been forced out of the South Sea Company
He would have lost his chance to outdo the French forever
He would have made even more money from a later boom
He would have seen Law’s scheme falling apart, and England would have been spared ruin
questions.explain: Greene’s parenthesis makes the point that time would have revealed the truth: Law’s scheme collapsed, and waiting would have spared England the crash.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the sanity and balance of an elevated perspective come naturally to most people once they are calm.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: such sanity and balance “do not come naturally” but are powers acquired through great effort, representing the height of human wisdom.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What is the significance of the Isaac Newton quotation that closes the opening story of Chapter 6?
questions.a: Newton says, “I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.” Coming from the paragon of rationality who himself was swept into the South Sea scheme and lost heavily, it underlines Greene’s point that shortsighted madness can overcome even the most logical minds when they are caught in a collective fever.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put these South Sea share price milestones in the order they occurred.
items: Shares start at £100
Price passes £300 and then £400
Price passes £500
Subscription price set at £1,000
questions.explain: The shares began at £100, rose past £300 and £400 during the spring frenzy, passed £500, and by June 15 Blunt set the subscription at £1,000.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each figure from the South Sea story to what Greene says about them.
pairs: Invested £7,000, sold, then re-entered and lost heavily
Wrote that London’s religion and business were South Sea stock
Compared Exchange Alley to lunatics escaped from a madhouse
Deposited £100,000 for shares when the bill passed
questions.explain: Each detail comes from Greene’s account of the mania: Newton’s double move, Swift’s letter, the Dutch banker’s madhouse image, and the king’s public show of confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which recent event does Greene name alongside the South Sea crash as a disaster produced by shortsighted thinking?
options: The fall of the Roman Republic
The crash of 2008
The collapse of the Mississippi Company in 1800
The Great Fire of London
questions.explain: When we react to a small piece of the puzzle, Greene says, our actions lead to unintended consequences or disasters like the South Sea crash or the more recent crash of 2008.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In Greene’s everyday scenarios of impatience, sort each into what we did in the moment and what time later revealed.

items.t: We pressed someone who was not returning our calls
We rushed a strategy to fix a troubled project
We befriended a charming new person
The person was overwhelmed with work
The problem was not really so urgent
The new friend was a destructive sociopath

questions.explain: Greene’s scenarios show that in the moment we lack perspective, while the passage of time brings new information that makes the truth visible in retrospect.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Greene calls time the greatest teacher of them all, the revealer of ____.
questions.explain: Because the passage of time adds information and cools emotion, it reveals what was invisible to us in the moment.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Explain Greene’s mountain metaphor for how time changes our perspective.
questions.a: Locked in the present, we are like someone at the base of a mountain in a thick forest, seeing only what is in front of us and unable to get our bearings. The passage of time is like a slow ascent: our emotions fade, we see more of the landscape, and we realize our earlier view was distorted. At the top we have a clear panoramic view, just as with enough time we understand what really happened.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene’s mountain metaphor in order, from the present moment to full hindsight.
items: At the base, in a thick forest, we see only what is before us
Moving up, we see how our surroundings relate to the landscape
Higher, we realize our earlier view was slightly distorted
At the top, we have a clear panoramic view
questions.explain: The climb stands for the passage of time: each stage adds information and cools emotion until the lay of the land is clear.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: Greene concludes that because wisdom mostly comes in hindsight, there is no way to gain an expanded view in the present moment.
questions.explain: He says wisdom seems to come too late, but there is a way to manufacture the effect of time in the present, which he calls the farsighted perspective.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Greene calls the way we can manufacture the effect of time and gain an expanded view in the present the ____ perspective.
questions.explain: The farsighted perspective approximates what time does for us, by detaching and then deepening and widening what we consider.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put the four elements of the farsighted perspective in the order Greene sums them up.
items: Distance from the present
A deeper look at the source of problems
A wider perspective on the overall context
A look further into the future
questions.explain: Greene summarizes the process as distance, deeper, wider and further: first detaching from the heat of the moment, then digging into causes, context and consequences.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each element of Greene’s farsighted perspective to what it involves.
pairs: Calming our excitement or fear in the heat of the moment
Considering other explanations and motivations behind a problem
Looking at the overall context, not just what grabs attention
Imagining consequences and realigning around long-term goals
questions.explain: Greene’s process starts with detachment, then deepens our view of causes, widens it to the whole context, and extends it into the future.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What does Greene say is the first step of the farsighted process when facing a problem, conflict or exciting opportunity?
options: Grab the most obvious explanation and act on it
Ask others what they would do
Detach from the heat of the moment and calm our excitement or fear
Write down every possible long-term goal
questions.explain: The process begins by training ourselves to get distance and calm down; only then do we deepen and widen our perspective.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these does Greene include in deepening and widening our perspective on a problem?
options: Responding at once so the problem does not grow
Choosing the explanation that first grabbed us in the moment
Imagining the negative consequences of the strategies we contemplate
Adding the lessons we have learned about our own patterns of behavior
Considering other possible motivations for the people involved
questions.explain: Greene asks us to dig past the immediate explanation, imagine negative consequences, and add lessons about our own patterns. Seizing the first explanation and reacting at once are short-term habits.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, is the farsighted perspective so rare among humans?
questions.a: Short-term thinking is hardwired into us: for our early ancestors it paid to notice what was immediately dangerous or what offered food, so the brain evolved to home in on the most dramatic features rather than the full picture. This worked in a simple environment and the tribe but not in today’s complex world, where it makes us notice what stimulates our senses and emotions and miss the larger picture.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which pair does Greene use to show that we attend more to immediate pain than to greater but more distant dangers?
options: War and famine
Crime and poverty
Terrorism and global warming
Disease and old age
questions.explain: Terrorism feels immediate and gets more attention, while global warming seems abstract in the present even though Greene calls it the greater danger.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Sort these into what our short-term wiring makes us notice and what it makes us neglect, according to Greene.

items.t: Terrorism as an immediate pain
The immediate pleasure of a cigarette or a drink
The most dramatic features of an event
Global warming as a distant danger
The long-term harm of self-destructive habits
The full picture and context of an event

questions.explain: Our brains evolved to home in on immediate, dramatic pain and pleasure, so abstract future dangers and the wider context get far less attention than they deserve.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Greene warns that our short-term tendencies are an even greater threat as our attention ____ decrease because of technology.
questions.explain: In a complex world with dangers looming in the future, shrinking attention spans make our short-term wiring even more dangerous.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Sort these into how Greene describes giving in to our animal nature and realizing our potential as the thinking animal.

items.t: Simply reacting to what we see and hear
Swinging from exuberance to panic at each piece of dramatic news
Seeking maximum pleasure in the moment
Considering the consequences of what we do
Weighing our long-term priorities

questions.explain: Greene says we are defined by our relationship to time: reacting and chasing momentary pleasure is the primitive side, while weighing consequences and priorities realizes our true human potential.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each icon of farsighted wisdom to what Greene credits them with.
pairs: Saw into the hearts of men and foresaw the future
Taught us to be less foolish and more consequential in our thinking
Could predict every movement of the enemy
Exposed the effects of deep time on the evolution of living things
Investor whose power rests on his farsighted perspective
questions.explain: Greene offers these figures as historical models of the farsighted perspective whose example inspires others.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to Greene, what effect can one individual who embodies the farsighted perspective have on others?
options: They make others more anxious about the future
They usually provoke envy and are pushed aside
They make others aware of the larger picture, and we want to imitate them
They have no effect, since farsightedness cannot be taught
questions.explain: Just as short-term thinking is contagious, a farsighted person reveals a mind-set we recognize as superior and want to imitate.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What practical advice about the company we keep does Greene draw from the contagiousness of time frames?
questions.a: Because short-term thinking spreads to those around us, Greene advises avoiding deep contact, where possible, with people whose time frame is narrow and who are in continual react mode. Instead we should strive to associate with people who have an expanded awareness of time, since a farsighted person makes us aware of the larger picture and we tend to imitate them.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: the subtitle of Chapter 6, The Law of Shortsightedness, names the flaw the chapter warns against, while the title Elevate Your Perspective names the remedy.
questions.explain: Like other chapters, Chapter 6 pairs a command (raise your perspective, the farsighted view) with the law naming the human tendency it counters (living in the immediate present).

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which later section of Chapter 6 builds directly on the Keys section’s call to recognize short-term thinking in ourselves?
options: The Inner Athena
Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
The Generational Phenomenon
The Supreme Desire
questions.explain: After explaining why we are shortsighted, the chapter turns to the four signs of shortsightedness and strategies against them, then ends with The Farsighted Human. The other titles belong to other chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each Chapter 6 section to its role in the chapter’s argument.
pairs: The South Sea story as a case of collective shortsightedness
Why we are shortsighted and how the farsighted perspective works
Common signs of short-term thinking and how to counter them
The ideal of an elevated perspective
questions.explain: Chapter 6 moves from a dramatic example, to the underlying human nature, to practical signs and strategies, and ends with the ideal it holds up.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these themes from earlier chapters of the book resurface in the South Sea story of Chapter 6?
options: The fear of death and mortality
The pull of desire for what others seem to have
Envy, as Blunt reacts to French success and Newton to others’ gains
The masculine and feminine sides of personality
Emotions overwhelming rational judgment
questions.explain: Blunt’s envy, the craving to have what others are getting, and the swamping of reason by emotion echo the laws of irrationality and covetousness. Gender and death are the subjects of Chapters 12 and 18.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How does the opening of Chapter 6 connect the South Sea story to the chapter’s later sections?
questions.a: The South Sea story ends by naming the problem (we live in the moment like animals) and the antidote (detach and elevate our perspective, often by waiting). The Keys section then explains why time reveals reality and how we can manufacture its effect through the farsighted perspective, and points ahead to the need to recognize short-term thinking in ourselves, which the Four Signs section and The Farsighted Human go on to develop.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In Greene's example of unintended consequences in ancient Rome, what did the conspirators who killed Julius Caesar in 44 BC end up bringing about?
options: A civil war that Caesar's loyal generals quickly won for the Senate
A de facto monarchy established by Caesar's great-nephew Octavius
A restored Republic that lasted for several more centuries
A permanent dictatorship held by the leader of the conspirators
questions.explain: In the chaos after the killing, Octavius rose to power and ended the Republic for good. The conspirators produced exactly what they had tried to prevent, and it later emerged that Caesar had never meant to found a monarchy.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In Greene's account of British rule in nineteenth-century Delhi, why did the cobra population end up three times larger than before?
options: The authorities stopped clearing the streets once the program began
Resentful breeders released their cobras when the bounty program was canceled
British residents imported cobras to sell back to the authorities
The reward was too small to persuade anyone to hunt the snakes
questions.explain: Locals bred cobras to collect the bounty; when the government caught on and canceled it, the angry breeders set their snakes loose. The problem was not a lack of hunting but the perverse incentive the reward created.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what did the Eighteenth Amendment establishing Prohibition in the United States in 1920 actually do?
options: It increased alcohol consumption by a substantial amount
It had no measurable effect on drinking either way
It moved drinking from cities to the countryside
It stopped the spread of alcoholism within a decade
questions.explain: Prohibition was meant to stop the spread of alcoholism but ended up raising consumption substantially. Greene lists it beside Pearl Harbor as a notorious case of an action producing the opposite of its aim.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say the very success of Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941 guaranteed the opposite of its intended result?
options: It exhausted Japan's fuel supplies for the rest of the war
It led Japanese commanders to grow overconfident and careless
It persuaded Japan's allies to abandon their alliance with it
It shook Americans out of isolationism and fully mobilized the country
questions.explain: The attack aimed to bring America to its knees, but it ended American isolationism and mobilized the country's superior manpower and resources. Japan wrongly assumed Americans would not be willing to go to war if attacked.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the source of the age-old syndrome of unintended consequences?
options: Alarmed by something in the present, we grab a solution without considering context, roots or consequences
We think so long about a problem that the chance to act passes us by
We trust our first instincts too little and overthink simple problems
We follow expert advice that turns out to rest on outdated research
questions.explain: Greene says that because we mostly react instead of think, our actions rest on insufficient information. The danger is hasty, simple thinking, not overthinking or slowness.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say good intentions often lead to cobra effects?
options: Noble people are blinded by self-righteousness and ignore others' complex, often malevolent motives
Good intentions attract envy from rivals who then sabotage the plan
Idealists spend so long planning that circumstances change around them
Well-meaning people are usually too timid to take decisive action
questions.explain: Greene rejects the belief that good intentions should produce good results. People with the noblest intentions feel self-righteous and fail to consider how others, with their own motives, will respond.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: What does Greene advise any group or team to do to guard against unintended consequences?
options: Ban any plan that has not already worked for a rival
Put at least one skeptical, prudent person in charge of gaming out possible consequences
Act quickly before competitors can see what the group is doing
Let the most optimistic member make the final decision
questions.explain: Greene says this matters even more for large organizations, where much is at stake. He adds that you can never go too far in this process and the time and money spent will be well rewarded.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: According to Greene, which feeling is almost a sure sign that you have descended into tactical hell?
options: Feeling overwhelmed by the amount of information you must absorb
Feeling defensive and petty, with your spirit drawn downward
Feeling exhilarated by a string of quick wins
Feeling bored by work that no longer challenges you
questions.explain: Caught in circular battles, you are always reacting to others' moves and cannot raise your perspective. Drowning in information is instead the mark of being lost in trivia.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In Greene's account of ticker tape fever before the 1929 Wall Street crash, what drew many people to the stock market in a physical way?
options: The crowded trading floor, where they could watch fortunes being made
The newspaper headlines printed several times a day with share prices
The clicking sound of the ticker tape, which felt like the heartbeat of Wall Street
The bells that rang whenever a stock reached a new high
questions.explain: The ticker tape registered each change in a stock's price, and its clicking told listeners that someone was trading and making a fortune. Greene compares it to today's news feeds and their narcotic ping.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In the ticker tape fever section, how did Abraham Lincoln read the larger picture at the outbreak of the Civil War?
options: The North should prevail with more men and resources; the only danger was time
Neither side could win, so an early negotiated peace was best
The South would win unless the North struck an immediate blow
The war would be decided by foreign powers joining one side
questions.explain: Lincoln needed time to build the army and find the right generals, but also victories before public opinion turned. Calls for negotiation or an immediate crushing blow came from his critics, not from him.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: What did Abraham Lincoln do in late August 1864, when his reelection seemed doomed?
options: He publicly offered the South terms of peace
He drafted a letter of peace terms, then felt ashamed and hid it in a drawer
He replaced Grant with a general who promised faster victories
He postponed the election until the war was over
questions.explain: Feeling the weight of the pressure, Lincoln wrote out peace terms but that very night felt ashamed for losing his resolve. A week later Sherman marched into Atlanta and the doubts about him vanished.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
