questions.q: In Greene's account of the Spanish Armada of 1588, what did King Philip II fail to pay enough attention to?
options: The strength of England's shoreline defenses
The state of England's finances
The weather reports, the most critical factor of all
The loyalty of the English people to Queen Elizabeth
questions.explain: Philip read every report on the English navy, finances, defenses and support for Elizabeth, yet neglected the weather. Storms at sea would spell the destruction of the armada.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: A new manager reads every email and report, frets as much about the brand of office coffee as about losing the company's biggest client, and gets headaches from it all. Which of Greene's four signs of shortsightedness fits best?
options: Tactical hell
Ticker tape fever
Lost in trivia
Unintended consequences
questions.explain: Like Philip II with his palace toilets and his war with the Turks, everything seems equally important because the manager has lost a sense of priorities. Greene's remedy is a mental filtering system based on long-term goals, and delegating information gathering.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to The Farsighted Human, why do most of us instinctively recoil from thinking deeply about the future and the past?
options: We associate the passage of time with aging and moving closer to death
We are too busy with work to find the time for reflection
We believe the future is impossible to predict, so thinking about it is useless
We were taught as children to focus on the present moment
questions.explain: Greene says we associate the passage of time with something negative, and thinking about past or future reminds us of it. So we mostly live within the present, reacting to what we see and hear.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In The Farsighted Human, why does Greene say the changes we go through over the years create only the illusion of real change?
options: Other people never notice how much we have changed
We return to the same habits after every period of change
Memory distorts the past so that we seem unchanged
Our character was set in our earliest years and only becomes more apparent with age
questions.explain: Greene points back to chapter 4: our character, likes, dislikes and inclinations were set early, and the changes are on the surface. Feeling connected to who we were gives a strong sense of identity.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to The Farsighted Human, what does awareness that a current problem will hardly seem important a year from now do for you?
options: It convinces you that no problem is ever worth acting on
It makes you more dependent on others' advice
It makes you ignore the problem until it solves itself
It lowers your anxiety and helps you adjust your priorities
questions.explain: Greene says this expanded sense of time affects you deeply in the present. It calms you and helps you set priorities, without meaning you should never act.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Why does Greene place the Four Signs of Shortsightedness after the Keys to Human Nature in Chapter 6?
options: The Keys list the signs, and the next section gives historical proof of each one
The Keys explain the farsighted process, and the signs help readers spot their own shortsighted thinking, since awareness is key
The Keys tell the South Sea story, and the signs show how the bubble finally burst
The signs are an appendix of examples unrelated to the Keys
questions.explain: The Keys describe the farsighted process of distance, depth, width and looking further ahead. The Four Signs section opens by saying we are in denial about our shortsightedness and that only by seeing its signs can we combat them.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In the title of Chapter 6, Elevate Your Perspective, what does the word elevate correspond to in the chapter's central image?
options: Climbing a mountain to see the lay of the land that is hidden at its base
Rising above other people to judge them more harshly
Lifting one's mood above sadness and fear
Raising one's ambitions to think bigger, as John Blunt did
questions.explain: The Keys compare living in the present to standing at the base of a mountain in a thick forest; time, and the farsighted perspective, move us up the mountain. Blunt's motto of thinking big was ambition without perspective, the opposite of elevation.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say we are fooling ourselves when we imagine we engage in long-term thinking?
questions.a: Talking to people about their plans reveals how vague they are and how little deep thought goes into them; they are more like hopes and wishes. Under the pressure of immediate events, such weak goals are easily overwhelmed, and we end up improvising and reacting with insufficient information. We are in denial because it is hard to have perspective on our own decision-making.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Explain Greene's criticism of A-leads-to-B thinking and what he recommends instead.
questions.a: The conspirators thought killing Caesar would bring back the Republic, a simple and lazy chain of action A leading to result B. In reality any action sets off a limitless chain of reactions, drawing in other actors whose motives are hard to predict. Greene urges consequential thinking: imagine the permutations to several degrees, which at least reveals the obvious negative consequences and often shows the wisdom of waiting.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Why does Greene think nonconsequential thinking is growing worse in the modern world?
questions.a: The speed and ease of access to information gives people the illusion that they are informed and have thought deeply. He points to self-destructive wars such as the 2003 invasion of Iraq, attempts to shut down the American government for short-term gain, and growing financial bubbles. Related to this is a disconnect from history, as people view present events as if isolated in time.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Using Greene's example of the wife who wants more intimacy, explain how unintended consequences arise in everyday life.
questions.a: She asks her partner what he is thinking and what happened in his day, hoping to bring him closer. He reads this as intrusiveness and closes up, which makes her more suspicious and prying, which closes him up further. Her well-meant solution grows from reacting without thinking about how the other person will respond, so it feeds the very problem it was meant to solve.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: What steps does Greene recommend for getting out of tactical hell?
questions.a: Back out of the battles temporarily or permanently, especially if they are on several fronts, and let your ego calm down. Remind yourself that winning an argument gets you nowhere in the long run, and create a ladder of values and priorities. With detachment you can plot a strategic response to the battles that matter and walk away from circular ones, because strategists always prevail over tacticians.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: A friend checks her investment app every few minutes and wants to sell everything after one bad day. How would Greene's discussion of ticker tape fever explain her mistake?
questions.a: She is basing decisions on snapshots of the moment, which give the deceptive impression that what is revealed now will only grow more pronounced. Greene says the trends of the moment are embedded in larger trends over weeks and months, which reveal real strengths and weaknesses that are often the opposite of the microtrends. She should step back, like Lincoln, and judge by the larger picture rather than the day's swing.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: What three-part antidote to ticker tape fever does Greene draw from Lincoln's example?
questions.a: First develop patience, which grows with training and repetition, and slow things down by waiting a day or two before acting. Second, on important issues, have a clear sense of your long-term goals and how to reach them, including the relative strengths and weaknesses of the parties. Finally, have faith that time will prove you right and maintain your resolve against others' emotional overreactions.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say King Philip II, though extremely detail oriented, was never quite on top of anything?
questions.a: His appetite for paperwork gave him a feeling of control, yet he gave as much attention to palace toilets and clergy titles as to spy reports and national security. By the time he had assimilated enough information on the Turks or England, the situation had changed, and he misjudged both, leading to an eighteen-year war and the armada's destruction. The strain of reading impaired his thinking and contributed to Spain's irreversible decline.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to The Farsighted Human, what price do we pay for living mostly within the present?
questions.a: Repressing the thought of death and aging creates a continual underlying anxiety, because we are not coming to terms with reality. Continually reacting to events puts us on a roller coaster ride, up and down with each change in fortune. Life seems to pass so quickly in the rush of events, which adds still more to our anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: What does Greene mean by seeing time as an ally rather than an enemy?
questions.a: Each stage of life has its advantages; youth's are obvious, but age brings greater perspective, so aging does not frighten you. Death too becomes a friend, motivating you to make the most of each moment and giving you a sense of urgency. Time becomes your great teacher and master, revealing the weaknesses of your plans so that you are more careful with them.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How does a connection to your past self help you, according to The Farsighted Human?
questions.a: Feeling organically connected to who you were as a child gives you a strong sense of identity, since your character was set in your earliest years. Knowing what you like and who you are helps you maintain the self-love that resists deep narcissism and supports empathy. You also pay more attention to the mistakes and lessons of the past, which people locked in the present tend to repress.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: How does The Farsighted Human tie Chapter 6 to other chapters of the book?
questions.a: It draws on chapter 4 for the idea that character is set in our earliest years, giving a cohesive identity across time. It links that identity to the self-love that resists narcissism and builds empathy in chapter 2. It also points ahead to chapter 18, where death is treated as a friend that gives urgency, so the chapter's widened relationship to time connects to the book's closing law.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Greene says good intentions often lead to what are known as ____ effects, named after the bounty program in Delhi.
questions.explain: The term comes from the Delhi bounty that led locals to breed cobras. People with noble intentions, blinded by self-righteousness, overlook how others will respond.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In nineteenth-century Delhi, British authorities offered a reward for every dead ____ residents brought in.
questions.explain: The authorities thought there were too many venomous cobras in the streets. The bounty instead encouraged locals to breed them.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: To escape tactical hell, Greene advises you to create a ____ of values and priorities in your life.
questions.explain: The ladder reminds you of what really matters, so you can judge which battles are worth fighting. Many turn out to be a waste of energy and time.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Greene ends his discussion of tactical hell by saying that in life as in warfare, strategists will always prevail over ____.
questions.explain: Greene writes that “strategists will always prevail over tacticians.” Tactical hell traps you in reacting to others' moves instead of calculating moves toward your goals.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In the ticker tape fever section, Greene says patience is like a ____ that requires training and repetition to make it strong.
questions.explain: Lincoln was a supremely patient man, and Greene treats patience as something built by practice. Slowing down and waiting a day or two before acting is the training.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: As a remedy for being lost in trivia, Greene says you need a mental ____ system based on a scale of priorities and your long-term goals.
questions.explain: Knowing what you want to accomplish lets you weed out the essential from the nonessential. You do not have to know all the details and can delegate the information gathering.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: King Philip II fussed over the placement of ____ in his new palace at Escorial and their distance from the kitchen.
questions.explain: This trivial concern sat beside matters like a war with the Turks, showing that everything had come to seem equally important. Meanwhile he sometimes neglected important reports on spies and national security.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Philip II's war against the Turks, launched after he misjudged their army's weakness, lasted ____ years and bled Spain of money.
questions.explain: Philip pored over endless reports on the Turkish army and concluded it was weak. The war had no definitive resolution.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: In 1864 the doubts about Lincoln suddenly vanished for good when General ____ marched into Atlanta.
questions.explain: This came only a week after Lincoln had drafted and hidden his letter of peace terms. Lincoln's long-term reading of the war proved right.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: In The Farsighted Human, Greene says you should not see the passage of time as an enemy but rather as a great ____.
questions.explain: Your task is to widen your relationship to time and slow it down. Each stage of life has its advantages, and time becomes your teacher.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: According to The Farsighted Human, continually reacting to events in the present puts us on a ____ ride, up and down with each change in fortune.
questions.explain: This ride only adds to the anxiety already created by repressing thoughts of death and aging. An expanded relationship to time makes us calmer.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as signs of shortsightedness in Chapter 6?
options: Lost in trivia
Moments of madness
Sunk-cost blindness
Tactical hell
Herd panic
Ticker tape fever
questions.explain: The four signs are unintended consequences, tactical hell, ticker tape fever and being lost in trivia. Moments of Madness is the title of the chapter's opening story, not one of the signs.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Which of these examples does Greene use to illustrate unintended consequences?
options: Philip II's armada against England
The Eighteenth Amendment establishing Prohibition
The cobra bounty in British-ruled Delhi
Lincoln's defeat at Bull Run
Japan's surprise attack on Pearl Harbor
questions.explain: Each of these produced the opposite of its aim. The armada belongs to being lost in trivia, and Bull Run to Lincoln's story in ticker tape fever.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene recommend for escaping tactical hell?
options: Redouble your effort to prove your point
Think again about your long-term goals
Fight on every front at once to finish quickly
Back out of the battles temporarily or permanently
Win through your actions, not your words
questions.explain: Greene says winning an argument gets you nowhere in the long run and that you should walk away from circular battles. Pressing harder or fighting on more fronts only deepens the trap.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: During the Civil War, which of these did Lincoln's critics urge him to do as the war's fortunes swung?
options: Throw everything into an immediate blow to crush the South
Negotiate peace with the South
Make Robert E. Lee commander of the Union Army
Hand the conduct of the war to Congress
questions.explain: Horace Greeley twice urged negotiation, and others wanted an immediate crushing blow though the army was not ready. Both reactions were based on momentary swings of fortune.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say result from assimilating too much information when you are lost in trivia?
options: Sharper focus on what matters
Mental fatigue
Faster, bolder decisions
Feelings of helplessness
Confusion
questions.explain: The brain has its limits, and too much information makes everything seem equally important. Greene says realistic assessment becomes harder, not easier, for a brain submerged in trivia.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these describe the farsighted human's relationship to time, according to Greene?
options: Greater pleasure comes from reaching long-term goals than from passing ones
Aging is resisted as the great enemy
Long-term goals are concrete objectives with a mapped path
Present pleasures are renounced, like a monk's
A deep sense of connection to one's childhood
questions.explain: Greene says the farsighted person is not a monk and still enjoys the present. Aging does not frighten them, since each stage of life has its advantages.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Which of these chapters does The Farsighted Human explicitly point the reader to?
options: Chapter 7, on defensiveness
Chapter 4, on character
Chapter 18, on death
Chapter 10, on envy
Chapter 2, on narcissism and empathy
questions.explain: Greene cites chapter 18 when calling death your friend, chapter 4 when saying character is set early, and chapter 2 when linking self-love to empathy. He does not refer to the chapters on defensiveness or envy here.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that after Caesar's death it came out that he had never intended to create a monarchical system.
questions.explain: This is what made the conspiracy so self-defeating: they acted on insufficient information and brought about precisely the monarchy they feared.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Prohibition reduced alcohol consumption somewhat, though not enough to stop alcoholism.
questions.explain: Greene says Prohibition ended up increasing alcohol consumption by a substantial amount. It is one of his notorious examples of an action producing the opposite of its aim.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says it is always better to walk away from a circular battle, no matter how deeply you feel personally invested in it.
questions.explain: Feeling petty and frustrated has reverberating effects on your ability to think strategically. Your energy and spirit are important considerations.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says a single poll or stock price, taken in isolation, reveals the true strengths and weaknesses of a candidate or investment.
questions.explain: Greene says such snapshots tell us little in isolation; larger spans of time reveal strengths and weaknesses, often the opposite of the microtrends of the moment.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Philip II's years of study of England meant his 1588 armada was planned around the weather at sea.
questions.explain: Philip failed to pay enough attention to weather reports, the most critical factor of all. Storms at sea would spell the armada's destruction.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the farsighted person is not a monk but enjoys the present and its passing pleasures.
questions.explain: The farsighted human connects to the trends of the moment, yet derives even greater pleasure from reaching long-term goals and overcoming adversity.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: True or false: Greene says repressing the thought of death and aging frees us from anxiety so we can live in the present.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: such repression creates a continual underlying anxiety, because we are not coming to terms with reality.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Put the events of the Delhi cobra bounty in the order Greene tells them.
items: Authorities offer a reward for every dead cobra
Enterprising locals breed cobras for the bounty
The government catches on and cancels the program
Resentful breeders release their cobras
The cobra population ends up tripled
questions.explain: Each step follows from the incentive the last created. A move partway up the mountain would have shown that poor residents would breed cobras for money.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Put these Civil War moments from Greene's account of Lincoln in chronological order.
items: The Union defeat at Bull Run
Victories at Vicksburg and Gettysburg
Grant bogged down pursuing Lee as casualties mount
Lincoln drafts peace terms and hides the letter
Sherman marches into Atlanta
questions.explain: Public opinion swung with each event, from doubt to praise and back to panic. Lincoln held to his long-term reading of the war throughout.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Put Greene's four signs of shortsightedness in the order he presents them.
items: Unintended consequences
Tactical hell
Ticker tape fever
Lost in trivia
questions.explain: Greene numbers them one to four in this order, each followed by strategies to overcome it.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene's example of the wife seeking more intimacy in order.
items: She asks what he is thinking and how his day went
He reads this as intrusiveness and closes up
She becomes more suspicious and prying
He closes up even further
questions.explain: Her solution feeds the problem in a loop. Greene uses it as an everyday case of unintended consequences.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Put the three parts of Greene's Lincoln-inspired antidote to ticker tape fever in the order he gives them.
items: Develop patience and slow things down
Gain a clear sense of long-term goals and the parties' strengths
Keep faith that time will prove you right and maintain resolve
questions.explain: Greene calls patience first and foremost, then clarity about goals on important issues, and finally faith in time and resolve.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 6, Elevate Your Perspective, in order.
items: Moments of Madness
Keys to Human Nature
Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
The Farsighted Human
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the South Sea story, to the explanation of shortsightedness and the farsighted process, to its practical signs, and ends with the ideal relationship to time.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Match each example to the sign of shortsightedness Greene uses it to illustrate.
pairs: The clicking of the 1929 stock ticker
Marital spats about imposing a point of view
The Delhi bounty on dead cobras
questions.explain: Each sign has its icon or example. Philip II is called the icon of being lost in trivia.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Match each actor in Greene's examples of unintended consequences to what actually resulted.
pairs: The Republic permanently ended by Octavius
A substantial rise in alcohol consumption
A fully mobilized, no longer isolationist America
questions.explain: In every case the action produced the opposite of its aim. Greene says the thinking behind each was simple: action A leads to result B.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Match each everyday attempt at a solution to the unintended result Greene describes.
pairs: Telling a depressed person her life is not so bad
She feels guilty, worthless and more alone
A wife asking her partner about his day
questions.explain: These are less dramatic versions of the historical cases. Each solution is grabbed without thinking about the other person's response.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Match each figure in Greene's account of Lincoln's Civil War to his or her role.
pairs: Finished off the siege at Vicksburg
Praised Lincoln's inflexible purpose after an 1864 visit
questions.explain: Greeley was a famous editor swayed by the day's reports. Stowe wrote that Lincoln listened to all but kept one inflexible, honest purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each dimension of time to the farsighted human's relationship with it, as Greene describes.
pairs: Concrete objectives with a mapped path
A felt connection to one's childhood self
Enjoyed, but not at the cost of long-term goals
A friend that gives a sense of urgency
questions.explain: Greene asks you to widen your relationship to time in every direction. He calls time “your great teacher and master.”

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 6 to its main content.
pairs: John Blunt and the South Sea Company bubble
The mountain image and the farsighted perspective
Common patterns of short-term thinking and their remedies
Widening and slowing down one's relationship to time
questions.explain: The chapter opens with a story of madness, explains it, makes it recognizable in daily life, and ends with the ideal to aim for.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Sort these examples of unintended consequences in Greene's chapter into historical and everyday cases.

items.t: Killing Caesar to save the Republic
A bounty on cobras in Delhi
Prohibition in the United States
The attack on Pearl Harbor
Restricting a rebellious teenager
Cheering up a depressed person
A wife prying to gain intimacy

questions.explain: Greene moves from dramatic historical cases to less dramatic ones from daily life. The same syndrome of grabbing a solution without thinking is at work in both.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Sort these matters from Greene's account of King Philip II into those he attended to closely and those he neglected.

items.t: The placement of palace toilets
How clergy should be addressed and paid
Endless reports on the Turkish army
Every detail of the English navy
Important reports on spies and national security
Weather reports before the armada sailed

questions.explain: Philip took in information without considering priorities. His attention to trivia came at the cost of what mattered most.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Sort these responses during a long workplace dispute into shortsighted reactions and farsighted strategies, as Greene describes them in tactical hell.

items.t: Insisting on winning the argument
Staying in the fight because so much is already invested
Responding to every move the other side makes
Backing out to get detachment
Recalling long-term goals
Winning through actions rather than words

questions.explain: Greene says tactical hell is about asserting ego and proving you are right. The remedy is detachment and a return to long-term goals.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.section: Four Signs of Shortsightedness and Strategies to Overcome Them
questions.q: Sort these into the reactions of Lincoln's contemporaries and Lincoln's own approach during the Civil War.

items.t: Questioning the president's competency after Bull Run
Hailing him as a genius after Gettysburg
Demanding an immediate crushing blow
Gauging the two sides' relative strengths
Giving the army time to develop
Keeping one inflexible purpose

questions.explain: Everyone else swung with day-by-day reports of the war. Lincoln's long-term thinking let him see how the war would eventually trend.

questions.unitTitle: Elevate Your Perspective
questions.q: Sort these traits into those of someone living in a narrow time frame and those of the farsighted human.

items.t: Plans that are more like daydreams
Feeling one's younger self is a stranger
Living for immediate pleasures as distraction
Seeing aging as bringing greater perspective
Concrete long-term goals with a mapped path
Paying attention to lessons of the past

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the anxious, reactive present-dweller with someone whose relationship to time is wide and slow. The farsighted person is calmer and more realistic.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: According to the Law of Defensiveness, why do we become defensive and resistant when others try to persuade or change us?
options: We assume every persuader is lying to us
Giving in exposes our ignorance to rivals
Giving in challenges our need to feel autonomous
Changing our minds feels like betraying our group
questions.explain: The law says we want to feel independent, doing our own bidding, so yielding to persuasion threatens that sense of autonomy. The other reasons are not the ones Greene gives.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: In the statement of the Law of Defensiveness, what does Greene call “the ultimate lure”?
options: Making people feel that by doing what you want they are being noble and altruistic
Praising people’s intelligence openly in front of their peers and rivals
Offering people a reward larger than what they must give up to help you
Promising people a share of the influence you will gain from their help
questions.explain: The law tells us to make people feel noble and altruistic for doing what we want, which flatters their sense of their own goodness rather than buying or bribing them.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: The Law of Defensiveness says that to move people from their defensive positions, you must make it seem that what they are doing is of their own ____.
questions.explain: Because giving in challenges our need to feel autonomous, people must feel they are acting of their own free will, not being pushed.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Defensiveness says that creating a feeling of mutual warmth helps soften people’s resistance.
questions.explain: The law states that mutual warmth softens resistance and makes people want to help, the opposite of pressure or argument.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Defensiveness warn you never to do when trying to influence people?
options: Make people feel noble for helping you
Create a feeling of mutual warmth
Make people feel insecure about their intelligence
Attack people for their beliefs
Make people feel insecure about their goodness
questions.explain: The law says attacking beliefs or making people insecure about their intelligence or goodness only strengthens their defensiveness. Warmth and making them feel noble are what it recommends.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why does the Law of Defensiveness end by telling you to tame your own stubborn nature?
questions.a: Greene turns the law inward: we too are defensive and resistant, and our minds harden into closed positions. Learning to tame this stubbornness frees the mind and unleashes our creative powers. This prepares the chapter’s final turn from influencing others to keeping our own minds flexible.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the ideas of the Law of Defensiveness statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: Life is harsh and people competitive
We want to feel independent, so we resist persuasion
Make it seem people act of their own free will
Never attack people’s beliefs, intelligence or goodness
Make them feel noble and altruistic
Tame your own stubborn nature
questions.explain: The statement moves from the cause of defensiveness, to the remedy of preserving free will and warmth, to what to avoid, to the ultimate lure, and ends by turning the lesson on ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: In the Lyndon Johnson story, what did Senator Tom Connally offer the newly elected Johnson in December 1948?
options: Help getting a seat on the Foreign Relations Committee
Help getting a seat on the Agriculture Committee
A place on the Armed Services Committee
His own seat on the Appropriations Committee
questions.explain: Connally offered the Agriculture Committee, one of the least coveted, knowing Johnson would find it insulting, after Johnson had hinted at Appropriations, Finance or Foreign Relations.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Senator Tom Connally told Johnson that to get a prestigious committee seat he must wait, because influence in the Senate came through ____, which usually took twelve to twenty years.
questions.explain: Connally reminded Johnson that the game was played by seniority, which had taken Connally himself nearly twenty years.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the moments of Johnson’s December 1948 meeting with Tom Connally in order.
items: Johnson reveals he wants a seat on a prestigious committee
Connally offers to help him onto the Agriculture Committee
Connally says he can prove he is a friend of the farmer
Connally says that later he can render real public service
Word spreads that Johnson is a potential hothead
questions.explain: Connally answered Johnson’s premature ambition with a mock favor, twisted the knife with the farmer remark, pointed him to the long wait of seniority, and the story of the snub then spread.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why did Tom Connally decide to put Lyndon Johnson in his place at their first meeting in the Senate?
questions.a: Johnson revealed that he wanted a seat on one of the three most prestigious committees and hinted that Connally, as a fellow Texan, could help. Connally felt Johnson did not understand how the senatorial system worked, where power came only through years of seniority. So he humiliated him with an offer of the lowly Agriculture Committee.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: After the Connally meeting, what reputation did Johnson have among senators before they met him?
options: A loyal follower of the Old Bulls
A potential hothead to keep an eye on
A brilliant speaker who would dazzle the chamber
A dull, timid man with no ambition
questions.explain: Word spread that Johnson was a potential hothead, which made his polite, deferential manner a pleasant surprise that worked to his credit.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these describe how Johnson behaved when he visited senators in their offices in his first months?
options: He asked about the senator’s family or favorite sports team
He pressed senators to support his committee ambitions
He asked for advice on bills and Senate procedure
He waited patiently in the outer office, sometimes for an hour
He lectured senators on how the Senate should change
questions.explain: Johnson waited without complaint, showed he had done his homework on each senator’s life, and came to ask for advice. He was careful not to push his own ambitions or criticize the institution.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Johnson often introduced himself with the self-deprecating nickname “____ Lyndon,” since he had won his Senate seat by the slimmest of margins.
questions.explain: The joke name mocked his own narrow victory, making him seem humble rather than ambitious.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How could the senators tell that Johnson was truly paying attention to their advice?
options: He acted on it or repeated their words to others, crediting them
He took notes on everything they said in their offices
He wrote them letters summarizing what he had learned
He brought up their advice in speeches on the Senate floor
questions.explain: Greene says Johnson would act on their advice or repeat their very words to someone else, always crediting the senator who had spoken them.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What set Johnson apart from every other senator on the Senate floor in his early years?
options: He rarely appeared, preferring to work in senators’ offices
He sat with the Old Bulls and asked them to sponsor his bills
He spoke in nearly every debate to make his name known
He attended every session and sat at his desk taking copious notes
questions.explain: Greene says that, unlike any other member, Johnson attended every session and studied procedure closely, the posture of a serious student.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why did Johnson’s attention appeal so strongly to the older senators known as the Old Bulls?
questions.a: Although the Old Bulls held great authority through seniority, many felt insecure about their age and their physical and mental capacities, some being in their eighties. Johnson visited them often, intent on absorbing their wisdom. This confirmed their worth and calmed their insecurity, so they came to appreciate him.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each senator in the Johnson story to their description.
pairs: Fellow Texan who offered Johnson the Agriculture Committee
Powerful Georgia bachelor whom Johnson called the Old Master
Armed Services chairman facing a reelection campaign in 1950
Minnesota liberal shunned for his strident idealism
Democratic leader from Arizona who lost in the 1952 election
questions.explain: Each is named in Greene’s account: Connally snubbed Johnson, Russell became his mentor, Tydings yielded the subcommittee, Humphrey became his bridge to the liberals, and McFarland’s defeat opened the leadership post.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Johnson began to call Senator Richard Russell “the Old ____,” and would say he would remember each lesson.
questions.explain: By casting Russell as the Old Master and himself as the student, Johnson flattered Russell’s wisdom and authority.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why did Johnson make sure he got a seat on the Armed Services Committee?
options: It was the most prestigious committee open to a junior senator
It was where most northern liberals sat, including Humphrey
It gave him the most access to Russell, who was second in seniority there
It let him chair the Korean War subcommittee right away
questions.explain: The Interpretation explains that Johnson chose Armed Services because Russell sat on it, so their encounters could multiply. The subcommittee chairmanship came only later, through Russell.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these did Johnson share or seem to share with Richard Russell to deepen their bond?
options: A love of hunting in Georgia
A strong work ethic and conservative values
An interest in the Civil War
A shared passion for liberal causes like FDR’s New Deal
A love of baseball
questions.explain: Johnson cultivated interests in baseball and the Civil War and mirrored Russell’s conservative values and work ethic. The hunting party was in Texas, and liberal idealism was what he mirrored to Humphrey, not Russell.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Johnson had always loved baseball and the Civil War, which is why he and Russell got along so naturally.
questions.explain: The Interpretation reveals that Johnson had never liked baseball and did not care about the Civil War; he quickly learned to cultivate an interest in both to mirror Russell.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What did Russell call Johnson that he had never called any other junior senator over his long career?
options: The Old Master
A disciple
A son
A hothead
questions.explain: Johnson was the only junior senator Russell referred to as a disciple, showing how fully Johnson had become an extension of Russell’s own ambitions.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why was Richard Russell, in Greene’s reading, the perfect target for Johnson?
questions.a: Russell was very powerful, yet lonely: a bachelor who spent almost all his time, even Sundays, in his Senate office. He was a believer in a cause without any real disciples. Johnson could fill that gap by becoming his friend, his worshipping son and disciple, and having one key ally near the top of the hierarchy “could move mountains.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: In 1950, what did Johnson propose to Senator Millard Tydings about the new war-preparedness subcommittee?
options: That Johnson chair it only until Tydings’s reelection, then step aside
That Tydings give the chair to Russell, who would advise Johnson
That the subcommittee be dropped to avoid embarrassing the military
That the two of them chair it jointly for the rest of the war
questions.explain: Johnson offered to chair it only until the election so Tydings could focus on campaigning. Tydings declined until Russell spoke to him.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: The war-preparedness subcommittee mattered because a similar one during World War II had been chaired by Harry ____, who rose to power through it.
questions.explain: Greene notes that Truman became famous through that chairmanship, which is why the post was such a prize for publicity.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these were part of Johnson’s handling of the press as chairman of the war-preparedness subcommittee?
options: He attacked journalists who wrote critical stories
He held daily open briefings for all reporters
He gave information to a select group of powerful journalists
He surrounded its work with mystery and drama
He allowed no leaks of the subcommittee’s findings
questions.explain: Johnson guarded the findings, created an air of drama, and doled out information to favored journalists, making the rest fight for crumbs. He was sympathetic to reporters, not hostile, and far from open with all of them.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How did Johnson win Russell over further while working with him on the recall of General MacArthur in 1951?
questions.a: Russell saw that Johnson’s staff was larger and better organized than his own, which made him feel out of step with the times. Sensing this, Johnson helped Russell build his own modern staff and gave him full access to his legal and public relations teams. By doing a favor rather than asking for one, Johnson tightened their bond, and Russell soon said Johnson could be president.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What problem had stalled Hubert Humphrey’s rise in the Senate before Johnson approached him?
options: He refused to serve on any committee he considered unimportant
He believed so stridently in liberal causes that he alienated almost everyone
He was too close to the southern Democrats to win liberal support
He was so dull a speaker that no one noticed his talent
questions.explain: Humphrey criticized the Senate in his first speech, was relegated to the worst committees and shunned, all because his stridency alienated his colleagues.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these into Johnson’s reputation before he took his Senate seat and how he actually behaved as a new senator.
groups: His behavior as a new senator

items.t: Brash and opinionated
A bit pushy
A potential hothead
Polite and very deferential
Self-deprecating about his narrow win
Listening with childlike focus

questions.explain: Senators expected the impatient, pushy man of the House years and the Connally meeting; instead they met a humble, attentive student, and the contrast worked to his credit.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: On their subway ride, Johnson only praised Humphrey and avoided any criticism, so as not to raise his defenses.
questions.explain: Johnson first praised Humphrey effusively, then surprised him by criticizing him for spending so much time making speeches that nothing got done.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these into what Johnson did in his first subway talk with Humphrey and what came afterward in their relationship.
groups: Later, in Johnson’s office and beyond

items.t: Praised Humphrey as articulate and knowledgeable
Told him he spent too much time making speeches
Said he needed to be more pragmatic and fit in
Shared his vote-counting method
Told stories about FDR and compromise
Reintroduced him to southern senators

questions.explain: The subway ride mixed praise with blunt advice, and ended with an invitation for drinks. The deeper teaching, the FDR stories and the social rehabilitation followed over later visits.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these did Johnson teach or give Humphrey in their meetings?
options: Techniques for giving more stirring public speeches
The intricacies of Senate procedure
A seat on the Armed Services Committee
Knowledge of other senators’ psychological weaknesses
His method of counting votes
questions.explain: Johnson shared procedure, his vote-counting method and what he had observed of senators’ weaknesses. He actually wanted Humphrey to make fewer speeches, and Armed Services was Johnson’s own route to Russell.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why did Johnson tell Humphrey that he himself could never become president?
options: He preferred to hold power behind the scenes
He had made too many enemies among the Old Bulls
He lacked the speaking skills a president needs
The nation was not ready for a president from the South
questions.explain: Johnson claimed a southerner could not yet win the presidency, so he could instead help Humphrey get there, which fed Humphrey’s ambition.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What sealed the deal for Humphrey, making him devoted to Johnson?
questions.a: Johnson made Humphrey’s life easier within the Senate. He spoke to fellow southern Democrats about Humphrey’s intelligence and humor, then reintroduced him to them, and above all got Russell to change his mind. Humphrey’s loneliness faded, and he felt compelled to return the favor by winning northern liberals over to Johnson.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene says that once Humphrey began winning liberals over to him, Johnson’s influence began to spread like an invisible ____.
questions.explain: The image of an invisible gas conveys influence that spreads quietly without seeming aggressive or purposeful.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each person to the way Johnson made them feel, according to Greene’s reading.
pairs: That he had a worshipping son and disciple
That he was liked and truly presidential material
That their wisdom was still worth absorbing
That he could focus on winning his reelection
questions.explain: Johnson tailored validation to each target’s need: Russell’s loneliness, Humphrey’s ambition, the Old Bulls’ insecurity about age, and Tydings’s campaign worries.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: When the Democratic leadership opened up after the 1952 election, why did Russell decline the position himself?
options: He feared the Republicans would target the leader
He was too old and tired to lead the party
He had promised the post to Humphrey
He felt he could have more power operating behind the scenes
questions.explain: Russell declined because he could wield more power behind the scenes, and instead offered to make Johnson the leader.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: When Russell said Johnson should become leader, how did Johnson respond?
options: He refused, saying Humphrey deserved the post more
He acted surprised and agreed only if Russell would keep advising him
He asked Russell to secure the votes of the liberals first
He accepted at once and began planning his committee changes
questions.explain: Johnson feigned surprise and made it a condition that Russell remain the Old Master advising him, which flattered Russell and needed no further words.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What did Johnson want to change about committee assignments after becoming leader, and why?
questions.a: Committee positions had been based on seniority for decades, so chairmen were often men in their seventies and eighties with ideas rooted in the past. With Republicans planning to roll back FDR’s achievements, Johnson wanted the power to shift some committees and chairmanships. He would bring in fresh blood, such as John Kennedy and Humphrey, to give the party energy and a fresh face.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: When Johnson sought power over committee assignments, Russell warned him that he was dealing with the most sensitive thing in the Senate and was “playing with ____.”
questions.explain: Russell gave tacit approval but warned that touching the seniority system was explosive.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these did Johnson use to win over senators who resisted his committee changes?
options: Threatening publicly to strip their chairmanships
Appeals to pragmatism and defeating the Republicans
Rehearsing their counterarguments alone until he found the perfect approach
Arguing with vehemence to force the issue
Offering numerous quid pro quos
questions.explain: Johnson prepared obsessively, tailored arguments to each senator and traded favors. Greene stresses that he never argued with vehemence or tried to force the issue.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put these events of Johnson’s rise in the Senate in chronological order.
items: Connally offers him the Agriculture Committee
He becomes chairman of the war-preparedness subcommittee
He befriends Humphrey on a subway ride
He becomes Democratic leader with Russell’s help
He gains control of committee appointments
questions.explain: The meeting with Connally came in 1948, the subcommittee in 1950, the Humphrey ride in 1951, the leadership after the 1952 election, and the committee powers weeks later.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: After gaining control of committee appointments, Johnson became known as the ____ of the Senate.
questions.explain: Greene says he was now the undisputed Master of the Senate, and colleagues said “Let Lyndon do it.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put these stages of Johnson’s Senate campaign, as Greene interprets them, in order.
items: Rein in his aggression and assume the front of a humble student
Lower senators’ defenses so he no longer seems a threat
Win over one key ally near the top: Russell
Win over a bridge to the northern liberals: Humphrey
Couch his power grab as a benefit to the party
questions.explain: The Interpretation traces a step-by-step campaign: transform himself, disarm, gain Russell, extend to the liberals through Humphrey, then present the committee change as serving everyone.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: According to Greene, why did Johnson’s career get bogged down in the House of Representatives?
options: He was too young to be taken seriously by its leaders
He had no allies from Texas in the House
The House was big and complex, and he was weak with large groups
He had offended its leaders with a fiery first speech
questions.explain: Greene says the House was too large and complex; Johnson was not an exciting public speaker and was far more charming one on one.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Touring the Senate floor before his inauguration, Johnson had an epiphany: the Senate was smaller, more like a cozy ____ for gentlemen.
questions.explain: Seeing the Senate as a small club told Johnson he could work one on one and slowly accumulate influence.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How did Johnson have to transform himself to succeed in the Senate, according to Greene?
questions.a: He was naturally aggressive and impatient, so he had to rein this in, slow down and step back. He stopped talking so much and getting into heated arguments, letting others feel like the star of the show. He assumed the inoffensive front of a junior senator learning the ropes, behind which he could observe people without seeming ambitious.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why did Johnson adopt the front of a serious, somewhat dull student of procedure?
options: It made the press see him as a future president
It was his genuine nature, which the House had hidden
Behind it he could observe people without seeming ambitious or aggressive
It was the only way to win Connally’s approval
questions.explain: The front lowered defenses and let him gather knowledge of how the Senate worked and of senators’ insecurities, which he could later trade for influence.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Johnson never asked Russell for favors but quietly did favors for him instead.
questions.explain: Johnson was careful never to ask for favors; he helped Russell modernize his staff and merely insinuated his desires when he wanted something.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: When Johnson wanted something from Russell, such as the subcommittee chairmanship, he would ____ his desire rather than directly express it.
questions.explain: Insinuating rather than asking let Russell feel he was acting of his own will, so he came to see Johnson as an extension of his own ambitions.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: According to Greene, what three things were the way to Humphrey’s heart?
options: Make him feel liked, confirm he was presidential material, give him practical tools
Defend his ideals, attack his critics, give him Russell’s committee seat
Share his love of baseball, invite him to dinner, praise his staff
Flatter his speeches, fund his campaigns, introduce him to Truman
questions.explain: Greene calls the approach threefold: make him feel liked, confirm his belief in his presidential future, and give him the means to realize it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these tactics by which of Johnson’s two key allies Greene links them to most directly.

items.t: Cultivating a sudden interest in baseball
Weekly dinners cooked by Lady Bird
Helping him modernize his staff
Sharing an adoration of FDR
Saying a southerner could never be president
Restoring him to favor with southern senators

questions.explain: With Russell, Johnson mirrored conservative tastes and did practical favors; with Humphrey he posed as a closet liberal who idolized FDR and would help him rise.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How did Johnson present his demand for control over committee assignments so that senators would accept it?
questions.a: His demand was a radical change to the seniority system, but he carefully couched it as a way to strengthen the Democratic Party and help individual senators in their battles with Republicans. He made it seem in their own interest to hand over the power. Because he had never appeared aggressive, by the time they realized what had happened he controlled the chessboard.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: According to Greene’s lesson from the Johnson story, what is the usual mistake we make when trying to win influence?
options: We give others too much credit and appear weak
We ask for advice too often and seem incompetent
We do favors for people who never return them
We put all the attention on ourselves, our ideas and accomplishments
questions.explain: Greene says we normally try to charm with our own ideas and hype ourselves, which in a self-absorbed world makes others turn inward and think of their own interests.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene calls putting the focus on others, letting them do the talking and be the stars of the show, the royal ____ to influence and power.
questions.explain: The royal road runs in the opposite direction from self-promotion: validation of others lowers their defenses.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says your first move in winning influence should be to step back and assume a superior position so others seek your approval.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: your first move is to step back and assume an inferior position, subtly, for example by asking for advice.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put Greene’s steps for gaining influence, drawn from the Johnson story, in order.
items: Step back and assume an inferior position
Ask for their advice and wisdom
Do something small for them that saves time or effort
They reciprocate the favor
They keep working on your behalf
questions.explain: Greene describes a sequence: validation through deference and advice-seeking, then a small favor that starts a cycle of reciprocity that sustains itself.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do people keep helping you once they have done you a favor?
questions.a: In doing something for you, they have judged you worthy of it. To stop helping you would call into question their original judgment and their own intelligence, which people are very reluctant to do. So the cycle of favors continues on its own.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as normal but counterproductive ways we try to charm people?
options: Asking for favors in the belief that honesty is best
Promising great things about ourselves
Asking for their advice
Hyping our past accomplishments
Letting them be the stars of the show
questions.explain: Self-promotion and direct requests keep the attention on us. Asking advice and letting others shine are the opposite approach Greene recommends.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each term or phrase from the Johnson story to what it referred to.
pairs: Older senators who held authority through seniority
Johnson’s joke about his narrow election victory
Colleagues’ byword after he gained his new powers
The system by which senators waited years for key committees
questions.explain: These phrases mark the stages of the story: the seniority system and its Old Bulls, Johnson’s humble self-mockery, and the byword that showed his eventual mastery.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: In the passage from Jean de La Bruyère that closes the Johnson story, what is the true spirit of conversation?
options: Amusing others so that they seek out your company
Matching others’ wit so they treat you as an equal
Instructing others in what you know so they respect you
Bringing out the cleverness of others rather than showing off your own
questions.explain: La Bruyère says most people want to be praised and applauded more than instructed or amused, so the one who leaves pleased with his own wit is pleased with you.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these into the usual way of seeking influence and Greene’s royal road to influence.

items.t: Charm people with our own ideas
Hype our past accomplishments
Ask directly for favors
Let others do the talking
Ask for their advice
Treat their causes as the noblest

questions.explain: The usual way puts attention on ourselves and makes others turn inward; the royal road puts the focus on others, giving them rare validation that lowers their defenses.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each age to the moment in Johnson’s career Greene attaches to it.
pairs: Elected to the House of Representatives
Became the youngest party leader in the Senate
questions.explain: Greene notes Johnson entered the House at twenty-eight, the Senate at forty, and became leader at forty-four.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these into what was genuine in Johnson’s relationship with Russell and what was strategic, according to Greene.

items.t: He genuinely liked Russell
He was always in search of father figures
Choosing the Armed Services Committee
Their hallway encounters
Taking up baseball and the Civil War

questions.explain: Greene grants that Johnson liked Russell and sought father figures, but says his attention and approach were highly strategic, down to rarely accidental encounters and borrowed interests.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each of Humphrey’s traits or troubles to how Johnson played on it.
pairs: Inviting him for drinks and making him feel liked
Offering to help him reach the presidency
Posing as a closet liberal who idolized FDR too
Reintroducing him to the southern senators
questions.explain: Greene reads Humphrey as lonely, ambitious and in need of validation, and Johnson answered each need while mirroring his deepest values.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What is the main lesson Greene draws from the Johnson story about how influence is gained?
questions.a: Influence is gained in the opposite way from what we imagine. Instead of promoting ourselves, we must put the focus on others, letting them talk and treating their opinions and causes as worthy. Such validation is so rare that it lowers people’s defenses and opens their minds to ideas we insinuate, while our ambitions stay disguised.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, how does Greene say our defensive side first begins in early childhood?
options: As a habit of hiding our feelings from others
As a sense of personal physical space others should not violate
As resentment of parents who coerce us
As fear of being judged by teachers and peers
questions.explain: It starts as a sense of physical space, then expands into a feeling of personal dignity: no one should coerce or manipulate us.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say make our defenses grow more rigid as we get older?
options: People continually judge and appraise us
One noticeable failure can bring crippling negative judgments
We feel people are always trying to take our time, money, ideas or labor
We are too often praised and validated by others
We lose our sense of personal physical space
questions.explain: Constant scrutiny, the fear of failure’s consequences and the sense that others want to take from us make us wall ourselves off. Greene says we almost never get the validation we crave.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the stages in the growth of our defensive side in the order Greene describes them.
items: A sense of personal physical space in early childhood
A feeling of personal dignity that rejects coercion
Rigid walls against judgment and those who want things from us
Settled systems of defense by our twenties
questions.explain: Greene traces defensiveness from a physical sense of space, to dignity, to rigid walls built in response to judgment, fully formed by our twenties.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as moments when our inner walls come tumbling down?
options: Falling in love when the feeling is reciprocated
Receiving an order from a demanding boss
A night of revelry with friends
An inspiring public rally for a cause
Losing an argument to a clever opponent
questions.explain: In revelry, at a rally and in reciprocated love we feel accepted rather than judged. Being ordered or defeated would raise our defenses instead.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What do the night of revelry, the public rally and falling in love have in common, according to Greene?
questions.a: In each we feel inwardly secure, not judged but accepted by friends, the group or the loved one. We see a reflection of ourselves in others and feel validated at our core. No longer needing to turn inward and defensive, we can direct our minds outward to a cause, a new idea or another person’s happiness.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene says that creating a feeling of ____ is the golden key that will unlock people’s defenses.
questions.explain: The moments when our walls fall all share a feeling of being validated, so creating that feeling is the key to influence.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that pleading, cajoling and making people feel guilty can win lasting support, as long as we are persistent.
questions.explain: He says these methods mostly make people more defensive, and even when they work the support is thin, with an undercurrent of resentment.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What dangerous dynamic does Greene say can develop if we keep butting up against people’s resistance and getting nowhere?
questions.a: We feel mounting frustration at people’s apparent indifference, and it subtly infects our attitude. When we try to influence people they sense our neediness and insecurity; we try too hard to please and seem slightly desperate. This becomes a negative self-fulfilling dynamic that keeps us marginalized without our seeing why.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene calls the perception people have about their own character and worthiness, accurate or not, their ____.
questions.explain: The self-opinion is the chapter’s central concept; whether it is accurate does not matter, only how people perceive themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each nearly universal quality of people’s self-opinion to Greene’s example of it.
pairs: Telling ourselves we chose to obey a boss
A plumber proud of his knowledge of houses
A strict boss calling discipline tough love
questions.explain: Greene illustrates each universal: we reframe obedience as choice, take pride in our own form of intelligence, and recast harshness as acting for others’ good.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: According to Greene, what do people do if they feel consciously coerced, as when obeying a boss?
options: Accept it calmly as the price of security
Openly confront the boss until the pressure stops
Lose their sense of autonomy for good
Tell themselves they chose to obey, or resent it and secretly rebel
questions.explain: Because we need to assert our free will, we either reframe obedience as a choice or resent the force and find a way to rebel in secret.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says people who admit they are not smart in the conventional way will at least think they are cleverer than others.
questions.explain: People are never comfortable feeling gullible or unintelligent, so they find their own form of intelligence or cleverness.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Besides the three universals, what does Greene say people’s more personalized self-opinions serve to do?
options: Mark them as members of a group
Hide their true ambitions from rivals
Regulate their particular insecurities
Make them easier for others to influence
questions.explain: Self-opinions like being a free spirit or a rebel regulate specific insecurities, and each implies a feeling of superiority in that area.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each kind of self-opinion to what Greene says lies behind it.
pairs: The rebel who disdains all authority
A disappointing father figure, or bullying
A very distant mother and fears of abandonment
The person with a low self-opinion
Expecting bad things calms fears about never succeeding
questions.explain: Greene says such self-opinions often stem from developmental issues: the rebel cannot bear feeling inferior and the self-reliant type built an image of rugged independence, while a low self-opinion protects people from hoping for success.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these self-opinions into the nearly universal qualities Greene names and the more personalized self-opinions.

items.t: I am autonomous, acting of my own free will
I am intelligent in my own way
I am basically good and decent
I’m a free spirit, one of a kind
I am a rebel and disdain all authority
I am good-looking and I can depend on that

questions.explain: Greene says three qualities are nearly universal, while personalized self-opinions regulate particular insecurities and each implies superiority in one area.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he says our self-opinion is primary, and how does the example of the tough Christian show it?
questions.a: Our self-opinion determines much of our thinking and values, and we will not entertain ideas that clash with it. A person who sees himself as tough and self-reliant gravitates to hard-core, unforgiving ideas. If he is Christian, he reinterprets the doctrine to stress self-reliance, tough love and destroying enemies, so even his religion bends to his self-image.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the three possible outcomes when you try to convince someone in the order Greene presents them.
items: You challenge their self-opinion
You leave their self-opinion neutral
You actively confirm their self-opinion
questions.explain: Greene moves from the worst outcome, where walls go up, through the neutral one, to the best, where minds open.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these effects into what happens when you challenge someone’s self-opinion and when you confirm it.

items.t: They become more defensive and resistant
Walls go up that will never come down
They feel stupid, brainwashed or less than good
They relax and direct their attention outward
Their minds open to suggestion and insinuation
They feel they help you of their own free will

questions.explain: Challenging the self-opinion, even subtly, implies you know better and hardens resistance; confirming it meets a deep emotional need and opens the mind.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: When you leave someone’s self-opinion neutral, for instance by being calm and reasonable, what does Greene say happens?
options: They feel validated and want to return the favor
They stay resistant, but you have some room for rational arguments
They open up completely and become easy to influence
Their walls go up and never come down
questions.explain: In the neutral case people remain dubious, but you have not tightened them up, leaving some room to maneuver with reason.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that we can feel independent, intelligent and decent on our own, without needing anyone else to confirm it.
questions.explain: He says we can imagine these qualities, but only other people can truly confirm them for us, and we almost never get that validation.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these are part of the task Greene sets for instilling inner security in people?
options: Point out gently where their self-image is wrong
Mirror their values
Make them feel you appreciate their wisdom and experience
Get them to laugh along with you
Remain coolly neutral so they trust your reasoning
questions.explain: Mirroring, appreciating and sharing laughter build warmth and rapport. Correcting their self-image challenges it, and neutrality leaves them resistant.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene says confirming people’s self-opinion works best if the feelings are not completely faked, which is more likely if you exercise your ____.
questions.explain: By getting inside people’s perspective through empathy, you are likely to genuinely feel at least part of the liking and respect you show.
