questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How should you influence someone who has a low self-opinion, according to Greene?
options: Ignore their self-opinion and argue purely from facts
Work from within it, empathizing with the injustices and difficulties they face
Challenge their pessimism directly so they see it is wrong
Insist that they can easily better their lives by following you
questions.explain: Insisting they can easily improve clashes with their belief that they do not deserve good things, so they resist. Validating their struggles first gives you latitude for gentle corrections.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why do people with a low self-opinion often feel relieved when bad things happen to them?
questions.a: They expect bad things to happen, telling themselves they are not worthy of good things or have too many problems. When bad things do happen, they feel justified. In this way the low self-opinion serves to calm their insecurities about ever getting success in life.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What does Greene say is the greatest obstacle to developing powers of influence?
options: The difficulty of reading people’s self-opinions
A cultural prejudice against the very idea of influence
People’s natural immunity to flattery
Our own lack of empathy for people unlike us
questions.explain: Greene names the cultural belief that we should simply be honest and transparent, and that being strategic is ugly and manipulative.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene says the ____, people who insist on complete honesty, often become passive-aggressive, pouting and making others feel guilty to get what they want.
questions.explain: Because they cannot square their angelic self-opinion with their need for influence, they pursue it indirectly through guilt and pouting.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these arguments does Greene make against the cultural prejudice that influence is manipulative?
options: We cannot avoid trying to influence others, since all we do is read for intentions
Influence should be practiced openly so that no one is deceived
Influence lets us change people who have dangerous or antisocial ideas
Those who disdain influence are often lazy and justify it as a moral choice
Honesty always produces more influence than strategy in the long run
questions.explain: Greene says the game is unavoidable, that the moral stance often masks laziness, and that skill at influence is socially beneficial. He tells us to nod along with the call for honesty while inwardly rejecting it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that even our silence can be read by others as an attempt at influence.
questions.explain: Everything we do is examined for clues to our intentions; silence may be read as being upset or as polite listening meant to impress.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is better to be skillful at influence than to refuse to play the game?
questions.a: As social animals we cannot avoid constantly influencing others, whether we are conscious of it or not, so refusing only leaves us improvising or in denial. Being good at influence is also socially beneficial, because it lets us move people with dangerous or antisocial ideas. And becoming persuasive requires immersing ourselves in others’ perspectives, exercising our empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 7, Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion, signal about Greene’s approach to persuasion?
options: Break people’s self-image so they become open to new ideas
Overcome resistance by presenting stronger evidence than the other side
Lower defenses by validating how people see themselves, not by out-arguing them
Avoid resistant people and work only with those who agree
questions.explain: The title names the defensiveness problem and its cure: confirming the self-opinion, which the Keys section defines and the strategies later apply.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 7 in the order they appear.
items: The Influence Game
Keys to Human Nature
Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
The Flexible Mind—Self-strategies
questions.explain: Like other chapters, it opens with a story, explains the law, gives practical strategies, and ends by turning the law on the reader’s own mind.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How does the Lyndon Johnson story set up the Keys to Human Nature section of Chapter 7?
questions.a: The story shows a man who rose to dominate the Senate by validating others rather than promoting himself. Keys to Human Nature then explains why this worked: people have a self-opinion of being autonomous, intelligent and good, and confirming it lowers their defenses. Greene even points back to the story, saying we must turn our dynamic around “as Johnson did at the age of forty.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene sends the reader back to chapter 2 for more on getting inside other people’s perspective through empathy.
questions.explain: When he says confirming the self-opinion works best through genuine empathy, Greene refers to chapter 2, Transform Self-love into Empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each part of Chapter 7 to its role in the chapter’s argument.
pairs: States why we resist persuasion and the cure in brief
Shows a master of influence at work in the Senate
Explains the self-opinion and why confirming it works
Turns the lesson on our own stubbornness
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the compressed law, to an illustrative story, to the explanation, and finally to applying the law to ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: The fifth of Chapter 7’s Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader, which Keys to Human Nature points ahead to when it mentions reverse psychology, is to use people’s resistance and ____.
questions.explain: The forward reference points to the fifth strategy, which turns people’s resistance and stubbornness to your advantage.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of the chapter’s Five Strategies most directly restates the central idea of Keys to Human Nature?
options: Infect people with the proper mood
Allay their insecurities
Confirm their self-opinion
Transform yourself into a deep listener
questions.explain: Keys to Human Nature argues that actively confirming the self-opinion opens minds, which becomes the third strategy by name.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How does Johnson’s front as a dull student of procedure connect Chapter 7 to the earlier chapter on people’s masks?
questions.a: Chapter 3, See Through People’s Masks, deals with role-playing and impression management. In Chapter 7 Johnson consciously assumes the inoffensive front of a junior senator learning the ropes. Behind that mask he could observe and gain influence without seeming ambitious or aggressive, a practical use of impression management in the service of persuasion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why, according to Greene's first persuasion strategy, is our attention usually divided when someone else is talking?
options: We are trying too hard to show them that we are listening politely
We are more interested in our own thoughts, feelings and experiences than in theirs
We distrust what they say and are checking it for hidden motives
We are distracted by their body language and miss their actual words
questions.explain: Greene traces divided attention to self-absorption: we plan our next story or daydream because our own inner monologue interests us more. That is why simply telling people to talk less and listen more is useless advice.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Greene's advice on deep listening, how should you steer a conversation without making it feel like a job interview?
options: Talk about yourself first so they feel obliged to open up in return
Prepare a list of probing questions in advance and work through them
Stay completely silent so that they are forced to fill the gaps
Watch for the topics that make their eyes light up and guide the talk there
questions.explain: Greene warns against barraging people with questions. Instead you read nonverbal cues, notice which subjects animate them, and steer toward those so they become chatty without realizing it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What does Greene call the best way to signal how deeply you are listening to someone?
options: Taking notes so they can see their words matter to you
Asking a fresh question as soon as they finish each point
Occasionally mirroring what they said in your own words, filtered through your own experience
Agreeing out loud with everything they say as they say it
questions.explain: Eye contact and nodding help, but the strongest signal is to reflect their words back in your own terms. This shows absorption without turning the exchange into an interrogation.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Henry James's novel The Ambassadors, as Greene presents it, what gives Marie de Vionnet her hypnotic hold over Lambert Strether?
options: Her air of mystery and deliberate coldness toward him
Her open promises of reward for his help
Her indulgent, nonjudgmental spirit expressed more in manner than in words
Her sharp wit and dazzling conversation
questions.explain: She listens deeply, seems to understand him completely and treats him as a friend through her manner rather than anything she says. Strether calls this “a beautiful conscious mildness.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: According to Greene, what did Lyndon Johnson secretly do to keep control while he drank with the men he was influencing?
options: He let an aide do the real negotiating afterward
He only pretended to sip and never swallowed
He had his own drinks greatly watered down
He left the room whenever the talk turned serious
questions.explain: Alcohol flowed freely in Johnson's office, but his own drinks were heavily diluted. The bawdy jokes and shared pleasures built a club-like rapport while he stayed clear-headed.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: When Greene discusses the power of a simple touch on the hand or arm, what caution does he add?
options: Never touch someone who is senior to you in status
Touch only at the end of an encounter, never at its start
Only touch people you have already known for some time
Do not maintain eye contact while touching, or it takes on a sexual connotation
questions.explain: Gentle taps create visceral rapport and make people think well of you without knowing why. Holding eye contact at the same time risks giving the gesture a sexual meaning.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What does Greene suggest doing before meeting a person you will eventually ask a favor of?
options: Rehearse your request until it sounds completely natural
Imagine them in the best light, as generous and caring
Find out what they want from you so you can bargain
Remind yourself of the favors you have already done for them
questions.explain: Your expectations are communicated nonverbally, as with teachers whose high hopes raise pupils' grades. Picturing the person as generous and caring infects the meeting with that expectation.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Greene's reading of the Tom Sawyer fence episode, what was the first thing that got Ben Rogers to see the whitewashing differently?
options: Tom's offer to share the apples he would collect
Tom's absorbed attention to the task and his body language
Tom's warning that his aunt would punish anyone who refused
Tom's promise to go swimming with Ben once the job was done
questions.explain: Before saying anything, Tom acted deeply engrossed, which made Ben curious and led him to reinterpret the chore as interesting. Only then did Tom frame it as a rare test of skill.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which question does Greene say all your attempts at influence should follow, drawing on the Tom Sawyer story?
options: How can you show others how much you have already done for them?
How can you make the cost of refusing your request too high to bear?
How can you get others to perceive the favor you want as something they already desire?
How can you prove to others that your request is the most rational option?
questions.explain: Tom could have pleaded and got nowhere; instead his friends begged to do the job. Greene recommends framing a request as pleasurable, rare and something others want to do.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: How did Billy Wilder get Marlene Dietrich to accept the role in A Foreign Affair after she had refused it?
options: He pleaded with her as an old friend until she gave in
He rewrote the cabaret singer so she had no ties to the Nazis
He asked her to judge screen tests of two actresses he knew would be terrible
He offered her a far larger fee than any other actress
questions.explain: Wilder knew pleading would fail with someone so stubborn. Watching two actresses make a mockery of the part triggered Dietrich's competitive instinct, and she volunteered.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does Greene advise giving smaller rather than larger gifts when trying to win people over?
options: Small gifts are easier to give in public where others can see them
Small gifts cost less, so you can afford to give them to more people
Large gifts make it obvious you are buying loyalty and offend people's sense of independence
Large gifts make people expect even larger ones in the future
questions.explain: Large gifts can breed resentment or suspicion. With small ones, spread over time, people can tell themselves they deserve them and are not being bribed, which binds them more strongly.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What happens, according to Greene, when you disagree with someone and impose your contrary opinion?
options: They feel you are implying you know better and cling harder to their opinion
They usually concede once they hear a better argument
They respect you more for your honesty and directness
They become neutral and willing to weigh both sides
questions.explain: Imposing your view implies you have thought things through more rationally, which challenges their intelligence. Greene notes that “Winning arguments is rarely worth the effort.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: How does Greene describe putting Disraeli's advice to “allow him to confute you” into practice?
options: Agree with everything from the start so that no argument ever arises
Begin by disagreeing, even vehemently, then slowly come round to their point of view
Challenge them in public, then concede to them in private
Let them win small points while you win the main argument
questions.explain: By being slowly won over, you confirm both their intelligence and their powers of influence. They feel slightly superior, which leaves them doubly vulnerable to your own countermove.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: How did Beaumarchais protect The Marriage of Figaro from the major cuts demanded by Louis XVI's censors?
options: He secretly published the uncut text abroad before the cuts were made
He dedicated the play to the king to flatter him into withdrawing his objections
He agreed to every cut the censors wanted and restored them after the premiere
He let a tribunal of notables make small changes, and they then defended him against the censors
questions.explain: By accepting trivial suggestions such as a witticism or the color of the page's ribbon, he flattered his tribunal's egos and intelligence. Won over, they stridently defended him, and Louis had to back down.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Under the self-opinion quality of goodness, how does Greene advise framing what you ask people to do?
options: As part of a larger cause they can take part in
As a duty they owe because of their position
As a personal favor that only they are able to grant
As a fair trade in which both sides gain equally
questions.explain: People want to see themselves, and be seen, as good. Framing a purchase as helping the environment or keeping jobs local lets them feel better about themselves while doing what you want.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does Greene say you should not remind people of what you have done for them when you need a favor?
options: Gratitude reminds them of their helplessness and dependence, which they dislike
It suggests you expect them to pay you back with interest
It makes you look weak and dependent on their goodwill
They will only remember the favors that went badly
questions.explain: We like to feel independent, so gratitude is rare. Reminding them instead of the good they have done for you confirms their self-opinion as generous and makes them want to live up to it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the purpose of committing a relatively harmless faux pas and then asking for forgiveness?
options: It implies the other person's moral superiority and makes them vulnerable to suggestion
It shows you are honest enough to admit your mistakes openly
It lowers their expectations so that later you can impress them
It tests whether the person is loyal enough to forgive you
questions.explain: Asking forgiveness puts you in the inferior, one-down position. People love to occupy the morally superior role, and in it they become open to your suggestions.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Greene's basketball illustration of strategic flattery, when does praise of someone's skill work best?
options: When the person knows they are awful and expects to be teased
When the person is already known as the best player around
When the person is uncertain about the skill and suspects they may not be so bad
When the person has never played and has no opinion either way
questions.explain: Praising a skill someone knows they lack rings false. The target is the quality they feel unsure about, where reassurance can work wonders.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: According to Lord Chesterfield's letter, as quoted by Greene, how did skillful flatterers win over Cardinal Richelieu?
options: By praising his abilities as a statesman above all others
By comparing him favorably with the king
By pretending to criticize him so that he would trust them
By praising him as a poet, the vanity he was insecure about
questions.explain: Richelieu, the ablest statesman of his time, wanted to be thought the best poet too and envied Corneille. Flatterers mentioned his statecraft only in passing and gave their incense to his poetry.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is better to praise people for their effort rather than their talent?
options: Praising talent makes people lazy and less willing to work
Praising talent implies they were merely lucky to be born with it
Praise of effort can be given more often without seeming excessive
Effort is easier to observe than talent, so praise sounds more informed
questions.explain: Extolling talent carries a slight deprecation, as if their success were a gift of birth. Everyone likes to feel they earned their good fortune through hard work.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which therapist does Greene describe redirecting a husband's wish for a “friendly divorce” into a night that saved the marriage?
options: Milton Erickson
Richard Fisch
Paul Watzlawick
Hakuin
questions.explain: Erickson agreed with the husband and used his own word, friendly, to plan a final night of champagne and kisses. Watzlawick and Fisch co-wrote Change, the source of the suspended teenager case.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What does Greene say made children's minds so remarkably flexible and quick to learn?
options: Their lack of any self-opinion to protect
Their natural skepticism toward what adults told them
Their feelings of weakness and vulnerability, which motivated them to learn
Their freedom from the pressure of having to earn a living
questions.explain: Sensing their inferiority to older people, children were hungry to learn and open to influence. In adults, a creeping sense of superiority does the reverse and closes the mind.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why, in Greene's account, did Socrates conclude that the Oracle of Delphi was right to call him the wisest man in Athens?
options: He had never repeated conventional wisdom on any subject
He out-argued every eminent man he questioned
He knew more about politics, the arts and business than anyone
He was aware of his own ignorance while the others were not
questions.explain: The eminent people he questioned were sharp in their own fields but spouted conventional wisdom outside them. Socrates was wiser only because he knew the limits of what he knew.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What lesson does Greene draw from the Zen master Bassui turning up drunk to a talk?
options: Rules are merely guidelines, and we must violate them from time to time to show our freedom
Even masters are weak and need their monks' forgiveness
Strict rules are needed because everyone eventually breaks them
Teachers must test whether their students are paying attention
questions.explain: Bassui had posted thirty-three rules, many forbidding alcohol, and wanted to disconcert his literal-minded monks. He never apologized; the point was that “such rules are merely guidelines.”

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How does the Five Strategies section of Chapter 7 relate to the three universal qualities of self-opinion set out in the chapter's Keys to Human Nature?
options: Its third strategy works through autonomy, intelligence and goodness one by one
It ignores them and focuses only on body language
It argues that the three qualities apply only to people with low self-opinion
It replaces them with five new qualities that matter more in practice
questions.explain: The third strategy, confirm their self-opinion, explicitly asks the reader to recall the universal qualities and then gives tactics for autonomy, intelligence and goodness in turn.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does Greene say the usual advice to talk less and listen more is meaningless, and what does he propose instead?
questions.a: The advice fails as long as we still prefer our own internal monologue to what the other person is saying. The only solution is to become motivated to reverse this: we already know our own thoughts too well, whereas each person is “an undiscovered country full of surprises.” Seeing listening as a journey into another mind makes it amusing and a source of lessons in psychology.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What does Greene say you gain by letting the other person do most of the talking in a conversation?
questions.a: The more they talk, the more they reveal about their insecurities and unmet desires. You let them be the star of the show and draw out their wittier, more fun-loving side, so they come away feeling better about themselves. They grow relaxed in your presence and look forward to seeing you, which gives you great latitude to plant ideas and influence their behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does an attitude of complete indulgence work so well in infecting people with the proper mood?
questions.a: We are social animals and extremely susceptible to others' moods, so a relaxed, accepting mood has a mirror-like effect. Indulgence means not judging people but accepting them as they are, which replicates the ideal mother figure with her unconditional love. Expressed in looks and body language more than words, it has a hypnotic effect on men and women alike, as Marie de Vionnet shows with Strether.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: According to Greene, what three pieces of basic psychology did Tom Sawyer use to get his friends to whitewash the fence?
questions.a: First, his absorbed attention and body language made Ben reinterpret the chore as something interesting. Second, he framed it as a test of skill and intelligence and a rare opportunity, appealing to competitive boys. Third, once the boys saw others working, it became a group activity no one wanted to be left out of, so they begged for the job.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why does Greene say no attempt at influence can work if people feel coerced, and what follows for the persuader?
questions.a: Autonomy is one of the universal qualities of self-opinion: people must feel they act of their own free will. If they sense they are being coerced or manipulated, they resist. So the persuader must arrange things so that people choose what you want, or at least experience it as their choice, and the more deeply this impression is created the better the chances of success.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: How does asking people for advice help lower their defenses, according to Greene?
questions.a: Asking for advice implies that you respect their wisdom and experience, which flatters their intelligence. Beaumarchais showed this by letting a tribunal suggest small changes to The Marriage of Figaro. Lowering defenses on matters that are not very important gives you latitude to move people on more important matters.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Explain Greene's advice to remind people of the good things they have done for you rather than what you have done for them.
questions.a: Gratitude is rare because it reminds us of our helplessness and dependence, and we like to feel independent. Reminding people of their own past kindness confirms their self-opinion of being generous. Once reminded, they want to live up to that image and do yet another good deed.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What two steps does Greene recommend once you have identified someone's particular insecurities?
questions.a: First, be extra careful not to trigger them, because people have sensitive antennae for any word or gesture that casts doubt on their looks, popularity or whatever they are insecure about. Second, praise and flatter the very qualities they are most insecure about. We crave this even when we see through it, because we never feel secure in a world that judges us continually, and we tend to like people who seem to like us.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: How does Greene suggest flattering a powerful, Machiavellian person, and why?
questions.a: Such people may feel insecure about their moral qualities, but praising their clever manipulations could backfire, and obvious praise of their goodness would be too transparent since they know themselves too well. Instead, tell them how you have benefited from their advice and how their criticisms improved your performance. This appeals to their self-opinion of being tough yet fair, with a good heart under a gruff exterior.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: List some of Greene's techniques for making flattery seem realistic and unforced.
questions.a: Do not follow praise with a request; let some time pass, and even show a little coldness at first so you have room to warm up. Get third parties to pass on your compliments as if overheard, avoid lavish praise and absolutes, and mix in small criticisms that do not trigger insecurities. Choose qualities you genuinely admire and try to feel the emotions, because stiff body language or a fake smile gives you away.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: What does Greene mean by playing a game of mental judo with resistant, stubborn people?
questions.a: In judo you do not counter an opponent's moves with your own thrust; you encourage their aggressive energy so they fall on their own. With rebellious people, often marked by deep insecurity and low self-opinion, you do not fight their resistance but use their emotions, their language and their rigidity to channel them in a productive direction.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do rigid people become more stubborn when you push them to change, and how did Hakuin get around this with the miserly pawnbroker?
questions.a: Rigid opposition stems from a deep fear of change and its uncertainty, so urging change gives them something to react against and justifies their rigidity. Hakuin used the pawnbroker's own nature instead, offering to pay him for each prayer as a strict business deal. The miser got so absorbed in the chanting that he forgot to count, no longer wanted payment, and became a generous donor to the temple.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What does Greene see as the danger of the mind tightening with age, and what ideal does he propose?
questions.a: As the body tightens, so does the mind: our creeping sense of superiority closes us off to new ideas, just as childhood vulnerability once made us eager to learn. Greene thinks this closing of the mind is a greater danger than too little skepticism, for individuals and for the culture. The ideal is a mind that keeps the flexibility of youth together with the reasoning powers of the adult and stays open to others' influence.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: What is Nietzsche's strategy for getting to know something new, as Greene presents it?
questions.a: You entertain the new thing with all possible love, averting your eyes from what seems hostile or false, and give an author the longest start, wishing them to reach the goal like a spectator at a race. This temporary suspension of the critical pendulum lets you reach the heart of the thing, its “soul.” Reason can make its reservations afterward, and even hostile writing may then enrich your mind.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why does Greene urge us to keep ironic distance from our own self-opinion?
questions.a: We are not as free and autonomous as we believe: we conform to our groups, buy things because of subliminal influence and can be manipulated, and we are not as good as our idealized image, being often self-absorbed. Awareness of this means we no longer need others to validate us. We can then work at becoming truly independent and concerned with others' welfare instead of clinging to the illusion of self-opinion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: How does Greene use the comparison between the seventeenth and the twenty-fifth centuries to argue for humility about our ideas?
questions.a: We scoff at the superstitious and irrational ideas people held in the seventeenth century, yet people in the twenty-fifth century will scoff at ours. Our knowledge is limited despite science, and our ideas are conditioned by the prejudices of our parents, culture and historical period, and by the mind's growing rigidity. A little more humility would make us more curious and open to a wider range of ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Why does Greene end Chapter 7 with a section on the flexible mind after teaching strategies for overcoming other people's resistance?
questions.a: The same defensiveness that makes others resist our ideas afflicts us too, though we are largely unaware of it, and it limits our creative powers. Just as we use strategies to melt people's resistance, we must apply them to ourselves to soften our rigid mental patterns. This fulfills the chapter's opening law, which ends by urging us to tame our own stubborn nature and free the mind from its defensive and closed positions.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene's first strategy for becoming a master persuader is to transform yourself into a deep ____.
questions.explain: Deep listening reverses our natural preference for our own inner monologue. It lets the other person be the star and reveals their insecurities and desires.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Greene's deep-listening advice, the other person may in the end do 80 ____ of the talking while still feeling it was a lively exchange.
questions.explain: You must not make the strategic purpose of your listening obvious. The exchange should feel lively even though they do most of the talking.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene's second persuasion strategy is to infect people with the proper ____.
questions.explain: Because we are social animals, we are highly susceptible to the moods of others. A relaxed, pleasurable mood in you communicates itself to them.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene says teachers who expect greater things from their ____ can raise their work and grades without saying anything.
questions.explain: This illustrates that your expectations of people are communicated nonverbally. Feeling excited about meeting someone conveys itself powerfully.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene's third persuasion strategy is to confirm people's ____.
questions.explain: This strategy draws on the three universal qualities of self-opinion described earlier in the chapter: autonomy, intelligence and goodness.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: In Billy Wilder's 1948 film A Foreign Affair, the role he wanted Marlene Dietrich to play was a German ____ singer with suspicious ties to Nazis.
questions.explain: The character, Erika von Shluetow, was distasteful to Dietrich because of her intense dislike of the Nazis. Wilder overcame this by appealing to her competitive instinct.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene quotes Benjamin Disraeli: if you wish to win a man's heart, allow him to ____ you.
questions.explain: Letting someone argue you round confirms both their intelligence and their powers of influence, making them feel slightly superior.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene notes it is better, for instance, to call someone a team ____ than an employee.
questions.explain: Under the quality of goodness, Greene stresses attention to words and labels, because they shape how people see themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: By asking for forgiveness after a minor faux pas, you put yourself in the inferior, ____ position.
questions.explain: Asking forgiveness implies the other person's moral superiority, a position people love to occupy and one that leaves them open to suggestion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene's fourth persuasion strategy is to allay people's ____.
questions.explain: Everyone has particular insecurities, about looks, creative powers, status or popularity. You identify them, avoid triggering them, and flatter those qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene says it is always better to praise people for their ____, not their talent.
questions.explain: Praising talent implies they were lucky to be born with natural skill. People like to feel they earned their fortune through hard work.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: With your superiors, Greene says, rather than flattering them it is best simply to agree with their opinions and validate their ____.
questions.explain: Flattering a boss is too transparent. With equals you have more room to flatter.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Greene compares the fifth strategy, using people's resistance and stubbornness, to a game of mental ____.
questions.explain: In judo you encourage an opponent's aggressive energy so that they fall on their own, rather than countering with a thrust of your own.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Socrates's motto, as Greene quotes it, was that the ____ life is not worth living.
questions.explain: Socrates examined and reexamined his own ideas over and over, seeing their inadequacies. This supreme openness of mind fascinated the youth of Athens.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Greene advises seeing the ideas and opinions you hold as toys or ____ blocks that you play with.
questions.explain: Some ideas you keep and others you knock down, but your spirit stays flexible and playful rather than rigidly attached to them.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list among the five strategies for becoming a master persuader?
options: Allay their insecurities
Use people's resistance and stubbornness
Transform yourself into a deep listener
Win every argument decisively
Remind people of what they owe you
questions.explain: The five are deep listening, infecting people with the proper mood, confirming their self-opinion, allaying their insecurities and using their resistance. Greene warns against both winning arguments and stirring gratitude.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these topics does Greene say almost everyone likes to talk about, making them useful when you are drawing people out?
options: The ins and outs of their work
Their family
Their childhood
Their debts
Their medical worries
questions.explain: Greene names childhood, family, work and some cause dear to them. Guiding the talk toward such topics makes people chatty without realizing it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these framings does Greene say will generally make people perceive a favor as something they already desire?
options: Something other people want to do
A rare opportunity
Something pleasurable
A painful duty
A way to repay a debt
questions.explain: Drawing on Tom Sawyer, Greene recommends framing the request as pleasurable, rare and popular. Framing it as duty or repayment works against people's sense of autonomy.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these are among the ways Greene says to use people's resistance and stubbornness?
options: Use their emotions
Use their rigidity
Use their fear of punishment
Use their guilt
Use their language
questions.explain: Greene's mental judo works through people's emotions, their language and their rigidity. Guilt is a tactic he associates with defensive, failed attempts at influence.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise when flattering someone?
options: Follow your praise straight away with your request
Choose qualities you actually admire if possible
Mix in some small criticisms to make the praise realistic
Get third parties to pass along your compliments
Use absolutes so the praise is unmistakable
questions.explain: Greene warns never to follow praise with a request and never to be too lavish or use absolutes. Overheard compliments, small criticisms and genuine admiration all make flattery seem sincere.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as insecurities that people commonly have?
options: Their popularity
Their looks
Their creative powers
Their cooking
Their handwriting
questions.explain: Greene's list includes looks, creative powers, masculinity, power status, uniqueness and popularity. You uncover a person's particular ones through the conversations you draw them into.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Which of these did Beaumarchais's tribunal contribute to The Marriage of Figaro, according to the account Greene quotes?
options: The color of the little page's ribbon
A witticism suggested by M. de Breteuil
A dedication to Louis XVI
A new ending in which the count is punished
questions.explain: These were small changes Beaumarchais happily accepted, saying the witticism would save the fourth act; the ribbon color even became fashionable. He refused the larger changes the censors later demanded.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say we must admit about ourselves when we keep ironic distance from our self-opinion?
options: We are as good as our idealized image of ourselves
We conform to the opinions of the groups we belong to
We are immune to advertising and subliminal influence
We can be manipulated
We can be quite self-absorbed
questions.explain: Greene says we are neither as autonomous nor as good as we like to believe. We buy products because of subliminal influence and are often obsessed with our own agenda.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these fields did the eminent people Socrates questioned come from, in Greene's account?
options: Medicine
The arts
Business
Politics
The army
questions.explain: Greene names politics, the arts and business. Each person seemed intelligent within their field but spouted conventional wisdom outside it.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Which of these earlier chapters does Chapter 7 point the reader back to?
options: Chapter 3, where the therapist Milton Erickson was introduced
Chapter 1, for the list of cognitive biases
Chapter 5, for the role of rare opportunities in desire
Chapter 2, for more on getting inside another's perspective through empathy
questions.explain: Chapter 7 refers to chapter 2 when urging empathy so that confirming self-opinion feels genuine, and marks Erickson with a reference to chapter 3. It makes no such cross-reference to the other chapters named.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the strategic purpose behind your deep listening should be made obvious so the other person feels respected.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: you cannot make the purpose too obvious. The other person must feel it is a lively exchange.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Marie de Vionnet's indulgent attitude replicates the ideal mother figure, unconditional in her love.
questions.explain: Greene adds that such indulgence is expressed more in looks and body language than in words, and works on men and women alike.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Billy Wilder persuaded Marlene Dietrich by pleading with her as an old friend.
questions.explain: Wilder did not plead, which would have been futile given her stubbornness. He asked her to judge screen tests of two terrible actresses, provoking her competitiveness.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that once Beaumarchais's tribunal had made their small changes, he also gave in to the larger changes requested by Louis's censors.
questions.explain: On the larger changes he did not relent. His tribunal, won over by having their small suggestions adopted, defended him so strongly that the king backed down.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises showing even a little coldness in your first encounter or two before you begin to flatter someone.
questions.explain: Appearing too ingratiating early is a giveaway. A little coldness leaves room to warm up, after which a few flattering words can melt resistance.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when people ask your opinion of their work or looks, they want the truth, so you should give it to them plainly.
questions.explain: Greene says “They do not want the truth; they want support and confirmation” given as realistically as possible.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: True or false: In the case from the book Change, the suspended teenager threw himself into his homework because he wanted to embarrass the principal.
questions.explain: The therapist had the mother say the principal believed the boy would fail outside class. The boy's desire for vengeance was channeled into exactly the work the therapist wanted.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the Oracle of Delphi answered that there was no wiser man in Athens than Socrates, and Socrates was delighted to hear it.
questions.explain: The oracle did say no one was wiser, but Socrates, being humble, was not pleased and set out to prove the oracle wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that in adolescence many of us fell under the sway of a great book or writer whose ideas affected us decades later.
questions.explain: Because we were so open to influence, such early encounters sank deep into our minds. Greene says our intelligence depends on this ability to absorb the ideas of older, wiser people.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: True or false: The law statement at the start of Chapter 7 ends by urging the reader to tame their own stubborn nature, which is the subject of the chapter's final section.
questions.explain: The law closes with learning to free your mind from its defensive and closed positions. The Flexible Mind section turns the chapter's persuasion strategies on the reader's own rigidity.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Put Greene's five strategies for becoming a master persuader in the order he presents them.
items: Transform yourself into a deep listener
Infect people with the proper mood
Confirm their self-opinion
Allay their insecurities
Use people's resistance and stubbornness
questions.explain: The strategies move from listening and mood, through confirming self-opinion and allaying insecurities, to the special case of the most resistant people.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Put the events of Tom Sawyer's whitewashing scheme in the order Greene tells them.
items: Tom is punished for fighting and must whitewash the fence
Ben Rogers walks by and teases him about swimming
Tom acts absorbed and calls the job a rare test of skill
Ben gives Tom his apple for a turn with the brush
A team of boys finishes the fence while Tom rests in the shade
questions.explain: Tom's absorbed manner and framing turned a punishment into something the neighborhood boys begged to do.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Put the steps of Billy Wilder's persuasion of Marlene Dietrich in order.
items: Dietrich turns down the role as too distasteful
Wilder says he has found two American actresses for the part
Dietrich agrees to view their screen tests
She is aghast at their performances
She volunteers to play the part herself
questions.explain: Rather than pleading, Wilder set up a comparison that stung Dietrich's competitive pride, so the decision felt like her own.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Put the stages of the Marriage of Figaro story in the order Greene tells them.
items: Louis XVI reads the manuscript and is furious
The play is privately performed at Versailles
Beaumarchais lets a tribunal suggest small changes
The censors demand larger changes
The tribunal defends him and Louis backs down
questions.explain: By yielding on small matters and flattering his tribunal's intelligence, Beaumarchais won allies who protected him on the important ones.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Put the events of Hakuin's dealings with the miserly pawnbroker in order.
items: The son asks Hakuin how to get his father to practice Buddhism
Hakuin offers to pay for each prayer and chant
The pawnbroker presents a daily bill for his prayers
On the seventh day he fails to show up
He becomes a generous donor to the temple
questions.explain: Hakuin used the man's rigid love of money rather than fighting it, and the miser discovered the value of prayer on his own.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the stages of Socrates's response to the oracle in the order Greene tells them.
items: Chaerephon asks the Oracle of Delphi if anyone is wiser than Socrates
The oracle answers no
Socrates sets out to prove the oracle wrong
He questions eminent people in many fields
He admits he is wiser because he knows his own ignorance
questions.explain: Socrates's humility led him to test the oracle, and the test showed that awareness of one's ignorance is the mark of wisdom.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Put the stages of the mind's development in the order Greene traces them.
items: As children we learn quickly, motivated by feelings of weakness
In adolescence a great book can sway us deeply
With age a creeping sense of superiority closes the mind
The ideal combines youthful flexibility with adult reasoning
questions.explain: Greene describes the mind tightening like the body with age, then proposes an ideal that recovers childhood openness without losing adult reasoning.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Match each figure to the persuasion technique Greene uses them to illustrate.
pairs: Rapport through laughter, drink and touch
Framing a chore as a rare opportunity
Flattering intelligence by inviting small changes
questions.explain: Each story illustrates one tactic for lowering resistance. Vionnet and Johnson belong to infecting people with mood; the others to confirming self-opinion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Match each quality of self-opinion to a tactic Greene recommends for confirming it.
pairs: Give smaller rather than larger gifts
Frame your request as part of a larger cause
questions.explain: Small gifts avoid seeming to buy loyalty, advice-seeking shows respect for wisdom, and a larger cause lets people feel good about themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Match each way of using resistance to the case Greene uses to show it.
pairs: The suspended teenager and the principal
The couple seeking a friendly divorce
The miserly pawnbroker paid to pray
questions.explain: In each, the therapist or master moves with the person's own energy rather than against it, channeling it in a productive direction.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Match each person Greene names to their role in the chapter's persuasion examples.
pairs: Friend who trades an apple for a turn at the fence
American captivated by Marie de Vionnet
Suggested a witticism for the fourth act
Chose the color of the little page's ribbon
questions.explain: These minor figures each appear in one of Greene's stories about lowering resistance or strategic flattery.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Match each target of flattery to the approach Greene recommends.
pairs: You have more room to flatter
Agree with their opinions and validate their wisdom
Say how their advice and criticisms helped you
questions.explain: Greene tailors flattery to the target. Flattering a boss is too transparent, and praise only fits people whose self-opinion is high.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each figure to the lesson about an open mind Greene draws from them.
pairs: Wisdom lies in awareness of your own ignorance
Entertain a new thing with all possible love
Rules are guidelines to break from time to time
Asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser
questions.explain: Socrates, Nietzsche and Bassui each model a way of loosening the mind; Chaerephon's question to the oracle sets Socrates's story in motion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each part of Nietzsche's advice, as Greene quotes it, to its meaning.
pairs: Allow the author the longest start
Give the work every chance, like a race you want them to win
Hold back criticism for a time
What actually moves the new idea at its heart
questions.explain: Nietzsche's method delays judgment so you can penetrate to the heart of a new idea before reason weighs in.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 7 to its role in the chapter.
pairs: States the law of self-opinion and its three universals
Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
Gives practical tactics for lowering people's defenses
Turns the strategies on the reader's own rigid mind
questions.explain: The chapter moves from understanding the law, to applying it to others, to applying it to oneself.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Sort these flattery practices into those Greene recommends and those he warns against.

items.t: Praising someone's effort
Passing compliments through third parties
Mixing in a small criticism
Praising someone's natural talent
Asking for a favor right after praising
Saying their latest book beats the last
Flattering your boss directly

questions.explain: Greene favors flattery that seems realistic and unforced. Comparing a new book with the last implies criticism, and praising talent implies mere luck.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Sort these examples into Greene's strategy of infecting people with the proper mood or confirming their self-opinion.

items.t: Marie de Vionnet's indulgent mildness
Lyndon Johnson's bawdy jokes
A touch on the arm
Tom Sawyer's fence
Disraeli's advice to be confuted
Beaumarchais's tribunal

questions.explain: Mood works through atmosphere, nonverbal cues and rapport; confirming self-opinion targets people's sense of autonomy, intelligence and goodness.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Sort these tactics by the quality of self-opinion Greene says they confirm.

items.t: Seeing their point of view and agreeing
Letting them argue you round
Asking for their advice
Asking forgiveness after a faux pas
Recalling the good they have done for you
Calling them a team member
Forgiving an enemy

questions.explain: Agreement, being confuted and seeking advice flatter people's minds; forgiveness, reminders of their kindness and prosocial labels confirm their moral self-image.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Sort these into the kinds of gift Greene says work better and the kinds that backfire when winning people over.

items.t: Small rewards spread out over time
A modest gift they feel they deserve
A lavish present that buys loyalty
A large reward accepted out of need

questions.explain: Large gifts offend people's sense of independence and later breed resentment or suspicion. Small ones let people feel they are not being bought.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.section: Five Strategies for Becoming a Master Persuader
questions.q: Sort these people by whether, in Greene's examples, they were the persuader or the one persuaded.

items.t: Billy Wilder
Hakuin
Milton Erickson
Marlene Dietrich
Ben Rogers
Lambert Strether
The pawnbroker

questions.explain: In each story the persuader lowered resistance indirectly, and the person persuaded came to feel the choice was their own.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these mental traits into those Greene links with the flexible mind and those he links with the closed mind.

items.t: A child's sense of vulnerability
Awareness of one's own ignorance
Treating ideas as toys
A creeping sense of superiority
Spouting conventional wisdom
Needing validation of one's self-opinion

questions.explain: Openness comes from humility and playfulness; rigidity comes from superiority and attachment to the illusion of self-opinion.

questions.unitTitle: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
questions.q: Sort these ideas into those first set out in Chapter 7's Keys to Human Nature and those developed in its later Five Strategies section.

items.t: Three universal qualities of self-opinion
Three possible outcomes of trying to convince someone
The cultural prejudice against influence
Mental judo with stubborn people
Praising effort rather than talent
Deep listening

questions.explain: The Keys section lays out the law and its rationale; the Five Strategies section turns that understanding into practical tactics.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In the Law of Self-sabotage, Greene gives the name ____ to our particular way of looking at the world and interpreting events and the actions of people around us.
questions.explain: The law opens by defining this way of seeing as our attitude and claims that it determines much of what happens to us in life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to the Law of Self-sabotage, what happens when our attitude is essentially fearful?
options: We see only the positive in things and take reckless chances
We see the negative in every circumstance and stop ourselves from taking chances
We learn from our mistakes faster than other people do
We become indifferent to both success and failure alike
questions.explain: Greene says a fearful attitude makes us see the negative everywhere, avoid chances, and blame others for mistakes instead of learning from them.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In the Law of Self-sabotage, how does Greene say we sabotage our careers and relationships?
options: By unconsciously creating the circumstances we fear the most
By trusting other people too quickly and too completely
By working too hard and neglecting our need for rest
By deliberately picking fights with the people above us
questions.explain: The sabotage is unconscious: a hostile or suspicious attitude makes others feel the same emotions, so we bring about exactly what we fear.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Self-sabotage holds that the human attitude is fixed early in life and cannot be changed.
questions.explain: The law says the opposite: “The human attitude, however, is malleable.” That is why making it more positive can spark a different dynamic.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Self-sabotage say we can do by making our attitude more positive, open, and tolerant of other people?
options: Create opportunities out of nothing
Make sure that no one ever criticizes us
Draw people to us
Do away with any need for willpower
Learn from adversity
questions.explain: A more positive attitude sparks a different dynamic in which we learn from adversity, create opportunities, and draw people to us. Greene promises no immunity from criticism, and he asks us to explore the limits of willpower, not abandon it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why does Greene frame the problem of a negative attitude as a law of self-sabotage rather than as bad luck?
questions.a: Because our attitude determines much of what happens to us. A fearful, hostile or suspicious attitude makes us see the negative, avoid chances, blame others and stir the same emotions in other people, so we unconsciously create the circumstances we fear most. The damage comes from within us, and since the attitude is malleable, we can also reverse it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the ideas of the Law of Self-sabotage statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: Our attitude determines much of what happens to us
A fearful attitude sees the negative and avoids chances
We unconsciously create the circumstances we fear
The human attitude is malleable
We must explore the limits of our willpower
questions.explain: The statement defines attitude, shows how a negative one sabotages us, then turns to the hope that attitude can change and ends with the challenge of testing our willpower.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In the story of Anton Chekhov’s childhood, how did his father Pavel Yegorovich explain beating his children?
options: He said he did it out of love, as God’s will to instill humility
He said it was to toughen them up for military service
He said it was punishment for stealing money from the shop
He said he did it only when drunk and later regretted it
questions.explain: Pavel claimed no malice: he said it was God’s will that children be beaten to instill humility, as he himself had been raised, which made the beatings doubly confusing.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Chekhov’s childhood, at the end of each beating young Anton had to kiss his father’s ____ and ask to be forgiven.
questions.explain: This ritual of submission foreshadows Greene’s later point that Pavel himself still bowed and kissed the hands of officials, a serf at heart.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: The Chekhov family lived in the backwater Russian town of ____, where the father owned a grocery shop.
questions.explain: Taganrog is the grim town of Anton’s childhood, and later the place where, left alone, he changed his attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s description of Anton Chekhov’s grim hometown, what was the only quiet and safe place for the boy?
options: The grocery shop after it had closed
The banks of the river outside the town
The graveyards that surrounded the town
The loft above the church choir
questions.explain: Greene says the surrounding graveyards were the only quiet and safe place, and Anton visited them often, wondering about himself and the world.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did young Anton Chekhov cope with the pain and boredom of his childhood in Taganrog?
options: He laughed at it all and became the family clown
He threw himself into his schoolwork every night
He withdrew into long hours of silent prayer
He ran away to join his brothers in Moscow
questions.explain: His only recourse was to laugh at it all, imitating the town’s characters, though his humor sometimes turned aggressive and cruel.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why did Pavel Yegorovich slip out of Taganrog one night in 1875?
options: He was chasing his sons, who had stolen money from him
He had been offered a post as a choir director in Moscow
He faced bankruptcy and likely debtor’s prison over the shop’s debts
He was being sued by the boarder who had taken the house
questions.explain: Years of mismanaging the grocery store left him with debts that came due, so he fled to Moscow without telling his wife.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In the Chekhov story, how did the family lose their house in Taganrog?
options: A boarder used his court connections to swindle them out of it
Anton sold it himself to pay for medical school
The creditors seized it and sold it at a public auction
The father sold it in secret before he fled the town
questions.explain: The boarder had offered to help the mother against the creditors but instead used his connections in court to take the house.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Left alone in Taganrog at sixteen, Anton Chekhov supported himself by hiring himself out as a ____ to as many families as possible.
questions.explain: Tutoring paid little, but it let him support himself, and he came to enjoy it and feel proud and dignified.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did the letters Anton wrote to his brothers Alexander and Mikhail while alone in Taganrog show his changing attitude?
questions.a: He told Alexander to stop obsessing over their father and start taking care of himself, and told Mikhail not to call himself worthless but to be aware of his worth among people. Having learned to support himself, Anton was gaining a sense of dignity, and even he was surprised by this new tone.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Anton Chekhov’s grandfather Yegor Mikhailovich had been born a ____, a form of indentured slavery, before buying the family’s freedom.
questions.explain: The Chekhovs had been serfs for generations; Yegor bought their freedom and set up Pavel as the family merchant.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What did Anton Chekhov conclude about his father after thinking through the family’s history?
options: He remained a serf at heart and was more a victim than an oppressor
He was cruel by choice and deserved no forgiveness at all
He was a gifted merchant held back by his lazy sons
He had been spoiled by a comfortable and easy upbringing
questions.explain: Anton saw a man with an artistic temperament trapped by his fate, beaten by his own father, who still bowed to every official: a helpless man rather than a tyrant.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What thinking prepared the ground for Anton Chekhov’s sudden rush of love for his parents?
questions.a: As a last resort against his bitterness, he analyzed his father as if he were a character in a story, going back through the generations of Chekhov serfs. He saw that Pavel had an artistic temperament, felt trapped by a grocery store and six children, and had been beaten by his own father. This understanding made Pavel seem helpless, more a victim than an oppressor, which laid the groundwork for unconditional love.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What vow did Anton Chekhov make after his rush of love for his parents?
options: Never again to speak to his father or answer his letters
No more bowing and apologizing, no more complaining and blaming, no more disorderly living
To leave Russia for good as soon as he became a doctor
To give up writing stories and devote himself to medicine
questions.explain: Freed of rancor, he vowed to stop bowing, complaining and wasting time, deciding that the answer to everything was work and love.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: After freeing himself from rancor in Taganrog, Anton Chekhov decided that the answer to everything was work and ____.
questions.explain: Greene repeats the phrase “work and love, work and love” to show the simple creed Anton wanted to spread to his family and to mankind.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these describe the Chekhov family’s situation when Anton arrived in Moscow in 1879?
options: They lived in a large apartment with a view
Alexander was drinking heavily and blaming their father
The younger siblings were no longer in school
The father had become a successful merchant again
They were crammed into a single basement room in the red-light district
questions.explain: Anton found the family in one dark basement room, the younger children out of school, and Alexander drinking. The apartment with a view came only after Anton’s efforts, and the father held odd jobs well below owning a business.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did Anton Chekhov set about changing his family’s spirits in the Moscow basement?
options: By having his father thrown out of the family’s room
By lecturing each of them every evening about their faults
By setting the proper example rather than preaching or criticizing
By moving out and sending them money from a distance
questions.explain: When others were moving out, Anton moved in to be the catalyst for change, deciding he would not preach or criticize but set the proper example.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these did Anton Chekhov do to improve his family’s lives in Moscow?
options: He put Mikhail, Ivan, and Maria back into school
He found his father a better job
He moved the family back to Taganrog
He forbade the family from reading books
He took charge of the housework
questions.explain: Anton did the housework until his brothers joined in, paid for schooling, found his father better work and moved them to a larger apartment. He also chose books for his siblings and discussed them late into the night.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: After Anton Chekhov reformed the family’s life in Moscow, his siblings began to call him Papa ____, the leader of the family.
questions.explain: The nickname marks how Anton had taken over the role their father had failed to play.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did Anton Chekhov deal with his brother Alexander, and what came of it?
questions.a: When Alexander came home drunk, insulted the mother and sister and threatened Anton, Anton told him he would lock him out and disavow him if he ever yelled at a family member again. The new family code demanded respect for the mother and sister, no blaming the father, and dignity in dress and conduct. It was a continual battle requiring patience and love, but Anton weaned him from drinking, helped his journalism career, and Alexander settled into a quiet, satisfying life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Anton’s brother Nikolai was weaned from drinking and settled into a quiet, satisfying life.
questions.explain: That was Alexander. Nikolai, the artist, was led by the family’s self-destructive streak to an early death from alcoholism.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Anton Chekhov’s mother was a gentle soul who tried to intervene on his behalf but was no match for her husband.
