questions.explain: She argued that the boy was too young to work and needed time to study, but the father overruled her, calling Anton lazy by nature.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: When Anton Chekhov first began to spit blood in 1884, he immediately had a fellow doctor examine him.
questions.explain: He refused to be examined by a fellow doctor, preferring not to know and to go on writing and practicing medicine without worrying about the future.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Anton Chekhov refused to ally himself with any revolutionary cause, and he was attacked by the political cliques of fellow writers.
questions.explain: As he grew famous, the envy and petty criticism of writers formed into cliques left him disenchanted with the literary world and depressed.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why did Anton Chekhov make the journey to Sakhalin Island at the end of 1889?
options: To research a play that the government had commissioned
To free himself from a depression caused by literary pettiness by connecting to something real
To escape the creditors who were still pursuing his family
To treat the many prisoners there who suffered from tuberculosis
questions.explain: Disenchanted with the envy of fellow writers, Anton hoped that studying Russia’s lowliest prisoners would reignite the generous mood he had crafted in Taganrog.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these did Anton Chekhov witness or learn about on Sakhalin Island?
options: Wives and daughters of convicts resorting to prostitution
Prisoners being sent home in comfort once their sentences ended
Gruesome torture sessions of prisoners
A model prison that treated inmates with dignity
Convicts working in the mines chained to wheelbarrows
questions.explain: Everything on the island was designed to degrade people’s spirits; freed prisoners often had to stay on in labor camps, which is why their wives and daughters were stranded there.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What did the trip to Sakhalin Island do for Anton Chekhov’s state of mind, and what came of it?
questions.a: Seeing the lowest rung of hell, a system designed to strip people of dignity that reminded him of his family dynamic on a vast scale, restored his sense of proportion. He was freed of the petty thoughts and concerns that had weighed him down and could get outside himself and feel generous again. The book he wrote, Sakhalin Island, caught the public’s attention and led to substantial reforms on the island.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did Anton Chekhov respond when, by 1897, a doctor advised him to retire and leave Moscow?
options: He gave up his plays to write a memoir about his illness
He would have none of it and lived as if nothing had changed
He moved into a sanatorium abroad to extend his life
He stopped receiving visitors in order to save his strength
questions.explain: Anton refused rest, kept receiving admirers, absorbed himself in their problems, and never talked about his illness, radiating a calm that astonished people.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put these events of Anton Chekhov’s life in the order they happened.
items: His brothers Alexander and Nikolai leave for Moscow
His father flees Taganrog to escape his debts
Anton is left alone in a corner of a room at sixteen
Anton moves to Moscow to attend medical school
Anton travels to Sakhalin Island
Anton takes a last open-sleigh ride
questions.explain: The brothers left and the father fled in 1875, Anton joined the family in Moscow in 1879, reached Sakhalin in 1890, and took his sleigh ride in the winter of 1904, months before he died.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the stages of Anton Chekhov’s inner change while alone in Taganrog in the order Greene describes them.
items: Angry, bitter and depressed at being abandoned
Supporting himself by tutoring
Absorbing his mind in study and books
Thinking long and hard about his father’s past
A sudden rush of love for his parents
A vow that the answer is work and love
questions.explain: Practical survival came first, then pride in his work and wider reading, then reflection on his father, which led to the rush of love and the vow.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put Anton Chekhov’s steps in reviving his family in Moscow in the order Greene describes them.
items: He moves into the cramped basement room
He takes charge of the housework
His brothers agree to share the chores
He puts the younger siblings back in school
He moves the family to a larger apartment
The family calls him Papa Antosha
questions.explain: Anton began by example with the housework, which drew his brothers in, then used savings for schooling and a better home, until the family accepted him as its leader.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chekhov story, what had changed when Anton went from feeling trapped in Taganrog to feeling liberated?
options: His attitude, which opened him to new experiences and possibilities
His father’s letters, which now praised his hard work
His circumstances, after a family friend began paying him
The town itself, which was becoming more prosperous
questions.explain: Greene stresses that his circumstances, the town and the corner of the room were all the same; only his attitude had changed.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say Anton came to feel about his life alone in Taganrog once his attitude changed?
options: His corner of the room was his kingdom
He needed someone to rescue him from the town
He actually liked his work as a tutor
His father had been right that he was lazy
The town’s odd characters supplied endless material for stories
questions.explain: He discovered he enjoyed tutoring, saw Taganrog as full of story material, and treated his corner as a kingdom. He now doubted his father’s charge of laziness and felt liberated rather than in need of rescue.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene’s interpretation, how did Anton Chekhov’s Sakhalin journey relate to his experience in Taganrog?
options: It was a punishment he imposed on himself for his success
It reproduced Taganrog in reverse, as he abandoned others to be alone and vulnerable
It was a way to return to the house where he was born
It was an attempt to reunite his scattered family in exile
questions.explain: In Taganrog he had been abandoned; this time he chose to abandon others so he could reexperience the freedom and empathy he had felt there.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What three crises does Greene identify in Anton Chekhov’s life, and how did he meet each one?
questions.a: First, being left alone at sixteen in Taganrog, which he met by changing his attitude and freeing himself of resentment toward his father. Second, about thirteen years later, depression over the pettiness of fellow writers, which he met by going to Sakhalin to be alone and vulnerable again. Third, the early death sentence of tuberculosis, which he met by letting go of his fear of death and living at full tilt, a final and ultimate freedom that gave him a visible radiance.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each member of the Chekhov family to Greene’s description of them.
pairs: The father who owned the grocery shop and beat his children
The grandfather, born a serf, who bought the family’s freedom
The most gifted yet troubled brother, whom Anton worked to reform
The artist brother who died early from alcoholism
The youngest son, who felt worthless and depressed
questions.explain: Each figure plays a part in Greene’s account of the family’s inherited bitterness and Anton’s efforts to break it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each crisis in Anton Chekhov’s life to how he responded.
pairs: Left alone in Taganrog at sixteen
Tutoring, reading, and rethinking his father
His family spiraling down in Moscow
Moving in and setting the proper example
A journey to the prison island of Sakhalin
Living at full tilt as if nothing had changed
questions.explain: In each case Anton answered a constricting situation by opening himself up rather than closing down.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each place in the Chekhov story to Greene’s description of it.
pairs: Backwater hometown with crumbling houses and muddy roads
The only place Anton could work in peace and quiet
A single crammed room with little light or ventilation
Russia’s most notorious prison, just north of Japan
questions.explain: These settings trace Anton’s path from a grim childhood, through self-education and family rescue, to the island that restored his sense of proportion.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s interpretation of the Chekhov story, match each part of Anton’s life alone in Taganrog to how he came to see it.
pairs: A way to get outside himself
A way to travel far beyond Taganrog
More a victim than an oppressor
questions.explain: Nothing about these things changed except how Anton saw them, which is Greene’s point about attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into Anton Chekhov’s childhood under his father and his life alone in Taganrog after the family left.

items.t: Minding a freezing grocery shop
Rehearsing for the church choir before dawn on Sundays
Playing cruel practical jokes as the family clown
Being beaten almost daily
Tutoring as many families as possible
Reading literature and philosophy in the town library
Writing stories at night in his corner
Going hungry when families went on vacation

questions.explain: The childhood items come from Greene’s account of life under Pavel; the second group describes the hard but freeing months after the family left for Moscow.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into what Anton Chekhov vowed to give up and what he vowed to embrace after his rush of love for his parents.

items.t: Bowing and apologizing to people
Complaining and blaming
Disorderly living
Wasting time
Work
Love

questions.explain: His vow ruled out bowing, complaining, blaming, disorder and wasted time, and named work and love as the answer to everything.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into the Chekhov family before and after Anton’s efforts in Moscow.

items.t: A complaining and self-pitying mood
Younger siblings out of school
Crammed into a single basement room
Younger brothers excited about future careers
Late-night discussions of science and philosophy
A much larger apartment with a view

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the despondent basement family Anton found with the bonded family that called him Papa Antosha.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into the effects of being generous toward others and of being generous toward ourselves, as Greene draws the lesson from Chekhov.

items.t: We stop taking everything personally
Others feel drawn to us and match our spirit
Our minds are freed from petty emotions about people
We stop playing the game of false humility
We get what we need on our own through our work
We stand tall and realize our potential

questions.explain: Accepting people frees our minds and draws them to us; generosity toward ourselves ends the bowing and scraping and lets us rely on our own work.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why does Greene call the story of Anton Chekhov a paradigm for what we all face?
questions.a: We all carry hurts from childhood, accumulate slights and disappointments, and feel moments of worthlessness and doubt. These emotions breed obsessive thoughts, make us curtail what we experience and numb ourselves with habits, so we assume a negative, fearful attitude that becomes a self-imposed prison. Chekhov shows that freedom comes from a choice, a change in attitude that anyone can make.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say our accumulated hurts and sense of worthlessness can lead us to do?
options: Seek out bold new adventures to prove ourselves
Develop obsessive thoughts that dominate our minds
Forgive other people too easily
Curtail what we experience to manage our anxiety
Turn to alcohol or other habits to numb the pain
questions.explain: Greene lists obsessive thoughts, a narrowing of experience and numbing habits as the path to a negative attitude, our self-imposed prison.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene mean by adopting a generous spirit toward others?
questions.a: It means accepting people, understanding them and, if possible, even loving them for their human nature. This liberates our minds from obsessive and petty emotions, so we stop reacting to everything people do and say and stop taking things personally. Mental space is freed for higher pursuits, and others feel drawn to us and want to match our spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene mean by being generous toward ourselves?
questions.a: It means we no longer feel the need to bow and scrape and play the game of false humility while secretly resenting our lack of success. Through our work and by getting what we need on our own, without depending on others, we can stand tall and realize our potential. We then stop reproducing the negative emotions around us.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Chekhov later described his Taganrog years as a young man who squeezes the ____ out of himself drop by drop.
questions.explain: In a letter to a friend he wrote of waking to find that his blood was “no longer the blood of a slave but that of a real human being.”

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: The William James epigraph in Chapter 8 says human beings can alter their lives by altering their ____ of mind.
questions.explain: James calls this “The greatest discovery of my generation,” which sums up the chapter’s claim that a change in attitude can change our circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: in the winter of 1904, the dying Anton Chekhov stayed indoors on his doctor’s orders rather than risk the cold.
questions.explain: He did the opposite: he took an open-sleigh ride into the country, one of his greatest pleasures, not caring about the consequences, and died a few months later.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why does Greene call Anton Chekhov’s father a walking contradiction, and how did young Anton respond to the hypocrisy around him?
questions.a: Despite his religious zeal, Pavel was lazy, a drunk, and dishonest with customers, and the townspeople were just as hypocritical, acting pious at funerals while whispering about the cakes they would eat afterward. Anton’s only recourse was to laugh at it all: he became the family clown, imitating the town’s characters and inventing stories about them, though his humor sometimes turned cruel.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the three crises Greene identifies in Anton Chekhov’s life in the order they occurred.
items: Being left alone in Taganrog
Depression over the pettiness of fellow writers
The death sentence of tuberculosis
questions.explain: Greene says the second crisis came some thirteen years after the first, and tuberculosis was the last crisis, met with the ultimate freedom of living at full tilt.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s scenario of two young Americans studying in Paris, why do they judge the city in opposite ways?
options: The young woman already spoke good French before arriving
Their different attitudes color how they perceive the same city
They happen to meet different classes of Parisians
They spend their year there in very different seasons
questions.explain: The city, its weather and its people are the same for both; the timid young man and the adventurous young woman add or subtract color through their own perspectives.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene, quoting Carl Jung, define attitude?
options: A set of moral rules we learn from our parents
A readiness of the psyche to act or react in a certain way
A conscious decision about how we choose to treat others
A passing mood that is triggered by recent events
questions.explain: Jung’s definition, “a readiness of the psyche to act or react in a certain way,” stresses an unconscious orientation, not a deliberate choice or a passing mood.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, why are we never conscious of how our attitude forms?
options: Our parents decide our attitude before we can speak
We form our attitude only during sleep and forget it
Other people shape it for us without our knowledge
We only experience the aftereffects of our brain’s sensitivities as an overall mood
questions.explain: Certain stimuli fire more strongly in us depending on our wiring and makeup; we only feel the result as a background mood such as depression or enthusiasm.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Jung’s illustration of hikers who come upon a stream, what does the fourth hiker do?
options: Crosses carefully, irritated by the obstruction in the path
Calculates the most effective way across as a mental challenge
Leaps across for the sheer physical pleasure of the jump
Turns back and rationalizes her fears by saying the hike has been long enough
questions.explain: Leaping for joy, calculating a route, and crossing with irritation belong to the first three hikers; the fourth sees no need to cross and covers her fear with a rationalization.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, why was Anton Chekhov better able than his siblings to reassess his father?
options: From an early age he had an ironic attitude that let him see things with detachment
He was the oldest child and remembered better times
He had been beaten far less often than the others
He had studied psychology in the medical school library
questions.explain: Greene uses the Chekhov children as evidence of genetic inclinations: Anton’s ironic bent let him distance himself, while the others were more easily enmeshed in the father’s brutality.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene mean by saying our attitude has a self-fulfilling dynamic?
options: It changes to match whatever happens to us each day
It shapes our behavior and others’ responses so as to bring about what it expects
It makes our predictions about the future always come true
It fulfills our needs without requiring effort from us
questions.explain: The young man’s insecurity makes learning and meeting people harder, which deepens his isolation; our attitude actively determines what happens to us.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: A coworker who assumes her colleagues are always judging her finds that they grow guarded and critical around her. Which idea of Greene’s best explains this?
options: The way we think about people tends to have a like effect upon them
Attitudes are fixed by genetics and cannot be influenced
People are naturally critical of anyone who works hard
Colleagues always resent a person who is more talented
questions.explain: Greene says that if we feel hostile and critical we inspire critical emotions in others, and if we feel defensive we make others defensive.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Maya notices that after friends leave a party she dwells on their flaws and bad opinions. What does Greene say this reveals?
options: A sign that she needs new friends who share her views
A sign of her own attitude, seen in how she judges people out of her presence
A healthy habit of rational and objective analysis
An accurate reading of her friends’ true characters
questions.explain: Greene lists how we judge people once they are out of our presence as one way to catch glimpses of our own attitude, negative or generous.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s lens metaphor, the negative attitude narrows the ____ of the lens, while the positive attitude expands it as far as possible.
questions.explain: If attitude is our lens on the world, the negative kind closes it down to limit experience, and the positive kind opens it wide.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: To illustrate attitude, Jung imagines hikers who come upon a ____ that must be crossed to continue the journey.
questions.explain: Each hiker sees the same rushing water differently, showing that our minds do not perceive just what is there.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says our earliest experiences and attachment ____ play a large role in shaping our attitude.
questions.explain: He refers the reader back to chapter 4 for attachment schemas and adds that we internalize the voices of our mother and father figures.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene tells the reader: you are not a ____ in a game controlled by others, but an active player who can move the pieces at will.
questions.explain: This image belongs to the second task, believing in the supreme power of your attitude to alter your circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says not to be afraid to exaggerate the role of willpower, because it is an exaggeration with a ____.
questions.explain: The point of the exaggeration is that it leads to a positive self-fulfilling dynamic, which is all that matters.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Explain in Greene’s terms what Jung means by calling attitude a readiness of the psyche to react in a certain way.
questions.a: Every day our minds respond to thousands of stimuli, and depending on our wiring and psychological makeup some fire more strongly and get more attention. If we are prone to sadness we pick up signs that promote sadness; if we are suspicious we notice and exaggerate any possible negativity in faces. We never see this process, only its aftereffect: an overall mood such as hostility or enthusiasm through which we see and interpret the world.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What are the roots of the attitude we carry through life, according to Greene?
questions.a: First, genetic inclinations toward hostility, greed, empathy or kindness, as shown by the different responses of the Chekhov children. Second, our earliest experiences and attachment schemas, including the internalized voices of our parents. Third, later experiences outside the family: people we love or admire shape us positively, while traumatic experiences constrict us. The attitude keeps being shaped, but vestiges of our earliest attitude always live on.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Using Greene’s Paris scenario, how does each young American’s attitude create its own dynamic?
questions.a: The tense, insecure young man reacts defensively to his mistakes in French, which makes learning harder, which makes meeting people harder and leaves him more isolated; his lowered energy and insecurities keep the cycle going and push people away. The adventurous young woman treats the language as a pleasant challenge, makes friends, improves her French, and her rising mood and energy make her more attractive to others, on and on.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, how can you catch glimpses of your own attitude in action?
questions.a: Watch how you judge people once they are out of your presence, whether you focus on their flaws or are generous and forgiving. Watch how you face adversity: whether you gloss over your mistakes, blame others, dread change, cling to routine, or bristle when your ideas are challenged. And watch how people respond to you nonverbally, whether they seem nervous or defensive, or whether you attract people who play a parent role.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What is the second task Greene sets for the student of human nature regarding attitude, and what does it involve?
questions.a: You must believe in the supreme power of your attitude to alter your circumstances, seeing yourself as an active player rather than a pawn. View your health, your intelligence and learning, your failures and the way people treat you as largely dependent on your attitude. Do not fear exaggerating the role of willpower, since it creates a positive self-fulfilling dynamic, and treat shaping your attitude as your most important creation in life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as roots of the attitude we carry through life?
options: People we love or admire outside the family
Earliest experiences and attachment schemas
The amount of money our family has
The climate of the region where we grow up
Genetic inclinations we are born with
questions.explain: Greene cites genetic inclinations, earliest experiences with our parents, and later experiences such as admired teachers or traumas. Climate and wealth are not among the roots he names.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say can show you signs of your own attitude?
options: How you face adversity or resistance
How people respond to you nonverbally
Which foods and music you prefer
How you judge people once they are out of your presence
How well you remember your dreams
questions.explain: Greene points to judgments of absent people, reactions to adversity, and others’ nervous or defensive responses as the places to catch your attitude in action.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene urge you to see as largely dependent on your attitude?
options: The year in which you were born
Your capacity for learning and intelligence
Your health
The weather where you live
The way people treat you
questions.explain: He says the mind and body are one, that intelligence is not fixed, and that how people treat you flows largely from your attitude. Things like the weather simply exist, as the Paris example shows.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say describe people with a negative attitude?
options: They operate from a basic position of fear toward life
They expand the lens as far as possible
They unconsciously limit what they see and experience to gain control
They see the world through a narrowed lens
They are open to new experiences, ideas, and emotions
questions.explain: Fear, a wish to limit experience for control, and a narrowed lens mark the negative attitude; openness and an expanded lens belong to the positive one.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that once we change our attitude, every trace of our earliest attitude disappears.
questions.explain: He says vestiges of our earliest attitude always live on; even Chekhov remained susceptible to depression and self-loathing.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if we feel defensive, we tend to make others feel defensive.
questions.explain: The way we think about people has a like effect on them, which is part of the self-fulfilling dynamic of attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene tells the reader not to be afraid to exaggerate the role of willpower.
questions.explain: He says: “It is an exaggeration with a purpose.” It leads to a positive self-fulfilling dynamic.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the steps of the young man’s negative cycle in Paris in the order Greene describes them.
items: He feels tense and insecure
He reacts defensively to his language mistakes
Learning French becomes harder
Meeting people becomes more difficult
He feels more isolated and his energy drops
questions.explain: Each step feeds the next, and the falling energy of depression perpetuates the cycle.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the four hikers in Jung’s stream illustration in the order Greene presents them.
items: The one who leaps across for physical pleasure
The one who enjoys calculating the best way across
The cautious one who crosses, irritated by the obstruction
The one who turns back and rationalizes her fear
questions.explain: Greene moves from the most carefree response to the most fearful, showing that no one simply sees the water over the rocks.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene’s Paris scenario, match each feature of the city to what it is as a matter of objective reality.
pairs: Has no positive or negative qualities
A subjective judgment depending on whom you meet
Merely an agglomeration of carved pieces of stone
questions.explain: Greene’s point is that the world simply exists; we add or subtract color through our perspective.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each root of attitude to Greene’s example or effect of it.
pairs: Being harsher on ourselves and more critical
An internalized presence that shapes a positive view
Closing our minds to avoid reexperiencing pain
questions.explain: Greene traces attitude to inborn wiring, internalized parental voices, admired figures, and constricting traumas.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each inclination to what Greene says it makes a person pick up on.
pairs: Facial expressions that display possible negativity
What is missing and what others are not giving
questions.explain: Each attitude is a readiness to notice certain stimuli, which then reinforces the attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these reactions into the young man and the young woman in Greene’s Paris scenario.

items.t: Finds the weather damp and gloomy
Finds Notre Dame disappointing because of the crowds
Concludes Paris is overrated
Finds learning the language a pleasant challenge
Finds the weather romantic
Finds the city enchanting

questions.explain: Both live in the same city, but his timid, depressive attitude and her adventurous one produce opposite experiences.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into the negative (narrow) attitude and the positive (expansive) attitude as Greene first describes them.

items.t: Operates from a basic position of fear
Limits experience to gain control
Narrows the aperture of the lens
A much less fearful approach
Open to new ideas and emotions
Expands the lens as far as possible

questions.explain: Greene sets up the two poles that the chapter’s later sections develop in detail.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these self-check questions into the two places Greene says you can catch your attitude: in how you face adversity, and in how people respond to you.

items.t: Do you gloss over your own mistakes?
Do you instinctively blame others?
Do you dread any kind of change?
Do you catch people being nervous around you?
Do people seem defensive in your presence?
Do you attract people who play a parent role?

questions.explain: The first group concerns your own reactions to resistance; the second concerns the mostly nonverbal signals others give off around you.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 8, Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude, signal about its argument?
options: That an inner shift in how we see the world can change what happens to us
That attitude is fixed and we should choose circumstances to suit it
That we must change our surroundings before our mood can improve
That other people’s attitudes control the circumstances of our lives
questions.explain: The chapter argues that attitude is a lens that actively shapes our circumstances, as Chekhov’s unchanged corner of a room became a kingdom.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which chapter of The Laws of Human Nature immediately follows the Law of Self-sabotage?
options: Soften People’s Resistance, the Law of Defensiveness
Beware the Fragile Ego, the Law of Envy
Confront Your Dark Side, the Law of Repression
Know Your Limits, the Law of Grandiosity
questions.explain: Chapter 9 on repression follows chapter 8; the Law of Defensiveness comes just before it, and envy and grandiosity come later.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does the order of the first two sections of Chapter 8 build Greene’s argument, and where does it lead next?
questions.a: The Ultimate Freedom opens with Chekhov’s story as a paradigm: a man who freed himself through a change in attitude rather than a change in circumstances. Keys to Human Nature then explains what attitude is, where it comes from, how it becomes self-fulfilling, and the reader’s two tasks. It ends by dividing attitudes into narrow and expansive, setting up the later sections on the constricted and expansive attitudes.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What earlier chapter does the Keys to Human Nature section of Chapter 8 point back to, and for what idea?
questions.a: It refers the reader to chapter 4, Determine the Strength of People’s Character, for attachment schemas. Greene uses that idea to show that our earliest experiences with parents, whose voices we internalize, are one of the roots of the attitude we carry through life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 8, the Keys to Human Nature section comes before the sections on the constricted and the expansive attitudes.
questions.explain: The chapter runs The Ultimate Freedom, Keys to Human Nature, The Constricted (Negative) Attitude, and The Expansive (Positive) Attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each chapter of The Laws of Human Nature to its law.
pairs: Soften People’s Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.explain: These are chapters 6 to 9 in order; chapter 8 sits between the laws of defensiveness and repression.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 8 in the order they appear.
items: The Ultimate Freedom
Keys to Human Nature
The Constricted (Negative) Attitude
The Expansive (Positive) Attitude
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Chekhov’s story, to the general analysis of attitude, to detailed portraits of its negative and positive forms.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Keys to Human Nature ends by sorting attitudes into the narrow kind and the ____ kind, which the last section of Chapter 8 develops as the positive attitude.
questions.explain: Greene says attitudes can be categorized as negative and narrow or positive and expansive, matching the chapter’s final two sections.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, why do people who feel particularly weak and vulnerable adopt a narrowing, constricted attitude toward life?
options: To punish the parents who failed to support them as children
To conserve their energy for a single great ambition
To attract protectors who will shield them from other people
To reduce the possibility of unexpected events in a chaotic world
questions.explain: Life is chaotic and unpredictable, and humans react badly to uncertainty, so the vulnerable narrow what they experience to cut down on surprises. The aim is control, not revenge or protection.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's account of the hostile attitude, how does a child who sees the world as full of hostility try to gain control over it?
options: By becoming the source of the hostility themselves
By pleasing everyone so that no one attacks without warning
By withdrawing from people and retreating into fantasy
By seeking out a strong protector among older children
questions.explain: If hostility is coming anyway, becoming its source makes it no longer so random and sudden. Pleasing people to disarm them is a disguise Greene links instead to the anxious attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's example of a husband with a hostile attitude who accuses his wife of not loving him, how does he read it if she is intimidated into silence?
options: As a sign that she needs more time to express her love
As proof that he has misjudged her and should apologize
As evidence that she is too fragile to be confronted
As a sign that he was right all along
questions.explain: Whatever the wife does confirms his view: protest means she is hiding the truth, and silence means he was right. Her confusion may then breed real hostility in her, completing the cycle.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What simple experiment does Greene suggest for someone who suspects they have a hostile attitude?
options: Spend a week avoiding all contact with strangers
Keep a diary of every slight received over a month
Silently hold positive thoughts about people you are meeting for the first time
Ask close friends to list the times you have provoked them
questions.explain: Approaching new acquaintances while feeling unspoken positive thoughts such as liking them will almost never draw a hostile response. That shows the source of hostile reactions was oneself.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene advise dealing with people at the extremes of the hostile attitude?
options: Shower them with praise until their suspicion melts away
Maintain your neutrality and do not respond with the antagonism they expect
Point out calmly how their own behavior provokes others
Confront them firmly so they learn their anger has consequences
questions.explain: Neutrality confounds them and halts their game for a time. In Greene's words, “They feed off your hostility, so do not give them fuel.”

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, what do people with the anxious attitude really fear?
options: Losing control of the situation
Being abandoned by those they love
Being outshone by more talented rivals
Being judged as lazy or incompetent
questions.explain: Their anticipation of obstacles and criticism stems from a fear of losing control, so they narrow the world they deal with. Fear of judgment on competence belongs to the avoidant attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's account, what did Sara Roosevelt do when her son Franklin came down with polio in 1921?
options: She tried to restrict his life and keep him to one room in the house
She urged him to return to politics as quickly as possible
She handed his care over entirely to his wife Eleanor
She moved him abroad to be treated by specialist doctors
questions.explain: Sara wanted him to give up politics and surrender to her care, disguising her anxious need to dominate as love. Eleanor, who knew what he needed, eventually won the battle.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the main goal in life of people with the avoidant attitude?
options: To take revenge on those who failed to recognize them
To win the approval of every authority figure they meet
To control every detail of their home and relationships
To avoid any responsibility or challenge in which they could be judged
questions.explain: Having come to dread their parents' judgment, avoidant types reason that if they do not try too hard they cannot fail or be criticized. Controlling every detail fits the anxious type instead.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, are avoidant types secretly afraid of success as well as failure?
options: Success would leave them with no further goals to pursue
Success brings responsibilities and the need to live up to them
Success would force them to admit their parents were right
Success would make their siblings envious and hostile
questions.explain: With success come responsibilities they must then meet, and standing out might also revive early fears about excelling. So escape routes protect them from both outcomes.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene's call, in the section on the expansive attitude, to explore repressed desires and the unconscious without fear points most directly toward which following chapter?
options: Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality
Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose
Chapter 7, Soften People's Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
Chapter 9, Confront Your Dark Side, the Law of Repression
questions.explain: Chapter 9 takes up repression and the dark side directly. Chapter 7 comes before this chapter, and the other two deal with purpose and death.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do children who feel unloved internalize the judgment that they are unworthy, forming the depressive attitude?
options: It lets them feel superior to their more favored siblings
It gives them an excuse to withdraw from schoolwork and chores
It earns them sympathy from the other adults around them
It preserves the illusion that their parents are strong and competent
questions.explain: Helpless and dependent children cannot bear to imagine their parents as flawed, so they decide something is wrong with themselves. The resulting sense of worthlessness haunts them for life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's account, what did the conductor Hans von Bülow do after Cosima Liszt left him to live with Richard Wagner?
options: He bombarded her with letters blaming himself and recounting his woes
He gave up music and retired to live alone in the country
He quickly remarried and never contacted Cosima again
He challenged Wagner and broke off all professional ties with him
questions.explain: His letters dwelt on his unworthiness, his career, his illnesses and suicidal tendencies, making her feel guilty; she likened each to “a sword twisted in my heart.” He did remarry, but only years later, and repeated the pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, how do people with the resentful attitude typically respond when they feel a lack of respect?
options: They withdraw into gloom and blame themselves for the slight
They let the hurt incubate and later take revenge through sabotage or passive aggression
They redouble their efforts to please the person who slighted them
They explode in anger immediately and then quickly forget the slight
questions.explain: Resentful types are cautious and control their emotions, so the hurt grows as they reflect on it until they strike in a plotted way. Immediate explosion is exactly what Greene recommends as healthier.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: A colleague carries his head a little too high, wears a faint smirk, never forgets a slight, and has a history of sudden breaks with people. Which constricted attitude does Greene's account best fit?
options: The avoidant attitude
The anxious attitude
The depressive attitude
The resentful attitude
questions.explain: Greene describes resentful types as arrogant in bearing, with a look of disdain, slow to forget hurts, and marked by past battles and breaks. Avoidant types instead show checkered careers and short relationships.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's advice on how to view other people, what is the advantage of not reacting emotionally when someone is truly malicious toward you?
options: You can avoid them entirely without them noticing
Others will notice your calm and take your side against them
They will soon feel guilty and apologize of their own accord
You will be in a better place to plot the proper countermove
questions.explain: Seeing their behavior as projected pain keeps you from getting upset or drawn into petty battles, so you can respond well. It also saves you from accumulating hurts and bitter feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, how do people get old and age prematurely?
options: By losing the support of family and friends
By accepting physical limits to what they can do
By living in stressful and crowded cities
By pushing their bodies too hard for too many years
questions.explain: Accepting limits makes a self-fulfilling cycle, while those who age well keep up physical activity, only moderately adjusted. Greene holds that excitement about a project lets us safely push past supposed limits.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What point does Greene draw from the medical shift, some fifty years ago, toward treating the human body as a whole?
options: That improving the overall attitude elevates everything else as well
That psychological problems should be treated one at a time
That depression is mainly a physical illness of the body
That diet and exercise matter more than one's state of mind
questions.explain: Just as better diet and exercise help every organ, our separate problems such as boredom or low motivation are governed by attitude. Improve it and creativity, stress-handling, confidence and relationships all rise.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How did Joan Crawford respond when Irving Thalberg punished her by casting her in a Western?
options: She complained to the studio until Thalberg withdrew the assignment
She took the role but quietly left MGM soon afterward
She refused the role and waited for a better part to come along
She made herself love the genre, became an expert rider, and studied the Old West
questions.explain: Crawford embraced the setback, aiming to become the leading actress of Westerns and at least expand her skills. Every setback became a chance to grow, which Greene presents as the right view of adversity.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: According to Greene, how did Malcolm Little (later Malcolm X) come to view his prison sentence that began in 1946?
options: As the best possible means of changing himself and his attitude
As proof that society would never give him a fair chance
As a period to endure quietly until he could resume his old life
As a chance to build alliances with other inmates
questions.explain: Through the prison library he fell in love with learning and used the time to study, gain discipline, and train as a speaker. Prison usually hardens and narrows criminals, but he embraced it without bitterness.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene say about humility in his advice on how to view yourself?
options: It is admirable but should be balanced with ambition
It wins the trust and support of more powerful people
It is not a virtue but a value people promote to keep you down
It is the surest protection against grandiose delusions
questions.explain: Greene writes, “Such humility is not a virtue but is rather a value that people promote to help keep you down.” Believing you are capable of more creates a different, self-fulfilling dynamic.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene interpret the cool, ironic attitude that many people affect in the postmodern world?
options: As a healthy defense against grandiose ambition
As a sign of mature and realistic thinking
As the natural result of greater knowledge about the world
As a clever mask for great fears of embarrassment, failure and emotion
questions.explain: Such people call the expansive attitude simpleminded, but Greene sees their nonchalance and false humility as hiding fear. He predicts the trend will fade, leaving the expansive attitude the more progressive one.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What did the psychologist Abraham Maslow call the kind of moment Chekhov had when he discovered his ultimate freedom?
options: A breakthrough insight
A flow state
A peak experience
A conversion moment
questions.explain: Maslow's peak experiences lift us out of the daily grind and reveal something larger and more sublime in life. Greene urges us to seek them out, since they can alter the attitude for good.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In his advice on how to view other people, what does Greene mean by seeing people as facts of nature?
options: Assuming people never change, so there is no point engaging
Treating everyone as fundamentally good underneath
Classifying people by their usefulness to your goals
Accepting that people come in all varieties, like flowers or rocks
questions.explain: Fools, saints, sociopaths and noble warriors all play a role in our social ecology, and we cannot reengineer human nature. Their differences should be welcomed rather than felt as a challenge to the ego.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why does Greene bring Chekhov back into the section on the expansive attitude, after telling his story at the start of the chapter?
options: To show that Chekhov's attitude eventually collapsed into the depressive type
To treat his Taganrog epiphany as a peak experience and his understanding of his father as a model for viewing people
To contrast Chekhov's methods with those of Maslow and William James
To argue that only people with genetic gifts like Chekhov's can change their attitude
questions.explain: Greene names Chekhov's epiphany a peak experience and asks readers to understand difficult people as Chekhov did his father. The story thus frames the chapter's practical road map.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Explain the self-sabotaging dynamic Greene sees in constricted attitudes.
questions.a: People with a constricted attitude make others feel the same negative emotion that dominates them, which seems to confirm their beliefs about people. They do not see their own role in instigating the response, only persecution or bad luck. By pushing people away they make success doubly hard, and in isolation the attitude gets worse, a vicious cycle.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do we often find several negative attitudes combined in one person?
questions.a: Negative emotions have a binding power: someone who is angry is more prone to also feel suspicion, insecurity and resentment. So the constricted attitudes tend to appear in combinations, each one feeding and accentuating the others.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How do the childhood origins Greene gives for the five constricted attitudes echo his earlier account, in Chapter 8, of where attitudes come from and of the Chekhov family?
questions.a: In Keys to Human Nature Greene traced attitude to genetic inclinations, earliest experiences and internalized parental voices, noting that negative and traumatic experiences have a constricting effect. Each constricted attitude is then rooted in a specific childhood experience, such as a punishing parent, fear of judgment, or a lack of love. The Chekhov family showed the same pattern: Pavel beat his children as he had been beaten, and the siblings grew bitter and secretly worthless.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Describe some of the subtle tricks Greene says people with a hostile attitude use to provoke the hostility they secretly want.
questions.a: They withdraw their cooperation on a project at just the wrong moment, are constantly late, do a poor job, or deliberately make an unfavorable first impression. Their hostility also shows in how they argue, the nasty undertone of their jokes, and their pleasure in others' failures. Yet they never see themselves as playing any role in the reactions they get.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What antidotes does Greene recommend for someone who notices the anxious attitude in themselves?
questions.a: Pour your energies into work, since focusing outward on a project calms you and channels the need for control into something productive, as long as you rein in perfectionism. With people, slowly open yourself to their habits and pace rather than imposing yours. Deliberately place yourself in the circumstances you most dread, discovering that the fears are grossly exaggerated, so you introduce a little chaos into an overly ordered life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do avoidant types find it hard to commit to a job or relationship?
questions.a: If they stayed in a job or relationship, their flaws might become apparent to others. By slipping away at the right moment they keep alive the illusion, for themselves and others, of their possible greatness. Their escape routes, such as sudden illnesses or starting too late, always come with a built-in excuse.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What strategy does Greene recommend for overcoming traces of the avoidant attitude in yourself, and why does it work?
questions.a: Take on a project of even the smallest scale and carry it all the way to completion, embracing the prospect of failure. If you fail, you have cushioned the blow by anticipating it, and it hurts less than imagined; your self-esteem rises simply because you tried and finished something. Either way you win, and once the fear diminishes progress becomes easy.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene suggest handling your own depressive tendencies?
questions.a: Recognize that depressive moods have a necessity: they are the body's and mind's way of making us slow down, lower our energies and withdraw. Realize they are temporary and ride them out, and find ways to raise your energy. For recurrent depression, channel your energies into work, especially the arts, using solitude to tap the unconscious and externalize your sensitivity and dark feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How should you deal with people who have a depressive attitude, according to Greene, and what should you avoid?
questions.a: Never try to lift them up by preaching about the wonderfulness of life. Instead go along with their gloomy opinion of the world while subtly drawing them into positive experiences that raise their mood and energy without any direct appeal. Be aware that they can attract helpers and then wound them, making it hard to disengage without guilt.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene say about the role of willpower and attitude in our energy and health?
questions.a: Though we are mortal and subject to illnesses beyond our control, our attitude plays an enormous role in health: when we fall in love or are excited by work we have more energy and recover quickly, and when depressed or stressed we fall prey to ailments. Feeling excited and challenged lets us safely push beyond supposed physical limits. People age prematurely by accepting limits, while those who age well keep active, so we have untapped wellsprings of energy and health.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: A friend has quit three jobs, each time just before a big deadline, citing a sudden illness, and says that without these setbacks he would have been a great entrepreneur. Using Greene's account, explain what is going on and how you should treat him.
questions.a: This fits the avoidant attitude: escape routes such as illness at the right moment protect him from being judged and keep alive the illusion of his possible greatness. Greene warns to be very wary of forming partnerships with such people, since they slip away at the wrong moment and leave you with the work and the blame. You should also resist the temptation to rescue them from their negativity.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he says to see yourself as an explorer in how you view the world?
questions.a: Most people cling to ideas adopted early in life and are secretly afraid of the unfamiliar; by thirty they act as if they know everything. The explorer leaves certainty behind, searches continually for new ideas, and does not mind seeming inconsistent, treating ideas as things to play with that die if held too long. This returns you to a childlike curiosity, unleashes creative powers, and extends to exploring your own unconscious.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene want us to view adversity, and how do Joan Crawford and Malcolm X illustrate it?
questions.a: Rather than avoiding or repressing difficult experiences, we should embrace obstacles as learning experiences and means of getting stronger. Crawford, punished with a Western, made herself love the genre and saw every setback as a chance to grow. Malcolm X used prison to study, gain discipline and train as a speaker, embracing it without bitterness; adversity may be beyond our control, but our response is not.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Why does Greene recommend feeling destined for something great or important, and how does this differ from the self-belief of Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar?
questions.a: Over time we internalize others' doubts, and accepting supposed limits makes them self-fulfilling. Alexander and Caesar believed they were part divine, and their confidence became a self-fulfilling prophecy; Greene says we need not indulge such grandiose thoughts. A milder sense of destiny gives resilience when people resist us, so we do not internalize their doubts and keep trying new things, confident we can bounce back.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: What does Greene advise about how to view other people when they criticize you or act against you?
questions.a: Drop the tendency to take what people do as personally directed at you; more often it stems from earlier pain they are reliving, and you are a convenient target for their projected frustrations. Seeing this, you avoid getting upset or drawn into petty battles, and if the person is truly malicious you are better placed to plot the proper countermove. You also save yourself from accumulating hurts and bitter feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: How does Greene connect the modern idea of attitude to the ancient concept of the soul?
questions.a: The soul was the overall spirit a person embodies, their way of experiencing the world, and some people were thought to have more of it than others. In the modern version, the external spiritual force is replaced by the life force, life's complexity and diversity. Those who try to inhibit and control it become soulless, dead inside, while the expansive person embraces uncertainty and lets the soul expand to the contours of life itself.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says negative emotions have a ____ power, so a person who is angry is more prone to also feel suspicion and resentment.
questions.explain: Because of this binding power, the constricted attitudes often appear in combination, each feeding the other.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: At work, Greene says, people with the anxious attitude become ferocious perfectionists and ____, eventually sabotaging themselves by trying to keep on top of too many things.
questions.explain: Their need to control everything spills into their work, where it ultimately undermines them.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says avoidant types are prone to all kinds of ____ maladies, such as an illness that strikes in the middle of a high-stakes project.
questions.explain: Illness gives them an escape route with a built-in excuse, so they cannot be judged for failing.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene, describing the explorer's attitude, says ideas are things to play with, and if you hold on to them for too long they become something ____.
questions.explain: The explorer keeps searching for new ideas and does not mind contradicting what they believed months before.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Cosima Liszt compared each of Hans von Bülow's self-blaming letters to a ____ twisted in her heart.
questions.explain: She compared each letter to “a sword twisted in my heart,” since his recounted woes made her feel guilty and depressed.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: As a child, Tiberius was described by his tutor as a pitcher molded with blood and ____.
questions.explain: The tutor's remark, “a pitcher molded with blood and bile,” showed that something was wrong with the boy early on, the root of his resentful attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In his antidote to the resentful attitude, Greene says respect is something that must be earned through your ____, not given simply for being human.
questions.explain: Resentful types feel they are owed recognition; Greene counters that respect has to be earned.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says that most people, secretly afraid of the unfamiliar, replace curiosity with ____.
questions.explain: By thirty such people act as if they know everything; the explorer instead leaves that certainty behind.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene's goal for the reader is to open the ____ of the lens as wide as possible, expanding what they see and experience.
questions.explain: The image continues the lens metaphor: the negative attitude narrows the aperture, the positive one expands it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene says Chekhov's epiphany in Taganrog was what Abraham Maslow called a ____ experience.
questions.explain: Peak experiences lift us out of the daily grind and can alter the attitude for good, so Greene urges seeking them out.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In his advice on how to view other people, Greene says to see people as facts of ____, coming in all varieties like flowers or rocks.
questions.explain: Seeing people this way means accepting diversity rather than trying to reengineer human nature.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: In Greene's modern conception of the soul, the ancient external spiritual force is replaced with life itself, or the ____.
questions.explain: Those who try to inhibit and control the life force veer toward the soulless; the expansive person fills the soul with it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Greene advises learning to measure the people you deal with by the depth of their ____, associating where possible with the expansive variety.
questions.explain: The soul here stands for a person's overall spirit and way of experiencing the world.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Chapter 8, Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude, presents the Law of ____.
questions.explain: The constricted attitudes illustrate the law directly, since each has a self-sabotaging dynamic that creates the very circumstances people fear.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these are tricks Greene says people with a hostile attitude use to provoke the hostility they secretly want?
options: Constantly being late
Withdrawing their cooperation on a project at just the wrong moment
Deliberately making an unfavorable first impression
Developing an illness in the middle of a big project
Flattering people lavishly to disarm them
questions.explain: These behaviors stir anger that confirms the hostile person's view of the world. Pleasing and sudden illness belong to the anxious and avoidant attitudes.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these are escape strategies Greene attributes to people with the avoidant attitude?
options: Wasting time and starting too late, with a built-in excuse
Plotting revenge against those who criticized them
Suddenly developing an illness in the middle of a high-stakes project
Micromanaging every detail of a project
Blaming an addiction, a so-called disease, for falling short
questions.explain: Each lets avoidant types escape being judged for mediocre results. Micromanaging fits the anxious type, and plotted revenge the resentful type.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these are antidotes Greene recommends for someone with the anxious attitude?
options: Deliberately place yourself in the circumstances you most dread
Slowly open yourself to other people's habits and pace
Withdraw from people until the anxiety passes
Explode into anger rather than letting worries build
Pour your energies into work or a project
questions.explain: Outward-focused work calms, adapting to others shows that loosening control is safe, and facing dreaded situations reveals fears are exaggerated. Exploding into anger is Greene's advice for resentment, not anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these are signs Greene gives for recognizing the resentful type?
options: A checkered career and short-term relationships
Carrying their head a little too high, with a slight smirk
A history of past battles and sudden breaks with people
Seeming brittle and demanding extra careful attention
Scanning faces for signs of disrespect
questions.explain: Arrogant bearing, a record of breaks, and constant scanning for slights mark resentful types. Brittleness is anxious, and a checkered career is avoidant.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say will elevate when you improve your overall attitude?
options: Your ability to handle stress
Your relationships with people
Your inherited genetic inclinations
Your creative powers
The events that happen to you by chance
questions.explain: Greene says attitude governs seemingly separate problems, so improving it lifts creativity, stress-handling, confidence and relationships. Chance events and genetic inclinations are not what he claims attitude changes.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as possible sources of a peak experience?
options: Exerting yourself past what you thought were your limits
Winning a heated argument
Taking a trip to a very different culture
Settling into a comfortable routine
Climbing a mountain
questions.explain: Greene also mentions overcoming great obstacles and the deep bonding of love. Comfortable routine is what the constricted attitude clings to.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene associate with people who veer toward the soulless?
options: Remaining true to ideas that have lost their relevance
Becoming obsessed with one goal such as making money or getting attention
Adapting to circumstances instead of complaining about them
Embracing uncertainty as a valuable quality of life
questions.explain: Trying to inhibit and control the life force leads to limited thought and petty obsessions, leaving people dead inside. Adapting and embracing uncertainty describe the expansive soul.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as ways insights from your own unconscious are revealed?
options: Careful logical analysis
Conversations with mentors
Your dreams
Repressed desires that leak out in certain moments
Moments of tiredness
questions.explain: Greene treats the unconscious as one more realm for the explorer to freely explore, with nothing to fear or repress there.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Which of these ideas from earlier in Chapter 8 reappear in the section on the expansive attitude?
options: Chekhov's epiphany in Taganrog
The two young Americans studying in Paris
Attitude as a lens whose aperture can be narrowed or widened
Chekhov's effort to understand his father
Jung's example of hikers crossing a brook
questions.explain: The expansive section calls Chekhov's epiphany a peak experience, urges opening the lens's aperture, and offers Chekhov's understanding of his father as a model. The brook and Paris examples stay in Keys to Human Nature.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says some children develop a hostile attitude because they interpret weaning and the natural separation from their parents as hostile actions.
questions.explain: Other children face a punishing parent; either way the child sees a hostile world and seeks control by becoming its source.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: In the battle over Franklin Roosevelt's care after he contracted polio, his mother Sara eventually won out over his wife Eleanor.
questions.explain: Eleanor, who knew Franklin needed to return slowly to his old life, eventually won. Sara had tried to confine him and make him a helpless invalid.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says avoidant types fear failure but are secretly drawn to success, since it would prove their greatness.
questions.explain: Greene says they are also secretly afraid of success, because it brings responsibilities and could revive early fears about standing out.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when we fall in love or feel excited by our work, we suddenly have more energy and recover quickly from illnesses.
questions.explain: He uses this common experience to show the role willpower and attitude play in health; depression and stress do the opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says people with the resentful attitude typically explode in anger the moment they feel disrespected.
questions.explain: Resentful types are cautious and control their emotions; the hurt incubates and later comes out as plotted sabotage or passive aggression.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene warns never to try to lift depressive people up by preaching to them about the wonderfulness of life.
questions.explain: Instead he advises going along with their gloomy view while subtly drawing them into positive experiences.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the cool, ironic attitude of the postmodern world is more progressive than the positive, expansive attitude.
questions.explain: Greene says the reverse: the cool attitude masks fear and will fade, while the expansive attitude is much more progressive.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: Greene says those who age well continue to engage in physical activity, only moderately adjusted.
questions.explain: People age prematurely by accepting physical limits, a self-fulfilling cycle; those who keep active tap reserves of energy.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 8, the section on the expansive attitude comes last, after the five forms of the constricted attitude.
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Chekhov's story to the nature of attitude, then the constricted forms, and ends with the expansive road map.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the five forms of the constricted attitude in the order Greene presents them.
items: The Hostile Attitude
The Anxious Attitude
The Avoidant Attitude
The Depressive Attitude
The Resentful Attitude
questions.explain: Greene begins with hostility and ends with resentment, noting that these forms often combine.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put these events in Greene's account of Joan Crawford's career in order.
items: She grows frustrated by the limited roles she is getting
She voices her opinion to Irving Thalberg
Thalberg casts her in a Western as punishment
She becomes an expert rider and studies the Old West
She treats every later setback as a chance to grow
questions.explain: Thalberg saw her assertiveness as impudence, but Crawford turned the punishment into a lifelong attitude toward adversity.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put these events in Greene's account of Hans von Bülow and Cosima Liszt in order.
items: Cosima, drawn to his air of sadness, marries him
He withdraws during bouts of depression and falls ill during her pregnancy
Cosima begins an affair with Richard Wagner
After she leaves, he bombards her with self-blaming letters
He remarries and repeats the pattern
questions.explain: The story shows the depressive cycle of attracting a helper, withdrawing, wounding through self-blame, and starting over.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put these events in Greene's account of the emperor Tiberius in order.
items: His tutor describes him as molded with blood and bile
Augustus apologizes to the Senate for his haughty manners
As emperor he coldly takes revenge on those who slighted him
He retires to Capri for the last eleven years of his reign
Rome celebrates his death
questions.explain: Greene uses Tiberius as the classic resentful type, from early signs through vengeance to universal hatred.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put the parts of Greene's road map for the expansive attitude in the order he presents them.
items: How to view the world
How to view adversity
How to view yourself
How to view your energy and health
How to view other people
questions.explain: After the road map, Greene closes by relating attitude to the ancient concept of the soul.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Put these stages of Malcolm Little's prison experience, as Greene tells it, in order.
items: He begins an eight-to-ten-year sentence for burglary
He falls in love with books in the prison library
He studies, builds discipline, and trains as a speaker
After release he treats every difficulty as a test to toughen himself
questions.explain: Instead of being hardened and narrowed by prison, he used it to change himself, then carried that attitude into life outside.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each constricted attitude to its core motive as Greene describes it.
pairs: Controls a hostile world by becoming the source of hostility
Fears losing control, so narrows where they go and what they attempt
Dreads being judged, so avoids responsibility and challenge
Manufactures gloom so that sadness is at least under their control
Never feels given enough recognition and nurses slights
questions.explain: Each constricted attitude is a strategy for controlling a frightening world, rooted in childhood experience.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
