questions.q: Match each constricted attitude to Greene's advice for overcoming it in yourself.
pairs: Approach new people with silent positive thoughts
Pour your energies into work and face the circumstances you dread
Finish a small project while embracing the prospect of failure
See the mood as temporary and channel it into work, especially the arts
Let go of hurts and become more generous toward people
questions.explain: Each antidote attacks the specific fear behind the attitude, from suspicion to dread of judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each constricted attitude to Greene's advice for dealing with others who have it.
pairs: Stay neutral and do not feed their antagonism
Provide a soothing influence and radiate calmness
Be wary of partnerships and do not try to rescue them
Go along with their gloom while drawing them into positive experiences
questions.explain: Greene's advice in each case avoids giving the attitude the fuel it seeks. For the resentful type he advises supreme caution and, if possible, avoidance.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each figure to their role in Greene's account of the constricted attitudes.
pairs: Disguised an anxious need to dominate as love for her son
Depressive conductor who wounded his wife with self-blame
Drawn to a man's sadness and hoped to rescue him
Resentful emperor who coldly avenged old slights
questions.explain: Each figure illustrates a constricted attitude or, in Cosima's case, how depressive types attract helpers.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each part of Greene's road map to its key advice.
pairs: See yourself as an explorer who plays with ideas
Feel destined for something great or important
Push beyond what you think are your physical limits
Do not take what people do as personally directed at you
questions.explain: Together these widen the aperture of the attitude in every area of life.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each name to its role in Greene's section on the expansive attitude.
pairs: First promulgated the idea of attitude in the 1890s
Embraced a punishing role in Westerns
Said the world shapes itself by how a man looks at it
questions.explain: James's idea is called a revolution waiting to happen; Schopenhauer's lines close the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Match each idea from the second half of Chapter 8 to the link Greene or the book's contents make with it.
pairs: Opening the aperture of the lens
The lens metaphor from Keys to Human Nature
questions.explain: Greene cites the Pleaser explicitly, reuses the lens metaphor and the Chekhov story, and his call to explore the repressed unconscious leads into the next chapter on the dark side.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these behaviors into the hostile or the anxious attitude, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Constantly being late
Nasty undertone in their jokes
Describes life as full of battles and betrayals
Subtly dominates domestic rituals and habits
Seems brittle and demands careful attention
Becomes fretful outside their comfort zone

questions.explain: Hostile types provoke conflict that confirms their view; anxious types narrow and control their world to avoid surprises.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these traits into the avoidant or the depressive attitude, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Checkered career and short relationships
Poses as a noble idealist
Starts too late, with a built-in excuse
Secretly drawn to the gloomy, seamy side of life
Withdraws from people to manage the mood
Feels deeply ashamed without knowing why

questions.explain: Avoidant types escape judgment; depressive types feel worthless from childhood and manufacture gloom to control it.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these descriptions into the depressive or the resentful attitude, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Felt unloved and decided they were unworthy
Wounds helpers, then withdraws
Develops blocks in their work after success
Always greedy for more attention as a child
Sees anyone with more as a personal affront
Carries an air of arrogance and disdain

questions.explain: Both attitudes start with a lack of love, but depressive types turn it inward as worthlessness, while resentful types turn it outward as a grievance.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into Greene's advice for overcoming a constricted attitude in yourself or his advice for dealing with others who have one.

items.t: Finish a small project and embrace possible failure
Introduce a little chaos into an overly ordered life
Stop seeing everything in personal terms
Maintain your neutrality against their antagonism
Radiate calmness rather than relying on words
Avoid the temptation to rescue them from their negativity

questions.explain: For each attitude Greene gives both an antidote for latent traces in yourself and a way to handle stronger versions in others.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these traits into Greene's constricted (negative) attitude or expansive (positive) attitude.

items.t: Expects bad things to happen in most situations
Builds elaborate defenses against other viewpoints
Blames others or bad luck for failures
Treats ideas as things to play with
Sees setbacks as chances to grow
Accepts people as they are

questions.explain: The constricted attitude narrows the lens out of fear; the expansive attitude opens it to new experience and people.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these into the soulless condition or the expansive soul, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Tries to inhibit and control the life force
Everything is about their petty needs
Obsessed with making money or getting attention
Rediscovers childlike curiosity
Sees their own role in any failure
Embraces uncertainty and the unexpected

questions.explain: The soulless close themselves off and grow dead inside; the expansive soul fills itself with the life force.

questions.unitTitle: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude
questions.q: Sort these pieces of advice under Greene's heading on how to view yourself or how to view other people.

items.t: Do not be so humble and self-effacing
Feel destined for something great or important
Seek out peak experiences
See people as facts of nature
Recognize that their criticism often stems from earlier pain
Accept diversity rather than feel it as a challenge

questions.explain: Viewing yourself expansively removes internalized limits; viewing others expansively removes petty reactions and builds tolerance.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to the Law of Repression, what lurks beneath people’s polite, affable exterior?
options: A calculating mind that consciously plans every social move
An inborn goodness that society has slowly corrupted
A shadow side of repressed insecurities and aggressive, selfish impulses
A deep fear of death that people refuse to discuss
questions.explain: The law says that under the pleasant front lies a dark, shadow side made of the insecurities and aggressive, selfish impulses people repress and hide. It is unconscious, not a deliberate plan.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Law of Repression, how does Greene tell you to read people’s overt traits, such as toughness or saintliness?
options: As reliable evidence of their true character
As proof that their Shadow is unusually thin
As covering up the opposite quality
As masks they consciously choose each morning
questions.explain: The law advises seeing overt traits such as toughness or saintliness as covering up the opposite quality, an idea the chapter later develops under contradictory behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: The Law of Repression says that by ____ the dark side into your personality, you will be a more complete human.
questions.explain: Greene’s goal is not to remove the dark side but to integrate it, which makes you more complete and authentic.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Repression says that by becoming conscious of your own dark side you can control and channel the creative energies in your unconscious.
questions.explain: The law states: “In being conscious of it you can control and channel the creative energies that lurk in your unconscious.”

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does the Law of Repression promise to the person who becomes aware of and integrates their own dark side?
questions.a: They can control and channel the creative energies lurking in their unconscious instead of being driven by them. By integrating the dark side into their personality they become a more complete human and radiate an authenticity that draws people to them.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Repression say about the dark side?
options: It consists of insecurities and aggressive, selfish impulses people repress
You should learn to recognize its signs before they become toxic
It leaks out in behavior that can baffle and harm you
It disappears once a person reaches adulthood
It exists only in criminals and openly cruel people
questions.explain: The law describes the Shadow as repressed insecurities and selfish impulses that leak out in harmful behavior, and urges you to spot its signs early. It says everyone has one, not just criminals, and it does not fade with age.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, what nickname did the young Richard Nixon earn for his inhuman work habits as a student?
options: RN
Iron Butt
Mr. Peace
The new Nixon
questions.explain: Too poor to pay for an elite education, Nixon made himself a superior student and was nicknamed Iron Butt for his work habits. RN and Mr. Peace were later names for his presidential persona.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, why did Eisenhower nearly drop Nixon as his running mate in 1952?
options: He felt uncomfortable with Nixon and used a secret-fund charge as an excuse
Nixon had just lost the race for governor of California
Nixon had publicly criticized Eisenhower’s handling of the war
Nixon had been caught spying on Democratic Party offices
questions.explain: Nixon had kept a secret fund he was accused of using privately; he was innocent, but Eisenhower disliked him and used it as an excuse. A televised speech saved his place on the ticket.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, whose persona of authority and love of country did Nixon set out to copy as president?
options: Dwight D. Eisenhower
Charles de Gaulle
Henry Kissinger
Abraham Lincoln
questions.explain: Nixon admired the French president Charles de Gaulle and wanted to craft the same kind of persona. Lincoln and Wilson were presidents he hoped to rank among, not the model for his persona.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, why did Nixon install a secret voice-activated taping system in the White House?
options: Because the CIA required all White House meetings to be recorded
To gather evidence against Larry O’Brien and the Democrats
To help Kissinger prepare for negotiations with China
To catch possible leakers and, later, to show posterity his greatness as a leader
questions.explain: Knowing loyalty was fleeting, Nixon wanted to keep tabs on his staff and, after his presidency, use edited tapes to show how clearly and rationally he made decisions. The tapes were meant to secure his legacy.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, how did Alger Hiss insult Nixon during their interview?
options: He noted he had attended Harvard Law School while Nixon had gone to Whittier
He said Nixon would never be elected to any office
He accused Nixon of keeping a secret political fund
He mocked Nixon’s Quaker upbringing
questions.explain: When Nixon reminded him of the perjury law, Hiss pointed out he had attended Harvard Law School and asked if Nixon’s school was Whittier, a jab at Nixon’s lowly college.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, what did Nixon urge Haldeman to assemble before the 1972 election?
options: A panel of intellectuals to advise him on policy
A team of nutcutters to spy and get dirt on the Democrats
A press office to promote him as Mr. Peace
A committee to investigate leaks about the Vietnam War
questions.explain: Wanting a landslide and certain O’Brien had tricks planned, Nixon told Haldeman to assemble a team of nutcutters to do the dirty work. Nixon expressly did not want intellectuals around him.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, what was the “smoking gun” among the tapes the Supreme Court ordered handed over?
options: Hunt’s demands for hush money in exchange for silence
A recording of Nixon directly ordering the Watergate break-in
The June 23, 1972, conversation approving use of the CIA to quash the FBI investigation
Nixon’s remarks about Jewish staff at the Bureau of Labor Statistics
questions.explain: The June 23 conversation showed Nixon had approved having the CIA pressure the FBI to drop the case, revealing his part in the cover-up from early on. Greene notes he never directly ordered the break-in.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, what simple way out of the Watergate mess does Greene say Nixon could not bring himself to take?
options: Hire an outside lawyer for a full internal investigation and bring everything to light
Resign immediately after winning the 1972 election
Publicly blame the break-in on the CIA
Destroy the tapes before an official subpoena arrived
questions.explain: Greene says an outside investigation would have damaged him but kept him politically alive; coming clean frightened him too much. Destroying the tapes was Haig’s later advice, a different decision.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, how did Nixon’s speechwriter Ray Price describe the relationship between the light Nixon and the dark Nixon?
options: They were at constant war with one another
They were two masks Nixon consciously switched between
The dark Nixon appeared only in public
The light Nixon had fully replaced the dark one by 1968
questions.explain: Price saw a considerate, generous light Nixon and an angry, vindictive dark Nixon, both “at constant war with one another.”

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the Nixon story, where did Henry Kissinger believe the key to Nixon’s split personality lay?
options: In his defeat by Kennedy
In his years as vice president
In his Quaker religion
In his childhood
questions.explain: Kissinger, who studied Nixon closely, thought the key lay in his childhood and wondered what Nixon would have been like if somebody had loved him.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Kissinger, as quoted in the Nixon story, what did Nixon fear more than anything?
options: Being thought weak
Losing an election
Being exposed as a liar
Being forgotten by history
questions.explain: Kissinger said there was nothing Nixon feared more than to be thought weak, which is why he built a supremely tough, decisive persona over his vulnerable side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: A colleague known for being unfailingly pleasant sends a cutting remark after weeks of stress, then insists it was just the pressure. In Greene’s account of the dark side, what is most likely happening?
options: They are deliberately testing your loyalty
Their pleasantness was always a conscious, calculated act
Stress has created a brand-new personality in them
Repressed traits from their dark side are leaking out under stress
questions.explain: Greene says the dark side leaks out under pressure in touchy moods and offhand comments people later regret, and that we tend to blame circumstances for them. The front is not a conscious lie; the repressed side is unconscious.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: After losing the 1962 race for governor of California, Nixon told the press they would no longer have Nixon to ____ around.
questions.explain: The bitter remark was widely seen as self-pity, and his political career seemed over, setting up yet another comeback.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In his notebooks, Nixon referred to the world-leader version of himself as ____.
questions.explain: RN was to be strong, resolute, compassionate yet completely masculine, the persona he wanted history to remember.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: As a junior congressman, Nixon relentlessly pursued the State Department staffer Alger ____, who was accused of being a communist spy.
questions.explain: Nixon got Hiss indicted for perjury; the victory made him famous but, he believed, earned him the lasting wrath of East Coast elites.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: The Watergate break-in was an attempt to plant bugs in the offices of the Democratic Party chairman, Larry ____.
questions.explain: Nixon saw O’Brien as the evil genius of politics, the man who had once had him audited by the IRS.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says depression and anxiety come from not being your complete self, from always playing a ____.
questions.explain: He argues it takes great energy to keep the dark side at bay, and the strain of playing a role shows up as depression and anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that once your dark side is subjected to conscious ____, it loses its destructive power.
questions.explain: The task of a student of human nature is to recognize and examine the dark side, because conscious scrutiny strips it of its destructive power.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that once you are aware of your dark side, you can turn your neediness and vulnerability into ____.
questions.explain: Awareness lets you channel dark energies productively: neediness becomes empathy, aggression goes into worthwhile causes and work.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Kissinger once asked what Nixon would have been like if somebody had ____ him.
questions.explain: The remark points to Nixon’s needy infancy with a cold father and an often absent, moody mother, which Greene sees as the root of his dark side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How did Nixon’s career before 1968 show his habit of turning setbacks into comebacks?
questions.a: Too poor for an Ivy League school, he worked so hard he won a scholarship to Duke law school. When Eisenhower tried to drop him in 1952 over a secret fund, he saved himself with a televised speech, and after the crushing defeats of 1960 and 1962 he laid low, then returned as the more relaxed new Nixon and won in 1968. Greene likens him to a cat with nine lives.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why was Nixon so bitter toward the East Coast elites, and how did the Alger Hiss case feed this?
questions.a: Nixon’s pursuit of Hiss, the darling of the liberals, made him famous but earned him the lasting wrath of East Coast elites, many of them Harvard graduates, who saw him as an upstart from Whittier. They kept him and Pat out of their social circles and their allies in the press ridiculed him. As president he kept reliving these wounds with his staff and believed these old enemies were still working against him.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why did Nixon not destroy the tapes, and how does Greene interpret his attachment to them?
questions.a: Nixon reasoned that destroying them would look like an admission of guilt and that they might even clear him, since he had never directly ordered the break-in. Greene reads deeper: Nixon never filtered what he said though he knew he was recorded, and he held on to the tapes mesmerized by the other Nixon on them. It was as if he secretly desired his own punishment, the denied child and dark side taking revenge.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, how did Nixon’s childhood shape both his public persona and his dark side?
questions.a: Nixon was a needy, crying infant, but his parents wanted a stoic, self-reliant child; his father could be cold and abusive and his mother was moody and often away nursing his sick brothers. To hide his vulnerability he built a tough, resilient, rational persona. The unmet needs of the weak child sank into the unconscious and became his dark side, stirring under stress as insecurity, suspicion, outbursts and the urge to harm enemies.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene say the story of Nixon is closer to your own reality than you might like to imagine?
questions.a: Like Nixon, you have crafted a public persona that stresses your strengths and hides your weaknesses, and you have repressed the less acceptable traits you had as a child. You too have a dark side of insecurities, revenge fantasies, suspicions and hunger for attention and power. It leaks out in moods and regretted comments, and you blame circumstances or others because you do not see its source.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does Greene say becomes possible once you learn to detect the signs of your own dark side?
questions.a: You can channel its darker energy into productive activity: turning neediness and vulnerability into empathy and aggressive impulses into worthwhile causes and work. You can admit your ambitions without guilt or stealth and monitor your suspicions and your projection of negative emotions onto others. Seeing that selfish impulses live in you too brings balance and greater tolerance for others.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene hold up Abraham Lincoln and Winston Churchill against the example of Nixon?
questions.a: Greene argues that straining to project constant strength and saintliness makes you seem phony. Lincoln and Churchill could examine their flaws and mistakes and laugh at themselves, so they came across as authentically human, and this was the source of their charm. Nixon’s tragedy was that he had immense talent but could not look within at the darker side of his character.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How did the release of the tape transcripts change the public’s view of Nixon?
questions.a: Even those who thought him slippery were horrified by the forceful language, the swearing, the hysterical, paranoid tone and the lack of hesitation in ordering illegal acts. On Watergate he seemed weak and indecisive, nothing like the de Gaulle image he wanted, and he never showed a desire to get at the truth and punish wrongdoers. Even his family was shocked; it was as if another person were on the tapes.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: in the 1972 election, Nixon won every state except Massachusetts.
questions.explain: Greene describes one of the biggest landslides in electoral history: Nixon swept every state except Massachusetts and the District of Columbia, before Watergate came back to haunt him.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Alexander Haig advised Nixon to keep the tapes and fight their release through executive privilege.
questions.explain: Haig told Nixon to tear out the taping system and destroy the tapes before a subpoena arrived. Invoking executive privilege was Nixon’s own decision after he chose not to destroy them.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: according to Greene, Nixon’s parents enjoyed fussing over their needy infant and encouraged his demands for attention.
questions.explain: His parents disliked his neediness; growing up in pioneer southern California, they preferred a stoic, self-reliant child.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that only people who project continual strength and saintliness can become successful.
questions.explain: Greene says this might seem true but is not: playing such a role emits a phoniness others pick up, while figures like Lincoln and Churchill charmed people by laughing at their own flaws.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these did Nixon name to his staff as old enemies still working against him?
options: Charles de Gaulle
Daniel Schorr of CBS
Katharine Graham of the Washington Post
Larry O’Brien of the Democratic Party
Henry Kissinger
questions.explain: Nixon railed against Schorr’s Vietnam reports, Graham’s newspaper and Georgetown circle, and O’Brien, who had had him audited. Kissinger was his own national security adviser and de Gaulle a hero he admired.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as ways your own dark side leaks out?
options: Touchy moods and sudden neediness
Moments of inexplicable depression
Unusual generosity toward rivals
Offhand comments you later regret
A steady growth in patience
questions.explain: Greene says the dark side haunts your dreams and leaks out in depression, anxiety, touchy moods, sudden neediness, suspicious thoughts and regretted comments.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these did the public discover when Nixon’s edited tape transcripts were released?
options: A strong desire to punish the wrongdoers
A decisive, de Gaulle-like handling of Watergate
A sometimes hysterical, paranoid tone
No hesitation in ordering illegal acts
Forceful language and swearing
questions.explain: The transcripts revealed swearing, paranoia and a lack of compunction about illegal acts. On Watergate he seemed weak and indecisive and never showed any desire to get at the truth.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say you can do once you are aware of your own dark side?
options: Monitor your projection of negative emotions onto others
Admit your ambitions without acting guiltily and stealthily
Stop ever feeling anxious or suspicious
Channel aggressive impulses into worthwhile causes and work
Eliminate the dark side from your character entirely
questions.explain: Awareness lets you channel and monitor the dark side, not erase it. Greene’s point is that selfish impulses always dwell within you; seeing them brings balance and tolerance.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put these events in Nixon’s career in the order they happened.
items: Chosen as Eisenhower’s running mate
Lost the presidency to Kennedy
Lost the race for governor of California
Defeated Humphrey for the presidency
Won a landslide against McGovern
questions.explain: The story runs from 1952 through the defeats of 1960 and 1962 to his comeback in 1968 and his landslide reelection in 1972.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put these stages of the Watergate affair in the order Greene describes them.
items: Burglars caught bugging O’Brien’s offices
Nixon approves using the CIA to pressure the FBI
The Senate launches an investigation
McCord implicates White House staff
The Senate learns of the taping system
Edited transcripts are released as a book
questions.explain: The break-in came in June 1972 and the CIA conversation a few days later; the Senate investigation began in January 1973, McCord talked in March, the tapes were discovered in July, and transcripts came out in April 1974.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the final steps of Nixon’s downfall in the order they happened.
items: He releases edited transcripts of the tapes
The Supreme Court orders the tapes themselves handed over
He decides to resign
He addresses his staff one last time
questions.explain: After the transcripts horrified the public, the Supreme Court’s order exposed the smoking gun, Nixon resigned in early August, and the next morning he spoke to his staff before leaving.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene’s explanation of Nixon’s dark side in order.
items: A needy infant who demanded attention
Parents who wanted a stoic, self-reliant child
A tough, resilient persona built to hide vulnerability
The unmet needs sink into the unconscious
Under stress, insecurity and suspicion erupt
questions.explain: Greene traces how the weak child’s needs were denied, covered by a tough persona, pushed into the shadows, and then resurfaced whenever Nixon felt stress or anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene’s lesson to the reader after the Nixon story in order.
items: You craft a persona that hides your weaknesses
You repress traits you had as a child
Your dark side leaks out in moods and remarks
You blame circumstances or other people
You examine the dark side so it loses its power
questions.explain: Greene moves from the persona and repression we share with Nixon, to the leaks and our misplaced blame, and ends with the task of examining the dark side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each member of Nixon’s team to their role.
questions.explain: Nixon chose loyal, clean-cut go-getters for his personal staff and Kissinger for national security. Haldeman and Ehrlichman were later fired over Watergate.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each figure Nixon resented to the reason he gave.
pairs: His Vietnam reports always made Nixon look bad
Her newspaper seemed to have a vendetta against him
He had managed to get Nixon audited by the IRS
His case earned Nixon the wrath of East Coast elites
questions.explain: Nixon kept reliving these old wounds with his staff, convinced his enemies were everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each figure in the Watergate story to their part in it.
pairs: Implicated White House staff in March 1973
Demanded hush money to keep quiet
Advised destroying the tapes at once
Ran the internal investigation and was told to stonewall
questions.explain: Each appears in Greene’s account of how the cover-up unraveled despite Nixon’s efforts.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each source to what it says about Nixon or the dark side.
pairs: Saw a light and a dark Nixon at constant war
Wondered what Nixon would be like if somebody had loved him
Said only a miracle could get Nixon elected again
To live is to war with trolls in heart and soul
questions.explain: Price and Kissinger are Greene’s witnesses to the two Nixons, Time wrote Nixon off in 1962, and Ibsen’s words close the story.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these traits into the two Nixons described by his speechwriter Ray Price.

items.t: Exceptionally considerate
Sentimental
Generous of spirit
Angry
Vindictive
Mean-spirited

questions.explain: Price listed caring, sentimental and generous traits for the light Nixon and angry, vindictive, ill-tempered traits for the dark one.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into Nixon’s intended presidential persona and what the tapes revealed.

items.t: Strong and resolute
A man of law and order
Mr. Peace
Swearing and forceful language
Paranoid revenge fantasies
Waffling over simple decisions
Insulting close friends behind their backs

questions.explain: Nixon meant to embody a strong, peaceful, law-and-order leader, but the tapes caught the other Nixon: paranoid, vengeful, profane and indecisive.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into what Nixon claimed about himself and what the story shows.

items.t: He never cried
He never held grudges
He did not care what others thought of him
He sobbed while firing Ehrlichman
He kept reliving old wounds from the Hiss case
He wanted to know what Georgetown elites said about him

questions.explain: Greene says Nixon denied his weakness with vehemence, insisting on the opposite of the truth, while his behavior kept exposing it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Jung, as Greene presents him, what determines the thickness of a person’s Shadow?
options: How many stressful events a person has lived through
How strict a person’s religious upbringing was
How deep the repression is and how many traits are concealed
How early in life a person first learned to lie
questions.explain: Greene reports Jung’s view that the Shadow’s thickness depends on the depth of repression and the number of traits concealed, and says Nixon had a particularly thick one.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene say the Shadow tends to emerge more as people get older?
options: They tire of the masks they have been wearing
Their childhood impulses grow stronger with age
Their memory weakens and they forget their roles
They face fewer social pressures to behave
questions.explain: When young we find even our social roles exciting, but later we tire of our masks, so the leakage is greater.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, what do we see of people when we know nothing of their Shadow?
options: A faithful mirror of our own personality
A dangerous stranger we should avoid
A grown child who never left childhood
A flattened, two-dimensional image of their pleasant social side
questions.explain: Greene says that without knowing the Shadow we see only a flat image; knowing its contours makes people come to life in three dimensions.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which sign of the Shadow does Greene call the most eloquent of all?
options: Vehement denial
Projection
Contradictory behavior
Emotional outbursts
questions.explain: Contradictory behavior, actions that belie a person’s carefully built front, is the most eloquent sign. Projection is the most common, not the most eloquent.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which way of dealing with the Shadow does Greene call by far the most common, because it offers almost daily release?
options: Emotional outbursts
Accidental behavior
Overidealization
Projection
questions.explain: Projection lets us attribute our own unadmitted desires for sex, money, power or superiority to others, then judge them, a release available nearly every day.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does Greene find telling about Richard Wagner’s attacks on Jewish influence in music?
options: Wagner refused ever to work with Jewish musicians
Wagner himself had the eclectic, sentimental qualities he condemned
Wagner’s charges were based on careful study
Wagner later publicly apologized for his views
questions.explain: Wagner’s charges were mostly made up, yet he shared the traits he blamed on Jews and relied on Jewish pianists and conductors. Greene uses him to show projection.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does Greene answer the idea that people today are less repressed than their ancestors?
options: It is true, because science has replaced organized religion
It is true, so the Shadow is now mainly a historical idea
We may be more split than ever, because of codes of correctness and shaming
It is true only of the younger generations
questions.explain: Greene argues the opposite: enforced correctness, social-media shaming and ideals of selflessness push the dark side even further underground.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What idea does Greene draw from Stevenson’s The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde?
options: Respectable people have no dark side to speak of
Science will one day separate good from evil in people
The more civilized and moral we outwardly become, the more dangerous the Shadow
Evil impulses are always punished in the end
questions.explain: Jekyll, a paragon of goodness, unleashes Hyde, the embodiment of his Shadow. Stevenson’s point, per Greene, is that fierce outward morality makes the denied Shadow more dangerous.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: A friend vows to quit drinking, relapses a week later, and says she just cannot help it because it is an illness. Which sign of the Shadow from Greene’s list does this fit?
options: Vehement denial
Accidental behavior
Contradictory behavior
Overidealization
questions.explain: In accidental behavior people fall into the very behavior they vowed to avoid and blame an uncontrollable illness or dependency, which salves their conscience. Greene says to ignore the excuse and see the Shadow releasing.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that what we glimpse in moments of acting out is the dark side of character, which Carl Jung called the ____.
questions.explain: Jung’s Shadow consists of all the qualities people try to deny about themselves and repress, so deeply that it operates unconsciously.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene quotes Horace: you can throw out Nature with a ____, but she will always come back.
questions.explain: The line captures why repressed impulses keep returning: concealing the Shadow takes energy, and it seeks release.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Freud, as Greene reports, the only way something unpleasant in the unconscious can reach the conscious mind is through active ____.
questions.explain: This is the basis of the sign Greene calls vehement denial: people express the very opposite of what is buried within.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that behind any vehement hatred there is often a secret and very unpalatable ____ of the hated person or people.
questions.explain: He draws this lesson from Wagner: hatred is how the repressed envy finds release from the unconscious.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says to consider yourself a ____ when piecing together people’s Shadow from the signs you pick up.
questions.explain: Like a detective, you fill in the outlines of repressed desires so you can anticipate future leakage, which never happens just once.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Stevenson’s novel, Dr. Jekyll says his devil had long been ____ and came out roaring.
questions.explain: The line illustrates Greene’s point that the more fiercely the Shadow is denied, the more violently it bursts out.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What two conflicting forces in our earliest years does Greene say create the Shadow?
questions.a: First, we came into the world bursting with energy and natural impulses, some of them aggressive and selfish: wanting to monopolize our parents, feel superior, even hurt people. Second, we were completely vulnerable and dependent on our parents, who pushed us to be nice, cooperative and quiet; later peers and teachers added pressure to fit in. To win approval we tamped down the dark side, and much of our nature moved underground into the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What price does Greene say we pay for becoming positive social animals?
questions.a: We lose the intensity, full range of emotions and creativity that came with our wilder childhood energy, and secretly yearn to recapture it, so we are drawn to the forbidden or to alcohol and stimulants. Accumulated hurts and resentments thicken the Shadow, and keeping up a nice, confident front is draining. So the Shadow seeks to release the inner tension and come back to life.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does overidealization serve as a cover for the Shadow, according to Greene?
questions.a: People go beyond enthusiasm for a cause, leader or new investment and see everything in black and white, glossing over every fault. They then feel sanctioned to lie, cheat, manipulate, take wild risks or be greedy for the cause. Greene says the overly strong conviction is simply cover that lets repressed emotions play out, so the bullying and greed should be taken at face value.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does projection work, according to Greene, and how might it play out in a conflict?
questions.a: We cannot admit certain desires, for sex, money, power or superiority, so we see them in others, either inventing them or exaggerating traces of them, and then judge and condemn those people. In a conflict we may accuse the other side of authoritarian desires when they are only defending themselves. In truth we secretly wish to dominate, and the accusation lets us vent that desire and justify our own authoritarian response.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene think modern audiences are drawn to Machiavellian characters, scandals and demagogues?
questions.a: Codes of correctness and pressure to be selfless drive our dark side further underground, so we hunger for expressions of it. Shows about manipulators, news of people caught acting out and fascination with killers give a relatively harmless release while we moralize. More dangerously, demagogues say what we dare not, and in the safety of a group we feel licensed to vent hostility on scapegoats.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What solution to the Shadow does Greene propose, and what does he reject?
questions.a: He rejects more repression and correctness, since human nature cannot be changed by enforced niceness, and he rejects seeking release in the group, which is volatile and dangerous. Instead we should see our Shadow in action and become more self-aware, because it is hard to project or overidealize once we know the mechanism. Through such self-knowledge we can integrate the dark side productively and creatively and become more authentic and complete.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the Shadow becomes disturbed and active in moments of stress or when deep wounds and insecurities are triggered.
questions.explain: Though buried deep, the Shadow stirs under stress or when old wounds are touched, and it also emerges more with age.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that when someone blames an emotional outburst on stress and says they did not mean it, you should accept that explanation.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: the Shadow has spoken, so take what they said at face value.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when people behave differently while drunk, it is often not the alcohol speaking but the Shadow.
questions.explain: Under accidental behavior Greene notes that drunken behavior often reveals the Shadow rather than the drink.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Shadow behavior usually occurs only once and stays confined to one area of a person’s life.
questions.explain: Greene says such behavior never occurs just once and tends to pop up in different areas; bullying in arguments will show up in other activities too.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as signs that someone’s Shadow is being released?
options: Laughing easily at one’s own mistakes
Overidealization
Projection
Vehement denial
Steady, even politeness in every setting
questions.explain: Greene’s signs include contradictory behavior, emotional outbursts, vehement denial, accidental behavior, overidealization and projection. Laughing at oneself is a mark of the authentic, integrated type instead.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these impulses does Greene say we had as young children, before learning to repress them?
options: A natural wish to sit still and cooperate
Finding some pleasure in hurting people
An inborn sense of acceptable behavior
Powerful dislikes, even of our parents
Wanting to monopolize our parents’ attention
questions.explain: Greene stresses that children are not innocent angels: they want attention and superiority and can be selfish and even cruel. Sitting still and knowing what is acceptable were what parents tried to instill.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as ways strong conviction lets repressed aggression leak out?
options: Intellectuals using obscure language to make others feel inferior
Bullying in arguments while calling it an exchange of ideas
Openly admitting the faults of one’s own cause
Giving the doubters’ arguments a fair hearing
Feeling sanctioned to lie, cheat or spy for a cause
questions.explain: Greene says overidealization and powerful convictions license manipulation, bullying and intellectual intimidation. Glossing over faults and seeing doubters as evil is the pattern, not fairness.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these scenarios illustrate projection as Greene defines it?
options: A manager calmly admits she wants a promotion
A woman who secretly wishes to dominate accuses her rival, who is only defending herself, of authoritarian desires
A man who repressed his own ambition sneers at an openly ambitious colleague as a shameless climber
A friend breaks a diet and blames an uncontrollable craving
questions.explain: Projection attributes our own unadmitted desires to others so we can condemn them. Admitting ambition openly is the opposite, and blaming a craving is accidental behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages in the formation of the Shadow in the order Greene describes them.
items: We are born full of energy and natural impulses
Parents push us to be nice and tone down our needs
Peers and teachers press us to fit in
We internalize cultural ideals and the dark side goes underground
We secretly yearn for the lost intensity
questions.explain: Greene moves from the child’s raw impulses, through parental then social pressure, to repression and the adult’s hidden longing for what was lost.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene’s argument about the Shadow in modern culture in order.
items: We assume we are less repressed than our ancestors
Codes of correctness and shaming push the dark side deeper
We thrill at Machiavellian characters and scandals
We are drawn to leaders who vent hostility
The answer is self-awareness, not more repression
questions.explain: Greene rejects the comfortable assumption, explains the pressure, shows its harmless and then dangerous outlets, and ends with his solution.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each sign of the Shadow to its description.
pairs: Actions that belie a carefully constructed front
Sudden loss of self-control and biting, hurtful words
Expressing the very opposite of what is buried within
Falling into avoided behavior and blaming a dependency
Seeing our own taboo desires in others to condemn them
questions.explain: These are the signs Greene lists for recognizing when someone’s Shadow is released.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each figure to the point Greene uses them to make in the Keys to Human Nature.
pairs: Named the dark side of character the Shadow
Nature returns however hard you throw it out
Buried material reaches consciousness through active denial
Hated in others qualities he himself had
The more civilized we become, the more dangerous the Shadow
questions.explain: Greene draws on each to build his picture of how the Shadow forms, hides and comes out.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each example to the sign of the Shadow it shows.
pairs: A tough exterior revealing hysteria at the wrong moment
Someone fulminating against what they secretly desire
Investors taking huge risks on a financial tool they believe is new
Accusing an opponent of authoritarian aims when they are only defending themselves
questions.explain: Each example comes from Greene’s descriptions of the signs of Shadow release.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into the two conflicting forces Greene says shaped us as young children.

items.t: Wanting to monopolize our parents’ attention
Fantasizing about getting revenge
Wanting to feel superior
Being chastised for too much energy
Being urged to play fairly
Needing to fit in with peers

questions.explain: The Shadow grows out of the clash between our raw childhood impulses and the pressure from parents, peers and teachers to be nice and fit in.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these outlets for the dark side into the relatively harmless and the more dangerous, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Watching shows about Machiavellian characters
Enjoying news of people caught acting out
Being enthralled by serial killers and cult leaders
Following demagogues who vent hostility
Venting our spleen on scapegoats in a group
Idealizing a leader to act as we would not alone

questions.explain: Greene calls entertainment and scandal relatively harmless release, but warns that group politics led by demagogues lets the Shadow explode.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into the excuses people give and how Greene says to read the behavior.

items.t: It was just stress
I can’t help it, it’s an illness
It’s just an exchange of ideas
Take what they said at face value
Ignore the justification and see the Shadow releasing
Pay attention to the bullying tone

questions.explain: For outbursts, accidental behavior and bullying arguments, Greene says to disregard the excuse and read the behavior as the Shadow speaking.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene says works against the Shadow and what does not.

items.t: Seeing our Shadow in action
Becoming more self-aware
Integrating the dark side productively
More repression and correctness
Enforced niceness
Seeking release in the group

questions.explain: Greene says the pitchfork does not work and group release is volatile; only self-awareness lets us integrate the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does the subtitle of chapter 9, The Law of Repression, signal about Greene’s argument?
options: People should repress their dark impulses even more firmly
The dark side is created by pushing unacceptable traits out of awareness
Only a few unusually repressed people have a dark side
Repression is a conscious strategy people use to deceive
questions.explain: The chapter argues that repressing natural traits from childhood creates the Shadow, and that more repression is not the cure; awareness and integration are.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does chapter 9 open with the long story of Richard Nixon before its Keys to Human Nature section?
options: It gives a vivid case of a thick Shadow that the Keys then explain in general terms
It argues that Nixon was uniquely evil among presidents
It shows that only politicians develop a dark side
It sets up a chapter mainly about American political history
questions.explain: Like other chapters, chapter 9 opens with a story and then generalizes. Greene insists Nixon’s story is closer to the reader’s reality than one might like, not a special case.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does chapter 9’s idea of the Shadow build on chapter 3, See Through People’s Masks?
questions.a: Chapter 3 teaches reading the masks and roles people play in social life. Chapter 9 goes beneath the mask to what it conceals: the repressed traits that form the Shadow. It explains why the strain of playing a role causes leakage, and why people tire of their masks with age.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does the first half of chapter 9 prepare for its later sections, Deciphering the Shadow: Contradictory Behavior and The Integrated Human?
questions.a: The Keys section lists the signs of Shadow release and singles out contradictory behavior as the most eloquent, which the next section examines in depth. It also ends by rejecting repression and group release in favor of self-awareness and integrating the dark side, the subject of The Integrated Human.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: in chapter 9, the section on deciphering contradictory behavior comes after the Keys to Human Nature, where Greene calls contradictory behavior the most eloquent sign of the Shadow.
questions.explain: The Keys section introduces contradictory behavior as the most eloquent sign and points ahead to the following section for more on reading it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the sections of chapter 9 in order.
items: The Dark Side
Keys to Human Nature
Deciphering the Shadow: Contradictory Behavior
The Integrated Human
questions.explain: The chapter moves from Nixon’s story, to the general theory of the Shadow, to reading contradictory traits, and ends with integrating the dark side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each chapter to the law it presents.
questions.explain: Chapter 9 sits between the law of self-sabotage and the law of envy, and builds on the masks of chapter 3.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these themes of later chapters are already previewed in the first half of chapter 9?
options: Hidden aggression leaking out (the Law of Aggression)
Facing our mortality (the Law of Death Denial)
Secret envy hidden behind hatred (the Law of Envy)
Generational patterns (the Law of Generational Myopia)
The volatile pull of the group (the Law of Conformity)
questions.explain: Greene’s point that hatred hides envy, his warning about release in the group, and his account of repressed aggression all anticipate later chapters. Generations and death are not touched on here.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene's discussion of emphatic traits, what generally lies beneath a person's unusually emphatic trait, such as exaggerated toughness or saintliness?
options: A milder version of the same trait that the person is ashamed of
A trait copied from a parent the person deeply admired
Nothing hidden at all, only a talent the person has honed for years
The opposite trait, which the emphatic one distracts from and conceals
questions.explain: Greene says the emphatic trait generally rests on top of its opposite and hides it from public view. It is not an exaggeration of the same quality but a cover for its contrary.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's account of emphatic traits, why do cracks in the façade tend to appear as such people get older or come under stress?
options: Playing a role to the extreme is tiring, and the repressed real self rebels
Their talents decline and they can no longer support the image
Other people finally learn the truth from their families and expose them
They consciously decide the image has served its purpose and drop it
questions.explain: Greene says these people are playing a role to the extreme and it is exhausting, so their real self rebels in moods, obsessions, secret vices and self-destructive acts. The deeper the repression, the more volatile the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, what does the Tough Guy's rough, intimidating masculinity actually conceal?
options: A secret contempt for the women he claims to have conquered
A cold calculation about how to win every negotiation
A hidden hunger for wealth and social status
An underlying softness and emotional vulnerability that terrifies him
questions.explain: Greene says such men have learned to hide a deep softness and emotional vulnerability. When it slips out, as tears or a tantrum or sudden compassion, they quickly cover it with a tough or cruel act.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's portrait of the Saint, which historical figure, nicknamed the Incorruptible, shows how the Shadow operates once such a person gains power?
options: Napoleon Bonaparte
Leo Tolstoy
Maximilien Robespierre
Richard Wagner
questions.explain: Robespierre rose to power in the French Revolution on a saintly image, and under his reign the guillotine was never busier. Tolstoy appears only as a cross-reference to the Saint's private demonic side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, how can you tell a genuine saint from the fake Saint type?
options: Ask their closest disciples whether they have ever seen any hypocrisy
Ignore their words and aura and look at their deeds and the details of their life
Listen closely to how sincerely and movingly they speak about their causes
Judge them by how many loyal followers they have attracted over the years
questions.explain: Greene advises ignoring the words and the aura they project and focusing on deeds: how much they enjoy power and attention, their wealth, their mistresses, their self-absorption. Genuine saints do not publicize their deeds or grab power.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's portrait of the Passive-Aggressive Charmer, what early sign tells you that you will one day be the target of their Shadow?
options: They smile less and seem more reserved after the first few weeks
Somewhat out of character, they indulge in malicious gossip about someone else
They refuse to accept any favor or help you offer them
They ask you detailed questions about your career and goals
questions.explain: Greene says that if such a person engages in malicious gossip about someone, the Shadow is speaking and you will be the subject of that gossip one day. Extreme niceness at first is the other warning sign.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, why do Fanatics often show radical shifts in their belief system over their past?
options: What matters to them is the intense conviction itself, not the particular belief
They are open-minded thinkers who keep learning from new evidence
Their followers push them to change positions to stay popular
They deliberately test which cause will make them the most money
questions.explain: Greene says it is not the particular belief that matters to the Fanatic but the intensity of conviction, which acts like a drug covering deep insecurity, so they shift it to fit the times.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What rule does Greene give for judging people who speak with great stridency and a flair for drama, like the Fanatic?
options: Stridency is a sign of a healthy and well-integrated Shadow
The greater the stridency, the deeper the underlying insecurities and doubts
The greater the stridency, the stronger their real commitment to the cause
The greater the stridency, the more likely they are to deliver on promises
questions.explain: Greene says to always operate by the rule that the greater the stridency in what they say, the deeper the hidden insecurities and doubts. Strong conviction is a mask, not proof of strength.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, what does true rationality look like, in contrast to the Rigid Rationalist?
options: It is sober and skeptical about its own powers and does not publicize itself
It rejects every form of irrational relaxation, including jokes and play
It treats science and technology with a firm, almost religious faith
It wins every argument with superior statistics and intellectual force
questions.explain: Greene says true rationality should be sober and skeptical about its own powers and not advertise itself. The Rigid Rationalist's faith in science has a religious air, and his anger in argument reveals the primitive stirring within.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's account of the Extreme Entrepreneur, what hidden desire does the outward show of total self-reliance often disguise?
options: A desire to have others take care of them, regressing to childhood dependency
A desire to punish the employees who failed to meet their standards
A desire to become famous for founding a great company
A desire to retire early and leave work behind altogether
questions.explain: Greene says the self-reliance often masks a secret wish to be cared for like a child. Unconsciously they create enough chaos to break down and become dependent on doctors or financiers.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, why are we so strongly drawn to people who seem authentic?
options: They are usually more successful and can help our careers
We secretly mourn the lost child part of our character, and they show it can be integrated
They flatter us and make us feel more comfortable with ourselves
They follow social codes perfectly, so we feel safe in their company
questions.explain: Greene says we all mourn the wildness, spontaneity and open mind of childhood that we lost in becoming adults. Authentic types show the possibility of integrating the child and the adult, the dark and the light.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's discussion of authenticity, which figure does he say in many ways epitomizes the inauthentic type?
options: Abraham Lincoln
Richard Nixon
Winston Churchill
Albert Einstein
questions.explain: Greene contrasts Richard Nixon, the chapter's opening subject, with authentic figures such as Churchill, Lincoln, Chaplin, Josephine Baker, Einstein and Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, which of the four steps for integrating the Shadow is the most difficult?
options: Exploring the Shadow
Embracing the Shadow
Showing the Shadow
Seeing the Shadow
questions.explain: Greene calls seeing the Shadow the most difficult step, because the Shadow is something we deny and repress, and it is far easier to dig up and moralize about other people's dark qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the step of seeing the Shadow, what does Greene suggest it means if you intensely loathe narcissistic or pushy people?
options: You have a strong and healthy moral sense that protects you
You are naturally humble and cannot understand such behavior
You have been badly hurt by such people in the past
You are probably brushing up against your own narcissistic tendencies and wish to be more assertive
questions.explain: Greene says this vehement hatred is likely a projection: we are especially sensitive to traits in others that we repress in ourselves, such as our own narcissism or secret desire for assertiveness.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene suggest looking back at moments in your late teens and early twenties when you acted insensitively or cruelly?
options: Because you need to apologize to the people you hurt before you can move on
Because those acts were the result of bad influences you have since escaped
Because you had less control of the Shadow then, so it came out more naturally
Because your character was not yet formed, so those acts reveal nothing about you
questions.explain: Greene says that when we were younger we had less control over the Shadow, so it emerged naturally rather than with the repressed force of later years. Those moments are clues to it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's story of Robert Bly, what had Bly long railed against in his writing that he eventually found in himself?
options: The bohemian artists of the counterculture
Religious leaders who preached against pleasure
Calculating, manipulative advertising men and businesspeople
The Romantic poets of the nineteenth century
questions.explain: Bly attacked advertising men and businesspeople as calculating and afraid of chaos, but looking inward he found those same qualities, a part of the stockbroker and advertising man within him.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, what should you pay attention to when looking at your dreams as a view of your Shadow?
options: Only the dreams that recur more than once a week
The people from your past who appear most often
The hidden symbols and their meanings in dream dictionaries
The emotional tone and overall feelings the dreams inspire
questions.explain: Greene tells readers not to look for symbols or hidden meanings but to hold on to the emotional tone and overall feelings of their dreams, and to write them down.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's account of Abraham Lincoln, what led Lincoln to vow never again to indulge his cruel streak?
options: A boxing match in which he badly injured an opponent
Anonymous letters mocking a politician that led to a duel challenge
A scathing courtroom joke that cost him an important case
A newspaper exposé revealing his harsh treatment of his family
questions.explain: Lincoln's anonymous letters against a politician so enraged the man that he challenged Lincoln to a duel, which became an embarrassment. Lincoln got out of it and redirected his aggression into debates and elections.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, how did Abraham Lincoln channel his soft, sensitive side instead of denying it?
options: Into a private life kept carefully hidden from the political world
Into strict temperance campaigns against drinking
Into writing poetry that he published under a pen name
Into deep empathy for the public and a non-retributive peace with the South
questions.explain: Lincoln turned his sensitivity into empathy for ordinary people, worked to end the war early, and did not project evil onto the South. He also joked about his ugliness, voice and brooding.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the step of exploring the Shadow, which discovery does Greene say Louis Pasteur made through a free association of ideas after an accident in his laboratory?
options: A new form of mathematics
A theory of relativity
His great discovery about immunization
A theory of evolution
questions.explain: Greene lists Pasteur's immunization discovery alongside Einstein's dream image, Hadamard's hunches on a bus or in the shower, and Steve Jobs's intuitions as products of less conscious thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, why is the unconscious such a valuable source of creative ideas?
options: It works only through careful logic, so its conclusions are more reliable than conscious thought
It holds an almost limitless store of memories, experiences and information, and associates them freely when we relax
It is free of any influence from our past and so produces completely original ideas
It is active only during sleep, when the conscious mind cannot interfere
questions.explain: Greene says conscious thinking can hold only so much, while the unconscious contains vast material. After long work on a problem, relaxing in dreams or banal activities lets it combine ideas, some of which bubble up.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In Greene's discussion of Steve Jobs under showing the Shadow, what is the main point?
options: Jobs's dark side was inextricably interwoven with his power and creativity
Jobs proves that being nice and agreeable is the key to creativity
Jobs learned to hide his rough side completely as he became successful
Jobs succeeded in spite of his dark side, which held him back
questions.explain: Greene argues that we tend to admire Jobs's creativity and subtract his dark qualities, but his roughness and refusal to listen were key parts of his success. Subtract the active Shadow and such people would be like everyone else.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does the Deciphering the Shadow section relate to the list of Shadow signs given earlier in Keys to Human Nature?
options: It argues that the earlier signs are misleading and should be ignored
It expands on contradictory behavior, the sign Greene called the most eloquent of all
It replaces the earlier list with a completely different theory of the Shadow
It applies the earlier signs only to historical figures, not everyday people
questions.explain: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene lists contradictory behavior first among the signs and points ahead for more on how to interpret it. The Deciphering section develops this with seven emphatic types.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene end chapter 9 with The Integrated Human after the sections on reading the Shadow in others?
options: To turn from detecting the Shadow in others to integrating one's own dark side
To return to Nixon's life story and complete the opening narrative
To argue that only others have a Shadow, while the reader can rise above it
To show that the Shadow can be eliminated entirely with enough discipline
questions.explain: The Law of Repression asks readers both to recognize others' dark side and to become aware of their own. The final section gives four steps for seeing, embracing, exploring and showing one's own Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Describe the two forms Greene says the emphatic trait can take as it develops early in life.
questions.a: In the first, a person senses a softness, vulnerability or insecurity that might be embarrassing and unconsciously develops the opposite, a toughness that sits outside like a protective shell. In the second, a person has a quality that seems antisocial, such as too much ambition or selfishness, and develops a strongly prosocial opposite. In both cases the hidden trait becomes part of their Shadow, and the public image is honed over years.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does Greene advise dealing with a Tough Guy, whether as an acquaintance or a rival?
questions.a: You should not be intimidated by the front, but you should also avoid stirring their deep insecurities by doubting their tall tales or masculinity, since they are touchy and thin-skinned. You might catch a micropout before they cover it with a scowl. If they are a rival, they are easy to bait into an overreaction that reveals something less than tough.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Explain why Greene says the Passive-Aggressive Charmer eventually lashes out at the people they befriended.
questions.a: Early in life they realized they had aggressive, envious tendencies and a desire for power that would make life hard, so they cultivated an opposite façade of niceness, which gave them social power. But they secretly resent having to be so deferential and cannot keep it up. Under stress or worn out, they lash out, using what they know of your weak spots, and then blame you.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, does the Fanatic tend to slip up at exactly the moment they could deliver on their promises?
questions.a: The Fanatic's great belief is a mask over massive early insecurities and doubts about self-worth. When the key moment arrives, the doubts return and they secretly know they cannot deliver, so under stress they become indecisive, burn out, fall ill or take ill-conceived actions. They may fire assistants to look active, but unconsciously they are sabotaging themselves and then blaming others.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does the repressed irrational side return in the Rigid Rationalist, according to Greene?
questions.a: Because they experience primitive thinking as softness and repress it, their faith in science takes on a religious air, and they argue with extra intellectual heft and a touch of anger that reveals a hidden need to bully. At the extreme they fall into a wildly irrational love affair, a bad career choice, a ridiculous financial scheme or a conspiracy theory. They are also prone to mood shifts and outbursts as the Shadow stirs.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does Greene say the Snob is really insecure about, and how do they cope with it?
questions.a: Snobs are especially sensitive to the banality that is part of every human life: boring tasks, ordinary parents with unglamorous jobs, and mediocre sides of their own character. They are deeply insecure about their origins and possible mediocrity, so they distract and deceive with appearances, special knowledge and refined tastes rather than real originality in their work. Often their exotic background turns out to be exaggerated or invented, as with Beau Brummell.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What traits, according to Greene, give certain people the impression of being comfortable with themselves and authentic?
questions.a: They can laugh at themselves and admit shortcomings and mistakes. They have a playful, sometimes impish edge, as if they kept more of the child within, and they can play their role in life with a little distance. At times they are charmingly spontaneous, in contrast to touchy, hypersensitive people who seem to have something to hide.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In the step of seeing the Shadow, what indirect signs does Greene tell you to look for in yourself?
questions.a: Note any one-sided, emphatic traits and assume the opposite lies buried. Look at your emotional outbursts and moments of extreme touchiness, which show an insecurity being stirred, and at your tendency to project bad qualities onto people or groups. Also examine moments in your late teens and early twenties when you acted cruelly, since the Shadow then came out more naturally.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What did Robert Bly gain from consciously scrutinizing his Shadow, and what lesson about other people does Greene draw from his story?
questions.a: Bly, depressed and blocked, found within himself the calculating, controlling, rigid and moralistic qualities he had attacked in businesspeople, and accepted others' view that he was rather classical. By being honest with himself he reconnected with the other half of his psyche, channeled the Shadow creatively, and his depression and writer's block lifted. Greene notes that other people can often see our Shadow better than we can, so it is wise to ask for their frank opinions.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Besides your adult behavior, where else does Greene tell you to look to rediscover the lost parts of yourself during the step of seeing the Shadow?
questions.a: He says to reexamine your earlier self: traits from childhood that parents and peers drummed out of you or made you feel ashamed of, such as introspective tendencies or interests your parents disliked. Look at emotions that once sparked awe or excitement and have gone missing. As you have aged you have become more like others, and you must rediscover these lost authentic parts.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Explain how Abraham Lincoln embraced and integrated both sides of his split personality, according to Greene.
questions.a: Lincoln saw in himself an ambitious, almost cruel streak and a sensitivity that made him depressed. After his anonymous letters nearly led to a duel, he admitted his cruel streak and poured his aggressive energy into winning debates and elections. He channeled his softness into deep empathy for the public and a non-retributive peace, and he joked about his own ugliness, voice and brooding, which made him seem tremendously authentic.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene argue that modern thinking dominated by statistics and big data can become sterile, and what does he recommend instead?
questions.a: As children our minds were fluid and made surprising associations, but as adults we tighten down and dismiss free associations, dream images, hunches and intuitions as irrational. This leads to sterile thinking because the unconscious, the Shadow side of the mind, has creative powers we ignore. Greene recommends unstructured time to play with ideas, widening options and taking seriously what comes in less conscious states.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Why does Greene encourage externalizing your darkest impulses in your work or in a journal?
questions.a: We all have aggressive and antisocial desires, even toward those we love, and traumas linked to emotions we prefer to forget. The greatest art expresses these repressed depths, which is why it causes such a powerful reaction, as in Ingmar Bergman's films or Dostoyevsky's novels. By externalizing your dark side you can gain the same power.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: According to Greene, what price do we pay for always being nice and following social codes?
questions.a: We gain comfort by fitting in, but we become defensive and secretly resentful. Niceness becomes a habit that turns into timidity, lack of confidence and indecision. Meanwhile the Shadow still shows itself, but unconsciously, in explosive fits and starts that often hurt us, so Greene says we pay a greater price for niceness than for consciously showing the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he calls showing the Shadow a form of exorcism?
questions.a: Once you show your hidden desires and impulses, they no longer lie concealed in corners of your personality, twisting and operating in secret ways. You have released your demons and gained presence as an authentic human. In this way the Shadow becomes your ally rather than a destructive force.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: How does The Integrated Human section answer the problem raised by the chapter's opening story of Richard Nixon?
questions.a: Nixon is presented as a man with a particularly thick Shadow who never looked within, so his repressed side eventually destroyed him; in the final section Greene says he in many ways epitomizes the inauthentic type. The Integrated Human offers the remedy he lacked: self-awareness, through four steps of seeing, embracing, exploring and showing the Shadow. Figures like Lincoln and Churchill, who could examine and laugh at their flaws, serve as the positive counterexamples.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that the deeper the repression, the greater the ____ of the Shadow, so cracks in an emphatic façade appear with age or stress.
