questions.explain: Greene states that the laws of human nature dictate this link: the more deeply a trait is repressed, the more volatile the Shadow becomes.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: The baseball player Reggie Jackson recognized the softness behind the bluster of Yankees manager Billy ____, a brawling Tough Guy type.
questions.explain: Jackson saw Martin's touchiness about his ego, changing moods and emotional outbursts as signs of glaring insecurities behind the tough front.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says the Saint's pure exterior developed early as a way to disguise a strong hunger for power and attention or strong sensual ____.
questions.explain: Behind the saintly image lies a hunger for power, attention or sensual pleasure; once in power, the Saint becomes intolerant and secretly drawn to the taboo.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene notes that some people propound a philosophy of free love and anything goes, but in fact they are after ____.
questions.explain: This variation on the Saint prefers sex with those who depend on them, and anything goes only on their terms.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Beau Brummell, the notorious snob and dandy of the early nineteenth century, actually came from a staunch ____ background.
questions.explain: Brummell's real background was the opposite of what he peddled, an example of the Snob's exaggerated or invented origins.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene suggests thinking of the pop star Michael ____ near the end of his life as an example of the Extreme Entrepreneur's slide into total dependence.
questions.explain: The Extreme Entrepreneur goes from complete control to total dependence on doctors or outside financiers.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says the path shown by authentic types largely centers on ____: conscious of our Shadow, we can control, channel and integrate it.
questions.explain: Greene says that the path to follow largely centers on self-awareness, which allows us to reconnect with the part of ourselves that sank into the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene warns that you are only half a ____ if you keep your Shadow buried.
questions.explain: In the step of seeing the Shadow, Greene urges readers to be intrepid in looking inward, because a buried Shadow leaves you incomplete.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Others told the writer Robert Bly that they saw him as rather ____ in his taste and writing, which bothered him because he thought the opposite.
questions.explain: Bly saw himself as a bohemian Romantic, but as he grew more honest he realized others were right, which shows that people can often see our Shadow better than we can.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that you should look at your ____ as the most direct and clear view of your Shadow.
questions.explain: Only in dreams will you find the behavior you carefully avoid in conscious life; Greene advises writing them down and attending to their feeling tone.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says Albert Einstein based one of his theories of relativity on an image from a ____.
questions.explain: Einstein is one of several examples, with Hadamard, Pasteur and Steve Jobs, of creative people who drew on unconscious, less structured thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: The mathematician Jacques ____ made his most important discoveries while boarding a bus or taking a shower.
questions.explain: Hadamard attributed these hunches that came out of nowhere to his unconscious, an example for the step of exploring the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Greene says that gender roles represent the most powerful social ____ of all, one that seems almost to represent biological differences.
questions.explain: Greene says that what men and women can do or say has been tightly controlled, and women in particular are socialized to be extra nice and agreeable.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: When Norman Mailer met Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis in 1960, he saw something droll and hard in her eyes, as if she were a very naughty ____-year-old.
questions.explain: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis played against the type of the traditional political wife, showed a malicious streak openly, and became a sensation because of her naturalness.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: In describing authentic people who can play their role in life with some distance, Greene refers the reader back to the last section of chapter ____.
questions.explain: Chapter 3, See Through People's Masks, ends with a section on the art of impression management, and the Integrated Human links back to it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say the Saint is secretly drawn to, or does once in power?
options: Refusing every position of power offered to them
Sex, money and the limelight
Becoming intolerant and punishing the impure
What is expressly taboo for their particular saintliness
Quietly giving away their wealth without telling anyone
questions.explain: Greene says that once in power the Saint becomes intolerant and is secretly drawn to sex, money, attention and the taboo. Quietly giving and refusing power describe the genuine saints, who do not publicize deeds or grab power.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as ways the Rigid Rationalist's repressed irrationality can burst out?
options: Falling for a ridiculous financial scheme
Indulging in some conspiracy theory
Becoming a devoted follower of a saintly guru
Giving up science entirely for religion
A love affair that is irrational and contrary to their image
questions.explain: Greene mentions the professor running off with the young model, bad career choices, ridiculous financial schemes and conspiracy theories. He does not describe them following gurus or abandoning science.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as positive qualities that the Extreme Entrepreneur shows at first?
options: Skill at delegating to trusted managers
Very high standards
Exceptional attention to detail
A strong habit of seeking and taking advice
questions.explain: The Extreme Entrepreneur has high standards, attends to detail and does much of the work personally. Their inability to listen to advice and failure to delegate are exactly what bring them down.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as signs of the softness behind the Tough Guy's bluster?
options: Exaggerated boasting about past exploits that feel hard to believe
A calm, even temper under stress
Emotional outbursts revealing insecurities
Changing moods
Touchiness about his ego
questions.explain: Reggie Jackson read Billy Martin's softness in his touchiness about his ego, changing moods and emotional outbursts. Boasting is the tough front itself, not a crack in it, and a calm temper is the opposite of what Greene describes.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as examples of authentic types who inspire us?
options: Josephine Baker
Richard Nixon
Maximilien Robespierre
Winston Churchill
Charlie Chaplin
questions.explain: Greene lists Churchill, Lincoln, Chaplin, Josephine Baker, Einstein and Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis. Nixon epitomizes the inauthentic type, and Robespierre is the false Saint.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these describe Abraham Lincoln's soft side, according to Greene?
options: He felt tremendous affection for animals
He had a scathing sense of humor in politics
He hated witnessing physical cruelty
He loved boxing and thrashing his opponents
He loved poetry
questions.explain: Poetry, love of animals, hatred of cruelty and drinking, and fits of melancholy were his soft side. Boxing and scathing humor belonged to his rough, ambitious side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as creative people who drew on the unconscious or less structured thinking?
options: Richard Wagner
Albert Einstein
Jacques Hadamard
Louis Pasteur
Beau Brummell
questions.explain: Einstein, Hadamard, Pasteur and Steve Jobs are Greene's examples for exploring the Shadow. Wagner appears as an example of projection and Brummell as a snob.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these women does Greene name as influential figures who broke with gender codes by bringing out their Shadow?
options: Eleanor Roosevelt
Marlene Dietrich
Coco Chanel
Sophia Tolstoy
questions.explain: Greene names Marlene Dietrich, Josephine Baker, Eleanor Roosevelt and Coco Chanel, who acted in traditionally masculine ways and blended gender roles. The Tolstoys are cited only in the chapter for the Saint's private demonic side.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these are among Greene's steps for showing the Shadow?
options: Assert yourself more and compromise less, under control and at opportune moments
Wait until everyone in the group agrees before acting
Care less about what people think of you
Always smooth over conflicts to keep others comfortable
Respect your own opinions more and those of others less, especially in your field
questions.explain: Greene's steps include respecting your own opinions, asserting more, caring less what people think, offending those who block you, playing the impudent child and flouting conventions. Smoothing every conflict and waiting for agreement are the overly nice habits he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Which of these cross-references to other parts of the book appear in the second half of chapter 9?
options: A chapter on envy, for the Passive-Aggressive Charmer
The story of the Tolstoys in chapter 2, for the Saint's private demonic side
The last section of chapter 3, for playing one's role with some distance
The story of Abraham Lincoln later in the chapter, as a truly original person who appears humble
questions.explain: Greene points to the Tolstoys in chapter 2, to the last section of chapter 3, and forward to Lincoln in the Integrated Human. He does not cross-refer to a chapter on envy for this type.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says it is very easy to get caught up in the appearance and first impression of people with emphatic traits, so you should watch over time for the emergence of the opposite.
questions.explain: Greene advises being extra wary around people with emphatic traits and watching for signs of the opposite over time, since dealing with them is much easier once you understand them.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that although the Tough Guy likes to dominate women, he will often end up with a wife who is submissive and easily controlled.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: he often ends up with a wife who clearly dominates him, which is a secret wish of his.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that Karl Lagerfeld's family inherited its money from an old aristocratic fortune, just as Lagerfeld claimed.
questions.explain: Greene says the family made its money in the most bourgeois fashion, contrary to the stories Lagerfeld told, an example of the Snob's invented background.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, those who are truly original and different do not need to make a great show of it and are often embarrassed by their difference.
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the Snob with truly original people who learn to appear more humble, pointing to Abraham Lincoln as an example.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that we humans are poor at sensing the difference between authentic people and those who have something to hide.
questions.explain: Greene says we are masters at smelling the difference, feeling it in body language, tone of voice, gaze and smile.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, as you keep seeing the outlines of your Shadow, the pain of the process eventually turns into excitement at what you are uncovering.
questions.explain: Greene says the process gets easier as the muscles of repression loosen, and at a certain point pain becomes excitement.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: In the step of embracing the Shadow, Greene says the goal is to keep only a surface awareness of your dark side so that it does not disturb you.
questions.explain: Greene says surface awareness is our natural reaction, but the goal is the opposite: complete acceptance and a desire to integrate the Shadow into your personality.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Abraham Lincoln made frequent jokes about his own ugliness, high-pitched voice and brooding nature.
questions.explain: Lincoln incorporated his soft, odd side into a healthy humor about himself, which helped give the impression of tremendous authenticity.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that successful people in their fields are generally more bound by social codes than others, and are rewarded for their restraint.
questions.explain: Greene says the successful are generally much less bound by such codes, more assertive and openly ambitious, and they are rewarded rather than punished for flouting conventions.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: True or false: The Deciphering the Shadow section points ahead to the story of Abraham Lincoln in the Integrated Human when discussing the Snob.
questions.explain: Greene says truly original people often appear humble and refers the reader to the story of Lincoln in the section below.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages of the Passive-Aggressive Charmer relationship in the order Greene describes.
items: They are amazingly nice and accommodating at first
You return the favor by helping their career
Cracks appear, such as a critical remark or gossip behind your back
A blowup, sabotage or betrayal occurs
They blame you for what followed
questions.explain: Greene traces how the charm draws you in, how small cracks appear, and how they finally lash out using what they know of you and then blame you.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages of the Extreme Entrepreneur's career in the order Greene describes.
items: High standards and hard work bring early success
They show an inability to listen or take advice
Growing responsibility arrives but they fail to delegate
The situation becomes chaotic and others take over
They become dependent on doctors or outside financiers
questions.explain: Greene shows the move from complete control to total dependence, driven by a hidden wish to be cared for.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages of the Fanatic's arc in the order Greene describes.
items: They show fervor and allow no compromise
Their strength and conviction gain them followers
At the key moment they slip up and become indecisive
They fire assistants to give the impression of action
It all falls apart and they blame others
questions.explain: The Fanatic's conviction masks deep doubts, which return at the moment of delivery and lead to unconscious self-sabotage.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put Greene's four steps for integrating the Shadow in order.
items: See the Shadow
Embrace the Shadow
Explore the Shadow
Show the Shadow
questions.explain: Greene begins with seeing, the hardest step, moves to accepting and integrating, then tapping its creative depths, and ends with consciously showing it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put these steps for showing the Shadow in the order Greene lists them.
items: Respect your own opinions more and others less
Assert yourself more and compromise less
Care less what people think of you
At times offend people who block your path
Play the impudent child who mocks hypocrisy
Flout the conventions others follow
questions.explain: Greene numbers these steps from first to fifth and ends with finally flouting conventions, leading into his discussion of gender roles.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the events of Lincoln's near-duel in the order Greene tells them.
items: Lincoln writes anonymous letters attacking a politician
The target, enraged, discovers Lincoln wrote them
The target challenges Lincoln to a duel
Lincoln manages to get out of the duel
Lincoln vows never to indulge his cruel streak again
questions.explain: The embarrassment led Lincoln to recognize his cruel streak and channel his aggression into debates and elections.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the stages of Robert Bly's confrontation with his Shadow in the order Greene describes.
items: He feels depressed and his writing becomes sterile
He looks inward at the Shadow side of his character
He finds calculating, controlling qualities like those he attacked
He accepts others' view that he is rather classical
His depression and writer's block lift
questions.explain: By honestly unearthing his dark qualities, Bly reconnected with the other half of his psyche and channeled the Shadow creatively.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Put the four sections of chapter 9 in the order they appear.
items: The Dark Side
Keys to Human Nature
Deciphering the Shadow
The Integrated Human
questions.explain: The chapter opens with Nixon's story, explains the Shadow and its signs, decodes contradictory behavior through emphatic types, and ends with integrating one's own Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each emphatic type with the hidden quality Greene says it conceals.
pairs: A hunger for power, attention or sensual pleasure
Massive insecurities and doubts about self-worth
A wish to be cared for like a dependent child
questions.explain: Each emphatic trait rests on its opposite: toughness over softness, purity over appetite, conviction over doubt, self-reliance over dependency.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each emphatic type with the advice Greene gives for handling it.
pairs: Keep some distance and, if they are enemies, expose their hypocrisy
Be wary of those too quick to charm and befriend
Bait them into overreactions to prick their intellectual superiority
Avoid getting entangled with them late in their careers
questions.explain: Greene tailors his advice to the way each type's Shadow emerges, from exposing hypocrisy to avoiding collateral damage.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each person with the emphatic type Greene uses them to illustrate.
questions.explain: Martin is the brawling manager, Robespierre the Incorruptible, Brummell the dandy with a middle-class background, and Jackson the example of a slide into dependency.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each emphatic type with how its Shadow typically breaks through.
pairs: Indecision or self-sabotage at the key moment
It comes out that their exotic background was invented
Tears or a tantrum, quickly covered with a cruel act
questions.explain: In each case behavior contrary to the public image emerges, especially under stress or over time.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each step for integrating the Shadow with what it involves.
pairs: Look for indirect signs such as touchiness and projection
Accept it fully and integrate it into your personality
Tap the unconscious for creative ideas and dark impulses
Openly assert yourself and flout social codes
questions.explain: Greene's four steps move from awareness to acceptance to creative use to open display.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each creative figure with how Greene says they drew on the unconscious.
pairs: Based a theory of relativity on a dream image
Got key hunches while boarding a bus or showering
Free association after a laboratory accident
Intuitions when his mind roamed most freely
questions.explain: Greene uses these examples to argue that the less conscious mind has great creative power when we pay attention to it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each dream experience with what Greene says it may reveal about the Shadow.
pairs: Hidden desires trying to rise to consciousness
Unexpected bold behavior on your part
Behavior you carefully avoid in conscious life
questions.explain: Greene says anxieties may relate to unconfronted insecurities while soaring and exploring are hidden desires, and dreams show behavior avoided in waking life.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Match each figure with how Greene uses them in The Integrated Human.
pairs: Found in himself the calculating traits he attacked
Integrated a cruel streak and a soft side into his persona
Played against the type of the traditional political wife
Made art whose power comes from expressing repressed depths
questions.explain: Bly illustrates seeing the Shadow, Lincoln embracing it, Bergman exploring it, and Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis showing it.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these traits into the public front and the hidden Shadow of the Passive-Aggressive Charmer.

items.t: Smiling a lot and always willing to help
Upbeat and accommodating
Quick to befriend and charm
Aggressive, envious tendencies
A desire for power
Resentment at having to be deferential

questions.explain: The niceness is a façade cultivated over years to cover aggressive, envious impulses that eventually lash out.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into the Snob's displayed image and the reality Greene says lies underneath.

items.t: Refined tastes in art, wine or food
An exciting, exotic ancestry
Being more alternative than others
Insecurity about origins
Fear of their own mediocrity
An ordinary person not so different from others

questions.explain: Snobs surround themselves with the extraordinary to distract from the banality that is part of every life.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into signs of a fake Saint and signs of a genuine saint, according to Greene.

items.t: Enjoys power and attention
Has accumulated astonishing wealth
Shows a demonic side to family in private
Does not publicize their good deeds
Does not grab for power

questions.explain: Greene says real saints exist but do not advertise themselves or seek power; the fake Saint is revealed by deeds and life details.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these traits into those of the authentic type and those of the opposite, inauthentic type.

items.t: Able to laugh at themselves
Admits mistakes and shortcomings
A playful, impish edge
Hypersensitive to any perceived slight
Seems to have something to hide
Tense body language and halting voice

questions.explain: Greene says we are drawn to authentic types and unconsciously repelled by their touchy, uncomfortable opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort Abraham Lincoln's traits into his rough side and his soft side, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Loved boxing and thrashing opponents
A scathing sense of humor in politics
An ambitious, almost cruel streak
Loved poetry
Tremendous affection for animals
Fits of deep melancholy

questions.explain: Lincoln felt his nature was split; instead of denying either side he channeled the rough into debates and elections and the soft into empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene says happens with overly nice conformity and what happens when you consciously show the Shadow.

items.t: Timidity and lack of confidence
Secret resentment
Explosive, unconscious outbursts
A tremendous sense of liberation
The Shadow becomes an ally
Enhanced presence as an authentic human

questions.explain: Greene argues we pay a greater price for niceness than for showing the Shadow, which acts as a kind of exorcism.

questions.unitTitle: Confront Your Dark Side
questions.q: Sort these ideas into the chapter section where Greene develops them.

items.t: Seven common emphatic traits
Wariness toward people who seem too nice
The Fanatic and the Snob
Four steps for working with your own Shadow
Dreams as a view of your Shadow
Flouting gender conventions

questions.explain: The first section teaches you to read the Shadow in others through emphatic types; the final section turns to integrating your own.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: The Law of Envy begins by saying that we humans are naturally compelled to ____ ourselves with one another.
questions.explain: The law starts from our constant measuring of status, respect and attention against others; envy is one outcome of this need to compare.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to the Law of Envy, what two directions can the human need to compare ourselves with others take?
questions.a: For some people, the need to compare serves as a spur to excel through their work. For others, it turns into deep envy: feelings of inferiority and frustration that lead to covert attacks and sabotage.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to the Law of Envy, among whom is envy most likely to crop up?
options: Between rivals in unrelated professions
Between people of very different social classes
Among strangers who meet only briefly
Among friends or peers in the same profession
questions.explain: The law says envy is most likely among friends or peers in the same profession, a point the Fatal Friends story then dramatizes with Jane Williams and Mary Shelley.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Envy name as early warning signs of envy?
options: Praise and bids for friendship that seem effusive and out of proportion
A refusal ever to spend time with you
Subtle digs at you under the guise of good-natured humor
Open declarations of rivalry
Apparent uneasiness with your success
questions.explain: The law lists overdone praise and friendship, digs disguised as humor, and unease at your success. Envy is never openly declared, and enviers tend to seek closeness rather than avoid you.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Envy says people will usually admit it when they are acting out of envy.
questions.explain: The law says the opposite: “Nobody admits to acting out of envy.” That is why you must learn its early warning signs.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What two remedies does the Law of Envy recommend?
options: Display your achievements more, and keep comparing yourself with rivals
Cut off every friend who competes with you, and hide all your successes
Confront enviers openly, and outshine them until they give up
Deflect envy by drawing attention away from yourself, and base your self-worth on internal standards
questions.explain: The law ends by advising us to deflect envy by drawing attention away from ourselves and to develop self-worth from internal standards rather than incessant comparisons.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the ideas of the Law of Envy statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: We are compelled to compare ourselves with others
For some, comparison spurs them to excel
For others, it turns into envy and covert sabotage
Recognize the early warning signs of envy
Deflect envy and build self-worth from internal standards
questions.explain: The statement moves from the universal need to compare, to its two outcomes, to the warning signs, and ends with the remedies.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each person in the story of Mary Shelley to their description.
pairs: Mary’s mother, perhaps the first great feminist writer
Mary’s father, a philosopher who argued for ending private property
Publisher who championed young poets, Shelley his favorite
Lawyer and Shelley’s best friend from his youth
Fellow poet and rebel who stood by Mary after Shelley’s death
questions.explain: Each figure is introduced in Greene’s account: Mary’s two illustrious parents, the publisher the men sailed to meet, the lawyer who later took up with Jane, and Byron, the one friend who did not turn cold.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What nickname did the English press give to the Shelleys and Lord Byron?
options: The Circle of Scandal and Exile
The League of Incest and Atheism
The Brotherhood of Rebel Poets
The Society of Free Love
questions.explain: Greene notes the three were a magnet for rumors, and the English press dubbed them “the League of Incest and Atheism.”

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How did Mary Shelley first describe Jane Williams in a letter to her husband?
options: Charming and gifted, a natural muse for any poet
Brilliant and well read, but cold and calculating in conversation
Plain-looking, but warm, lively and quick-witted in company
Very pretty, but lacking animation and sense, with a slow, monotonous way of talking
questions.explain: Mary at first found Jane dull and pretentious, writing that she was pretty but wanted animation and sense and spoke in a slow, monotonous tone.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these early warnings about Jane Williams did Mary Shelley have before she grew dependent on her?
options: Lord Byron openly accusing Jane of being a thief
A letter from a common friend warning her to keep her distance from Jane
Edward Williams confessing that Jane envied her
Her own first impression that Jane was dull and pretentious
Catching Jane staring at her with an unpleasant look, quickly covered by a cheerful smile
questions.explain: Mary saw the unpleasant looks, received a friend’s warning letter, and formed a poor first impression, then forgot her misgivings. Byron and Edward made no such accusations.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why did Mary Shelley come to depend on Jane Williams despite her early misgivings?
questions.a: Mary was in a turbulent, lonely period: grieving her children and drifting from her husband. She was moved by the Williamses’ love story, and once Jane had her second child the two could bond as young mothers in a foreign land. The Shelleys had no English friends in Italy, so Mary welcomed daily companionship and forgot her doubts about Jane.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Percy Shelley was obsessed with ____, despite the fact that he had never learned to swim.
questions.explain: Edward Williams boasted of his navigational skills, and together he and Shelley designed the boat that later went down in a storm.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In the story of the Shelleys, why was Percy Shelley drawn to Jane Williams?
options: She was a gifted poet whose ideas challenged and sharpened his own
She was wealthy and offered to fund the publication of his poems
She reminded him of Mary as she had been when they first met
She never argued, admired him and seconded everything he said, so she could be his new muse
questions.explain: Shelley liked that Jane was cheerful, never argued and looked at him admiringly; he could teach her and she could be the muse his depressed wife no longer was.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Mary Shelley saw her husband’s infatuation with Jane as a repeat of his pattern of seeking a woman very different from the one he was with.
questions.explain: Mary knew he had left the pretty, simple Harriet for the complicated Mary, and now saw him falling for the simpler Jane. Even so, she did not fear losing him.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these events in the story of Mary Shelley and Jane Williams in order.
items: The Williamses arrive in Pisa and visit the Shelleys
The two couples move to a villa on the Bay of Lerici
Shelley and Edward drown when their boat sinks
Mary returns to London and finds herself a celebrity
Jane abruptly throws Mary out when Hogg arrives
Isabel Robinson reveals the stories Jane has spread
questions.explain: The story runs from the first meeting in Pisa in 1821, to the shared villa and the drowning in 1822, to Mary’s return to London in 1823 and the later revelations there.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How did Percy Shelley and Edward Williams die?
options: They caught fevers in the isolated villa on the coast
Their boat capsized on the way out to visit Lord Byron
They were attacked by local peasants near the villa
Their badly designed boat went under in a storm on the voyage home
questions.explain: They had sailed up the coast to meet the Hunts and, on the homeward journey, ran into a storm; the boat had indeed been badly designed and went under.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How did Mary Shelley react to her husband’s death, and what did she resolve to do?
questions.a: She was seized with remorse and guilt, replaying every angry word, critique and doubt she had given him. She resolved then and there to devote the rest of her life to making Shelley’s poetry famous.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: When Mary Shelley asked for advice about returning to London, what did Jane Williams urge?
options: That she marry Thomas Hogg to secure her finances
That she come back at once so the Shelley family could meet Percy
That she give up her son Percy and not come to England
That she publish Shelley’s poems before the gossip spread
questions.explain: Jane adamantly advised Mary to give up Percy and stay away, framed in practical terms; Mary later saw that this would have meant giving up their inheritance.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: After Shelley’s death, Jane Williams had an affair with, and became pregnant by, Shelley’s old friend Thomas ____.
questions.explain: Hogg had been courting Jane, and the night Jane abruptly threw Mary out of her house made it clear the two were having an affair.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these stages of Mary Shelley’s life after her husband’s death in order.
items: She stays in Italy as Leigh Hunt turns cold
She writes to Jane and Hogg for advice about returning
She returns to London and finds herself famous
She moves near Jane in a remote part of London
Hogg’s arrival one night exposes Jane’s affair
questions.explain: Mary first stayed in Italy, then sought advice, returned in August 1823 to find Frankenstein a sensation, moved near Jane to hide from gossip, and was thrown out the night Hogg arrived.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Who finally revealed to Mary Shelley the stories Jane Williams had been telling about her?
options: Lord Byron, shortly before his death
Isabel Robinson, a young woman Mary was helping
Leigh Hunt, in an apologetic letter
Thomas Hogg, after quarreling with Jane
questions.explain: While Mary was helping Isabel Robinson escape a scandal, Isabel confided in detail what Jane had been telling her for months.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these stories had Jane Williams told Isabel Robinson about Mary Shelley?
options: That Mary had secretly damaged his boat
That Mary had made him so unhappy he secretly wanted to die
That Shelley had never really loved his wife
That Mary had stolen Shelley’s unpublished poems
That Jane was the great love of Shelley’s life
questions.explain: Jane claimed Shelley had never loved Mary, that Jane was his great love, and hinted Mary made him want to die and was somehow responsible. She did not claim sabotage of the boat or theft of poems.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: After learning of Jane’s stories, Mary Shelley wrote in her journal that her friend had proved false and ____.
questions.explain: Mary’s journal entry asks whether she had not been a fool, as she sees that Jane had been a competitor all along.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: After Isabel Robinson’s revelation, what past events suddenly made sense to Mary Shelley?
questions.a: She understood the sudden coldness of Hogg, Leigh Hunt and others who must have heard Jane’s stories, the looks Jane threw at her when Mary was the center of attention, and Jane’s face when she threw her out. Jane’s vehemence that Mary give up her son and stay away also made sense. Jane had been not a friend but a competitor, who had actively seduced Shelley.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: When Mary Shelley finally confronted Jane Williams, how did Jane respond?
options: She burst into tears, denied the betrayal and accused Mary of being cold and unaffectionate
She refused to speak and left London for good
She calmly blamed Thomas Hogg for spreading the stories
She admitted everything at once and begged for forgiveness
questions.explain: Jane created a scene, demanded to know who had spread the story, denied it and turned the blame on Mary; Mary now saw the fake outrage and phony love.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: after confronting Jane, Mary Shelley immediately cut off all ties with her.
questions.explain: Mary did not cut off ties at once; the relationship continued on her terms, and only slowly, as Mary’s fame grew, did she cut off contact.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Mary Shelley later wrote that Jane, staining past years, took sweetness from memory and gave it instead a serpent’s ____.
questions.explain: The journal image captures how one envier’s betrayal poisoned even Mary’s good memories, the lasting damage the chapter warns about.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each quoted source in the Fatal Friends section to what it said.
pairs: Every time a friend succeeds, I die a little
Called the Shelleys and Byron the League of Incest and Atheism
Jane is pretty but wants animation and sense
Jane gave memory a serpent’s tooth
questions.explain: Vidal’s line closes the section on envious friends; the press nickname, Mary’s first letter and her later journal mark stages of the story.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene’s interpretation, what conflicting emotions did Jane Williams first feel toward Mary Shelley?
options: Pity for Mary’s grief mixed with fear of her husband
Liking and admiration mixed with a deep sense of inferiority
Romantic interest in Mary mixed with jealousy of Percy
Indifference that only later turned into admiration
questions.explain: Greene says there was much to like and admire in Mary, but she made Jane feel deeply inferior, lacking things Jane felt she deserved.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Using Jane Williams as his example, how does Greene describe what envy is?
questions.a: Envy is the desire to have the same things as another person, the sense of being entitled to them, and the apparent inability to get them easily or legitimately. With it comes a secret desire to hurt, wound or steal from the envied person, to right the unfairness of their supposed superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these reasons does Greene give for Jane Williams concealing and even repressing her envy?
options: Envy is a painful admission of one’s own inferiority
Mary had asked her to keep her feelings private
Displaying envy is socially toxic and pushes people away
She and Edward depended on the Shelleys for their future livelihood
Edward had threatened to leave her if she showed it
questions.explain: Greene gives three reasons: envy is socially toxic, the Williamses relied on the generous Shelley, and envy admits our inferiority, which we cannot bear to face.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says it is socially ____ to display envy, because it reveals deep insecurity along with hostility.
questions.explain: He calls the mix of insecurity and hostility a very ugly brew that is certain to push people away, one reason enviers hide the feeling.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, how did befriending Mary Shelley help Jane Williams deal with her envy?
options: It gave her direct access to Lord Byron’s fortune and fame
It let her hide the envy from herself, since she could hardly envy someone she had chosen as a friend
It ended her envy by showing her Mary’s many real flaws
It let her learn the craft of writing from Mary and so stop feeling inferior
questions.explain: Greene asks how Jane could imagine herself envious of Mary if she had chosen to become her friend; friendship disguised the envy. Closeness actually made it worse.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the stages of Jane Williams’s envy, as Greene interprets them, in order.
items: She feels attraction to Mary mixed with inferiority
She befriends Mary, disguising the envy
Daily closeness makes the imbalance plain and envy grows
She mentally turns Mary into an unsympathetic character
She feels justified in seducing Shelley and spreading stories
questions.explain: Greene traces envy’s transformations: mixed feelings, friendship as disguise, growing envy through proximity, a hostile narrative, and finally harmful action that feels justified.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, must enviers like Jane Williams create a narrative about the person they envy?
questions.a: In order to feel entitled to take harmful action, enviers must believe that everything the other person does reveals some negative trait and that they do not deserve their superior position. To build this story Jane had to willfully ignore the context: Mary’s loss of two children, Shelley’s coldness and his pursuit of other women.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these into what Mary Shelley actually had, which fed Jane’s envy, and the narrative Jane built to justify it.

items.t: An illustrious, handsome husband
A possibly large inheritance
A deep friendship with Lord Byron
A rich imagination and talent
Merely lucky, not talented
Owed everything to famous parents and men
Did not deserve her fame
Moody, clinging and no fun

questions.explain: Greene lists the real advantages Jane saw daily, then the story she told herself to recast Mary as undeserving and unlikable.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these were part of the narrative Jane Williams built about Mary Shelley, according to Greene?
options: Mary cared too little about her son
Mary was too generous with her money
Mary was moody, depressive, clinging and no fun
Mary owed her position to her famous parents and the men around her
Mary was merely lucky rather than talented
questions.explain: Jane’s narrative made Mary undeserving and unpleasant. Greene stresses the opposite of the wrong options: Mary was generous and totally devoted to her son, facts that did not fit Jane’s story.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what story did Jane spread after Shelley’s death that made Leigh Hunt and others distance themselves from Mary?
options: That Mary had refused to pay for the funeral
That Mary was having an affair with Lord Byron
That Mary had stolen Shelley’s manuscripts
That Mary did not seem particularly sad at the loss
questions.explain: Greene says Jane vented her envy by spreading the malicious story that Mary did not seem sad, which troubled Hunt and others enough to turn cold.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that envy occurs most commonly and painfully among friends.
questions.explain: Greene’s lesson from the story is plain: “Envy occurs most commonly and painfully among friends.”

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What paradox about envious people does Greene ask us to grasp in the Fatal Friends section?
options: People who feel envy are often motivated to become our friends
Envy is strongest among strangers who never meet
The more we succeed, the less our friends envy us
People who feel envy usually avoid us altogether
questions.explain: Greene says enviers, like Jane, feel interest, attraction and envy at once, and becoming our friend lets them disguise the envy, often with extra eagerness.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, does envy grow worse as an envious person becomes our friend?
questions.a: As they draw closer, the underlying envy is continually stirred, because the traits that made them feel inferior, such as our good position, solid work ethic or likability, are now witnessed every day. So, as with Jane, they gradually construct a narrative that we are lucky, overly ambitious and not nearly so great.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says an envious friend gradually constructs a ____ in which the envied person is lucky, overly ambitious and not nearly so great.
questions.explain: The narrative lets the envier justify hostility while hiding the envy behind it, the same move Jane made with Mary.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these advantages does friendship give an envier, according to Greene?
options: They are better positioned to sabotage us or steal our spouse
They gain a share of our income
They can discover our weak points and what will wound most
Our angry reaction to their attack feeds their story of our unlikable nature
They become immune to any criticism from us
questions.explain: From within a friendship enviers learn our weak points and can do the most damage, and if we respond angrily it only feeds their narrative.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does Greene describe our reaction to being attacked by an envious friend, and why does the envier gain from it?
questions.a: We tend to feel guilty and confused, wondering if we deserve some of the criticisms, and if we respond angrily this only feeds the narrative of our unlikable nature. Because we were friends we feel doubly wounded and betrayed, and the deeper the wound, the greater the envier’s satisfaction. Greene even speculates that enviers are unconsciously drawn to befriend the envied to gain this wounding power.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these warning signs of an envious friend does Greene mention in the Fatal Friends section?
options: Sudden looks and disparaging comments
A refusal to talk about their own life
Puzzling advice that seems against your interests
Lavish gifts given on every occasion
A first impression that the person is false
questions.explain: Greene advises heeding first impressions and watching for leaked looks, disparaging comments and puzzling advice meant to lead us into mistakes.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, enviers will give puzzling ____, something that seems against our interests but well reasoned on their part.
questions.explain: Enviers want us to make mistakes and try to lead us into them, as Jane did when urging Mary to give up her son and stay away.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene say Mary Shelley’s story teaches about first impressions and the opinions of others?
questions.a: Pay deeper attention to first impressions: we often intuit that someone is false but forget it as they make friendly overtures, because we always feel better about people who seem to like us, and enviers know this. We should also rely on the opinions of friends and neutral third parties; many of Mary’s friends found Jane conniving and even a bit scary.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that once you spot envy you should become suspicious and paranoid about everyone who befriends you.
questions.explain: Greene says it is not a question of becoming paranoid but simply of being alert once you pick up some signs of possible envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: A new colleague, very eager to befriend you, keeps urging you to turn down a promotion, with reasons that sound sensible but seem against your interests. What would Greene suggest?
options: This shows true friendship, since only a friend would risk upsetting you
This may be envy leaking out as puzzling advice meant to lead you into a mistake
This proves the colleague is a wiser strategist whom you should follow
This means the colleague is simply indifferent to your career
questions.explain: Greene warns that enviers give puzzling advice against our interests, and that any success we enjoy causes greater leakage of their true feelings.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Ana’s close friend stays warm to her face but increasingly describes Ana to others as merely lucky and overly ambitious. What does Greene’s account of Jane Williams suggest?
options: The friend is offering honest feedback to help Ana grow
The friend is constructing an envious narrative to justify hostility
The friend is drifting away from Ana in a harmless way
The friend is really jealous of Ana’s partner, not of Ana
questions.explain: Greene says envious friends gradually build a narrative that the envied person is lucky and overly ambitious, then vent it to others, as Jane did about Mary.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: The Fatal Friends section closes with Gore Vidal’s line: Every time a friend succeeds, I ____ a little.
questions.explain: Vidal’s confession captures Greene’s point that envy is most intense and painful among friends.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each of Jane Williams’s actions to the role Greene gives it in her envy.
pairs: Disguised her envy even from herself
Took what Mary had and set him against his wife
Saying Mary was not sad at his death
Made Hunt and others turn cold to Mary
A weaker imitation of stealing Mary’s husband
questions.explain: Greene reads each step as envy at work: friendship as disguise, seduction as theft, gossip as venting, and the affair with Hogg as a repeat of the original sin.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these into what drew Mary Shelley to Jane Williams and the warning signs she overlooked.

items.t: Bonding as young mothers in a foreign land
Empathy for the Williamses’ love affair
Having no other English friends in Italy
Jane’s cheerfulness when Mary needed cheering
An unpleasant stare covered by a quick smile
A friend’s letter urging her to keep away
Her first impression of Jane as dull and pretentious
Jane’s cold advice to give up her son

questions.explain: Mary’s loneliness and empathy pulled her toward Jane while she dismissed the looks, the warning letter, her first impression and the puzzling advice.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each further figure in the story of Mary Shelley to their description.
pairs: Charming admirer of Shelley who boasted of his navigational skills
Shelley’s pretty, simple first wife, whom he left for Mary
Young woman with an illegitimate child whom Mary tried to help
Woman who dressed as a man to pose as a father in Paris
questions.explain: Each appears in Greene’s account: Edward helped design the fatal boat, Harriet fit Shelley’s pattern, and Mary’s plot to help Isabel with Miss Dods led to the revelation about Jane.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene say envy is harder to detect than anger?
options: We know when we feel anger, but we disguise envy even from ourselves
Anger is rarer than envy, so people hide it less skillfully
Envy produces no feelings until it is finally acted upon
Only a few disturbed people ever feel real envy
questions.explain: With anger we are aware we feel hostile and the target usually knows why; with envy we almost never express it directly and convince ourselves it is something else.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these traits into anger and envy, as Greene contrasts them in the Keys to Human Nature section of Chapter 10.

items.t: We are aware that we feel hostile
The target usually knows what caused it
Can be analyzed and defused
Disguised even from ourselves
Leaves the target confused about the motive
Shows up as poisonous praise

questions.explain: Greene says anger is felt consciously and understood by its target, while envy is hidden, recast as something else, and leaves its victims confused.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says envy entails the admission to ourselves that we are ____ to another person in something we value.
questions.explain: Admitting inferiority is painful, and it is worse for others to see it, which is why we disguise envy almost as soon as we feel it.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene say we tell ourselves instead of admitting envy, and what do others then see?
questions.a: We tell ourselves it is not envy but unfairness in the distribution of goods or attention, resentment at this unfairness, even anger, and that the other person is not superior but simply lucky, overly ambitious or unscrupulous. Having convinced ourselves, we make the envy hard for others to detect: they see only our anger, indignation, hostile criticisms and poisonous praise.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each Old Testament figure Greene mentions to the act of envy.
pairs: Threw him in a ditch in the desert to die
Tried several times to kill the younger David
questions.explain: Greene uses these stories to show how, in ancient times, intense envy was often acted on through open violence.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How do enviers today usually act, compared with those in ancient times, according to Greene?
options: Not at all, since modern people no longer act on envy
More violently, by seizing what others own
Indirectly, by sabotaging work, ruining relationships and sullying reputations
Openly, by confessing their envy and demanding fairness
questions.explain: Greene says people are now more political and indirect, harming us while keeping their social position and leaving us unaware that envy was the motive.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these ways of acting on envy into ancient times and today, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Open violence
Forcefully taking what the other had
Resorting to murder
Sabotaging the other’s work
Sullying a reputation
Criticisms aimed at basic insecurities

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the violent envy of the Old Testament with modern enviers, who control overt aggression and attack by indirect means.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that being unable to see the envy behind a hostile act leaves us confused, and this confusion doubles the pain.
questions.explain: If we cannot see the underlying envy we are confused by the attack, and Greene says “this confusion doubles the pain we experience.”

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene say an envy attack is so painful when we cannot see the envy behind it?
questions.a: If someone is angry with us, we can analyze the anger and find a way to defuse it or defend ourselves. But when we cannot see the underlying envy we are confused by the hostile action, asking why people are suddenly cold or why a project failed, and this confusion doubles the pain we experience.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says your task as a student of human nature is to transform yourself into a master ____ of envy.
questions.explain: Greene treats spotting envy as an intellectual challenge: its signs are subtle, but their language can be mastered.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these benefits does Greene say come from learning to decode envy?
options: Ridding yourself of all envy for good
Understanding in hindsight that you suffered an envy attack, which helps you get over it
Learning to provoke envy in others without risk
Seeing the warning signs in advance so you can defuse or deflect an attack
Weeding out false friends from the ones you can truly trust
questions.explain: Greene promises less confusion, the chance to defuse attacks early, and better judgment of whom to trust, without becoming paranoid. He does not promise freedom from all envy or safe ways to provoke it.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene distinguishes between passive envy and ____ envy, the more acute form that leads to harmful action.
questions.explain: Passive envy is the everyday pang we all feel; active envy is the dangerous form that turns into harmful action.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these into passive envy and active envy, as Greene distinguishes them.

items.t: Pangs we all feel in the course of a day
Little put-downs and offhand comments
To be tolerated as part of social life
Inferiority too strong to vent in a comment
Doing something to harm the other person
To be detected before it turns dangerous

questions.explain: Passive envy does no meaningful harm to a relationship and should be tolerated; active envy acts on hostility and is what Greene wants us to spot early.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, why does passive envy sometimes turn active?
options: The envied person confronts the envier about their feelings
The underlying sense of inferiority is too strong to be vented by a comment or put-down
The envier finally achieves the same success as the envied person
The envier’s friends encourage open rivalry
questions.explain: Greene says active envy arises when the inferiority is too strong, producing hostility that a remark can no longer release.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene say acting on envy can feel better to the envier than simply living with it?
questions.a: Sitting with envy over a long time is painful and frustrating, while feeling righteous indignation against the envied person is invigorating. Doing something to harm the other person brings satisfaction, as it did to Jane, though the satisfaction is short-lived because enviers always find something new to envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the satisfaction of acting on envy is lasting, because it settles the envier’s sense of unfairness for good.
questions.explain: Greene says the satisfaction is short-lived, because enviers always find something new to envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: A colleague makes a slightly mean remark now and then when you are praised, but is otherwise supportive and does nothing to harm you. What would Greene advise?
options: End the relationship before the envy turns active
Report the colleague, since the remarks prove sabotage
Confront the colleague at once, since all envy is dangerous
Tolerate it as passive envy, a normal part of being a social animal
questions.explain: Greene says little put-downs and offhand comments are signs of passive envy that we should simply tolerate; alert mode is for the more acute, active form.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the three ways Greene gives for detecting active envy in the order he lists them.
items: Learn the signs of envy that leak through
Know the types of people prone to acting on envy
Understand the circumstances that trigger active envy
questions.explain: Greene lists signs, types and triggers, and says using all three decoding devices increases your chances of detection.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What three decoding devices does Greene offer for detecting active envy, and can they catch all of it?
questions.a: We can learn the signs of envy that leak through, be aware of the types of people more prone to acting on envy, and understand the circumstances and actions that might trigger active envy. Greene admits we can never see all envious actions, since people are too good at disguising them, but using all three devices increases our chances of detection.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises looking for combinations or repetitions of the signs of envy, a pattern, before moving to alert mode.
questions.explain: A single sign in isolation might indicate only passive or weak envy, so Greene says to look for a pattern before going on alert.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene say first impressions should be given added weight in detecting envy?
options: When people first feel envy they have not yet fooled themselves into thinking it is something else, so it leaks more
We observe strangers more closely than we observe friends
Envy is strongest at a first meeting and then fades away
Enviers deliberately show their envy early to test how we react
questions.explain: Early on the envier has not yet disguised the feeling to themselves, so microexpressions leak through more readily than later.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: The root of the Latin word for envy, ____, means to look through, to probe with the eyes like a dagger.
questions.explain: Greene notes envy is most associated with the eyes, and the word’s early meaning was tied to the evil eye.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does Greene describe the envious microexpression?
questions.a: The envier’s eyes momentarily bore into you with a look of disdain and a touch of hostility, like a child who feels cheated. The corners of the mouth turn down, the nose is in a sneering, somewhat upturned position, and the chin juts out. The look is a little too direct and held a little too long, but lasts no more than a second or two and is usually followed by a strained, fake smile.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each part of the face to how it looks in the envious microexpression Greene describes.
pairs: Momentarily boring into you with disdain
In a sneering, somewhat upturned position
questions.explain: Greene says envy is most associated with the eyes but the microexpression affects the entire face, before a strained smile covers it.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What test for envy did Arthur Schopenhauer devise, as Greene describes it?
options: Ignore suspected enviers for a time and see how they react
Ask suspected enviers directly whether they envy you and watch their eyes
Tell suspected enviers some good news about yourself and watch for a quick look of disappointment
Praise suspected enviers lavishly and see whether they return the praise
questions.explain: Schopenhauer’s quick test is to share good news, such as a promotion, and notice the flash of disappointment and strained tone; sharing a misfortune reveals the opposite flash of glee.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: The uncontrollable flash of joy an envier shows at your misfortune is commonly known as ____.
questions.explain: Greene says envious people cannot help feeling glee at the bad luck of those they envy, and their eyes light up for a fleeting second.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these reactions of a suspected envier by whether, in Schopenhauer’s test, they follow your good news or your bad news.

items.t: A very quick expression of disappointment
Tension and strain in their congratulations
Eyes lighting up for a fleeting second
A flash of glee at your pain

questions.explain: Good news brings out disappointment and strained congratulations; misfortune brings out schadenfreude.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each sign of envy to its description, as Greene presents them.
pairs: Fleeting looks of disdain, or glee at your misfortune
Compliments that leave you confused and uncomfortable
Gossip that vents hostility to third parties
questions.explain: These are the four signs of envy Greene lists; he advises watching for them in combination or repetition.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the four signs of envy in the order Greene presents them.
items: Microexpressions
Poisonous praise
Backbiting
The push and pull
questions.explain: Greene moves from the fleeting looks of first envy, to little envy bites, to gossip, and ends with the full pattern seen in the Jane Williams story.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Your new film gets a good reception, and a friend immediately says you must be thrilled about all the money you will make. Which sign of envy does Greene say this is?
options: Backbiting, venting hostility to a third party
A microexpression of joy at your misfortune
The push and pull, alternating warmth and criticism
Poisonous praise, implying you did it for the money
questions.explain: Greene’s example of poisonous praise is praising the money a project will make, implying you sold out, timed just when you feel a flush of joy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these forms of poisonous praise does Greene describe?
options: Toasting your success in front of your family
Noting the least likable parts of your audience
Praising the craft and effort that went into your work
Praising the money your project will make, implying you sold out
Praising something just after you have lost it
questions.explain: Poisonous praise praises in a way that wounds: money over merit, guilt by association, or regret for what you lost. Praise for the work itself is exactly what enviers withhold.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these behaviors into poisonous praise and backbiting, two signs of envy Greene describes.

items.t: Saying Wall Street executives will love your work
Calling your lost house beautiful, what a shame
Praising the money your project will earn
Eyes lighting up while telling stories of acquaintances
Gossip that no one is really that great
Spreading a negative story about you to others

questions.explain: Poisonous praise wounds you directly under cover of a compliment; backbiting vents hostility behind your back to third parties.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene say backbiting by a friend is a sign of active envy?
questions.a: Gossip is a frequent cover for envy, a convenient way to vent it through malicious stories, and people who gossip a lot about common acquaintances will gossip about you. What indicates active envy is that they are your friend yet feel the need to vent their hostility to a third party rather than keep it to themselves. Serial gossipers do not make loyal and trustworthy friends.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that with backbiting you should wait until several negative stories about you have spread before raising your antennae.
questions.explain: Greene says that if you ever get wind of a story they have spread about you, only one such instance should be enough to raise your antennae.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the stages of the push and pull pattern of envy in the order Greene describes them.
items: They eagerly befriend you and saturate you with attention
Through closeness they gather material and find your weak points
Once your emotions are engaged, they criticize you pointedly
They return to their initial warmth, and the pattern repeats
When you break away, they tell others you are cruel
questions.explain: Greene traces the push and pull from effusive early friendship, through confusing criticism alternating with warmth, to the final twist of blaming you when you defend yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does the push and pull pattern of envy work, according to Greene?
questions.a: Enviers show unusual eagerness to befriend you, saturate you with attention and praise you too effusively too early. The closeness lets them find your weak points; then, once your emotions are engaged, they criticize you in confusing ways unrelated to anything you did, before returning to warmth, so you are trapped between friendship and occasional pain. Underneath, they befriend people they envy and then subtly torture them.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In the push and pull, Greene says enviers pick out your flaws and regretted words like ____ building a case against you.
questions.explain: The image stresses how deliberately they gather and emphasize material against you.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In the push and pull pattern, what does Greene say enviers do when you finally defend yourself or break off the friendship?
options: They ascribe to you a mean or even cruel streak and tell others
They apologize sincerely and the envy comes to an end
They admit their envy and ask for your help
They leave quietly and never mention you again
questions.explain: Your reaction gives them new material: they can now claim you are mean or cruel. Greene adds that their past shows other dramatic breakups, always the other person’s fault.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says criticism of you that seems sincere but is not directly related to anything you have actually done is usually a strong sign of envy.
questions.explain: Greene concludes the push and pull by saying such criticism lets enviers wound you while covering any tracks of envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego, signal about the Law of Envy?
options: Envy grows from a fragile sense of self-worth, so we must watch for it in others and build self-worth from internal standards
We should avoid anyone with a big ego, since they are always envious
Only the ego of the envied person is at risk, so we should protect our image
Strong, inflated egos are the main source of envy and must be humbled
questions.explain: Envy rests on a painful sense of inferiority, which is why the law warns us to watch for it and to develop self-worth from internal standards rather than comparisons.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 10 in the order they appear.
items: Fatal Friends
Keys to Human Nature
Signs of Envy
Envier Types
Envy Triggers
Beyond Envy
questions.explain: The chapter follows the book’s pattern: a story, the general explanation, then practical decoding tools, ending with how to move beyond envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 10 to its role in the chapter.
pairs: A story of envy within a close friendship
Why envy is elusive, and passive versus active envy
Clues that leak out of envious people
People especially prone to acting on envy
Circumstances that can set off active envy
questions.explain: The Keys section promises three decoding devices, signs, types and triggers, and the next three sections deliver them in that order after the Mary Shelley story.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does the end of the Keys to Human Nature section in Chapter 10 set up the sections that follow?
questions.a: It names three ways to detect active envy before it turns dangerous: learning the signs of envy that leak through, knowing the types of people prone to acting on envy, and understanding the circumstances that trigger it. The chapter then takes these in turn in Signs of Envy, Envier Types and Envy Triggers.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Chapter 10 follows Chapter 9, Confront Your Dark Side (the Law of Repression). What links the two?
options: Both argue that envy is mainly a problem of whole generations
Both teach how to become an elusive object of desire
Both focus on facing our own mortality
Both deal with feelings we hide even from ourselves, as Jane concealed and repressed her envy
questions.explain: Greene says Jane had reasons to conceal and even repress her envy, which leaks out only indirectly, much like the repressed dark side of Chapter 9.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these earlier chapters of the book connect closely with the first half of Chapter 10 on envy?
options: Seize the Historical Moment (Chapter 17), on generations
Determine the Strength of People’s Character (Chapter 4), on patterns of behavior
Meditate on Our Common Mortality (Chapter 18), on death
See Through People’s Masks (Chapter 3), on reading nonverbal cues such as microexpressions
Confront Your Dark Side (Chapter 9), on feelings we repress
questions.explain: Decoding envious microexpressions draws on the skills of Chapter 3, hidden envy echoes the repression of Chapter 9, and the envier’s repeated dramatic breakups is a pattern like those in Chapter 4. Generations and death belong to later chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein, when does a lifelong proneness to envy begin?
questions.explain: Klein traced chronic envy to the first months of life, when some infants feel the mother's growing absences more keenly and come to see father and siblings as rivals.
options: In early adulthood, after the first serious career setback
In school, when children are first ranked against classmates
In adolescence, when teenagers first compete with peers for status
In early infancy, when some infants are especially sensitive to the mother's withdrawal

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: The psychoanalyst ____ argued that people prone to envy their entire lives begin feeling it in early infancy.
questions.explain: Klein, who specialized in infancy and early childhood, noticed that some children feel extra hostility toward father, siblings and mother over the attention they receive.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene notes that some parents create or intensify a child's envy by playing favorites or withdrawing on purpose.
questions.explain: Greene says there are parents who intensify such envy by playing favorites and by withdrawing to make the child more dependent.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Melanie Klein, how do envy-prone people differ from most of us in the way childhood feelings carry into adult life?
questions.a: Most of us balance moments of feeling deprived with moments of undeniable love and gratitude, and later transfer these positive emotions to siblings, teachers, friends and partners. Envy-prone people instead transfer their early envy and hostility to a series of others they see as disappointing them. Their moments of gratitude are rare, and nothing is ever quite good enough for them.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these steps of Klein's account of how chronic envy develops in the order they occur.
items: Infant and mother are almost never apart
The infant must cope with the mother's longer absences
A sensitive infant grows greedy for more feeding and attention
Father and siblings come to be seen as rivals
As an adult, nothing ever feels quite good enough
questions.explain: Klein describes a sequence from early closeness, through painful adjustment to absence, to rivalry with father and siblings, setting a lifelong pattern of feeling deprived.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these strategies, according to Klein, do envy-prone people use to mitigate or repress their envy?
options: Devaluing themselves so they need not compete
Denigrating anything or anyone good in the world
Seeking out mentors to emulate
Becoming extremely independent so they need no one
Openly confessing their envy to the people they envy
questions.explain: Klein lists denigrating the good, extreme independence and self-devaluation. Emulating mentors and confessing envy are healthy responses the envy-prone avoid.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Klein, what happens to the coping strategies of envy-prone people under stress such as a career downturn or wound to the ego?
questions.explain: Klein calls these strategies brittle. Under stress the latent envy from their earliest years resurfaces, and they look for people to envy so they can reexperience the primal emotion.
options: They harden, making these people immune to envy for years
They break down, and the latent envy is directed at new targets
They make the person openly admit their envy to others
They turn into healthy ambition and emulation

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these patterns into Klein's envy-prone child and most other children.

items.t: Feels continually deprived despite the attention received
Grows up feeling nothing is ever quite good enough
Transfers early hostility to a series of disappointing people
Balances jealous moments with moments of undeniable love
Transfers positive feelings to teachers, mentors and friends
Alternates between wanting more and feeling grateful

questions.explain: Klein's envy-prone child rarely feels satisfied or grateful, while most children counterbalance feelings of deprivation with experiences of love and gratitude.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the five envier types in the order Greene presents them.
items: The Leveler
The Self-entitled Slacker
The Status Fiend
The Attacher
The Insecure Master
questions.explain: Greene moves from the cynical leveler and the lazy slacker, through the status fiend and the attacher, to the insecure master who envies from a position of power.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what separates the Leveler from people with genuine empathy for underdogs?
questions.explain: Both types seem to care about injustice, but levelers cannot appreciate excellence in almost anyone, except those who are dead, because achievement makes them feel insecure.
options: Levelers secretly admire the powerful people they mock
Levelers cannot recognize or appreciate excellence in almost anyone except the dead
Levelers act on behalf of the underdogs rather than just talking
Levelers only defend underdogs who are members of their own family

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: To soothe their insecurities, Levelers have come to associate excellence with ____.
