questions.explain: Levelers cover their envy with indignation, railing at high achievers for gaming the system or being lucky, so that success itself looks unfair.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says Levelers make excellent professional ____, since this lets them tear down those they secretly envy and be rewarded for it.
questions.explain: As critics, levelers can attack the people they envy in public and be paid for it.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does the Leveler disguise the envy first felt toward successful people?
questions.a: The envy is quickly covered up by indignation. Levelers rail at high achievers for gaming the system, for being far too ambitious, or for simply being lucky. They associate excellence with unfairness, which soothes their own insecurity, and they cast themselves as blameless victims of injustice.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the Leveler's main goal?
questions.explain: Greene says levelers want to bring everyone down to their own mediocre level, including people who are simply enjoying themselves or have a strong sense of purpose.
options: To collect material signs of status
To attach themselves to a powerful patron
To bring everyone down to the same mediocre level they occupy
To win praise for their own hidden talents

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In the workplace, the Leveler begins with passive-aggressive comments that taint you with the ugly word ____.
questions.explain: Greene warns that levelers make you feel guilty for your impulse to excel, labelling you ambitious before moving to hurtful criticism and sabotage.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these are signs Greene gives for recognizing a Leveler?
options: A wicked sense of humor that deflates the powerful and pretentious
Generous praise for living high achievers
Not taking easily to jokes at their own expense
A strong, clear sense of purpose in life
Many stories of injustices done to them in which they are always blameless
questions.explain: Levelers mock others but cannot take a joke, and paint themselves as blameless victims. They praise almost no living achievers and lack the sense of purpose they resent in others.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these traits into the Leveler and the Status Fiend.

items.t: Celebrates low culture and trash
Uses cynical humor to deflate the powerful
Tells stories of injustices inflicted on them
Asks how much money you make
Reduces everything to material considerations
May pose as the consummate monk or idealistic hippie

questions.explain: Levelers attack excellence through humor and grievance, while status fiends measure their self-worth by money and possessions, sometimes hiding this behind a show of indifference.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does the Self-entitled Slacker move so quickly from envy to hostility around high achievers?
questions.a: Slackers feel they deserve attention and rewards as if these were naturally due to them, but deep down they are insecure about their ability to get what they want, which is why they never developed discipline. People who work hard and earn real respect make them aware of the self-doubts they have been trying to repress, and this envy turns quickly into hostility.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: In the story of Christopher Wren, William Talman was a lower-level architect appointed as Wren's assistant who believed their roles should have been reversed.
questions.explain: Talman had an extremely high opinion of himself and a lazy streak, and he resented serving under Wren, whom he thought he should have outranked.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What was the outcome of William Talman's years-long campaign against Christopher Wren?
questions.explain: Talman so muddied the waters that the king gave him important commissions, and he incorporated many of Wren's innovations, while the battle affected Wren emotionally for years.
options: Wren and Talman reconciled and designed St. Paul's Cathedral together
Wren lost all his commissions and left architecture for science
Talman was dismissed after Wren exposed his laziness to the king
The king gave some important commissions to the less talented Talman, who stole Wren's innovations

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these events in the story of Christopher Wren and William Talman in order.
items: Talman is appointed as Wren's assistant
Accidents on Wren's projects kill some workmen
Talman accuses Wren of negligence and digs up past misdeeds
The king gives important commissions to Talman
Talman incorporates many of Wren's innovations
questions.explain: Talman used the accidents as an opening for a long smear campaign, won commissions from the king, and then took Wren's ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: If you are of a higher social status than a Status Fiend, how does Greene say the Status Fiend will conceal envy?
questions.explain: Toward those above them, status fiends hide envy behind admiration. Toward peers and coworkers they sniff for favoritism and attack in underhanded ways.
options: By openly mocking your wealth in public
By competing with you to earn more
By appearing to admire your success
By cutting off all contact with you

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: For the Status Fiend, status is more than a way of measuring social position: it is the most important determinant of their ____.
questions.explain: All of us monitor rank, but status fiends let it decide their whole sense of their own value.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these questions does Greene say a Status Fiend is likely to ask you?
options: What you see as your calling in life
Whether you occasionally fly business class
How much money you make
Which books have most influenced your thinking
Whether you own your home and what neighborhood it is in
questions.explain: Status fiends gather petty points of comparison about money, property and privileges. Questions about calling or ideas do not serve their need to compare status.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Status Fiends always give themselves away by expensive clothes and cars.
questions.explain: Greene warns not to be fooled by an older car or shabby dress: status fiends may assert status in the opposite direction, as a monk or idealistic hippie, while secretly yearning for luxury.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In Reggie Jackson's account, what most embittered his Yankee teammate Graig Nettles?
questions.explain: Nettles constantly compared salaries and resented Jackson's pay and press, deciding Jackson was a manipulator who played the media and the owner.
options: Jackson's refusal to share batting tips with teammates
The size of Jackson's salary and the media attention he received
Jackson's criticism of Nettles in his autobiography
Jackson's friendship with Nettles's former manager

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Reggie Jackson felt there was some tacit racism in Graig Nettles's envy of him.
questions.explain: Jackson felt Nettles acted as if a black athlete could not possibly earn a salary so much larger than his own.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says the Attacher conceals an undercurrent of envy through excessive ____.
questions.explain: Attachers make themselves useful to the powerful and fawn over them, while secretly feeling entitled to some of their attention.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How did Yolanda Saldivar first attach herself to the Tejano singer Selena?
questions.explain: Saldivar ingratiated herself through the fan club and the clothing stores, grew powerful and sycophantic, then embezzled funds and, when confronted, murdered Selena.
options: She was Selena's childhood friend who later became her agent
She started a major fan club, then became manager of Selena's clothing stores
She produced Selena's records, then ran her concert tours
She was hired as Selena's backup singer, then her personal stylist

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What trait does Greene say the Attacher shares with all enviers, and how does it drive the Attacher's behavior?
questions.a: Like all enviers, attachers lack a clear sense of purpose: they do not know their calling, drift between jobs and feel empty inside. They naturally envy people who act with purpose and attach themselves to such a person's life, partly to get some of what they are missing and partly out of a desire to harm the other person.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as warning signs or methods of the Attacher?
options: Gathering information on you to leak or spread as gossip
Refusing to make themselves useful to you
Openly criticizing your work in meetings
Drawing you in by flattery and attention rather than experience and competence
questions.explain: Attachers are too eager to be useful and win you over with flattery, then attack through leaked information and gossip, not open criticism.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these traits into the Self-entitled Slacker and the Attacher.

items.t: Writes the briefest outline of a novel and expects praise
Feels rewards are naturally due without hard work
Keeps their position by charm and politics, not results
Becomes a friend or assistant to someone powerful
Fawns excessively on the person they envy
Wanders between jobs without a calling

questions.explain: Slackers are narcissists who avoid discipline and resent hard workers; attachers lack purpose and fasten themselves to a purposeful, successful person they secretly want to wound.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What reason did Michael Eisner give for firing Jeffrey Katzenberg from Disney in 1995?
questions.explain: Greene says the stated reason hid the truth: Katzenberg's films had become Disney's main source of revenue, and Eisner envied his golden touch.
options: Katzenberg's abrasive personality and not being a team player
Katzenberg's films losing money for the studio
Katzenberg's plan to leave and start a rival studio
Katzenberg's leaking of company secrets to rivals

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Maya joins a firm, works extra hard, and delivers clearly excellent results. After several months her confident-seeming boss suddenly demotes her with a vague story about her attitude. Which envier type best explains this?
questions.explain: Greene describes exactly this pattern: insecure bosses envy a subordinate's youth, energy and talent, then justify a firing or demotion with a concocted narrative.
options: The Attacher
The Self-entitled Slacker
The Leveler
The Insecure Master

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says Insecure Masters will inevitably have a track record of ____ people for strange reasons.
questions.explain: A pattern of unexplained firings, as with Eisner and the creative people he brought in, is a sign of a boss's insecurity and envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does Greene advise you to protect yourself from an Insecure Master?
questions.a: Watch those above you for signs of insecurity, such as a track record of firing people for strange reasons. Play it safe by deferring to such bosses, making them look better and earning their trust. Couch your brilliant ideas as their ideas and let them take the credit; your time to shine will come if you do not stir their insecurities.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each envier type to Greene's example of it.
pairs: William Talman, envious assistant of Christopher Wren
Graig Nettles, teammate of Reggie Jackson
Yolanda Saldivar, fan-club founder and manager for Selena
Michael Eisner, who fired Jeffrey Katzenberg
questions.explain: Each story shows the type in action: Talman's smear campaign, Nettles's salary comparisons, Saldivar's fawning turned murderous, and Eisner's envy of a talented subordinate.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each envier type to its typical form of attack.
pairs: Passive-aggressive digs about ambition, then sabotage as retributive justice
Gathering information to leak or spread as gossip
A sudden demotion or firing justified by a concocted story
Underhanded attacks that undermine your position in the group
questions.explain: Each type attacks in a way suited to its position and disguise, from the leveler's moralizing to the boss's unexplained firing.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each envier type to Greene's advice for dealing with it.
pairs: Downplay what you have and talk up their possessions and status
Hire people with experience rather than just a pleasing manner
Defer, make them look good and present your ideas as theirs
Beware colleagues who rise by charm and politics, not results
questions.explain: Greene's defenses aim to avoid triggering each type's particular insecurity or to keep such people out of your working life.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the most common trigger of envy?
questions.explain: Greene calls a sudden rise in status the most common trigger, especially among people in your own profession.
options: A sudden change in your status that alters your relationship to friends and peers
Openly criticizing the work of rivals
A long period of failure that makes others pity you
Moving to a new city where nobody knows you

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene quotes Hesiod: The potter envies the ____, the craftsman the craftsman, the writer the writer.
questions.explain: Hesiod's line shows that envy has long been known to be strongest among people in the same profession.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What point does Greene use Hesiod's line about potters, craftsmen and writers to make?
questions.explain: Greene cites Hesiod to show that envy among peers in one's own profession has been known for a very long time.
options: Envy can be cured by changing one's profession
Envy is strongest among people in the same field with similar aspirations
Envy is a modern problem created by competitive markets
Craftsmen are more envious than people in other walks of life

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when you succeed, you should treat every faint praise and veiled criticism from peers as a dangerous attack.
questions.explain: Greene advises being reasonably tolerant, since you would probably feel the same in their place, and not taking faint praise personally; only signs of active envy call for distance.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: When discussing your success with people who might envy you, what does Greene say you should always emphasize?
questions.explain: Playing up luck makes your success less of a judgment on others' abilities and so blunts their envy.
options: The element of luck in your success
The hard work and sacrifice it took
The rewards still to come
The mistakes of your rivals

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene warns never to praise a writer in front of another writer, or an artist in front of an artist, unless the person being praised is ____.
questions.explain: Praising a living peer in front of someone in the same field stirs that person's envy; the dead pose no threat.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene advise you to do when sudden success may stir envy in peers in your field?
questions.a: Be reasonably tolerant of their envy, since you would probably feel the same. Use self-deprecating humor, do not rub people's faces in your success, and play up the element of luck. Offer help to those closest to you without seeming patronizing, and if you see signs of active envy, get as far away from those people as possible.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says people who are getting older, with their careers in decline, have delicate egos and are prone to envy.
questions.explain: Greene flags aging people whose careers are declining as especially prone to envy, as with Paul Iribe in the Coco Chanel story.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why do people with natural gifts often attract even more envy, according to Greene?
questions.explain: Gifted people who do not feel envy cannot understand it, so unaware of the danger they show their talents and attract more envy, as Mary Shelley did.
options: They tend to hide their gifts, which makes people suspicious
They usually refuse to work hard, which offends others
They tend to be naive: not feeling envy themselves, they display their talents freely
They tend to be arrogant and openly mock less gifted people

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these does Greene recommend for people with natural gifts who want to blunt envy?
options: Strategically revealing some flaws
Avoiding contact with people in their own field
Displaying their talents openly so others can be inspired
Showing intellectual clumsiness in subjects outside their expertise
Discussing mistakes they have made in the past
questions.explain: Greene advises masking natural superiority with selective flaws and past mistakes that do not diminish one's reputation; flaunting talent invites envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what happened to John F. Kennedy's popularity after the failed Bay of Pigs invasion?
questions.explain: Kennedy had seemed almost too perfect to identify with; the debacle and his acceptance of responsibility made him more likeable.
options: His popularity fell until he blamed the military for the failure
His poll numbers collapsed because the public lost faith in his judgment
His popularity stayed the same because the public blamed his advisers
His poll numbers skyrocketed because the mistake, for which he took full responsibility, humanized him

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says Kennedy's big mistake at the Bay of Pigs had ____ him in the eyes of the public.
questions.explain: By showing a flaw, Kennedy became easier to identify with and like, which is why his poll numbers rose.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do successful women tend to attract envy rather than admiration?
questions.a: We often admire people who achieve great things because we do not feel personally challenged by them. A high-achieving woman, however, inflicts greater feelings of inferiority in both women and men, which leads to envy and hostility instead. This hostility is veiled as something else, so such women are called too cold, ambitious or unfeminine.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Coco Chanel met Paul Iribe when his career was at its peak and hers was in decline.
questions.explain: It was the reverse: Chanel was at the height of her power in 1931, while Iribe's career was on the decline, and her growing celebrity eclipsed his.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these events in the story of Coco Chanel and Paul Iribe in order.
items: Chanel meets Iribe at the height of her power
Iribe, an expert seducer, wins her over
He begins criticizing her extravagance and other flaws
He tries to control every aspect of her life
Chanel later writes that he hoped to destroy her
questions.explain: The relationship moved from seduction to criticism and control, showing Greene's point that love and envy are not mutually exclusive.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene say Robert Rubin's career at Goldman Sachs shows about envy?
questions.explain: Rubin became more deferential as he rose, seeking the views of junior staff, and few people had anything bad to say about him despite the competitive environment.
options: Envy disappears once you reach the very top of an organization
Envy is best handled by openly confronting your rivals
You can short-circuit envy by placing attention on other people instead of yourself
Competitive firms are free of envy if pay is high enough

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these habits helped Robert Rubin defuse envy at Goldman Sachs?
options: Making sure he was credited publicly for each success
Answering subordinates' questions about a crisis by first asking what they thought
Reminding colleagues that his view was just one man's opinion
Asking the most junior associate in a meeting for an opinion and listening intently
Correcting junior staff sharply in front of others
questions.explain: Rubin's humility, as one colleague put it, meant deferring to others and taking their answers seriously. Seeking credit or humiliating juniors would have stirred envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: If you find yourself under an envy attack, what does Greene call your best strategy?
questions.explain: The envier feeds on your overreaction to justify their actions and draw you into more drama, so composure comes first, followed by physical distance.
options: Controlling your emotions and keeping your composure
Publicly explaining that the attacker is envious
Generously trying to repair the relationship
Planning careful revenge on the envier

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene advise against trying to repair the relationship with someone who has made an envy attack on you?
questions.a: Your generosity in trying to repair things will only intensify the envier's feelings of inferiority, and they will strike again. Instead you should get physical distance, defend yourself against public attacks or gossip, and not harbor revenge fantasies. Their chronic unhappiness is punishment enough, so let them stew in their cold poison from a distance.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise when you are under an envy attack?
options: Defend yourself against public attacks or gossip
Maintain your composure at all costs
Imagine and plan your revenge
Get some physical distance, for example by cutting off contact
Try hard to win the envier back as a friend
questions.explain: Greene recommends composure, distance and self-defense, but warns that reconciliation attempts intensify the envier's inferiority and that revenge fantasies are pointless.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Envy among the public can turn against public figures in the form of ____, pleasure at their misfortune, as with the hostility toward Martha Stewart.
questions.explain: Greene says public envy shows itself as schadenfreude when public figures suffer a misfortune, and gossip about the powerful becomes an industry.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene argue that envy is more prevalent now than ever before?
questions.a: Social media gives us a continual window into the lives of friends, pseudofriends and celebrities, but what we see is a highly idealized image of their lives. Comparing ourselves with it leaves us with a generalized dissatisfaction, a low-grade envy that waits to be triggered into the acute variety when something intensifies our insecurities.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these stages of social-media envy, as Greene describes them, in order.
items: We see idealized images of others' lives
We wonder whether we are missing out
A generalized feeling of dissatisfaction sets in
Low-grade envy sits inside us, waiting
Something we read intensifies insecurity and envy turns acute
questions.explain: Greene traces how a steady diet of idealized images breeds diffuse dissatisfaction that can flare into acute envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each person to the point Greene uses them to make about envy.
pairs: Envied the younger Raphael and tried to block his commissions
A public mistake made a too-perfect figure likeable
Deference to others defused envy in a competitive firm
A successful woman tormented by an envious lover
The public piles on with schadenfreude after a misfortune
questions.explain: Each figure illustrates a different trigger or defense: peer rivalry, humanizing flaws, humility, envy of successful women, and public schadenfreude.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each envy trigger to Greene's advice for handling it.
pairs: A sudden rise in status among peers
Play up luck and use self-deprecating humor
Strategically reveal some flaws and past mistakes
Success and fame as a woman
Be adept at deflecting envy and play the humble card
Being targeted by an envy attack
Keep your composure and get physical distance
questions.explain: Greene pairs each trigger with a way of lowering the envy it provokes or limiting the harm it can do.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these actions into what Greene advises and what he warns against when dealing with envy.

items.t: Emphasizing luck when discussing your success
Showing selective awkwardness in some areas
Keeping your composure under attack
Praising a living writer in front of another writer
Trying to repair the relationship with an envier
Harboring revenge fantasies
Flaunting your natural talents

questions.explain: Greene's advice lowers others' sense of inferiority or limits the envier's ammunition; the warned-against actions provoke more envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these into Greene's envier types and his envy triggers.

items.t: The Leveler
The Status Fiend
The Insecure Master
A sudden rise in status among peers
Natural gifts and talents
Success and fame achieved by a woman

questions.explain: Types are people especially prone to envy; triggers are circumstances that can set off envy in almost anyone.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do we tend to deny that we ever feel envy?
questions.explain: Greene says the initial pang is quickly disguised, so we notice only the resentment that follows and so are not being honest with ourselves.
options: Envy is so rare in modern life that most people never feel it
Envy is felt only in childhood and fades in adulthood
We are conscious only of the indignation or resentment that covers up the first pangs of envy
We feel envy only toward strangers, never toward friends

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene mentions studies showing that monkeys feel envy.
questions.explain: Greene cites this to show that comparing ourselves with others and feeling envy is wired into our nature.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What simple experiment does Greene suggest for catching your own envy?
questions.a: The next time you hear or read about the sudden success of someone in your field, notice the feeling of wanting the same, the pang, and the hostility, however vague, that follows toward that person. The transition happens quickly and is easy to miss, so try to catch it. There should be no guilt, since the sequence is natural, and monitoring it helps in moving beyond envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene's experiment for observing your own envy in order.
items: Hear of the sudden success of someone in your field
Notice the pang of wanting the same
Notice the vague hostility toward that person
Catch the transition without feeling guilt
questions.explain: Greene's experiment trains you to see the quick sequence from pang to hostility, which normally passes unnoticed.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Why does Greene not ask us to stop comparing ourselves with others, and what does he propose instead?
questions.a: Greene thinks it is almost impossible to rid ourselves of the compulsion to compare, because it is too ingrained in our nature as a social animal. Instead we should slowly transform this comparing inclination into something positive, productive and prosocial, using his five exercises.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put Greene's five exercises for moving beyond envy in the order he presents them.
items: Move closer to what you envy
Engage in downward comparisons
Practice Mitfreude
Transmute envy into emulation
Admire human greatness
questions.explain: The exercises move from correcting our view of others, through gratitude and shared joy, to turning envy into effort and admiration.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these are among Greene's five exercises for moving beyond envy?
options: Engage in downward comparisons
Stop comparing yourself with anyone
Practice Mitfreude
Level down those you envy
Move closer to what you envy
questions.explain: Greene explicitly says moving closer is not leveling people down, and he holds that comparison cannot be stopped, only redirected.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene's account of the last ten years of Aristotle Onassis's life illustrate?
questions.explain: Greene uses Onassis, rich and married to Jacqueline Kennedy yet plagued by unloving children, to show that looking closely at an enviable life reveals its miseries.
options: Mitfreude: he took joy in the success of his children
Admiring human greatness: his fortune was an achievement to celebrate
Transmuting envy into emulation: he rose by copying richer rivals
Moving closer to what you envy: great wealth brought him endless nightmares

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that moving closer to what you envy means diminishing the achievements of great people.
questions.explain: Greene says this is not the same as leveling them down: you look behind façades and imagine the disadvantages of their position without diminishing real achievement.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the best antidote to envy that downward comparisons stimulate?
questions.explain: Looking at those with less stirs empathy and gratitude, and Greene calls such gratitude the best antidote to envy.
options: Pride in being better than others
Indifference to how others live
Pity for those who have more than you
Gratitude for what you actually possess

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene says gratitude is a ____ that requires exercise or it will atrophy.
questions.explain: Greene suggests writing down the good things in your life that you take for granted to keep gratitude strong.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Nietzsche's term ____ means joying with others, the opposite of schadenfreude.
questions.explain: Instead of taking pleasure in others' pain, Greene urges us to actively feel the joy of others as a form of empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does Greene say practicing Mitfreude differs from simply congratulating someone?
questions.explain: Congratulations are easy and easily forgotten; Mitfreude means imagining and sharing the other person's happiness, which also creates rare rapport.
options: You actively try to feel their joy as a form of empathy, rather than saying easily forgotten words
You congratulate them only when their success does not threaten you
You congratulate them publicly rather than in private
You hide your envy behind especially lavish praise

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Besides cleaning our minds of envy, what does Greene say practicing Mitfreude does for our relationships and for ourselves?
questions.a: It creates an unusual form of rapport: when we are the targets of Mitfreude, we feel the other person's genuine excitement at our good fortune and are induced to feel the same for them. Because this is so rare, it has great power to bond people. And by internalizing other people's joy, we increase our own capacity to feel joy in our own experiences.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene's fourth exercise is to transmute envy into ____, so that it becomes a spur to excellence.
questions.explain: Instead of wanting to hurt or steal from someone who has achieved more, we try to raise ourselves to their level.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Leo is jealous of a colleague's skill at design. Instead of sniping, he starts practicing every evening and joins a workshop with people slightly better than him. Which of Greene's exercises is he following?
questions.explain: Greene advises redirecting the comparing mechanism into raising ourselves up, even seeking people slightly above us in skill to stimulate competitive desire.
options: Practice Mitfreude
Move closer to what you envy
Transmute envy into emulation
Engage in downward comparisons

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as psychological shifts needed to transmute envy into emulation?
options: Believing that we have the capacity to raise ourselves up
Avoiding people who are more skilled than we are
Congratulating rivals politely while hiding our feelings
Developing a solid work ethic to back this up
questions.explain: Confidence in our ability to learn and a rigorous, persistent work ethic make emulation possible; avoiding the more skilled defeats the purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does having a sense of purpose immunize you against envy, according to Greene?
questions.a: With a feel for your calling, you are focused on your own life and plans, which are clear and invigorating. Your satisfaction comes from realizing your potential rather than from fleeting public attention, so you have much less need to compare. Your sense of self-worth comes from within, not from without.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene calls admiration the polar ____ of envy.
questions.explain: In admiration we acknowledge and celebrate people's achievements without feeling insecure or pained by their superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: What does Greene say we gain from the exercise of admiring human greatness?
questions.a: Admiration lets us acknowledge others' superiority without pain and, beyond that, celebrate the highest potential of our species, a kind of Mitfreude with the best in human nature. It lifts us above the pettiness of daily life and has a calming effect. Though it is easier to admire the dead, we should include at least one living person in our pantheon.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: True or false: Greene says we should admire only great figures from the past, since admiring living people inevitably breeds envy.
questions.explain: Greene grants that the dead are easier to admire without envy, but urges us to include at least one living person among those we admire.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each of Greene's exercises for moving beyond envy to its core idea.
pairs: Move closer to what you envy
Look behind glittering façades and imagine the disadvantages
Look at those who have less, building gratitude
Actively feel other people's joy as empathy
Raise yourself to the level of those who achieve more
Celebrate the highest potential of our species
questions.explain: Each exercise redirects the comparing instinct away from hostility toward a more accurate, grateful or productive response.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each term from Beyond Envy to its meaning.
pairs: Pleasure in the pain of other people
Joying with others in their happiness
Called the best antidote to envy
questions.explain: Greene sets Mitfreude against schadenfreude and treats admiration and gratitude as the healthy counterparts of envy.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these into what feeds envy and what eases it, according to Greene.

items.t: Seeing only others' triumphs and best face
Being lazy and undisciplined
Focusing on those who seem to have more
Seeing the quarrels behind closed doors
Gratitude for what you possess
A sense of purpose and calling
Awe before mountains, sea or forest

questions.explain: Envy thrives on idealized views, idleness and upward comparison; it fades with a closer look, gratitude, purpose and sublime moments free of comparison.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: In describing the Attacher's lack of purpose, Greene points the reader to which later chapter?
questions.explain: Greene says lack of purpose is common to all enviers and refers ahead to Chapter 13, which is also why a sense of purpose returns in Beyond Envy as a defense against envy.
options: Chapter 5, Become an Elusive Object of Desire (the Law of Covetousness)
Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group (the Law of Conformity)
Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose (the Law of Aimlessness)
Chapter 11, Know Your Limits (the Law of Grandiosity)

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Greene ends his advice on surviving an envy attack by recalling which earlier part of Chapter 10?
questions.explain: Greene advises letting the envier stew from a distance, as Mary did to Jane, tying the practical advice back to the chapter's opening story.
options: The Fatal Friends story, in which Mary Shelley let Jane stew in her cold poison from a distance
The Latin root of the word invidia
The Old Testament story of Cain and Abel
Melanie Klein's account of envy in infancy

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does the Envier Types section build on the Keys to Human Nature section of Chapter 10?
questions.a: Keys to Human Nature names three ways to detect active envy before it turns dangerous: signs, types and triggers. Envier Types delivers the second, describing five kinds of people most likely to turn active with their envy, so that you can recognize them early. Envy Triggers then covers the third, the circumstances that provoke envy in almost anyone.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: How does the final section, Beyond Envy, change the focus of Chapter 10?
questions.a: The earlier sections teach you to detect and defend against envy in others. Beyond Envy turns to the reader's own envy, arguing that we all compare and feel envy, especially now with social media, and must manage it in ourselves. It offers five exercises to transform the comparing instinct into something positive, productive and prosocial.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Which of these other chapters of the book does the second half of Chapter 10 refer to explicitly?
options: Chapter 17, on generational patterns
Chapter 12, on gender rigidity
Chapter 5, where Coco Chanel's origins as an orphan are discussed
Chapter 13, on the Law of Aimlessness and a sense of purpose
Chapter 18, on death denial
questions.explain: Greene refers ahead to Chapter 13 for the Attacher's lack of purpose and back to Chapter 5 for Chanel's background; the other chapters are not cited here.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Put these stages of the second half of Chapter 10 in the order Greene takes them.
items: People especially prone to envy
Circumstances that trigger envy in almost anyone
Defending yourself against an envy attack
Why social media makes envy more prevalent
Exercises for transforming your own envy
questions.explain: Greene moves from envious types to triggers, then to defense, the modern spread of envy, and finally to managing envy in ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Match each point in the second half of Chapter 10 to the link it makes elsewhere.
pairs: Coco Chanel's origins as an orphan
Mary Shelley in the Fatal Friends story
The Aeschylus verse that closes the chapter
questions.explain: The second half of the chapter ties its points back to the opening story and its closing verse, and across to other chapters of the book.

questions.unitTitle: Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.q: Sort these topics into the first and second halves of Chapter 10.

items.t: The story of Mary Shelley and Jane Williams
Passive versus active envy
Envious microexpressions
Five types of envier
Circumstances that trigger envy
Five exercises for moving beyond envy

questions.explain: The first half tells the Fatal Friends story and explains and decodes envy; the second half covers types, triggers and moving beyond envy.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: The Law of Grandiosity says that if our opinion of our goodness, greatness and brilliance diverges enough from reality, we become ____.
questions.explain: Greene starts from our deep need to think highly of ourselves; when that self-opinion drifts far enough from reality, it becomes grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to the Law of Grandiosity, what often elevates our natural grandiosity to even more dangerous levels?
options: Strict parents who refused to praise us as children
Harsh criticism that makes us defend our talents
A long run of failures that makes us crave recognition
A small measure of success that seems to confirm our high self-opinion
questions.explain: Greene says a small success confirms our high self-opinion by events, so we forget luck and the help of others. Failure and criticism are not what he names as the trigger here.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Grandiosity name as signs of elevated grandiosity, in yourself or others?
options: A disdain for any form of authority
A habit of crediting mentors for every success
Overbearing certainty in the positive outcome of your plans
Excessive touchiness if criticized
Frequent doubts about whether a plan will work
questions.explain: The law lists overbearing certainty, touchiness about criticism and disdain for authority. Crediting others and doubting your plans are the opposite of grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Grandiosity advises tying any feelings of greatness to your work, your achievements and your contributions to society.
questions.explain: The law ends by telling us to keep a realistic assessment of our limits and to anchor any sense of greatness in real work and contribution.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to the Law of Grandiosity, why does our success often not last?
questions.a: A small success seems to confirm our already high self-opinion, so we forget the role luck and other people played and imagine we have the golden touch. Losing contact with reality, we make irrational decisions, and these undo the success.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the steps of the Law of Grandiosity’s account of how success turns against us in order.
items: We have a deep need to think highly of ourselves
A small success seems to confirm our high self-opinion
We forget the role of luck and the contributions of others
We lose contact with reality and make irrational decisions
Our success does not last
questions.explain: The law moves from the universal need for a high self-opinion, to success confirming it, to forgetting luck and others, to irrational decisions that end the success.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Michael Eisner, which company was he president of in 1984, before moving to Disney?
options: Warner Bros.
DreamWorks
Creative Artists Agency
Paramount Pictures
questions.explain: Eisner went from ABC to Paramount, where he ran the film studio under Barry Diller. Warner Bros. was Frank Wells’s former studio, CAA was Ovitz’s agency, and DreamWorks was founded later by Katzenberg.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What was Michael Eisner’s formula for creating profitable films at Paramount?
questions.a: Eisner was obsessed with keeping costs down. A film had to start from a great concept that was original, easy to summarize and dramatic; such films would market themselves. A studio could churn these relatively inexpensive films out in volume, and even moderate hits would ensure a steady flow of income, against the blockbuster mentality of the late 1970s.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Eisner’s Paramount formula held that a film had to begin with a great ____, one that was original, easy to summarize and dramatic.
questions.explain: In Eisner’s formula, a weak underlying concept wasted all the money spent on stars and writers, while a strong one would market itself.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Michael Eisner, why did the run-down Walt Disney Company seem to him the perfect target for his ambitions?
options: Roy Disney offered to sell him a controlling stake in the company
It had just produced a string of hits he could take credit for
Its dilapidated state meant it could only move up, and he could dictate his terms
Its animation department was already the most profitable in Hollywood
questions.explain: Disney had not had a hit since 1968 and its board was desperate to avoid a hostile takeover, so Eisner could work his magic and set his own terms of leadership.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each person in the story of Michael Eisner to their role.
pairs: Former head of Warner Bros., named Disney president to run the business side
Eisner’s right-hand man from Paramount, named chairman of Walt Disney Studios
Walt’s nephew and largest shareholder, who later led a shareholder revolt
Head of Creative Artists Agency, hired as president and fired after fourteen months
Paramount chairman who argued endlessly with Eisner over his ideas
questions.explain: Each figure appears in Greene’s account of Eisner’s rise and fall, from his partner at Paramount to the president who balanced him, the rival he fired, the hire he humiliated and the shareholder who ousted him.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: After reviving The Wonderful World of Disney with himself as host, Eisner began to feel he was the natural son and successor to ____.
questions.explain: Hosting Walt’s old show, Eisner felt magically connected to him, as if he were more than just the head of the corporation.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Euro Disney, which site did Eisner choose for the new park?
options: The site near Barcelona, because the weather there was better
A site near Tokyo, to repeat the success of Tokyo Disneyland
The site near Paris, though the Barcelona site made more economic sense
The site near Paris, because his advisers said it would be cheapest
questions.explain: Barcelona’s better weather made it the sounder economic choice, but Eisner picked France because he wanted a cultural statement, not just a theme park.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as reasons Euro Disney disappointed when it opened in 1992?
options: The rides were copied from Tokyo and felt stale to Europeans
The French were unwilling to wait in line for rides, especially in bad weather
The hotel rooms were too expensive for a family to stay more than a night
The castles were cheap fiberglass copies of those in other parks
No beer or wine was served on the premises
questions.explain: Eisner misread French tastes and vacation habits: lines, no wine, pricey hotels. The castles were in fact built of pink stone at great cost, yet still looked kitschy.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: when Euro Disney turned into a disaster, Eisner decided that Frank Wells was to blame.
questions.explain: Eisner reasoned that overseeing the project’s financial health had been Wells’s job, and began to complain about him and consider firing him.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Michael Eisner, what about Jeffrey Katzenberg’s 1990 memo made Eisner uncomfortable?
options: It blamed Eisner personally for the cost of Euro Disney
It demanded the president’s job if Frank Wells ever left
It criticized bigger-budget event movies like Dick Tracy, Eisner’s pet project
It proposed buying Miramax without Eisner’s approval
questions.explain: Katzenberg’s memo said Disney had fallen for the blockbuster mentality; Eisner read it as an attack on his own project and an imitation of his famous Paramount memo.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Eisner had once referred to Jeffrey Katzenberg as his golden ____, so loyal and hardworking.
questions.explain: The affectionate nickname shows how far Eisner’s view of Katzenberg fell as Katzenberg’s own fame grew.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put these events in Michael Eisner’s career in order.
items: Becomes head of prime-time programming at ABC
Takes over Paramount’s film studio
Is named chairman and CEO of Disney
Opens Euro Disney
Fires Jeffrey Katzenberg
Fires Michael Ovitz
questions.explain: Eisner rose at ABC, ran Paramount from 1976, took over Disney in 1984, opened Euro Disney in 1992, fired Katzenberg in 1994 and fired Ovitz in December 1996.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How did Eisner treat Michael Ovitz after hiring him as Disney’s president, and with what result?
questions.a: Eisner narrowed Ovitz’s responsibilities and kept a tight leash on him, putting him in an unimpressive fifth-floor office and having his spending and moves watched. He would let Ovitz explore deals and then refuse them at the last moment, so word spread that Ovitz had lost his touch. Isolated within the company, Ovitz was fired after fourteen months with an enormous severance package.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Michael Ovitz at Disney, what pattern made the industry think Ovitz had lost his touch?
options: Ovitz openly feuded with Katzenberg in the press
Ovitz spent lavishly on parties that never produced any deals
Eisner let him explore deals, then gave a firm no when it came time to agree
Ovitz moved to New York and neglected his duties at the studio
questions.explain: Eisner never discouraged Ovitz from exploring a deal but always refused to close it, so Ovitz looked unable to close deals. Eisner refused his offer to move to New York.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these were disasters that hit Disney in the later years of Eisner’s leadership?
options: Pearl Harbor became the biggest of a run of expensive flops
Katzenberg was forced to pay Disney $280 million
The Go internet portal flopped and had to be shut down
A costly purchase of Yahoo! collapsed
Steve Jobs made it clear Pixar would never work with Disney again
questions.explain: Go, the Pixar split and Pearl Harbor were among the wave of disasters. Eisner had nixed the Yahoo! purchase, and it was Disney that had to pay Katzenberg $280 million.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Instead of buying Yahoo!, Eisner had Disney start its own internet portal, called ____.
questions.explain: Eisner believed it was always best to run your own show; Disney poured vast resources into Go, and it flopped.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the story of Michael Eisner, how did he respond when Roy Disney told him it would be best for him to resign?
options: He resigned at once to avoid a public fight
He offered Roy the position of chairman
He made Roy head of the animation department
He forced Roy to resign from the board
questions.explain: Enraged at what he saw as betrayal, Eisner struck back and pushed Roy off the board, which only emboldened Roy to organize a shareholder revolt.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: After being forced off the board, Roy Disney organized a shareholder revolt known as ____.
questions.explain: The revolt led shareholders to rebuke Eisner in March 2004, the board then stripped him of the chairmanship, and he resigned in 2005.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the stages of Michael Eisner’s fall from Disney in order.
items: Roy Disney tells Eisner he should resign
Eisner forces Roy off the board
Shareholders rebuke Eisner in the Save Disney revolt
The board strips Eisner of the chairmanship
Eisner resigns from Disney
questions.explain: Eisner’s counterattack on Roy backfired: the revolt came in March 2004, then the loss of the chairmanship, and finally his resignation in September 2005.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each film to its place in the story of Michael Eisner.
pairs: Already in preproduction when Eisner arrived at Paramount; sparked the turnaround
Eisner’s pet project, a bigger-budget event movie
Katzenberg’s baby, one of the most profitable films in Hollywood history
The biggest of Disney’s expensive flops, opening in May 2001
Disney’s last hit film before Eisner arrived
questions.explain: The films trace the story: luck at Paramount, Eisner’s own taste for grand projects, Katzenberg’s success, the late flops, and the drought Eisner inherited.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what strengths gave the young Michael Eisner a solid grasp on reality at ABC?
questions.a: Eisner was fiercely practical and exploited his strengths: his ambitious, competitive nature, intense work ethic, keen sense of the average American’s entertainment tastes, quick mind and ability to get others to think creatively. His confidence was confirmed by real promotions, and his cockiness was affordable because his skills had genuinely improved on the job.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what began the subtle unbalancing of Eisner’s mind at Paramount?
options: The failure of his first films at the studio
Attention from the media and millions of admirers who saw him as a genius
Pressure from corporate CEOs to cut his budgets
Constant arguments with Barry Diller that wore down his confidence
questions.explain: Unlike promotions at ABC, magazine covers and public admiration were intoxicating and inflated his view of his skills. Diller’s arguments actually helped him sharpen his ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say were parts of Eisner’s success at Paramount that were not completely his own doing?
options: Frank Wells balanced him on the business side
Ovitz’s deal making brought in major stars
Saturday Night Fever was already in preproduction when he arrived
Katzenberg’s animated hits fed the studio’s profits
Barry Diller argued with him endlessly, forcing him to sharpen his ideas
questions.explain: At Paramount, timing and Diller’s pushback helped him. Katzenberg’s animation, Ovitz and Wells belong to the later Disney years.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that part of Eisner’s good luck at Disney was inheriting its library of classic cartoons just as the home video market was exploding.
questions.explain: Greene notes Eisner quickly forgot this incredible luck, along with the role Wells played in balancing him out.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why did Eisner need a project like Euro Disney?
questions.a: Eisner had become addicted to the attention that came from making a splash and could not be content with simple success and rising profits. He had to keep adding to the myth of his greatness, so Euro Disney would prove he was not just a corporate executive but a renaissance man.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says Euro Disney would show the world that Eisner was not just a corporate executive but rather a ____ man.
questions.explain: Eisner believed his skills as a studio head could transfer to theme parks and architecture, which Greene calls overestimating his creative powers.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why can the mental imbalance of grandiosity only get worse once it takes hold?
options: Our advisers stop telling us the truth once we are powerful
The brain becomes addicted to risk and needs ever larger bets
Success keeps growing, so there is never a reason to doubt ourselves
Coming back down to earth means admitting our earlier high self-opinion was wrong
questions.explain: Greene says the human animal will almost never admit its high self-opinion was wrong, so it blames others for every failure instead.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene call the firing of Jeffrey Katzenberg Eisner’s most serious mistake?
questions.a: The Disney system depended on a steady flow of animated hits that fed the stores and theme parks, and Katzenberg had the knack for creating them, as The Lion King showed. Firing him put the whole assembly line at risk, and he took his skills to DreamWorks, whose hits drove up the price of animators and threatened Disney’s profit system. Eisner sacrificed profit and practicality to soothe an ego threatened by Katzenberg’s rise.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: After he was fired from Disney, Katzenberg cofounded a new studio, ____, which churned out more animated hits.
questions.explain: The new studio raised the cost of skilled animators, threatening the profit system that depended on Disney’s animated hits.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does Greene interpret Eisner’s acquisition of ABC?
options: As a sound move to secure television outlets for Disney films
As a play for publicity based on the belief that bigger is better
As a defensive purchase to block a hostile takeover of Disney
As a favor to Michael Ovitz to lure him from his agency
questions.explain: Greene says television was a dying business model and the deal created a behemoth without a clear identity, which revealed Eisner’s growing detachment from reality.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each of Eisner’s decisions to Greene’s interpretation of it.
pairs: Overestimating his creative powers by assuming studio skills transfer to parks
Sacrificing profit to soothe an ego threatened by a rival’s rise
A play for publicity driven by the belief that bigger is better
Treating people as instruments, perhaps to humiliate the most feared man in town
questions.explain: Greene reads each decision as a sign of a mind growing detached from reality: attention and ego, not practical business sense, drove the choices.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these traits into the young Eisner’s real strengths and the later Eisner’s delusions.

items.t: An intense work ethic
A keen sense of the average American’s entertainment tastes
The ability to encourage others to think creatively
Belief that he had the golden touch
Belief that his studio skills would transfer to theme parks and architecture
Belief that bigger is better

questions.explain: Greene praises the practical young Eisner who exploited real strengths, then shows how attention led him to imagine a golden touch and chase size and splash.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why is the story of Michael Eisner much closer to you than you think?
questions.a: We all share a latent weakness: a natural tendency to overestimate our skills and to need to feel superior in something. Once we have any success, such as attention, a promotion or funding, our confidence rises too quickly, and a growing gap opens between our self-opinion and reality. So Eisner’s fate could be ours, only on a smaller scale.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say any success in life inevitably depends on, beyond our own merit?
options: The size of our ambitions
The teachers who helped us along the way
Our naturally superior self
The contributions of others
Some good luck and timing
questions.explain: Greene lists luck, timing, others’ contributions, teachers and the whims of the public. Imagining success comes from our superior self is exactly the tendency he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why is a degree of confidence a positive thing?
options: It lets us transfer our skills easily to new fields
It impels us to take on challenges, push past our supposed limits and learn
It ensures that others will give us the attention we deserve
It protects us from ever having to admit a mistake
questions.explain: Greene grants that confidence helps us grow; the danger comes when success makes it rise too quickly, opening a gap with reality.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the stages of the success delusion, as Greene describes it in our own lives, in order.
items: We have some success and gain attention
Our confidence rises too quickly
We forget luck and others and credit our superior self
We take on new challenges before we are ready
We blame others for the failures that follow
questions.explain: Greene traces the same arc in us as in Eisner: success, inflated confidence, forgetting luck and help, overreaching, and finally blaming others.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these are part of Greene’s advice for what to do after any kind of success?
options: Expand into new fields while your momentum lasts
Analyze its components and see the element of luck
Pay closer attention to the applause as it grows louder
Raise your vigilance, since success brings complacency
Wipe the slate clean and start each new project from zero
questions.explain: Greene tells us to analyze luck and others’ help, raise vigilance and start fresh. He warns against believing bigger is better and says to pay less attention to the applause.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene advises that with each new project you should wipe the slate ____, starting from zero.
questions.explain: Starting from zero counters the complacency of success, in which old strategies get repeated and attention matters more than the work.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that in Euro Disney the castles were built of fiberglass, as at the other theme parks, to keep costs down.
questions.explain: Eisner insisted on castles of pink stone with handcrafted stained glass, unlike the usual fiberglass castles, and let costs mount.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: after Frank Wells died, Eisner made Jeffrey Katzenberg president of Disney.
questions.explain: Eisner announced he would take over Wells’s position himself, even though Katzenberg reminded him he had been promised the job.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: A chef whose first restaurant is a hit immediately opens three more in cuisines he has never cooked, sure his touch will carry over. Which idea from Greene does this illustrate?
options: Grandiose humility, a public show of modesty to feel superior
Imagining we have the golden touch and can transfer our skills to any field
Practical grandiosity, energy channeled into honing real skills
The grandiose victim, who creates drama to feel important
questions.explain: Greene warns that after success we imagine our skills can magically move to another medium or field, as Eisner assumed of theme parks.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, how should you compensate for the drug-like effect of success, and what kind of power results?
questions.a: You should keep your feet firmly on the ground: see your limits and work with what you have, consolidate rather than assume bigger is better, and avoid offending allies with a growing sense of superiority. Power built this slow and organic way is more real and lasting, while the gods punish those who fly too high on the wings of grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the Keys on grandiosity, what does Greene’s image of the block of marble say about a realistic attitude toward a goal?
questions.a: The task is like a block of marble, larger than you and resistant, that you must slowly sculpt into something precise and beautiful. It is not impossible: with effort, focus and resiliency you can carve it. A realistic attitude begins with a proper sense of proportion, since goals are hard, people are resistant and you have limits, and this lets you summon patience and get to work.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene’s block-of-marble image, how does the disease of grandiosity change the way you see the task?
options: The block seems hard, so you ask others to carve it for you
The block seems impossibly large, so you give up before starting
The block seems fragile, so you work too slowly and cautiously
The block seems small and malleable, so it will not take long to shape
questions.explain: Grandiosity reverses normal proportions: the task and other people shrink while the self grows larger than anything around it.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene notes that the root of the word grandiosity means big or ____.
questions.explain: Grandiosity is seeing yourself as enlarged, superior and worthy of being adored, not merely needing to be the center of things.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does Greene distinguish grandiosity in chapter 11 from the deep narcissism of chapter 2?
options: Narcissism is rare in leaders; grandiosity is found only in leaders
Narcissism makes everything revolve around you; grandiosity enlarges you to feel godlike
Narcissism is about envy; grandiosity is about fear of death
Narcissism is a feeling of smallness; grandiosity is a feeling of guilt
questions.explain: Greene says grandiosity goes beyond needing everything to revolve around you. “It is a feeling of being not merely human but godlike.”

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says grandiosity is a disease mostly confined to powerful, egotistical leaders in the public eye.
questions.explain: Greene says that assumption is very wrong: beside the high-grade version of leaders like Eisner, a low-grade everyday version is common to almost all of us.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that besides the high-grade version found in leaders like Eisner, there is an everyday, ____ version of grandiosity common to almost all of us.
questions.explain: Low-grade grandiosity stems from the deep need to feel important and superior in something, and we are rarely aware of it.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as effects of everyday, low-grade grandiosity?
options: Spending many years mastering a single craft
Underestimating your own skills and overestimating obstacles
Becoming slightly passive and expecting others to give you what you want
Restlessly changing careers instead of mastering anything
Having dozens of great ideas you never attempt to execute
questions.explain: Low-grade grandiosity makes us overestimate our skills and underestimate obstacles, flee work that does not confirm our greatness, avoid testing our ideas and feel entitled to praise.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why does low-grade grandiosity lead people to change careers restlessly?
questions.a: Their present work is not confirming their greatness and superiority, because being truly great would take more years of training and new skills. It feels better to quit and be lured by the possibilities of a new career, which let them entertain fantasies of greatness. In this way they never quite master anything.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the threefold task of a student of human nature when it comes to grandiosity?
questions.a: First, understand grandiosity itself: why it is embedded in human nature and why there are more grandiose people today. Second, recognize its signs in others and learn to manage the people who show them. Third, and most important, see the signs in yourself, control your grandiose tendencies and channel that energy into something productive.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the three parts of Greene’s task for the student of human nature regarding grandiosity in his order.
items: Understand grandiosity and why it is spreading
Recognize its signs in others and manage them
See it in yourself, control it and channel its energy
questions.explain: Greene calls the third part the most important and points ahead to the chapter’s closing section on practical grandiosity for how to channel the energy.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which psychoanalyst does Greene cite for the idea that grandiosity has its roots in the earliest years of our life?
options: Sigmund Freud
Carl Jung
Heinz Kohut
Melanie Klein
questions.explain: Greene draws on Heinz Kohut’s account of the infant’s sense of omnipotence and the painful discovery of its own smallness.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the stages of early childhood in Kohut’s account of grandiosity in order.
items: The infant bonds completely with the mother, with no separate identity
The infant feels omnipotent, as if its needs were magically met
The child confronts that the mother is a separate being
The child feels small and dependent and fantasizes about powers
questions.explain: In Kohut’s account, the omnipotence of the first months gives way to a painful sense of smallness, which we spend our lives alternately feeling and denying.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Kohut’s account, in our first months we felt ____: all we had to do was feel a need, and the mother was there to meet it.
questions.explain: The infant even believed the breast that fed it was part of itself, as if it had magical powers to control the mother.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why does our sense of insignificance get worse as we grow older?
questions.a: We realize we are one person in a globe of billions, with short lives, limited skills and brainpower, and little control over careers and global trends. The idea of dying and being quickly forgotten is intolerable. So we alternate between sensing our smallness and denying it, which makes us prone to imagining our superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, which children are most vulnerable to deeper forms of grandiosity later in life?
options: Children with strict fathers who demanded discipline
Neglected children who had to fend for themselves early
Children with many siblings who competed for attention
Pampered children who never had to confront their own smallness
questions.explain: Pampered children skip the phase of confronting their smallness; their parents make them feel like the center of the universe, which marks them for life.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these traits does Greene give to children who were pampered and shielded from confronting their smallness?
options: They need to be adored
They fear and obey father figures
They become masters at manipulating others to pamper them
They come to disdain any form of authority
They alternate often between feeling small and feeling great
questions.explain: Pampered children know only feelings of greatness, never the alternation others feel, and see the father figure as weak compared with themselves.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Eisner had a cold mother and a doting father who completed his homework for him.
questions.explain: It was the reverse: Eisner’s mother met his every need and did his homework, sheltering him from his cold and sometimes cruel father.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, how did religion once channel our grandiose needs?
questions.a: Our smallness came partly from our weakness before the hostile powers of nature, which gods and spirits represented. By worshipping them we gained protection and, connected to something larger, we felt enlarged; the gods cared about our tribe and our soul, a sign of our significance. Later the same energy went into worshipping leaders of great causes, such as Napoleon or Mao.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the objects toward which, in Greene’s account, people have directed their grandiose energy in historical order.
items: Gods and spirits representing the powers of nature
Leaders of great causes promising a future utopia
The self
questions.explain: As religion and then great causes lost their binding power in the West, the need to feel larger did not disappear; it turned toward idealizing the self.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each object of worship in Greene’s account of grandiose energy to how it enlarged people.
pairs: Connection to powers larger than ourselves made us feel enlarged and protected
Worshipping a leader who stood for a great cause and a future utopia
A second leader and cause that absorbed the same grandiose energy
Where the energy goes today when religions and great causes lose their binding power
questions.explain: Greene traces the same need for significance through religion, leader-and-cause worship, and finally the self once the older channels weaken.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what more than anything spreads the grandiosity virus today?
options: Social media
Fast online learning
Pampering in childhood
The decline of religion
questions.explain: Pampering, disrespect for experts and technology all contribute, but Greene says social media above all lets us feel the adoration of thousands, like kings or gods.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that more than anything it is social media that spreads the grandiosity ____.
questions.explain: Social media gives the illusion of near-limitless presence and the attention or even adoration of thousands or millions of people.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these into factors Greene says are increasing grandiosity today and older outlets that once channeled it away from the self.

items.t: More people pampered in childhood
Little respect for authority or experts
Technology’s promise of quick, easy mastery
Social media’s illusion of adoration
Worship of gods and spirits
Worship of leaders of great causes

questions.explain: Greene says religion and great causes once absorbed our need to feel larger; with them weakened, pampering, disdain for experts, technology and social media turn it toward the self.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says technology has made people more willing to spend years learning a skill.
questions.explain: Greene says the reverse: technology makes everything seem fast and simple, so people think a few tricks and a few hours a week can make them proficient.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these behaviors into grandiose humility and the grandiose victim.

items.t: Publicly declares no interest in possessions or a car
Makes a show of being happy with a small lot in life
Feels morally superior through a display of modesty
Keeps falling for the worst types in relationships
Puts themselves where they are sure to fail and suffer
Feels superior in suffering

questions.explain: Both are negative forms of grandiosity: one gains attention and moral superiority through a public show of humility, the other through creating the drama of being a victim.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What does Greene mean by grandiose humility?
questions.a: It is a negative form of grandiosity in which people disguise their grandiose urges, even from themselves. They make a show of not caring about power, possessions or status and of being content with their small lot. But they need to display this humility publicly, because it is their way of getting attention and feeling morally superior.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: A friend constantly recounts her misfortunes, keeps choosing the worst partners and expects every friendship to revolve around her suffering. Which form of grandiosity does Greene’s account fit?
options: Practical grandiosity
Grandiose humility
The grandiose victim
Idealizing a leader
questions.explain: The grandiose victim creates the drama that turns her into a victim and feels important, even superior, through her suffering.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene name as compensations people turn to when disappointed in their careers yet still believing they are great?
options: Retraining patiently in a new skill
A superior, mocking attitude
Seeking out mentors for honest feedback
Drugs or alcohol
Shopping
questions.explain: Greene lists drugs, alcohol, many sexual partners, shopping and a mocking superiority. Patient retraining and honest feedback are the realistic path he recommends instead.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene count idealizing and worshipping a leader as a form of grandiosity?
options: Followers feel some of the leader’s greatness and superiority to non-believers
Followers secretly plan to replace the leader one day
Followers are humble people with no need to feel great
Followers worship leaders only out of fear of punishment
questions.explain: By believing someone else will make everything great, followers share in the greatness and soar with the rhetoric, much as lovers feel reflected power from an idealized partner.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each form of grandiosity Greene describes to its description.
pairs: Wanting admiration while claiming to care only about the work
Manic energy about great plans, then depression as reality intrudes
Raising a partner to god or goddess status and feeling the reflected power
A public show of modesty to gain attention and moral superiority
Creating the drama of suffering to feel important
questions.explain: Greene shows that grandiosity takes many forms, from open prestige seeking to disguised, negative forms like humility and victimhood.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each sign Greene describes to what it reveals about a grandiose person.
pairs: Their sense of greatness has been called into doubt
Unable to relax and laugh at themselves in private
They have come to believe in their own myth
Claiming to have foreseen trends that cannot be verified
They are big talkers who invent successes
A faraway look when the spotlight is elsewhere
They have low levels of empathy
Big gestures, a loud fast voice, lots of personal space
questions.explain: Greene gives several simple ways to measure grandiosity, from reactions to criticism and private behavior to talk, empathy and body language.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
