questions.q: According to Greene, why do people in the public eye with potent grandiosity suddenly say things that get them into trouble for being insensitive?
questions.a: They are so attuned to their own great opinions that they assume everyone else will interpret their words in the right spirit and agree with them. Their grandiosity blinds them to how others will actually react.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these behaviors into signs of high grandiosity and signs of normal realism.

items.t: Becoming enraged and hysterical when criticized
Inventing past successes
Taking up a lot of personal space in meetings
Feeling a bit defensive when criticized
Relaxing and laughing at oneself in private
Moments of coming back down to earth

questions.explain: Greene says some defensiveness and swings of feeling great are normal; look for moments of realism. Rage, invented successes and dominating space mark high grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what should you do if you cannot avoid working with a highly grandiose boss or partner?
options: Confront them firmly to bring them back down to earth
Mirror their confidence so they will see you as an equal
Flatter them until they trust you with real decisions
Maintain your skepticism and judge their ideas apart from their self-belief
questions.explain: Their confidence can distract you from flaws in their ideas, so look at the ideas themselves. Confronting them may trigger a rage response.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises trying to confront highly grandiose people to bring them back down to earth.
questions.explain: Greene says not to entertain that illusion, since confronting them may trigger a rage response; keep your skepticism instead.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene advises with highly grandiose people and what he warns against.

items.t: Maintaining your skepticism about their certainty
Looking at the ideas themselves
Avoiding entanglements when you can
Baiting them into overreactions if they are rivals
Trying to confront them and bring them down to earth
Getting caught up in their seductive self-belief

questions.explain: Greene says to keep skeptical and judge their ideas, but not to confront them, since you may trigger a rage response, or be swayed by their confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that if highly grandiose types are your rivals, you should consider yourself ____, since they are easy to bait into overreactions.
questions.explain: Casting doubt on their greatness makes them furious and doubly irrational, which a rival can exploit.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each type of person to Greene’s advice for dealing with them.
pairs: Be indulgent, since almost all of us swing up and down
Highly grandiose people you can avoid
Avoid relationships or entanglements with them
Highly grandiose bosses or partners you cannot avoid
Keep your skepticism and look at the ideas themselves
Taunt them and bait them into overreactions
questions.explain: Greene scales his advice to the level of grandiosity: tolerance for normal swings, distance or skepticism for the extreme, and provocation for rivals.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What does Greene say a realistic attitude toward yourself includes, as the greatest protection against grandiosity?
questions.a: You know which subjects and activities you are naturally drawn to and accept that you cannot be skilled at everything, so you play to your strengths. You understand your energy levels, how far you can push yourself and how this changes with age. And you have a solid grasp of your social position: your allies, the people you have rapport with and the natural audience for your work, since you cannot please everyone.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these physical signals into signs you are working with your natural strengths and signs you have taken on too much.

items.t: Feeling ease in the effort
Learning faster
Withstanding the tedium of learning
Feeling exhausted
Feeling irritable and nervous
Getting headaches

questions.explain: Greene says self-awareness has a physical side: activities that mesh with your inclinations bring ease and energy, while overreaching brings exhaustion, irritability and headaches.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these attitudes into a realistic approach to a project and the grandiose approach.

items.t: Expecting success to need effort and some luck
Expecting people to respond in surprising ways
Examining your own mistakes to learn from them
Believing people need you more than you need them
Blaming malicious or envious others for failure
Focusing on what you feel you deserve

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the sculptor who respects a resistant block of marble with the person whose sense of proportion is reversed and who feels entitled.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that after success you will naturally feel a touch of fear about rising too high. What does he compare it to?
options: Seasickness
A hangover
Vertigo
Stage fright
questions.explain: Greene likens it to vertigo: the anxiety is your body telling you to come back down to earth.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that self-knowledge and acceptance of limits will serve as a ____ mechanism, pulling you back down when you think too highly of yourself.
questions.explain: Like gravity, self-knowledge pulls you back toward the actions and decisions that best serve your particular nature.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene say that in becoming more realistic you are simply becoming more human?
options: Humans are naturally humble, and grandiosity was learned only recently
Realism lets us hide our weaknesses from others more easily
Accepting limits frees us from needing other people at all
Pragmatism is how we overcame our weakness and became the preeminent social animal
questions.explain: Greene says being realistic let early humans survive a hostile environment, cooperate and build communities and tools. “In becoming more realistic, you are simply becoming more human.”

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as nonverbal signs of grandiosity?
options: Big, dramatic gestures
A loud voice and a fast pace that leaves no room to interrupt
Close attention while others speak
A soft, hesitant voice
Taking up a lot of personal space at a meeting
questions.explain: Greene says grandiose people take up space, gesture big and talk loud and fast. They are poor listeners who grow animated only in the spotlight.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What does the title of chapter 11, Know Your Limits, signal about the chapter’s argument?
options: That the cure for grandiosity is a realistic assessment of yourself and your limits
That we should avoid ambition and settle for a small life
That other people’s limits are what we must exploit
That success comes from ignoring others’ doubts about us
questions.explain: The law counters grandiosity by keeping a realistic sense of self and limits, while still tying greatness to real work. Greene even mocks a showy embrace of a small lot as grandiose humility.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: The Keys on grandiosity say the energy can be channeled into something productive. Which later section of chapter 11 develops this?
options: The Grandiose Leader
The Integrated Human
Beyond Envy
Practical Grandiosity
questions.explain: Greene points ahead to Practical Grandiosity, where energy goes into work and real achievement. The Grandiose Leader deals with leaders’ illusions, and the other two close earlier chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does the story of Michael Eisner in The Success Delusion prepare for the Keys to Human Nature section of chapter 11?
questions.a: The story shows a high-grade case of grandiosity, where success and attention pushed a talented man into delusion and ruin. The Keys then widen the lens: they explain that a low-grade version is common to almost all of us, trace its roots to early childhood, describe its forms and signs, and show how to manage it in others and ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: chapter 11, on the Law of Grandiosity, comes directly after the chapter on the Law of Envy.
questions.explain: Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego, covers envy; chapter 11 follows with the inflated self-opinion of grandiosity, and chapter 12 turns to gender rigidity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each section of chapter 11 to its content.
pairs: The rise and fall of Michael Eisner
The roots, forms and signs of grandiosity and how to manage it
The theatrical illusions grandiose leaders use to awe us
Channeling grandiose energy into work and real achievement
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a story, to analysis of the trait, to its most dangerous public form, and ends with how to turn the energy to good use.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the sections of chapter 11, Know Your Limits, in order.
items: The Success Delusion
Keys to Human Nature
The Grandiose Leader
Practical Grandiosity
questions.explain: Like other chapters, it opens with a story, explains the law in the Keys, examines a key type, and ends with the positive ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's account of the grandiose leader, what do these leaders fundamentally depend on to keep their high self-opinion alive?
options: The loyalty of a small circle of advisers
Accurate feedback from trusted experts
Inherited wealth and family connections
The attention and adoration of the public
questions.explain: Greene says grandiose leaders depend on the attention we give them; without being adored, their self-opinion is not validated and the confidence they rely on withers.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says grandiose leaders employ theatrical devices and lists six common ____ that they like to create.
questions.explain: The section is organized around six illusions, such as being destined or invulnerable, which Greene calls stage tricks we must see through.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why must we demythologize grandiose leaders, and what fact about them makes this possible?
questions.a: Grandiose leaders mesmerize us with their image, so we fail to see the irrationality in their decisions and follow them into disaster. But they depend on our attention: without public adoration their high self-opinion cannot be validated and their confidence withers. By seeing through their stage tricks and scaling them back down to human size, we resist their allure.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says grandiose leaders usually rise to power in times of stability and prosperity.
questions.explain: In the illusion “I will deliver you,” Greene says these types often rise to power in times of trouble and crisis, when their self-confidence comforts the public or shareholders.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I will deliver you,” why must the grandiose leader's promises be both large and vague?
options: Large to inspire dreams, vague so no one can hold them to account
Large to attract money, vague to keep the plans secret from enemies
Large to frighten opponents, vague to leave room for compromise
Large to impress experts, vague to avoid offending rivals
questions.explain: Greene explains that large promises inspire dreams, while vagueness means there are no specifics to hold the leader to if the promises never come to pass.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the six illusions of the grandiose leader in the order Greene presents them.
items: I am destined
I’m the common man/woman
I will deliver you
I rewrite the rules
I have the golden touch
I’m invulnerable
questions.explain: Greene moves from the leader's mythic origins and identification with the people, through promises and rule-breaking, to the legend of never failing and the final sense of invulnerability that precedes the crash.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's account of Indira Gandhi, which detail shows that her “Mother Indira” image was stagecraft?
options: She refused to wear traditional dress at public events
She came from political royalty and was educated in Europe, yet ate with her fingers in villages
She grew up in a poor village and later forgot her roots
She avoided large crowds and spoke only to the elites
questions.explain: Gandhi was the daughter of India's first prime minister, educated in Europe and far from the poor, yet she wore her sari like local women and ate with her fingers to seem one with the people.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these did Indira Gandhi do, in Greene's account, to present herself as one with the people?
options: Wore her sari as local women wore them
Used homely metaphors when visiting small villages
Gave up her political office to live in a village
Altered her language when speaking in front of large crowds
Spoke publicly about her European education
questions.explain: Greene lists her changed language, homely metaphors, local way of wearing the sari and eating with her fingers; she did not give up power, and she hid rather than advertised her privileged background.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I’m the common man/woman,” what trick lets grandiose leaders seem ordinary despite their wealth?
options: They hide their wealth by living in modest homes
They place the emphasis on their cultural tastes rather than their actual class
They give away most of their money in public ceremonies
They hire ordinary people to speak on their behalf
questions.explain: Greene says they may fly first class and wear expensive suits, but they seem to share the public's tastes in food and films and ridicule the elites.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I’m the common man/woman,” how does identifying with the masses enlarge the grandiose leader beyond simply gaining attention?
questions.a: The leader comes to embody an entire nation or interest group rather than being one person. Following the leader becomes loyalty to the group itself, and criticizing the leader becomes a betrayal of the cause. This quasi-mystical identification is dangerous because the leader feels licensed to do whatever he or she wants in the name of the public.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say grandiose leaders do under the illusion “I’m the common man/woman”?
options: Stop flying first class and wearing expensive suits
Seem to share the public's tastes in food and films
Give up relying on expert advisers
Ridicule the elites
questions.explain: Greene says they keep their luxuries but stress shared cultural tastes and mock the elites, even though they probably depend on such experts to guide them.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these facts about Indira Gandhi into her public act and her actual background, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Wore her sari as local women wore them
Ate with her fingers in small villages
Used homely metaphors with villagers
Was educated in Europe
Her father was India's first prime minister
Lived far apart from India's poorer people

questions.explain: Greene contrasts her privileged, political-royalty background with the motherly, common-woman stagecraft that won her elections.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I will deliver you,” the grandiose leader requires convenient ____, often the elites or outsiders, to tighten group identification.
questions.explain: Greene says the movement crystallizes around hatred of these scapegoats, and the leader's promise to bring them down increases his power exponentially.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says the grandiose leader's message must be simple to digest and reducible to a ____.
questions.explain: A simple message that promises something large stirs the emotions and can be reproduced everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I will deliver you,” whom does Greene say grandiose leaders often use as scapegoats?
options: Their own most loyal followers
Former leaders of rival nations
The elites or outsiders
Younger members of their own movement
questions.explain: Greene says the convenient scapegoats are often the elites or outsiders, who come to stand for every pain and injustice the crowd has experienced.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene say that the grandiose leader of “I will deliver you” is creating a cult more than leading a political movement or a business?
questions.a: The leader's name, image and slogans are reproduced in large numbers and take on a godlike ubiquity. Colors, symbols and music bind the group identity and appeal to the basest instincts. Believers become doubly mesmerized and ready to excuse any action, so nothing will dissuade them; Greene advises keeping our own internal distance and analytic powers.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say mark the cult that forms around the leader who promises “I will deliver you”?
options: The leader's name, image and slogans reproduced in large numbers
Colors, symbols and music used to bind the group identity
Open debate welcomed among the believers
Detailed, measurable promises that followers can check
questions.explain: Greene describes godlike ubiquity of name and slogans and the use of colors, symbols and music; the promises are deliberately vague, and true believers will not be dissuaded.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why are we secretly excited when a grandiose leader claims to rewrite the rules?
questions.a: Greene says a secret human wish is to do without the usual rules and conventions of a field and gain power simply by following our own inner light. When grandiose leaders claim such powers, we want to believe them. But most rules have common sense and rationality behind them, as the Heaven's Gate disaster showed.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What lesson does Greene draw from Michael Cimino's Heaven's Gate?
options: The traditional contract served a purpose in reining in a director's grandiosity
Great directors should always be given unlimited freedom
Studio executives were jealous of Cimino's earlier success
Films with a strong concept will market themselves
questions.explain: After costs soared and the first cut ran over five hours, Greene concludes the usual contract had served to make directors work within limits, since most rules have common sense behind them.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: The Academy Award–winning film that came before Michael Cimino's disaster Heaven's Gate was ____.
questions.explain: Cimino directed The Deer Hunter (1978), and its success helped him win the unique contract for Heaven's Gate (1980).

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Michael Cimino negotiated a unique contract that let him increase the ____ as he saw fit on Heaven's Gate.
questions.explain: The no-strings contract let costs soar, and the film became one of the greatest disasters in Hollywood history.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put these events in Michael Cimino's story, as Greene tells it, in order.
items: Wins an Academy Award for The Deer Hunter
Negotiates a contract with no strings attached
Spends weeks rehearsing actors in roller-skating
Turns in a first cut over five hours long
His career is virtually destroyed
questions.explain: Greene uses Cimino to show how the claim to rewrite the rules leads from a celebrated success, through unchecked spending on set, to disaster.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How, according to Greene, do grandiose leaders use their intuition, and how should we treat their claims to be mavericks?
questions.a: Grandiose leaders rely on their hunches and disregard focus groups or any scientific feedback, claiming a special inside connection to the truth. They build a myth that their hunches led to great successes, but close scrutiny shows their hunches miss as often as they hit. When a leader poses as a maverick who can do away with rules and science, we should see this as “a sign of madness, not divine inspiration.”

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says that when leaders present themselves as the consummate ____, able to do away with rules and science, we should see a sign of madness.
questions.explain: The maverick pose plays on our wish to do without rules, but Greene says it reflects madness, not divine inspiration.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, Douglas MacArthur claimed he had never lost a battle, although in fact he had lost many.
questions.explain: Greene uses MacArthur to show how grandiose leaders create the legend that they have never really failed by finding excuses such as betrayal for every loss.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Under the illusion “I have the golden touch,” why does Greene call the belief that skills can easily be transferred often a fatal move?
questions.a: Because they think they are magically gifted, grandiose leaders believe they can try their hand at anything, as when a movie executive becomes a theme park designer or a businessman a national leader. They then attempt things beyond their expertise and are quickly overwhelmed by the complexity and chaos that come from their lack of experience.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these behaviors by whether they show the maverick who claims to rewrite the rules or the leader who claims never to fail.

items.t: Demanding a contract with no strings attached
Relying on hunches instead of focus groups
Posing as a maverick who can ignore science
Blaming every failure on betrayal by others
Claiming never to have lost a battle
Believing a movie executive can design theme parks

questions.explain: Rule-breaking and reliance on intuition belong to the maverick illusion, while denying failure and assuming skills transfer anywhere belong to the legend of the golden touch.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I have the golden touch,” what does Greene advise doing when dealing with such leaders?
options: Look at their record and publicize their failures as neutrally as possible
Ignore them until they fail on their own
Confront them privately about their weaknesses
Flatter them so they will listen to reason
questions.explain: Greene says to look carefully at their record, notice the glaring failures, and publicize the truth neutrally, even though people under their spell may not listen.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why can the grandiose leader in the illusion “I’m invulnerable” never rest or retreat?
options: They must keep making a splash to keep the attention coming
Their followers would immediately elect a rival
Retreat would expose the failures they hid from the public
Their contracts require constant new projects
questions.explain: Greene says their boldness is not really under control: they need actions that create a splash, because resting would cause a lapse in the publicity that feeds their self-opinion.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In the illusion “I’m invulnerable,” what does Greene say Stan O'Neal, CEO of Merrill Lynch, did?
options: Moved his company into theme parks abroad
Fired his second-in-command after a run of successes
Stuck with mortgage-backed securities when everyone else was getting out
Launched a grand tour of the country to win attention
questions.explain: Greene lists O'Neal's decision, which essentially destroyed one of the oldest financial institutions in the country, as a fatal hubristic maneuver.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as examples of the fatal hubristic maneuver that shatters a grandiose leader's aura of invulnerability?
options: Churchill's confidence during World War II
Stan O'Neal sticking with mortgage-backed securities
Mao's decision to unleash the Cultural Revolution
Indira Gandhi eating with her fingers in villages
MacArthur's grandiose tour of the United States after the Korean War
questions.explain: Greene names these three as moments when leaders finally went too far; Gandhi's behavior illustrates the common-woman act, and Churchill is his example of healthy, practical grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put these stages of the grandiose leader's path, as Greene describes it under “I’m invulnerable,” in order.
items: Takes bold risks that attract attention
Gets away with risky maneuvers many times
Comes to feel invulnerable and needs bigger stakes
Makes a fatal hubristic maneuver
The aura of invulnerability is shattered
questions.explain: Greene describes boldness becoming a drug: repeated success breeds a feeling of invulnerability until one maneuver goes too far and reality catches up in one hard blow.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, why does the grandiose leader who feels invulnerable eventually crash?
questions.a: Their risky actions are driven not by rational considerations but by the need for attention and glory, and the daring itself becomes a drug requiring bigger stakes. Because they have so often gotten away with risky maneuvers, they come to feel godlike. Eventually they make a hubristic move that goes too far, and reality catches up in one hard blow.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when you deflate a grandiose leader's image, their followers quickly and calmly abandon the leader.
questions.explain: Greene warns that such leaders will overreact and their followers become rabid; only slowly may a few followers have second thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In dealing with grandiose leaders, Greene says creating a viral ____ is your best hope.
questions.explain: Greene ends the section saying “Creating a viral disenchantment is your best hope.” after deflating the leader's sacred image.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What is Greene's general advice for dealing with the grandiose leader at the close of his discussion of the six illusions?
options: Compete with them by making even larger promises
Wait patiently for the leader to retire
Try to deflate the sacred, glorious image they have forged
Join their movement and change it from within
questions.explain: Greene says to deflate their glorious image; though the leader overreacts and followers grow rabid, a few may slowly have second thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each illusion of the grandiose leader to the example Greene uses for it.
pairs: Indira Gandhi presenting herself as Mother Indira
Michael Cimino's contract for Heaven's Gate
Douglas MacArthur claiming he never lost a battle
Stan O'Neal holding on to mortgage-backed securities
questions.explain: Each figure illustrates one stage trick: Gandhi's common-woman act, Cimino's rule-breaking, MacArthur's legend of never failing, and O'Neal's fatal risk.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each illusion of the grandiose leader to what the leader claims or does.
pairs: Tells childhood stories showing fate singled them out
Makes large, vague promises in a time of crisis
Trusts their intuition over focus groups and science
Creates the legend that they have never really failed
questions.explain: Greene describes each illusion by the myth it builds: destiny, deliverance, freedom from rules and an unbroken record of success.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each illusion of the grandiose leader to Greene's advice for countering it.
pairs: Find the mundane facts behind the tales and publicize them
Stand back and analyze the reality of what is going on
Keep your internal distance and analytic powers
See the maverick pose as a sign of madness
Look at their record and publicize their failures
questions.explain: For each illusion Greene offers a way to scale the leader back down to human size by looking past the myth to the facts.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these tactics by whether a grandiose leader uses them to promise deliverance from a crisis or to build a myth of personal destiny.

items.t: Using elites or outsiders as scapegoats
Reducing the message to a slogan
Binding the group with colors, symbols and music
Telling stories of unusual toughness in youth
Reinterpreting the past to show early creativity
Relating early career tales of beating impossible odds

questions.explain: Deliverance relies on simple slogans, scapegoats and cult symbols, while destiny relies on reworked stories from childhood and early career.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these are among the six illusions that Greene says grandiose leaders create?
options: I serve only the cause
I’m invulnerable
I am destined
I am misunderstood
I rewrite the rules
questions.explain: The six illusions are destined, common man/woman, deliver you, rewrite the rules, golden touch and invulnerable; being misunderstood and serving only the cause are not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What does Greene call the usual form of grandiosity, which makes us imagine we are greater and more superior than we are?
options: Grandiose humility
Practical grandiosity
Fantastical grandiosity
Negative grandiosity
questions.explain: Greene names it fantastical grandiosity because it rests on fantasies and the skewed impression we get from attention; practical grandiosity is the reality-based alternative.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does Greene distinguish fantastical grandiosity from practical grandiosity?
questions.a: Fantastical grandiosity is the natural form: it makes us imagine we are greater than we are, based on fantasies and the skewed impression attention gives us. Practical grandiosity is harder to reach but is based on reality: the energy is channeled into our work, skills and goals, so our self-esteem is tied to real achievements. In it, the desire for attention is under control and subordinate.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says the problem is not with grandiose energy itself but with the ____ it takes.
questions.explain: Grandiosity is a primal energy that can fuel ambition; what matters is whether it flows into fantasy or into real work.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says practical grandiosity comes naturally to us.
questions.explain: Greene says practical grandiosity is not easy to achieve and does not come naturally, though it can be the source of tremendous power and self-fulfillment.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In practical grandiosity, where does Greene say the greater sense of gratification comes from?
options: The work itself and overcoming our own weaknesses
The praise and attention of a large audience
Comparing our achievements with those of rivals
Imagining the success of future projects
questions.explain: Attention from our work is gratifying, but Greene says the greater gratification comes from the work and from overcoming our weaknesses, with the desire for attention kept subordinate.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these describe practical grandiosity as Greene defines it?
options: It is based on reality rather than fantasy
The desire for attention is under control and subordinate
It comes naturally and needs no effort
Self-esteem is tied to subjective fantasies of greatness
Its energy is channeled into our work and goals
questions.explain: “Practical grandiosity is based not on fantasy but on reality.” Self-esteem built on fantasies belongs to the fantastical form, and Greene says the practical form does not come naturally.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put Greene's five principles of practical grandiosity in the order he presents them.
items: Come to terms with your grandiose needs
Concentrate the energy
Maintain a dialogue with reality
Seek out calibrated challenges
Let loose your grandiose energy
questions.explain: Greene begins with honesty about our needs, moves through focus, feedback and calibrated difficulty, and only at the end allows the tamed energy to run free.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Come to terms with your grandiose needs,” what does he call your worst enemy?
options: Envy
Ambition
Denial
Criticism
questions.explain: Greene says you must admit you want to feel important and superior; “Denial is your worst enemy,” since only self-awareness lets you transform the energy.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene say practical grandiosity must begin with coming to terms with your grandiose needs?
questions.a: You must start from honesty, admitting that you want to feel important, superior and the center of attention, which is natural. You can then acknowledge and analyze the bad decisions your grandiose needs led you into. Denial is the worst enemy, and only with this self-awareness can the energy be transformed into something practical and productive.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says fantastical grandiosity will make you ____ from one fantastic idea to another, never realizing any of them.
questions.explain: Under the principle of concentrating the energy, Greene says you must do the opposite of flitting: focus deeply on a single project.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Concentrate the energy,” what kind of goal should you set?
options: A goal chosen by others so you stay humble
A grand goal that will take many years to reach
Several goals pursued at once to keep things fresh
A relatively simple goal within a time frame of months
questions.explain: Greene advises a relatively simple goal within months rather than years, broken down into mini steps, so you can focus deeply on a single project.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Concentrate the energy,” the objective is to enter a state of ____, in which ideas come to you at odd hours.
questions.explain: Greene says this absorbed state should feel pleasurable and addicting; if you do not reach it, you are multitasking and breaking the focus.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Concentrate the energy,” what matters more than the number of hours you put in?
options: The intensity and consistent effort you bring
The number of projects you have planned
The prestige of the project
The size of the audience for the work
questions.explain: Greene says it is not the hours but the intensity and consistent effort, and the project could even be one outside your job.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put these steps of Greene's principle “Concentrate the energy” in order.
items: Choose a single, relatively simple project
Break it down into mini steps and goals
Absorb yourself until you reach a state of flow
See continual improvement in your skill level
Feel your confidence rise and keep advancing
questions.explain: Greene describes focusing on one achievable project, breaking it down, going deep enough to enter flow, and letting the resulting skill gains raise confidence.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these signs into whether, in Greene's principle “Concentrate the energy,” you have entered a state of flow or not.
groups: Not in a state of flow

items.t: Your mind becomes increasingly absorbed in the work
Ideas come to you at odd hours
The work feels pleasurable and addicting
You keep multitasking
You fantasize about other projects on the horizon
You keep stopping the focus

questions.explain: Greene describes flow as deep, pleasurable absorption; multitasking and fantasies about other projects are what break it.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene's principle “Maintain a dialogue with reality” in order.
items: Start with an idea and let your imagination take flight
Move from planning to execution
Actively seek feedback and criticism
Analyze what you did wrong as brutally as possible
Return to the project or start a new one, using the lessons
questions.explain: Greene describes an endless cycle between imagination and reality, in which each round of feedback and analysis feeds the next round of imagining.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Describe the cycle Greene calls “Maintain a dialogue with reality,” and say what goes wrong if either side dominates.
questions.a: You begin with an idea and let your imagination roam, then move to execution and actively seek feedback and criticism from people you respect or your natural audience. You analyze failures brutally and return to the project or a new one, incorporating what you learned. Staying too long in imagination makes the work grandiose and detached from reality; only following feedback makes it conventional and flat.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Maintain a dialogue with reality,” what happens if you only listen to feedback and make the work reflect what others want?
options: The work will be conventional and flat
You will win a large but short-lived audience
You will be overwhelmed by too many ideas
The work will be grandiose and detached from reality
questions.explain: Greene says pure feedback produces conventional, flat work, while too much time in the imagination phase produces grandiose work; the dialogue between them creates something practical and powerful.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these activities into the two sides of Greene's dialogue with reality.

items.t: Letting your imagination take flight
Being open to various possibilities in planning
Letting your imagination loose again on a new project
Seeking criticism from people you respect
Hearing about the flaws in your plan
Analyzing in depth what you did wrong

questions.explain: Greene asks you to cycle between these two sides, since either alone yields work that is grandiose or flat.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene's principle “Maintain a dialogue with reality,” what should you do when a project succeeds?
options: Repeat the same approach on a larger scale
Move into a field where you have no experience
Take a long rest to enjoy the praise
Step back from the attention and see yourself back at square one
questions.explain: Greene says to look at the role of luck and others' help, resist the success delusion, and treat the next project as a new challenge needing the same focus.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: In “Maintain a dialogue with reality,” Greene says you should treat a failed project as the best way to learn.
questions.explain: Greene says if the project fails or the problem is not solved, you should embrace this as the best way to learn and analyze what you did wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Seek out calibrated challenges,” what level of challenge should you look for?
options: Challenges exactly at your current skill level
Challenges just above your skill level
Challenges well below your skill level, to build confidence
The greatest challenge you can imagine
questions.explain: Greene says challenges below or at your level bore you, while overly ambitious ones crush you; moderately harder challenges are the optimum path toward learning.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each level of challenge to the result Greene predicts in “Seek out calibrated challenges.”
pairs: Below or at your skill level
You become easily bored and less focused
You feel crushed by your failure
Moderately harder than the last project
questions.explain: Greene's point is that only a moderate step up in difficulty keeps focus high and makes both success and failure useful.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene call challenges just above your skill level the optimum path toward learning?
questions.a: Projects below or at your level bore you and weaken focus, while overly ambitious ones crush you when you fail. A challenge moderately harder than the last one excites and energizes you, so your focus rises. If you fail, you are not overwhelmed and learn more; if you succeed, your confidence grows but stays tied to the work, satisfying your need for greatness.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: In Greene's principle “Seek out calibrated challenges,” what does he call failing in a large fashion after an overambitious attempt, blaming others and never learning?
options: The success delusion
The Euro Disney syndrome
The grandiose victim
Grandiose humility
questions.explain: Greene names it after Eisner's overreach with Euro Disney; the success delusion is the broader blindness after success, and grandiose humility and the grandiose victim are disguised forms of grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if you fail at a properly calibrated challenge, you will feel overwhelmed and learn very little.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: with a calibrated challenge, failure does not overwhelm you and you learn even more.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene compares tamed grandiose energy to a wild ____ that needs to roam free now and then or it will go mad from restlessness.
questions.explain: This image introduces the fifth principle, letting loose your grandiose energy once it has been tamed.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene suggest as ways to let loose your grandiose energy once it is tamed?
options: Give freer rein to your imagination when planning
Quit your job to chase your biggest fantasy
Develop a new skill in an unrelated field
Stop seeking feedback for good
questions.explain: Greene suggests occasional bigger challenges, such as a new skill or a once-postponed novel, and freer imagination in planning; he never advises abandoning feedback or chasing fantasies blindly.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which leader does Greene use to illustrate letting loose grandiose energy to inspire a group in crisis?
options: Douglas MacArthur
Mao Zedong
Winston Churchill
Napoleon Bonaparte
questions.explain: Greene says Churchill's grandiose confidence during World War II lifted and inspired others; MacArthur and Mao appear as grandiose leaders who went too far.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is safe to let loose your grandiose energy, and what are some ways to do it?
questions.a: Once the energy is tamed and serves your goals, you have earned the right to feel godlike through improved skills and real achievements. You might take on greater challenges, develop a skill in an unrelated field, give your imagination freer rein, or let self-belief animate you when performing or leading in a crisis, as Churchill did. Having worked through the other principles, you naturally return to earth after a few days or hours.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: Greene says someone who has worked through the other principles will naturally come back down to earth after a few days or hours of grandiose exuberance.
questions.explain: Greene ends the fifth principle by saying the earlier principles act as a safeguard, so exuberance is temporary.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, if you are in the public eye and let your grandiose energy fill you with self-belief, what effect will it have?
options: It will lead you into the success delusion
It will make you lose touch with your allies
It will animate your gestures and give you greater charisma
It will make your audience more critical of you
questions.explain: Greene says that when performing before others, letting go of restraint animates your gestures and adds charisma, because this confidence rests on real achievement.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the source of our infantile grandiosity, and how can we satisfy the urge it leaves us with?
questions.a: It lies in the intense, complete connection we felt with our mother as infants, which we spend much of life trying to recapture. We get glimmers of it in intimate relationships and unconditional love, but these are rare. Entering a state of flow with our work or cultivating deeper empathy with people gives us more such moments of oneness, and we can go further by connecting to life itself.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say will give us more moments of the oneness we felt in our original connection to the mother?
options: Gaining social prestige and accolades
Entering a state of flow with our work
Worshipping a leader who promises a utopia
Cultivating deeper levels of empathy with people
questions.explain: Greene names flow and deeper empathy as ways to feel oneness with the work or with people; prestige and leader worship are forms of grandiosity he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What term from Sigmund Freud does Greene use for experiencing a deeper connection to life itself?
options: The success delusion
The state of flow
The oceanic feeling
The Sublime
questions.explain: Greene cites Freud's “the oceanic feeling”; the Sublime is Greene's own name for fully taking in the improbable reality of being alive.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene cites Sigmund Freud's phrase “the ____ feeling” for a deeper connection to life itself.
questions.explain: The phrase leads into Greene's reflection on the improbability of life and his idea of the Sublime.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Fully taking in the improbable reality of life and of your own brief consciousness is what Greene calls the ____.
questions.explain: Greene says it cannot be put into words and refers to chapter 18 for more.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene says feeling part of the tenuous experiment of life is a kind of ____ grandiosity, in which you are ecstatic to be a drop in the ocean.
questions.explain: Instead of being disturbed by our smallness, we rejoice in it, which turns grandiosity's usual direction around.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: What does Greene mean by the Sublime at the end of his discussion of practical grandiosity, and why does he call it a kind of reverse grandiosity?
questions.a: The Sublime is fully taking in how improbable the formation of life on Earth was, how astonishing evolution has been, and how unlikely your own birth and brief consciousness are. It is too awesome to put into words. It is reverse grandiosity because, rather than being disturbed by your relative smallness, you feel ecstatic at being a drop in the ocean of life.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each term from Greene's discussion of practical grandiosity to its meaning.
pairs: Based on fantasies and the skewed impression attention gives
Energy channeled into real work, skills and goals
Freud's term for a deeper connection to life itself
Fully taking in the improbability of life and of being alive
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the two forms of grandiosity, then points beyond both toward connection with life itself.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each of Greene's principles of practical grandiosity to its core instruction.
pairs: Come to terms with your grandiose needs
Admit you want to feel important and superior
Focus deeply on a single project until you enter flow
Take on projects just above your skill level
Occasionally entertain greater challenges and self-belief
questions.explain: Each principle channels grandiose energy toward reality: honesty, focus, feedback, measured difficulty, and finally controlled release.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these traits into fantastical grandiosity or practical grandiosity, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Flitting from one fantastic idea to another
Self-esteem tied to nebulous fantasies
Failing hugely on an overambitious goal and blaming others
Focusing deeply on a single project
Self-esteem tied to real achievements
Seeking challenges just above your skill level

questions.explain: Greene's contrast is between energy lost in fantasies of acclaim and energy channeled into real, focused, calibrated work.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: In the Xenophon passage that closes Greene's chapter on grandiosity, the god's answer to Croesus was that by knowing himself he would live and be happy.
questions.explain: Croesus admits that, flattered and puffed up, he thought himself fit to be the greatest but did not know himself, a fitting end for a chapter titled Know Your Limits.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does the section “Practical Grandiosity” relate to the earlier part of Greene's chapter on the Law of Grandiosity?
options: It fulfills the promised third and most important task: channeling your own grandiosity productively
It retells the Michael Eisner story from a new angle
It lists the warning signs for spotting grandiose leaders
It contradicts the earlier claim that grandiosity is natural
questions.explain: Earlier in the chapter Greene sets a threefold task and points ahead to “Practical Grandiosity” for how to channel the energy into something productive.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Greene's discussion of the Sublime at the end of “Practical Grandiosity” points ahead for more to which chapter?
options: Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality
Chapter 2, Transform Self-love into Empathy
Chapter 17, Seize the Historical Moment
Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.explain: Greene writes “For more on this, see chapter 18,” the book's closing chapter on death, where the Sublime is developed further.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Why does the section “The Grandiose Leader” follow the general discussion of grandiosity in chapter 11, and how does it link back to the chapter's opening story?
questions.a: The earlier discussion shows grandiosity as an everyday trait and how to measure it in people around us. The leader section then turns to the high-grade type: people with talent and assertive energy who rise to great power and can lead followers into disaster. Michael Eisner, the subject of the opening story, reappears as a leader who presented himself as embodying the whole Disney spirit, and his Euro Disney overreach echoes later.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: How does the second half of chapter 11 move from other people to the reader, and why does the chapter end with practical grandiosity and the Sublime?
questions.a: Greene first teaches us to see through grandiose leaders and scale them down to human size, then turns to our own grandiose energy. Rather than asking us to suppress it, he shows how to channel it into real work, the most important part of the task he set. Ending with the Sublime offers a healthy outlet for the urge to feel larger: a reverse grandiosity of connection to life, fitting the chapter's title, Know Your Limits.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Which of these chapters does the second half of chapter 11 explicitly refer the reader to?
options: Chapter 2, Transform Self-love into Empathy
Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality
Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego
questions.explain: Greene refers to chapter 2 when recommending deeper empathy and to chapter 18 for more on the Sublime; chapters 10 and 14 are not cited there.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: True or false: In “Practical Grandiosity,” Greene refers to a Euro Disney syndrome, linking back to the story of Michael Eisner that opens chapter 11.
questions.explain: Greene warns that overambitious types may end up in the Euro Disney syndrome, recalling Eisner's costly overreach told in The Success Delusion.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Match each section of chapter 11 to its main focus.
pairs: Michael Eisner's rise and fall at Disney
The childhood roots of grandiosity and how to measure it
Six illusions that powerful grandiose types create
Five principles for channeling grandiosity into work
questions.explain: The sections move from story to analysis, then to grandiose leaders, and finally to a practical program for the reader.

questions.unitTitle: Know Your Limits
questions.q: Sort these topics from the second half of chapter 11 by whether they help you deal with grandiosity in others or in yourself.

items.t: Seeing through the six illusions
Indira Gandhi's common-woman act
Creating a viral disenchantment
Seeking calibrated challenges
Maintaining a dialogue with reality
Coming to terms with your grandiose needs

questions.explain: The Grandiose Leader section equips us to demythologize others, and Practical Grandiosity turns to managing and channeling our own energy.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: The Law of Gender Rigidity says our masculine and feminine qualities are partly genetic and partly come from the profound influence of the ____ of the opposite sex.
questions.explain: The law names two sources of our contrasexual qualities: our genes and the parent of the other sex, whose influence the Keys section later explains in depth.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to the Law of Gender Rigidity, what leads us to repress our masculine or feminine qualities?
options: The need to present a consistent identity in society
The wish to attract members of the opposite sex
A natural lack of those qualities from birth
Bad experiences in our first romantic relationships
questions.explain: The law says it is the need to present a consistent identity in society that makes us overidentify with the expected role. It insists we are born with these qualities, so they are not simply missing.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Gender Rigidity name as prices we pay for overidentifying with our expected gender role?
options: We become physically weaker over time
Our thinking and ways of acting become rigid
We lose the ability to fall in love
We project our own fantasies and hostilities onto the opposite sex
We lose valuable dimensions to our character
questions.explain: The law lists lost dimensions, rigid thinking and acting, and relationships damaged by projection. It never says we stop falling in love; in fact projection is what drives infatuation.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: the Law of Gender Rigidity advises you to play the gender role expected of you more convincingly.
questions.explain: It says the reverse: “Do not play the expected gender role, but rather create the one that suits you.”

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to the Law of Gender Rigidity, what do you gain by becoming aware of your lost masculine or feminine traits and slowly reconnecting to them?
questions.a: Reconnecting unleashes creative powers and makes your thinking more fluid. By bringing out the masculine or feminine undertone to your character, you fascinate people by being authentically yourself, creating the role that suits you rather than the expected one.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: The Law of Gender Rigidity promises that by bringing out the masculine or feminine ____ to your character, you will fascinate people by being authentically yourself.
questions.explain: Undertone is Greene’s recurring word for the contrasexual side that colors a character, as in Caterina’s masculine undertone.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Put the steps of the Law of Gender Rigidity statement in the order Greene presents them.
items: We all have masculine and feminine qualities
The need for a consistent identity makes us repress them
Our character becomes rigid and we project onto the opposite sex
Become aware of the lost traits and reconnect to them
Create the gender role that suits you
questions.explain: The statement moves from our double nature, to its repression, to the cost, then to the remedy and the final advice to create one’s own role.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: In the Law of Gender Rigidity, how do our relationships with members of the opposite sex suffer when we overidentify with our gender role?
options: We project onto them our own fantasies and hostilities
We compete with them for status and power
We avoid them out of shyness and fear
We imitate them and lose our own identity
questions.explain: The law says our relationships suffer because we project our own fantasies and hostilities onto the other sex, an idea the Keys section develops through Jung’s anima and animus.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: As Duke of Milan, Galeazzo had his daughter Caterina brought into the castle of Porta Giovia and raised like any ____ member of the Sforza family.
questions.explain: Although born out of wedlock, Caterina was raised as a legitimate Sforza, and her stepmother treated her as one of her own.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: In the story of Caterina Sforza, why was it significant that Francesco Filelfo became her tutor?
options: He taught only military subjects, preparing her for war
He had been her father’s own tutor, signaling Galeazzo’s identification with her
He was a woman, offering her a rare female role model
He was the pope’s favorite scholar, linking her to Rome
questions.explain: In the Interpretation Greene notes that giving her his own tutor signaled an identification Galeazzo felt between them, perhaps seeing a female reflection of himself.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these subjects did Francesco Filelfo teach Caterina Sforza?
options: Law
Music composition
Military history
Latin
Greek
questions.explain: Filelfo taught her Latin, Greek, philosophy, the sciences and even military history. Law and music composition are not on Greene’s list.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Match each book or kind of book to how it figures in Caterina Sforza’s girlhood reading.
pairs: Written by Filelfo in the style of Homer
Boccaccio’s book on the deeds of celebrated women
Stories of real-life knights in armor
Stories of past leaders she read alongside the others
questions.explain: Greene lists these as the books that converged in her mind as she daydreamed of the family’s future glory with herself in the midst of it.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How did Caterina Sforza’s father treat her, and how did she relate to him as a girl?
questions.a: Although their encounters were brief, they were intense: Galeazzo treated her as an equal, marveled at her intelligence and encouraged her studies. From early on she identified with him, experiencing his traumas and triumphs as if they were her own, and he stood at the center of her fantasies as a legendary figure.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What methods did Galeazzo Sforza confide to his daughter Caterina?
options: Trust no one, strike first, and show no mercy
Wait patiently and let enemies make mistakes
Think ahead, plot several moves in advance, and seize the initiative
Win people with charm, gifts, and spectacle
questions.explain: He told her to think ahead and plot several moves in advance, always aiming to seize the initiative, methods she later used at Sant’Angelo and Ravaldino.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Sort these traits of Galeazzo Sforza into his hard, warrior side and his softer, artistic side as Caterina saw them.

items.t: Fearless in the hunt against the largest animals
Superior and impetuous horseman
Diplomat who kept the upper hand at court
Orchestrated colorful spectacles on tour
Wore the latest bejeweled silk fashions
Cried like a baby at choral music

questions.explain: Greene shows Galeazzo blending a virile, commanding side with a love of spectacle, fashion and music, and says this second side deepened Caterina’s identification with him.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: as a girl, Caterina Sforza was kept from the sword fighting and hunting that her brothers learned.
questions.explain: All the Sforza children, girls included, were taught sword fighting and rigorous physical training, and Caterina hunted boars and stags in the woods of Pavia.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Whom did Galeazzo Sforza arrange for ten-year-old Caterina to marry in 1473?
options: Giovanni de’ Medici of Florence
Giacomo Feo, a former stable boy
Cesare Borgia, son of the pope
Girolamo Riario, nephew of Pope Sixtus IV
questions.explain: The marriage to Girolamo Riario, the thirty-year-old papal nephew, forged an alliance between Rome and Milan. Feo and Medici were her later husbands, and Borgia her final enemy.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: As part of Caterina’s marriage arrangement, the pope purchased the city of ____ and christened the new couple its Count and Countess.
questions.explain: The pope bought Imola, which the Sforzas had taken decades before; later he added nearby Forlì.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these describe Girolamo Riario as Caterina Sforza came to know him?
options: Moody, self-absorbed and high-strung
A gentle man who worshipped her
Paralyzed with fear when the pope died
A brilliant strategist she admired
A hothead who made enemies wherever he turned
questions.explain: Greene paints Girolamo as moody, hotheaded and, after the pope’s death, unable to decide anything. She found him weak compared with her father; worship came later, from Giacomo Feo.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Botticelli used Caterina Sforza as a model for some of his greatest paintings.
questions.explain: Greene notes that she reveled in attention as the most fashionable woman in Rome, Botticelli using her as a model.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why were Caterina Sforza and her husband in grave danger after Pope Sixtus IV died in 1484?
questions.a: Girolamo had started a feud with the powerful Colonna family, the Romans hated him, and the new pope was likely to be a friend of the Colonnas. Without papal protection, and with the Sforzas weak in Milan, they stood to lose everything, including Forlì and Imola.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: When Pope Sixtus IV died, what did Caterina Sforza do while her husband hesitated outside Rome?
options: She rode secretly into Rome and seized the Castel Sant’Angelo
She fled to Milan to raise a Sforza army
She persuaded the cardinals to elect a friendly pope
She negotiated a truce with the Colonna family
questions.explain: Thinking as her father would, she snuck out of camp, rode to Rome and took the castle whose cannons commanded the city, preventing the conclave from meeting.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Caterina Sforza could enter Rome unrecognized because she was seven months ____ with her fourth child.
questions.explain: In her condition no one recognized her, and she headed straight for the Castel Sant’Angelo.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why did holding the Castel Sant’Angelo give Caterina Sforza leverage over the cardinals?
options: It housed the cardinals’ families as hostages
It held the papal treasury that the cardinals needed
It controlled the only bridge into the city from the north
Its cannons covered the roads to the Vatican, so the conclave could not meet
questions.explain: With the cannons aimed at all roads to the Vatican, the cardinals could not gather in one place to elect a new pope until they met her terms.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why were the Romans astonished when Caterina Sforza walked out of the Castel Sant’Angelo?
questions.a: They had taken her for a frivolous young woman addicted to clothes, the pope’s little pet. Now she emerged after controlling Rome for eleven days wearing a silk gown with a heavy sword hanging from a man’s belt, her pregnancy evident. They had never seen such a blend of the feminine and the warlike.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: In Forlì, what step did Caterina Sforza take that later saved her after her husband’s murder?
options: She installed a trusted ally as commander of the castle Ravaldino
She moved her children to Milan for safety
She lowered taxes to win the people’s loyalty
She hired a bodyguard of French soldiers
questions.explain: Thinking ahead, she put a trusted ally in charge of Ravaldino, the castle that dominated the area, and when the assassins struck she ordered that it never be surrendered.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: In 1488 Girolamo Riario was stabbed to death by men led by Ludovico ____, a member of a powerful family he had made enemies of.
questions.explain: Girolamo’s heavy taxes and quarrels made enemies of the Orsi family, and Ludovico Orsi led the armed men who killed him.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Put these events from Caterina Sforza’s life in chronological order.
items: Marriage to Girolamo Riario arranged
Seizure of the Castel Sant’Angelo
Murder of Girolamo by the Orsi conspirators
Murder of Giacomo Feo at a picnic
Marriage to Giovanni de’ Medici
Siege of Ravaldino by Cesare Borgia
questions.explain: The arranged marriage came in 1473, Sant’Angelo in 1484, Girolamo’s death in 1488, Feo’s killing in 1495, the Medici marriage in 1498 and Borgia’s siege in late 1499.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How did Caterina Sforza trick the Orsi conspirators into letting her into the fortress of Ravaldino?
questions.a: She and the commander Tommaso Feo, communicating through messengers, staged a drama: she seemed to beg him to surrender, and he agreed only if she entered alone to pay his wages and sign a letter absolving him. Once inside she was safe, and Feo announced he was holding her hostage, while she played for time until the Milanese army arrived.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Match each person to their part in the Ravaldino episode of Caterina Sforza’s story.
pairs: Commander of Ravaldino who staged the surrender drama with her
Conspirator who pressed his lance against her chest
Leader of the men who killed her husband
Her first husband, stabbed and thrown into the square
questions.explain: Greene identifies Feo as the commander she had installed, Ronche and Orsi as the conspirators who marched her to the castle, and Girolamo as their victim.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: When the assassins threatened to kill her children unless she surrendered Ravaldino, how did Caterina Sforza respond?
options: She defied them, saying she could have more children
She bargained for the children’s release with gold
She offered herself as a hostage in their place
She surrendered the castle to save them
questions.explain: She shouted that she was already pregnant again and had the means to make more, having calculated that the assassins were too weak to kill them in cold blood.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why did Caterina Sforza calculate that the Orsi conspirators would not kill her children?
questions.a: She judged them weak and indecisive, since they should have killed her family on the first day amid the mayhem. They knew the Sforzas, already on their way, would take terrible revenge for such a deed. And she knew that surrendering would only lead to prison and poison, so she had to keep stalling.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these did Caterina Sforza do during the Ravaldino crisis after her first husband’s murder?
options: Fled to Milan disguised as a servant
Shuffled her six children into a room in the palace tower
Shouted instructions that the castle must never be surrendered
Signed away Forlì to the conspirators
Had the castle cannons fire at the Orsi palace
questions.explain: She protected her children, sent orders through allies below her window, and showed her resolve with cannon fire until the Milanese army arrived. She never fled or signed anything away.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: After the Ravaldino crisis, the new pope confirmed Caterina Sforza as ____ until her eldest son, Ottaviano, came of age.
questions.explain: She was quickly restored to power as regent, and the legend of the warrior countess of Forlì spread across Italy.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these did Caterina Sforza do after falling in love with Giacomo Feo?
options: Had him knighted and married him in secret
Listened closely to her sons’ warnings about him
Made him commander of Ravaldino
Sent him to negotiate with the pope in Rome
Handed him governing powers and retired from public affairs
questions.explain: To soothe his insecurity she gave him the castle, a knighthood, a secret marriage and her powers. She ignored, rather than heeded, the warnings of courtiers and her sons.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: after Giacomo Feo was murdered in 1495, Caterina Sforza fell into a deep depression and even contemplated suicide.
questions.explain: After punishing the conspirators she sank into depression, asking herself how she had lost her way and given up her power, before recovering through religion and ruling.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: The pope who set his eye on Forlì, Alexander VI, used his son Cesare ____ as commander of the papal forces.
questions.explain: Alexander VI, formerly Roderigo Borgia, wanted to extend the papal domains through conquest, with Cesare Borgia leading the army.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Cesare Borgia rode up to Ravaldino on December 26, the anniversary of the assassination of Caterina Sforza’s father.
questions.explain: As she looked down at Borgia, she thought of her father on the anniversary of his murder and resolved not to disappoint him.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How had Caterina Sforza prepared Ravaldino for Cesare Borgia’s siege, and what was her overall plan?
questions.a: She forged an alliance with the Venetians and fortified Ravaldino so that she could keep retreating behind barricades if the walls were breached. As her father would have, she thought ahead and planned to play for time until her allies came, forcing Borgia to take the castle by force while she was ready to die sword in hand.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What trick did Caterina Sforza try to play on Cesare Borgia at the drawbridge of Ravaldino?
options: She pretended to surrender and then fired the cannons
She lured him with flirtation onto the drawbridge, which began to rise
She offered a forged letter from the French king
She sent out a double dressed in her clothes
questions.explain: Seeming to fall for his charm, she invited him to follow her into the castle; as he stepped onto the drawbridge it rose, and he leaped back just in time.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Match each figure to their role in the last years of Caterina Sforza’s story.
pairs: Besieged Ravaldino and took her prisoner
French captain who won her release
Pope who wanted Forlì for the papal domains
questions.explain: Greene closes the story with Medici’s death, the Borgia pope’s ambitions, Cesare’s siege and the chivalric d’Allegre who got her freed.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What happened to Caterina Sforza after her capture by Cesare Borgia, up to her death?
questions.a: She refused to sign away her domain even under duress and was thrown into the prison at Castel Sant’Angelo, enduring a year of loneliness and torture in a windowless cell. The French captain Yves d’Allegre, who had fallen under her spell, demanded her release and got her safe passage to Florence. In retirement she received letters from admiring men all over Europe and died in 1509.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to Greene’s Interpretation, what roles were open to a woman in Caterina Sforza’s time?
options: Wife, soldier, or regent for a young son
Good mother and wife, religious life, or in rare cases courtesan
Mother, merchant, or teacher of noble children
Only nun or wife, never any public role
questions.explain: Greene says a woman’s primary role was mother and wife; unmarried, she could devote herself to religion or rarely become a courtesan, as if a circle were drawn around her.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Greene says that in Caterina Sforza’s time it was as if a ____ had been drawn around every woman, which she dared not explore beyond.
questions.explain: The image of the circle captures how restricted women’s roles were, restrictions internalized through a limited early education.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did a woman’s early education matter so much for the roles she could later play in Caterina Sforza’s time?
questions.a: It was in her earliest years and education that a woman internalized the restrictions on her role. If she studied only a few subjects and practiced only certain skills, she could not expand her role even if she wanted to. As Greene puts it, knowledge was power.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did the Sforzas train their daughters in hunting and sword fighting?
options: They hoped their daughters would one day rule Milan alone
Italian law required noble daughters to bear arms
They had no sons and needed heirs who could fight
They were new to power and saw that strong wives made valuable marriage pawns
questions.explain: Having found in their rise that a strong, capable wife was a great help, they toughened their daughters to be fearless, important qualities in marriage pawns.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Greene calls Caterina Sforza’s upbringing at Porta Giovia a unique experiment, in which she was isolated and given great freedom to develop in any direction.
questions.explain: Isolated and free, she could explore all knowledge, indulge her interests in fashion and the arts, and give rein to her bold physical spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Sort these roles Caterina Sforza played into those within the conventional circle for women and those beyond it.

items.t: Loyal wife
Devoted mother
Most fashionable woman at the papal court
Daring soldier seizing a city
Keen strategist plotting moves ahead
Leader of troops, sword in hand

questions.explain: Greene stresses that she could play the expected roles of wife, mother and beauty, but in crisis also became soldier, strategist and commander, roles she had fantasized about as a girl.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Greene says Caterina Sforza had a feminine spirit with a pronounced masculine undertone, the ____ of her father.
questions.explain: Galeazzo was a masculine man with a feminine side for spectacle and music; Caterina was the mirror image, and the two traits blended into her unique style.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene cite as signs of Caterina Sforza’s feminine empathy as a ruler?
options: She endured prison to safeguard her children’s inheritance
She was ambitious and proud of it
She comforted the sick when plague struck Forlì
She had no tolerance for the incompetent or weak
She tried to outwit opponents and avoid bloodshed
questions.explain: Comforting plague victims, self-sacrifice for her children and avoiding bloodshed show her empathy; her intolerance of weakness and her open ambition are the tough, masculine side of the blend.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Sort these qualities of Caterina Sforza as a ruler into her feminine and her masculine sides, as Greene presents them.

items.t: High degree of empathy when ruling
Comforting the plague-stricken
Self-sacrifice for her children
Shrewd and tough negotiating
No tolerance for the incompetent
Open pride in her ambition

questions.explain: Greene presents her as blending empathy and self-sacrifice with toughness and ambition, a blend he calls the source of her power.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to Greene, what was the source of Caterina Sforza’s power?
options: Her beauty, which made men obey her
Her ability to play many roles, blending the masculine with the feminine
Her ruthlessness toward every enemy
Her family’s wealth and its Milanese armies
