Reconnecting to a bold, adventurous spirit, they should widen their options to both offense and defense, remembering that action for its own sake can be therapeutic.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that for those with the feminine style, action for its own sake is never helpful.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: action for its own sake can be therapeutic, and taking aggressive action can discomfit opponents, especially for those who overthink.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to Greene, how do men tend to respond when they make mistakes?
options: They look inward and blame themselves too harshly
They ask others for help in finding what went wrong
They credit luck for both their failures and successes
They look outward and blame other people or circumstances
questions.explain: Because men's sense of self is tied to success, they avoid looking inward after failure, which makes it hard to learn. Looking inward is the feminine tendency.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What does Greene advise people with the masculine style of self-assessment to do?
options: Look outward for the causes of both failure and success
Look inward when they make mistakes and outward when they succeed
Avoid asking for feedback so as not to seem weak
Raise their self-opinion to keep their confidence high
questions.explain: He tells them to reverse their habit, ask for help and feedback, and lower their self-opinion, since they are not as skilled as they imagine.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as the feminine style of self-assessment and learning?
options: Taking complete credit for any success
Overestimating their abilities
Blaming themselves and looking inward after failure
Finding it easy to ask for assistance
Looking at the role of others in helping them succeed
questions.explain: Women tend to look inward at failure, credit others for success and ask for help readily; overconfidence and taking full credit are the masculine tendencies.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Greene says Jung called the internalized critical voices of men who judged women for their looks and intelligence ____ voices.
questions.explain: Greene advises catching these voices as they occur and ridding yourself of them, since low self-esteem in women is acquired, not natural.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the low self-esteem many women suffer from is natural rather than acquired.
questions.explain: He says it is “not natural but acquired”, coming from critical voices of others that women have internalized.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What does Greene advise people with the feminine style of self-assessment to do?
options: Ask others to judge their work more often
Avoid trying again after a criticism to protect themselves
Adopt more masculine self-confidence and take events less personally
Credit others even more generously for their successes
questions.explain: Because failures can hit too deeply and make them afraid to try again, they should adopt more confidence, without the attendant stupidity, and view events from a distance.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene describe as the masculine style of relating to people and leadership?
options: Emphasizing results, however they are achieved
Using some element of fear to keep the group cohesive
Treating the process as just as important as the results
Forming hierarchies and punishing those who fall out of line
Involving each member in the decision-making process
questions.explain: Hierarchy, fear and results describe the masculine style, which Greene compares to male chimpanzees; involving everyone and valuing process are feminine traits.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: Greene cites studies showing that boys are as empathetic as girls, but that empathy is slowly drummed out of men.
questions.explain: Boys are highly attuned to the mother's emotions, but empathy fades as they develop an assertive style; great leaders like Shackleton and Lincoln kept theirs.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why does Greene mention Ernest Shackleton and Abraham Lincoln in the Law of Gender Rigidity?
options: As leaders who ruled through fear and strict hierarchy
As leaders who were no less masculine for considering their men's emotions, and were stronger for it
As examples of leaders who avoided all conflict
As men whose empathy made them weaker in a crisis
questions.explain: Greene says Shackleton was simply a stronger and more effective leader for his constant consideration of his men's feelings, and the same could be said of Lincoln.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise people with the feminine style of leadership to do?
options: Avoid instilling any fear in their lieutenants
Not be afraid of assuming a strong leadership role, especially in a crisis
Know when to stop listening and go with the chosen plan
Incorporate the ideas of as many people as possible before acting
Fire the fools, incompetents and hyperselfish who drag the group down
questions.explain: Greene warns that incorporating too many ideas weakens a plan, and says a touch of fear in lieutenants is not always bad.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Sort these into the masculine and feminine styles of relating to people and leadership, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Requires a leader and designated deputies
Highly status conscious
Identifies clear goals and reaches them
Maintains group spirit and smooth relationships
Considers the feelings of each member
Treats the process as equally important as results

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the hierarchical, goal-driven masculine style with the empathetic, process-minded feminine style.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: A team leader spends weeks gathering everyone's opinions on a plan and keeps an underperforming, selfish colleague out of fear of hurting him. What does Greene advise for her feminine leadership style?
options: Keep listening until everyone agrees
Focus only on smoothing relationships and ignore results
Know when to stop listening, commit to her plan, and remove those who drag the group down
Hand the decision to the most senior person on the team
questions.explain: Greene says incorporating too many ideas weakens a plan and that she should even find pleasure in getting rid of those who bring the group down.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Put the four areas in which Greene compares masculine and feminine styles in the order he presents them.
items: Styles of thinking
Styles of action
Styles of self-assessment and learning
Styles of relating to people and leadership
questions.explain: Greene moves from how we think, to how we act, to how we learn from experience, and finally to how we lead others.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Match each style to Greene's advice for balancing it.
pairs: Widen the fields you look at and allow freer associations
Dig into one problem and take pleasure in structure
Train yourself to step back before taking any action
Confront people in small ways before larger conflicts
Look inward at mistakes and ask for help
questions.explain: In each area Greene's advice is to lean toward the opposite style to correct the imbalance.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How does Greene conclude the Law of Gender Rigidity about the idea of the muse?
options: Men need women as muses, but women do not need muses
The muse, for both genders, lies within
A muse is best found in a partner of the opposite sex
The idea of a muse is an illusion to be abandoned
questions.explain: Greene says “the muse, for both genders, lies within”; moving closer to your anima or animus brings you closer to the creative treasures of your unconscious.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he ends the Law of Gender Rigidity by saying the muse lies within?
questions.a: Nature compels us to move toward the feminine or masculine in the form of attraction to another person, but the wise realize they are equally compelled to move toward it inwardly. Moving closer to your anima or animus brings you closer to your unconscious and its untapped creative treasures. The fascination you once felt for the opposite sex in others you will feel for your work, your thinking and life, and like the shaman's inner wife or husband it becomes a source of uncanny powers.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise for those with an aggressive, masculine style of action?
options: Train yourself to step back before taking any action
Withdraw and reflect on your true interests when your career is blocked
Stay on the offensive so opponents never gain time
Act quickly, since waiting shows a lack of strength
Consider how each group or individual in your relationships will be affected
questions.explain: Greene says acting without proper consideration reveals weakness and a lack of self-control, so balance comes from stepping back, weighing interdependence and reflecting.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Greene compares the masculine style in a group setting to that of male ____, requiring a leader and loyal followers.
questions.explain: Like male chimpanzees, men form hierarchies, are highly status conscious and punish those who fall out of line.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: According to Greene, why should those with the masculine style of leadership enlarge their concept of leadership?
questions.a: Thinking more deeply about the individuals on the team and strategizing to involve them engages the energy and creativity of the group and produces superior results. Boys are as empathetic as girls, but empathy is drummed out of men as they develop an assertive style. Leaders like Shackleton and Lincoln kept their empathy and were stronger and more effective for it.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Put these steps of Greene's argument in The Original Man/Woman in the order he presents them.
items: The midlife crisis is really a crisis of identity
The shaman draws power from an inner wife or husband
We must overcome the prejudice that the feminine is weak
Masculine and feminine styles are compared in four areas
The muse, for both genders, lies within
questions.explain: Greene moves from the problem of a rigid identity, to the lost original wholeness, to clearing away prejudice, to practical balance, and ends with the inner muse.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How does the Gender Projection—Types section of Chapter 12 build on the Keys to Human Nature section before it?
options: It drops the idea of anima and animus and turns to biology
It turns the general idea of projecting the anima or animus into six concrete, recognizable patterns
It offers statistics on how often couples break up
It retells the opening story of Caterina Sforza in detail
questions.explain: The Keys explain how the anima and animus form and are projected; the next section shows six common forms this projection takes, each traced to a parent of the opposite sex.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Within Chapter 12, which section does the Keys to Human Nature point to for more on integrating repressed masculine or feminine traits into your everyday self?
options: The opening law statement
The Original Man/Woman
The Authentic Gender
Gender Projection—Types
questions.explain: The Keys end their discussion of integrating repressed traits by referring the reader to the final section of the chapter, The Original Man/Woman.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: When Greene says men's habit of taking full credit for success feeds their grandiose tendencies, which earlier chapter does he refer the reader to?
options: Chapter 6, Elevate Your Perspective (The Law of Shortsightedness)
Chapter 11, Know Your Limits (The Law of Grandiosity)
Chapter 2, Transform Self-love into Empathy (The Law of Narcissism)
Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego (The Law of Envy)
questions.explain: In the discussion of masculine self-assessment Greene adds a cross-reference to chapter 11 for more on grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Why does Chapter 12 end with The Original Man/Woman after describing the six gender projection types?
questions.a: The projection types diagnose the problem: repressed masculine or feminine traits get projected onto partners in fantasies that always disappoint. The final section turns to the cure, showing how to reclaim those traits within by leaning toward the opposite style in thinking, action, learning and leadership. It completes the law's arc, ending with the idea that the muse lies within.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: How does The Original Man/Woman section explain the word Reconnect in the title of Chapter 12?
questions.a: Greene argues that our original nature was fluid and contained both masculine and feminine qualities, which we repressed to build a consistent social self. The shaman with an inner wife or husband and the ancient myths of original humans who were both male and female show this lost wholeness. Reconnecting means returning to that original nature, which releases repressed energy and creativity.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: In the leadership discussion of Chapter 12, Greene refers back to chapter ____ for the story of Sir Ernest Shackleton.
questions.explain: Shackleton appears in chapter 2 on narcissism and empathy, and Greene reuses him to show that empathy makes male leaders stronger.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Chapter 12 states the Law of Gender ____, the price we pay for overidentifying with the masculine or feminine role expected of us.
questions.explain: The title names the cure, reconnecting to the masculine or feminine within, and the law names the problem, a rigid gender identity.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Which of these earlier chapters does Chapter 12's final section explicitly cross-reference?
options: Chapter 11, on grandiosity
Chapter 9, on repression
Chapter 14, on conformity
Chapter 2, on narcissism (for Shackleton)
Chapter 7, on defensiveness
questions.explain: Greene points to chapter 2 for Shackleton and to chapter 11 for grandiose tendencies; the other chapters are not cited in this section.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: True or false: In Chapter 12, the Gender Projection—Types section comes before the Keys to Human Nature section.
questions.explain: The order is The Authentic Gender, Keys to Human Nature, Gender Projection—Types, and The Original Man/Woman; the types follow the Keys that explain projection.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 12 to its role in the chapter.
pairs: Explains Jung’s anima and animus and how we project them
Describes six common patterns of projection
Shows how to reclaim the inner opposite in four styles
questions.explain: The chapter follows Greene's usual structure: a story, the keys, practical types, and a closing ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
questions.q: Sort these examples by which section of Chapter 12 they appear in.

items.t: Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis
Charles Swann and Odette
Dorothea Brooke
Queen Elizabeth I and the armada
Warren Buffett
The shaman with an inner wife or husband

questions.explain: The projection types use real and fictional relationships, while the final section uses leaders, thinkers and shamans to show balanced styles.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The Law of Aimlessness opens by noting that, unlike animals, which have ____ to guide them past dangers, we humans have to rely upon our conscious decisions.
questions.explain: Animals are guided by instinct; humans must make conscious decisions, which is why we can drift without a sense of direction.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to the Law of Aimlessness, what pulls us this way and that, leaving us with an overall lack of direction?
options: Our parents' rules and our teachers' plans
Our ambition and our fear of death
Our moods and the opinions of others
Our instincts and bodily appetites
questions.explain: The law says we sense a lack of direction as we are pulled about by our moods and by what other people think, which leads to drifting.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Aimlessness says that, once we have a sense of purpose, even our moments of doubt and our failures have a purpose: to toughen us up.
questions.explain: The opening says that with a sense of purpose even doubts and failures serve us, because they toughen us up.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to the Law of Aimlessness, what is the way to avoid drifting into dead ends, and what does it give us?
questions.a: The way out is to develop a sense of purpose: to discover our calling in life and use that knowledge to guide our decisions. We come to know our tastes and inclinations more deeply, trust ourselves, and know which battles and detours to avoid. With such energy and direction, our actions have unstoppable force.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does the Law of Aimlessness say a sense of purpose brings us?
options: Freedom from ever doubting or failing
Actions with unstoppable force
A deeper knowledge of our own tastes and inclinations
Trust in ourselves and knowing which battles and detours to avoid
The steady approval of the people around us
questions.explain: Purpose brings self-knowledge, self-trust and force; it does not abolish doubt or failure, which instead serve to toughen us, and it frees us from others' opinions rather than winning their approval.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: A woman in her thirties suddenly wonders how she ended up in this job, in this place. In the Law of Aimlessness, what is this feeling a sign of?
options: A shortsighted focus on short-term gains
Drifting without an overall sense of direction
A healthy phase of free exploration
Envy of more successful peers
questions.explain: The opening uses exactly this question, how we ended up in this job and place, as the symptom of drifting that can lead to dead ends.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The Law of Aimlessness says the way to avoid aimless drifting is to discover our ____ in life and use that knowledge to guide our decisions.
questions.explain: Developing a sense of purpose means discovering our calling in life, the theme the whole chapter develops.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In The Voice, what kind of childhood did Martin Luther King Jr. have?
options: A pleasant, carefree one in a staunchly middle-class black neighborhood of Atlanta
A troubled one marked by frequent racist violence
A lonely one in an integrated neighborhood of Boston
A hard one in a poor rural district of Alabama
questions.explain: King grew up comfortably in middle-class Atlanta, the son of a thriving pastor; his few encounters with racism left him relatively unscathed.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How did Martin Luther King Sr. discipline his son, and why did Martin Jr. feel guilt rather than resentment?
questions.a: Martin Sr. was a strict disciplinarian who whipped his son until he was fifteen and once scolded him vehemently in front of friends for dancing at a church social. But the discipline carried no hostility; the father's affection was real and palpable, so the boy felt only guilt for disappointing him. That guilt was heavier because of the high hopes his father placed on him.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Martin Luther King Sr.'s strict discipline came with open hostility, which drove Martin Jr. into rebellion against his father.
questions.explain: The book stresses that the discipline came without the slightest hint of hostility; the boy felt guilt for disappointing a loving father, and he never mindlessly rebelled.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put Martin Luther King Sr.'s plan for his elder son in order.
items: Attend Morehouse College in Atlanta
Be ordained as a minister
Serve as copastor at Ebenezer
Inherit his father's position as pastor
questions.explain: Martin Sr. wanted his son to follow in his footsteps through Morehouse, ordination and the copastorship to eventually inherit Ebenezer, as he had inherited it from his father-in-law.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In The Voice, sort these traits between Martin Luther King Jr. and his father, Martin Sr.

items.t: Easygoing, fond of parties and nice clothes
A fundamentalist who read the Bible literally
A cool, rational and practical temperament
Sermons aimed at the emotions of parishioners
More interested in improving life on earth
More concerned with helping people in the afterlife
Not complicated at all
A social side and a solitary, reflective side

questions.explain: The son was complex, easygoing and rational, more interested in life on earth; the father was simple, strong in a literal faith, and preached to the emotions with an eye on the afterlife.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How did young Martin Luther King Jr. handle the tension of possible confrontation with his father?
options: He asked his grandmother to plead his case for him
He always said yes to his father and postponed any decision that might cause a rift
He argued openly and then apologized afterward
He rebelled by refusing to attend his father's church
questions.explain: Since it was impossible to argue with his father, King developed the strategy of saying yes to everything and postponing decisions, such as attending Morehouse while planning to choose his own path.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these careers did Martin Luther King Jr. consider in his first months at Morehouse?
options: Law
Sociology
Medicine
Engineering
Journalism
questions.explain: Excited by all the subjects open to him, he thought of medicine, then sociology, then law, before deciding by his last year to be ordained.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: At Crozer Theological Seminary, Martin Luther King Jr. discovered a side of Christianity that emphasized social commitment and political ____.
questions.explain: At Crozer he found a socially committed, activist Christianity, read the major philosophers and Marx, and became fascinated by Gandhi.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: As he prepared to graduate from Boston University in 1954, what two comfortable options did Martin Luther King Jr. face, and what did he choose instead?
questions.a: His father had lined up a copastorship at Ebenezer plus part-time teaching at Morehouse, while Coretta wanted to stay in the North, where he could teach at almost any university. Both promised a comfortable life. But he had a vision he could not rationally explain: to return to the South and lead a large congregation in a good-sized city, though not Atlanta, where he could make a practical difference. He would have to resist the easy path and displease his father.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why did the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery suit Martin Luther King Jr.'s temperament?
options: It had the strongest NAACP chapter in Alabama
Its congregation was more solemn and thoughtful than Ebenezer's
Its congregation was larger and more emotional than Ebenezer's
It was close to his father and the family church
questions.explain: On his visit he found the Dexter congregation more solemn and thoughtful, which matched his cool, reflective side rather than his father's emotional style.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Coretta urged Martin Luther King Jr. to accept the Dexter position because she had grown up near Montgomery and loved the city.
questions.explain: Coretta tried to dissuade him: having grown up near Montgomery, she knew how fiercely segregated it was and the ugly tensions beneath the surface.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: When the Dexter Avenue Baptist Church offered Martin Luther King Jr. the job, how did he respond?
options: He accepted only after his father gave his blessing
He accepted it as a temporary post before teaching in the North
He felt certain, without his usual ambivalence; the choice seemed fateful and right
He agonized for months before reluctantly agreeing
questions.explain: Despite opposition from Coretta and his father, he did not need to think it over; the choice felt fateful, an early case of following his inner intuitions.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: At Dexter, the key theme Martin Luther King Jr. began to develop in his sermons was the power of ____ to transform people.
questions.explain: He preached that love was a desperately underused power that black people would have to adopt toward their white oppressors to change things.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why did Martin Luther King Jr. turn down the presidency of the local NAACP chapter in Montgomery?
options: He disagreed with the NAACP's legal tactics
His first child had just been born, and his duties as father and minister were enough
His father forbade him to enter politics
He felt he was too young to lead older activists
questions.explain: He stayed active in local politics but felt his duty was to his church and family, and he reveled in the simple, satisfying life he was then leading.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put these events of the Montgomery bus protest in order.
items: Rosa Parks is arrested for refusing to give up her seat
Activists call a one-day boycott of the buses
The boycott stretches into weeks with substitute transport
The Montgomery Improvement Association is formed and King is made president
questions.explain: Parks's arrest was the catalyst for a one-day boycott that kept growing; when the local NAACP proved too small to handle it, leaders formed the MIA and nominated King.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each person in The Voice to their role in Martin Luther King Jr.'s story.
pairs: Refused to give up her bus seat and was arrested
Boycott organizer who first asked King to take a leading role
Birmingham activist who begged King to help desegregate stores
Birmingham police chief who relished the chance to use force
Team member who proposed enlisting local students
questions.explain: Each figure marks a turning point: Parks sparked Montgomery, Nixon's request King initially declined, Shuttlesworth brought him to Birmingham, where Connor's overreaction and Bevel's idea made the campaign succeed.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why did the founders of the Montgomery Improvement Association nominate Martin Luther King Jr. as its president?
options: Because of his wealth and connections in the North
Because of his long record as an NAACP officer
Because of his youth, his eloquence and his seemingly natural leadership skills
Because of his father's fame across the South
questions.explain: They chose him for youth, eloquence and leadership, half expecting him to refuse given his past hesitations.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: The founders of the Montgomery Improvement Association half expected Martin Luther King Jr. to refuse its presidency, but he accepted without his usual careful premeditation.
questions.explain: Feeling the energy in the room and their faith in him, King suddenly decided to accept, another moment of following intuition rather than overthinking.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In his speeches at Montgomery Improvement Association meetings, Martin Luther King Jr. developed his theme of ____ resistance, invoking the name of Gandhi.
questions.explain: He told crowds they would defeat the other side through peaceful protests and justified boycotts, the method he never abandoned.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these pressures did Martin Luther King Jr. face in his first weeks as leader of the Montgomery Improvement Association?
options: A whispering campaign of rumors, including that he was a communist
His father publicly disowning him
His congregation at Dexter turning against him
An arrest, ostensibly for speeding, and a night in a cell with hardened criminals
Phone calls almost every night threatening his life and family
questions.explain: The authorities spread rumors, threats came nightly, and he was arrested on a pretext; his father and congregation, by contrast, remained loving and supportive.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: On the night of the threatening phone call, what did Martin Luther King Jr. realize about himself as he sat in his kitchen?
questions.a: Shaking and losing his nerve, he realized he had never really known true adversity; his life had been easy and his parents had given him everything. Going deeper, he saw he had simply inherited religion from his father and had never personally communicated with God or felt His presence within. Panicking, he prayed with an urgency he had never felt before, confessing that he was weak and losing his courage.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What did the voice Martin Luther King Jr. heard in his kitchen tell him?
options: To make peace with his father before going any further
To stand up for righteousness, justice and truth, and that it would be with him until the end of the world
To leave Montgomery and return quietly to Ebenezer
To take his struggle to Birmingham and win there
questions.explain: The voice told him: “Stand up for justice. Stand up for truth.” It promised never to leave him, and he immediately felt relief.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: After hearing the voice in his kitchen, Martin Luther King Jr. felt a tremendous relief, as if the burden of his doubts and anxiety had been lifted.
questions.explain: He felt the burden lifted and could not help but cry; days later he stayed calm even when his house was bombed.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: When Martin Luther King Jr.'s house was bombed, how did he address the angry crowd outside?
options: He called on them to arm themselves in self-defense
He announced he would move his family back to Atlanta
He told them not to advocate violence but to love their enemies
He demanded that the city's police chief resign
questions.explain: Calm after the voice, he told the crowd, “We want to love our enemies,” and with Coretta's support he refused his father's plea to leave.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put these milestones in Martin Luther King Jr.'s public career in order.
items: Becomes pastor at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church
Is made president of the Montgomery Improvement Association
Founds the Southern Christian Leadership Conference
Leads the largely failed campaign in Albany, Georgia
Wins a settlement in Birmingham
Supports the sanitation workers' strike in Memphis
questions.explain: Dexter led to the MIA; after the bus victory he founded the SCLC; Albany's failure taught him lessons he applied in Birmingham; Memphis came at the very end of his life.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why did Martin Luther King Jr.'s campaign in Albany, Georgia, largely fail, and how did it affect him?
questions.a: The whites in power negotiated and agreed to compromises, then found loopholes and backtracked once protests stopped. In Albany the mayor and police chief made a show of exaggerated calmness, making King and the SCLC look like unreasonable outsiders stirring up trouble. The failure left King depressed and exhausted, yearning for the simpler days of his past and thinking of retiring from leadership.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Because protests against segregation there were met with violence and terrorism, Birmingham, Alabama, had come to be known as “____.”
questions.explain: Birmingham was among the most fiercely segregated cities, overseen by Bull Connor, which made it King's most dangerous campaign so far.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: When the voice returned to Martin Luther King Jr. before Birmingham, how did he come to understand its message more deeply?
questions.a: He saw that standing up for justice meant bringing it about in a real and practical way, not just talking or settling for useless compromises. His fears of disappointing people and failing had made him too cautious. This time he would have to be more strategic and courageous, raise the stakes, and win.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Birmingham, what did Martin Luther King Jr. say the campaign needed to do?
options: Negotiate quietly with local merchants away from the press
Avoid confrontation so that moderate whites would not be alienated
Provoke a national crisis that made Southern racism visible to whites watching television
Win a federal court ruling before any demonstrations began
questions.explain: Since racism was largely invisible to moderate whites, the aim was a bloody, visible crisis that would stir their consciences and pressure the Kennedy administration.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Whose cooperation was Martin Luther King Jr. counting on most for his Birmingham plan?
options: The downtown merchants, who wanted calm
The local NAACP chapter and its members
Bull Connor, whose overreaction would be key to the drama
President Kennedy, who had promised new laws
questions.explain: King expected Connor to overreact with force, producing the scenes that would shock the nation; Kennedy, by contrast, had proven very cautious.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these reasons explain why local black support for the Birmingham campaign was at first tepid?
options: Many thought Martin Luther King Jr. too young to lead
Many rejected nonviolence as weak and antiquated
Many resented Fred Shuttlesworth's autocratic style
Many reasonably feared the violence Bull Connor would unleash
questions.explain: Resentment of Shuttlesworth and fear of Connor kept crowds small; the Black Power criticism of nonviolence came later, after Birmingham.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: In Birmingham, Martin Luther King Jr. argued that no one under the age of twelve should be brought into the campaign.
questions.explain: King argued against bringing in anyone under fourteen, but James Bevel reminded him of the stakes and the need for numbers, and King relented.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put these stages of the Birmingham campaign in order.
items: Sit-ins and demonstrations begin, and King gets himself arrested
The national press starts to leave for lack of a story
Students fill the streets and then the jails
Fire hoses and attack dogs appear on national television
Frightened merchants push for a settlement
Kennedy addresses the nation and proposes new civil rights laws
questions.explain: Tepid support nearly sank the campaign until the students arrived; Connor's force drew the cameras, merchants pushed for a deal, and Kennedy was caught in the trap.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each outcome to its place in Martin Luther King Jr.'s story.
pairs: Formed because the local NAACP was too small for the boycott
Founded to take the movement beyond Montgomery
Followed Kennedy's televised address after Birmingham
Made possible by the Civil Rights Act
Won soon after Birmingham made King the movement's undisputed leader
questions.explain: The MIA and SCLC were organizations King led; the laws and the prize followed the Birmingham triumph, which pricked Kennedy's conscience.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these troubles did Martin Luther King Jr. face in the years after Birmingham?
options: Being booed by an audience at a Chicago Baptist church
Black Power activists criticizing nonviolence as weak and antiquated
Learning that the FBI had bugged his hotel rooms and leaked rumors
Losing the support of Coretta
The SCLC running out of money
questions.explain: Victory brought new burdens: surveillance, criticism from a new generation, and hostile crowds; money in fact poured into the SCLC, and Coretta is never shown abandoning him.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What did the Vietnam War and his tour of Watts lead Martin Luther King Jr. to conclude about America?
questions.a: He concluded that America had a cancer in its system: extreme inequalities of wealth and a willingness to spend vast sums on an absurd war, while black people in inner cities were left to rot and riot, largely invisible. In Watts, in the heart of an affluent city, he saw people living in poverty with no hope for the future. His depression mixed with growing anger, and he widened the struggle to poverty and the war.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: At a staff retreat Martin Luther King Jr. said that power without love is reckless, and love without power is ____.
questions.explain: King argued that power and love fulfill each other rather than being opposites; love without the power to change things is merely sentimental.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What new tactic did Martin Luther King Jr. say nonviolence must mature into in his later years?
options: Quiet lobbying of Congress and the White House
Armed self-defense in the inner cities
Mass civil disobedience that interrupts society's functioning at some key point
Boycotts aimed only at segregated stores
questions.explain: He never abandoned nonviolence as the means, but said there must be a force that interrupts society's functioning, aimed at altering America's values at the root.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these objections did critics raise to Martin Luther King Jr.'s April 1967 speech widening the struggle to include the Vietnam War?
options: It would alienate the public from the cause of civil rights
It was not part of his mandate to speak so broadly
It would anger the Johnson administration, whose support they needed
It would bankrupt the SCLC
It would cost him the Nobel Peace Prize
questions.explain: Even his most ardent supporters criticized the speech on these three grounds, and he had never felt so alone.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The day he died, Martin Luther King Jr. told an aide that fear should not stop them, saying that he would rather be dead than ____.
questions.explain: Revitalized by his mountaintop speech, he insisted that fear should not stop an upcoming march; that evening he was shot on his motel balcony.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these sides of Martin Luther King Jr.'s character does Robert Greene identify in his interpretation?
options: A sensitive, introspective side
A practical side that wanted to solve people's problems
A pleasure-loving side
A cynical side indifferent to people's suffering
A combative side that relished confrontation
questions.explain: Greene names the pleasure-loving, practical and introspective Kings, whose conflicts made him agonize over decisions; King was deeply sensitive to suffering and hated confrontation.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Robert Greene contrast Martin Luther King Jr. with his younger brother, A.D. King?
questions.a: A.D. lacked Martin's awareness of the danger of being overwhelmed by their father's dominating presence. He became a minister but could never assert his independence: his career was erratic, he developed an alcohol problem and a self-destructive streak, and he lived in his father's shadow. The contrast shows why Martin had to create distance and autonomy to find his own path.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Robert Greene, why would mindless rebellion against his father have failed Martin Luther King Jr.?
options: It would simply have shown how defined he was by his father, in reverse
It would have alienated the congregation he needed
It would have cost him his inheritance of Ebenezer
It would have made him as rigid as his father
questions.explain: Greene says real autonomy meant understanding the differences between them and using them as levers to create space, not defining himself as his father's opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these qualities does Robert Greene say Martin Luther King Jr. took from his father?
options: His high sense of principle
His discipline
His emotional style of preaching
His caring nature
His literal interpretation of the Bible
questions.explain: King took the best of his father, his discipline, principle and caring nature, while going his own way in faith and temperament.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Robert Greene interpret the voice Martin Luther King Jr. heard in his kitchen?
questions.a: Greene sees it as the inclinations and intuitions that had already guided King, at Dexter and the MIA, transformed at a moment of crisis into an actual voice, the voice of God, clarifying his destiny and offering continual support. With it his doubts, fears and debilitating inner conflicts fell away and he felt integrated on a whole new level. His moods returned over the years, but so did the voice, making his mission clear.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Robert Greene, why was Martin Luther King Jr.'s strategic pragmatism, such as using students in Birmingham, connected to his mission rather than at odds with it?
options: Because the voice had ordered him to win at any cost to his principles
Because he had abandoned his spiritual role for politics
Because a minister had a duty to obey the movement's majority
Because merely inspiring people was sentimental, and ignoring results only fed the ego
questions.explain: King hated mere inspiration as sentimental; not thinking about results meant seeking attention for appearing righteous. He wanted to palpably change conditions, which required leverage.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene says that in bringing the ugly reality of Southern life into white America's living rooms, Martin Luther King Jr.'s strategic objective was their ____.
questions.explain: The aim was to strike whites' consciences so that outrage would pressure those in power to change.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Robert Greene's account of Martin Luther King Jr.'s pragmatism, sort these between what King embraced and what he rejected.

items.t: Keeping up sit-ins and boycotts even while negotiating
Maximizing the attention of the press
Using students to fill the jails
Deep analysis of the other side after each campaign
Merely inspiring people with speeches
Seeking attention for appearing righteous
Settling for useless compromises

questions.explain: King treated the struggle as a game of leverage and studied each campaign, while seeing inspiration alone as sentimental and righteous posturing as ego.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene says Martin Luther King Jr.'s bouts of depression came partly from his deep sensitivity to the zeitgeist, sensing the mood of America before others did.
questions.explain: Greene links the depression to King's sensitivity to the war, the despair of the inner cities and the restless young, and to his sense of doom; the voice let him rise above it.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In what sense does Robert Greene say Martin Luther King Jr. came to serve as the voice for black America?
questions.a: Just as the voice had guided him, King took on a similar role for the movement. He strove to bring unity to the cause and keep it focused on practical results instead of debilitating infighting. He also had to keep the movement united against a growing desire for violence among younger black activists.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Martin Luther King Jr.'s story, sort these moments between those where he felt certain and guided from within and those where he hesitated or wanted to retreat.

items.t: Accepting the job at Dexter Avenue Baptist Church
Accepting the presidency of the MIA
Staying calm after his house was bombed
Deciding to go to Birmingham once the voice returned
Postponing his career decision through his Morehouse years
First declining E. D. Nixon's request to lead
Shaking in his kitchen after the death threat
Yearning for a simpler life after Albany

questions.explain: Greene shows King's intuitions and later the voice cutting through his habit of overthinking, while his many conflicting sides produced doubt and the urge to retreat.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each line from Martin Luther King Jr.'s story to when it was said.
pairs: Stand up for justice. Stand up for truth.
The voice he heard in his kitchen in Montgomery
We want to love our enemies.
To the crowd outside his bombed house
At a retreat with his staff
I’d rather be dead than afraid.
To an aide on the day he was killed
questions.explain: Each line marks a stage of his mission, from the voice's charge to his final acceptance in Memphis that fear should not stop them.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each place to its role in Martin Luther King Jr.'s education and career.
pairs: Where he found a socially committed, activist Christianity
Where he earned a PhD in systematic theology
questions.explain: Ebenezer was the path his father planned; Crozer and Boston formed his thinking; Dexter was his own choice, the start of his public career.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each city to what happened to Martin Luther King Jr. there.
pairs: Officials' exaggerated calmness made his campaign look unreasonable
Students, fire hoses and television forced a settlement
A housing settlement was attacked as too little, and he was booed
The poverty after the riots overwhelmed him
He supported striking sanitation workers and was killed
questions.explain: Albany was a failure, Birmingham his greatest triumph, Chicago and Watts marked his later despair, and Memphis was his last mission.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put Martin Luther King Jr.'s education and first post in order.
items: Morehouse College
Crozer Theological Seminary
Boston University
Dexter Avenue Baptist Church
questions.explain: He went to Morehouse at fifteen, then Crozer for a divinity degree, then Boston University for his PhD, before choosing Dexter over Ebenezer and the North.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the events of Martin Luther King Jr.'s night in the kitchen in order.
items: A caller threatens to kill him and bomb his house
Unable to sleep, he goes to the kitchen to make coffee
He realizes he has only inherited his father's religion
He prays, confessing that he is losing his courage
He hears a voice telling him to stand up for justice
He feels tremendous relief and cries
questions.explain: The threat brought his inner crisis to a peak; self-examination led to an urgent prayer, and the voice that answered lifted his burden.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What dilemma does Robert Greene say Martin Luther King Jr.'s story reveals that all of us face?
questions.a: We are all complex, presenting a consistent front while inside we have many moods and faces: practical, social, introspective, irrational. This inner chaos causes pain and leaves us without cohesion or direction, pulled by shifting emotions. We wander, never reaching our goals or our potential, and soothe the pain with addictions, new pleasures or passing causes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Robert Greene, what is the only solution to the dilemma of our inner chaos and aimlessness?
options: Following the plan our parents laid out for us
Joining a popular cause that interests us for a while
Pursuing new pleasures to soothe the pain
A higher sense of purpose, a mission that gives us our own direction
questions.explain: Greene calls it King's solution: a mission tied to our individuality, not the direction of parents, friends or peers; passing causes and pleasures only soothe the pain.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. said we have a responsibility to discover what we are made for, to discover our life’s ____.
questions.explain: Greene adopts King's term life's work for what we were intended to do, as dictated by our particular skills, gifts and inclinations: our calling.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Robert Greene say the inner voice of our life's work does?
options: Directs us toward activities and goals that mesh with our nature
Speaks so loudly that it needs no effort to hear
Warns us, through uneasiness, of entanglements and unsuited career paths
Seeks attention and quick gratification
Gives us a feeling of greater clarity and wholeness
questions.explain: The voice warns, directs and unifies us; it is not the ego's voice, which wants attention, and it is hard to hear over others' voices, needing introspection and practice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene says the inner voice that guides us to our life's work is the voice of the ego, which wants attention and quick gratification.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: the ego's voice divides us further from within, whereas the voice of purpose absorbs us in our work.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: An accountant feels a nagging uneasiness every time she considers a promotion into a sales role that does not suit her. In Robert Greene's terms, what is this uneasiness?
options: Low self-esteem from a lack of accomplishments
The inner voice warning her of a path unsuited to her character
Envy of colleagues who are better at selling
A fear of success she should push past
questions.explain: Greene says the voice warns us, through the uneasiness we feel, when we are about to follow career paths unsuited to our character.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The Voice ends with Nietzsche's line: He who has a ____ to live can bear with almost any how.
questions.explain: The quotation sums up the section: a sense of purpose, a why, lets us endure the hardships that King faced.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Robert Greene, what does it take to hear the inner voice of purpose, and what happens when we follow it?
questions.a: The voice is sometimes hard to hear because our heads are full of others' voices telling us what to do, so hearing it takes introspection, effort and practice. When we follow it, positive things tend to happen: we have the inner strength not to be swayed by people with their own agendas, and we become more strategic, focused and adaptive. Once we hear it there is no going back, and deviating from our course causes anxiety and pain.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What predicament does Robert Greene say people face today as soon as their schooling ends?
questions.a: We are suddenly thrown into a ruthless, fiercely competitive work world with little or no life experience, having to make choices that affect our whole future. In the past, career choices were limited and mentors, family members or religious leaders could offer direction. Today the world changes ever more quickly, everyone is preoccupied with their own needs, and our parents' advice may be totally antiquated.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene describes two ways people react to today's chaotic world. Sort these behaviors between them.

items.t: Experiment with many jobs and relationships
See commitment as a restriction on freedom
Regard obeying authority figures as old-fashioned
Quickly choose a practical, lucrative career
Settle on an intimate relationship
Continue to cling to parents

questions.explain: Some are dazzled by the opportunities and value freedom above all; others, frightened by the chaos, grab whatever stability they can.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, what problem eventually catches up with people who embrace the freedom of trying many jobs and adventures?
options: They are trapped in one job they chose too early
They become overly dependent on their parents
They never develop solid skills, so their career possibilities narrow
Their careers feel lifeless by their thirties
questions.explain: Flitting from thing to thing makes focus and learning hard, so they get trapped moving from job to job; a lifeless career is instead the fate of those who chose stability.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, what problem eventually catches up with people who quickly choose a practical, lucrative career for stability?
options: They lose their jobs as the world changes
They cannot tolerate the compromises a relationship needs
Their career begins to feel lifeless, just a job, because it has little connection to their interests
They never develop solid skills in any one area
questions.explain: Chosen for practical reasons in their twenties, the career feels lifeless in their thirties; their minds disengage, and midlife brings the temptation of new adventures.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each form of pain from aimlessness to its description in Keys to Human Nature.
pairs: We need ever newer and stronger diversions
A brittle ego too fragile for criticism, so skills stagnate
Having avoided difficulties, we are overwhelmed when they come
An emptiness from lacking meaning or connection to something larger
questions.explain: Greene says we are generally unaware that all four pains come from the same source, a lack of purpose and direction.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene says that, by the law of ____ returns, bored people need to keep finding new and stronger forms of diversion.
questions.explain: Each distraction satisfies less, so we chase new trends, exotic travel, gurus and addictions while the chronic boredom eats away at us.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene says we are generally well aware that the source of our boredom, insecurity and anxiety is a lack of purpose in our lives.
questions.explain: Greene says we are generally unaware of the source of our discomfort, the lack of purpose and direction, and we ascribe our depression to other factors.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, how does insecurity trap people who have drifted aimlessly?
options: They avoid all opinions so as not to be criticized
Learning requires admitting what we don't know, but they feel too insecure to admit it, so their skills stagnate
They copy successful people so closely that they lose themselves
They take on too many responsibilities and burn out
questions.explain: With no solid accomplishments, their ego becomes brittle; unable to take criticism or admit ignorance, they cover the insecurity with strong opinions or moral superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Robert Greene say our feeling of being lost and confused is not anyone's fault?
questions.a: It is a natural reaction to being born into times of great change and chaos. The old support systems, religions, universal causes and social cohesion, have mostly disappeared, at least in the West, along with the conventions, rules and taboos that once channeled behavior. We are all cast adrift, so it is no wonder many lose themselves in addictions and depression.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene writes that, unlike animals guided by instinct, we depend on consciousness, but the human mind is a bottomless ____.
questions.explain: Our imagination can take us in a hundred directions; without belief systems or conventions we have no obvious compass points, which can be maddening.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Robert Greene say inscribe each person's radical uniqueness?
options: The culture's ideas of what is cool
The one-of-a-kind configuration of our DNA
The particular way our brains are wired
Our experiences, unlike anyone else's
Our parents' expectations of us
questions.explain: Uniqueness comes from DNA, brain wiring and experience, a seed planted at birth; parents and culture are what later drown out its voice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What point does Robert Greene make by comparing human culture to an ecosystem?
options: Individuals should adapt to fit in with their surroundings
Only the strongest individuals survive the competition of culture
Diverse ecosystems thrive, so by cultivating our uniqueness we add to a culture's needed diversity
Cultures stay healthy by keeping individuals in fixed roles
questions.explain: Rich ecosystems depend on diversity, and the most creative cultures, such as ancient Athens and the Italian Renaissance, encouraged individual diversity, unlike sterile, conformist dictatorships.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene calls the subjects and activities we were naturally drawn to in early childhood our ____ inclinations.
questions.explain: These primal inclinations speak to us like a voice, but as we grow older they are drowned out by parents, peers, teachers and the culture.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does the example of Leonardo da Vinci show about following one's path in Keys to Human Nature?
options: Talent matters more than years of practice
Great achievers must narrow their focus to a single field
The path need not be one simple line; it can combine several mastered skills inventively
Genius depends on a guiding mentor in youth
questions.explain: Leonardo mastered art, science, architecture and engineering and combined them, a way of following the path that suits modern, eclectic tastes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene explains how a sense of purpose turns boredom into creative energy. Put the steps in order.
items: Embrace the tedium of practice
Become absorbed and focus deeply
Gain momentum and retain what we learn
Learn at a faster rate
Fresh ideas come, bringing creative energy
questions.explain: Because we are emotionally engaged, focus brings momentum and retention, faster learning fills the mind, and ideas start to come out of nowhere.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, when people with a sense of purpose have moments of doubt, what are those doubts usually about?
options: The quality of their work rather than their self-worth
Whether other people approve of them
Whether they deserve their accomplishments
Whether they chose the right calling at all
questions.explain: Focused on the work and its quality rather than on what people think, they can tell practical criticism from malicious criticism and bounce back from failure.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Robert Greene, how does a sense of purpose turn anxiety and stress into productive emotions?
questions.a: In pursuing a goal such as a book or a business, we learn not to think too much about how far we have to go and instead focus on smaller goals while keeping a degree of urgency. We learn to regulate anxiety, enough to keep us going and improving the work but not enough to paralyze us. We also develop a high tolerance for stress and even feed off it, since humans are built to handle stress.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each example in Keys to Human Nature to the point it illustrates.
pairs: Healthy cultures encourage diversity among individuals
A path can combine several mastered skills
Fighting for a cause multiplies force
Without stress and activity, the mind deteriorates
questions.explain: Each example supports Greene's case for purpose: uniqueness serves culture, paths can be eclectic, causes multiply force, and some stress keeps us healthy.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Robert Greene say people with a sense of purpose experience low moments?
options: As inevitable and even welcome, because they make us withdraw and reassess, as they did for King
As rare events that purpose eliminates entirely
As problems to be solved by new distractions
As signs that they have chosen the wrong calling
questions.explain: Greene says purpose makes us less prone to depression, but low moments still come and can serve us; more often we feel lifted above daily pettiness.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In military history, fighting for a cause is known as a force ____: the greater the connection to the cause, the higher the morale.
questions.explain: Greene then applies the idea to life: operating with a high sense of purpose is a force multiplier for all our decisions and actions.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Explain Robert Greene's comparison between armies and individuals with a sense of purpose.
questions.a: Armies that fight for a cause, like Napoleon's spreading the French Revolution, fight with greater intensity than those fighting for money, and can defeat larger, less motivated forces; this is called a force multiplier. Likewise, a high sense of purpose gives all our decisions and actions greater power, channeling the many sides of our character into one aim. Our focus and resilience give us momentum, and in a world of meandering people we spring past them and attract others.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Robert Greene say are true of an army fighting for a cause?
options: It can often defeat a larger but less motivated army
It depends on harsh discipline to hold together
Its battalion leaders are more creative
Its soldiers must be paid more to keep fighting
It fights with greater intensity
questions.explain: Soldiers tie their fate to the cause, the less enthusiastic are swept up in the group spirit, and the general can ask more of them; pay and harsh discipline are not the source of its strength.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene's example of an army fighting for a cause is the armies of Napoleon Bonaparte fighting to spread the French Revolution.
questions.explain: Greene uses Napoleon's armies to show how fighting for an idea, rather than for money as a job, raises intensity and unity.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these between an army that fights for a cause and one that fights largely for money, as Robert Greene contrasts them.

items.t: Soldiers tie their fate to the cause and the nation
More willing to die in battle
Less enthusiastic soldiers are swept up in the group spirit
Battalion leaders are more creative
Fights as part of a job
Can be beaten by a smaller but more motivated army

questions.explain: Connection to a cause raises morale and multiplies force, so a motivated army can defeat a larger one that fights only for pay.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each kind of person to how Robert Greene advises you to treat them.
pairs: Someone driven by a false purpose
Avoid hiring or working with them
Someone struggling to find their calling
Help them, or help each other
A young person with a high sense of purpose
Befriend them and catch their enthusiasm
An older person with many accomplishments
Associate with them in any way possible
questions.explain: People driven by false purposes drag you down with unproductive energy, while those with a high sense of purpose draw you upward.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Robert Greene call false purposes that lead to obsessive behavior and dead ends?
options: Attention
The pursuit of pleasure
Money
Mastering skills tied to our inclinations
Raising a family in the best way possible
questions.explain: Greene lists freedom to do as we please, pleasure, money, attention, power for its own sake and causes to join as false purposes; skills and raising a family can be real callings.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What is the twofold task Robert Greene gives you as a student of human nature in Keys to Human Nature?
questions.a: First, become aware of the primary role a sense of purpose plays in human life: observe what guides the people around you, recognize false purposes, and seek out those with a high sense of purpose. Second, find your own sense of purpose and deepen your connection to it. If you are young, give your restless energy a framework and above all accumulate skills; if you are older and have gone astray, gently channel your skills toward your inclinations.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Robert Greene advise someone older who has gone astray from their calling?
options: Quit at once and start over in the field they loved as a child
Explore freely without any framework until something clicks
Gently channel the skills they already have toward their inclinations, avoiding drastic career changes
Accept that it is too late and find meaning outside work
questions.explain: Greene warns against sudden, impractical career changes; existing skills can be channeled gradually to mesh with one's inclinations and spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene says some callings, such as becoming an entrepreneur, are superior to others, such as a craft or raising a family.
questions.explain: Greene insists that no calling is superior to another; what matters is that it is tied to a personal need and inclination and moves us toward continual improvement.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: A carpenter takes great pride in the excellence of his work and keeps improving his craft. By Robert Greene's account, does this count as a calling?
options: Only if he eventually starts his own business
No, because a calling requires an influential public role
Yes, if it is tied to his personal inclinations and keeps him learning and improving
No, because a calling must change the wider culture directly
questions.explain: Greene says a path can involve physical labor and craft, leaving one's stamp on the quality; you need not be an entrepreneur or figure on the world's stage.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Robert Greene concludes that, by cultivating your uniqueness, in a world of people who seem largely interchangeable you cannot be ____.
questions.explain: Your combination of skills and experience is not replicable, which Greene calls true freedom and the ultimate power humans can possess.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Robert Greene says the signs of our uniqueness are usually clearest in early childhood and are later drowned out by parents, peers, teachers and the culture.
questions.explain: As children we are drawn to particular subjects despite our parents' influence; later we are told what to like and lose a sense of what makes us different.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these between the pains of aimlessness and the benefits of a sense of purpose described in Keys to Human Nature.

items.t: Chronic boredom needing ever stronger diversions
A brittle ego too fragile for criticism
Low-grade, continual anxiety
An emptiness blamed on other factors
Embracing the tedium of practice
Inner resiliency after failure
The ability to regulate anxiety
Moments of great fulfillment

questions.explain: Greene argues that the guidance system of purpose neutralizes each pain of aimlessness and turns it into a positive emotion.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, sort these later problems between the two reactions to the modern world.

items.t: Never developing solid skills in one area
Finding it hard to focus for long
Bristling at the restrictions of a lasting relationship
A career that feels lifeless in their thirties
Minds disengaging from work that is just a job
Being tempted by new adventures at midlife

questions.explain: The freedom-seekers end up skill-less and restless; the stability-seekers end up disengaged and tempted at midlife. Both suffer from a lack of real purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Robert Greene say is the purpose of our individual uniqueness, and why is it hard to connect to?
questions.a: Our uniqueness, stamped on us by nature, has a purpose: by bringing it to flower through our particular skills and work, we contribute to the diversity a healthy culture needs, and it gives us an internal guidance system through life. It is hard to connect to because its signs, our primal inclinations, are clearest in childhood and are later drowned out by parents, peers, teachers and the culture. We must strengthen that connection and learn to trust the voice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the steps of Robert Greene's argument in Keys to Human Nature in order.
items: The modern world throws us out on our own
We react by embracing freedom or seeking stability
Both paths lead to boredom, insecurity, anxiety and depression
Our uniqueness offers an internal guidance system
Purpose turns these pains into positive emotions
Your twofold task: read others' purposes, then find your own
questions.explain: Greene diagnoses the modern predicament and its pains, offers individual purpose as the way out, shows its benefits, and ends with the reader's task.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Robert Greene say diversity among individuals matters, and how does cultivating our uniqueness contribute to it?
questions.a: Greene compares human culture to a thriving ecosystem: healthy ecosystems have high diversity, and the healthiest, most celebrated cultures, such as ancient Athens and the Italian Renaissance, encouraged the greatest diversity among individuals. By bringing our uniqueness to flower through our particular skills and work, we contribute our share to that needed diversity. He contrasts this with the conformity and cultural sterility of dictatorships.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, sort this advice between people who are young and people who are older and have gone astray.
groups: Advice for the older who have gone astray

items.t: Explore the world freely and accumulate adventures
Give your restless energy an overall framework
Above all, accumulate skills
Gently channel the skills you already have toward your inclinations
Avoid sudden, drastic and impractical career changes
Look for a path that eventually meshes with your inclinations and spirit

questions.explain: For the young, Greene says to explore but within a framework and to build skills. For the older who have strayed, he advises gentle channeling of existing skills rather than abrupt change.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Chapter 13 is titled Advance with a Sense of Purpose. What does its law, the Law of Aimlessness, name?
options: The human tendency to drift, pulled by moods and others' opinions, without direction
The tendency to chase pleasures that lead us downward
The tendency to conform to the group's goals
The tendency to overestimate our own powers
questions.explain: The title gives the remedy, the law names the problem: drifting without direction. Conformity and grandiosity are the subjects of other chapters.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Robert Greene open Chapter 13 with the story of Martin Luther King Jr.?
options: King showed that a strong father is the key to finding one's purpose
King showed that great leaders never doubt themselves
King was a complex man whose conflicting sides were unified by a voice of purpose, the dilemma all of us face
King proved that purpose comes from joining a popular cause
questions.explain: Greene says King's dilemma is everyone's dilemma; his many sides, doubts and moods were integrated by the voice, which models the solution the Keys section explains.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does the Keys to Human Nature section prepare for the rest of Chapter 13?
questions.a: Keys diagnoses the modern predicament and argues that our uniqueness gives us an internal guidance system, but it repeatedly points ahead. For how to connect to our uniqueness, it refers to Discover your calling in life, the first of the next section's strategies for developing a high sense of purpose. For pursuits like pleasure, money, attention and power, it names them false purposes and refers to the chapter's last section, The Lure of False Purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 13 in order.
items: The Voice
Keys to Human Nature
Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
The Lure of False Purposes
questions.explain: The chapter moves from King's story to the general law, then to practical strategies, and ends with the false purposes to avoid.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each theme in the first half of Chapter 13 to the chapter of the book it echoes.
pairs: The envy and infighting King faced after each victory
King sensing the mood of America before others did
With purpose, even death can lose its sting
Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality
Others' voices drowning out our primal inclinations
Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.explain: Greene's laws interlock: envy, the spirit of the times, mortality and the pull of the group all bear on whether we can follow our purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Keys to Human Nature warns that parents, peers, teachers and the culture drown out the voice of our primal inclinations. Which following chapter takes up this pressure from others most directly?
options: Chapter 11, Know Your Limits
Chapter 5, Become an Elusive Object of Desire
Chapter 6, Elevate Your Perspective
Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.explain: Chapter 14, the Law of Conformity, deals with the group's downward pull, the same social pressure that makes it hard to hear our own voice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The law that Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose, addresses is the Law of ____.
questions.explain: The chapter's remedy, a sense of purpose, answers the problem the law names: drifting through life without direction.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Greene say the five strategies for developing a high sense of purpose should be approached?
options: In any order at all, since none matters more than another
Starting with losing yourself in the work, which makes the others possible
In a strict sequence, each mastered fully before moving to the next
In a loose order, with discovering your calling as the essential starting point
questions.explain: Greene says the strategies are in a loose order, the first being the essential starting point, and that you should put them all into practice. They are neither a rigid sequence nor interchangeable.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Greene's account of Marie Curie's primal inclination, what mesmerized her at the age of four?
options: A schoolbook full of diagrams of the elements and their properties
A telescope her mother kept by the window of the family home
A visit with her class to a university laboratory in Warsaw
Tubes and measuring devices behind a glass case in her father's office
questions.explain: Curie recalled entering her father's office and being mesmerized by chemistry equipment behind a polished glass case, and she felt the same thrill in laboratories all her life.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
