questions.q: What point does Greene use Ingrid Bergman's remark that she did not choose acting, it chose her, to make about early fascinations?
options: That acting is a calling unlike any other profession
That talent must be spotted and encouraged early by parents
That a calling is usually chosen deliberately after long reflection
That such moments are signs of something beyond our personal control
questions.explain: Greene says these moments of visceral attraction come suddenly, without prodding from parents or friends, and are signs of something beyond our personal control. Bergman's remark, he says, expresses this best.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In Greene's account, what finally opened the aimless young Akira Kurosawa's eyes to his calling?
options: Watching the director Kajiro Yamamoto at work in 1936
Seeing a foreign film that his father took him to
Quitting film work to return to painting full time
Winning a prize for one of his early paintings
questions.explain: Kurosawa had tried painting and hated being an assistant director, but when assigned to Kajiro Yamamoto he saw the magical possibilities of film. Greene uses him to show a calling can be revealed by observing a master.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Greene bring up Howard Gardner's book Frames of Mind in the strategy of discovering your calling?
options: To show that most callings combine all forms of intelligence equally
To argue that social intelligence matters more than any other kind
To prove that intelligence is mostly fixed by the age of four
To help you identify the particular form of intelligence your brain is wired for
questions.explain: Greene cites Gardner's forms of intelligence so you can find the one you have a particular gift for; the activity that feels right will correspond to it. Social intelligence is Greene's own addition to the list, not the point of citing Gardner.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Greene, what should an older person with more experience do when working on their calling?
options: Explore a wide field of activities until something finally fits
Accept that it is too late and focus instead on helping the young
Take the skills already developed and adapt them toward the true calling
Abandon the old career entirely and start again from nothing
questions.explain: Greene says the young should explore a relatively wide field related to their inclinations, while the older person should adapt existing skills more in the direction of the true calling.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene says a calling could combine several fields that fascinate you. What was the combination for Steve Jobs?
options: Business and spirituality
Engineering and music
Technology and design
Electronics and marketing
questions.explain: Greene writes that for Jobs the calling was the intersection of technology and design, an example of a calling that fuses several fascinations.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In the strategy of using resistance and negative spurs, how does Greene interpret frustration during practice?
options: As a sign you need more rest and fewer deadlines
As a sign of progress, as the mind sees higher skill levels yet to reach
As a warning that you have chosen the wrong calling
As proof that others' envious criticisms have got to you
questions.explain: Greene says frustration is a sign you are making progress, because your mind is becoming aware of levels of skill you have yet to attain. It is something to embrace, not a reason to change course.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, did Thomas Edison talk up the future greatness of his inventions to journalists?
options: To put himself in a position where he had to deliver soon or be ridiculed
To gain the fame he felt he had been denied as a young man
To discourage rival inventors from working on the same ideas
To attract investors who would pay for his laboratory
questions.explain: Edison knew he could take far too long, so the publicity acted as a manufactured deadline. He then had to rise to the occasion, and Greene says he almost always did.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How did the Zen master Hakuin, in Greene's account, push himself past his lack of progress with koans?
options: He promised his fellow monks he would teach them within a year
He vowed to kill himself if he failed to master a koan in seven days
He asked his master for easier koans to rebuild his confidence
He left his master and studied alone in the mountains
questions.explain: Hakuin made a deadly serious seven-day vow, an extreme deadline that Greene says kept working for him until he attained total enlightenment.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Greene say you can recognize criticism that comes from envy rather than a constructive impulse?
options: It is personal and vehement, targets your ability, and lacks specifics on what to improve
It comes from people who have more experience than you
It focuses closely on one technical flaw in your work
It is delivered calmly and only in private
questions.explain: Greene says envious critics go a little too far, make it personal, stress your personality more than the work, and lack specific details about how to improve. Precise, work-focused criticism is the constructive kind.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In the strategy of absorbing purposeful energy, who was the mentor who gave the young Coco Chanel confidence and taught her about business?
options: A charismatic painter who shared her love of the arts
A famous Parisian couturier who took her on as an apprentice
An aristocratic patroness who introduced her to society
A wealthy older English businessman named Arthur Capel
questions.explain: Chanel met Arthur Capel at twenty-five, drawn to his ambition, experience and ruthless practicality. He instilled confidence, taught her business and gave tough criticism she accepted out of respect.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: When looking for people to absorb purposeful energy from, what kind does Greene tell you to seek?
options: Online mentors who can be reached at any time
Visionaries whose big ideas will inspire you to dream
Pragmatic people, not merely charismatic ones or visionaries
People in your own field who are at your exact level
questions.explain: Greene wants their practical advice and their spirit of getting things done, so pragmatic people matter more than charisma or vision. He also warns not to settle for virtual mentors.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What problem is Greene's ladder of descending goals mainly designed to solve?
options: The lack of mentors willing to set goals for you
The boredom of having goals that are too easy
The envy of rivals who see your ambitions
The anxiety generated by ambitious long-term goals
questions.explain: Long-term goals bring clarity but also anxiety when you see all there is to do from where you stand. Smaller goals reaching down to the present give a sense of progress and manage that anxiety.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which psychologist does Greene credit with the term peak experiences for moments of flow beyond the ego?
options: Viktor Frankl
Abraham Maslow
Howard Gardner
Carl Jung
questions.explain: Greene says Abraham Maslow called these moments peak experiences, and that once you have them you are forever changed. Gardner appears earlier in the strategies for his forms of intelligence.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Greene, which two elements of human nature create the gravitational pull toward finding a purpose?
options: Our envy of others and our wish for status
Our love of pleasure and our fear of pain
Our need to belong to a group and our dread of being alone
Our lack of guiding instincts and our awareness of our puniness and mortality
questions.explain: Greene says we cannot rely on instincts as animals do, so we need direction, and we feel our smallness and mortality, so we need to connect to something that transcends us.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What is the first way Greene contrasts a real purpose with a false one?
options: A real purpose is shared by many; a false one is private
A real purpose comes from within; a false one comes from external sources
A real purpose is religious; a false one is secular
A real purpose brings money; a false one brings only fame
questions.explain: Greene says the real purpose is our own, a calling nobody imposed or can take away, while false purposes are belief systems swallowed whole and conformity to what others do.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What dynamic does Greene say the pursuit of pleasure tends to lead to, whatever its objects?
options: Diminishing returns, as pleasures grow duller with repetition
A balanced life once enough pleasure has been collected
Steady growth in skill and self-knowledge
Envy of those who have fewer pleasures
questions.explain: Greene says the moments of pleasure dull with repetition, so we need more of the same or new diversions, and the need often becomes an addiction that diminishes health and mental powers.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Greene's contrast between racing through many books and absorbing one excellent book illustrate?
options: That deeper pleasure requires learning to limit ourselves
That entertainment should be avoided entirely by purposeful people
That variety is the secret of lasting satisfaction
That reading is the only pleasure that never leads to addiction
questions.explain: Reading many books in rapid succession overstimulates and dulls satisfaction, while one book absorbed deeply is relaxing and uplifting. Greene does not reject pleasure outside work, only overstimulation in place of depth.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Greene, how can you recognize a microcause or cult?
options: By its detailed, practical plan for reaching its goals
By its long history stretching back generations
By the vagueness of what its disciples want
By the size and wealth of its membership
questions.explain: Greene says adherents cannot describe the world they desire in concrete, practical terms and have no strategy for reaching their nebulous goals, a sign the group is merely about releasing emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What historical episode does Greene cite to show how short-term thinking in the pursuit of money leads to big mistakes?
options: The derivatives frenzy leading up to the crash of 2008
The stock market crash of 1929
The dot-com bubble of the late 1990s
The tulip mania in seventeenth-century Holland
questions.explain: Greene points to those who went all in on derivatives before the 2008 crash as an example of the obsessive, short-term thinking of people driven by money and success.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Greene mean by the effects of hyperintention?
options: That ambitious people intend too many things at once
That setting very high goals guarantees eventual success
That desperately wanting something makes it less likely to happen
That intentions matter more than results in judging people
questions.explain: Desperately needing sleep keeps us awake and desperately needing a great talk makes it worse. Greene applies this to money and success: the dogged pursuit tends to backfire.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Greene, what has changed about the false purpose of pursuing attention?
options: Social media has democratized it, so almost anyone can seek huge attention
It is now limited to kings, conquerors and celebrities
It has become harmless because attention is now so easy to get
It has largely disappeared as people turn toward privacy
questions.explain: Greene says this false purpose has become greatly democratized through social media, so almost anyone can have attention past kings could only dream of, at the cost of an exhausting, alienating quest.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Greene call cynicism, the feeling that life has no purpose or meaning?
options: The pleasure principle
The crowd as purpose
The void as purpose
The absurd as purpose
questions.explain: Drawing on Nietzsche's line that man would rather have the void as purpose than be void of purpose, Greene calls cynicism having the void as purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: According to Greene, what lies behind the cool, sardonic air of the cynic?
options: A great fear of trying and failing, of standing out and being ridiculed
A secret hunger for money that has been frustrated
A deep and well-founded knowledge of how the world works
A mature acceptance that has replaced childish hopes
questions.explain: Greene calls it an adolescent pose of not caring that disguises fear of failure and ridicule, stems from laziness, and consoles believers for their lack of accomplishments.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How do the two closing sections of 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose' relate to each other?
options: The first lists false purposes; the second shows how to escape them
The first gives strategies to build a real purpose; the second exposes cheap substitutes to eliminate
The first is about work; the second is about personal relationships
Both retell the story of Martin Luther King Jr. from different angles
questions.explain: The strategies section shows how to develop a high sense of purpose, then the last section warns against false purposes that supply only the illusion of purpose. Greene says eliminating the lower forms lets us gravitate toward the higher.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose', what is the relationship between the Keys to Human Nature and the final section on false purposes?
options: The Keys never mention false purposes at all
The Keys briefly name false purposes and point ahead to the final section for more
The final section is a summary repeating the Keys word for word
The final section contradicts the Keys and revises its claims
questions.explain: When assessing others, the Keys name pleasure, money, attention, power and causes as false purposes and refer the reader to the last section of the chapter, which then examines them in detail.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The Coco Chanel example in the strategy of absorbing purposeful energy refers back to which earlier chapter?
options: Chapter 10, Beware the Fragile Ego
Chapter 5, Become an Elusive Object of Desire
Chapter 15, Make Them Want to Follow You
Chapter 3, See Through People's Masks
questions.explain: Greene adds a cross-reference to chapter 5, where Chanel's story is told, linking her mastery of desire to the sense of purpose she absorbed from mentors.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What obstacles does Greene say you will face once you commit to developing a sense of purpose?
questions.a: Greene lists the distracting voices of others who instill doubts about your calling and uniqueness, your own boredom and frustration with the work and your slow progress, and the lack of trustworthy criticism. He adds the anxiety you must manage and the burnout that often comes with focused labor over long periods. The five strategies are designed to move you past these obstacles.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What signs of primal inclinations does Greene tell you to look for in your earliest years?
questions.a: You look for moments when you were unusually fascinated by a subject, certain objects, or particular activities and forms of play, such as Curie with laboratory equipment or Chekhov at his first play. These moments of visceral attraction came suddenly and without prodding from parents or friends, and are hard to put into words. Greene treats them as signs of something beyond personal control.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Besides childhood fascinations, what other sign of your calling does Greene describe, involving how certain activities feel?
questions.a: Greene says to examine moments when certain tasks felt natural and easy, like swimming with a current. In such activities you tolerate the tedium of practice better, are not easily discouraged by criticism, and want to learn. You can contrast these with tasks that feel deeply boring, unfulfilling and frustrating.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Greene describe discovering your calling as a process of subtracting external influences, and what does it give you?
questions.a: Later in life we often lose contact with our own preferences, influenced by what others are doing and by the culture. Discovering your calling reacquaints you with your natural likes and dislikes, what predates the opinions of others. The deeper this connection, the more you can resist the bad ideas of others and engage your internal guidance system.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Greene call experimenting with your calling perhaps the most important step in life in general?
questions.a: He says it is the single most essential step in developing a high sense of purpose, and that it rarely comes in a lightning-bolt moment but requires continual introspection and effort. Knowing deeply who you are and what makes you unique makes it much easier to avoid all the other pitfalls of human nature.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In the strategy of using resistance and negative spurs, why does Greene urge you to move toward pain and adversity rather than away from it?
questions.a: Success requires developing skills in various areas, a tedious and painful process that exposes your limitations, and most people try to avoid criticism and failure. Greene says to embrace negative experiences, limitations and pain as the perfect means of building skill and sharpening purpose. As with exercise, manageable pain and discomfort later yield strength and stamina.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Greene say deadlines intensify a sense of purpose?
questions.a: He says if you give yourself a year for a project you will generally take a year or more, while three months makes you finish sooner. The concentrated energy of a tight deadline raises your skill level and improves the result. If necessary you should manufacture reasonably tight deadlines, as Edison did by overselling his inventions to journalists.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: How does Greene advise you to deal with criticism that comes from envy as you progress on your path?
questions.a: First recognize it by its emotional tone: it goes too far, is too vehement, is personal and attacks your overall ability, and lacks specific details on how to improve. Then do not internalize it in any form; becoming defensive is a sign it has got to you. Instead use these negative opinions to motivate you and add to your sense of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Describe how Greene's ladder of descending goals works.
questions.a: You set ambitious long-term goals for clarity and resolve, then create smaller goals reaching down to the present, each simpler and quicker to realize, down to daily or weekly microgoals. These give satisfaction and focus, while you keep returning to the larger vision to stay inspired. The process includes flexibility: you periodically reassess and adjust the goals, aiming for practical results rather than unrealized dreams.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What three things does Greene say you can do to set the stage for peak experiences in your work?
questions.a: First, wait until you are further along, at least halfway through a project or several years into your field, so your mind is full of information and practice. Second, give yourself as much uninterrupted time as possible, rigorously eliminating distractions, like a religious retreat. Third, keep the emphasis on the work, never on yourself or the desire for recognition, since ego and self-doubt interrupt the flow.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Greene say humans feel a gravitational pull toward finding a purpose?
questions.a: First, unable to rely on instincts as other animals do, we need some sense of direction to guide and restrict our behavior. Second, we are aware of our puniness among billions of others and of our mortality, so we need to feel larger than ourselves and connected to something that transcends us. Many people satisfy this pull on the cheap, with false purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Explain the two ways Greene contrasts real purposes with false purposes.
questions.a: A real purpose comes from within: a calling we feel personally connected to, which nobody imposed and nobody can take away, while false purposes come from external belief systems swallowed whole and from conformity. A real purpose also leads upward to a more human level, improving skills and contributing to society, while false purposes lead downward to the animal side: addictions, loss of mental powers, mindless conformity and cynicism.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does Greene consider the pursuit of pleasure a false purpose?
questions.a: Pleasures of every kind tend toward diminishing returns: they grow duller through repetition, so we need more of the same or new diversions, and the need often becomes an addiction that saps health and mental powers. It goes against the principle that deeper pleasure requires limiting ourselves. People with a sense of purpose still relax outside work but choose depth of experience over overstimulation.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What does Greene say happens to people in the large public gatherings that causes and cults depend on?
questions.a: People in a crowd are highly suggestible: through short, simple, repeated phrases they can be made to chant slogans and swallow absurd ideas. They feel relieved of personal responsibility, which can lead to violence. They feel transported and less puny, but this is an illusion; they are actually made smaller by losing their will and individual voice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Under what conditions does Greene say allying with a cause can be part of a real sense of purpose?
questions.a: It must emerge from an internal process of deep thinking, with the cause committed to as part of your life's work, as it was for Martin Luther King Jr. You act as an active contributor bringing your uniqueness into play, not a cog mimicking the company line. And you join out of a hunger for justice and truth, not to gratify the ego or vent ugly emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Give the reasons Greene offers for why making money and success your purpose often yields impractical results.
questions.a: Such people enter fields that pay most and fastest, unconnected to their inclinations and crowded with fierce competition; they grow restless and bored and make short-term mistakes. They never cultivate their uniqueness, so someone younger and hungrier supplants them. And when the aim is simply to have more than others, there is never enough, so the quest is endless and exhausting, alienating and soulless.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What is hyperintention, and how does Greene apply it to the pursuit of money and success?
questions.a: Hyperintention is the effect where desperately wanting something makes it less likely: needing to sleep keeps us awake, needing a perfect talk makes us anxious, needing friends pushes people away. The most pleasurable things come without being directly intended. Likewise the dogged pursuit of money backfires, while people like Steve Jobs who focus on high-purpose work find success flows to them naturally.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: What attitude does Greene propose as the opposite of cynicism?
questions.a: He says reality is not brutal and ugly but contains much that is sublime, beautiful and worthy of wonder, seen in the great works of other achievers and in the human brain itself. We should seek more encounters with the Sublime, realize our own potential, and see a purpose behind everything we experience. In the end we want to fuse a child's curiosity and excitement toward the world with adult intelligence.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Why does it make sense that 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose' ends with a section on false purposes after its five strategies?
questions.a: Greene argues that our search for meaning is unavoidable and that everyone falls for false purposes at some point because they are easy, popular and cheap. Having shown how to build a real purpose, he names the cheap substitutes so readers can recognize and eliminate them. If the impulse toward these lower forms is removed, he says, we naturally gravitate toward the higher.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene's first strategy begins by looking for signs of ____ in your earliest years, when they were often the clearest.
questions.explain: Greene's term for these early, unprompted fascinations is primal inclinations, which point toward a person's calling.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene cites the psychologist Howard Gardner's book ____, which lists forms of intelligence for which people usually have one particular gift.
questions.explain: Gardner's Frames of Mind lists forms such as mathematics and logic, physical activity, words, images and music.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: To Gardner's forms of intelligence, Greene adds ____ intelligence, a superior sensitivity to people.
questions.explain: Greene says we could also add social intelligence, a superior sensitivity to people, to Gardner's list.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene says that the deeper your connection to your calling, the more you can resist the bad ideas of others and engage your internal ____ system.
questions.explain: Connecting to your calling engages the internal guidance system that the chapter presents as the remedy for aimlessness.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: The Zen master Hakuin was frustrated by the ____, paradoxical anecdotes designed to spark enlightenment, that his master presented to him.
questions.explain: Greene defines koans as paradoxical anecdotes designed to spark enlightenment; Hakuin's seven-day vow was about mastering them.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In the ladder of descending goals, Greene says that each day or week you must have ____.
questions.explain: Breaking tasks into microgoals helps you focus and avoid detours that waste energy, while you keep the larger goal in mind.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Abraham Maslow called the moments of flow in which the mind is transported beyond the ego ____.
questions.explain: Greene says these peak experiences change you forever and make the more immediate pleasures of the world pale in comparison.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene's second strategy for developing a sense of purpose is to use resistance and negative ____.
questions.explain: The strategy treats tedium, pain, deadlines and even envious criticism as spurs that sharpen your skill and sense of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: In the strategy of absorbing purposeful energy, Greene warns: do not settle for ____ associations or mentors, since they will not have the same effect.
questions.explain: Greene wants real, in-person associations with people of high purpose, because virtual ones will not have the same effect.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene says false purposes lead downward, to the ____ side of our nature: addictions, loss of mental powers, mindless conformity and cynicism.
questions.explain: Real purposes lead upward to a more human level, while false purposes lead downward to the animal side of our nature.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Whatever the objects pursued, Greene says the pursuit of pleasure tends to lead to a dynamic of diminishing ____.
questions.explain: Pleasures grow duller with repetition, so we need more of them or new ones, often ending in addiction.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: During their brief existence, adherents of microcauses and cults substitute extreme conviction and ____ for a clear vision of what they are after.
questions.explain: Greene says such groups replace a clear, practical vision with extreme conviction and hyperbelief, and quickly find enemies to blame.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene says people in a crowd are highly ____ and can be made to chant back slogans and swallow absurd ideas.
questions.explain: Through short, simple, repeated phrases, crowds can be led to accept irrational ideas, which wily rulers have exploited.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene's term for the effect in which desperately needing to fall asleep makes us less likely to fall asleep is ____.
questions.explain: Hyperintention explains why the dogged pursuit of money, success or happy moments tends to disappoint.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Greene calls cynicism, the feeling that there is no purpose or meaning in life, having the ____ as purpose.
questions.explain: The phrase comes from Nietzsche's remark that man would rather have the void as purpose than be void of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: As an answer to cynicism, Greene says we want to have more encounters with the ____.
questions.explain: Greene insists reality contains much that is sublime, beautiful and worthy of wonder, seen in the great works of other achievers.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose' presents the Law of ____.
questions.explain: The table of contents names chapter 13's law the Law of Aimlessness, the condition that a high sense of purpose overcomes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these are among the obstacles Greene says you will face when developing a sense of purpose?
options: A shortage of opportunities in the modern world
Burnout from long periods of focused labor
Too much praise from mentors
A lack of trustworthy criticism
Boredom and frustration with slow progress
questions.explain: Greene lists distracting voices, boredom and frustration, lack of trustworthy criticism, anxiety and burnout. He does not name a lack of opportunities or excessive praise.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these people does Greene describe as having a moment of fascination with their calling as a child?
options: Akira Kurosawa
Jean-Paul Sartre
Martin Luther King Jr.
Tiger Woods
Anton Chekhov
questions.explain: Chekhov at his first play, Woods watching his father hit golf balls, and Sartre with printed words were childhood moments. Kurosawa found his calling as a young man watching a master, and King when older, during the Montgomery bus boycott.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these forms of intelligence does Greene list from Howard Gardner's Frames of Mind?
options: Mathematics and logic
Moral intelligence
Financial intelligence
Words
Music
questions.explain: Greene names mathematics and logic, physical activity, words, images and music. Financial and moral intelligence are not on the list.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as signs that a criticism comes from envy?
options: It offers concrete suggestions for improving the work
It emphasizes your personality more than the work
It lacks specific details on what and how to improve
It is expressed with a bit too much vehemence
questions.explain: Envious critics go too far, make it personal and lack specifics. Concrete, work-focused suggestions mark constructive criticism worth heeding.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these skills does Greene say Coco Chanel later sought from other people she learned from?
options: Sewing technique
Marketing
Social graciousness
Legal knowledge
A nose for cultural trends
questions.explain: Later in life Chanel kept returning to the strategy, finding people with skills she lacked such as social graciousness, marketing and a nose for cultural trends.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these are among Greene's conditions for setting the stage for peak experiences?
options: Keeping the emphasis on the work rather than on yourself
Thinking about the recognition the work will bring
Giving yourself long stretches of uninterrupted time
Waiting until you are well along in a project or field
Starting at the very beginning of a project while enthusiasm is highest
questions.explain: Greene says to wait until your mind is full of practice, to clear uninterrupted time, and to focus on the work, never on yourself or recognition, which interrupt the flow.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these are among the five common false purposes Greene describes?
options: Cynicism
Absorbing purposeful energy from mentors
The pursuit of pleasure
Causes and cults
Mastery of a craft
questions.explain: The five false purposes are pleasure, causes and cults, money and success, attention, and cynicism. Mastery and absorbing energy from mentors belong to the real path of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as marks of a microcause or cult?
options: Definitions built mostly on getting rid of certain people or practices
Enemies blamed for all that is wrong in the world
A clear strategy for reaching its goals
Vagueness about the society its members want
A concrete, practical vision of the future
questions.explain: Greene says such groups are vague, define themselves negatively, and quickly find enemies to blame. Their lack of strategy and practical vision shows they are mainly about releasing emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these are reasons Greene gives for why making money and success your purpose tends to fail in the long run?
options: You never truly cultivate your uniqueness
There are always people with more, so there is never enough
The fields chosen are crowded with fierce competition
Wealth always arrives too late in life to be enjoyed
Money cannot be earned without first finding a calling
questions.explain: Greene cites crowded fields, failure to cultivate uniqueness so younger rivals supplant you, and the endless comparison with those who have more. He does not claim money is impossible without a calling.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these beliefs does Greene list as part of cynicism, having the void as purpose?
options: Everything is relative
Reality contains much that is sublime and beautiful
Life is absurd, meaningless and random
We should fuse childhood curiosity with adult intelligence
All politicians are corrupt, so getting involved is not worth it
questions.explain: Absurdity, relativism and blanket political distrust are among the cynic's beliefs. The sublime and childlike curiosity belong to Greene's purposeful alternative.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Which of these examples does Greene use to illustrate hyperintention?
options: Needing to give the best possible talk and performing worse
Practicing a skill daily and slowly improving
Desperately needing a partner or friends and pushing them away
Desperately needing to sleep and staying awake
questions.explain: All three examples show desperate wanting making the result less likely. Steady practice leading to improvement is not an example of hyperintention.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if you give yourself a year to finish a project, you will generally take a year or more.
questions.explain: Greene uses this to argue for tight deadlines: three months would make you finish sooner and work with more concentrated energy.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says peak experiences can be manufactured on demand once you master the right technique.
questions.explain: Greene says these experiences cannot be manufactured, but you can set the stage for them and vastly increase your odds.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: In the strategy of absorbing purposeful energy, Greene says the best people to learn from are charismatic visionaries above all.
questions.explain: Greene says to find people who are pragmatic and not merely charismatic or visionaries, so you can absorb their spirit of getting things done.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Steve Jobs would close his office door, stay holed up all day, and wait until he fell into a state of deep focus.
questions.explain: Greene gives Jobs as an example of clearing uninterrupted time so that deep absorption in the work can occur.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Martin Luther King Jr. realized his mission in early childhood while watching his father preach.
questions.explain: Greene gives King as an example of the moment coming when older: he realized his mission as he got pulled into the Montgomery bus boycott.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says microcauses and cults tend not to last very long and within ten years already seem passé.
questions.explain: Greene notes the short life of such groups, during which adherents substitute hyperbelief for a clear vision.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that in a crowd, people gain a stronger individual voice and a greater sense of responsibility.
questions.explain: Greene says crowds relieve people of personal responsibility and make them smaller by losing their will and their individual voice.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Steve Jobs amassed a fortune but actually cared very little for material possessions.
questions.explain: Jobs focused on creating the best and most original designs, and Greene says good fortune followed him as a result.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says attention we strive hard for is more pleasurable than attention that comes unexpectedly.
questions.explain: Greene says the opposite: attention that is unexpected, like sudden success, is all the more pleasurable.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that inevitably all of us at some point fall for false purposes because they are so easy, popular and cheap.
questions.explain: That is why he says it is critical to become aware of them: eliminating the impulse toward lower forms lets us gravitate toward the higher.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: True or false: In 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose', the five strategies for developing a high sense of purpose come before the final section on false purposes.
questions.explain: The chapter runs from The Voice to the Keys, then the strategies, and ends with The Lure of False Purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put Greene's five strategies for developing a high sense of purpose in the order he presents them.
items: Discover your calling in life
Use resistance and negative spurs
Absorb purposeful energy
Create a ladder of descending goals
Lose yourself in the work
questions.explain: Greene says the strategies are in a loose order, starting with discovering your calling and ending with the deep absorption that offsets burnout.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the stages of Akira Kurosawa's path to his calling in the order Greene describes.
items: He tried painting
He worked as an assistant director, a job he hated
He was assigned to work for Kajiro Yamamoto
Watching Yamamoto, he realized his calling
questions.explain: Kurosawa was aimless and ready to quit until working under Yamamoto opened his eyes to the magical possibilities of film.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the stages of Coco Chanel's use of mentors in the order Greene describes.
items: She began life as an orphan with few resources
In her early twenties she realized her calling was to design clothes
At twenty-five she met Arthur Capel
Later she sought out others with skills she lacked
questions.explain: Chanel found her calling, then absorbed confidence and business sense from Capel, and kept returning to the strategy later in life.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put Greene's three conditions for setting the stage for peak experiences in the order he gives them.
items: Wait until you are further along in the process
Give yourself uninterrupted time with the work
Keep the emphasis on the work, never on yourself
questions.explain: Greene labels them first, second and third: ripeness of the mind, uninterrupted time, and a focus on the work rather than the ego.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the five false purposes in the order Greene discusses them.
items: The pursuit of pleasure
Causes and cults
Money and success
Attention
Cynicism
questions.explain: Greene moves from pleasure through causes, money and attention, and ends with cynicism, the void as purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the stages of the pursuit of pleasure in the order Greene describes them.
items: We pursue pleasure outside work
The pleasures grow duller through repetition
We need more of the same or new diversions
The need turns into an addiction
Health and mental powers diminish
questions.explain: Greene traces the dynamic of diminishing returns from dulling pleasures to dependency and a loss of health and mental powers.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the stages of the money-and-success seeker's career in the order Greene describes.
items: They enter the field that pays the most the fastest
They do quite well for a while
As they get older, they feel restless and slightly bored
They try different avenues and need new challenges
questions.explain: Greene shows how a career chosen only for money leads, over time, to restlessness and a constant need to find new motivation.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put the sections of 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose' in order.
items: The Voice
Keys to Human Nature
Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
The Lure of False Purposes
questions.explain: The chapter opens with Martin Luther King Jr.'s story, explains the law, gives strategies, and ends by exposing false purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Put these chapters of The Laws of Human Nature in order.
items: Know Your Limits
Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You
Advance with a Sense of Purpose
Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.explain: Chapter 13 on purpose sits between the chapter on gender rigidity and the chapter on conformity to the group.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each person with the childhood fascination Greene describes.
pairs: Chemistry equipment behind glass in her father's office
His first play in a theater in his small town
Gadgets in the window of an electronics store
His father hitting golf balls into a net in the garage
Printed words on a page and their magical meanings
questions.explain: Each moment came suddenly and without prodding, which Greene treats as a sign of a primal inclination.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each figure with the role Greene gives them in the strategies for developing purpose.
pairs: Oversold inventions to journalists to force a deadline
Vowed to master a koan in seven days or die
Absorbed purpose and business sense from a mentor
Fused with her film roles in peak experiences
Became so absorbed he lost himself in city streets
questions.explain: Edison and Hakuin illustrate deadlines, Chanel absorbing purposeful energy, and Bergman and Einstein losing themselves in the work.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each strategy with the obstacle Greene says it helps overcome.
pairs: Losing contact with your own preferences under others' influence
The urge to avoid tedium, pain and criticism
Our susceptibility to the moods of low-purpose people
Create a ladder of descending goals
Burnout and the tedium of long commitment
questions.explain: Each strategy targets a specific obstacle on the path to a high sense of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each term from Greene's strategies with its meaning.
pairs: Early, unprompted fascinations pointing to a calling
Flow beyond the ego bringing calm and joy
Small daily or weekly objectives on the ladder
Adversity and criticism turned into motivation
questions.explain: These terms name the key ideas of the strategies, from finding a calling to sustaining it through flow.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each false purpose with the trap Greene says it leads to.
pairs: Losing your will and voice in the crowd
An endless race since others always have more
Becoming ever more outrageous, like a clown
A pose that hides fear of trying and failing
questions.explain: Each false purpose offers an easy illusion of transcendence but leads downward to the animal side of our nature.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each aspect with how Greene describes it when contrasting real and false purposes.
pairs: Within: a calling no one imposed
Belief systems swallowed whole and conformity
Upward, to a more human level
Downward, to addiction and mindless conformity
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the two by where they come from and where they lead.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each false purpose with the better alternative Greene offers.
pairs: Limit yourself and choose depth of experience
Commit to a cause after deep inner thought
Focus on high purpose and let success follow
Create work that naturally draws people
Seek the Sublime with childlike curiosity
questions.explain: For each false purpose Greene points to a higher path rooted in a real, inner sense of purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each example with the point Greene uses it to make about false purposes.
pairs: Success follows from focus on original work, not money
A cause can be part of a real purpose
Short-term money thinking causes big mistakes
People prefer the void as purpose to no purpose
questions.explain: Greene uses these figures and events to show the failures of false purposes and the shape of real ones.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Match each section of 'Advance with a Sense of Purpose' with its role in the chapter.
pairs: The story of Martin Luther King Jr. finding his calling
The predicament of aimlessness and the inner guidance system
Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
Five practical ways to build and sustain purpose
Common substitutes offering only an illusion of purpose
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a story to the law itself, then to practical strategies, and ends by warning against false purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these into signs that an activity points to your calling and signs that it does not, according to Greene.
groups: Does not point to your calling

items.t: It feels natural and easy, like swimming with a current
You tolerate the tedium of practicing it
Criticism makes you want to learn rather than quit
It fascinated you as a child without anyone prodding you
You find it deeply boring and unfulfilling
It constantly frustrates you

questions.explain: Greene contrasts activities that feel natural and engage you even through tedium with those that feel boring, unfulfilling and frustrating.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these features into constructive criticism and criticism that comes from envy, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Gives specific details on what and how to improve
Focuses on the work itself
Is expressed with a bit too much vehemence
Instills doubts about your overall ability
Emphasizes your personality more than the work

questions.explain: Envious criticism is personal, vehement and vague; Greene says some criticism is constructive and worth attention.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these into people Greene says to seek out and people to avoid when absorbing purposeful energy.
groups: Avoid or do not settle for

items.t: People with a high sense of purpose
Pragmatic people who get things done
Friends from different fields with similar energy
People with a low or false sense of purpose
Virtual mentors
Merely charismatic visionaries

questions.explain: Because we are susceptible to others' moods, Greene says to associate with pragmatic, high-purpose people in person and limit contact with those of low or false purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.section: Strategies for Developing a High Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these features into those of the long-term goal and those of the smaller goals down Greene's ladder of descending goals.

items.t: Ambitious enough to bring out the best in you
Brings clarity and resolve
Can generate anxiety from the present vantage point
Realized in relatively short time frames
Gives moments of satisfaction and a sense of progress
Set each day or week

questions.explain: The large goal gives direction but breeds anxiety; the smaller rungs reaching to the present give quick wins and focus.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these features into real purposes and false purposes, as Greene contrasts them.

items.t: A calling nobody imposed and nobody can take away
Leads us upward, sharpening skills and minds
Religious belief made inward through introspection
Belief systems swallowed whole
Conformity to what other people are doing
Leads to addictions and loss of mental powers

questions.explain: Greene says real purpose comes from within and leads upward, while false purpose comes from outside and leads downward.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these into Greene's picture of deep pleasure and of diminishing pleasure, from his book-reading example.

items.t: Absorbing yourself in one excellent book
Discovering hidden riches in what you read
Thinking of the book again when not reading
Reading many books in rapid succession
Feeling overwhelmed and overstimulated
Reaching for a new one right away

questions.explain: Greene's example shows that deeper pleasure requires limiting ourselves, choosing depth of experience over overstimulation.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these into a cause embraced as part of a real purpose and membership in a microcause or cult, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Emerges from deep thinking about the subject
Brings your uniqueness into play
Springs from a hunger for justice and truth
A means to vent frustration, envy and hatred
Mimicking the company line
Feeling superior in a clique with special truth

questions.explain: Greene says a cause, as for Martin Luther King Jr., must come from an internal process, not ego gratification or emotional release.

questions.unitTitle: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
questions.q: Sort these into the cynic's beliefs and the view of the hunter for purpose, as Greene describes them.

items.t: Life is absurd, meaningless and random
Look behind people's motives and you find selfishness
It is hard to take anything seriously
Reality contains much that is sublime and beautiful
The human brain is awe-inspiring
Fuse a child's curiosity with adult intelligence

questions.explain: Greene says purpose hunters move in the opposite direction from the cynic's slacker attitude, toward wonder and realized potential.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The Law of Conformity says that in a group we unconsciously ____ what others are saying and doing.
questions.explain: The opening says that in the group setting we unconsciously imitate others, and that we care more about fitting in and believing what others believe.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to the opening of Chapter 14, what is the only solution to the loss of independent thought that groups cause in us?
options: Joining only groups whose values match our own exactly
Developing self-awareness and a superior understanding of how we change in groups
Rebelling against whatever the group believes at every opportunity
Avoiding group settings so that others cannot shape our thinking
questions.explain: Greene says the only solution is awareness and understanding of the changes that occur in us in groups, not withdrawal or rebellion.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Conformity says that with enough awareness we can outwardly fit in and cooperate at a high level while keeping our independence and rationality.
questions.explain: The opening promises that self-awareness lets us become superior social actors who fit in outwardly yet keep our own thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does the opening of Chapter 14 say happen to us in a group setting?
options: We become more prone to taking irrational risks because everyone else is
We think more about fitting in and believing what others believe
We feel emotions infected by the group mood
We feel less pressure to match the people around us
We reason more carefully because others check our ideas
questions.explain: In groups our thinking, feelings and risk-taking all shift toward the group; careful, independent reasoning is what tends to be lost.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What side of our character does the opening of Chapter 14 say we are generally unaware of, and what is its danger?
questions.a: It is our social personality, the different person we become in groups. There we imitate others, think and feel as the group does, and take irrational risks. If this social personality comes to dominate, we slowly lose our sense of uniqueness and our ability to think for ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How was Yizhen Middle School, where Gao Jianhua studied, labeled in communist China?
options: A school for the children of party officials only
A technical school preparing students for factory work
A model school run entirely by army officers
A key school, with over 90 percent of students going on to college
questions.explain: YMS was a prestigious key school that was hard to get into, and Jianhua hoped to use it to reach Beijing University and a writing career.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Gao Jianhua's story of the Cultural Revolution at his school comes from the nonfiction book Born ____.
questions.explain: Greene's interpretation says the story comes from Gao Yuan's account Born Red, written by the same boy under his later name.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each character in Gao Jianhua's story to who he or she was.
pairs: Zealous communist friend who rose to rule the school
Student who proposed parading teachers in dunce caps
Leader of the more tolerant Red Rebels
Party secretary later paraded with a drum around his neck
Artist friend who made the best posters and later fled
questions.explain: Fangpu and Little Bawang became the aggressive core of the East-Is-Red Corps, while Mengzhe led the rival Red Rebels; Ding and Zongwei were among those swept aside.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In May 1966, what news did Fangpu bring to Jianhua that signaled something was in the air?
options: Chairman Mao had died and the party was in turmoil
The school was to be closed for the summer by order of the army
Students from Beijing were arriving to take over the classes
Famous writers were being accused of hiding counterrevolutionary messages in their work
questions.explain: Fangpu had read in the Beijing papers of a literary debate in which intellectuals accused respected writers of veiled attacks on Mao; the debate soon spread across China.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Mao told young people it was right to rebel, using a Chinese phrase, zao fan, which literally means to turn everything ____.
questions.explain: Zao fan meant turning everything upside down, and Mao said it was the young people's duty to question authority.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Mao called those who secretly worked to pull China back into its past ____, and he asked students to root them out.
questions.explain: Mao's enemy figure was the revisionist, someone clinging to the past, which gave the students a target to hunt for.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Fangpu claim that Secretary Ding was a revisionist?
options: Ding's ban on attacking teachers showed he was suppressing the questioning spirit Mao encouraged
Ding had secretly fought on the side of the nationalists
Ding had hidden food coupons and a radio in his office
Ding had refused to hold any assembly about the debate
questions.explain: Fangpu's audacious poster argued that the ban on posters about teachers proved Ding opposed Mao's call to question authority; the hidden coupons and radio came out only later.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: When the work team from Beijing arrived at the school, what did it do about the posters?
options: It praised the poster against Ding and made Fangpu the principal
It banned all posters and restarted classes under military drill
It lifted the ban on posters criticizing teachers and also suspended classes and exams
It ordered Ding to apologize to Fangpu before the whole school
questions.explain: The work team made Fangpu apologize to Ding but freed the students to attack teachers and put all classes aside so they could make revolution.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Jianhua make a poster attacking Teacher Wen even though he liked almost all of his teachers?
options: Fangpu had ordered him to pick a teacher as a test
He felt compelled to join in and did not want to seem like a revisionist
The work team demanded one poster from every student
He sincerely believed she was a hidden counterrevolutionary
questions.explain: Jianhua felt pressure to take part, wanted to avoid suspicion, and resented her old criticism of his lack of interest in politics, so he wrote a poster as gently as he could.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's account, Teacher Wen was condemned as a revisionist even though she was radical in her beliefs, because she liked Western-style fashion.
questions.explain: The students judged by appearances, and such appearances could be quite deceptive; Wen's taste in clothes outweighed her actual beliefs.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: On what did the YMS students tend to base their judgments about who was a revisionist?
options: Careful study of each teacher's lectures and writings
Appearances such as clothes, food, drink, manners and family background
Sworn statements gathered by the work team
Votes cast by the whole student body in assemblies
questions.explain: Greene stresses that the students judged by surface signs, which shows how groups replace careful analysis with simple, appearance-based thinking.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Where did Little Bawang get his idea of parading teachers with dunce caps and heavy boards around their necks?
options: From a story Teacher Li had told in class
From a poster that arrived from the army unit
From the orders of the party secretary Ding Yi
From Mao's description of peasants humiliating notorious landlords in the 1940s
questions.explain: He had read how peasants paraded landlords in this way, and the students hoped the same shame would make teachers confess.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these early events at Yizhen Middle School in the order they happened.
items: Fangpu brings news of the literary debate
Students make posters copied from Beijing
Fangpu posts an attack on Secretary Ding
The work team lifts the poster ban and suspends classes
Teachers are paraded in dunce caps
questions.explain: The campaign built step by step, from news of the debate, to copied posters, to Fangpu's audacious poster, to the work team freeing the students to attack teachers.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: When teachers confessed to crimes they mostly had never committed, the students concluded their suspicions had been wrong.
questions.explain: The confessions, made to avoid escalating punishment, only seemed to confirm the students in their paranoia, which made their thinking even more simplistic.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each teacher or official in the story to what the students held against him.
pairs: Talked about China's landscapes but seldom quoted Mao
Had an American father who served in the U.S. Navy
Had first fought for the nationalists before switching sides
Discovered to be the son of a notorious landlord
questions.explain: Each suspicion rested on appearances or family background rather than on anything the person had actually done.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Jianhua become a member of the Red Guards at his school?
options: He was the best writer for the school newspaper
His father had an illustrious past as a communist war veteran
He had informed on a teacher to the work team
Fangpu used his power to place him there
questions.explain: Only the purest revolutionaries could join, and Jianhua's red armband came from his father's past, which later made him fear for his place once his father was denounced.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The student groups formed to support and defend Mao were called the ____ Guards, whose members wore bright red armbands.
questions.explain: Mao approved the Red Guards, and the red armband became a mark of revolutionary elite status that students competed to win.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: When Jianhua learned that students had denounced his father as a revisionist, he was anxious mainly that the East-Is-Red Corps would punish his family.
questions.explain: Although he loved and worried for his father, he feared that news of the disgrace would cost him his red armband and get him ostracized, showing how strongly group status can weigh on a person.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did the Red Rebels' leader Mengzhe differ from Fangpu?
options: He wanted a revolution that was more tolerant and based on reason rather than violence
He rejected Mao's authority and wanted to restore the old order
He preferred a revolution led by teachers instead of students
He wanted the army to take permanent control of the school
questions.explain: Mengzhe claimed his tolerant approach was the purer Maoism, yet Greene notes the two sides soon seemed to fight about little except power over each other.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these steps in the struggle between the rival student groups in the order they happened.
items: Fangpu forms the East-Is-Red Corps and ousts the chairman
The Red Rebels emerge under Mengzhe
The army's 901 unit orders all factions to disband
The Red Rebels take over the school after the Corps leaves
The county military sides with the Corps and the Rebels are crushed
questions.explain: Power passed from Fangpu's Corps to the rival Rebels and back again, until the military settled the matter by choosing a side.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did the students respond when the army unit ordered the factions to disband and classes to resume?
options: They handed over the leaders to the soldiers at once
They gratefully returned to their desks and burned the posters
They could not accept a sudden return to discipline, so they sulked and skipped classes
They agreed to merge into a single student committee
questions.explain: After eight months of upheaval the students refused to go back, and Fangpu even led a campaign against the soldiers, which shows how deeply the group spirit had taken hold.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Gao Jianhua gave a name to his torturers under pressure and afterward felt intense regret that he had been a coward.
questions.explain: Beaten and blindfolded, he panicked and named a fellow Red Rebel, Dusu, and then regretted it deeply.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these events of the story's ending in the order they happened.
items: Jianhua is beaten and names Dusu
Zongwei dies in Jianhua's arms
The Corps rewrites the past with a doctored exhibition
Jianhua returns to his hometown in the summer of 1968
Jianhua and his brother join the army
questions.explain: The torture and Zongwei's death came first, then the Corps' rewriting of history, then Jianhua's flight, his return to a wrecked school, and his enlistment.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Jianhua see his school when he came back in September 1968, and what questions did it raise for him?
questions.a: After months away he saw it with fresh eyes: torn-up classrooms, empty science labs, rubble, unmarked graves, a bombed music hall, and hardly a reputable teacher left. He asked what Heping, Yulan, Zongwei and so many others had died for and what they had been fighting over. He could not answer, and he felt disgust and despair, so he joined the army to bury the memories.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene's interpretation, what was the Cultural Revolution in essence?
options: Mao's attempt to alter human nature itself
A cultural movement to promote literature among the young
A military plan to take over the schools of China
A spontaneous uprising of the peasants against the party
questions.explain: Greene reads Mao's wish to wipe the slate clean and start over as an experiment on human nature, which he says failed.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says that in Mao's experiment, human nature could not be uprooted; try to alter it and it merely ____ in different shapes and forms.
questions.explain: The events in Born Red show in miniature that old patterns of group behavior return in new guises however radically a scheme tries to reengineer them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Mao pictured the nation as a clean ____ of paper on which the newest and most beautiful pictures could be painted.
questions.explain: Mao wanted to wipe away old habits and ways of thinking, including mindless respect for authority, so that a fresh generation could build a classless society.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Mao start the Cultural Revolution, and what outcome did he hope for?
questions.a: He feared that China was slipping back into its feudal past, that bureaucracies were becoming breeding grounds for a new elite, and that peasants stayed powerless. He wanted a wake-up call that would let the young experience revolution firsthand. He hoped to uproot old habits and mindless obedience to authority and produce a fresh generation that could forge a classless society.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What was the three-part strategy Mao used in his experiment?
questions.a: He focused people's attention on a legitimate enemy, the revisionists who clung to the past. He encouraged the young to fight both this reactionary force and any entrenched authority. By struggling this way, the Chinese were supposed to free themselves from old thinking, get rid of elites and ranking systems, and unify as a revolutionary class clear about what it was fighting for.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these were parts of Mao's strategy for his experiment, as Greene describes it?
options: Building a cult around his image from the outset
Hoping to get rid of elites and ranking systems
Installing a police state from the start
Focusing attention on revisionists as a legitimate enemy
Urging the young to fight entrenched forms of authority
questions.explain: The police state and the cult of Mao came later, as desperate remedies by spring 1968, after the strategy failed.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What fatal flaw does Greene find at the core of Mao's strategy?
options: The young were too well educated to follow orders
People in groups do not think in a nuanced way and mainly want to fit in
The enemy he named was not a legitimate one
Mao underestimated the strength of the army
questions.explain: Only calm, detached individuals can think with nuance, whereas people in groups are emotional, simplistic and eager to belong, so the plan could not produce clear, independent thinkers.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say people in groups tend to do?
options: Look for some authority to simplify matters
Put independence ahead of fitting in with the group spirit
Feel emotional and excited
Engage in nuanced thinking and deep analysis
Think in simple terms such as good versus evil
questions.explain: Greene says that deep analysis requires individual calm and detachment, and that the primary desire of people in groups is to fit in.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say that deliberately creating chaos, as Mao did, backfired?
questions.a: Humans find too much confusion and uncertainty frightening. Chaos therefore makes a group more certain to fall back on primitive patterns of thinking: simplistic, us-against-them judgments and a search for some authority to simplify things. The students merely made Mao into the new authority and swallowed his ideas with very little reflection.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did the students, though freed from the old order, stay emotionally tied to it?
options: They missed the discipline of the daily military drills
They feared the work team would return and restore the teachers
They kept the teachers' orders in force through the committee
The teachers still seemed all-powerful, but now as scheming counterrevolutionaries
questions.explain: Their old resentment at having to obey boiled over into a desire to be the ones punishing and oppressing, so they changed roles from obedient students to oppressors without becoming more rational.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did the students' role shift once they were freed from the old order, and why was the result the opposite of Mao's intentions?
questions.a: The students moved from obedient subjects to oppressors, venting repressed resentment on the teachers. When the teachers confessed to avoid escalating punishment, this confirmed the students in their paranoia. Their thinking became more simplistic and irrational, not the clear, independent thinking Mao wanted.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these dynamics did Greene see emerge once Mao had created a power vacuum?
options: More passive students receded into the background as followers
The students settled into a natural egalitarian order
Naturally aggressive types pushed their way to power
A new elite formed that handed out perks and privileges
questions.explain: Fangpu and Little Bawang rose while Jianhua and Zongwei receded; an egalitarian order did not appear, because the students kept straining to occupy superior positions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A manager abolishes all job titles and rules, hoping the staff will run themselves as equals. Within weeks the most assertive staff members are giving orders and handing out favors. Which dynamic from the Cultural Revolution story does this resemble?
options: Aggressive types filling the power vacuum and forming a new elite
The cult of a leader to restore order
Teachers confessing to crimes to avoid punishment
Tribal factions fighting over a shared enemy
questions.explain: When authority is removed, the more assertive members push forward and create a new hierarchy, as Fangpu and Little Bawang did at YMS.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did the students' obsession with status show itself in the confusion of the Cultural Revolution?
questions.a: They kept asking who was in the red category and who was in the black, and whether it was better to come from the peasantry or the proletariat. They schemed to get into the Red Guards and win the red armband that marked revolutionary elite status. Instead of moving toward an egalitarian order, they strained to occupy superior positions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
