questions.q: Sort each item by whether it was part of what Mao intended or what actually happened.

items.t: A unified, classless revolutionary class
Getting rid of elites and ranking systems
Freedom from old patterns of thinking
Aggressive types forming a new class of elites
Groups splitting into tribal factions
A police state and a cult around Mao

questions.explain: Mao hoped for equality, unity and fresh thinking, but group dynamics produced new elites, factions and a repressive state.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each person by the group role Greene says the person took in the power vacuum.
groups: Receded into the background as a follower

items.t: Fangpu
Little Bawang
Jianhua
Zongwei

questions.explain: Greene says the more assertive, aggressive and even sadistic students rose, while the more passive ones, such as Jianhua and Zongwei, faded back.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, what triggers the split of a group into tribal factions once the students ran the school themselves?
options: Open debate over which ideas were the most loyal to Mao
Orders from the army to divide the students into teams
A total monopoly of power shuts out other ambitious people and leaves members feeling lost in a large grouping
A shortage of food and supplies in the school
questions.explain: People reject complete monopolies of power, and smaller factions give members closer bonds and a charismatic leader of their own, as Mengzhe was for the Rebels.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says that groups almost automatically split into rival smaller factions and ____, in which members identify more easily with fewer comrades.
questions.explain: The split into tribes follows from large groups making members feel lost, so each person seeks a tighter bond with a smaller set of comrades.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, what do people most want when they join one tribe or the other?
options: The chance to speak openly with a variety of views
Protection from the army and the work teams
A sense of belonging and a clear tribal identity
The chance to prove which set of ideas is correct
questions.explain: People may think they join for ideas or goals, but belonging is what they want most; Greene notes that it was hard to say what the two student groups were fighting for.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's account, the differences between the East-Is-Red Corps and the Red Rebels were what drove the fighting, and each side could see merit in the other.
questions.explain: As the battle intensified it was hard to say what they fought for beyond power, and there was no middle ground; the tribe is always right and questioning it is betrayal.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does Greene explain the escalating violence between the East-Is-Red Corps and the Red Rebels?
questions.a: Each side felt certain it embodied the true cause, and any act of violence by one side called for a reprisal from the other. There was no middle ground and no questioning the rightness of the tribe, since doing so was betrayal, as Zongwei found. The violence became cut off from the original purpose of the Cultural Revolution.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: By spring 1968, what was Mao's only remaining recourse, according to Greene?
options: To restore the old party bureaucracy and the old schools
To invite the rival tribes to share a single committee
To dissolve the Red Guards and hand power to the teachers
To install a police state and turn himself into a cult figure
questions.explain: With crime soaring and the economy halted, Mao imprisoned hundreds of thousands, let the army take over, and made himself a figure to be worshipped.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each result of the Cultural Revolution to the cause or purpose Greene gives for it.
pairs: To avoid escalating punishment, which only fed the students' paranoia
Crime soaring and the economy halting
Hardly anyone felt compelled to work or make anything
Mao turning into a cult figure
To help restore order and respect for authority
The most repressive, superstitious regimes were what the new order came to resemble
questions.explain: Each outcome in Greene's telling grew out of group dynamics rather than the revolution's stated ideals.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What did the failed Cultural Revolution leave China with, and what did Jianhua's father say about it?
questions.a: China ended with a police state, soaring crime, a halted economy, and a leader turned into a worshipped cult figure. Fangpu's repression at the school, with its torture, rewriting of history and control of all media, mirrored what Mao did nationally. The new order resembled the repressive, superstitious regimes of feudal China, just as Jianhua's father kept saying: a thing turns into its opposite if pushed too far.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Jianhua's father kept telling his son, ‘A thing turns into its ____ if pushed too far.’
questions.explain: The saying captures Greene's point that the new revolutionary order came to resemble the old repressive regimes it wanted to destroy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the lessons of the Cultural Revolution apply mainly to adolescents, because young people are more susceptible to groups.
questions.explain: Greene says young people show human nature in a purer form, but what happened at the school occurred throughout China among people of all ages, in offices, factories and the army.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In the closing part of the story's interpretation, what does Greene say we tend to imagine about the Cultural Revolution tale?
options: That it shows the dangers of every kind of leader
That it is mostly an account of a single cruel school principal
That it proves young people are more rational than adults
That it is an extreme example with little relevance to our own groups
questions.explain: Greene says we picture ourselves as polite, civilized and independent, but this is largely an illusion, since we also slip into primitive modes in groups.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes what we like to believe about ourselves or what actually happens to us in groups, per Greene.

items.t: We are sophisticated and polite in our workplaces
We have our own progressive ideals and think independently
We shape our thoughts to the group orthodoxies
We unconsciously imitate others in appearance, words and ideas
We worry about where we rank in the hierarchy

questions.explain: Greene says much of our self-image is an illusion: the moment we enter a group we slip into primitive modes of thinking and behaving without realizing it.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, why do we worry so much about status in the group?
options: It is the primate part of our nature, which we share with chimpanzees
It is a symptom of reading too much news
It is a habit learned only in modern offices
It is forced on us by the leaders of the group
questions.explain: Greene ties the question ‘Am I getting as much respect as my colleagues?’ to the status obsession we share with chimpanzee relatives.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as signs that a group is influencing us?
options: Imitating others in appearances, expressions and ideas
Feeling immune to the moods of the people around us
Getting heated and exaggerating the faults of the group's rival
Feeling awed and intimidated around leaders
Choosing our beliefs entirely by our own reflection
questions.explain: These are the subtle signs of group influence; Greene adds that we also get swept up in the group mood.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says that depending on patterns from early childhood, in a group we become more passive or more ____ than usual.
questions.explain: Group settings bring out the less developed sides of our character, either in a more passive or in a more aggressive direction.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say happen to a seemingly civilized group when an outside threat or crisis arrives?
options: We are subject to stronger waves of viral emotion such as panic or hatred
Our thinking about the rival becomes more simplistic and heated
We feel greater pressure to prove our loyalty
The group's differences disappear and factions are avoided
The group grows calmer and more tolerant of dissent
questions.explain: Stress intensifies the group effects, and the group could even split into factions with tribal dynamics that charismatic leaders can exploit.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the stages Greene gives for how a group's downward dynamic develops under outside stress in order.
items: Pressure to prove loyalty grows
Thinking about the rival grows more simplistic
Waves of panic, hatred or grandiosity spread
The group splits into tribal factions
Charismatic leaders exploit the volatility
questions.explain: Greene lists the effects in this order: loyalty pressure and simpler thinking about the enemy, viral emotions, factional splitting, and then leaders who exploit the situation.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What can happen even when a group does not turn to open violence, according to Greene?
questions.a: The primitive dynamic can still have grave consequences, because the group overreacts and makes decisions based on exaggerated fears or uncontrollable excitement. The potential for aggression lies under the surface of almost any group if it is pushed far enough. This is why Greene says we must learn to detach from the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What is the first step of the different experiment in human nature that Greene proposes?
options: Choosing a strong leader to follow
Doing away with all status and rank
Accepting the reality of the powerful effect the group has on us
Leaving every group we belong to
questions.explain: The experiment starts with brutal honesty about how our need to fit in can shape and warp our thinking, such as asking whether our outrage is our own or inspired by the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to Mao's experiment or to the experiment Greene proposes.

items.t: Deliberately create chaos
Wipe the slate clean by uprooting old habits
Urge the young to attack any authority
Detach from the group to create mental space
Accept human nature and work with it
Earn status through excellent work

questions.explain: Mao tried to remake human nature by shaking things up, while Greene proposes accepting it and working productively with what we have.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each aspect of human nature to Greene's constructive way of working with it.
pairs: The need for status and recognition
The need to belong and prove loyalty
Question group decisions that will harm it and offer divergent views
Spread a calm, patient focus on results
Respect their accomplishments without deifying them
questions.explain: Greene says the aim is not to deny the needs of human nature but to channel them in productive ways.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The goal of Greene's experiment is to develop the ability to ____ ourselves from the group and create mental space for independent thinking.
questions.explain: Detachment from the group, combined with outward cooperation, is the end point: truly independent and rational individuals.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says we should be especially careful around people with charismatic appeal and try to pull them down to earth.
questions.explain: He asks us to demystify charismatic figures and not blindly venerate leaders, while still respecting what they have accomplished.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In Greene's experiment, how does he suggest we use the viral nature of emotions in the group?
options: Spread calm, patience and a practical focus on results instead of panic
Promote strong anger to keep the group motivated
Avoid all feeling by staying silent in meetings
Match the group's mood so that nobody feels left out
questions.explain: Greene wants us to play on a different set of emotions so that the group's emotional contagion works in a more rational direction.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Fangpu's poster against Secretary Ding cause such a stir, and how did the work team respond?
questions.a: The students had been reared to obey authority unquestioningly, especially respected party members like Ding, and Fangpu broke that taboo. The work team ordered Fangpu to apologize publicly to Ding. At the same time it lifted the ban on posters criticizing teachers and suspended all classes and exams so students could devote themselves to making revolution.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Jianhua's own conduct in the story show the pull of the group even though he disliked what was happening?
questions.a: He liked almost all his teachers yet felt compelled to join in, writing a poster against Teacher Wen as gently as he could. He followed the parade of Teacher Li from a distance, repressing his uneasiness, and later guarded the room where the vice principal hanged himself. He also feared losing his red armband if his father's disgrace became known, so he went along and kept quiet.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did the East-Is-Red Corps control the school once it held power, and what did Greene notice about this?
questions.a: Its paper Battlefield News was the only one allowed, classes became recitations of Mao's quotes, and an exhibition of doctored photographs and fake news rewrote the past. A giant statue of Mao stood at the gate, and the defeated Rebels wore white armbands and kowtowed. Greene notes that this torture, rewriting of history and control of all media mirrored what Mao was doing across the country.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these did the victorious East-Is-Red Corps do at the school?
options: Held an exhibition with doctored photographs and fake news
Made former Red Rebels wear white armbands listing their crimes
Let the Red Rebels keep a newspaper of their own
Allowed only its own paper, Battlefield News
questions.explain: The Corps controlled the media and rewrote history, much as Mao did nationally; the Rebels were the ones cowed and silenced.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these reasons did students have for choosing a side when the army unit was suddenly recalled?
options: The Corps was larger and offered better positions
They hated Fangpu and Little Bawang
They thought one group was more truly revolutionary
The army had assigned each student to a group by lottery
questions.explain: Students joined for position, for personal dislike, or for ideological conviction, which fits Greene's point that people join tribes for belonging more than for ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these developments among the students after Mao's call in the order Greene presents them.
items: Students make Mao their new authority
Students judge teachers by appearances
Students turn from obedient pupils into oppressors
Aggressive types take power in the vacuum
The group splits into tribal factions
questions.explain: Greene moves from the students' conventional imitation and appearance-based judgments, through their role reversal and the rise of aggressive types, to status obsession and finally tribal factions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene call the energy that affects and binds a group through shared sensations and creates an intense feeling of connection?
options: The group instinct, a hidden drive to dominate
The tribal bond, a loyalty based on blood ties
The social force, a kind of invisible force field
The herd reflex, a fear of being left behind
questions.explain: Greene labels this energy the social force, which we feel as automatic bodily sensations such as goose bumps and a racing heartbeat.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene calls the energy that binds a group through shared sensations the ____ force.
questions.explain: The social force is felt in concerts, rallies, speeches and urgent group work, and it is a physiological part of our nature.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says the social force exists inside us and ____ us at the same time.
questions.explain: We feel the force within, yet we think of it as outside ourselves as well, in the people sharing the sensations.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says we can feel the intense rush of the social force just as strongly when alone or with just a few other people.
questions.explain: Greene says these emotions cannot arise when we are alone or with just a few people; in general the larger the group, the more intense the effect.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the three elements of the social force that Greene lists in the order he gives them.
items: It exists inside and outside us at once
It differs with the size and chemistry of the group
We are drawn to it
questions.explain: Greene lists first its inside-and-outside quality, then its variation with group size and chemistry, then our attraction to crowds.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each situation by whether it gives us a rush of belonging or leaves us feeling uneasy as outsiders.

items.t: Sitting in a large audience at a concert
Giving a talk to a crowd that is on our side
Working in a group toward a critical deadline
Starting a job where people have a secret language
Traveling to a place with a very different culture
Walking through a neighborhood of a different social class

questions.explain: Greene shows the social force as a rush when we belong and as anxiety and alertness when we confront it as outsiders.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each situation to how Greene says the social force shows up in it.
pairs: Sitting in a crowd at a rally
Waves of shared excitement, anger or joy rise in us automatically
Giving a talk to a friendly audience
We feed off the crowd; our voice and gestures change
The speaker seems invested with a special force that commands respect
Racing a critical deadline as a team
We work extra hard and almost anticipate colleagues' thoughts
questions.explain: In each case the feelings come to us as automatic bodily sensations rather than as rational thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene cites Richard E. Byrd's account of his five months in isolation in Antarctica, in his book ____.
questions.explain: Byrd's account and the reports of solitary prisoners show that, without others' eyes on us, our sense of self begins to disintegrate.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does prolonged isolation reveal about the social force, according to Greene?
questions.a: People in solitary confinement or remote isolation feel disconnected from reality, sense their personalities disintegrating, and become prone to hallucinations. What they miss most is the eyes of others looking back at them. Greene links this to infancy, when our mother's gaze told us who we were, and says that only other people's eyes reassure us that we are real, whole and belonging.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the social force can be felt in a weaker, phantom-like way through our screens, as we use smartphones like a substitute pair of eyes upon us.
questions.explain: Virtual crowds carry a less intense version of the force, which we sense inside us and outside us through the screen.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, why do we so rarely discuss or analyze the social force?
options: It is a recent development of modern media
It reminds us of our animal roots and offends our self-opinion as conscious, civilized individuals
It cannot be felt except in small gatherings
It affects only a small minority of people
questions.explain: Part of the silence is the difficulty of studying it scientifically, but Greene also sees willful ignorance: our group behavior shatters the myth that we consciously control what we do.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these ways of working in groups does Greene say humans share with other social animals?
options: Basing the group's rank only on individual merit
Sensing and feeling what others in the group feel
An urgent need to fit in and play a role
Settling every disagreement by open vote
Unconsciously imitating gestures, especially of leaders
questions.explain: Greene says that human group life is a more complex version of what all social animals experience, played out on a subverbal level.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each social-animal behavior to its human counterpart that Greene describes.
pairs: Imitating those higher in the rank
We unconsciously imitate gestures and expressions, especially leaders'
We sense and feel what others in the group are feeling
We vent our anger together through social media
Religious or political assemblies, spectacles and warfare
questions.explain: Greene says we seem much more sophisticated, but the same dynamic operates in us on a subverbal level.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say the deep suspicion we feel toward outsiders is a dangerous part of the social force today?
options: It only affects people who live in large cities
It makes us trust strangers too easily
It prevents groups from forming at all
It evolved to cope with disease and rival hunter-gatherers, yet with modern technology it can fuel genocidal violence
questions.explain: Reactions that helped our earliest ancestors survive are no longer relevant in the twenty-first century but can now be the source of our most violent behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Greene associates it with the downward pull or the upward pull of the social force.

items.t: Demonizing outsiders to the group
Losing the ability to think independently
Genocidal violence made possible by technology
High-level cooperation and empathy
Creating something together in a group
The reality group

questions.explain: The force is neither positive nor negative: it pulls downward to primitive behavior when it degrades rational thought and upward when it supports cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say the social force is neither positive nor negative, and what is the difference between its downward and upward pull?
questions.a: It is simply a physiological part of our nature that evolved long ago. Insofar as it degrades our ability to think independently and rationally, it exerts a downward pull into primitive behavior unsuited to modern life. It can also be shaped for an upward pull, as when we create something together in a group through high-level cooperation and empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene reject becoming a nonconformist as the answer to the pull of the group?
options: Rebelling for its own sake is just as mindless and leaves us marginalized
Nonconformity is impossible once we have joined a group
Groups reward the nonconformist with more status
Nonconformists always end up leading the group
questions.explain: We are social creatures who depend on working with others, so blind rebellion is as unthinking as blind conformity and just as self-destructive.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What is group intelligence, and why does Greene call it a delicate dance?
questions.a: It is a thorough understanding of the effect groups have on our thinking and emotions, together with an understanding of the laws and dynamics by which human groups operate. With it we can become gifted social actors who outwardly fit in while inwardly keeping some distance and mental space to think for ourselves. We can then make decisions suited to who we are and our circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put Greene's four individual effects of the group on us in the order he gives them.
items: The desire to fit in
The need to perform
Emotional contagion
Hypercertainty
questions.explain: Greene numbers them as the first and primary effect (fitting in), the second (performing), the third (contagion) and the fourth (hypercertainty).

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In the first effect, the desire to fit in, which of the two ways of fitting in does Greene call the more important?
options: Arriving earlier than the others each day
Adopting the ideas, beliefs and values of the group
Speaking more quietly than the others
Dressing the way the others dress
questions.explain: Appearances are the first way, but taking on the group's ideas and values is the second and more important, and it works below the surface of awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the desire to fit in work, and why does Greene urge us to confront it?
questions.a: The first and primary effect of a group is the desire to fit in, which we satisfy through appearances and, more importantly, by taking on the group's ideas, beliefs and values. Over time the parts of our thinking that were a little different are trimmed away like a shrub, so on almost all issues we agree with the group, without noticing. Greene urges us to confront this conformity so we can become aware of it and control the process to some degree.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A new hire starts using the same phrases as her colleagues and insists that she reached her views entirely by herself. Which effect of the group does this show?
options: Hypercertainty about a risky plan
The desire to fit in, working unconsciously
Emotional contagion of anxiety
The group court around a leader
questions.explain: Greene says conformity happens unconsciously, and we tend to deny it and believe we chose our ideas ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The second effect of the group on us is the need to ____, as we exaggerate our agreement to show that we belong.
questions.explain: Greene says that in the group we become actors, molding what we say and do so others accept and like us.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A junior employee deliberately acts obsequious around the boss, aware it is an act. After years of this, she finds she smiles automatically without thinking. What does Greene say has happened?
options: She has become a nonconformist who rebels
The inner distance has melted and the mask has fused into her personality
She has joined a faction of the group's elites
She has escaped the group's influence
questions.explain: In acting the part, we begin to feel what we show, and the mask we wear fuses with our personality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Greene describes for how our group performances change us.
items: We act with some inner distance
In acting the part we begin to feel what we show
The mask fuses into our personality
questions.explain: Greene says we may start aware that we are performing, but over time the inner distance melts and the mask becomes part of us.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say we should not try to curb the need to perform in groups, and what should we do instead?
questions.a: He says nothing is more unnatural than curbing this need, which even chimpanzees display. Those who sulk and refuse to perform end up marginalized as the group unconsciously expels them. Instead, we should feel no shame, keep an inner distance, and become conscious, superior actors who alter their expression to suit each subgroup and impress people with their positive qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, which emotions are the most contagious of all in a group?
options: Pride and loyalty
Joy and excitement
Anxiety and fear
Boredom and apathy
questions.explain: Greene says anxiety and fear are the strongest, because among our ancestors it was important that everyone sensed a danger; joy, anger, apathy and desire are also contagious.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The third effect of the group on us is the ____ of emotions, where others' moods can displace our own.
questions.explain: Primed from infancy to pick up others' emotions, we absorb a group's mood, especially among those with whom we feel we belong.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list among the highly contagious emotions in a group?
options: Desire to follow a new trend or own something
Anxiety and fear
Reflective self-doubt
Joy and excitement
Calm detachment
questions.explain: Group emotions also include tiredness, apathy, anger and hatred; reflective doubt is what the group neutralizes.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Explain the self-fulfilling dynamic of emotional contagion that Greene describes, and what he suggests doing about it.
questions.a: If three people are anxious, there must be a good reason, so we become the fourth, and the emotion gains a reality others find compelling. The more people feel it, the more intense it becomes in each of us. Greene urges us to ask whether our fear comes from something right in front of us or is secondhand, to discern which emotions are most contagious for us, and so gain power to control them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that when everyone around us seems sure about a plan, we feel more certain about it and become more willing to take risks.
questions.explain: This is the fourth effect, hypercertainty: the doubting, reflective mechanism is neutralized and the group's confidence makes risk seem safe.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The fourth effect on us in a group, in which doubt melts away and we feel more certain about what we are doing, is called ____.
questions.explain: Greene says that in the group we feel the pressure to decide and get behind the decision, and that makes us prone to taking risks.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say that being covered by thousands doing the same thing makes us more willing to take a risk such as buying a bubble stock?
options: We have learned the facts from the group's experts
We are certain that the group will rescue us
We are shielded from feeling accountable if it fails
We can sell the stock without anyone noticing
questions.explain: Alone, a failed purchase would leave us feeling ridiculous and responsible, but a crowd doing the same spreads the blame and makes the gamble feel safe.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the group make us overconfident, according to Greene's discussion of hypercertainty?
questions.a: Alone we feel doubts, but in a group the doubting mechanism is neutralized: arguing is tiring, dissent risks marginalization, and if everyone agrees we feel compelled to feel confident. In financial bubbles like tulips, South Sea stock or subprime mortgages, those who raise doubts seem too cautious, and the group's validation lets even delusional schemes appear sound. Greene advises that when we feel unusually certain, we should step back and ask whether the group is working on us.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A team votes unanimously for a very risky expansion. No one voices a doubt, and anyone who hesitates is told they are being too cautious. Which of Greene's group effects is this?
options: Group culture, in which the founders' style dominates
Hypercertainty, in which the group's agreement neutralizes doubt
Group factions, in which cliques form
The group court, in which flattery wins favor
questions.explain: The unanimity and the dismissal of doubters show the group generating certainty and risk-taking, as in a financial bubble.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are among the group dynamics Greene tells us to study in the groups we belong to?
options: Group rules and codes
Emotional contagion
Group factions
Group culture
Hypercertainty
questions.explain: Contagion and hypercertainty belong to the earlier list of the individual effects of the group on us, not to the list of group dynamics.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the group dynamics Greene describes in the order he gives them.
items: Group culture
Group rules and codes
The group court
The group enemy
Group factions
questions.explain: Greene moves from the group's overall style, to its tacit rules, to the court around the leader, to the enemy, and finally to the splitting into factions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that Presidents Kennedy and Johnson succeeded in changing the Pentagon's hawkish culture so as to avoid war in Vietnam.
questions.explain: The Pentagon's aggressive culture instead altered their ideas and dragged them into the war.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say about group culture?
options: The longer a group exists and the larger it grows, the more conservative it becomes
Leaders who enter an established group can usually reshape its culture
It often reflects the founders, especially strong personalities
It often centers on an ideal the group imagines for itself, which works as a binding myth
A group's culture is best judged by what it says about itself
questions.explain: Greene warns that leaders are likely to be absorbed by an entrenched culture, and he says to judge a culture by actions, not by claims.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says the longer a group exists and the larger it grows, the more ____ it becomes, which can be the death of the group because it loses the ability to adapt.
questions.explain: People want to hold on to what they have built and rely on tried-and-true ways, so creeping conservatism sets in.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say about group culture and about group rules and codes, and what should we do when new to a group?
questions.a: Every group has a culture shaped by an ideal it imagines for itself and often by its founders, and the larger and older it is, the more likely it will control you and the more conservative it becomes. Rules and codes are implicit; a group enforces them without active policing by making violators nonentities or firing them. When new, look at who is rising and falling, how hard people work when unobserved, and the sacred cows and any de facto policing member, and avoid those trip wires.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says that in any group there are inevitably ____ cows, meaning people or beliefs never to be criticized.
questions.explain: Sacred cows are among the trip wires that a newcomer must avoid, along with friction with the member who polices the codes.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does Greene advise flattering a leader, given that leaders have large egos and a hunger for validation?
options: Copy the leader's exact words in every meeting
Compliment the leader in public as often as possible
Praise the leader's business success as loudly as possible
Tailor it to the leader's particular insecurities and keep it indirect, praising qualities no one else notices
questions.explain: Flattery that is too obvious makes the flatterer look desperate; the best courtiers aim at what the leader needs validated and mirror ideas without using exact words.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that flattery that is too obvious makes the flatterer look desperate and easy to see through.
questions.explain: He advises making flattery as indirect as possible and adapting it to the style of each court.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these courtier behaviors does Greene recommend?
options: Downplaying your successes and giving others credit in meetings
Making the leader's flattery indirect and tailored to the leader's insecurities
Refusing to take part in court politics to prove your honesty
Making your bosses comfortable in the superiority they believe they possess
Making yourself seem as brilliant and charming as possible
questions.explain: Standing out stirs envy, and acting superior to the court game marginalizes you, since there is no way to opt out of it.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each courtier tactic Greene describes to its purpose.
pairs: Flattering qualities no one else praises
Validates the leader without looking desperate
Mirroring the leader's ideas in different words
A highly effective form of indirect flattery
Avoids stirring the envy of other courtiers
Not seeming too good at your job
Keeps bosses from fearing their dependence on you
questions.explain: Greene's courtier strategies all aim to win the leader's favor without alarming the leader or the other courtiers.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Greene says a good courtier does it or avoids it.

items.t: Flatter indirectly and tailor it to the leader
Downplay successes and credit others
Question people's motives without paranoia
Act superior to the political games
Seem too brilliant or charming in front of colleagues
Make flattery obvious

questions.explain: Greene says the best courtiers act well and question motives, while a holier-than-thou attitude only gets you marginalized.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What are the three behavior patterns Greene says to note about courtiers in the group court?
questions.a: First, courtiers must gain a leader's attention and ingratiate themselves, usually through indirect flattery and by showing their usefulness without alarming the leader. Second, they must pay great attention to other courtiers, avoid standing out too much, and downplay their successes to avoid envy. Third, they should be aware of the types of courtiers and the dangers they pose, since one aggressive, clever courtier with little conscience can dominate the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the three behavior patterns of courtiers in the order Greene gives them.
items: Gain the attention of the leader and ingratiate yourself
Pay great attention to the other courtiers
Be aware of the types of courtiers and their dangers
questions.explain: Greene says the first is ingratiation with leaders, the second is attention to fellow courtiers, and the third is knowing the types of courtiers.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A staff keeps bonding over complaints about a rival firm, and the manager says little about the real differences. According to Greene, why does a group reflexively focus on an enemy?
options: Groups cannot function without a clear business plan
Leaders cannot stay in power without a rival firm
It helps unite the tribe, and the need to belong matters more than the actual differences
The enemy always poses a real and immediate danger
questions.explain: Rival tribes had the positive side effect of uniting a group, and the brain also sorts the world into opposites such as us versus them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene cites Chekhov's observation that common ____ for something unites people more than love, friendship or respect.
questions.explain: Chekhov's remark illustrates why any group reflexively focuses on a hated enemy, real or imagined.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that when we see through the group's picture of its enemy, we should openly display our skepticism to show our independence.
questions.explain: He says not to overtly display skepticism, since we might be seen as disloyal, and to keep our minds open instead so we can resist the overreactions that come from tribal emotions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say about the group enemy?
options: Leaders have long exploited the enemy reflex to justify actions and distract from their own shortcomings
The enemy is always as bad as the group says it is
Learning from the enemy is a sign of disloyalty to be avoided
Any group reflexively focuses on some enemy, real or imagined, to bring the tribe together
The differences between the groups are usually greatly exaggerated
questions.explain: Greene even suggests learning from the enemy by adapting its superior strategies, while detaching from the distortions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the stages of how factions form and grow in the order Greene gives them.
items: We get a narcissistic boost from those who share our values
The group becomes too large and abstract for that boost
We form subgroups with those even more like us
Factions split again from within
A strong faction puts its interests above the group's
questions.explain: Greene describes factions as an unconscious process of group fission that continues until a faction becomes strong enough to favor itself over the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does Greene say elites behave in a group, and what should we do about it?
questions.a: Elites may split into rival factions, but when push comes to shove they usually unite to preserve their status and bend the rules in their favor. In democratic times they pose as acting for the group's greater good, saying that if the elites prosper, so will everyone else. You will never see them lessen their power or make true sacrifices, so we should not fall for their rationalizations and should see this faction for what it is.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A company slowly breaks into cliques, each convinced it best represents the firm's values, and workers care more about their clique than the company. Which dynamic does Greene say this shows?
options: Group rules and codes, kept by an implicit policeman
The group court, formed around a powerful leader
Hypercertainty, driven by an unquestioned plan
Group factions, formed to give members a narcissistic boost
questions.explain: Greene says that in a group above a certain size, members seek smaller subgroups of like-minded people, and strong factions put their interests above the group's.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each example from Greene's discussion of group effects to the idea it illustrates.
pairs: Tulips, South Sea stock and subprime mortgages
The Pentagon and the Vietnam War
An entrenched culture absorbing the leaders who try to change it
Hollywood directors and the producers' notes
A top-down culture that no individual has been able to alter
Isolation showing how much we need the eyes of others
questions.explain: Greene uses each example to show a different way that groups, or the lack of them, shape the individual.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Greene says it makes us more permeable to the group or lowers our permeability.

items.t: Insecurity about our self-worth
Hunger for the group's approval
Needing constant attention to feel validated
Confidence in what makes us unique
Anchoring our self-opinion in our work and accomplishments
Scrutinizing the group's ideas against our own experience

questions.explain: The less certain we are about our worth, the more we blend into the group; raising self-esteem reduces the need for approval.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says our goal must be to lower our permeability to the group by raising our ____.
questions.explain: If we feel strong about our tastes, values and experience, we can more easily resist the group effect.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each piece of Greene's advice to what it is meant to achieve.
pairs: Lower your permeability to the group
Entertain the opposite of the group's view as a thought experiment
See whether going against the grain has value
Keep strategic options and room to maneuver
Understand the group's culture and codes with detachment
questions.explain: Each piece of advice helps us fit in outwardly while keeping inner independence.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene tells us to consider ourselves an ____ studying the strange customs of an alien tribe when we observe our groups.
questions.explain: This detached stance helps us see the group's culture and rules in action and keeps us from trying to change what cannot be changed.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put Greene's two tasks and his closing ideal in the order he gives them.
items: Become a consummate observer of yourself
Become a consummate observer of the groups you belong to
Imagine the reality group
questions.explain: He gives the self-observation task first, the group-observation task second, and then the ideal of the reality group with its upward pull.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What are the two tasks Greene gives the student of human nature, and what is the aim of the second one?
questions.a: The first is to become a consummate observer of yourself in groups, assuming you are less of an individual than you think and raising your self-esteem to lower your permeability. The second is to observe your groups like an anthropologist, looking at their culture, codes and factions and staying unaligned. The aim of the second is to keep as tight a grip on reality as possible, despite group tendencies toward one-sided beliefs, exaggerated enemies and overoptimism.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene calls the group that exerts an upward ____, whose members offer diverse opinions and focus on cooperation, the reality group.
questions.explain: The reality group is the opposite of a group that exerts a downward pull: its minds are open and its focus is on cooperation.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these reasons does Greene give for why the ability to observe and detach from groups is more critical now than ever?
options: We are hungry for the approval of people who share our values and so are more permeable
Social media makes tribes larger and longer-lasting
Groups are now more stable and secure than in the past
Large-scale belief systems have lost power, so we have lost inner security but not the need to belong
We are open to cults and unscrupulous populist leaders who prey on the need to belong
questions.explain: Social media spreads the narrow views of tribes, but those tribes are small and do not last long, so the need to belong goes unsatisfied.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each modern feature Greene names to its effect on tribalism.
pairs: The decline of large-scale belief systems
A loss of inner security, though the need to belong remains
Makes narrow tribal views easy to spread and viral
A greater narcissistic boost but no lasting sense of belonging
Makes tribalism far more dangerous than it was for our ancestors
questions.explain: Greene says that tribalism has ancient roots but now has technological power, which could threaten our extinction.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Greene recommends it or warns against it.

items.t: Outwardly fitting in while inwardly keeping distance
Learning group intelligence
Seeing humanity as one large reality group
Rebelling against the group for its own sake
Denying the social force exists
Seeing our group's enemy as purely evil

questions.explain: Greene wants awareness and detachment together with cooperation, not blind rebellion, blind conformity or tribal hatred.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does every group reflexively focus on an enemy, and how should we respond to this dynamic?
questions.a: Our ancestors feared outsiders, and rival tribes had the positive side effect of uniting the group; the brain also sorts the world into pairs such as us versus them. Leaders have long exploited this reflex to justify almost anything and distract from their shortcomings, and the need to belong outweighs the actual differences, which are exaggerated. We should detach and see the enemy without distortion, hide our skepticism so as not to look disloyal, and even learn from the enemy's superior strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each of Greene's four effects of the group to what it does to us.
pairs: We adopt the group's appearance, ideas, beliefs and values
We exaggerate our agreement and act the part so others accept us
Others' moods can displace our own, fear and anxiety most of all
Doubt is neutralized, so we feel sure and take bigger risks
questions.explain: These are the four effects that Greene describes as the individual effect of the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each group dynamic to its main point in Greene's account.
pairs: Reflects an imagined ideal and the founders, and grows more conservative over time
Implicit standards enforced without active policing
Courtiers compete for the favor of the person on top
Hatred of outsiders helps bind the tribe together
Subgroups give members a narcissistic boost and tend to split again
questions.explain: Greene presents these five patterns as dynamics that human groups fall into almost automatically.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether Greene lists it among the individual effects of the group on us or among the group dynamics.

items.t: Hypercertainty
The need to perform
Emotional contagion
The group court
Group factions
Group rules and codes

questions.explain: The effects describe what happens inside each person, while the dynamics describe the patterns the group as a whole falls into.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which law does Chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group, address?
options: The Law of Envy
The Law of Fickleness
The Law of Aimlessness
The Law of Conformity
questions.explain: The chapter's remedy, resisting the group's pull, answers the problem the law names: the way groups bend our thinking to theirs.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which chapter comes immediately after Chapter 14 in the book?
options: Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose (The Law of Aimlessness)
Chapter 16, See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade (The Law of Aggression)
Chapter 12, Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You (The Law of Gender Rigidity)
Chapter 15, Make Them Want to Follow You (The Law of Fickleness)
questions.explain: After the chapter on how groups pull us down comes the chapter on gaining authority over others.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The title of Chapter 14 says to resist the downward pull of the group. How does the Experiment section lead into the Keys section?
options: It ends by proving that groups never harm anyone
It ends by describing the army's rescue of the school
It ends by proposing a different experiment, detaching from the group, which Keys then equips us for
It ends by telling the reader to leave all groups
questions.explain: After Mao's failed experiment, Greene proposes an experiment of detachment and independent thought, and Keys explains the social force and group dynamics we must understand to carry it out.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene says that when we lose contact with what makes us unique we lose the source of our power. Which earlier chapter does he point back to?
options: Chapter 9, Confront Your Dark Side
Chapter 13, Advance with a Sense of Purpose
Chapter 7, Soften People's Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion
Chapter 3, See Through People's Masks
questions.explain: He refers readers to chapter 13 on our uniqueness and sense of purpose, which links the chapter on following our inner voice to the chapter on the group's pull.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Chapter 14 begins by stating the Law of Conformity and the social personality before it moves to Gao Jianhua's story.
questions.explain: The opening gives the law in brief, then the chapter turns to a long story from the Cultural Revolution and its interpretation.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: The Keys to Human Nature section of Chapter 14 refers readers forward to The Court and Its Courtiers for more on the ideal group that offers an upward pull.
questions.explain: For the ideal group with an upward pull, Greene points to the closing section, The Reality Group; the courtiers section is where he sends us for the types of courtiers.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Chapter 14 begin with Gao Jianhua's story and then move to the Keys section?
questions.a: The story shows in a school how group dynamics play out when authority is removed: conformity, simplistic thinking, new elites, tribal factions and repression. Its interpretation and Understand paragraphs then turn this into a lesson about our own groups and end by proposing a different experiment of detaching from the group. Keys then names the social force and sets out its individual effects and group dynamics, so the reader knows what to observe in order to resist.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the Keys section of Chapter 14 point to the rest of the chapter?
questions.a: It points ahead to the next section, The Court and Its Courtiers, for more on the types of courtiers. It also points to The Reality Group, at the chapter's end, for the ideal of a group with an upward pull, which Greene says we can help create by keeping our individual spirit. It points back to chapter 13 on uniqueness and to chapter 6 for the South Sea bubble.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 14 in order.
items: An Experiment in Human Nature
Keys to Human Nature
The Court and Its Courtiers
The Reality Group
questions.explain: The chapter runs from the story and experiment, to the general principles of the social force, to the types of courtiers, and ends with the ideal group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each section of Chapter 14 to its main focus.
pairs: The Law of Conformity and our social personality in brief
Gao Jianhua's story and Mao's failed experiment
The social force, its individual effects and group dynamics
The types of courtiers found in most courts
The ideal group that exerts an upward pull
questions.explain: Each section builds on the one before it, from story to principles to tactics to the ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort each item by whether it appears in An Experiment in Human Nature or in Keys to Human Nature.

items.t: Teacher Wen condemned for Western fashion
Mao's image of a clean sheet of paper
The Red Guard armbands
The social force and its three elements
Hypercertainty and financial bubbles
The Pentagon and the Vietnam War

questions.explain: The first section tells the story and interprets it, while Keys sets out the general concepts and examples.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The title of Chapter 14 tells us to resist the downward ____ of the group.
questions.explain: The downward pull is the group's drag on our rational, independent thinking, as opposed to the upward pull of a group like the reality group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are sections of Chapter 14?
options: The Narcissistic Spectrum
Strategies for Establishing Authority
The Court and Its Courtiers
An Experiment in Human Nature
The Reality Group
questions.explain: The other two titles belong to other chapters of the book, namely Chapter 2 and Chapter 15.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why is the position of the Favorite dangerous, and what does Greene advise instead?
questions.a: The Favorite's rise rests on a friend-like bond, and the leader's friendly feelings are fickle, so disappointment can flip to hatred. Special treatment makes Favorites arrogant and envied, so their fall is hard, with no skill to fall back on. Greene says to make your power depend on accomplishments and usefulness.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these childhood patterns does Greene link to courtier behavior?
options: A wish to monopolize a parent's attention, leading to a wish to monopolize the leader's
Resentment of siblings, leading to the envious type with passive aggression
A deep need to please parents, leading to the pleaser type
A fear of the dark, leading to the Gatekeeper
questions.explain: Greene's examples are pleasing, envy of siblings, and monopolizing attention. Fear of the dark is not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the steps by which childhood shapes courtier behavior in order.
items: We idealize our parents to feel secure about their power
Authority figures in the court regress us to childhood
Our adaptation to parents and siblings replays in adult form
We fall into a recognizable courtier type
questions.explain: Greene links the court to the family dynamic: the pattern from childhood returns when we face power at work.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Alexander Haig first rise within Henry Kissinger's little court?
options: By outshining Kissinger's academic staff in policy debates
By tailoring himself to Kissinger's needs and doing even the lowliest tasks rather than joining policy arguments
By befriending reporters who then praised him to the president
By exposing Kissinger's weaknesses to Nixon during meetings
questions.explain: Haig could not compete with the brilliant academics, so he stayed out of policy arguments and made himself indispensable by organizing Kissinger's desk and schedule. The dirt on Kissinger only mattered later.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these pieces of advice by whether Greene says to do them or to avoid them.

items.t: Befriend the Punching Bag
Make your power depend on accomplishments
Keep a polite distance from the Shadow Enabler
Stay on good terms with a powerful Gatekeeper
Insulting a known Stirrer
Taking the first step into an Enabler's dubious plan
Imitating the Jester's flamboyant behavior
Joining in the ridicule of the Punching Bag

questions.explain: Each item is advice the author gives for surviving court dynamics.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Gatekeepers are motivated mainly by a secret disdain for the leader.
questions.explain: Gatekeepers are motivated by intense adoration of the person on top, unlike the Intriguer.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Frances Perkins, the consummate Mirrorer, served as secretary of labor under ____.
questions.explain: She read FDR's moods and framed ideas as stories, or as his own earlier thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What signs does Greene say help you identify an Intriguer early?
questions.a: Look past the efficient, loyal, even charming front to the maneuvers and the impatience to rise. Check the past record for intrigue, and notice the little extra zeal to please the boss and become useful. Intriguers make leaders dependent on their efficiency, and when looking at you they think of how to use you.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene warn leaders to beware of Gatekeepers?
options: They spread rumors that turn the group against the leader
They steal the leader's ideas and present them as their own
They tend to isolate the leader from the group, and isolation is dangerous
They push the leader to take reckless risks
questions.explain: Because Gatekeepers monopolize access and filter information to the leader, they cut the leader off from the group. Greene stresses that this isolation is the danger.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What role does the Punching Bag play in a court, and how does Greene say you should respond?
questions.a: In almost every court someone becomes the target everyone laughs at and feels superior to because of supposed incompetence, unorthodox opinions, or lack of sophistication, mostly behind the back. Greene says not to join in, since it coarsens and debases you. Instead see everyone as a potential ally and befriend the Punching Bag.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether they describe the Intriguer or the Gatekeeper.

items.t: Secretly disdains the boss
Aims to take over the leader's power
Plays to the real boss behind the immediate boss's back
Wears a mask of loyalty and efficiency to hide ambition
Motivated by adoration of the leader
Monopolizes the flow of information to the leader
Buffers the leader from petty struggles
Polices the group to follow the leader's ideas

questions.explain: The Intriguer wants the position; the Gatekeeper wants exclusive access to the leader.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these did Frances Perkins do to charm Roosevelt?
options: Challenged his decisions in front of others
Framed recommendations as his own past ideas, slightly modified
Presented ideas with a story line
Referred verbatim to something brilliant he had said
questions.explain: These are all forms of mirroring and listening. Public challenge would run against her method.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are dangers Greene says the Favorite faces?
options: The Favorite's fall is hard, with no one to defend them
The leader's friendly feelings are inevitably fickle
Privileged treatment makes the Favorite arrogant and entitled
Other courtiers are indifferent to the Favorite
questions.explain: The Favorite is envied by other courtiers, not ignored. Fickle feelings, arrogance, and a lonely fall are the dangers Greene names.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each role with its description in Greene's account.
pairs: Has license to poke fun at almost everyone, even the leaders
Allowed to break dress codes and voice wild opinions
Cultivates a personal, friend-like bond with the leader
Target whom everyone feels encouraged to laugh at
questions.explain: The first two are varieties of the Jester; the last two sit at the top and bottom of the court.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The Mirrorer's power is based on the idea that everyone at heart is a ____.
questions.explain: Mirrorers reflect people's own moods and ideas back, making them feel validated.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say is the key risk in dealing with a known Stirrer?
options: Ignoring the Stirrer's rumors lets them spread unchecked
Any sign of disrespect to the Stirrer, who is hypersensitive to it, will bring a passive-aggressive campaign against you
Befriending the Stirrer exposes you to the Stirrer's envy
Challenging the Stirrer in public makes the rest of the court side with you
questions.explain: Although Stirrers are insensitive to those they malign, they are hypersensitive to disrespect toward themselves. Greene therefore advises against insulting them directly or indirectly.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Frances Perkins present a recommendation that might meet resistance from Franklin Roosevelt?
options: She waited for a public crisis to force the issue
She presented hard statistics to overwhelm his objections
She couched it as one of his own earlier ideas, with a slight modification of her own
She had other cabinet members raise it first
questions.explain: Perkins adapted to FDR's moods, told stories, and framed new proposals as extensions of his own thinking. That is mirroring rather than confrontation.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these steps of Alexander Haig's rise in the order they happened.
items: Hired as one of several assistants to Kissinger
Tailored himself to Kissinger's needs and quickly rose
Worked late where Nixon would notice him
Appointed Nixon's chief of staff in 1973
Told reporters he was in control as Reagan's secretary of state
questions.explain: Haig rose through Kissinger's office, caught Nixon's attention, became chief of staff in 1973, and later claimed control after the 1981 shooting of Reagan.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether they describe the Court Jester or the Mirrorer.

items.t: Secretly fears responsibility and failing
Is allowed to voice wild opinions
Has little actual power
Makes others feel comfortable conforming
Reflects back moods and ideas
Confirms the leader's idealized self-image
Appears nonthreatening to other courtiers
Needs to read nonverbal cues well

questions.explain: The Jester is tolerated for comic relief; the Mirrorer succeeds by charming everyone.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, what usually becomes of Shadow Enablers in the end?
options: They retreat into private life with their influence intact
Their careers are generally short and they often serve as the fall guy
They rise to replace the leader they have corrupted
They are promoted to become the leader's Favorite
questions.explain: If what the Enabler advocated or acted on becomes public, the Enabler tends to take the blame. Greene says to take heart that these careers are short.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each court type with the advice Greene gives about it.
pairs: Keep your distance, being neither pawn nor enemy
Never show direct or indirect disrespect
Recognize the power and stay on good terms
Refuse to take the first step into dubious actions
Base power on accomplishments, not friendly feelings
questions.explain: Greene gives each type its own defensive or avoidance advice.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Stirrers are hypersensitive to any disrespect shown toward them.
questions.explain: Even though insensitive to those they malign, they retaliate against perceived disrespect.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each court type with what defines it.
pairs: Seems loyal while secretly despising the boss and amassing power
Spreads rumors and anxieties to stay at the center of the action
Monopolizes access and information to a leader they adore
Draws out the leader's repressed desires and acts on them
Reflects back people's moods and ideas to charm them
questions.explain: Each type has its own method and motive in Greene's account.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say you need in order to play the Mirrorer yourself, and why does it work even when people see through it?
questions.a: You must be a great reader of people, sensitive to nonverbal cues, mirroring their moods and not just their ideas. With leaders, you confirm their idealized opinion of themselves. Even if people see through mirroring, they remain charmed and want more, because those on top are lonelier and more insecure than you imagine.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The ____ Enabler is a courtier who draws out the leader's repressed desires, as Charles Colson did for Nixon.
questions.explain: The Enabler detects the leader's Shadow and gives it a way out, with the Enabler handling everything.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Shadow Enablers typically enjoy long, secure careers beside the leader.
questions.explain: Their careers are generally short, and they often serve as the fall guy when their advice becomes public.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why did Richard Nixon start borrowing Alexander Haig for his own tasks?
options: Haig had written a memo on the Watergate crisis
Haig had flattered Nixon openly in public speeches
Kissinger formally recommended Haig for his war record
Nixon, a workaholic, kept seeing the light on in Haig's office at all hours
questions.explain: Haig made sure he worked in the evenings when Nixon was around to notice, and Nixon admired this. It was a staged display of zeal, not a recommendation or a memo.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each figure with the role Greene assigns.
pairs: National security adviser whose assistant used him
questions.explain: Greene uses these historical figures to illustrate each type.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says there is rarely more than one Jester per court.
questions.explain: Greene says this is the reason you should not imitate the Jester's behavior.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A coworker keeps 'innocently' sharing rumors about a colleague, stirs up worry about vague threats, and is quick to express outrage at others' disloyalty. Which court type does Greene say this most resembles?
options: The Stirrer
The Favorite
The Court Jester
The Intriguer
questions.explain: Stirrers spread rumors and viral anxiety and cover their tracks with hyperrighteous indignation. Greene says to be wary of courtiers who innocently share rumors, since you may be the next target.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say is the secret reason people fall into the Court Jester role?
options: A real desire to challenge the leader's decisions
A fear of responsibility and a dread of failing
A wish to be the leader's closest confidant
A talent for reading the leader's moods
questions.explain: As Jesters they are not taken seriously and have little power, which spares them the stress of getting things done. Their rebelliousness never threatens the status quo.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What are the two varieties of Court Jester, and why does the court keep one around?
questions.a: One is the court cynic and scoffer, who may poke fun at everyone, even the leader. The other is the domesticated rebel, allowed to break dress codes and voice wild opinions. They signal that the leader welcomes dissent, give others a feeling of superiority, and never threaten the status quo, since the Jester fears responsibility.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these figures by whether Greene places them in Nixon's circle or Roosevelt's circle.

items.t: Alexander Haig
Charles Colson
Henry Kissinger
Frances Perkins
Franklin Roosevelt
Richard Nixon

questions.explain: Haig, Colson, and Kissinger worked with Nixon; Perkins was Roosevelt's secretary of labor.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: To avoid the Favorite's fate, Greene says to make your power dependent on your accomplishments and your ____.
questions.explain: Power based on a leader's friendly feelings is fickle, whereas usefulness is lasting.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the Stirrer typically cover his or her tracks?
options: By openly mocking the leader to appear honest
By being hyperrighteous and indignant about the supposed betrayals of others
By volunteering to act as the group's peacemaker
By staying silent in meetings and avoiding all gossip
questions.explain: Greene says Stirrers project such loyalty and devotion that they are hard to suspect, and they use indignation about others' betrayals as cover. Silence or open mockery would not hide what they do.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which court type wears a mask of intense loyalty and efficiency while secretly disdaining the boss and working to amass power?
options: The Mirrorer
The Gatekeeper
The Favorite
The Intriguer
questions.explain: The Intriguer seems the hardest-working and most loyal member of the group, but behind the scenes feels he or she could do the boss's job better. The Gatekeeper, by contrast, adores the leader and does not want to take over.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the Stirrer operate within a court, and how should you treat one?
questions.a: The Stirrer is insecure and envious, so he or she spreads rumors, doubts, and anxieties, often targeting a rival courtier, which puts the Stirrer at the center of the action and closer to the leader. Cover comes from hyperrighteous indignation. Never show the Stirrer disrespect, since Stirrers are hypersensitive to it and retaliate passive-aggressively.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put these court types in the order Greene presents them.
items: The Intriguer
The Stirrer
The Gatekeeper
The Shadow Enabler
The Court Jester
The Mirrorer
questions.explain: Greene's seven types run Intriguer, Stirrer, Gatekeeper, Shadow Enabler, Court Jester, Mirrorer, and then the Favorite and the Punching Bag together.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does the Stirrer infect the group with doubts and anxieties?
options: It tests the loyalty of the other courtiers on the leader's behalf
It forces the leader to hold open meetings about problems
The turmoil puts the Stirrer at the center of the action and may bring him or her closer to the leader
It lets the Stirrer quietly take over the leader's position
questions.explain: The Stirrer is riddled with insecurity and envy and benefits from drama, which brings attention and access to the leader. Taking over the leader's job is the Intriguer's goal, not the Stirrer's.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In Greene's account of the court, which childhood dynamic does courtiers' idealizing of their leaders repeat?
options: Idealizing our parents so as to feel more secure about the power they held over us
Competing with siblings for toys and then pretending to share them
Copying older children in order to be accepted into their games
Rebelling against parental rules in order to test where the limits lay
questions.explain: Greene says we idealized our parents because it was too frightening to see them as weak, and dealing with authority figures in the court regresses us to that state. The other options are not the pattern he names.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are things Greene says about the Court Jester?
options: Leaders tolerate the Jester because it shows a lack of insecurity
There is rarely more than one per court
The Jester's rebelliousness seriously threatens the status quo
The Jester secretly fears responsibility and failing
questions.explain: The Jester is tolerated and has little real power. Rebelliousness that never challenges the status quo is the point.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: A manager's assistant praises the boss's genius constantly, screens out annoying colleagues, and is the only person who sees the boss's calendar. Which court type does this most resemble?
options: The Mirrorer
The Court Jester
The Gatekeeper
The Stirrer
questions.explain: Gatekeepers rise through fawning and by monopolizing access and information, buffering the leader from petty struggles. A Mirrorer reflects moods to many people, not to one leader alone.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are among the court types Greene describes?
options: The Peacemaker
The Gatekeeper
The Court Jester
The Whistleblower
The Shadow Enabler
questions.explain: Greene's seven types include the Intriguer, Stirrer, Gatekeeper, Shadow Enabler, Court Jester, Mirrorer, and the Favorite and Punching Bag. He does not describe a Whistleblower or a Peacemaker.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Gatekeepers ingratiate themselves with leaders by giving them a great deal of narcissistic ____.
