questions.explain: By supplying admiration and flattery, Gatekeepers bind leaders and gain exclusive access.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which weaknesses of Richard Nixon did Charles Colson play upon?
options: Loneliness and a craving for a close personal friend
Paranoia about enemies and insecurity about his own masculinity
Vanity about his war record and a fear of public speaking
Boredom with routine duties and a wish to retire
questions.explain: Nixon felt surrounded by enemies and wanted to punish them and display some swagger. Colson let him vent and then suggested revenge schemes, which also let Colson live out his own Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each childhood pattern with the courtier behavior Greene links to it.
pairs: A deep need to please parents
Resenting siblings who drew parental attention
Becoming the envious type, with passive aggression
Trying to monopolize a parent's attention
Wanting to monopolize the leader's attention
questions.explain: Greene says courtiers fall into types depending on deep patterns stemming from childhood.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In Nixon's court, Alexander Haig epitomized the ____ type, loyal on the surface but secretly seeking power.
questions.explain: Haig stayed away from policy arguments, tailored himself to Kissinger, and rose from within.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise in dealing with a Shadow Enabler?
options: Maintain a polite distance
Join in gradually to gain influence over the Enabler
Protect your clean reputation
Do not take the first step into dubious actions
questions.explain: Greene says your clean reputation is the most important thing you possess, so keep your distance. Joining in is the opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In the court there is almost always a ____ Bag, a person everyone feels encouraged to laugh at and feel superior to.
questions.explain: Greene advises against joining in, and suggests befriending that person.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Describe how the Shadow Enabler works on a leader and what the example of Charles Colson shows.
questions.a: The Enabler senses the leader's repressed desires, raises taboo topics jokingly, and then proposes ways to act on them while handling the details. Colson played on Nixon's paranoia and sexual insecurity, letting him vent and then suggesting revenge schemes. Such types often become the fall guy, and you should refuse their first dubious step and keep a polite distance.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene recommends that you follow the Court Jester's example and show your rebelliousness openly.
questions.explain: Greene advises keeping rebellion subtle and saving nonconformity for private life or until you have more power.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Explain how the Gatekeeper gains and uses power, and what Greene advises both courtiers and leaders to do.
questions.a: The Gatekeeper idealizes the leader, supplies narcissistic supply, and monopolizes access and information, buffering the leader from petty struggles and learning the leader's weaknesses. Once installed, such types can cut anyone off. Courtiers should recognize their power and stay on good terms, while leaders should beware, since the Gatekeeper isolates them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Describe how Alexander Haig rose in Nixon's court and what Greene advises about dealing with the Intriguer type.
questions.a: Haig made himself indispensable to Kissinger through lowly service, then won Nixon's notice by working late where Nixon would see, and became chief of staff in 1973. Greene says to look behind the loyal, efficient front at the maneuvers and the extra zeal, and to keep your distance so you are neither a pawn nor an enemy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: On what idea does the Mirrorer's power rest?
options: That everyone secretly distrusts those in power
That everyone at heart is a narcissist
That flattery is the surest way to win favor
That groups reward the courtier who disagrees most
questions.explain: Mirrorers reflect back people's own moods and ideas so that they feel validated without sensing manipulation. Greene contrasts this with overt flattery, which people can see through.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say the Favorite's fall from grace is so hard and painful?
options: The Favorite is always blamed for the leader's mistakes
The leader publicly humiliates the Favorite
The Favorite has made open enemies of the Gatekeeper
No one defends the Favorite, and the rise did not depend on any special skill, so there is nowhere else to go
questions.explain: The Favorite is envied, grows arrogant, and relies on the leader's fickle friendly feelings. Greene's remedy is to rest your power on accomplishments and usefulness instead.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What motivates the Gatekeeper, in contrast to the Intriguer?
options: A hidden belief that he or she could do the leader's job better
A desire to expose weak courtiers to the leader
A fear of responsibility and of failing
Intense adoration of the person on top, not a secret disdain for others
questions.explain: Greene says the Gatekeeper may use people like the Intriguer does, but wants exclusive access to the leader, not the leader's power. The disdain and the urge to take over belong to the Intriguer.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says courtiers tend to see their leaders as smarter and more perfect than they are.
questions.explain: The idealizing makes fawning easier to justify and echoes childhood idealizing of parents.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the Favorite's typical trajectory in order.
items: Acts relaxed and chummy with the leader
The leader shares secrets and bestows favors
Other courtiers grow envious
The Favorite becomes arrogant and entitled
The leader tires and the Favorite falls hard
questions.explain: The Favorite's rise depends on a friendly bond, and the privileges that follow breed envy and arrogance, which end in a painful fall.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Frances Perkins serve as a model Mirrorer in Roosevelt's court?
questions.a: She sensed Roosevelt's moods and adapted to them, presented ideas as stories, listened closely and quoted him later, and framed proposals as modified versions of his own ideas. She confirmed his noble image of himself, and presented herself as nonthreatening to other courtiers so they did not envy her influence.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, the Mirrorer's power rests mainly on overt flattery of the leader.
questions.explain: The Mirrorer reflects back moods and ideas instead of using overt flattery, which people can see through.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does the Intriguer do, according to Greene?
options: Openly criticizes the boss in meetings
Hides disdain for the boss behind a mask of loyalty
Makes leaders dependent on his or her efficiency
Works late when the real boss will notice
questions.explain: Intriguers conceal their contempt, show zeal for those who matter, and bind others through efficiency. Open criticism would reveal the very disdain they hide.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the Gatekeeper's motive differ from the Intriguer's, and why might they still be confused?
questions.a: Both may use people to reach the leader. But the Intriguer secretly holds the boss in contempt and wants to take over power. The Gatekeeper is driven by adoration of the leader and wants exclusive access to, and control over, the flow of information to the leader, not the leader's position.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, do courtiers tend to fall into recognizable types, and what do the idealizing and regressing have to do with it?
questions.a: Courtiers idealize those in power, as we idealized our parents to feel secure, and authority figures in the court regress us to the family dynamic. How we adapted to our parents' power and to our siblings replays in adult form, so deep childhood patterns, such as the need to please or resentment of siblings, shape the type we become.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the Shadow Enabler's approach to a leader in the order Greene describes.
items: Broach taboo subjects in a jocular, nonthreatening way
The leader falls into the spirit and opens up
Suggest actions that let the leader vent frustrations
Handle everything and serve as the leader's protection
questions.explain: The Enabler first gets contact with the leader's Shadow and then moves to action, with the Enabler managing the details.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does the Shadow Enabler first make contact with a leader's repressed desires?
options: By criticizing the leader's closest advisers in private
By offering formal advice on how to manage public scandals
By broaching somewhat taboo subjects in a nonthreatening, jocular way
By reporting on the group's mood in written memos
questions.explain: Greene says the Enabler begins with jokey conversation about taboo topics, and once the leader opens up, moves on to suggesting actions. Serious advice or memos would not draw out the Shadow.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: One variety of Court Jester is the domesticated ____, allowed to break the dress code and offer wild opinions.
questions.explain: Such nonconformists prove that the leader appears to encourage a free exchange of opinions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Dealing with authority figures in the court tends to ____ us to our childhood and the family dynamic.
questions.explain: Greene says the way we adapted to our parents and siblings replays in adult form in the court.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The Stirrer is quite insensitive to the feelings of those they malign, but is hypersensitive to any sign of ____ toward themselves.
questions.explain: This is why Greene says not to insult or show disrespect to a known Stirrer.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says courtiers will tend to ____ those in power, seeing them as smarter and more perfect than they are.
questions.explain: Idealizing leaders makes it easier to justify fawning behavior and mirrors how we idealized our parents.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these descriptions by whether they fit the Favorite or the Punching Bag.

items.t: Cultivates a friend-like relationship with the leader
Receives secrets and favors
Becomes arrogant and entitled
Is envied by other courtiers
Is laughed at, mostly behind the back
Is seen as incompetent or unsophisticated
Lets others feel superior
Is best befriended to take the fun out of the cruel game

questions.explain: These roles occupy the highest and lowest rungs of the court.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene advise about copying the Court Jester's flamboyant nonconformity?
options: Do so only in meetings, where wild opinions are always welcome
Do so as long as there are several Jesters already in the court
Do so openly, because leaders reward visible independence
Do not; keep any rebelliousness subtle and save it for private life or until you have more power
questions.explain: Greene notes there is rarely more than one Jester per court, and that modern courts tolerate differences in appearance more than in ideas. The Jester's license does not extend to you.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these approaches to lieutenants by whether Greene favors or rejects them.

items.t: Selecting for competence
Weighing character
Choosing people with skills you lack
Diverse temperaments and ideas
Hiring for charm
Hiring friends
Keeping brilliant but poisonous personalities
Special privileges for favorites

questions.explain: The standards he favors build a capable, equal team; the ones he rejects breed politics.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises choosing lieutenants mainly for their charm and personal friendship.
questions.explain: He says not to base selection on charm and never to hire friends.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each productive emotion or habit with what Greene says about it.
pairs: Helps players execute and not overreact, as Phil Jackson found
Not upset by setbacks; keeps advancing and working on problems
Should stem from a track record, not slip into grandiosity
Makes members less defensive and more independent in thought
questions.explain: These items are all drawn from the fourth strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the steps by which a bubble forms around a leader in order.
items: Lieutenants try to ease the leader's burdens
They isolate the leader and filter the information
They tell the leader what they think will please
The leader's perspective on reality becomes distorted
The leader's decisions reflect the distortion
questions.explain: Greene warns this is the slow, unnoticed danger as the group evolves.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say creates a functional, healthy group dynamic?
options: The group's ability to maintain a tight relationship to reality
A charismatic leader who inspires loyalty
A strict hierarchy with clear rewards for the loyal
A culture of friendly competition among members
questions.explain: Greene defines the reality group by its grip on reality: it exists to get things done, has particular resources, and works in a competitive, changing environment.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In a dysfunctional culture, why do people begin to form factions?
options: They have been ordered by the leader to compete
They are confused about roles and direction, so they think more of their own interests and status
They want to protect a failing leader from criticism
They have too many resources and too little work
questions.explain: Amid confusion, people turn to their own agendas, grow touchy about status, and obsess over who is getting more. Greene links this to the rise of bad apples.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, what role should making money or being successful play for a group with a collective purpose?
options: An embarrassing topic to avoid altogether
The main goal that the ideal supports
The reward for the leader alone
A natural result of the ideal, not the goal itself
questions.explain: The ideal is excellence and creating something of the highest possible quality. Success should follow from it.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each strategy with its core idea.
pairs: Instill a collective sense of purpose
A clearly stated ideal that is practiced, not just preached
Assemble the right team of lieutenants
Competence and character over charm, with equal treatment
Let information and ideas flow freely
Unfiltered, diverse information, as Napoleon gathered
Infect the group with productive emotions
Spreading calm, resolution, and grounded confidence
Gauging inner toughness through challenge before a crisis
questions.explain: Each strategy addresses a different part of the group's health.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the steps in Greene's argument at the start of the Reality Group section in order.
items: A group fails and blame falls on individuals
The real fault is the group's dysfunctional dynamic
We must shift focus from individuals to the overall dynamic
A healthy dynamic depends on a tight relationship to reality
This ideal is named the reality group
questions.explain: Greene diagnoses the problem before offering the ideal and the strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each problem with the consequence Greene describes.
pairs: People turn to their own agendas and form factions
The leader's mind is clouded by details and courtier battles
The leader's view of reality becomes distorted
Mediocrity rises to become the lieutenants
questions.explain: Greene shows how each failing of the group erodes its grip on reality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How did Phil Jackson differ from many other coaches, according to Greene?
options: He instilled calmness rather than revving the team up and getting them excited or angry
He demanded total obedience to the game plan
He rotated players to avoid favoritism
He avoided talking about opponents
questions.explain: Jackson found that calmness helped players execute the game plan and not overreact to the ups and downs of the game. Greene presents this as a productive emotion a leader can spread.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which standards does Greene give for the team of lieutenants?
options: Skills you lack
Willingness to speak up and take initiative
Competence for the job
Personal charm
Diversity of temperament and ideas
questions.explain: Charm is explicitly rejected as a basis for selection. The other standards match his advice for a diverse, capable, speaking-up team.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does the fourth strategy mean by infecting the group with productive emotions?
questions.a: People in groups are permeable to moods, and especially the leader's. The leader should spread calmness, as Phil Jackson did, keep the group on concrete tasks, show resolution in setbacks, and show confidence grounded in a track record rather than grandiosity. Changing routines and showing openness and lack of fear make members less defensive and more independent in thought.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the typical first reaction when a group fails in some enterprise?
options: To disband the group and start afresh
To look at the individuals involved and affix blame
To reduce the group's resources
To examine the group's overall dynamic
questions.explain: Greene says groups blame an overambitious leader, an incompetent lieutenant, or a shrewd adversary, and may fire people. This leaves the real cause untouched.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What danger does the third strategy address, and how does Napoleon illustrate the remedy?
questions.a: The danger is a bubble forming around the leader as lieutenants filter information and tell the leader what will please. The remedy is open communication up and down the line. Napoleon reviewed concise reports from everyone down to the foot soldiers, and their diversity gave him a clear picture.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why should a leader avoid signaling a preference during group discussions?
options: It encourages the group to blame the leader afterward
It makes the leader look indecisive
It shortens the discussion too much
It will subtly tip the team into following the leader's lead
questions.explain: Greene wants lively meetings with a diversity of opinions and little worry about bruised egos. A visible preference narrows the deliberation and weakens the group's connection to reality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these practices by whether they belong to the collective-purpose strategy or the battle-tested-group strategy.

items.t: Publicize a clear mission
Remind the group of its mission
Practice what you preach
Give shorter deadlines than usual
Lead the team into a novel, slightly riskier action
Review people's inner strength after a crisis

questions.explain: The first strategy builds shared purpose; the fifth tests the group under stress.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these habits by whether they keep the leader connected to reality or distort the leader's view.

items.t: Reading concise reports from all levels
Transparency about how decisions were made
Frank discussion up and down the line
Self-criticism focused on the group, not scapegoats
Lieutenants who filter what the leader hears
Signaling the leader's preferred option in meetings
Hurried decisions on highly filtered information
Blaming scapegoats after failure

questions.explain: Greene stresses diverse, unfiltered information and honest review.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The leader's greatest obstacle to focusing on the larger picture is the fear of ____ authority.
questions.explain: Micromanaging clouds the leader's mind and the confusion filters down through the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says a group's confidence should mostly stem from a successful track record.
questions.explain: This keeps confidence from slipping into grandiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these into productive and counterproductive emotional states for a group.

items.t: Calmness
Resolution after setbacks
Confidence from a track record
Openness to new ideas
Hysteria at slight shifts in fortune
Anger whipped up before a game
Confidence that has slipped into grandiosity
Complacency after success

questions.explain: Greene wants leaders to spread the first four and guard against the rest.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: With high esprit de corps, a group will ____ itself, isolating those who are petty and all about ego.
questions.explain: Members who share a purpose notice and isolate ego-driven colleagues.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Phil Jackson tried to rev up his players before games to make them excited and angry.
questions.explain: Jackson noticed that other coaches did this but found calmness more productive.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says a true reality group is a rare occurrence in history.
questions.explain: He says we see it to some degree in a few famous cases.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as examples of groups that approached the reality group ideal?
options: Napoleon Bonaparte's battalions
The Chicago Bulls under Phil Jackson
The early years of IBM under Thomas Watson
Nixon's White House staff
questions.explain: Greene also names Roosevelt's initial cabinet and John Ford's film team. Nixon's court appears as a source of court types, not as a reality group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene warns that a leader's confidence must not slip into ____.
questions.explain: Confidence should stem from a successful track record.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say will destroy the effort to instill a collective purpose?
options: Rewarding results more than effort
Letting the mission change in any way
Any hypocrisy or noticeable gap between the stated ideal and the group's reality
Publicizing the mission too widely
questions.explain: Greene says the group must practice what it preaches and build a track record of results that match the ideal. He does allow the mission to be adapted, as long as the group does not drift from its core.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, replacing a failed leader and lieutenants is usually enough to prevent the same failure from recurring.
questions.explain: The dysfunctional dynamic stays and infects the replacements, so the problem returns.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these features by whether they belong to a dysfunctional group or the reality group.

items.t: Members form factions around status
Mediocrity is rewarded
Leaders are surrounded by flattering courtiers
Politics thrives and the work suffers
Primary emphasis is on the work itself
A tight relationship to reality
Members feel an upward pull
A clearly stated shared mission

questions.explain: The first three belong with the dysfunctional pattern; the other five belong with the reality group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What is the reality group, and what three facts about reality does it stay in touch with?
questions.a: It is Greene's ideal group, with a tight relationship to reality. It exists to get things done, make things, and solve problems. It has resources, the labor and strengths of its members and its finances. It operates in an environment that is competitive and constantly changing. Putting the work first, it can accomplish ten times more than a dysfunctional group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are productive emotions or attitudes Greene wants the leader to spread?
options: Resolution in the face of setbacks
Anger before key moments
Openness and a lack of fear
Calmness
questions.explain: Greene contrasts calmness with other coaches' practice of getting players excited or angry. Openness and lack of fear make members less defensive.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How should a leader run discussions and handle mistakes to keep information flowing, according to Greene?
questions.a: Encourage frank, lively meetings with diverse opinions, avoid signaling a preference, and bring in experts and outsiders. Be transparent about how and why decisions were made. After failures, let the group criticize its own functioning without scapegoats, so that it keeps learning and becomes more confident.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Napoleon Bonaparte personally reviewed concise ____ sent by everyone down the chain of command, including foot soldiers.
questions.explain: The diversity of the reports gave him several lines of perspective.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the typical cycle of group failure and recurrence in order.
items: The group looks at the actors and affixes blame
The leader or lieutenants are fired and a new team is brought in
A few lessons are shared and everyone feels satisfied
Years later nearly the same failure recurs
questions.explain: Because the dynamic is untouched, the recycled solutions fail to prevent a repeat.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says a healthy group puts its primary emphasis on the work itself.
questions.explain: Not wasting time on political games, such a group can accomplish ten times more.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does nearly the same failure recur years after a group fires its leader or lieutenants?
options: The group's rivals learn to exploit its mistakes
The replacements are chosen for the same personal flaws
Lessons from the first failure are never shared
The dysfunctional dynamic of the group remains and produces incompetent lieutenants and grandiose leaders
questions.explain: Greene says the next leaders are simply infected and transformed by the dysfunctional culture. The lessons are shared, but they do not touch the dynamic.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are ways Greene suggests to find out a team's inner toughness?
options: Wait for a real crisis and then see
Give some members challenging tasks or shorter deadlines
Lead the team into a novel, slightly riskier action
Review people's reactions after crises or failures
questions.explain: Greene wants to gauge strength before a crisis arrives, and then use real crises as further reviews.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are among Greene's five strategies for building a reality group?
options: Forge a battle-tested group
Rotate the leadership regularly
Instill a collective sense of purpose
Let information and ideas flow freely
questions.explain: The other two strategies are assembling the right team of lieutenants and infecting the group with productive emotions. Rotating leaders is not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How does a dysfunctional culture come to reward mediocrity and produce grandiose leaders?
questions.a: Confusion about roles and direction leads members to pursue their own interests, form factions, and obsess over status. Bad apples such as Stirrers stir trouble, and those who excel at politics rise to become lieutenants. Leaders, dragged down, surround themselves with courtiers who tell them what they want to hear and encourage grandiose plans.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each of Greene's lieutenant-selection or team-management guidelines with its content.
pairs: Skills you lack, in diverse temperaments
Equal treatment, with no special privileges
The leader shares in them as much as any member
questions.explain: These are all part of the second strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene call the leader's greatest obstacle to focusing on the larger picture?
options: A preference for fast decisions
A lack of any strong personal ambition
The fear of delegating authority, which leads to micromanaging
Too many outside advisers
questions.explain: Micromanaging clouds the leader's mind with details and with battles among courtiers, and the confusion then filters down. Hence the second strategy: cultivate trusted lieutenants.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Phil Jackson found it more productive to instill a sense of ____ in his players than to rev them up.
questions.explain: Calm helped players execute the game plan and avoid overreacting.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What do leaders in a dysfunctional group do when they feel vulnerable and dragged down by dissension?
options: Withdraw from all major decisions
Hand authority to the most competent lieutenants
Open the group's decisions to outside review
Surround themselves with courtiers who tell them what they want to hear
questions.explain: Inside this court cocoon, leaders hatch ill-conceived, grandiose plans that the spineless courtiers encourage. This connects the two halves of the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the five strategies for building a reality group in the order Greene gives them.
items: Instill a collective sense of purpose
Assemble the right team of lieutenants
Let information and ideas flow freely
Infect the group with productive emotions
Forge a battle-tested group
questions.explain: Greene says the strategies should all be put into practice, and he presents them in this sequence.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these are features of a dysfunctional group culture, according to Greene?
options: Mediocrity that is preferred and rewarded
Confusion about roles and overall direction
Factions and touchy egos obsessed with who gets more
A clearly stated and practiced mission
questions.explain: A clear mission is a mark of the reality group. The other three are described as the dysfunctional pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says that what is really at fault in a repeated group failure is the dysfunctional ____ of the group.
questions.explain: Firing individuals changes nothing because the next ones are transformed by the same dysfunctional culture.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why should a leader give members challenging tasks or short deadlines before a real crisis?
options: To keep members too busy for politics
To make sure the group's finances can absorb losses
To punish low performers early
To gauge people's inner toughness, since stress reveals a side of them that daily work hides
questions.explain: Greene says people can seem motivated in day-to-day work and then disconnect or become anxious under pressure. Those who rise to the occasion are a treasure to hoard.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does Greene say about the link between group dynamics and the psychological health of individuals?
questions.a: People focus on the health of individuals, but a dysfunctional group can make individuals unstable and neurotic. The opposite is also true: taking part in a high-functioning reality group makes us healthy and whole. We learn to cooperate on a higher level, develop empathy, gain confidence, and feel connected to reality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each leader with the group Greene cites as approaching the reality group ideal.
pairs: The film team that worked with him for decades
questions.explain: Greene says that a true reality group is rare, and these are the examples he cites.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Describe the typical cycle after a group fails, and why Greene says the problem comes back.
questions.a: The group blames the actors, fires the leader or lieutenants, shares a few lessons, and feels ready to move on. Years later nearly the same failure recurs. The real fault is the dysfunctional dynamic of the group, which produces incompetent lieutenants and grandiose leaders, so unless it is fixed the problems return with different faces.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What social force does the first strategy tell the leader to capture and channel for a higher purpose?
options: The fear of being dismissed
The desire to outdo rivals within the group
The wish for money and recognition
The urge that makes people want to belong and fit in
questions.explain: Greene wants the group's conformist pull put to work for a clearly stated ideal. The ideal must be real, because members must see it practiced.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The fifth strategy is to forge a ____-tested group, one that has been through a few wars.
questions.explain: Such a group welcomes obstacles and feels an upward pull to meet challenges.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which examples does Greene give of near-reality groups, and what warning does he give about inheriting a dysfunctional culture?
questions.a: He cites Napoleon's battalions, early IBM under Thomas Watson, Franklin Roosevelt's initial cabinet, John Ford's film team, and the Chicago Bulls under Phil Jackson, noting a true reality group is rare. If you inherit a set dysfunctional culture, the job is harder and slower: be resolute and patient, treat the dynamic as the enemy, and take care that it does not assimilate you.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene say the leader must watch for the group's slow formation of a bubble, and how does this tie back to the court?
questions.a: Lieutenants trying to ease the leader's burdens can isolate the leader and filter information, so the leader hears what pleases and the perspective on reality slowly distorts. This is the court dynamic of Gatekeepers and flattering courtiers. Greene's remedy is to treat open communication of ideas and information as the lifeblood of the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the steps of testing a group's toughness, from the fifth strategy, in order.
items: Give some members challenging tasks or shorter deadlines
Lead the team into a novel, slightly riskier action
Observe how individuals react to the chaos and uncertainty
Use crises as a chance to review inner strength
Expand the limits of what you ask of the group
questions.explain: Greene wants testing before and after crises, and a battle-tested group can then be asked for more.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Making money or being successful should be a natural ____ of the group's ideal, not the goal itself.
questions.explain: The ideal is excellence and creating something of the highest possible quality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Explain the first strategy, instilling a collective sense of purpose.
questions.a: The leader captures the urge to belong and fit in and channels it into a clearly stated, publicized ideal, emphasizing excellence, with money and success as results. The group must practice what it preaches, since hypocrisy destroys the effort. Members feel part of something important, so the group polices itself and has fewer factions.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The ideal group that maintains a tight relationship to reality is what Greene calls the ____ group.
questions.explain: Its primary emphasis is on the work itself rather than on political games.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Explain the fifth strategy, forging a battle-tested group.
questions.a: Stress reveals what daily work hides, so the leader tests members with challenging tasks and short deadlines and with novel, slightly riskier actions, and reviews inner strength after crises. Those who rise to the occasion are a treasure, and a few fearful types can be tolerated. A group that has been through a few wars can be asked for more and feels an upward pull.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Greene says to select lieutenants for competence and character, and never to hire ____.
questions.explain: Charm and friendship are poor standards for choosing the team.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which standards does Greene give for choosing lieutenants?
options: The most loyal people, whatever their skills
The most competent people with good character, not the most charming, and never friends
The people who have served longest
People similar in temperament to the leader
questions.explain: Charm and friendship are rejected, and Greene also warns that brilliant people with poisonous egos drain the group's spirit. He wants diversity of skills, temperament, and ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of these does Greene recommend to keep information flowing to the leader?
options: Share how and why decisions were made
Encourage frank discussion up and down the line
Let lieutenants filter reports to save time
Bring in experts and outsiders
questions.explain: Filtering by lieutenants is the cause of the bubble Greene warns about. Transparency and outside voices broaden the group's connection to reality.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: The first strategy for building a reality group is to instill a collective sense of ____.
questions.explain: A clearly stated, positive mission unites the members.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Put the stages of the way a dysfunctional culture degrades a group in order.
items: Members are confused about roles and direction
People pursue their own agendas and form factions
Bad apples stir trouble and politicians rise to be lieutenants
Leaders surround themselves with flattering courtiers
Leaders hatch grandiose plans that are encouraged
questions.explain: Greene traces how confusion leads to politics, mediocrity, and finally a leader in a cocoon.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What gave Napoleon Bonaparte a clear picture of his army and the enemy?
options: Several lines of unfiltered information, from concise reports sent by people all the way down the chain of command
Personal inspection of every unit before a battle
Intelligence gathered by a network of spies
Daily summaries compiled by his chief of staff
questions.explain: He personally reviewed short reports from field marshals down to foot soldiers, and their diversity gave him perspective. He kept the number manageable.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does Greene advise periodically changing the group's routines or giving it something new and challenging?
options: To reduce the leader's workload
To test which lieutenants are loyal
To wake the group from the complacency that can settle in after success
To keep members from learning each other's roles
questions.explain: A group that succeeds can grow complacent. Surprise and challenge bring it back to attention.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: Greene says being in a dysfunctional group can actually make individuals unstable and neurotic.
questions.explain: The reverse is also true: a high-functioning reality group can make individuals healthy and whole.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: What does the second strategy say about assembling a team of lieutenants?
questions.a: The leader must avoid micromanaging by delegating to trusted lieutenants imbued with the group's purpose. They are chosen for competence and character, not charm, and never friends. They have complementary skills and diverse temperaments, speak up, and are treated equally with no special privileges. The leader shares sacrifices and removes those who do not live up to the ideal.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Who tends to thrive and rise to the top in a dysfunctional culture?
options: The members who speak most frankly
Those who excel at schmoozing and playing politics but little else
The newest recruits with fresh ideas
The most technically brilliant members
questions.explain: Greene says that mediocrity is preferred and rewarded in such a culture. Lieutenants who play politics rise, and capable but unpolitical people do not.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each law with the chapter title Greene gives it.
pairs: Advance with a Sense of Purpose
Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
Make Them Want to Follow You
See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Facade
questions.explain: Chapters 13 to 16 run in this order. Chapter 14 comes after the chapter on purpose and before the chapter on authority.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which earlier chapters does Greene explicitly cite in the court and reality group sections?
options: Chapter 12, on gender
Chapter 4, on judging character
Chapter 7, on persuasion
Chapter 9, on the Shadow
questions.explain: The Shadow Enabler points to chapter 9, and selecting lieutenants points to chapter 4. The others are not cited in these sections.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: When describing the Shadow Enabler, Greene sends readers back to an earlier chapter on which law?
options: The Law of Repression, from the chapter on confronting your dark side
The Law of Envy, from the chapter on the fragile ego
The Law of Grandiosity, from the chapter on knowing your limits
The Law of Role-playing, from the chapter on masks
questions.explain: The Enabler works on the leader's Shadow, the repressed side that chapter 9 explains. The other laws are related to themes in the court but are not the cross-reference.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which of the court types in this chapter echo themes from earlier chapters of the book, and how?
questions.a: The Stirrer acts out resentment and envy, a theme of the chapter on envy. The Shadow Enabler works on the leader's repressed Shadow, which Greene cites from chapter 9. The Mirrorer relies on the narcissism in everyone, and the Gatekeeper supplies narcissistic supply. The court is thus the earlier laws of human nature at work in groups.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Chapter 14 is built around the Law of ____.
questions.explain: Its law is conformity, which is why the chapter speaks of the downward pull of the group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Why does the chapter end with the Reality Group after the section on the court?
options: It argues that all groups should be avoided
It shows how a leader can replace the downward pull of the group with an upward pull
It turns to the leader's own Shadow
It repeats the same types in a more detailed way
questions.explain: The court shows how group dynamics drag people down; the Reality Group shows what a healthy dynamic looks like and how to build one. The chapter title promises a way to resist the downward pull.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: True or false: In chapter 14, the section on the Reality Group comes before the section on the court and its courtiers.
questions.explain: The court comes first and shows the downward pull; the Reality Group closes the chapter with the remedy.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: How do the two sections covered here, the court and the reality group, relate to the chapter's title about the downward pull of the group?
questions.a: The court shows the downward pull in action: leaders idealized, courtiers of several types scheming and flattering, and a dysfunctional dynamic. The reality group is the remedy: a leader shapes a group tied to reality so that it produces an upward pull instead. Together they move from diagnosis to prescription.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Match each court type with the earlier theme of the book that it echoes.
pairs: The Stirrer's resentment of what others have
The Enabler's work on the leader's hidden desires
The Mirrorer's reliance on everyone's self-love
questions.explain: The court types are earlier laws of human nature at work in a group.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: In chapter 14, which section directly follows the one on the court and its courtiers?
options: Keys to Human Nature
The Reality Group
An Experiment in Human Nature
The Inner Authority
questions.explain: The chapter's four sections run: An Experiment in Human Nature, Keys to Human Nature, The Court and Its Courtiers, The Reality Group. The last is the constructive counterpart to the court.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Which law gives chapter 14, Resist the Downward Pull of the Group, its theme?
options: The Law of Conformity
The Law of Aimlessness
The Law of Fickleness
The Law of Aggression
questions.explain: Chapter 14 is built around conformity. Aimlessness is chapter 13's law, and fickleness is chapter 15's law, on making people want to follow you.

questions.unitTitle: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group
questions.q: Sort these features of the chapter by whether they belong with the downward pull or the upward pull of the group.

items.t: A Stirrer spreading rumors
A Favorite's arrogance
Courtiers telling a leader only what pleases
Ridicule of a Punching Bag
A shared mission people believe in
Open flow of information
A battle-tested team
Calm and resolute emotions

questions.explain: The court produces the downward pull; the reality group is the remedy that produces the upward pull.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the opening statement of the Law of Fickleness, what mixed wish does Greene say people have about those who lead them?
options: They want to be led but also to feel free
They want to be led but also to be consulted on every decision
They want a strong ruler but also a ruler who stays out of sight
They want to be equals but also to be rewarded like the leader
questions.explain: The opening says people are always ambivalent about those in power: they want to be led yet feel free. Consultation and equal rewards are not the pair Greene names.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to the opening of the Law of Fickleness, what happens if a leader tries to win loyalty by seeming to be the group's equal or friend?
options: People stay loyal but grow bored with the leader's ordinary manner
People feel respected but start to demand a share of the leader's power
People relax, work harder, and give the leader more affection
People doubt the leader's strength, grow suspicious of motives, and feel hidden contempt
questions.explain: Greene warns against the prejudice of the times that leaders must look like friends; the result is doubt, suspicion, and hidden contempt rather than loyalty.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In the opening of the Law of Fickleness, Greene defines authority as the delicate art of creating the appearance of power, legitimacy, and fairness while getting people to identify with you as a leader in their service.
questions.explain: This is the definition given in the opening. Note it blends strength (power, legitimacy) with a sense of serving the group.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the opening, Greene says that once you have gained people's ____, they will stand by you as their leader no matter the bad circumstances.
questions.explain: The payoff of mastered authority is trust that survives setbacks, in contrast to the fickle support a leader gets from mere position.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does the opening of the Law of Fickleness say about people's attitude toward a leader?
options: They stay devoted as long as the leader acts like one of them
They want protection and prosperity without making sacrifices
They both worship the king and want to kill him
They are ready to turn on a leader who seems weak or has a setback
questions.explain: Greene lists ready-to-turn-on, worship-and-kill, and wanting protection without sacrifice. The friend-like leader is exactly the strategy he says fails.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene say a person who wants to lead must do, and when should they begin?
questions.a: Greene says you must master the art of authority: creating the appearance of power, legitimacy and fairness while getting people to identify with you as a leader who serves them. You must learn it early in life, because once trust is earned people stand by you even in bad circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the story of Elizabeth's coronation procession, what did the English see that they had never witnessed in a monarch?
options: A queen who handed out money to every petitioner
A queen who rode in silence to show her semidivine status
A queen who seemed to enjoy mingling and listened to the poorest Londoners
A queen who refused all pageants to show her seriousness
questions.explain: Unlike distant, pomp-surrounded monarchs, Elizabeth wept and listened to petitions in a natural, folksy manner, which charmed the crowd.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, what was William Cecil's plan for the new queen's rule?
options: He would rule openly as regent until she turned thirty
He would form a council of Catholics and Protestants to share power
He would persuade her to marry Robert Dudley at once
He and his cohorts would take the reins, and she would marry quickly so a husband could rule
questions.explain: Cecil thought ruling was not for women: the queen would mostly follow her ministers' guidance and be married off, preferably to a Protestant. Dudley was the match he feared.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, how did she answer Cecil's attempt to route foreign correspondence to his desk first?
options: She let him keep it but had a spy report on his reading
She dismissed Cecil and appointed a new secretary of state
She ordered all diplomatic correspondence to go through her, citing her command of the languages
She asked Parliament to forbid him from reading foreign letters
questions.explain: Cecil had hoped to keep the queen in the dark. She learned of it and argued she spoke and read all the major European languages and understood their nuances, so she should handle diplomacy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, why did she keep entertaining marriage proposals year after year?
options: She was hunting for a husband who would accept a limited role
She feared the Spanish would invade if she refused all suitors
She hoped to marry Dudley once Cecil's opposition faded
It let her play foreign powers against each other and secure funds from Parliament, while she never married
questions.explain: She played the French, Austrians and Spanish off each other, softening when Parliament threatened to cut funds and then finding an excuse to break off talks.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's Interpretation, what was Elizabeth's one major mistake while she was gaining credibility?
options: Her refusal to give Essex any money
Her choice of Cecil as secretary of state
Her handling of Mary, Queen of Scots, when she let personal qualms override the greater good
Her decision to go to war with Spain too early
questions.explain: In the Mary case Elizabeth became somewhat entitled herself, believing her feelings trumped her ministers' advice, and the people's respect began to drain away.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, how did she eventually resolve the problem of Mary, Queen of Scots, in a way that regained public trust?
options: She let Parliament decide Mary's fate without involvement
She exiled Mary to France in exchange for peace
She had her intelligence chief lure Mary into a plot, and then signed the death warrant despite her feelings
She sent Mary back to Scotland under guard
questions.explain: With solid evidence of Mary's complicity, Elizabeth could take the dreaded step. Going against her own feelings and admitting her mistake gained even more trust.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the story of Philip II's armada, what did Philip believe made Elizabeth unfit to lead a war?
options: That she was a woman who seemed afraid of armed conflict and neglected her military
That she was too young and had never held a command
That she was Protestant and would lose the support of her sailors
That she trusted only her admirals and ignored strategy
questions.explain: Philip saw her as crafty but a woman who always negotiated to avoid war, with a small navy and a pitiful army. He underestimated her toughness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the story of the Spanish armada, what did the English do on the night the fleet was anchored at Calais?
options: They negotiated a truce that split the Spanish fleet
They sent unmanned fireships loaded with flaming wood and pitch toward the galleons
They boarded the galleons with a large landing force
They blockaded the harbor with a chain of ships
questions.explain: The fire spread from ship to ship in the high winds, scattering the Spanish formation, which was then hit by the faster English ships.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, what finally broke Essex on the night before his execution?
options: The sight of the crowd calling for his death
A letter from the queen offering him a pardon
News that his friends had testified against him
Her chaplain relaying her last words, which brought back his sense of her authority
questions.explain: Faced with her representative, Essex saw the queen's majestic face again, felt the full weight of his betrayal, and went to his death with a quiet dignity no one expected.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene's Interpretation, what was a consequence for government ministers of the royal sense of entitlement under rulers like Henry VIII?
options: They grew rebellious and formed factions against the crown
They worked harder to prove their loyalty to the people
They were cowed and spent their energy appeasing the king instead of using their own creative powers
They became too independent and ignored royal orders
questions.explain: Entitled monarchs intimidated their ministers, whose energy went into pleasing the ruler rather than into thinking and creating.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which two modern causes does Greene suggest might help explain our present-day sense of entitlement?
options: Rising wealth and the loss of religion in daily life
Being spoiled by parents who made us feel everything we did was golden, and technology that gives powers with little effort
Competition at work and the pressure of social media
Democratic politics and the decline of public education
questions.explain: Greene offers parental spoiling and technology that grants immense power without effort, which leads us to expect everything fast and easy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why, according to Greene, are entitled leaders unaware of how their followers really feel?
options: They assume followers will always respect their position
They notice only people's smiles and nods of approval, not the resentment beneath
Their advisers deliberately hide bad news from them
They are too busy with the details of governing
questions.explain: Followers see through the entitlement they feel projected at them, but leaders only read the visible approval until a tipping point and a sudden turn against them.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's Interpretation, Elizabeth's common touch with the crowd was merely a faked performance.
questions.explain: Greene says she was not faking it: having felt powerless in her youth, she could identify with the poorest charwoman, and she built on that empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In the Essex story, Elizabeth gave Essex political power when he asked for high positions for himself and his friends.
questions.explain: She indulged his requests for money and perks but drew a line at political positions, saying he had to prove himself and rise to her level first.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In the Elizabeth story, Elizabeth overruled her admirals on one point, wanting the armada fought as close to England as possible.
questions.explain: She otherwise left battle strategy to them, but fighting near home suited English ships, unsuited the Spanish galleons for stormy northern seas, and would make her soldiers fight harder.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In the Essex story, when Essex marched on London in early 1601, thousands of Londoners rallied to his cause as he had predicted.
questions.explain: The Londoners stayed in their houses and ignored him, his fellow soldiers deserted, and he retreated to his house to be arrested.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene's Understand passage, a leader who feels entitled tends to blame mistakes on others, circumstances, or a momentary inner demon.
questions.explain: Greene lists this among the habits of the entitled: never really to blame, defensive when challenged, and expecting exemption from sacrifices.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, King Philip II's invasion fleet was known as the Spanish ____.
questions.explain: Philip's invincible armada of some 130 ships was launched in 1588 and ended in disaster, leaving Spain bankrupt.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Interpretation, Greene says Elizabeth decided to turn her weak position into an advantage by feeling no sense of ____.
questions.explain: Instead of delusively expecting loyalty from her post, she kept her weakness in mind and set out to earn trust through her actions.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, the secretary of state she appointed, who tried to manage her, was Sir William ____.
questions.explain: Cecil served as her most trusted minister but had to give up on managing her and on the marriage issue.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, the English captain who raided Cádiz in 1587 and destroyed Spanish ships was Sir Francis ____.
questions.explain: Drake's raid destroyed many ships and seized treasure, delaying the invasion and making it more costly for Philip.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Essex story, Essex was sent to put down a rebellion in ____ led by Hugh O'Neill, Earl of Tyrone.
questions.explain: The campaign in Ireland bogged down in winter weather and boggy terrain, and the failure pushed Essex toward the plot that led to his downfall.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene describes the modern attitude of expecting respect and help without earning it as the entitlement ____.
questions.explain: He argues that this sense of entitlement is a curse that makes us lazy, insensitive, and a source of resentment.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How did Elizabeth manage her ministers, according to the Interpretation of her story?
questions.a: She made clear she was all business, would work harder than all of them, and cut court expenses at her own cost. She flashed anger at ministers with personal agendas but was mostly warm and attuned to their moods. They came to want her approval and had to earn her trust, so she ended up with a team working for her agenda.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why did Greene say rulers' sense of entitlement made their emotional connection with the people shallow, and how did Elizabeth go the opposite way?
questions.a: Entitled rulers expected obedience as a right of bloodline and semidivine status, so subjects felt the distance and how little they were considered. Elizabeth refused to assume loyalty; she turned active and earned trust through actions over time, showing that she acted for the greater good of the country.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Describe how Elizabeth handled Philip II's threat, and what it shows about authority.
questions.a: She built an elaborate spy system to know Spain's plans, financed Drake's raids, and built many smaller, faster ships only when the launch was near, doing war economically. After victory she did not take the battle to Spain, since she wanted war only to safeguard the country. This showed her credibility came from efficient action for the group's interests.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say that Elizabeth, even after the armada victory, kept her guard up, and what happened with Essex?
questions.a: She knew that age and success bring a creeping sense of entitlement and insensitivity, which a woman ruling alone could not afford. She stayed receptive to moods, saw the younger men's respect was only for her position, indulged Essex's perks but limited his power, stayed calm at his tantrums, and let his conspiring ruin him.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene's Understand passage, what does an entitled leader do and what attitude should replace it?
questions.a: Entitled leaders sit back, expect loyalty for their position, get defensive when challenged, expect perks and blame others for errors. Greene says we should expect nothing, be active, earn everything including respect, show we put the group's welfare ahead of our egos, be empathetic yet tough, and practice what we preach.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What effects does Greene say the new attitude has on a group, as the Entitlement Curse section ends?
questions.a: People open themselves to our influence and want to win our approval, we are more easily forgiven for mistakes, and group energy goes toward goals instead of infighting. Over time this builds an aura of authority in which what we say and do carries extra weight.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does the Essex story illustrate the difference between nominal authority and real authority?
questions.a: Essex saw Elizabeth as a woman he could manipulate and came to test her limits, but she stayed calm and kept power from him. When he rebelled, Londoners ignored him and she signed the death warrant. At the end, her aura overwhelmed him and he confessed, showing her authority was earned and deeper than her position.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say are consequences of a ruler's sense of entitlement, in the Interpretation?
options: Ministers put energy into appeasing the ruler
Wars of conquest become a chief source of glory
Rulers pay less attention to the boring details of governing
Rulers grow more attuned to the moods of the people
questions.explain: Entitlement blunted effectiveness, led to neglect of governing details and glory-seeking wars. It did not make rulers more attuned to the people; it kept them distant.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these were part of Elizabeth's plan to earn credibility with her ministers?
options: Reducing court expenses at the cost of her own income
Letting them make all major decisions on foreign affairs
Showing superior knowledge of the country's finances
Working harder than all of them
questions.explain: She showed she was all business and knew the finances. She kept diplomacy in her own hands, so ceding foreign affairs is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these did Greene list among the ways modern entitlement shows up in our lives?
options: Feeling entitled to respect for work no matter how little we accomplished
Expecting people to take our ideas seriously however little thought went in
Believing we must work harder than others to deserve any reward
Expecting help in our careers because we are sincere
questions.explain: Needing to work harder to deserve rewards is the opposite of entitlement; the other items are the royalty-like expectations Greene lists.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these were reasons given in the Philip II story for Philip's confidence before the armada sailed?
options: England's army was pitiful compared with Spain's
He had gold from the New World to help finance the effort
Elizabeth had already agreed to marry a Catholic prince
England's navy was relatively small and its ships smaller than Spain's galleons
questions.explain: Philip looked at navy, army, and money. No marriage deal existed; Elizabeth had played at marriage talks for years without agreeing.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, match each person to their role.
pairs: Her secretary of state who planned to have her married off
Spanish king who launched the Enterprise of England
Catholic cousin held under mild house arrest, later executed
Young Earl of Essex who rose as her favorite then rebelled
questions.explain: Each figure is tied to a stage of Elizabeth's reign: Cecil to rule and marriage, Philip to the armada, Mary to the conspiracy problem, Essex to the late challenge.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, match each event to its outcome.
pairs: The Spanish invasion was postponed a year
Execution of Mary, Queen of Scots
Londoners ignored him and he was arrested
questions.explain: Each event had a clear consequence in the story, showing Elizabeth's strategy playing out.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's Interpretation, match each of Elizabeth's audiences to how she won them.
pairs: A common touch mixed with royal pomp and visible empathy
Working harder, saving money, warm but occasionally intimidating
Economical war, spies, and letting them underestimate her
Indulging perks, limiting power, calm firmness
questions.explain: Greene shows Elizabeth adapting one principle of earned authority to each audience.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's Understand passage, match each entitled habit to its effect on others.
pairs: Expecting people to trust us for our position
They feel their willpower negated and resent us
Our intelligence seems tied to our ego, reducing respect
People see through us and feel disconnected
We are shocked when people turn on us suddenly
questions.explain: Greene lays out how entitlement is read by others, culminating in a tipping point.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Essex story, match each stage of his career to what happened.
pairs: He charmed the queen and she indulged his requests
Raid on the Spanish coast in 1596
A bold success that made him the people's darling
Weather, terrain, disease and desertion hobbled his army
He was placed under house arrest within hours
questions.explain: The stages mirror the slow loss of his standing, ending in rebellion and execution.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these events from Elizabeth's reign in the order they happen in the story.
items: Coronation procession through London
Cecil learns she routed diplomacy through herself
Mary, Queen of Scots, is executed
The armada is destroyed
Essex is executed
questions.explain: The story runs from her coronation in 1559, through the Mary execution (1587), the 1588 armada, and Essex's death in 1601.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these steps in the order they happen in Essex's downfall.
items: He asks for command of the army against Tyrone
He negotiates a truce and marches to London
He is placed under house arrest
The queen refuses his wine monopoly
He leads a failed march and is arrested
questions.explain: After Ireland went badly, he returned and was held, then lost his income, then staged a final failed rising.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these steps in the order of Greene's account of Elizabeth's handling of Mary, Queen of Scots.
items: Mary flees to England and is kept under mild house arrest
Calls for Mary's execution grow as she conspires
Proof of a plot to murder Elizabeth emerges
Elizabeth signs the death warrant
questions.explain: Elizabeth hesitated for years, then acted only once clear proof of Mary's plot existed.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these steps in the order of the arc Greene gives in his Understand passage, from entitlement to authority.
items: We feel entitled and sit back
People feel the entitlement and lose respect
We realize we are in a weak position
We earn trust through effort and empathy
People move toward us and an aura of authority grows
questions.explain: Greene shows how the curse leads to resentment, and how adopting the opposite attitude creates connection.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into attitudes of the entitled leader versus the leader who earns authority, as in the Understand passage.

items.t: Expects respect because of position
Gets defensive when ideas are challenged
Blames mistakes on others
Expects exemption from sacrifices
Works harder than the group
Is accountable for mistakes
Attunes to people's moods
Puts the group's welfare first

questions.explain: Greene contrasts passive expectation with active earning of respect.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these features of the Elizabeth story into how entitled rulers behaved and how Elizabeth behaved.

items.t: Expected obedience as a birthright
Used wars of conquest for glory
Kept distance from the people
Cowed ministers by intimidation
Listened to the poorest Londoners
Reduced her own income to cut costs
Fought economically and defensively

questions.explain: Greene presents Elizabeth as deliberately opposite to the usual royal pattern.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into things Elizabeth did to Essex and things Essex did to the queen.

items.t: Indulged him with money and perks
Set limits on political power
Stayed calm in his tantrums
Let his conspiring go far enough to ruin him
Criticized her in front of courtiers
Burst into her bedchamber in mud
Tried to rally nobles to take over

questions.explain: Her patient management contrasts with his escalating tests of her.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into who held the view that ruling was not for a woman and who proved it wrong.

items.t: Cecil, at the start of her reign
Philip II, planning the armada
The young men at the late court
Elizabeth through finances and diplomacy
The defeat of the armada

questions.explain: Each doubter underestimated Elizabeth, while her record corrected them.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In the Elizabeth story, Elizabeth let Cecil remove her authority in diplomacy because she did not speak the major European languages.
questions.explain: It was the opposite: she spoke and read all the major European languages, unlike Cecil, which is why she took over foreign correspondence.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's Interpretation, why did Elizabeth consider marriage bad for both her and the country?
options: A foreign prince husband would use England as a pawn in the Continent's power games and drain its resources
Parliament would then lose its power over the throne
A husband would force her to convert to Catholicism
Her ministers would resent sharing power with a foreign court
questions.explain: Greene says she felt capable of ruling, and any foreign husband's allegiance would be to his own country, not England.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Interpretation, Greene says kings and queens of Elizabeth's time ruled with entitlement due to their bloodline and ____ status.
questions.explain: Rulers felt that obedience came with their position, without any need to earn it.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Elizabeth story, Henry VIII had Elizabeth's mother, his second wife Anne ____, executed on trumped-up charges.
questions.explain: Elizabeth was not yet three, and she was then shunted from stepmother to stepmother.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these were part of Elizabeth's difficult early life, according to the story?
options: She was shunted from stepmother to stepmother
Queen Mary threw her into the Tower of London in 1554
She grew up as a favorite at the center of her father's court
Her mother was executed when she was not yet three
questions.explain: Her presence in the court was minimal, so being a favorite at its center is wrong.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these events from Elizabeth's early life in the order they happen in the story.
items: Henry VIII has her mother executed
Elizabeth is shunted from stepmother to stepmother
Mary imprisons her in the Tower of London
Mary dies and Elizabeth is crowned
questions.explain: Her mother's death came before she was three, the Tower in 1554, and the coronation after Mary's death in late 1558.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene, where does the ambivalence in our emotions begin?
options: In our adult relationships with employers
In the history of early human societies
In our experience of school and teachers
In childhood, in our relationship with our parents
questions.explain: He says ambivalence began in childhood and set the pattern for life, with resentment of dependence mixed in even with loving parents.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why do we remain unaware of our own ambivalence, according to Greene?
options: Strong emotions are easy to recognize and we ignore weaker ones
Our parents taught us to hide mixed feelings
Contemplating the complexity of our emotions is baffling, so we prefer simple explanations
Mixed feelings only appear in relationships with leaders
questions.explain: We reduce our own and other people's feelings to something simple and digestible; catching ambivalence would take effort and honesty.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why do we crave leaders, according to Greene?
options: We believe leaders are wiser than ordinary members
Groups have narrow agendas and competing interests, and someone must see the larger picture and make hard decisions
We fear freedom and want someone else to carry our responsibility
We want to be rewarded for loyalty to someone powerful
questions.explain: Without leaders who stand above competing interests, hard decisions would never be made and no one would be guiding the ship.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why do we fear and despise those above us, according to Greene?
options: They remind us of failures in our own careers
They usually ignore the needs of the group
They may use privilege to accumulate power and enrich themselves, and we dislike inferiority and dependence
They tend to be less talented than they appear
questions.explain: We are willful creatures who want to feel our autonomy, we fear abuse of power, and we secretly envy leaders' recognition and privileges.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene, how did early cultures treat chiefs and kings who showed signs of aging or weakness?
options: They were exiled to live among other tribes
They were forced to share power with a council
They were honored and given a ceremonial role
They were routinely put to death, with the executions as moments of celebration
