questions.explain: Greene cites Frazer's The Golden Bough for chiefs killed on weakness, lost battles, or drought, releasing pent-up hostility.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does the Latin root of authority, auctoritas, mean, according to Greene?
options: To command or compel
To increase or augment
To found or inherit
To protect or defend
questions.explain: He says authority reverts to its original sense, an augmented presence with extra weight to what a leader says and does.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's Roman example, what was the essential ingredient of authority?
options: Winning military victories abroad
Making passionate speeches to the people
Controlling the senate through patronage
Embodying the ideals of the founders and adherence to a higher purpose
questions.explain: Roman leaders had authority to the extent that they returned to the founders' wisdom; they did not need speeches or force.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What are the twin pillars of authority that Greene names in Keys to Human Nature?
options: Force and persuasion
Fairness and consensus
Vision and empathy
Wealth and reputation
questions.explain: Leaders provide a far-reaching vision and attune to group moods; Elizabeth showed toughness and empathy are not incompatible.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: If leaders become pliant and plead for more support, what does Greene say members feel?
options: Even less respect, as if the group were now leading the leader
More gratitude and loyalty toward the leader
Fear that the leader may punish them
Greater willingness to cooperate with the leader
questions.explain: Forceful, demanding leaders get passive-aggressive responses, and pliant ones get less respect.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene advise doing about the bad apples in a group who will not be won over?
options: Hold a meeting to hear their complaints
Recognize them quickly and either fire or marginalize them
Ignore them and hope the group wins them over
Give them extra empathy until they change
questions.explain: He says they live to be passive-aggressive and undermine leaders, so empathy will not work; a tight group makes them easier to control.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, which is NOT among the fake forms of authority Greene lists in an age of chaos?
options: The panderer
The visionary
The chummy leader
The strongman
questions.explain: He lists the strongman, panderer, chummy leader, and the authority of the group, all of which lead to turmoil and bad decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene, what happens when parents no longer see themselves as authority figures?
options: Children become more respectful of teachers
Children turn to their peers for their values only briefly
Children cannot go through the stage of adolescent rebellion and grow up lost, searching for identity
Children grow more independent and self-reliant
questions.explain: Without parental authority, we cannot reject their ideas and discover our own identity, so we search outside ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that ambivalence toward leaders is largely a modern product of fiercely democratic times.
questions.explain: He says the idea that ancestors were obedient is wrong: ancient chiefs and kings were executed on weakness, and underneath obedience lay tremendous wariness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that those who show deference to leaders do so because their personal fate is in the leaders' hands and they cannot show their true feelings.
questions.explain: This is why leaders mistake smiles and applause for reality and are shocked when support turns.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that a leader who establishes authority removes the group's ambivalence entirely.
questions.explain: He says the ambivalence does not go away since that would violate human nature, but it becomes manageable.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if members lose respect and trust, the leader should see it as the members' fault.
questions.explain: He says it is always within our capacity to reach the ideal, so we should see such loss as our own fault.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says we unconsciously associate leaders with ____ figures, which explains the ambivalence we feel toward them.
questions.explain: Our feelings toward leaders mirror childhood ambivalence toward parents, a mix of dependence, love, and resentment.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's account, Latin auctoritas gives the word ____, meaning a presence augmented with prestige and credibility.
questions.explain: He reverts to the original meaning of the word: to increase or augment.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says a leader's primary task is to provide a far-reaching ____ for the group.
questions.explain: Leaders must see the global picture, work for the greater good and maintain unity.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says leaders who fail to establish authority create endless friction and feel as though they must ____ the group up a hill.
questions.explain: The friction from inattentiveness is why many leaders get little done and are mediocre.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene warns that data and ____ are mistakenly seen by some as the real authority today.
questions.explain: He says data and algorithms are treated as determining direction, a fake substitute for leaders with vision.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says that much of the progressive push for consensus and the minimal leader is a fear of ____.
questions.explain: He says it hides a fear of the tough choices, of standing out and taking the heat.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says we no longer kill our chiefs but symbolically do so in our elections and in the ____.
questions.explain: Symbolic executions replace the real ones of the past, with joy at the fall of the powerful.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene tells the student of human nature to observe authority using as a measuring device the influence people wield without force or motivational ____.
questions.explain: Authority is measured by influence without the use of force or speeches.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Explain why, according to Greene, our feelings toward leaders are ambivalent.
questions.a: We feel emotions that are rarely pure, a pattern that began in childhood. We crave leaders because groups need someone above competing interests to make hard decisions. We also fear their abuse of power, resent dependence, and envy their privileges. When leaders show abuse or incompetence the ambivalence tips negative.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How do leaders usually misread their support, and what happens when the ambivalence surfaces?
questions.a: Leaders notice only the smiles of employees and applause at meetings, not realizing people defer because their fate is in the leaders' hands. When mistakes happen or power looks shaky, the hidden mistrust and lost respect suddenly turns against them with surprising intensity.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Describe the Roman idea of authority and why Greene finds it useful.
questions.a: For Romans, the founders' wisdom was shown by the lasting institutions they built, and leaders who embodied those ideals had an augmented presence, prestige and credibility. They did not need speeches or force, and they were not judged only by their latest success. Greene sees this adherence to a higher purpose as the essential ingredient of authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What are the two tasks of a leader that Greene says produce authority, and why must empathy be limited?
questions.a: A leader must provide a far-reaching vision and work for the greater good and unity, and must be attuned to the group's moods, showing trust to engage their willpower. Empathy must never make the leader soft and pliant, as that signals weakness. On the vision the leader must be stern and immovable, merciless toward saboteurs.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What happens in a group whose leader lacks vision and empathy?
questions.a: Members feel distance and see themselves as replaceable pawns, notice the lack of direction, and become resentful. They listen less, think of their own interests, form factions, and work at reduced speed. Forceful leaders get passive-aggression and pliant ones get less respect, creating friction.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What is the student of human nature's threefold task regarding authority, as Greene describes it?
questions.a: First, to be a consummate observer of authority in family, teachers, bosses and public leaders, noticing when it waxes or wanes. Second, to develop habits for projecting authority and reflect on one's effect on people, watching actions rather than smiles. Third and most important, to avoid the prejudice of the times that despises authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say the modern prejudice against authority is harmful, and what does he propose instead?
questions.a: Today authority is confused with leaders who serve themselves, and fiercely democratic values make people resent it. Without authority in arts, parenting, teaching and leadership, we lose things to rebel against, learn from or be guided by, and fake authority proliferates. He proposes accepting that authority is a human need and can be democratic, embracing the risks of leadership.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does Greene describe the fake forms of authority that arise in times of chaos?
questions.a: The strongman gives an illusion of direction but serves his ego. The panderer mimics what the public wants to hear. The chummy leader affects everyone's style and offers fairness and fun. The authority of the group treats numbers, especially on social media, as truth. All lead to turmoil and bad decisions.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he says that the need for true figures of authority has never been greater?
questions.a: Humans have become more self-absorbed, more tribal in holding to narrow agendas, consumed by information, and even more fickle about leaders. So figures with an elevated perspective, a high attunement to the group and a feel for what unifies it are needed, and we are tasked with establishing our authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say members of a group with no real authority above them tend to do?
options: Join or form factions
Listen less attentively to the leaders
Work at half or three-quarter speed
Spend more time thinking about the group's mission
questions.explain: These are the signs of resentment and lost respect; thinking about the mission is what happens when authority is established.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as the fake forms of authority?
options: The strongman
The chummy leader
The founder of the group
The panderer
questions.explain: The fourth form he lists is the authority of the group, not a founder.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these did Greene say people did to chiefs and kings in early cultures?
options: Put them to death after a lost battle
Elect them again every year
Put them to death if they showed signs of aging
Put them to death if a drought occurred
questions.explain: Executions followed aging, defeat, drought or favoring one's own clan. Annual elections are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are modern leaders or figures Greene gives as examples of those who built solid authority?
options: Martin Luther King Jr.
Warren Buffett
Abraham Lincoln
Napoleon Bonaparte
questions.explain: His list includes Moses, Asoka, Pericles, Scipio Africanus, Elizabeth I, Lincoln, King, Buffett, Merkel, and Jobs.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say heightened sensitivity to others involves for a student of authority?
options: Noticing tension as people nod
Trusting smiles and assent as reality
Paying attention to their actions
Taking any grumbling as a reflection on your authority
questions.explain: Greene says not to take smiles and assent for reality, so trusting them is wrong; noticing tension, watching actions and treating grumbling as a signal are his advice.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's account of ambivalence, match each emotion to the reason given.
pairs: Groups need someone above competing interests
They may use privilege to gain more power
We are willful and dislike dependence
We want their recognition and privileges
questions.explain: Greene gives each side of the ambivalence its own root.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's discussion of the prejudice against authority, match each area to what is lost.
pairs: There is nothing to rebel against, only trends
No stage of rebellion, so identity is lost
No masters to learn from or surpass
No one with long-term vision to guide us
questions.explain: He shows consequences in four areas of removing authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's account of fake authority, match each type to what it gives.
pairs: Illusion of direction serving his ego
Mimicking what the public wants to hear
Truth by sheer numbers, magnified on social media
questions.explain: Each type imitates a part of true authority without vision.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the threefold task, match each source to what you gauge about authority.
pairs: Which parent had greater authority over you and your siblings
Whose words and example still reverberate
Their effect on individuals and on the group
The source of their authority or lack of it
questions.explain: Greene tells students to examine family, teachers, bosses, and public leaders.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Greene gives for how authority is undermined when a leader lacks vision and empathy.
items: Group feels distance and lack of direction
Members feel resentment and lose respect
Members spend time on their own interests and form factions
Leader gets little done and is mediocre
questions.explain: Greene traces how disconnect leads to friction and mediocrity.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these in the order Greene mentions them in the history of leader ambivalence.
items: Chiefs and kings in early cultures are executed
Romans use authority to control their fractiousness
Moderns execute leaders symbolically in elections and media
questions.explain: Greene moves from ancient executions to Rome to the modern symbolic form.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these in the order Greene lists the three tasks of a student of human nature.
items: Become a consummate observer of authority
Develop habits and strategies that project authority
Resist the prejudices of the times against authority
questions.explain: The third task is called most important.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these steps in the order of the growth of authority once a leader earns it.
items: The leader shows vision and empathy
Members trust and forgive mistakes
Members feel engaged in the mission
Everything the leader says carries added weight
questions.explain: Greene describes trust turning friction into channeled energy and then augmented presence.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into the reasons we crave leaders and the reasons we fear them.

items.t: Groups have competing interests
Someone must see the larger picture
Hard decisions must be made
Without a guide we feel disoriented
They may use privilege to enrich themselves
Serving under a leader implies inferiority
We want to exercise our own will

questions.explain: Greene splits ambivalence into the need and the threat.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into signs of true authority and signs of fake authority.

items.t: A far-reaching vision
Attunement to the group's moods
Toughness with empathy
Mimicking what the public wants to hear
Affecting everyone else's mannerisms
Ideas serving the ego of the leader

questions.explain: True authority rests on vision and empathy; the fakes imitate parts of it.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these into what leaders do when they lose authority and how members respond.

items.t: Become more forceful and demanding
Become pliant and plead for support
Become passive-aggressive
Feel less respect, as if leading the leader
Join or form factions

questions.explain: Greene shows leader reactions only worsening member friction.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says that without leaders who see the larger picture, hard decisions would never be made and no one would be guiding the ____.
questions.explain: He uses the ship image to show why groups with competing interests crave leaders.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does Greene say leadership works as a dynamic relationship with followers?
questions.a: Our slightest gesture has an unconscious effect, so we must pay attention to our attitude and tone, attune to the group's shifting moods, and never assume support. When we show respect and trust toward those below us, those feelings flow back, and members open up to our influence and identify with the mission.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: The Law of Fickleness comes after chapters on conformity and before one on aggression. What does the chapter title Make Them Want to Follow You signal about its approach?
options: It proves that all groups need strict hierarchy
It shows how to mimic leaders for personal gain
It shifts to the leader's side, showing how to earn followers' willing loyalty
It tells followers how to avoid manipulation by leaders
questions.explain: After a chapter on resisting the group's downward pull, this one asks what a leader must do to earn followers; the title is about drawing willing followers.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene begin this chapter with the Entitlement Curse before the Keys to Human Nature?
options: The Elizabeth story and modern entitlement show the pitfall first, before the theory of ambivalence and authority
He wants the chapter to open with theory and place the story last
He needs to prove history repeats before offering advice
He wants to defend monarchy before turning to modern democracy
questions.explain: The story shows a ruler avoiding entitlement; Keys then explains why the ambivalence toward leaders makes that avoidance necessary.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does the section Keys to Human Nature connect to the section that follows it?
options: Keys lists strategies, and the next section gives the history
Keys describes the inner authority, and the next explains it
Keys defines authority and the ambivalence behind it, while the next section gives strategies for establishing it
Keys is separate from the strategies and from the rest
questions.explain: Keys ends with the call to build habits and strategies (see the next section), which is where the chapter goes next.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: The Entitlement Curse section comes before Keys to Human Nature, which moves from Elizabeth's story to the general psychology of ambivalence toward leaders.
questions.explain: The chapter opens with a story and the modern lesson on entitlement, then widens to the theory of ambivalence and authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does the Elizabeth story in The Entitlement Curse prepare the reader for the later Keys to Human Nature section?
questions.a: The story shows a ruler with weak standing who avoids entitlement and earns trust through action, empathy and toughness, winning over commoners, ministers, and rivals. Keys then explains the ambivalence in human nature that makes this necessary and defines authority as vision and empathy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Keys to Human Nature says forceful leaders meet passive-aggressive members. Which later chapter takes up passive aggression, and how does it connect to this chapter?
questions.a: Chapter 16, on the Law of Aggression, includes a section on passive aggression, its strategies and how to counter them. In this chapter, members who resent a leader who lacks vision and empathy turn passive-aggressive, so the next chapter develops that hidden hostility in more detail.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these describe how the first half of the chapter is organized?
options: A long historical story with an Interpretation
A section on human nature and the ambivalence toward leaders
An epigraph-like statement of the Law of Fickleness
A section of case studies of modern CEOs
questions.explain: The chapter starts with the law, tells Elizabeth's story, then explains ambivalence and authority. There are no modern CEO case studies.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these parts of the chapter in the order they appear.
items: Statement of the Law of Fickleness
The Entitlement Curse
Keys to Human Nature
Strategies for Establishing Authority
The Inner Authority
questions.explain: The table of contents gives this order, with the first half ending after Keys to Human Nature.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each part of the chapter to its role in the argument.
pairs: Story of Elizabeth and the warning about entitlement
Ambivalence toward leaders and the concept of authority
The internal strength behind outward authority
questions.explain: These roles follow the book's structure for the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort these ideas into those introduced in The Entitlement Curse and those introduced in Keys to Human Nature.

items.t: Elizabeth earning trust through actions
Essex's downfall
The modern royalty attitude
Auctoritas and its meaning
The fake forms of authority
The three tasks of a student of human nature

questions.explain: The first section is a story and its lesson; the second is theory and instruction.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the essence of authority?
options: People willingly follow your lead and choose to adhere to your advice
People are carried along by inspiring speeches that stir their emotions
People obey because they fear the consequences of defying you
People are kept loyal by a steady stream of rewards and promotions
questions.explain: Greene says force, rewards and speeches may sometimes be needed, but the less you need them the greater your authority. Authority is willing following, not compelled following.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In Greene's list of authority archetypes, which one is determined to deliver people from evil and has an acute dislike of injustice?
options: The Founder
The Deliverer
The Truth Seeker
The Healer
questions.explain: Moses and Martin Luther King Jr. are his examples of the Deliverer. The Truth Seeker is tied to intolerance of lies, not to rescuing a group from injustice.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which authority archetype does Greene describe as having a keen sense of trends, an aversion to the status quo and a joy in tinkering and inventing something new?
options: The Teacher
The Quiet Pragmatist
The Deliverer
The Founder
questions.explain: Founders establish a new order in politics or business and attract followers because they represent progress. The Quiet Pragmatist, by contrast, simply wants to fix what is broken.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say your authority style must come naturally from your own character and strengths?
options: A natural style lets you avoid having to show any toughness
Without that naturalness your bid for authority looks opportunistic and manipulative
A borrowed style is always weaker than an invented one
People only follow leaders who share their own temperament
questions.explain: A natural style makes your cause seem like something beyond you, a gift rather than a ploy. Without it, support for a cause or trend can look like a mere play for power.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Under the Attitude strategy, what does Greene say you do about the respect of others?
options: Wait for it to arrive naturally as your reputation grows
Trade it for popularity by being liked by everyone
Demand it early so that people know your position
Dedicate yourself to earning it rather than feeling entitled to it
questions.explain: Greene says you earn respect by respecting people's individual needs and showing you work for the greater good. Feeling that people owe you respect is an inward turn.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What drives a leader who has the outward-focused attitude Greene recommends?
options: A strong wish to be recognized as the group's most talented member
Bringing about the best results for the most people, not getting attention
A desire to be as popular and liked as possible
A need to protect the leader's own reputation at any cost
questions.explain: Such a leader treats leadership as a tremendous responsibility and absorbs themselves in the work, not the ego. Paradoxically, this earns far more attention than signaling a desperate need to be liked.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why was Xenophon, who had no military experience, chosen as the de facto leader of the trapped Greek soldiers?
options: He was the only survivor among the captured commanders
His escape vision was so complete, and delivered so confidently, that the soldiers trusted it
He promised the soldiers a share of Persian treasure
He had been appointed by the Persian prince they served
questions.explain: Xenophon, a student of Socrates, conjured the details of a fast retreat in a few hours. The captured commanders had all been executed, but his authority came from the quality of his vision.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which feature was central to the plan Xenophon envisioned for the Greek mercenaries' escape?
options: Fighting directly through the Persian army at full strength
Moving swiftly and stealthily, sacrificing everything for speed
Negotiating a surrender with the victorious Persian king
Fortifying the camp and waiting out the winter
questions.explain: He saw them dropping their wagons, living off the land and using surprise to gain distance. Staying put or surrendering was the fate they were trying to avoid.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why did people facing Napoleon Bonaparte often feel he could read their minds?
options: He relied on a mysterious natural gift for predicting plans
He had simply thought forward more thoroughly than the other side
He copied the strategies of the enemy commanders
He had a network of spies inside every enemy camp
questions.explain: Greene uses Napoleon, like Goethe, to show that the apparent power to see the future comes from deep, patient, global thinking and not from a gift.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: After forming a vision of the future, what does Greene say you do next?
options: Work backward to the present, creating a reasonable and flexible way to reach the goal
Announce the finished plan and avoid revising it
Wait for events to confirm the vision before planning
Gather opinions from the group and adopt the majority view
questions.explain: Working backward from the vision builds a plan you feel confident in, and that confidence infects others. The plan is meant to be flexible, not rigid.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What should you conclude, according to Greene, if you fall short of the goals your vision set?
options: That the vision itself should be abandoned
That the group failed to follow you properly
That you did not take your thinking far enough
That circumstances were against you
questions.explain: Greene treats failure as a signal to think more deeply, not as a reason to drop the method. If people doubt your vision, you stay inwardly firm because time will prove you right.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say you must set the tone of leading from the front from the very beginning?
options: Early habits are the only ones that people can imitate
Leaders who change style are always seen as weak
A later attempt to lead from the front looks forced and lacks credibility
Members decide within a year whether they will stay
questions.explain: First impressions are critical. Showing you work as hard as anyone and make sacrifices first only convinces if people see it from the start.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: In the Tone strategy, why does Greene advise showing some initial toughness?
options: A soft start prevents people from forming any impression
Toughness is the main thing that makes people like a leader
Harsh punishment alone keeps a group productive
If people think early on that they can maneuver you, they will do so mercilessly
questions.explain: Starting soft signals you are a pushover, whereas you will always have time to reveal your softer, kinder side later. The toughness should still stay fair and not stir fears of abuse of power.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene advise sending slightly contradictory signals as part of the Aura strategy?
options: It makes people sympathetic to your inner conflicts
People stop categorizing you instantly, and the more they think about you the larger your presence
It keeps people too confused to question your decisions
It hides your real intentions from rivals
questions.explain: Most people are too predictable. A mysterious mix makes people wonder who you really are, which adds to your authority. Greene warns the mix must be an undertone or you will seem insane.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene compares the mixed signals of a good leader to which kind of figure?
options: Judges, who stay neutral between rival parties
Friends, who accept others as they are
Parents, who show love while indicating limits and boundaries
Teachers, who reward effort with grades
questions.explain: A child caught between affection and a touch of fear develops respect out of that tension. Leaders can create a similar effect with kindness plus an undertone of harshness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: On the balance between presence and absence, what does Greene recommend?
options: Be as visible as possible so that everyone feels close to you
Alternate evenly between presence and absence
Stay completely aloof so that nobody can identify with you
Lean slightly more toward absence, so that your appearances generate excitement
questions.explain: Too much presence makes you banal and gives no room for people to idealize you, while too much aloofness stops them identifying with you. A slight lean toward absence works best.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: A department head posts every detail of her day on social media to seem relatable. How would Greene judge this?
options: It is harmless as long as she posts only positive things
It makes her seem like everyone else, making authority impossible to project
It helps only if she posts on a very regular schedule
It strengthens her authority by showing openness
questions.explain: Greene says today's overexposure may make you relatable, but an ordinary presence cannot project authority. Excess talking is another form of overpresence that reveals weakness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: When a leader makes a mistake, how does Greene say the leader should respond?
options: Accept responsibility quietly, avoid overexplaining and overapologizing, and move on
Apologize repeatedly until everyone is satisfied
Defend the decision firmly to avoid looking weak
Offer a detailed account of the circumstances behind the error
questions.explain: Quiet contrition, followed by actions showing that you learned the lesson, preserves authority. Appearing defensive or whiny when attacked does not.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why is taking something from people that they assumed they possessed so damaging to a leader's authority?
options: It proves that the leader has strong willpower
It lowers people's expectations of future leaders
It creates insecurity and stirs doubts about the leader's legitimacy
It teaches the group to be more self-reliant
questions.explain: People start to ask what more will be taken and whether the power is being abused. Even a hint of that harms reputation, so Greene says never to appear to take, always to give.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: According to Greene, why does overpromising erode authority?
options: Failing to deliver on a promise feels to people like something taken away
People forget promises quickly and lose interest
Promising too much makes you seem arrogant
Promises always raise the group's expectations beyond what is realistic
questions.explain: People have an acute memory for promises, and blaming others or circumstances will not erase it. A second failure makes authority erode sharply.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why can a leader's established authority become a problem as the leader gets older?
options: Older leaders lose the ability to think about the future
Authority naturally fades after a fixed number of years
Younger members refuse all forms of leadership
It can turn rigid and stodgy, and a new generation sees the leader as a relic
questions.explain: Greene's remedy is to keep empathy and sensitivity and to look for new audiences while adjusting your style. Picasso, Hitchcock and Chanel are his examples.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of our two sides does Greene say is naturally the stronger one?
options: Neither, because they are exactly balanced
Whichever side was strengthened in childhood
The lower self, the more primitive and animal part of our nature
The higher self, which acts as soon as we think
questions.explain: Left alone we become indolent, crave quick pleasures and brood over petty matters. Taming the lower half and bringing out the higher one takes great effort and awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does Greene define the inner authority?
options: The approval we receive from leaders we respect
The authority we inherit from our parents
The habit of obeying the rules of our group
The voice and conscience of our higher self
questions.explain: This voice is already there but weak, and we must increase how often and how loudly we hear it. It dictates a code of behavior that we make ourselves listen to every day.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does the inner voice say you have a responsibility to contribute to your culture and times?
options: You are living off the fruits of millions of people before you and should not feel entitled to them
Society will punish anyone who only consumes
Culture will stop improving unless you personally add to it
Contributing is the surest way to gain recognition
questions.explain: Greene calls the view that all of this simply came about naturally the view of spoiled children. We are here to make and contribute, not merely to gratify impulses and consume.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene say moments of depression are, in light of the inner authority?
options: A result of listening too closely to your lower self
A sign that your group is not supporting you
A sign that you are working too hard
A call to listen again to your inner authority and cultivate your uniqueness
questions.explain: He says that not following the course of cultivating what is unique about you is the real reason you feel depressed at times.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene say about the first thought or idea that comes to you?
options: It should be recorded exactly and left unchanged
It should be tested by asking others before developing it
It is usually the most authentic, so you should protect it
It is most often incomplete and inadequate, so you should treat it roughly
questions.explain: To keep to the highest standards, think more thoroughly and deeply, and be willing to discard some ideas rather than become attached to your initial ones.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What was Leonardo da Vinci's motto, which Greene uses to illustrate the inner authority?
options: Fare e tacere, do and be silent
Ars longa, art is long
Sempre avanti, always forward
Ostinato rigore, relentless rigor
questions.explain: Leonardo went well beyond every commission, poring over details, and no one had to tell him to. His inner authority pushed him past the limits of his unprivileged start.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene follow the strategies for establishing outer authority with a section on the inner authority?
options: Inner authority concerns only artists, whereas outer authority concerns leaders
Authority over oneself works like authority over a group, making you your own leader
Inner authority replaces the need for any outer strategies
Outer authority is impossible unless inner authority is perfected first
questions.explain: He says the outer authority keeps a group unified and channels energy toward higher ends, and the inner authority gives you cohesion and force. You then no longer need the guidance of a parent or leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: The strategies for establishing authority follow the chapter's discussion of human ambivalence toward leaders. What are they designed to do?
options: Engage people's willpower and overcome their natural resistances and ambivalence
Help leaders use force and rewards more effectively
Remove people's ambivalence for good
Replace the need for a vision with practical habits
questions.explain: Greene says ambivalence never disappears, as that would violate human nature, but authority makes it manageable. The strategies aim to engage willpower so that people follow willingly.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say that the less you need force, rewards and speeches, the greater your authority?
questions.a: Authority is people willingly choosing to follow your lead and adhere to your advice. Force, rewards and punishments, and inspiring speeches may sometimes be needed, so it is a matter of degree. But every time you rely on them you show people are not following willingly, so you should keep striving to engage their willpower and overcome their ambivalence.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What is the Authenticity strategy and why does Greene say it matters?
questions.a: You find an authority archetype, such as the Deliverer, Founder or Visionary Artist, that suits your natural character and strengths. Bringing out a natural style makes it seem beyond you, like a gift, so people see you as someone who cannot help but fight for a cause. Without it your authority looks opportunistic and manipulative, and the earlier you find the style the more time you have to hone it.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What are the three ways Greene says you can reverse your natural self-absorption in the Attitude strategy?
questions.a: First, you hone your listening skills, reading words, nonverbal cues, moods and needs, and not taking smiles for reality. Second, you dedicate yourself to earning respect by respecting people's needs and working for the greater good, without feeling entitled. Third, you treat leadership as a great responsibility and focus on results rather than attention, which makes you stand out.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Tell the story of Xenophon and explain what Greene uses it to show.
questions.a: Ten thousand Greek mercenaries were trapped deep in Persia after their leaders were executed. Xenophon, a student of Socrates with no military experience, envisioned a swift, stealthy retreat that dropped the wagons and lived off the land. His vision was so complete and confidently communicated that he was made leader and brought them home. Greene says this shows that a global vision is the essence of authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does Greene tell us to cultivate the third eye of vision?
questions.a: You train yourself to disconnect from the emotions of the group, raise your vision and imagine the larger picture. You consider the enemy's perspective, listen to outsiders and game out how things might play out and go wrong. Then you work backward from the vision to the present to build a flexible plan, stay inwardly firm if people doubt it, and treat any shortfall as a sign you did not think far enough.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Explain the Tone strategy of leading from the front, including why it should start early.
questions.a: You must be seen working as hard as or harder than anyone, set the highest standards for yourself, be consistent and accountable, and be the first to make sacrifices. Members will then internalize your values and imitate you without lectures. It must start at the beginning because a later attempt looks forced. You also show initial toughness and set fair limits, because starting soft marks you as a pushover.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does the Aura strategy work, and what warning does Greene give about it?
questions.a: Instead of being predictable, you send slightly contradictory signals, such as kindness with an undertone of harshness, or prudence with occasional bold action. People pause their instant categorizing and keep thinking about you, which enlarges your presence. Greene warns not to make the mix too strong or you will seem insane, and that it means bringing out your natural complexity rather than faking qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene say about balancing presence and absence, silence and apologies?
questions.a: Being too present and familiar makes you banal, while being too aloof stops people from identifying with you, so lean slightly toward absence. Talking too much is overpresence, while silence signals self-control and gives your words more effect. After a mistake you accept responsibility without overexplaining or overapologizing, and you avoid sounding defensive when attacked.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Describe the Taboo strategy of never appearing to take, always to give.
questions.a: Taking away money, rights, privileges or time that people thought they owned makes them insecure and questions your legitimacy. If sacrifices are needed, you make them first and for real, and you frame any loss as temporary. You husband resources, as Queen Elizabeth I did, so you can afford generosity. You also avoid overpromising, because a failure to deliver feels like something taken away.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What are the two steps Greene gives for rejuvenating your authority as you age?
questions.a: First, maintain the sensitivity Elizabeth showed, noting people's moods and your effect on newcomers and young people, since losing empathy is the greatest danger. Second, look for new markets and audiences, which forces you to adapt, and gradually alter your style without trying foolishly to imitate a younger crowd. This keeps authority from turning rigid and entitled, as Picasso, Hitchcock and Chanel showed.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say you should not feel entitled to people's respect, and how does that tie to his idea about attention?
questions.a: Feeling entitled to respect because of your position or greatness is an inward focus on your own feelings. Greene wants you to earn respect through attention to others' needs and by working for the greater good. Because it is rare to meet a leader so sensitive and result-focused, you gain far more attention this way than by signaling a desperate need to be popular.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What are the higher and lower selves, and how does the inner authority help?
questions.a: We all have a higher self, felt when we accomplish things, think of others and step back to strategize, and a lower self, felt when we are petty, escapist or wasteful. The lower self is stronger and more primitive, so we need effort to bring out the higher one. The inner authority is the conscience and voice of the higher self, and we strengthen it by listening to its code of behavior every day.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: List the four parts of the code of behavior that the inner authority dictates.
questions.a: First, you have a responsibility to contribute to your culture and times rather than just consume. Second, you must cultivate what is unique about you. Third, you must focus and prioritize, avoiding time-wasters and low-natured people. Fourth, you must hold to the highest standards in your work, with self-discipline, attention to detail and a sense of urgency.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does Greene mean when he calls the attitude that you are entitled to the world's benefits that of spoiled children?
questions.a: You live off the work and inventions of millions before you and an education that holds thousands of years of wisdom. Assuming that this all arose naturally and you are entitled to it is spoiled and, Greene says, shameful. The world needs constant improvement, so you are here to make and contribute and serve a higher purpose.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How does Greene tell you to cultivate your uniqueness?
questions.a: Stop letting others tell you who you are and what to like. Judge things for yourself, question your thoughts and feelings, and know your innate tastes and inclinations. Work daily on skills that mesh with your spirit and purpose, create something reflecting your uniqueness, and embrace what makes you different.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: What does holding to the highest standards require, according to the inner authority?
questions.a: You strive for excellence to create something that resonates with the public and lasts, since falling short disappoints your audience and shames you. That requires self-discipline, good work habits, attention to detail and a premium on effort. You must think deeper than your first, incomplete idea, discard some ideas, feel urgency because life is short, and find motivation within, not from deadlines.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene present Leonardo da Vinci as the model of operating with an inner authority?
questions.a: His motto was ostinato rigore, relentless rigor. He went beyond every commission and examined every detail without being told to, and he was ferociously diligent and hard on himself. He worked with complete focus on each problem while pursuing a personal mission to serve mankind. His inner authority helped him push past his limits as an illegitimate son with little early direction.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene say that living by an inner authority does not make life harsh?
questions.a: Nothing is more disorienting than watching the years pass without direction and chasing shifting goals. The inner authority gives you cohesion and force, like the outer authority does for a group, and relieves the anxiety of living below your potential. With the higher self ascendant you can occasionally indulge the lower self without being a prisoner of your Shadow, and you become your own mother, father and leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: How do the two halves of this chapter's second part, outer strategies and inner authority, fit together under the title Make Them Want to Follow You?
questions.a: The strategies show how to win willing followers by engaging their willpower through style, attitude, vision, tone, aura, giving and adaptability. The inner authority turns the same idea inward: you listen to the higher self's voice and lead yourself, so you need no parent or leader. Both rest on a higher purpose, and the second shows that real authority begins with command over yourself.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Why does Greene end the chapter on authority by moving from other people to the individual's inner voice?
questions.a: The chapter opens with our ambivalence toward leaders and the need for true authority, and its strategies deal with winning willing followers. The lower self is also a source of resistance within us, so authority must work inside as well. Ending on the inner authority shows the same logic of a higher purpose and unity applied to the self, leaving you independent, your own leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene advises you to find an authority ____ that suits your character, such as the Deliverer, the Founder or the Healer.
questions.explain: The Authenticity strategy asks you to pick a natural style from archetypes. Naturalness avoids looking opportunistic.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Pablo Picasso, John Coltrane and David Lynch are Greene's examples of the ____ Artist archetype.
questions.explain: Visionary Artists learn their field's conventions and then turn them upside down, creating a new style and finding followers.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: The strategy of focusing outwardly rather than inwardly is labeled the ____ in Greene's list.
questions.explain: Attitude involves listening, earning respect and treating leadership as a responsibility.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Xenophon had been a student of the philosopher ____, which shaped his belief in rational, global thinking.
questions.explain: Greene notes his philosophical training and years of practicing the skill of seeing the whole picture.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Cultivating the third eye lets you gain a feel for the overall shape of a situation, which Greene calls its ____.
questions.explain: Seeing the gestalt means stepping back from partisan opinions to grasp the whole.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: The great thinker Goethe seemed to predict trends, but Greene says this came from years of study and ____ thinking.
questions.explain: Like Napoleon, Goethe seemed gifted but had simply thought more broadly and thoroughly.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: The strategy of working as hard as anyone and being first to sacrifice is called Lead from the front: the ____.
questions.explain: Tone is set from the beginning, and members subtly imitate the leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene warns that if you start soft, you signal that you are a ____.
questions.explain: Initial toughness prevents people from maneuvering you, while your kinder side can be revealed later.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sending slightly contrary signals to fascinate people is the strategy of Stir conflicting emotions: the ____.
questions.explain: The Aura keeps people wondering about you, as long as the mix stays an undertone.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says it is generally best to lean slightly more toward ____ than presence, so that your appearances generate excitement.
questions.explain: Too much presence makes you banal, but too much aloofness blocks identification.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Taking from people something they assumed they owned is the subject of the strategy Never appear to take, always to give: the ____.
questions.explain: Taking breeds insecurity and doubts about your legitimacy as a leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: An aging leader's authority can turn rigid and stodgy, like a ____ figure who has monopolized power too long.
questions.explain: A new generation then sees the leader as a relic, which is why the Adaptability strategy matters.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene calls the inner authority the voice, or ____, of our higher self.
questions.explain: It is already present but weak, so it needs to be heard more often and more loudly.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Leonardo da Vinci's motto, ostinato rigore, means relentless ____.
questions.explain: It describes his thoroughness in every commission and problem.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says the first thought or idea that comes to you is most often ____ and inadequate.
questions.explain: This is why you must think more deeply and discard some ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Greene says moments of ____ are a call to listen again to your inner authority.
questions.explain: They reflect not cultivating what is unique about you.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: With the inner authority in place, you become your own mother and father, your own ____.
questions.explain: You no longer need the comfort and guidance of a parent or leader.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are authority archetypes that Greene names?
options: The Deliverer
The Diplomat
The Healer
The Conqueror
questions.explain: The Deliverer and Healer are on Greene's list. The Conqueror and the Diplomat are not.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are among the three ways Greene says to focus outwardly?
options: Treating leadership as a tremendous responsibility
Signaling your need to be popular and liked
Earning people's respect without feeling entitled to it
Sharpening your listening skills
questions.explain: Greene lists listening, earning respect and responsibility. Signaling a desperate need to be popular is what he says to avoid.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these were part of Xenophon's vision for the escape?
options: Moving swiftly and stealthily
Using citizens who revolted against the Persians
Getting rid of the wagons
Fortifying a position in the mountains
questions.explain: He saw speed, surprise, living off the land and help from revolting citizens. Fortifying a position is not in his plan.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say leading from the front involves?
options: Making sacrifices first for the good of the group
Working as hard as or harder than everyone else
Setting the highest standards for yourself
Delegating unpleasant tasks while staying distant
questions.explain: Leading from the front means visible effort, accountability and first sacrifices. Staying distant from hard work would undercut the tone.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are mixtures of qualities Greene suggests for the Aura strategy?
options: Being constantly available and visible
Deliberation with occasional audacity
A consistent, always-jovial persona
Kindness with an undertone of harshness
questions.explain: Greene suggests mixing contrary qualities. A single consistent persona and constant visibility are what he warns makes you predictable and banal.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say damage a leader's authority?
options: Overpromising and then failing to deliver
Making sacrifices before asking others to
Taking away money, rights or time people thought they owned
Framing a necessary loss as temporary and promising to restore it
questions.explain: The first two are what Greene calls taboo. Framing losses as temporary and making sacrifices first are his advice.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these steps does Greene give for rejuvenating your authority over time?
options: Refusing to change your style so you remain consistent
Maintaining empathy for people's moods, including those of the young
Looking for new markets and audiences
Imitating youthful fashions to look young
questions.explain: He advises sensitivity and expanding the reach of your authority while altering your style somewhat, without foolishly trying to appeal to a crowd you cannot understand.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are parts of the code that the inner authority dictates?
options: Focus and prioritize in a world of distractions
Cultivate what is unique about you
Take your cues about who you are from others' opinions
Contribute to your culture and times
questions.explain: Greene says to stop listening to others' opinions about who you are, so the last item is the opposite of the code.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these does Greene associate with the lower self?
options: Finishing what you start
Taking everything personally and becoming petty
Trying to escape reality through addictive pleasure
Thinking of others before yourself
questions.explain: The last two are signs of the higher self.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are said of Leonardo da Vinci as a model of inner authority?
options: He needed deadlines from patrons to finish work
He felt a personal mission to serve mankind
He went well beyond what each commission required
He focused completely when attacking a problem
questions.explain: No one had to tell Leonardo what to do, since his motivation came from within.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Which of these are true of how Greene links the outer and inner authority?
options: Both channel energy toward higher ends
The inner authority gives the individual cohesion and force
Both depend on force and punishment
The inner authority works only for artists
questions.explain: The outer authority unifies a group and the inner one unifies the self. Neither is described as resting on force.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that true authority means a leader never uses force, rewards or punishments.
questions.explain: He says that at times you may have to use them. It is only a matter of degree, and the less you need them, the greater your authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's account, leaders who focus outwardly on others and results end up gaining far more attention than those who signal a desperate need to be liked.
questions.explain: The rarity of a person so sensitive to moods and focused on results makes them stand out.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Xenophon, who led the Greek mercenaries out of Persia, had extensive military experience.
questions.explain: He had no military experience. His authority came from the completeness of his vision and his confidence in communicating it.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises that if people doubt your vision, you should quickly drop it and adopt the group's view.
questions.explain: You stay inwardly firm because, he says, time will prove you right.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that showing initial toughness helps a new leader, since people can respect strength as long as it does not stir fears of abuse.
questions.explain: Showing toughness early prevents being maneuvered, and a softer side can be revealed later.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene recommends making the mix of contrary qualities in your aura as strong as possible.
questions.explain: He warns that a mix that is too strong makes you seem insane. It should be an undertone that makes people wonder in a good way.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, silence is a form of absence that draws attention and signals self-control.
questions.explain: When you do talk, it has a greater effect, while talking too much reveals weakness.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that if you fail to deliver on a promise, people will forget it as long as you blame outside circumstances.
questions.explain: People have an acute memory for promises, and failure sticks even if you blame others or circumstances.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the higher self is naturally the stronger half of our nature.
questions.explain: The lower self is the stronger and more primitive part, so it takes effort and awareness to bring out the higher side.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that the voice of the inner authority already exists in us but is weak.
questions.explain: We hear it at times, and the task is to increase its frequency and volume.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: True or false: In this chapter, the section on inner authority comes after the strategies for establishing authority over others.
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the outer strategies to turning authority inward, with Greene ending on the individual.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put the last five strategies in the order Greene presents them.
items: Vision
Tone
Aura
Taboo
Adaptability
questions.explain: The sequence is Vision, Tone, Aura, Taboo and then Adaptability, after Authenticity and Attitude.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put the events of the Xenophon story in order.
items: The Persians execute the Greek commanders
Xenophon conceives a plan of escape overnight
The soldiers nominate him as their leader
He leads them home over several years
questions.explain: The soldiers' leader selection followed his confident vision, and he proved it by leading them to safety.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put the steps for cultivating vision in order.
items: Disconnect from the emotions roiling the group
Imagine the larger picture and the enemy's perspective
Game out possible trends and how things could go wrong
Work backward to the present with a flexible plan
questions.explain: Greene moves from detachment to the larger view, to forecasting, then to planning backward.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put Greene's three ways of focusing outwardly in order.
items: Hone your listening skills
Dedicate yourself to earning respect
Consider leadership a tremendous responsibility
questions.explain: These are first, second and third in the Attitude strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these stages of aging authority and its renewal in the order Greene describes.
items: Authority grows with trust-inspiring actions
The leader begins to seem oppressive after monopolizing power
A new generation sees the leader as a relic
The leader looks for new markets and audiences to adapt
questions.explain: Greene describes the growth and rigidity, the generational problem, then the steps to renew authority.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put the four parts of the inner authority's code in the order Greene gives them.
items: Contribute to your culture and times
Cultivate what is unique about you
Focus and prioritize
Adhere to the highest standards in your work
questions.explain: The code runs from responsibility, to uniqueness, to focus, to standards.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these points about the highest standards in the order Greene gives.
items: Strive for excellence that will last
Develop self-discipline and work habits
Pay attention to details and value effort
Treat first ideas roughly
Feel a sense of urgency because life is short
questions.explain: They follow in this order in the text.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put these parts of the Inner Authority section in order.
items: The higher and the lower self
The inner authority as the voice of the higher self
The four-part code of behavior
Leonardo da Vinci as the model
Why the inner authority leads to a fuller life
questions.explain: Greene moves from the two selves, to the voice, to its code, to Leonardo, and finally to the benefits.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Put the chapter's four main sections in the order they appear.
items: The Entitlement Curse
Keys to Human Nature
Strategies for Establishing Authority
The Inner Authority
questions.explain: The chapter moves from the problem and the keys to the strategies, and finally turns inward.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each of these three authority archetypes (Deliverer, Founder, Visionary Artist) to the trait Greene gives it.
pairs: Determined to deliver people from evil and dislikes injustice
Establishes a new order and has an aversion to the status quo
Learns a field's conventions, then turns them upside down
questions.explain: These are Greene's first three archetypes.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each strategy label to the idea it names.
pairs: Focus outwardly on others and on results
Cultivate the third eye to see the larger picture
Lead from the front by working hard and sacrificing first
Never appear to take, always to give
questions.explain: Each label pairs with the strategy's core idea.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each figure to how Greene uses him or her in the strategies.
pairs: Led Greek mercenaries out of Persia with a complete vision
Seemed to read minds because he thought ahead more thoroughly
Seemed to predict trends through years of global thinking
Husbanded resources so she could afford generosity
Blended the spiritual with earthy pragmatism
questions.explain: Each is used to illustrate a strategy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each pair of qualities to the leader's example in the Aura strategy.
pairs: With an undertone of harshness toward certain behavior
questions.explain: These are Greene's examples of blending contrary qualities.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each of these four other archetypes (Truth Seeker, Pragmatist, Healer, Teacher) to the trait Greene gives it.
pairs: Has no tolerance for lies and politicking
Wants to fix what is broken and has infinite patience
Has a knack for finding what will fulfill and unify people
Gets people to initiate action and learn from their mistakes
questions.explain: These are four more of Greene's archetypes.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each leadership problem to Greene's remedy.
pairs: You are too present and familiar
People think they can maneuver you
questions.explain: Each problem has a specific remedy.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each part of the inner authority's code to what it asks.
pairs: Serve a higher purpose rather than only consuming
Judge for yourself and know your innate tastes
Pay attention to detail and treat first ideas roughly
questions.explain: These are the four parts of the code.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each term from the inner authority section to its meaning.
pairs: The conscience and voice of the higher self
Assuming one is entitled to all the powers handed down
A call to listen again to the inner authority
questions.explain: These terms are drawn from the section.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Match each section of the chapter to its role.
pairs: Explains ambivalence toward leaders and why authority matters
Gives practices for engaging willpower so people follow willingly
Turns authority inward so you become your own leader
questions.explain: The sections move from the problem to the outer strategies to the inner version.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it builds or erodes authority, according to Greene.

items.t: Leading from the front
Accepting responsibility without overexplaining
Making real sacrifices first
Keeping anger infrequent so it carries weight
Overpromising
Overapologizing for a mistake
Constant presence and familiarity
Taking away privileges people assumed they had

questions.explain: Each item comes from the strategies on tone, aura and the taboo.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each habit by whether it reflects an inward or outward focus.

items.t: Feeling entitled to respect because of your position
Dwelling on your own wounds and fantasies
Signaling a need to be popular
Reading between the lines of what people say
Earning respect by meeting people's needs
Absorbing yourself in the work, not the ego

questions.explain: The Attitude strategy asks you to reverse the human tendency toward self-absorption.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each example by the archetype Greene uses it for.

items.t: Pablo Picasso
John Coltrane
David Lynch
Moses
Martin Luther King Jr.

questions.explain: Moses and King illustrate the Deliverer, while the three creators illustrate the Visionary Artist.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each behavior by whether it is overpresence or absence.

items.t: Posting every move on social media
Talking too much
Always being available and visible
Overexplaining a mistake
Staying silent
Appearing before the group only occasionally
Withdrawing so that people think of you
Leaving room for people to idealize you

questions.explain: Greene says to lean toward absence, using silence and withdrawal to draw attention.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each move by whether it protects or harms authority under the Taboo strategy.

items.t: Making the first sacrifice, and a real one
Framing a loss of resources as temporary
Husbanding resources so you can afford generosity
Letting people hear of the great things you will do
Failing to deliver and blaming circumstances
Taking time or money people thought was theirs

questions.explain: The Taboo strategy is about never appearing to take, and overpromising feels like taking.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each trait by whether Greene associates it with the higher or the lower self.

items.t: Finishing what you start
Thinking of others before yourself
Stepping back to strategize
Taking everything personally
Escaping reality through addictive pleasure
Wasting time

questions.explain: These are drawn from Greene's description of the two sides of our nature.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each attitude by whether it is the spoiled child's view or the inner authority's view.

items.t: Assuming the world's powers came about naturally for you
Believing you are entitled to consume what others made
Seeing yourself as living off the fruits of past struggles
Seeking to make and contribute as well as consume
Serving a higher purpose

questions.explain: Greene calls the first two the view of spoiled children and shameful.

questions.unitTitle: Make Them Want to Follow You
questions.q: Sort each item by the section it belongs to.

items.t: The Deliverer archetype
Xenophon's escape vision
The Taboo of taking
Leonardo da Vinci's relentless rigor
Treating first ideas roughly
The voice of the higher self

questions.explain: The first three are outer strategies and the last three concern the inner authority.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to the opening statement of the Law of Aggression, what lies beneath the polite and civilized surface of the people around you?
options: A fear of being judged that makes them avoid all conflict
A quiet envy of anyone who has more talent than they do
A steady wish to cooperate that is hidden by shyness
Frustrations and a need to influence people and gain power over circumstances
questions.explain: Greene says people wear a mask of politeness but are dealing with frustrations and a need for influence and power, so they often assert themselves in manipulative ways.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the opening of the Law of Aggression, what do dangerous aggressive types depend on in order to get their way with you?
options: Flattering you until you drop your guard completely
Convincing you that their goals are the same as yours
Making you emotional, afraid or angry, so you cannot think straight
Keeping you ignorant of the rules of the organization
questions.explain: The opening warns that aggressors rely on stirring up fear and anger. The remedy is not to hand them that power.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the opening of the Law of Aggression, Greene tells you to suppress your own aggressive energy completely so that it never harms anyone.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: tame and channel your own aggressive energy into productive uses such as standing up for yourself, attacking problems, and realizing ambitions.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The opening says you must become a superior observer of people's unsatisfied ____ desires.
questions.explain: The law asks you to watch for the unsatisfied aggressive desires of the people around you, especially chronic and passive aggressors.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does the opening of the Law of Aggression tell you to do?
options: Avoid thinking about aggressors so they cannot upset you
Give up your own wish to influence events
Look for past patterns of behavior and an obsessive need to control the environment
Pay extra attention to chronic aggressors and passive aggressors
questions.explain: The opening asks for sharp observation of the dangerous types and their signs, and it asks you to channel your own aggressive energy rather than to give it up.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the opening of the Law of Aggression, why does Greene say you should watch for particular signs in other people, and what should you do with your own aggressive energy?
questions.a: He says the dangerous types, chronic aggressors and passive aggressors, can be spotted by their past patterns of behavior and an obsessive need to control everything around them. They try to make you afraid or angry so you cannot think straight. Your own aggressive energy should be tamed and channeled into productive purposes like standing up for yourself and realizing great ambitions.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Rockefeller story, why did Maurice Clark choose the young bookkeeper John D. Rockefeller as his business partner?
options: Rockefeller was Clark's cousin and trusted heir
Rockefeller was efficient and honest, and so young that Clark could dominate the relationship
Rockefeller had a gift for charming big buyers
Rockefeller was a famous banker whose name would attract customers
questions.explain: Clark thought Rockefeller's reputation for efficiency and honesty was valuable and expected to dominate him because of his youth. Rockefeller had only been a clerk.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Rockefeller story, what was Clark's reaction when Rockefeller first showed fierce enthusiasm for the oil refinery business?
options: He took the idea as his own and ran it alone
He refused outright and left the firm
He demanded that Rockefeller sell his share first
He was lukewarm at first, but gave in to the pressure and agreed to fund a refinery
questions.explain: Clark thought oil was too volatile, especially with the Civil War raging, but Rockefeller's enthusiasm convinced him to join Andrews in a refinery.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the story of the dissolution of Clark and Rockefeller, what did Clark expect to happen after he angrily proposed splitting up?
options: That Rockefeller would accept the loss and retire
That the two would settle the matter in court
That Andrews would buy Rockefeller's share
That Rockefeller was bluffing and would back down and ask to resume the partnership
questions.explain: Clark, an experienced poker player, felt sure Rockefeller was bluffing and would be humbled. Instead Rockefeller placed a newspaper notice of the dissolution the next day.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How did Rockefeller behave when Clark exploded at him over the loans and the dissolution of their partnership?
options: He wept and asked Clark for forgiveness
He shouted back and threatened to expose Clark
He left town for several months
