He stayed calm and businesslike, agreeing with Clark and saying he was only doing what Clark suggested
questions.explain: Rockefeller's dull, businesslike manner and apparent agreement infuriated Clark while Rockefeller quietly carried out his own plan.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What did Clark come to suspect after Rockefeller bought the refinery at the 1865 auction?
options: That the auction had been rigged by the bank
That Andrews had intended to buy it himself
That Rockefeller had stolen the plans of the refinery
That Rockefeller had been planning this for months, with bank loans and Andrews lined up in advance
questions.explain: Clark reassessed what happened and thought his sober partner might have been acting, since Rockefeller must have secured funds and Andrews beforehand.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the story, how did Rockefeller treat Colonel Oliver Payne, the Cleveland aristocrat with the second-biggest refinery?
options: He threatened to ruin him unless he joined the Southern Improvement Company
He sued him for sabotaging the railroads
He offered a buyout at a good price, Standard Oil stock, and a high-level title, and let him see the ledgers
He offered to merge the firms as equals with equal control
questions.explain: Payne was offered generous terms and a look at Standard Oil's books, which showed higher profit margins, and he accepted.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What did the Southern Improvement Company turn out to be, according to the story?
options: A real alliance that dominated the railroads for decades
A government agency that regulated railroad rates
A rumor that never really took effect, which Standard Oil seems to have spread
A rival company formed by Payne and Fawcett
questions.explain: The SIC remained just a rumor, with Standard Oil as its principal source, and Rockefeller used it as a bogeyman to scare refinery owners into selling.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What was the Cleveland Massacre in the Rockefeller story?
options: A court case that broke up Standard Oil
A violent railroad strike that destroyed freight cars
The few months in which Rockefeller bought out twenty of the twenty-six refineries outside his control
A fire that wiped out the Cleveland refineries
questions.explain: The name refers to Rockefeller's quick takeover of rival refineries. The destructive strike came later in the war with Tom Scott.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the story, how did Rockefeller respond when Tom Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad tried to build his own pipelines and refineries to check him?
options: He negotiated a shared monopoly with Scott
He bribed Scott's board to remove him
He shut down almost all his Pennsylvania refineries and undersold Scott, absorbing losses until Scott gave in
He sold his pipelines to Scott at a loss
questions.explain: Rockefeller starved Scott's pipelines and railroads of oil and cut prices, and Scott ran out of money and had to sell most of his assets.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What happened to Tom Scott after Rockefeller's campaign against him ended?
options: He sold the lion's share of his assets to Rockefeller and suffered a stroke a year later
He retired to run an independent refinery
He sued Rockefeller and won damages
He took control of Standard Oil's pipelines
questions.explain: The defeat was humiliating and sudden: Scott never recovered and died within a few years at the age of fifty-eight.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What was Byron Benson's idea for challenging Rockefeller's control over oil transport?
options: One long, continuous pipeline from western Pennsylvania to the Eastern Seaboard
A fleet of ships carrying oil around the continent
A secret price-fixing agreement with the railroads
A railroad owned by the independent refiners
questions.explain: Rockefeller's pipelines were short, so independents depended on his network. A long pipeline, the Tidewater, would bypass it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these did Rockefeller do to obstruct Benson's Tidewater pipeline?
options: Bought up tank cars, got an exclusive pipeline charter in Maryland, and bought land in the pipeline's path
Persuaded the army to seize the land
Forced Benson's investors to withdraw their money
Sabotaged the pumps with hired saboteurs
questions.explain: Greene lists the tank cars, the bribed Maryland legislature, and a real estate buying spree, plus rumors among farmers that Tidewater would leak.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How did Rockefeller finally bring Benson and Tidewater under his control?
options: By cutting rates on his own lines to near free, then buying more and more Tidewater shares
By hiring Benson as a Standard Oil engineer
By suing Tidewater for patent infringement
By buying Benson's investors' loyalty with bribes
questions.explain: Tidewater could not find oil to ship, so Benson made a deal in 1880. Rockefeller then bought up shares until he controlled it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What was Rockefeller's reputation among the public in the early 1900s after he testified in court cases against Standard Oil?
options: He seemed arrogant and evasive, confirming his bad name
He seemed ill and frightened, asking the court for mercy
He seemed bored and indifferent to all questions
He seemed calm, sweet, and serene, nothing like the devil the public had imagined
questions.explain: A newspaper writer called him the embodiment of sweetness and light. Meanwhile he kept the monopoly together through secret agreements.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the Rockefeller story, Clark first met Rockefeller when they worked together at the produce firm Hewitt and Tuttle.
questions.explain: Clark had befriended Rockefeller at a commercial college they both attended. Rockefeller was a bookkeeper at Hewitt and Tuttle while Clark was a buyer and seller at a produce firm.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the Interpretation, Greene concludes that Rockefeller's success came mostly from supreme intelligence and creative vision.
questions.explain: He says Rockefeller had some of those qualities but nothing strong enough to account for the success; the main cause was relentless force of will, which Greene calls aggressive energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the Interpretation, Greene says Rockefeller's father, William, was a con artist who left the family for months at a time.
questions.explain: The father's absences and sudden returns left the family unsure when he would reappear, which fed Rockefeller's later need for order.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: According to the Interpretation, Rockefeller felt guilty and conflicted about using ruthless methods to ruin his rivals.
questions.explain: He built an aggressor's narrative in which his actions served a divine mission to bring order to the oil business, so his conscience was not troubled.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: According to the section, primitive aggressors tend to rise to top positions and stay there, while sophisticated aggressors usually burn out early.
questions.explain: It is the other way around: primitive aggressors have short fuses and lack self-control so they do not get far, while sophisticated aggressors cloak their maneuvers and rise.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises never to bring sophisticated aggressors on as partners, no matter how friendly or charming they seem.
questions.explain: He warns that they like to piggyback on your hard work and then wrest control.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Interpretation, Greene calls Rockefeller's relentless force of will to dominate every situation and rival ____ energy.
questions.explain: Greene says that more than anything else, Rockefeller's rise can be attributed to what he calls aggressive energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Rockefeller's need for control, the author says, grew out of an unpredictable childhood with a con-artist ____.
questions.explain: The father came and went unpredictably, so John needed to make everything orderly and predictable.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Rockefeller built what Greene calls the aggressor's ____ to convince himself that his quest for power served a higher purpose.
questions.explain: The narrative cast the creation of an oil monopoly as a divine mission to bring order and cheap prices.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The author says Rockefeller turned himself into a superior reader of men, and the quality he most wanted to gauge in rivals was their willpower and ____.
questions.explain: He read rivals' willpower and resiliency from body language and patterns of action.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says anger burns itself out quickly, and so Rockefeller always played for the ____ term.
questions.explain: He aimed to outlast emotional opponents, who tended to surrender or overreact.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says that the more sophisticated aggressors proclaim their convictions, the more certain you can be that they are ____ something.
questions.explain: The louder they are, the more likely they conceal a hidden agenda behind the narrative.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In dealing with sophisticated aggressors, Greene says to look at the individual, not the myth or ____.
questions.explain: Looking at the real person helps you lower the emotional temperature and see the anxiety under the reputation.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says that you must see the frightened ____ within an aggressor like Rockefeller, terrified by anything unpredictable.
questions.explain: The aggressor's need for control covers vast layers of anxieties and insecurities.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: At the Southern Improvement Company stage, Rockefeller offered Colonel Payne money, stock, and a high-level ____ to give up his refinery.
questions.explain: Payne was vain and greedy, and a nice title and plenty of money were enough.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these were among the ways Standard Oil squeezed George Rice, the independent Ohio refiner?
options: Salesmen who anticipated his visits and undersold him
A court order that closed his refinery
Pressure that pushed him to ever-smaller towns until he could sell nothing
A railroad that had agreed to ship his oil suddenly refused
questions.explain: Rice faced blocked shipments, underselling, and a shrinking market. No court order is mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these did Standard Oil do in the 1880s to control the kerosene market, according to the story?
options: Set up storage tanks and tank wagons across the country
Gave retailers free shares in the company
Sold stoves and heaters directly to homeowners at the lowest prices
Secretly owned and ran a supposed rival, Republic Oil
questions.explain: These are the practices Greene describes. Free shares for retailers are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as telltale signs of the sophisticated aggressor in the Interpretation?
options: They get where they are going mainly through aggressive energy rather than talent
They value amassing power more than the quality of their work
They always lose their temper in public
They do not like to share power
questions.explain: The signs are aggressive energy over talent, valuing power over quality, and refusing to share power. Hot tempers describe primitive aggressors.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise for fighting a sophisticated aggressor?
options: Threaten to expose the hypocrisy in their narrative or hidden past deeds
Appear weak to bait them into a rash attack you have prepared for
Confront them directly and loudly
Band together with others who have suffered at their hands
questions.explain: Greene says direct confrontation fails because they are too relentless and have the power to overwhelm you.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are ways Rockefeller made opponents emotional and prone to mistakes, according to the Interpretation?
options: He made Scott angry so Scott became rash
He used the SIC as a bogeyman to scare refinery owners
He fed Clark's arrogance and made him irritable
He gave opponents long periods to plan their responses
questions.explain: He also rushed opponents. Giving them plenty of time was the opposite of his approach.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say aggressors want you to feel or believe?
options: Fear or anger that clouds your thinking
That surrender is inevitable and the best way out
That you have no options
That they are weaker than you
questions.explain: The aggressor wants to control your thoughts and reactions, not to appear weak.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these rivals in the order in which Rockefeller dealt with them in the story.
items: Maurice Clark
Oliver Payne
Tom Scott
Byron Benson
George Rice
questions.explain: The story goes from his partner Clark, to the Cleveland refiners, to the railroad war with Scott, to the Tidewater pipeline, to the small independent Rice.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these events in the partnership with Clark in the order they happened.
items: Rockefeller borrows $2,000 to join Clark
Andrews pitches the oil refinery and Rockefeller sparks
Clark threatens to dissolve the partnership
The auction for the business
Clark begins to feel he had been played
questions.explain: The partnership forms, moves into oil, breaks down, ends at the auction, and only afterward does Clark reassess.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the steps of Rockefeller's method in each refining town in order.
items: Aim at the biggest refineries first
Show them his books
Get a few big fish to surrender
Instill panic in the others
Undersell and drive out the holdouts
questions.explain: Greene describes the method as always the same in Pittsburgh, Philadelphia, and New York, following the Cleveland pattern.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the steps by which the Interpretation explains Rockefeller's drive in order.
items: His father's unpredictability and absences
A need to make life orderly and predictable
Attraction to the chaotic oil business as a way to conquer the father
The overwhelming need for control
A second need to justify his actions
questions.explain: Greene traces a path from childhood anxiety to the need for control and then to the aggressor's narrative.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the advice for handling a sophisticated aggressor in the order Greene gives it.
items: Lower the emotional temperature
Look at the individual, not the myth
Understand their motivation to gain control
Focus on actions and strategies, not feelings
See through their narrative and distractions
questions.explain: Greene starts by calming your emotions and then moves through understanding the person to seeing through the narrative.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each opponent to how Rockefeller read and played him.
pairs: Fed his arrogance and made him irritable
Vain and greedy, so offered money and a title
Scared with the SIC and made to feel isolated and weak
Treated as a hothead to be outlasted
Seen as enamored with his own brilliance and easy to wear down
questions.explain: Each rival was read for a weakness, such as vanity, fear, anger, or pride.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each person in the Rockefeller story to his role.
pairs: Inventor who pitched Clark on the oil refinery
Independent Ohio refiner who published Black Death
Rockefeller's former boss who sold his refinery
questions.explain: These roles come directly from the story.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each term from the Rockefeller story to its meaning.
pairs: Buyout of twenty of the twenty-six outside refineries
Rumored railroad-refinery pact, mostly a rumor
Secret Standard Oil front that caught angry retailers
questions.explain: These items are named in the Rockefeller story.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each type of aggressor to the description Greene gives.
pairs: Explodes when feeling inferior and lacks self-control
Cloaks maneuvers and presents a distracting façade
Tends not to get far, hurting too many people
Rises to top positions and stays there
questions.explain: Greene contrasts the explosive primitive type with the controlled, cunning sophisticated type, and says the difference decides how far each goes.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each piece of Greene's advice about aggressors to the reason he gives.
pairs: Never bring them on as partners
They piggyback on your work and then wrest control
They are relentless and can overwhelm you head-on
Look at their patterns of behavior
If they have taken before, they will take again
It creates strength and leverage in numbers
questions.explain: These pairs come from the closing advice of the section.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether the Interpretation attributes them to Rockefeller's success or says they do not account for it.

items.t: Relentless force of will
Need for control rooted in childhood
Skill at reading rivals' weaknesses
Aggressive energy used on every rival
Supreme intelligence
A particular talent
Creative vision

questions.explain: Greene says Rockefeller had some intelligence, talent, and vision, but not enough to account for his outrageous success.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these traits by whether they describe primitive or sophisticated aggressors.

items.t: Very short fuse
Lacks self-control
Bullies and hurts too many people to get far
Cloaks maneuvers with a distracting façade
Rises to and stays in top positions
Plays on people's emotions

questions.explain: The primitive type explodes and gets stuck; the sophisticated type is trickier and more successful.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these events by whether they belong to Rockefeller's conflicts with Cleveland refiners or his conflicts with Scott and Benson.

items.t: The Southern Improvement Company rumor
Payne examining Standard Oil's ledgers
Fawcett surrendering to Rockefeller's terms
A railroad strike that turned violent
A bribed Maryland legislature
Real estate buying along the pipeline route

questions.explain: The Cleveland phase relied on rumor and the books; the later wars with Scott and Benson used price wars, bribery, and blocking the route.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these pieces of Greene's advice into things to do and things to avoid when facing a sophisticated aggressor.

items.t: Lower the emotional temperature
Focus on their actions and your strategies
Band together with others they have harmed
Fight them directly and openly
Get mesmerized by their charm
Take them on as a partner

questions.explain: Greene recommends calm, indirect, collective methods and warns against being charmed or fighting head-on.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these into things Greene says the aggressor wants to control and things he says you should focus on.
groups: What the aggressor wants to control

items.t: Your thoughts
Your reactions
Your sense that you have no options
Their real goals
Their past patterns of behavior
Your own strategies

questions.explain: The aggressor wants to control your inner responses; Greene says to deny that power by focusing on their goals, patterns, and your plan.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Interpretation, what question does Greene ask about Rockefeller, and what does he say is the answer?
questions.a: He asks how one man with little help accumulated so much power in so little time. The answer is not supreme intelligence or a particular talent but the sheer relentless force of will to dominate every situation and rival, which he calls aggressive energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What two needs does Greene say drove Rockefeller, and where did they come from?
questions.a: The first was an overwhelming need for control, which came from his childhood with an unpredictable con-artist father and led him to bring order to the chaotic oil business. The second was a need to justify his aggression, which produced the aggressor's narrative that his monopoly was a divine mission.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What is the aggressor's narrative, and how did it help Rockefeller?
questions.a: It is the story an aggressor tells himself and others that his quest for power serves a higher purpose. Rockefeller saw ordering the oil business as a crusade for cheap, predictable oil, so he felt no conscience about ruining rivals, bribing legislators, or bending laws. It also confused his opponents about whether he was really a demon.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How did Rockefeller read most people's weaknesses, and how did he use that to win?
questions.a: He judged that most people are weak: led by emotions, wanting things easy, and with little stomach for long battles. He made them afraid, confused, frustrated, or angry, or offered an easy way out, and they surrendered. He also rushed opponents so that they could not strategize.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How does Greene distinguish the sophisticated aggressor from the primitive aggressor?
questions.a: Primitive aggressors have short fuses, explode when they feel inferior, and lack self-control, so they do not get far. Sophisticated aggressors cloak their moves, present a distracting façade, and play on emotions, so they rise to top positions. They also depend on our docility as much as on their own aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What simple sign does Greene give for recognizing a sophisticated aggressor in your own workplace?
questions.a: They get to where they are going mainly through their aggressive energy, not their particular talents. They value amassing power over the quality of their work, do whatever is needed to secure their position and crush challenges, and do not like to share power.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say we often end up surrendering to aggressors, and what is his remedy?
questions.a: We become angry or fearful, enlarge their presence, and obsess over their evil character rather than their actual actions, so we surrender to the illusion of strength they project. The remedy is to lower the emotional temperature and look at the individual, not the myth, focusing on their motives and our own strategies.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to the Interpretation, how should you act against an aggressor if open confrontation is out of the question?
questions.a: Do not fight directly, because they are relentless and powerful. Outwit them by finding unexpected angles, such as threatening to expose the hypocrisy of their narrative or past dirty deeds, appearing weak to bait a rash attack, or banding together with others they have hurt. Even if you must submit now, keep your inner independence and wait for their mistake.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say you should calculate when you fear that fighting an aggressor costs too much?
questions.a: He says aggressors win because you fear losing too much in the present, but you should calculate what you lose in the long term. Once they dominate, your options for power and expansion shrink, and your dignity and self-worth suffer by not standing up. Surrender can become a habit with devastating consequences.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How did Rockefeller's public image change in the early 1900s, and what does the story suggest about his behavior behind the scenes?
questions.a: After he testified in the court cases, the public saw a calm, gentle, serene man instead of a devil, and his philanthropy and cheap oil improved his image. Behind the scenes he kept the monopoly together through loopholes and secret agreements and would not let anyone, including the government, block his path.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, how do people usually explain their own aggressive moments to themselves and others?
options: They rationalize them, saying they had no choice, felt threatened, or did not start it
They blame it on a rare illness or an inherited flaw
They claim the behavior was a deliberate plan to help others
They admit the behavior and promise to avoid it in future
questions.explain: Greene says we rationalize in order to keep our self-opinion as peaceful creatures. We rarely admit the behavior for what it was.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, what does the author say happens when we face people who are clearly weaker and meeker than we are?
options: We become more shy and avoid them altogether
We become more sycophantic to win their affection
The lion in us emerges, mixing help with contempt or a wish to push them around
We lose all aggressive feeling because there is no threat
questions.explain: Our unconscious aggression level rises when we compare ourselves with weaker people, even when we think we are helping. Sycophancy is how we act toward stronger, more aggressive types.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, how do most people think about the word aggression?
options: They use it for stronger manifestations in others and exclude themselves
They use it only for physical violence between nations
They use it as a polite word for ambition in themselves
They use it for any firm or confident behavior in anyone
questions.explain: Greene says we block the idea of a spectrum, defining aggression as what extreme others do, so the aggressive person is always the other.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, what does the Latin root of the word aggression mean, according to Greene?
options: To step forward
To take by force
To hold ground
To strike first
questions.explain: The root means to step forward, which links aggression to asserting ourselves in the world and trying to create or change anything.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, what often happens if people feel uncomfortable with their own assertive impulses and try to repress them?
options: They gradually lose all their assertive energy
They become the most effective and calm leaders
They channel the energy into work without effort
They appear paragons of humility and goodness but turn passive-aggressive
questions.explain: The chapter says this energy cannot be denied or repressed and will emerge in some way, often as passive-aggressive behavior.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene claims that aggression is a tendency that exists only in a minority of unusually hostile individuals.
questions.explain: He calls that a profound misconception: aggression is latent in every human and wired into our species, with some people simply higher on the spectrum.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In Keys to Human Nature, Greene says the positive and negative sides of aggression are two sides of the same coin.
questions.explain: The same energy that lets us fight injustice and create can push us into grabbing too much or pushing people around.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Keys to Human Nature says there is a ____ of human aggression, and we are all on it.
questions.explain: Greene argues that our mild aggressive moments and the extreme kind lie on a single continuum, and we are all somewhere on the spectrum.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, we became the preeminent animal on the planet because of our aggressive energy, supplemented by our intelligence and ____.
questions.explain: The chapter credits aggressive energy, plus intelligence and cunning, for our rise.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Keys to Human Nature says that when we feel our job security is threatened or our career blocked, we may do something extreme, and afterward we ____ our behavior.
questions.explain: The section notes that most often we rationalize such behavior to ourselves and to others.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, the author says that to control and channel aggression we must understand where it comes from, how it turns negative, and why some people are more ____ than others.
questions.explain: These are the three questions that Keys leaves for the next section.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Keys to Human Nature give as examples of everyday places where our split between self-image and behavior shows up?
options: Coworkers who take credit for our work or push us off a project
The delight people take in outrage and attacks on social media
The press exposing every flaw in those in power
Athletes who calmly accept defeat in a championship
questions.explain: Greene lists the workplace, social media, the press, and violent films and games. Calm sportsmanship is not among them.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Keys to Human Nature list as moments when ordinary people cross the line into aggression?
options: Sensing that a partner is going to abandon them
Receiving an unexpected promotion
Feeling frustrated in an intimate relationship
Feeling that their job security is threatened
questions.explain: Job insecurity, relationship frustration, and fear of abandonment appear in the chapter. A promotion is not described as a trigger.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put in order the way the first part of Keys to Human Nature unfolds.
items: We see ourselves as peaceful and agreeable
In some moments we cross a line
We rationalize what we did
We split aggression into us versus extreme others
Greene says aggression is latent in everyone
questions.explain: Greene moves from our self-image, through our actual crossing of lines and rationalizing, to the false divide and then his correction.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put in order the three things Keys to Human Nature says we must understand, as Greene lists them.
items: Understand the source of all human aggression
Understand how aggression turns negative
Understand why some people are more aggressive than others
questions.explain: Keys ends by naming these three things we must understand before we can control and channel our aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each situation described in Keys to Human Nature to the aggressive act it can lead to.
pairs: Trying to push a colleague out of the way
Reaching for a dubious scheme for fast money
Going too far to get noticed
questions.explain: These are among the examples the section gives of how frustration, insecurity or impatience pushes us over the line.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these behaviors by the kind of person they are directed at in Keys to Human Nature.

items.t: Acting more submissive than usual
Becoming a bit sycophantic
Mixing help with contempt and superiority
Being forceful with advice and ordering their life
Using them for our own purposes
Pushing them around

questions.explain: The section says we raise or lower our aggression depending on whom we compare ourselves with.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether they are the positive or the negative side of aggression described in Keys to Human Nature.

items.t: Attacking problems and altering the environment
Fighting injustice
Creating anything on a large scale
Grabbing too much
Pushing people around
Antisocial behavior

questions.explain: Greene presents these as two sides of the same energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Keys to Human Nature, what is the split Greene sees between what we think of ourselves and how we act, and what common ways of handling aggression follow from not seeing it?
questions.a: We think of ourselves as peaceful and cooperative, yet in moments of frustration or insecurity we act aggressively and then rationalize it. Because we do not see our own tendency, we may turn aggressive without realizing it and pay for going too far, or we may repress it and become passive-aggressive.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say it is a misconception to treat aggression as something only other, more extreme people have?
questions.a: He says aggression is a tendency latent in every human and wired into the species. It is on a continuum, so our occasional aggressive moments and extreme cases differ by degree. Treating the aggressor as always the other person blinds us to our own nature.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Keys to Human Nature, what does the Latin root of aggression suggest, and why does this matter for how we judge aggressive energy?
questions.a: The root means to step forward, so any time we assert ourselves to create or change something we tap into this energy. That means aggression can serve positive purposes, and the positive and negative aspects are two sides of the same coin.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Describe the subtler way our aggression shows up in Keys to Human Nature, depending on whether we face stronger or weaker people.
questions.a: With intimidating, more aggressive types we act more submissive and even sycophantic if they have power. With people clearly weaker and meeker than us, the lion in us emerges: we may help them with a feeling of contempt, order their lives, or use and push them around. This happens unconsciously, so we do not experience it as aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to The Source of Human Aggression, what is the ultimate source of human aggression?
options: A desire for wealth for its own sake
Learned habits from a competitive culture
An inborn urge to hurt or take from others
Feelings of helplessness arising from our awareness of weakness and vulnerability
questions.explain: Greene says aggression stems from underlying insecurity rather than a simple impulse to hurt, and the desire for power is a natural response to our essential weakness.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In The Source of Human Aggression, how does Greene describe the human desire for power?
options: A natural response to our weakness, not evil or antisocial in itself
A learned taste from modern capitalism
A trait found only in men
An evil drive that must be stamped out
questions.explain: The desire for power is a way to have control over circumstances and feel a link between what we do and what we get, which makes life's unpredictability tolerable.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does the author mean by guardrails in The Source of Human Aggression?
options: Mental habits that keep us from feeling anxious
The limits others set to prevent us from rising
Safety rules that stop us from physical harm
The patience and social codes and laws we stay within to gain power while being liked and respected
questions.explain: Guardrails are the tacit codes and laws we observe, which require patience and let us gain power while keeping respect.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to The Source of Human Aggression, what do most of us do after we cross the guardrails in a moment of frustration?
options: We abandon ambition altogether
We keep going and enjoy the results
We blame our family for the behavior
We feel uncomfortable or remorseful and scurry back within them
questions.explain: For most people such aggressive acts are occasional and do not become a pattern, unlike the chronically aggressive.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In The Source of Human Aggression, why does Greene say feelings of love can turn into hostility and aggression?
options: Love tends to make us envious of our partners
Love removes our social skills
Love makes us confuse affection with power
In love we are most dependent, vulnerable, and helpless
questions.explain: Greene notes in a parenthetical that love is where we feel most dependent and helpless, which can trigger aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What did the psychoanalyst Melanie Klein notice about some babies, according to The Source of Human Aggression?
options: Some were bored by the mother's attention
Some were more anxious and greedier, attacking the breast and being almost impossible to calm
Some were silent and withdrawn from birth
Some showed no fear of strangers
questions.explain: She speculated that chronically aggressive adults could be grown versions of the greedy baby, born with a greater need to control.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Erich Fromm as cited in The Source of Human Aggression, how can parenting lead to adult aggression?
options: Domineering parents who repress a child's need for power can produce adults who dominate and tyrannize others
Indulgent parents create adults who expect obedience
Strict teachers create children who rebel against parents
Absent parents create adults who fear all rules
questions.explain: Children whose need for power was repressed turn that enforced passivity into active control as adults, and beaten children may later beat others.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say hypersensitivity to criticism and intolerance of dissent in domineering people reveals?
options: A sign of dedication to a cause
A sign of high moral standards
A sign of great inner weakness
A sign of unusual intelligence
questions.explain: A person who is truly strong from within can endure criticism and open discussion without feeling threatened.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to The Source of Human Aggression, why is chronic aggression more common among men than women?
options: Men are physically stronger and so get away with it
Women are taught to hide aggression more effectively
Men find it harder to manage dependency and helplessness and are more insecure about their status
Men receive less affection in infancy than women
questions.explain: Greene points to male infants and the male tie between self-esteem and power, control, and respect, so less is needed to trigger the aggressive response.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene call the phenomenon in which more power and a bigger empire create more points of vulnerability for aggressors?
options: The tyrant's circle
The aggressor's trap
The control paradox
The monopolist's dilemma
questions.explain: More power brings more rivals and enemies, which sparks a need for yet more aggression. Greene says Rockefeller fell victim to this dynamic.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say aggression can easily become addictive for aggressors?
options: Aggression is encouraged by their followers' praise
Aggression is rewarded with money every time
Getting the best of people gives a jolt of adrenaline that makes ordinary pleasures seem tepid
Aggression relieves guilt from earlier acts
questions.explain: The adrenaline of overt, immediate action is stimulating, so safer ways of relieving boredom seem dull by comparison.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to The Source of Human Aggression, how do aggressors treat the people around them?
options: As partners whose opinions they value
As rivals to be defeated at once
As teachers to learn from
As objects to use, with charm that is only for effect
questions.explain: Because their need for control is so strong, they use people, and the habit degrades any empathy they once had.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say attracts followers to aggressors, despite their negative qualities?
options: The aggressor's real generosity and kindness
The security of a stable, long-term job
The followers' own frustrated aggressive desires, which make them fall in love with the narrative
The aggressor's reputation for fairness
questions.explain: Followers get to act out aggression on others, but turnover is high and morale low, as Sophocles' remark about a tyrant's court suggests.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What are the three directions the author says our assertive energy tends to go in?
options: Into anger, into fear, or into envy
Into leadership, into friendship, or into hobbies
Into work as controlled aggression, into aggressive or passive-aggressive behavior, or inward as self-loathing
Into competition, into cooperation, or into retreat
questions.explain: The third direction, self-loathing, activates what Greene calls the internal saboteur.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: According to The Source of Human Aggression, the awareness of our own mortality is one of the sources of our feeling of helplessness.
questions.explain: Humans alone know they could die at any moment, and this joins other insecurities such as job loss and unreliable people.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In The Source of Human Aggression, Greene says positive aggression, such as fighting an injustice, arises with no anxiety at all.
questions.explain: He says feelings of anxiety and insecurity precede the positive type too; it remains an attempt at control for positive purposes.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, once a chronic aggressor takes a step back, you can assume the aggressor has changed.
questions.explain: He says any step back is only momentary because aggressors are addicted and trapped, and are rarely capable of changing the essential pattern.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the first myth Greene discusses, humans were once peaceful, and civilization and capitalism made them aggressive.
questions.explain: This is the myth of the noble savage, which Greene rejects, citing anthropology and archaeology showing brutal warfare long before civilization.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene argues that technology like the internet has reduced human aggression by making people less able to attack each other.
questions.explain: He says technology makes it easier to express aggression, for example through hostile online arguments and cyberwar, because aggression adapts to new media.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In The Source of Human Aggression, Greene says that people who are domineering often surround themselves with ____.
questions.explain: Domineering types need constant reminders of their greatness and superiority.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says the aggressor's ____ is that the more power they get, the more vulnerabilities they create.
questions.explain: The trap leads to more aggression and more power in an escalating cycle.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The first of the two myths Greene discusses is the myth of the noble ____.
questions.explain: It says our ancestors were peace-loving and corrupted by civilization.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, the second myth holds that we are evolving beyond aggression, guided by our better ____.
questions.explain: He answers that the signs of aggression are as prevalent now as ever.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the three tasks, Greene says the first is to stop denying your own aggressive ____.
questions.explain: You must admit you are on the spectrum before you can channel your energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says aggressors have a ____ tolerance for feelings of helplessness and anxiety than the rest of us.
questions.explain: What frustrates us can trigger rage in them.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Flaubert, quoted by Greene, said that even when you take out the canines of a tiger, his heart remains that of a ____.
questions.explain: Greene uses this to argue that progress does not remove the aggressive nature underneath.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Chronically aggressive people are often described as having ____ personalities, with meticulous habits and a predictable environment as their way of holding control.
questions.explain: Meticulous habits and a controlled environment give them a sense of control.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does The Source of Human Aggression list as sources of our feelings of helplessness?
options: A lack of any natural desire for power
Unpredictable people who do not always come through
Insecure positions in life, such as job and status
Awareness of our own mortality
Wounds from childhood that can be reopened
questions.explain: Greene lists the first four as reasons we are plagued by helplessness. He calls the desire for power a natural response to it, not a source.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as telltale signs of a chronic aggressor?
options: An unusually high number of enemies built up over the years
Obsessive physical habits like not being passed on the street
A loud narrative casting themselves as crusader or victim
A sudden shortage of friends in one month
questions.explain: The signs include many enemies, an extreme narrative, and obsessive habits and physical cues. A short-term shortage of friends is not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are among the explanations Greene gives for why some people are chronically aggressive?
options: Domineering parents who repressed their power
Too much success early in life
Being beaten as a child, then beating others as an adult
A possible genetic component, as in the greedy baby
questions.explain: Klein, Fromm, and the abuse example are given; early success is not cited.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as evidence that human aggression is as prevalent in our era as in the past?
options: A decline in violent entertainment
Worsening depredation of the environment
Cycles of war and acts of genocide
Growing inequality in power and wealth
questions.explain: Greene points to war, environmental damage, inequality, and the popularity of violent entertainment, which has not declined.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene suggest you do when you face a chronic aggressor whose battle with you is inevitable?
options: Match them in open anger
Never engage in direct confrontation
Make the easy victory they expect seem more expensive
Look for the vulnerabilities they are covering up
questions.explain: He advises indirect fighting and exposure of what they hide, not open anger.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these steps in the order Greene uses to build the case for why people become aggressive.
items: Awareness of mortality and vulnerability
Feelings of helplessness
A natural craving for power and control
Staying within the guardrails by patience and skill
Crossing the guardrails when frustration overwhelms patience
questions.explain: Greene moves from weakness to helplessness to the craving for control, then to the guardrails and what happens when we break them.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the author's three tasks for a student of human nature in the order given.
items: Stop denying your own aggressive tendencies
Become a master observer of aggression in others
Rid yourself of denial about aggression in human nature
questions.explain: These are the three tasks listed in the closing part of the section.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the points of Greene's argument about the two myths in order.
items: Myth one: humans were once peaceful
Evidence of ancient warfare and ecological damage
Myth two: we are evolving beyond aggression
Evidence from war, inequality, and technology today
We must own the fact that aggression is in all of us
questions.explain: The first myth and its evidence precede the second myth and its evidence, with the conclusion last.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each thinker to his idea in The Source of Human Aggression.
pairs: Some babies are greedier and more anxious, and chronic aggressors may be grown versions
Domineering parents can produce adults who dominate others
Whoever enters a tyrant's court becomes his slave
A tiger without canines still has a carnivore's heart
questions.explain: Each thinker is quoted or cited in the section to support a point about aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each task for the student of human nature to what it requires.
pairs: Admit your own aggression and channel it productively
Observe aggression in others and spot chronic aggressors
Give up the myths denying aggression in human nature
questions.explain: Greene gives the three tasks in this order.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each quality of the chronically aggressive to how Greene describes it.
pairs: Lower than average, so they feel rage
Hypersensitive, a sign of inner weakness
questions.explain: These are four of the qualities he calls out.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each myth or fact to the way Greene treats it.
pairs: Rejected, as ancestors waged brutal warfare
Rejected, as war, inequality, and online hostility persist
Gives aggression new tools such as cyberwar
Expects more aggression as more people feel helpless
questions.explain: Greene dismisses both myths and expects more, not less, aggression ahead.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene says they happen to ordinary people or to chronic aggressors.

items.t: Cross the guardrails only on occasion
Feel remorse and scurry back
Make aggression a lasting pattern
Exaggerate threats and grab for more than necessary
Find normal ways of getting stimulation too dull

questions.explain: Ordinary people slip over the line in moments, while chronic aggressors keep crossing it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these directions of assertive energy by whether Greene presents them as productive or unproductive.

items.t: Channeling energy into patiently achieving things
Developing higher social and technical skills
Lashing out and regretting it
Turning anger inward as self-loathing
Passive-aggressive behavior

questions.explain: Controlled aggression is the productive route; the other directions bring problems.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these methods by whether Greene advises them for dealing with an aggressor or lists them as aggressor tactics.

items.t: A last-minute change to an agreed deal
Spreading rumors and disinformation
Charming you with a favor to entrap you
Anticipating their maneuvers
Appearing weaker than you are
Disengaging mentally to control your emotions

questions.explain: The aggressors use surprises and traps, while Greene advises anticipation, deception for defense, and emotional detachment.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Explain in The Source of Human Aggression how feelings of helplessness lead to a desire for power and how most people satisfy it.
questions.a: Humans are aware of mortality, insecure in their positions, dependent on unpredictable others, and carry childhood wounds, so helplessness is unavoidable. The craving for power is a natural response, a wish for control over circumstances. Most of us satisfy it through work skills, social skills, and accepted activities, staying within the guardrails by being patient.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What are the guardrails in The Source of Human Aggression, and what makes some people cross them chronically?
questions.a: Guardrails are the patience, social codes, and laws that let us gain power while remaining liked and respected. Most people cross them only in moments of frustration or old wounds and scurry back, but chronic aggressors feel helpless more deeply and often, so their need for power overrides patience and social responsibility.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, what are the possible roots of chronic aggression?
questions.a: A genetic component is possible, as Klein's observation of greedy, anxious babies suggests, and early family life can matter, as Fromm argued: domineering parents who repress children's need for power often produce adults who dominate others. Those who were beaten may later beat others, turning passivity into activity.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say we should look for the underlying insecurity when we see a chronic aggressor?
questions.a: He says aggression stems from an underlying insecurity rather than a simple wish to hurt. Aggressors process feelings of helplessness and anxiety first, perceive or exaggerate threats, and strike to preempt them. Seeing their inner fragility helps us control our own fear and intimidation, which aggressors love to stimulate.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Describe how the aggressor's trap and addiction mean that the aggressor's past pattern will continue.
questions.a: Aggression gives a jolt of adrenaline that can become addictive, and each increase in power creates more rivals and vulnerability, which leads to more aggression. They also feel stopping would look weak. So they are both addicted and trapped, and we must not be naive: any step back is momentary.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say a student of human nature should do about the aggression in the people around them (the second task)?
questions.a: Become a master observer: watch actions and nonverbal cues rather than words, be tolerant of ordinary aggression, and spot chronic aggressors who cannot tolerate challenge and want more control. Telltale signs include many enemies, an extreme narrative as crusader or victim, and obsessive habits. Disengage mentally and fight indirectly.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say you may sometimes need to step outside the guardrails when dealing with an aggressor?
questions.a: Aggressors have the advantage of going outside the guardrails often, with last-minute changes in negotiations and rumors, so you must anticipate them. Occasionally you must venture outside yourself, as a temporary and defensive measure, by deception, appearing weak to bait an attack, or spreading rumors to unbalance them. Defeating aggressors matters more than keeping your purity.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What are the two myths about aggression in the third task, and how does Greene answer each?
questions.a: The first is the noble savage, the idea that ancestors were peaceful until civilization corrupted them; Greene answers that early humans made murderous war and damaged their environments. The second is that we are evolving beyond aggression; he answers with war, genocide, environmental harm, inequality, and online hostility as evidence of aggression in our own era.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene conclude that we must own the fact of aggression in human nature?
questions.a: He says insecurity is rising for many groups, so we should expect more aggression, with dirtier wars and more confrontation, and better ways to justify it. The denial that it is always the other person or culture is stronger than ever. Only by awareness that it is all of us can we think of progress.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the book's order of chapters, which law comes immediately before the Law of Aggression?
options: The Law of Generational Myopia, on seizing the historical moment
The Law of Fickleness, on making people want to follow you
The Law of Conformity, on resisting the pull of the group
The Law of Repression, on confronting your dark side
questions.explain: Chapter 15 on the Law of Fickleness comes just before Chapter 16. Generational Myopia is the chapter that follows it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which law does the book take up immediately after the Law of Aggression?
options: The Law of Envy
The Law of Aimlessness
The Law of Generational Myopia
The Law of Death Denial
questions.explain: Chapter 17 is Seize the Historical Moment, the Law of Generational Myopia. Death Denial is the final chapter, number 18.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does the title of Chapter 16, See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade, tell the reader to do?
options: Treat every friendly person as an enemy
Show a friendly surface while hiding your own aims
Look past a polite surface to the aggressive drives beneath it
Avoid any person who shows open anger
questions.explain: The title signals the chapter's theme: people look civilized, but frustrated aggressive desire lies under the mask, and you must learn to see it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the book's table of contents, the chapter on the Law of Aggression comes before the chapter on the Law of Fickleness.
questions.explain: Fickleness is Chapter 15 and Aggression is Chapter 16, so Fickleness comes first.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The Law of Aggression appears in the chapter whose title speaks of the hostility behind the friendly ____.
questions.explain: The chapter title is See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are sections of the Law of Aggression chapter, in addition to the three in its first half?
options: Passive Aggression, Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
The Reality Group
Controlled Aggression
The Narcissistic Spectrum
questions.explain: The chapter's second half has the sections on passive aggression and controlled aggression. The other two titles belong to other chapters.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the chapter's sections in the order they appear.
items: The Sophisticated Aggressor
Keys to Human Nature
The Source of Human Aggression
Passive Aggression
Controlled Aggression
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a case study to the theory of aggression, then to its source, then to the hidden form, and ends with the productive form.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these steps of the first half of the chapter in order.
items: A story of Rockefeller's rise
An interpretation naming the sophisticated aggressor
An account of our own hidden aggressiveness
An account of why aggression arises
Three tasks and two myths about aggression
questions.explain: Greene starts with Rockefeller and his analysis, widens to everyone's aggressive tendencies, explains the roots, and ends with tasks for the student of human nature.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each section of the Law of Aggression chapter to its main job.
pairs: A long case study of Rockefeller with lessons on handling aggressors
The claim that everyone is on a spectrum of aggression
Why helplessness leads to aggression, plus three tasks for the student
How to channel aggressive energy to productive ends
questions.explain: Each section has a distinct role: story, claim about human nature, causes, and finally the productive use of aggressive energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each chapter of the book to its law.
questions.explain: These are consecutive chapters in the book's table of contents.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these sections of the chapter by whether they are in its first half or its second half.

items.t: The Sophisticated Aggressor
Keys to Human Nature
The Source of Human Aggression
Passive Aggression
Controlled Aggression

questions.explain: The first three sections cover the Rockefeller story, our nature, and the roots of aggression; the last two cover the hidden form and the productive form.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene begin the chapter with the long story of Rockefeller before turning to everyone's nature in Keys to Human Nature?
questions.a: The story presents Rockefeller as a specimen of a highly aggressive person, so the reader can see aggressive energy at work without the usual emotional reactions. The Interpretation draws lessons about the sophisticated aggressor. Keys then widens the lens, claiming that aggression is present in every human on a spectrum.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How does the section The Source of Human Aggression follow from the end of Keys to Human Nature?
questions.a: Keys ends by saying that to control and channel aggression, we must understand the source of all human aggression, how it turns negative, and why some people are more aggressive than others. The Source section then answers this by tracing aggression to feelings of helplessness and describing the chronic aggressor.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In Greene's account of passive aggression, why is the behavior called passive?
options: We act only when we are certain no one is watching us
We avoid every kind of action and simply wait for others to give way
We appear to be merely being ourselves rather than actively trying to influence anyone
We let a third person deliver the message so we stay out of it
questions.explain: The label refers to appearance: the passive aggressor seems not to be manipulating, yet a message still gets sent. It does not mean the person does nothing or hides behind a go-between.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what is true of people who engage in everyday, low-grade passive aggression such as slow replies or subtle digs?
options: They are never quite as passive as they seem, since part of them knows what they are doing
They are truly unaware of their behavior and mean no harm
They are chronic aggressors who should be avoided entirely
They are acting from a deep fear of every kind of authority
questions.explain: Greene says that in the back of our minds we know we are delaying a reply or inserting a dig, while pretending to be innocent. He advises tolerance of this everyday version.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: What does Greene say about how to treat the low-grade passive aggression that thrives in polite society?
options: Cut off anyone who shows even a trace of it
Treat it as an irritating part of social life and be as tolerant as possible
Answer it in kind so the other person learns a lesson
Confront it every time so that it never becomes a habit
questions.explain: Greene separates the everyday version, which we are all guilty of and should tolerate, from the chronic passive aggressor, who is the real danger.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what in a chronic passive aggressor's childhood often explains the adult pattern?
options: Early success that taught them they could ignore rules
Domineering or neglectful parents, which made indirect tactics their way to get attention while avoiding punishment
A lack of any siblings, which left them without rivals
Overly indulgent parents who gave in to every demand
questions.explain: Passive aggression was a way of asserting their will without risking punishment, and they repeat what worked in childhood. Greene says the manipulative child can be seen peeking through the adult mask.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say chronic passive aggressors are hard to resist when they are very good at their strategies?
options: Their open threats make us afraid to disagree with them
Their ambiguity makes us unsure they are attacking us at all, and the confusion gives them power
Their constant flattery makes us lower our guard
Their strong reputations make other people take their side
questions.explain: They are masters at being elusive, so we may think we are imagining things or being paranoid. Direct aggression would make us angry and resist, but indirection sows confusion that they exploit.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the key to defending ourselves against passive aggressors?
options: Waiting for them to reveal themselves through a mistake
Asking a mutual friend to confront them for us
Matching their behavior with open anger straight away
Recognizing what they are up to as early as possible
questions.explain: Greene says early recognition is the key, and then lists the common strategies and counters. Open anger is the reaction passive aggressors want.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Subtle-Superiority strategy, what lies at the root of the person's chronic lateness and forgetfulness?
options: A fear that you secretly dislike them
A need to show themselves and you that they are in some way superior
A wish to avoid the work they have been given
A genuine inability to keep track of time
questions.explain: Greene says that putting you in the inferior position lets them define the relationship. They cannot state their superiority outright without ridicule, so they let you feel it while denying it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: A friend is chronically late to your plans but always arrives with a logical excuse and a sincere-sounding apology. According to Greene, what should you attend to most?
options: The pattern of the behavior, more than the apologies
How sincere the apology sounds the first time
Whether other friends are also kept waiting
The quality of each individual excuse
questions.explain: Greene tells you to pay attention to the pattern more than the apologies, and to notice nonverbal signs such as a whiny tone and apologies laid on extra thick.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In Greene's account, what did Milton Erickson do when his student Anne arrived late yet again, with her usual profuse apology?
options: He took her aside and warned her she would fail the course
He had the whole class stand and bow to her in mock reverence, and he did so too
He began the lecture again so that she missed nothing
He marked her absent and refused to let her take part in the lab
questions.explain: The bowing conveyed that everyone saw through her, and her embarrassment made her stop being late. Anne was a straight-A student, so grades were not the lever he used.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How does Greene say you should react to a boss or powerful person who makes you wait as a show of superiority?
options: Complain openly to their colleagues
Arrive late to their meetings to mirror them
Keep calm and show your own superiority by staying patient and cool
Bow to them to show that you see through them
questions.explain: With someone in power the assertion is not subtle and mirroring is risky, so the best available response is calm patience. Mirroring and shaming is advised for peers and underlings.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Sympathy strategy, what do passive aggressors want once they have drawn out your sympathy?
options: A promise that you will defend them in public
Favors, extra care, and attention, which give them control
Your agreement that others have it worse
Your advice on how to solve their problems
questions.explain: Greene notes that they do not want advice or any suggestion that they are partly to blame. Their goal is the favors and attention that tilt the relationship in their favor.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How does Greene say genuine victims differ from the sympathy-seeking passive aggressor in telling their stories?
options: Genuine victims tell their stories at length, while passive aggressors keep quiet
Genuine victims seek advice, while passive aggressors seek only money
Genuine victims feel shame and tell their stories reluctantly, while passive aggressors are eager to share and bask in attention
Genuine victims exaggerate their pain, while passive aggressors understate it
questions.explain: Greene ties the reluctance of true victims to an old superstition that bad luck signals something wrong with a person. Passive aggressors are dying to tell what happened to them.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: According to Greene, how can you gain the distance needed to see through a sympathy-seeking passive aggressor?
options: Convince them that others are suffering more than they are
Let yourself feel anger and resentment at the time and energy wasted for so little in return
Tell them directly that their symptoms are not real
Offer them more help until they no longer need you
questions.explain: Greene says the only way to build distance is to feel anger at how much you give and how little comes back. He adds that you should not feel bad about leaving and that they will quickly find another target.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: A new acquaintance showers you with attention and help, then occasionally turns cold, and you find yourself trying to please them. Which of Greene's strategies does this fit?
options: The Dependency strategy
The Blame-Shifter strategy
The Subtle-Superiority strategy
The Passive-Tyrant strategy
questions.explain: Greene describes the Dependency strategy as unusual early attentiveness, then coldness that leaves you puzzling over what you did, until the sympathy and concern shift from them to you.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In Greene's description of the Insinuating-Doubt strategy, what are the people who use it most often driven by?
options: A wish to be admired
Envy
A need for sympathy
Fear of abandonment
questions.explain: Greene says such people want to strike blows at your self-esteem, and most often they are operating out of envy. Sympathy-seeking belongs to a different strategy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: A colleague congratulates you on your promotion with a faint smile and says you must be pleased with the money. According to Greene, what is the best counter?
options: Demand an explanation of exactly what was meant
Show the remark has no effect, calmly agree, and perhaps return the faint praise
Tell others about the remark so they will judge it
Answer with a sharper insult to teach a lesson
questions.explain: The insinuator wants to get a rise out of you, so Greene advises calm, an agreeable reply, and perhaps a hint that you see through them. Demanding an explanation gives them the reaction they want.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: What does Greene advise you to do in the moment a Blame-Shifter is irritating you?
options: Say nothing and walk away until they apologize
Ask other people to confirm that you were right
Write down what they are doing so you can later trust your own feelings
Quote their past mistakes back to them in detail
questions.explain: Writing it down memorializes the behavior, so you can check whether you overreacted and, if not, remind yourself you are not crazy and stop the blame-shifting in its tracks.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the logic behind the Passive-Tyrant strategy?
options: People who are praised often will work harder for the leader
People who are paid well will accept almost any treatment
People who fear unemployment will stay no matter how they are treated
People who cannot tell what earns praise or punishment have no power or independence and can be made to do anything
questions.explain: If underlings knew exactly what pleased the tyrant, they would hold some power. Moodiness and occasional praise, like a pat for a dog, keep them anxious and submissive.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that actively aggressive types, such as Rockefeller, can also be passive-aggressive, using it as an additional weapon in their attempts at control.
questions.explain: Greene says active aggressors can be quite passive-aggressive at times, and that for them it is simply one more weapon of control.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: Greene says chronic passive aggressors typically have low energy and little need for control.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: like active aggressors they have a high degree of energy and need for control, but they fear outright confrontation.
