questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: In the Subtle-Superiority strategy, Greene advises you to show open irritation, since passive aggressors respect strength.
questions.explain: He says you must not get angry or display overt irritation, because passive aggressors thrive on getting a rise out of you. Stay calm and subtly mirror them instead.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: In the Dependency strategy, Greene says a person who is too solicitous too early in a relationship should be treated with some wariness.
questions.explain: He says this is unnatural since we are normally a bit suspicious at first, and advises keeping some distance until you can gauge their motives.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: In the Blame-Shifter strategy, Greene says the passive aggressor typically behaves badly toward everyone, not only toward you.
questions.explain: He says they are often quite nice and polite to other people and play their games only on the person they want to control, which is why confiding in others brings no sympathy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: In Greene's discussion of the Sympathy strategy, the symptoms such as headaches or anxiety attacks tend to recur when the person needs a favor or feels you pulling away.
questions.explain: Greene says to look for this pattern: the symptoms appear when they need something, feel you withdrawing, or feel particularly insecure.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: True or false: In the Passive-Tyrant strategy, Greene says open rebellion against the tyrant is usually the most effective response.
questions.explain: He says overt rebellion will only make things worse. Because such tyrants hold real power and are hypersensitive, the only real counter he gives is to quit and recuperate.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Greene says the behavior of a chronic passive aggressor works like a ____ strategy, acting on a person over time in a personal or work relationship.
questions.explain: Greene says chronic types use drip-drip passive-aggressive strategies that take effect on an individual over time.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Greene says that if we look closely at a passive aggressor we can often see the manipulative ____ peeking through the adult mask.
questions.explain: The pattern comes from childhood strategies that worked, so the manipulative child shows through the adult.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Subtle-Superiority strategy, Greene says the passive aggressor tries to turn the tables by making you seem ____ and unsympathetic.
questions.explain: When confronted, the chronically late person suggests that you are uptight and unsympathetic, and may even say you add to their stress.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Greene says that to counter the Subtle-Superiority strategy you should stay calm and subtly ____ their behavior.
questions.explain: Mirroring, for instance by showing up impossibly late with a sincere apology laced with irony, lets them brood on what it means.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Sympathy strategy, Greene says the passive aggressor is always the ____ of unfair circumstances, hostility, or society in general.
questions.explain: The person always plays the victim and relishes the drama of the story.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Greene says sympathy-seeking passive aggressors often prey on those who are prone to feel ____, the sensitive caregiving types.
questions.explain: These types target people prone to guilt, which makes disengaging hard.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Dependency strategy, the person made to feel dependent is returned to the position of the needy and vulnerable ____.
questions.explain: The strategy is all about gaining power over another, returning the dependent person to a childlike, wanting position.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In Greene's story of the Insinuating-Doubt strategy, the Terror leader Robespierre aimed his insinuations at his friend and fellow leader Georges ____.
questions.explain: Robespierre came to see Danton as an enemy of the revolution but chose to insinuate this rather than say it outright.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: When insinuators are challenged, Greene says they may say they were only kidding, asking whether they can take a ____.
questions.explain: This is one of the variations Greene lists on the insinuating-doubt strategy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Blame-Shifter strategy, you are left feeling that perhaps you overreacted or were ____, even doubting your own sanity.
questions.explain: The shifting of blame leaves you unable to trust your own feelings and feeling guilty for the tension.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: In the Passive-Tyrant strategy, Greene says Michael Eisner exercised dictatorial control over everyone around him, including Jeffrey ____.
questions.explain: Greene points to Eisner and Katzenberg as the example of this strategy and refers the reader to chapter 11 for more.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as everyday examples of ordinary passive aggression?
options: Taking extra time to answer someone's message to signal slight disdain
Praising someone while slipping in a subtle dig
Openly refusing a request and explaining why
Making a neutral comment while tone and expression show you are upset
questions.explain: The first three are his examples of indirect assertion. An open refusal is direct and so is not passive aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these are traits Greene attributes to chronic passive aggressors?
options: A fear of outright confrontation
A strong preference for open arguments
Reliance on strategies that worked in childhood
A high degree of energy and need for control
questions.explain: Chronic types combine energy and a need for control with fear of confrontation, and repeat childhood tactics. They avoid open arguments.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say are nonverbal signs of the insincere apologies in the Subtle-Superiority strategy?
options: A tone that suggests it is really your problem
Apologies laid on extra thick
A whiny tone of voice
A long and detailed written explanation
questions.explain: Greene lists the whiny tone, the thick apologies, and the sense that the problem is yours. Written explanations are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these are described as ways the sympathy-seeking passive aggressor attracts pain to themselves?
options: Being negligent with details so things fall apart
Refusing every offer of help
Choosing partners who will disappoint them
Having a bad attitude at work that draws criticism
questions.explain: Greene says they are masters at attracting pain through these choices. Refusing help is not on his list, since they in fact seek attention and favors.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these are variations of the Dependency strategy that Greene describes?
options: A boss who rewards quick work with extra pay
Someone who makes promises of money or a job but delivers only part
A partner in a couple who makes the other dependent
A parent who showers a child with affection and treats independence as unloving
questions.explain: Greene mentions the mother and daughter, couples, and promise-makers who forget or deliver partially. A boss paying for fast work is not an example.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise when dealing with a Blame-Shifter?
options: Stay calm and be fair, even accepting some of the blame if that seems right
Avoid trading recriminations with them
Try to make them as angry as you are
Write down their behavior as it happens
questions.explain: He warns that they are better at the drama game, so he advises calm and notes. Making them angry is the trap he tells you to avoid.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Which of these are features of the Passive-Tyrant strategy as Greene describes it?
options: Appearing disorganized, absentminded, or like a helpless child
Giving clear and consistent instructions
Replacing underlings who quit with more submissive ones
Occasional praise mixed with temperamental rants
questions.explain: The strategy depends on unpredictability and feigned helplessness. Clear, consistent instructions would give underlings power, which is just what the tyrant avoids.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Put Greene's six passive-aggressive strategies in the order he presents them.
items: Subtle-Superiority
Sympathy
Dependency
Insinuating-Doubt
Blame-Shifter
Passive-Tyrant
questions.explain: This is the order in the text: the first three concern superiority, victimhood and dependency, followed by doubt, blame and tyranny.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Put the steps of Greene's account of the Blame-Shifter's tactics in the order they unfold.
items: You feel irritated by something they did
They seem to sense it and sulk before you speak
When confronted they go silent with a hurt look
They conjure up a past wrong or push your buttons
You end up feeling guilty and doubting yourself
questions.explain: Greene walks through the sulking, the hurt silence, the counter-accusation, and the guilt that leaves you doubting your own feelings.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Put the stages of the Dependency strategy in the order Greene describes them.
items: Someone becomes unusually attentive to you
You grow dependent on what they give
They show occasional coldness
You try hard to please them
The sympathy and concern shift from them to you
questions.explain: The attention comes first and builds dependence; the coldness makes you work to please, and the dynamic then reverses.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Put the steps of Erickson's handling of the late student Anne in order.
items: Anne arrives late once more
Erickson has the class stand and bow to her
Erickson bows as well
The students keep bowing in the hall afterward
Anne, embarrassed and ashamed, stops coming late
questions.explain: The mock reverence was carried beyond the room, conveying that the class saw through her, and the shame ended the pattern.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Put Greene's logic of the Passive-Tyrant strategy in order.
items: A boss seems brimming with energy but disorganized
You strain to anticipate their needs
They alternate rare praise with angry rants
You cannot tell what earns praise or punishment
Having no independence, you can be made to do anything
questions.explain: Unpredictability prevents underlings from learning what works, and without that knowledge they lose power and independence.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each passive-aggressive strategy to its main tell or tactic.
pairs: Chronic lateness or forgetting, always with a ready excuse
Always the victim, relishing the drama of their own story
Unusual early attentiveness followed by coldness
Faint praise and comments that make you wonder
Sulking and a hurt silence that leave you feeling guilty
questions.explain: Each pairing follows the opening scenario Greene gives for the strategy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each strategy to Greene's main counter.
pairs: Stay calm, mirror their behavior, induce some shame
Create inner distance and quit the relationship
Show the insinuations have no effect on you
Write down their behavior and trust your own feelings
Detach emotionally and, in the end, quit and recuperate
questions.explain: These are the counters Greene gives for each strategy in turn.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each person from Greene's examples to the strategy or story they illustrate.
pairs: Responding to a chronically late student
Insinuating that a friend was an enemy
Dictatorial control through being hard to please
An active aggressor who also used passive aggression
questions.explain: Each figure is tied to one point in the section on passive aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each phrase in the Passive Aggression section to the strategy it belongs to.
pairs: You did quite well for someone of your background
Fine. Whatever. If that’s how you feel
They have too much on their mind and are overwhelmed
questions.explain: These phrases come from the examples Greene uses to illustrate each strategy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each type of person to how Greene says they treat sympathy and their own troubles.
pairs: Feels shame and tells the story reluctantly
Is eager to share and bask in your attention
Seems vaguely bored by other people's problems
Passive aggressor who feels you pulling away
May show symptoms such as headaches or depression
questions.explain: The contrast between reluctant true victims and attention-hungry passive aggressors is Greene's way to tell them apart.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Match each passive-aggressive tactic to the feeling it is meant to leave in the target.
pairs: Self-doubt that gets under your skin
Guilt and doubt about your own feelings
Anxiety and a need to try harder
questions.explain: Each tactic works on a different emotion, but all aim at control.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene describes them as a trait of everyday passive aggression or of the chronic passive aggressor.

items.t: Slow reply to signal slight disdain
Tone of voice that stirs up guilt
A thing nearly everyone is guilty of
Repeats strategies that worked in childhood
Drip-drip tactics aimed at one person over time
Uses ambiguity to sow confusion and gain power

questions.explain: Greene treats the first as irritating but tolerable, and the second as a pattern that can make your life miserable.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Sort these responses by whether Greene recommends them or warns against them when dealing with passive aggressors.

items.t: Staying calm and not showing overt irritation
Noticing the pattern more than the apologies
Writing down their behavior in the moment
Getting angry so they see how you feel
Exchanging recriminations with a blame-shifter
Rebelling openly against a passive tyrant

questions.explain: Greene repeatedly says passive aggressors thrive on a rise out of you, and that open rebellion or recrimination plays to their strengths.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Sort these strategies by whether the person using them mainly plays the victim or mainly puts the target down.
groups: Puts the target down or under pressure

items.t: Sympathy strategy
Blame-Shifter hurt silence
Insinuating-Doubt comments
Subtle-Superiority lateness
Passive-Tyrant rants

questions.explain: Sympathy and the hurt look of the blame-shifter draw on being wounded, while the others work by lowering the target or making the target anxious.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Sort these statements by whether they describe the real victim or the passive aggressor who plays the victim.

items.t: Feels shame at their fate
Tells their story reluctantly
Relishes the drama of their story
Looks bored when others share problems
Resents advice that suggests they are partly to blame

questions.explain: Greene uses these differences in attitude toward the story, rather than the amount of suffering, to tell the two apart.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Why do all of us engage in some passive aggression, according to Greene?
questions.a: Most of us fear outright confrontation and want to seem polite, yet we cannot always get what we want without asserting ourselves, and we need release from the tension of being deferential. So we assert ourselves indirectly, for example by being slow to reply or inserting digs. Greene says we are not as innocent as we seem, since part of us knows what we are doing.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How does Greene distinguish a chronic passive aggressor from ordinary people, and what is the origin of the pattern?
questions.a: Chronic passive aggressors have a high degree of energy and need for control but fear outright confrontation. They often had domineering or neglectful parents and used passive aggression to get attention or assert their will without punishment. They repeat the same strategies as adults, so the manipulative child can be seen behind the mask.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Why does Greene say passive aggression can be more damaging than direct aggression?
questions.a: Because it is ambiguous and elusive, we can never be sure they are attacking us and may think we are paranoid. Direct aggression would make us angry and resist, but indirection sows confusion that they exploit for power and control. If they reach our emotions, they can make our lives miserable.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Explain the Subtle-Superiority strategy and how Greene says to counter it.
questions.a: The person is chronically late or forgetful, with logical excuses and thick apologies, and turns the tables if confronted. The root is a need to be superior while denying it, which defines the relationship. You should watch the pattern, stay calm without showing irritation, and subtly mirror their behavior to call attention to it and induce shame.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: What happened in Greene's story of Milton Erickson and his student Anne, and what does it show about countering passive aggression?
questions.a: Anne, a straight-A student, kept arriving late and apologizing sincerely, holding up others. Erickson had the whole class stand and bow to her in mock reverence, and the students kept doing so afterward. The message was that they saw through her, and the embarrassment made her stop, showing that shaming calmly can end the pattern.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How does the Sympathy strategy work, and how can you tell it from real suffering?
questions.a: The person is always the victim, draws your sympathy, then asks for favors and attention, which is the control they want. They resist advice and any hint of blame, and often attract pain through their own choices. Real victims feel shame and tell their stories reluctantly, while passive aggressors are eager to share and bask in your attention.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How does Greene advise you to deal with a sympathy-seeking passive aggressor, and why is this hard?
questions.a: You need distance, which is hard because they soak up your time and prey on guilt-prone, caregiving people. Greene says you get it by feeling anger and resentment at the time you waste and how little they return, which lets you see through them and leave the relationship. You should not feel bad, because they quickly find another target.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Describe the Dependency strategy and the warning signs Greene gives.
questions.a: Someone is unusually attentive and helpful early on, you become dependent, and then they turn cold, leaving you trying to please them until concern shifts from them to you. Warning signs are being too solicitous too early, coldness that confuses you, and anger when you seek distance. Greene advises keeping some distance, being wary of promises, and making it a priority to get out.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: How did Robespierre use the Insinuating-Doubt strategy against Danton, and what is Greene's counter to the strategy?
questions.a: Defending Danton at an assembly, Robespierre repeated every charge against him in detail and concluded that he deserved praise as a family man, which planted doubt while pretending support. The point of the strategy is to hurt self-esteem, most often out of envy. The counter is to stay calm, show the insinuations have no effect, even agree with faint praise, and perhaps hint that you see through them.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: Explain the Blame-Shifter strategy and Greene's advice for dealing with it.
questions.a: The person sulks or goes silent with a hurt look when confronted, may dredge up a past wrong or push your buttons so they can call you hostile, and leaves you feeling guilty and doubting yourself. They are often nice to others, so you get no sympathy. Greene advises staying calm and fair, avoiding recriminations, and writing down their behavior in the moment so you can trust your own feelings, then disengaging.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: What is the logic of the Passive-Tyrant strategy, and why does Greene say the only real counter is to quit?
questions.a: If people do not know what earns praise or punishment, they have no power or independence, so the tyrant mixes moodiness, rants, and occasional praise to keep them submissive and anxious. The tyrant often holds real power and is hypersensitive, so resistance or detachment makes things worse. Greene says no position is worth the damage to your self-esteem, so you should quit and recuperate.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.section: Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
questions.q: You work for a charismatic but disorganized boss who rails at you after rare praise. Using Greene's ideas, explain what is happening and how you should think about it.
questions.a: This is the Passive-Tyrant strategy: the boss seems helpless and temperamental, but it is more conscious than it looks, and the unpredictability keeps you from knowing what pleases and therefore powerless. Greene advises you to dwell on their manipulations and harshness rather than the praise, and detach emotionally. If they sense your distance and get worse, the real answer is to leave.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How does Greene describe the human energy he calls willpower, assertiveness, or aggression in its purest state, in childhood?
options: Cautious and rule-bound, shaped by what adults allowed
Calm and patient, content to wait for others to act first
Bold and adventurous in body and mind, relentless in solving problems and getting what we want
Selfish and cruel, aimed at taking things from other children
questions.explain: Greene says this energy made us explore ideas, seek friends, and be relentless and bold in asking. It could turn combative only after long frustration.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the more common outcome than becoming chronically aggressive as we grow older?
options: We become uncomfortable with and frightened of our own assertive energy
We express it openly but only toward strangers
We lose the energy completely and feel nothing
We direct it all into competitive sports
questions.explain: Failure, exposure, dislike from others, conflict, and parental shame make us see the aggressive part of ourselves as dangerous.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In Greene's account, what happens to aggressive energy that we judge dangerous but that cannot disappear?
options: It turns inward and becomes what Ronald Fairbairn called the internal saboteur
It splits into ambition and anger with nothing left over
It turns outward and becomes passive aggression in every case
It fades slowly until it is replaced by calm
questions.explain: Greene uses Fairbairn's term for the inner persecutor that continually judges and attacks us. The outward routes (chronic or passive aggression) are separate outcomes.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these is something Greene says the internal saboteur does?
options: It makes us openly confront whoever blocks us
It reminds us of the potential for failure whenever we are about to attempt something
It pushes us to take risks so we can prove ourselves
It encourages us to express deep emotion freely
questions.explain: The saboteur tamps down exuberance, ambition, and strong feeling, and urges us toward a humble fake self. It does not encourage risk or open expression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say the internal saboteur and the aggressor have in common?
options: Both rely on persistence to wear down opposition
Both use sympathy to get what they want
Both are driven by envy of other people's success
Both seek control over uncertainty, though through opposite means
questions.explain: The aggressor seeks control by attacking, the saboteur by lowering our energy and making the world manageable, but also quite dead.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, how does the internal saboteur affect our thinking?
options: It discourages bold ideas and leads us to settle for the conventional opinions of the group
It sharpens our judgment by making us doubt ourselves
It makes us argue with every opinion that we hear
It leaves our thinking unchanged and affects only behavior
questions.explain: Creative people are aggressive in their thinking, trying many options. By rooting out aggressive impulses we also thwart our own creative energies.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say is the real problem with human aggressive energy?
options: Children express it too early and should be taught restraint
Aggression has no positive uses in modern society
We do not know how to harness it in an adult, productive, and prosocial manner
Humans are by nature too aggressive and must suppress it
questions.explain: He says the problem is not that we are assertive, since the positive and negative aspects are two sides of one coin. The task is to tame and train the energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, what lies behind much of the sneering at ambition and ambitious people in our culture?
options: A belief that ambition causes aggression
Envy at the accomplishments of others
Concern for people who fail
A well-founded distrust of power
questions.explain: Greene says much of the sneering stems from a great deal of envy, and that tamping down youthful ambitions signals that you no longer respect yourself.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: A woman always dreamed of writing a particular book but now says she is too modest to be ambitious. Using Greene's ideas, what is wrong with that stance?
options: Her humility is its own ambition and display, and by lowering her ambitions she limits her possibilities and energy
She should drop the book and aim for general success
She should keep the dream secret so as not to provoke envy
Her modesty is sincere but will lose her friends
questions.explain: Greene says being so humble and saintly is itself an ambition, and that the remedy is to revisit the early ambition and make it specific, not to hide it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say vague ambitions such as wanting success, money, and attention can lead to aggressive behavior?
options: With no clear idea of what is enough, the person cannot limit their desires and keeps wanting more
Vague goals reward persistence too slowly
Vague goals make the person doubt their own worth
Vague goals attract the envy of rivals
questions.explain: He asks what constitutes enough money, success, or power; without a limit, people continually want more and do not know when to stop.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, how should the ambitions you adopt be sized?
options: Challenging, but not so far above your capacity that you only set yourself up for failure
Left open-ended so that you never feel finished
As large as possible, since only grand goals produce energy
Small enough that failure is impossible
questions.explain: Greene wants the end point and route to be clearly visible, with each finished ambition followed by a new one to build momentum.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: According to Greene, what causes us to give up on a problem too soon?
options: We lack the intelligence to find a clever solution
We run out of time before we have tried every method
A slight loss of self-belief reduces the energy of our attack, which makes the doubts louder
We do not feel enough anger toward the problem
questions.explain: He describes a downward spiral: doubts weaken our blows, weaker results amplify the doubts, and we surrender inwardly long before outwardly.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as examples of persistence carried over many years?
options: Edison and the telephone, Newton and gravity, and Hakuin and Zen
Hannibal and the Alps, Marie Curie and the lightbulb, and Edison and radium
Edison and the lightbulb, Marie Curie and radium, Einstein and relativity, and Hakuin and Zen enlightenment
Einstein and the lightbulb, Hakuin and radium, and Curie and relativity
questions.explain: Greene credits Edison with the proper lightbulb, Curie with radium, Einstein with relativity after ten years of thought experiments, and Hakuin with enlightenment after about twenty years.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How does Greene say we come to be timid, according to the section on Fearlessness?
options: Timidity is acquired as fears mount and we lose confidence in our power to get what we want
Timidity is inherited, so we cannot change it
Timidity comes from too much early success
Timidity is taught by teachers who value obedience
questions.explain: He says we are bold by nature and become overly concerned with how people see us, internalize their doubts, and develop a habit of backing down.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Where does Greene say anger becomes toxic?
options: When it is disconnected from reality, aimed at vague enemies and scapegoats
When it is directed at specific people who deserve it
When it is kept simmering for a long time
When it is felt at all, since it is an ugly emotion
questions.explain: He says natural frustration turns toxic when channeled into anger at scapegoats or grand conspiracies spread by demagogues, without thought behind it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the section on anger, what does Greene say gives an orator such as Malcolm X much of his effectiveness?
options: A calm and neutral manner
A sense of contained rage
The support of a large movement
Skill at humor and storytelling
questions.explain: Greene says contained rage makes an orator effective and was the source of much of Malcolm X's charisma.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the problem is that humans are assertive and aggressive, so these traits should be removed as far as possible.
questions.explain: He says the problem has never been that we are assertive, which would make a problem of our own nature. The task is to tame and train the energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the internal saboteur makes us forge a fake self that is humble and self-effacing.
questions.explain: This is one of the saboteur's effects, along with tamping down ambition and pleasure and pulling us inward, even toward depression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the Persistence section, Greene says people tend to give up outwardly long before they have given up inwardly.
questions.explain: He says the reverse: we surrender inwardly long before we surrender outwardly, which is why we give up too soon.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that incremental practice, such as speaking up in everyday situations, is how to recover fearlessness.
questions.explain: He says to begin with small everyday acts of speaking up and then ramp up, building the muscle slowly before risking a large-scale battle.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises using a giant cathartic release of anger, since a loud protest is the most satisfying outcome.
questions.explain: He says most people vent in one release and then slip back into complacency or bitterness. He prefers cooled anger at a simmer, with real satisfaction coming from defeating the bully.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that restrained anger in a film or book can feel like a fresh wind because most of us are so careful and correct.
questions.explain: He says such channeled anger attracts our own frustrations and resentments and lets them out, and that we recognize it as real and authentic.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Ronald Fairbairn, whom Greene calls a great English psychoanalyst, named the inner persecutor that judges and attacks us the internal ____.
questions.explain: The internal saboteur lowers our energy and constrains what we do.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says the positive and negative aspects of aggressive energy are two sides of the same ____.
questions.explain: Trying to tamp down the negative only dulls the positive.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says that instead of being chronically aggressive, passive-aggressive, or repressed, we can make our aggressive energy focused and ____.
questions.explain: Concentrated and sustained energy has far more force behind it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says Controlled Aggression gives us ____ potentially positive elements of this energy that we can discipline and use.
questions.explain: The four are ambition, persistence, fearlessness, and anger.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Ambition section, Greene says to revisit your earliest ambitions, adapt them to your current reality, and make them as ____ as possible.
questions.explain: Specific goals let you visualize the endpoint and the route, making success likelier.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says that if you observe infants, you will notice how willful and ____ they are when they want something.
questions.explain: He uses infants to show that persistence is natural to us before confidence fades.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Persistence section, Greene cites Hannibal's motto about finding a way or making a ____.
questions.explain: The motto is used to show the determination he wants the reader to adopt.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Fearlessness section, Greene says building boldness must be done slowly, like a ____ that has atrophied.
questions.explain: Slow building prevents a large-scale battle before you have toughened up.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: In the Anger section, Greene says you want to cool your anger and bring it more to a ____ than a boil.
questions.explain: A simmering anger gives you the resolve and patience for a longer struggle.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The chapter ends with a quotation from Rollo ____ about the self-assertion that honest communication requires.
questions.explain: The closing quotation says power is required for communication and may even require aggression at times.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say the internal saboteur makes us uncomfortable with?
options: The expression of deep emotion
Standing out from the group
Quiet and routine work
Strong sensations of pleasure
questions.explain: The saboteur wants us to tamp down pleasure, emotion, and ambition so we fit into the group. Routine work is not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are the four positive elements of aggressive energy that Greene describes?
options: Cunning
Ambition
Fearlessness
Persistence
questions.explain: He names ambition, persistence, fearlessness, and anger. Cunning is not one of the four.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as consequences of tamping down your ambitions?
options: You are more likely to fail
You become more adult and mature
You limit your possibilities
You diminish your energy
questions.explain: He says lowering ambitions does not make you more adult, only more likely to fail, with fewer possibilities and less energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise for recovering the fearlessness you had as a child?
options: Call people on their passive-aggressive behavior
Pick a major fight right away to test yourself
Begin by speaking up in everyday situations when people are insensitive
First convince yourself that you deserve better things in life
questions.explain: Greene stresses incremental steps. Starting with a large-scale battle is what he warns against.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are examples Greene gives of toxic anger disconnected from reality?
options: Anger at a specific person who unfairly blocks your advancement
Anger at scapegoats conjured up by demagogues
Blaming outside forces for one's lack of success instead of one's own impatience
Imagining grand conspiracies behind inescapable realities
questions.explain: The first three are toxic anger. Anger aimed at a specific blocker is the healthy, targeted form he recommends.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are questions Greene says you should ask to control your anger?
options: Do you understand the cause of the anger and what it should be directed at?
How loudly can you express it to be heard?
Are you certain the frustration does not stem from your own inadequacies?
What is the best way to channel it to defeat your opponents?
questions.explain: He asks you to analyze the emotion, its target, and the best strategy. Loudness is not his concern; he wants it cooled and targeted.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say about using anger in creative or expressive work?
options: You should capture and channel anger and not shy away from it
Restrained anger behind lasting works of art can be felt by the audience
Anger should be kept out of creative work so it stays pure
Contained rage can make an orator effective
questions.explain: He cites Malcolm X and lasting art, and tells you to channel anger into your work. He does not say to keep it out.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the four positive elements of aggressive energy in the order Greene presents them.
items: Ambition
Persistence
Fearlessness
Anger
questions.explain: This is the order in the Controlled Aggression section, moving from goals to endurance to courage to emotion.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the stages of Greene's account of how aggressive energy ends up as the internal saboteur in order.
items: Childhood energy is bold and assertive
Frustration, failure, and shame make it feel dangerous
We become frightened of our own assertiveness
The energy turns inward as an internal persecutor
The saboteur lowers our energy and makes the world dead
questions.explain: Greene traces the path from a pure childhood energy through shame and fear to an inward attack that constrains our lives.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the stages of the downward spiral to giving up, as Greene describes in the Persistence section, in order.
items: We attack the problem with energy
Background doubts slightly reduce our self-belief
Our action loses force and the result is weaker
The doubts grow louder and weaken the next blow
We admit defeat and give up
questions.explain: Self-doubt reduces energy, which brings poorer results and louder doubts, until we surrender.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the steps Greene recommends for building boldness in order.
items: Convince yourself you deserve better things
Speak up in everyday situations
Try this in small ways every day
Make greater demands that people treat you well
Bargain harder and defend your interests against bullies
questions.explain: Greene says to build the fearless muscle step by step, from belief, to small acts, to larger demands and negotiations.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put the steps Greene recommends for handling anger in order.
items: Feel the anger toward a specific target
Analyze whether it is justified and where it should be directed
Work out the best strategy for defeating your opponents
Cool it to a simmer for the longer struggle
Find satisfaction in defeating the bully
questions.explain: Greene wants anger analyzed, targeted, and held at a simmer so that it supports a longer struggle rather than a single release.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each figure or example in the Controlled Aggression section to what it illustrates.
pairs: Years of painstaking persistence on the lightbulb
Twenty years of relentless effort toward Zen enlightenment
Contained rage as the source of an orator's charisma
Finding a way or making a way
questions.explain: Each is used by Greene to illustrate one of his points.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each element of controlled aggression to the problem it counters.
pairs: Tamping down dreams because we fear seeming self-absorbed
Giving up too soon as doubts erode self-belief
The habit of backing down and failing to set boundaries
Vague, scapegoating fury that leads nowhere
questions.explain: Each element is presented as the healthy counterpart to a way we lose or misuse our energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each element of controlled aggression to a practice Greene recommends.
pairs: Revisit early dreams and make them specific
Keep attacking from new angles with full force
Start by speaking up in small everyday ways
Analyze it, aim it, and cool it to a simmer
questions.explain: These are the main instructions in each of the four subsections.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each effect to the force Greene says produces it.
pairs: Lowering energy and making the world dead
Getting more by never knowing when to stop
questions.explain: Each pairing follows a cause-and-effect link that Greene draws in this section.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each stance toward aggressive energy to its result in Greene's account.
pairs: Frustration and resistance leave the person combative
Energy turned inward as the internal saboteur
Focused, rational energy with more force
questions.explain: Greene contrasts three poor ways of handling the energy with the fourth, trained and disciplined one.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these effects by whether they come from the internal saboteur or from the controlled aggression Greene recommends.

items.t: Tamps down ambition to fit in with the group
Makes us settle for conventional opinions
Builds a humble, self-effacing fake self
Gives us momentum from one ambition to the next
Lets us feel bolder, more integrated, more authentic
Concentrates energy so it has more force

questions.explain: The saboteur dulls and constrains us, while trained aggressive energy adds focus and force.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene treats them as healthy or toxic uses of anger.

items.t: Aimed at a specific individual who blocks you unfairly
Analyzed to check it is not your own inadequacy
Cooled to a simmer for a long struggle
Aimed at a vague enemy or scapegoat
Fed by a belief in grand conspiracies
Released in one spasm and then followed by complacency

questions.explain: Greene separates anger that is realistic, targeted, and sustained from anger disconnected from reality or spent in one burst.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these examples by whether they illustrate persistence or fearlessness in Greene's account.

items.t: Edison inventing the proper lightbulb
Marie Curie discovering radium
Einstein's ten years of thought experiments
Asking for a raise or a promotion
Telling people what you think of their bad ideas
Making bolder demands in negotiations

questions.explain: Persistence examples are sustained efforts to solve a problem, while fearlessness examples are standing up to people.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene describes them as part of the childhood state or as acquired later in life.

items.t: Bold requests for what we want
Willful persistence of infants
Big dreams with no shame
Timidity and a habit of backing down
Fear of how others perceive us
Shame about our aggressive outbursts

questions.explain: Greene says boldness, persistence, and ambition are original, while timidity and shame are learned.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these by whether they describe a sign of stifled ambition or a sign of well-directed ambition.

items.t: Keeping dreams secret and acting modestly
Wanting only success, money, and attention
Having no sense of what is enough
Seeing the end point and how to get there
Turning to a new project after reaching a goal
Putting full energy in without doubts or guilt

questions.explain: Greene contrasts hiding or blurring ambitions with making them specific and pursuing them in sequence.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Describe the aggressive energy Greene says we are born with and what happens to it as we grow up.
questions.a: Greene calls it willpower, assertiveness, or aggression mixed with intelligence; in childhood it made us bold, curious, relentless, and open to the world. With frustration, resistance, and shame, some of us become chronically aggressive, but more commonly we grow frightened of the energy. It then turns inward and becomes the internal saboteur.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What is the internal saboteur, and how does it limit our lives?
questions.a: Named by Ronald Fairbairn, it is a persecutor within that judges and attacks us, reminds us of failure, and tamps down exuberance, pleasure, deep emotion, and ambition. It pushes us to retreat inward, even into depression, and to present a humble fake self. It lowers our energy and makes life manageable but dead, and it dampens our mental boldness.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say we should not try to eliminate our aggressive energy, and what should we do instead?
questions.a: He says the problem is not that we are aggressive, since the positive and negative aspects are two sides of one coin, and suppressing the negative dulls the positive. The real problem is that we do not know how to harness it in an adult, productive, prosocial way. We should tame and train it so it becomes focused and rational, which brings back some of our childhood spirit.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene say about ambition, and why do people stifle it?
questions.a: Greene says we all had big dreams as children but later stifled them, partly to avoid seeming self-absorbed, and partly because the culture sneers at ambition out of envy. Lowering ambitions signals low self-respect and only limits possibilities and energy, and being humble is itself a display. He advises reviving early dreams and making them specific.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How should you shape and pursue your ambitions, according to Greene?
questions.a: Revisit your earliest ambitions, adapt them to your current reality, and make them specific so you can see the end point and how to reach it. They should be challenging but not far beyond your capacity. After reaching one, move on to a new ambition to build momentum, putting full energy in without doubts or guilt.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why do we tend to give up too soon, and what does Greene say about the power of persistence?
questions.a: A slight fall in self-belief reduces the energy of our attack, which gives weaker results and louder doubts, so we surrender inwardly before we do outwardly. Greene says almost nothing can resist persistent human energy, citing Edison, Curie, Einstein, and Hakuin. He wants us to drop background doubts and keep attacking from new angles.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What does Greene mean by persistence being aggressive energy that is undivided from within?
questions.a: He means the infant, the scientist, or the Zen practitioner wants something so badly that no inner doubt dilutes their effort, so nothing deters them. Knowing the value of persistence, they summon the energy and self-belief to solve the problem, and it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. He recommends wanting a goal badly enough that nothing will stop you.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How does Greene say we lose our natural fearlessness, and how can we recover it?
questions.a: We are bold by nature, but as we age we worry about how others see us, fear conflict, and develop a habit of backing down, failing to set boundaries or ask for what we deserve. To recover it, first believe you deserve better, then speak up in small everyday situations, and gradually make greater demands, stand up to bullies, and negotiate harder. It is built slowly like an atrophied muscle.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Greene say fearlessness is worth the effort, and what does he expect you will discover?
questions.a: He says losing our bold spirit is losing a deep part of ourselves and is painful. When you try speaking up, you will often find you have less to fear than you imagined, and may even gain respect. Once developed, the muscle gives confidence to meet any adversity with a fearless attitude.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: What distinguishes healthy anger from toxic anger in Greene's account?
questions.a: Greene says anger at those who unfairly block you or at fools with power is natural and can energize action. It becomes toxic when disconnected from reality, as when people blame scapegoats or conspiracies spread by demagogues instead of their own impatience. Healthy anger is aimed at specific individuals and forces, analyzed, controlled, and realistic.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says to cool anger to a simmer rather than a boil. Why, and how can anger be used in creative work?
questions.a: Most people release anger in one cathartic spasm and then slip back into complacency or bitterness. Simmering anger keeps you energized, patient, and resolved for a possibly longer struggle, with real satisfaction in defeating the bully. In creative or expressive work, contained anger gives life and movement and attracts an audience, as with Malcolm X and lasting art.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Someone is passed over for a promotion and starts blaming a vague 'system' while stewing for weeks. Using Greene's ideas on anger, how would you advise them?
questions.a: Greene would say their anger is drifting toward a vague enemy and risks becoming toxic. They should analyze whether the frustration stems from their own shortcomings, find the real cause and target, and plan the best strategy to defeat the obstacle. They should keep the anger controlled and simmering as motivation rather than venting it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Why does Chapter 16 end with Controlled Aggression after the section on passive aggression?
options: It returns to the opening aggressor to show how he can be avoided
It moves from the personal to the historical, setting up the next chapter
After showing the harmful forms aggression takes, it presents the remedy of training the same energy for productive ends
It shows that passive aggression is the best form of aggression
questions.explain: The final section recasts aggressive energy as something to tame and use, in contrast with the chronic, passive-aggressive, or repressed ways of handling it.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The title of Chapter 16 speaks of hostility behind a friendly façade. Which section of the chapter most directly deals with this?
options: Controlled Aggression
The Source of Human Aggression
Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
Keys to Human Nature
questions.explain: Passive aggressors present a pleasant or innocent front while exerting control, and the section teaches readers to see through it. Controlled Aggression is about channeling energy, not about masks.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Greene says the Insinuating-Doubt strategy usually comes from envy. Which other chapter of the book is organized around that theme?
options: Chapter 9, on confronting your dark side (the Law of Repression)
Chapter 10, on beware the fragile ego (the Law of Envy)
Chapter 8, on changing circumstances by changing attitude (the Law of Self-sabotage)
Chapter 11, on knowing your limits (the Law of Grandiosity)
questions.explain: Chapter 10 is the Law of Envy, so the remark connects this chapter to it. The Eisner example, by contrast, points to chapter 11.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the book's table of contents, Chapter 16 (the Law of Aggression) falls between the chapter on fickleness and the chapter on generational myopia.
questions.explain: Chapter 15 is Make Them Want to Follow You (Fickleness) and Chapter 17 is Seize the Historical Moment (Generational Myopia).

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: True or false: In the chapter's structure, Controlled Aggression comes before Passive Aggression.
questions.explain: The table of contents gives the sections in this order: The Sophisticated Aggressor, Keys to Human Nature, The Source of Human Aggression, Passive Aggression, and finally Controlled Aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these parts of Chapter 16 in the order they appear.
items: The Sophisticated Aggressor
Keys to Human Nature
The Source of Human Aggression
Passive Aggression—Its Strategies and How to Counter Them
Controlled Aggression
questions.explain: This is the order in the table of contents, moving from the aggressor to human nature, then source, then disguised aggression, and finally the constructive use of the energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Put these three laws in the order of their chapters.
items: The Law of Fickleness
The Law of Aggression
The Law of Generational Myopia
questions.explain: The table of contents gives Chapter 15, 16, and 17 in this order.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Match each idea from the second half of Chapter 16 to its link elsewhere in the book.
pairs: Eisner and Katzenberg, discussed in chapter 11
Passive aggression as an extra weapon
Used by active aggressors too, such as Rockefeller
The way to harness the energy rather than be chronically aggressive, passive-aggressive, or repressed
questions.explain: Greene ties these threads to other parts of the book or chapter.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Sort these items by which of the chapter's two later sections they belong to.

items.t: Robespierre and Danton
Milton Erickson and Anne
The Blame-Shifter
Ronald Fairbairn
Hakuin and Zen
Malcolm X

questions.explain: The first group are strategies and stories about disguised hostility; the second are the figures in Greene's case for harnessing aggressive energy.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: Which of these are sections of Chapter 16 in the book's table of contents?
options: The Sophisticated Aggressor
The Inner Authority
The Source of Human Aggression
Controlled Aggression
questions.explain: The Inner Authority is a section of Chapter 15, not Chapter 16.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: The law of Chapter 16, See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade, is the Law of ____.
questions.explain: The table of contents lists Chapter 16 as the Law of Aggression.

questions.unitTitle: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Façade
questions.q: How do the two later sections of Chapter 16 relate to each other, and what does the contrast say about Greene's view of aggression?
questions.a: The Passive Aggression section shows how hidden hostility and indirect control work and how to counter it, which is the friendly façade of the title. The Controlled Aggression section shows that the same energy, rather than being suppressed, can become ambition, persistence, fearlessness, and anger put to productive use. Greene's view is that aggression is part of human nature and must be trained, not denied.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to the opening statement of the Law of Generational Myopia, what happens to generational values and ideas as you get older?
options: They matter only in your relationships with your parents.
They make you more open to the views of younger people.
They tend to close you off from other points of view, constraining your mind.
They gradually fade as personal experience replaces them.
questions.explain: The author says generational values harden over time and narrow your outlook, which is why the law is called generational myopia. They do not fade or open the mind.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: In the Law of Generational Myopia, what does the author say deep knowledge of the spirit of your generation and times lets you do?
options: Return to the values of your parents with more conviction.
Exploit the zeitgeist and anticipate the trends your generation hungers for.
Avoid ever being influenced by any trend.
Win the approval of the older generation that holds power.
questions.explain: Understanding the spirit of the times lets you anticipate and set trends and free your mind from generational constraints. It is not about pleasing elders or rejecting all trends.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The Law of Generational Myopia says your generation defines who you are less than you imagine.
questions.explain: The opening says the opposite: your generation defines who you are more than you can imagine.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The chapter's law, the Law of ____ Myopia, says your generation shapes how you see the world.
questions.explain: The chapter is titled as the Law of Generational Myopia: seeing narrowly through the lens of your generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does the opening of the chapter say about a generation?
options: It is easy for individuals to see because they stand outside it.
It becomes less constraining on the mind as its members age.
It forms tastes, values and ways of thinking that its members internalize.
It wants to separate itself from the previous generation and set a new tone.
questions.explain: The opening describes a generation distancing itself from the last and imprinting its tastes and values on individuals. It adds that these values close the mind with age, so they are not less constraining.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author say your task is regarding the influence of your generation, and what do you gain by doing it?
questions.a: Your task is to understand as deeply as possible the powerful influence your generation has on who you are and how you see the world. In return you can exploit the zeitgeist, anticipating and setting the trends your generation hungers for. You also free your mind from the generational constraints on it and become more of the individual you imagine yourself to be.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes the problem the law warns about or the benefit the author promises.

items.t: Generational values close you off from other points of view
Your mind is constrained without your noticing
You can anticipate the trends your generation craves
You free your mind from generational constraints
You become more of the individual you imagine yourself to be

questions.explain: The first two describe the constraining influence of generational values; the others are the rewards of understanding that influence.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which outcome does the author hold out for someone who frees their mind from generational constraints?
options: A guarantee that the older generation will accept them.
A permanent return to the values of their childhood.
Immunity from the opinions of anyone in their own generation.
More of the individuality they imagine for themselves, with the power that freedom brings.
questions.explain: The opening promises that you become more of the individual you imagine yourself to be, with the power that freedom brings.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did Louis XVI's mood change as he prepared for his coronation in 1775?
options: He learned the ritual was only a symbolic tradition.
Studying the ritual convinced him he would be elevated above mortals and guided by God.
His advisers promised him a quick end to the nation's debts.
The French people greeted him with unexpected enthusiasm.
questions.explain: The legend of the sacred oil, which made the king God's lieutenant on earth, filled him with the confidence he lacked. For him the rite's ancientness was comforting rather than empty.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Many progressive French people saw the coronation ritual as a relic of a superstitious past. How did Louis XVI respond?
options: He ignored it and stressed practical reforms instead.
He found its ancientness comforting and chose to reenact it in a more original form.
He simplified it to please the progressive clergy.
He canceled the public parts of the ceremony.
questions.explain: Louis felt the opposite of the progressives: he leaned on the rite's antiquity and even surrounded himself with Roman-god imagery to dazzle his subjects.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did fifteen-year-old Danton sneak off to Reims to see the coronation?
options: His father had ordered him to see the king.
He hoped to be hired by the royal court.
He wanted to describe it vividly in an essay and win his school's prize.
He wanted to protest against the monarchy.
questions.explain: Danton knew he was weak at writing, so he planned to compensate with an eyewitness account for the essay prize. The adventure also suited his bold character.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What was at the root of France's perpetual financial crisis under Louis XVI?
options: An antiquated financial structure in which the clergy and nobility were largely exempt from taxes.
Corruption among the bankers who lent to the court.
Heavy taxes that fell mainly on the nobility.
A string of lost wars that emptied the treasury.
questions.explain: Onerous feudal-era taxes fell on the lower and middle classes while the clergy and nobility largely escaped them, so revenue never matched the court's lavish spending.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did Danton turn down a higher position on the King's Council in 1788?
options: He wished to return to his family's farm.
He feared the king's ministers would betray him.
He had been offered a lower salary than he wanted.
He believed the country was on the brink of revolution and the monarchy was doomed.
questions.explain: He told the minister the matter was no longer about modest reforms and asked whether he could see the avalanche coming. He had read the signs of change before others.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did Louis decide to hold the Estates General at Versailles despite his advisers' warnings?
options: Versailles was cheaper than any hall in Paris.
He wanted to avoid the agitators of the nobility.
He hoped the grandeur would impress the delegates and remind them of the monarchy's divine origin.
He wanted the delegates close to the army for protection.
questions.explain: Louis reasoned that the splendor of Versailles would move the moderate Third Estate to gratitude, but advisers warned it was too close to Paris and its agitators.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What did the Third Estate do that was described as unthinkable for the French king?
options: It refused to attend the opening ceremony.
It proposed to abolish taxes forever.
It asked the church to crown a new king.
It declared itself the true representative of the people and disobeyed a royal order to disband.
questions.explain: Calling itself the National Assembly and refusing a royal decree was unprecedented insubordination from the lower classes.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How did Louis explain the starving, swearing crowd surrounding his carriage on the way to Paris?
options: He recognized them as victims of his mismanagement.
He believed they had been misled by the Third Estate.
He thought they were soldiers disguised as peasants.
He decided they must be outside agitators, not his real subjects.
questions.explain: He could not recognize his own subjects and concluded they were outsiders brought in to destroy the monarchy. This shows him still viewing events through the lens of the divine monarchy.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What did the revolutionaries do with Louis's coronation carriage, the Sacre?
options: They preserved it as a museum of the monarchy.
They sold it to a foreign collector for the treasury.
They gave it to Danton as a trophy.
They melted its gold, sent its bronze to the foundries and burned its painted panels.
questions.explain: Finding it a hideous grotesquerie no one would buy, they salvaged its gold for the treasury and bronze for cannons and burned the mythological panels.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: In the author's interpretation, why did the subtle signs of discontent in prerevolutionary France go unnoticed by the king?
options: They were subtle and disparate, and could pass as novelties without underlying meaning.
The king had banned the writers who recorded them.
They were hidden by the church from the court.
They appeared only after the Estates General.
questions.explain: Enlightenment ridicule, secret societies and popular theaters were hard to connect into a trend until the late-1780s crisis made them combine into a force.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What was the one instance in which Danton's sense of timing was off?
options: He joined the Cordeliers too early.
He moved to end the Terror months before the public was ready.
He called for a republic too late.
He turned down the position on the King's Council.
questions.explain: Danton understood before others that the Terror was a mistake, but acting months ahead of the public gave his rivals an opening to destroy him.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What cultural movement does the author say Danton's youthful generation represented?
options: Absolutism, valuing the king's divine right.
The Enlightenment, valuing reason over feeling.
Classicism, valuing order and strict etiquette.
Romanticism, valuing emotions and sensations over the intellect and formalities.
questions.explain: The author calls it the first real explosion of Romanticism, and Danton's emotional speeches and the disinterment of his wife exemplified it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to the author, why are intellectuals often the last to discern the spirit of the times?
options: They fear speaking out against the powerful.
They are so grounded in theories and conventional frameworks.
They pay too much attention to fashion.
They isolate themselves from young people.
questions.explain: The author insists you must first feel the change in the collective mood, and says intellectuals are bound by theories that blind them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author conclude about trying to revive something that has lost its spell?
options: It can be revived by ritual and spectacle.
Force works if applied early enough.
No amount of force can bring it back to life.
It can be revived by a charismatic leader.
questions.explain: Louis turned to force to make the past prevail, but once something no longer enchants, force cannot restore it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to the author, why is Louis XVI closer to you than you think?
options: Like him, you are likely to inherit great power.
Like him, you are likely to be betrayed by allies.
Like him, you probably fear public speaking.
Like him, you probably look at the present through the lens of the past.
questions.explain: Things look much as they did a month ago, so we assume life goes on as always, while the tide moves below the surface.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What happened to Danton after he began openly working to end the Terror?
options: Robespierre accused him of lost fervor, and he was arrested for treason and executed.
He was welcomed back by the sans-culottes.
He was named leader of the Committee of Public Safety.
He was exiled to Belgium.
questions.explain: His campaign against the Terror played into Robespierre's hands. Robespierre packed the Committee and ensured a guilty verdict.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Louis XVI had longed all his life to become king and felt fully ready for the role.
questions.explain: Ever since he was a boy, he had dreaded becoming king, finding the role beyond his capacities.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Danton won his school's essay prize after witnessing Louis XVI's coronation firsthand.
questions.explain: Inspired by the images he saw in Reims, Danton wrote his best essay yet and won the prize.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: At the time of the Estates General in 1789, the previous Estates General had been held only a few years earlier.
questions.explain: The previous one had been held in 1614, so convening one was a measure of last resort and an anomaly.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: When Danton visited Louis at the Tuileries, he bowed graciously but refused to kiss the king's hand.
questions.explain: This was a breach of protocol that, along with his manner and clothes, frightened and unsettled the king.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: After the monarchy fell, the revolutionaries sold the Sacre for a large sum to fund the republic.
questions.explain: They found it hideous and unsellable, so they melted and burned it for useful materials.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Danton remained a supporter of the Terror until the day he was arrested.
questions.explain: Danton grew sick of the bloodshed, was no longer in favor of the Terror, and worked openly to end it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says Danton compared the rising mood of the people to a strong tide in a river that he jumped into.
questions.explain: Danton, an avid swimmer, told a friend it was like seeing a strong tide in the river and jumping in to let it carry him.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Louis XVI was anointed at Reims with sacred oil that, according to legend, was deposited by a ____.
questions.explain: The legend said a dove sent from the Holy Spirit left the oil kept at the church in Reims.
