questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The coronation carriage, designed to represent the chariot of Apollo, was named the ____.
questions.explain: The Sacre was meant as a symbol of the monarchy, dazzling and mythical, yet seemed oddly out of place.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Danton joined a club of bohemian artists and political agitators called the ____.
questions.explain: The club was near his apartment, and its raucous debates drew him into the revolutionary spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The lowest classes, the most revolutionary in spirit, were called the ____, meaning without breeches.
questions.explain: Danton came to identify with them, feeling ostracized himself, and his call for a republic resonated among them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Voltaire and Diderot ridiculed the church and monarchy, and their ideas became known as the ____.
questions.explain: These ideas spread among the expanding middle class, which was excluded from power.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The author says intellectuals are often the ____ to discern the spirit of the times.
questions.explain: Because they are grounded in theories and conventional frameworks, intellectuals trail those who feel the mood.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The author calls the cultural movement of Danton's youth the first real explosion of ____.
questions.explain: It valued emotions and sensations above the intellect and formalities.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: After losing his title, the former king was to be known as Louis ____.
questions.explain: Capet was the family name of the founder of the tenth-century kingship that would end with Louis.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these were subtle signs of discontent below the surface of prerevolutionary France?
options: Plays mocking the monarchy at the popular Paris theaters
Freemason lodges that were hotbeds of discontent
Open revolt by the army before 1780
Writers such as Voltaire and Diderot ridiculing church and monarchy
questions.explain: The author lists Enlightenment ridicule, secret societies and brazen theater among the cracks. The army turned unreliable only once the revolution was underway.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these did Danton and the young king Louis have in common?
options: They were not far apart in age.
Both were dreaded as orators.
Both were large and considered decidedly unhandsome.
Both came from the middle class.
questions.explain: The text notes the similarity in age and in looks. Louis was shy and a king; Danton was a middle-class orator.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does the author tell you to do in order to see the tide of change?
options: Drop the habit of moralizing and judging
Ignore the clichéd interpretations others spout
Rely on established theories to interpret events
Look for undercurrents of discontent below the surface
questions.explain: The author asks you to see things as they are and look for connections among signs of discontent. Established theories are exactly what blind intellectuals.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these did Louis XVI plan for the Estates General?
options: An opening ceremony rivaling his coronation
Equal power for all three estates
Some tax reforms but no loss of other privileges
Hold it at Versailles
questions.explain: He meant to impress with majesty, grant tax reform, and keep the rest. Equal power was the Third Estate's demand, which he refused.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these did the National Assembly vote to do in 1789?
options: Eliminate the privileges of the nobility and clergy
Proclaim all French citizens equal
Take over the Catholic Church and auction its lands
Abolish the monarchy entirely
questions.explain: The monarchy was at first allowed to survive with shared power. Danton's coup that ended it came later, in August 1792.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these wants did Danton's young generation have, according to the interpretation?
options: More elaborate outfits and hairstyles
More spontaneous, open expression of emotion
Looser clothing with less ostentation
Open mingling of all the classes
questions.explain: They were tired of empty formality and wanted freer, more natural expression, the opposite of elaborate outfits.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these events in the order in which they happened.
items: Louis XVI's coronation
The Estates General convenes at Versailles
The Parisians take the Bastille
The mob forces the royal family to Paris
The monarchy is ended by the assembly
questions.explain: The coronation was in 1775; the Estates General in spring 1789; the Bastille in July 1789; the march on Versailles in October 1789; and the monarchy ended in August 1792.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these steps in Danton's career in order.
items: Clerks in the Paris law courts
Becomes a lawyer on the King's Council
Joins the Cordeliers
Turns down a higher council position
Is named minister of justice
questions.explain: He moved to Paris in 1780, took the council post in 1787, joined the Cordeliers, refused promotion in 1788, and became minister of justice after the monarchy fell.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these events in the order in which the Third Estate's challenge unfolded.
items: The Estates General opens with royal ceremony
The Third Estate declares itself the National Assembly
Louis orders it to disband and is disobeyed
Louis calls in the army
Parisians arm themselves and march on the Bastille
questions.explain: Each step escalated the conflict until force failed and the Parisians took the Bastille.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these events in order, from Danton's arrest to the end of the revolutionary tribunal.
items: Danton is arrested for treason
Danton is executed
Robespierre unleashes the Great Terror
Robespierre is arrested by the assembly
The assembly abolishes the revolutionary tribunal
questions.explain: After Danton's death Robespierre ran the Great Terror, but the public turned and he was guillotined, after which the tribunal was ended.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the author's advice on responding to the spirit of the times in the order given.
items: Feel the change in the collective mood
Analyze why people are dissatisfied
Notice idols that no longer cast a spell
Respond boldly, voicing what others feel
Avoid getting too far ahead of the public
questions.explain: The author starts with feeling, then analysis, then telltale disenchantment, and finally bold but careful action.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the places where Louis XVI was held or lived, in order, after the Estates General.
items: Versailles
The Tuileries
The Temple
The Place de la Révolution
questions.explain: He was forced from Versailles to the Tuileries, imprisoned in the Temple, and taken to the guillotine at the Place de la Révolution.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the fate of the Sacre in order.
items: Built for the coronation
Rediscovered by the new leaders
Judged hideous and unsellable
Gold removed and melted
Painted panels burned
questions.explain: The leaders had hoped to sell it for funds, but found it a grotesquerie and broke it up.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each person to the role he or she plays in the story.
pairs: King who found comfort in the ancient ritual of the coronation
Orator who sensed the tide and led the Cordeliers
Rival who spread the rumor that Danton had lost his fervor
Queen whose parties and love of finery added to the court's costs
questions.explain: Each figure's role in the story of the revolution is described.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each event to its date.
pairs: The mob's arrival at the palace to bring the king to Paris
questions.explain: These dates are given in the narrative of the revolution.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each speaker to what he did or said at his end.
pairs: Pointed at Robespierre's apartment and predicted he would follow
Told Robespierre that Danton's blood chokes him
Tried to defend himself but the words came out haltingly
questions.explain: Robespierre fell with remarkable speed after the public turned against the executions.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each name to its role in the story.
pairs: Danton's wife, whose grave he dug up
Roman orator whose speeches Danton memorized
Philosopher who called frivolity and boredom heralds of change
Royalist unit whose banquet trampled revolutionary badges
questions.explain: Each name appears in the narrative or in the closing epigraph.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each signal of change to what it showed in prerevolutionary France.
pairs: Ridiculed church and monarchy as backward and superstitious
Hotbeds of discontent with the monarchy
Plays that mocked the monarchy brazenly
No longer understood the rituals they performed
questions.explain: Each of these subtle signs showed that the monarchy's symbols had become masks with nothing behind them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each point by whether it reflects how Louis XVI or Danton viewed the unrest in France.

items.t: The unruly subjects are a noisy, godless minority
Disobedience to the king is sacrilege
The monarchy is a façade that no longer stirs the masses
The signs of discontent point to a rising tide
A constitutional monarchy has no middle ground left to stand on

questions.explain: Louis clung to the divine monarchy and read the unrest through it; Danton read the same signs as a tide moving toward a republic.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each item by whether the author says it was visible on the surface to Louis XVI or hidden below it.

items.t: Versailles as the glittering jewel of Europe
The king's role as absolute ruler
Stable distinctions among the estates
Aristocrats loathing the king's weak absolute power
Enlightenment ridicule of the church
Freemason lodges with secret rituals

questions.explain: The king saw a stable, glittering order; the discontent was subtle and disparate.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did Louis XVI find the coronation ritual comforting, and how did he act on this?
questions.a: Louis was shy and fearful of failing as king, and the legend that sacred oil elevated the king above mortals and linked him to God and the people gave him confidence. Where progressives saw a relic of a superstitious past, he found the ancientness reassuring. So he reenacted the ritual in a more original form and surrounded himself with Roman-god imagery to overwhelm his subjects.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What did Danton glimpse as a fifteen-year-old at the coronation, and how did it set him apart from the king?
questions.a: Danton saw the king up close and was surprised to find him quite ordinary despite his jewels, and the huge Sacre seemed oddly out of place and swallowed him up. He glimpsed for a moment how empty the monarchy and its symbols had become. Unlike Louis, he was not insecure and had no inner need to rely on the past.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why did Louis XVI's plan for the Estates General fail?
questions.a: He planned to overwhelm the delegates with the grandeur of Versailles and then grant a little tax reform while keeping all other privileges. But the Third Estate was unmoved by the pomp and demanded equal power. They declared themselves the National Assembly and defied a royal order to disband. Force failed too, since troops would not fire on compatriots and Paris armed itself.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Explain Danton's tide metaphor and how he used it.
questions.a: As an avid swimmer, Danton saw the discontent in France as a tide in a river: sometimes the river seems placid but is still moving, and at other times a rush that no king can hold back. He told a friend he had jumped into the tide and let it carry him. He read signs from the clubs, the lawyers and the lower classes and saw before others that it led toward a republic.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How did Louis XVI interpret the unrest, and why does the author say this was mistaken?
questions.a: Louis viewed events through the lens of the divine monarchy he inherited, so those who disobeyed him had to be godless individuals and a noisy minority or outside agitators. He planned to use force to make the past prevail. The author says that once something has lost its spell and no longer enchants, no amount of force can bring it back to life.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Describe the signs of discontent beneath the calm surface of prerevolutionary France.
questions.a: Enlightenment writers like Voltaire and Diderot ridiculed the church and monarchy, which influenced the excluded middle class. Aristocrats loathed the weak king and wanted more power, and Freemason lodges were hotbeds of discontent. The theater mocked the monarchy, and the rituals and mythological art seemed empty masks. These signs were subtle until the crisis of the late 1780s combined them into a force.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How did Danton rise after the king's failed escape, and what did he achieve?
questions.a: After the king was caught, Danton declared the monarchy meaningless and called for a republic, which resonated with the sans-culottes. He was elected deputy prosecutor for the commune, filled it with sympathizers and gained control. On August 10 crowds invaded the Tuileries and the assembly voted to end the monarchy, making Danton minister of justice and de facto leader.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How did Danton fall from power, and what does the author say about his timing?
questions.a: Danton unleashed the Terror through the tribunal but grew sick of the bloodshed, after losing his wife, and worked to end it. Robespierre spread the rumor that he had lost his fervor and had him arrested for treason. The author says his sense of timing was off in this one instance, since he moved months ahead of the public, giving rivals an opening.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the author say that Louis XVI is closer to you than you think?
questions.a: Like Louis, you probably look at the present through the lens of the past, so the world seems the same as a month or year ago. Below the surface, though, younger people respect old values less, power dynamics shift, and new symbols form. Some will cling to the past like the king, while others are carried along without understanding. The power you want is Danton's vision from a fresh angle.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author say you must do to read the spirit of the times, and why isn't it merely an intellectual exercise?
questions.a: You must drop clichéd interpretations, moralizing and old mental habits, and see things as they are, looking for undercurrents of discontent and connections among them. First you must feel the change in the collective mood, since intellectuals are often last to discern the spirit of the times. Then you analyze what people crave, notice idols that no longer enchant, and respond boldly without getting too far ahead.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to the author, what drives the continual changes in fashions, styles and ideas?
options: The succession of new generations of young people trying to create something more relevant to their experience.
The tastemakers who decide each season's styles for the masses.
The effort of older generations to hold on to their power.
The random desire for novelty with no deeper meaning.
questions.explain: After weighing top-down and bottom-up explanations, the author concludes that new generations of young people drive the changes, going in a different direction from the previous one.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: About how many years does the author say a generation comprises?
options: Around forty years.
Around fifteen years.
Around ten years.
Around twenty-two years.
questions.explain: He adds that those at the earliest and latest parts of the period often identify more with the previous or following generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author call the knowledge of the generational patterns that shape history and our place in them?
options: Historical determinism.
The zeitgeist.
Collective consciousness.
Generational awareness.
questions.explain: The author names it generational awareness, which requires understanding our own generation's effect on us and the larger generational patterns.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author conclude about the apparently superficial shifts in styles?
options: They have no relation to psychology.
They are decided by a handful of tastemakers at the top.
They reflect deeper alterations in people's mood and values emerging from the bottom up.
They reflect economic cycles alone.
questions.explain: The author says nothing is innocent in this realm: even a preference for brighter colors or a harder sound says something about the collective mind.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What pattern does the author find in the way books argue, over the past fifty years and since the eighteenth century?
options: A rise of shorter books only.
A steady move away from statistics.
A back-and-forth between a literary, speculative style and a sober, data-driven one.
A permanent shift to speculation.
questions.explain: Fifty years ago arguments rested on psychoanalysis and sociology and were speculative; now they rest on genetics, brains, studies and statistics.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Besides social power, what other benefit does the author say generational awareness can give you?
options: Immunity from generational influences.
A calming effect, letting you view events with distance and equanimity.
Approval from all generations.
The ability to predict the exact date of crises.
questions.explain: The author notes a therapeutic effect: you rise above the chaotic changes of the moment.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says changes in clothing style are limited in number and recur in waves over decades or centuries.
questions.explain: He lists several categories, such as looser and more romantic, or more classic and elegant, which come back at irregular but regular-enough intervals.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author argues that shifts in style are only superficial and say nothing about people's values.
questions.explain: He argues they reflect deeper alterations in mood and values. Even a shift to looser clothing in the 1780s reflected an overall psychological shift.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says some people deny the generational phenomenon because they prefer to think they shape their own beliefs or that class, gender and race matter more.
questions.explain: He also admits that the study of generations is imprecise, but says generations are more of an influence than we imagine.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The knowledge of generational forces and where our time fits in history is called generational ____.
questions.explain: This is the term the author coins for the knowledge he describes.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: A generation, the author says, comprises around ____ years.
questions.explain: Those at the edges of the period often identify with neighboring generations.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The author argues that changes in styles emerge from the ____ up, from the society as a whole.
questions.explain: This is the bottom-up dynamic that he favors, rather than the tastemaker top-down one.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does the author list as kinds of change in fashion styles?
options: More military and uniform
More classic and elegant
Looser and more romantic
More overtly sexual and body conscious
questions.explain: The author describes looser, body-conscious, classic and gaudy trends. A military style is not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these benefits of generational awareness does the author name?
options: Freedom from all conventions of any kind
Seeing what shaped our parents' mind-set and ours in turn
A calming distance from the chaos of events
Anticipating future trends
questions.explain: He names understanding our parents and ourselves, anticipating trends, and social power plus equanimity.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the author's line of reasoning in the order he develops it.
items: Fashion changes are visible over decades
Do these shifts reflect deeper changes in psychology?
Do they come from the top down or the bottom up?
New generations drive the changes
Generational awareness
questions.explain: He moves from observing fashion to asking about deeper causes, then to bottom-up dynamics, generations and finally awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each description by whether it fits arguments of fifty years ago or arguments now.

items.t: Rooted in psychoanalysis and sociology
Loose, literary and speculative
Environment seen as the main influence on behavior
Revolve around genetics and the brain
Backed up by studies and statistics
Shorter sentences that communicate information

questions.explain: The author contrasts the speculative style of the past with the sober, data-driven style of the present.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each statement by whether it describes a top-down or a bottom-up view of how styles change.

items.t: Tastemakers initiate a change and the masses pick it up
A style spreads virally from individual leaders
Tastemakers respond to signs of change in society
Change comes from the social force of the group

questions.explain: The author opts for bottom-up: tastemakers themselves respond to what is stirring in the collective mind.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each term from the Keys section to its meaning.
pairs: Individuals and tastemakers initiate change that the masses adopt
Tastemakers respond to signs of change within society as a whole
Knowledge of the generational effect and patterns that shape history
About twenty-two years, with overlapping edges
questions.explain: These are the terms the author uses to frame the question and its answer.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the author say changes in fashion are not trivial?
questions.a: Though they might look trivial, shifts in clothes, music or theorizing reflect deeper alterations in people's mood and values that rise from the bottom up. A desire for looser clothing in the 1780s reflected an overall psychological shift. Nothing is innocent in this realm, and the shifts are limited in range and recur, suggesting patterns in human nature.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does the author answer the question of whether style changes come from the top down or the bottom up, and what does he say drives them?
questions.a: He concludes that the changes emerge from the bottom up, with tastemakers responding to signs of change in the society as a whole. What drives them is the continual succession of new generations of young people, who try to create something more relevant to their experience and different from the previous generation. This is part of a larger pattern in history going back thousands of years.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What is generational awareness and what two steps are needed to attain it?
questions.a: Generational awareness is the knowledge of the generational phenomenon and its patterns that gives social power and a calming perspective. First we must understand the profound effect our own generation has on how we view the world. Second, we must understand the larger generational patterns that shape history and recognize where our time period fits into the overall scheme.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why might people deny the influence of generations, and how does the author respond?
questions.a: Some people like to imagine that they alone shape what they think and believe, or that class, gender and race play a greater role. The author admits that the study of generations is imprecise, subtle and elusive, and that other factors matter. But looking in depth reveals that generations are more of an influence than we generally imagine, a great generator of what happens in history.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the world of adults seem alien to a child, according to the author?
options: Children lack any ability to imitate adults.
The child sees it from a peculiar angle: physically smaller, helpless, dependent and with little life experience.
Adults deliberately hide their concerns from children.
Children are shielded from entertainment.
questions.explain: The child encounters the same reality as everyone else, but from the angle of a child, so adult cares can seem odd or comical.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to the author, how do decisive events during youth, such as a war or an economic boom, shape the generational personality?
options: They matter less than family upbringing.
They affect the old more deeply than the young.
A war or crash makes the generation cautious, while prosperity or stability makes it hungry for adventure.
They make all young people rebel in the same way.
questions.explain: Because the young are impressionable, such events have a decisive influence on the forming personality, and they view them differently from their parents.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the Babylonian clay tablet complaining about today's youth illustrate?
options: Proof that youth really are lazy.
A pattern of older generations condemning the young that has existed for at least three thousand years.
Evidence that Babylonian culture was preserved.
A unique decline in discipline in ancient Babylon.
questions.explain: The author cites it to show that such complaints appear in all cultures and time periods, and are not objective judgments.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the author say older people judge the younger generation as immature and soft?
options: They have no contact with the young.
They have studied young people objectively.
They succumb to an illusion of perspective, along with some hidden envy of youth.
They are protecting the values of their grandparents.
questions.explain: We think we judge objectively but follow a pattern; there is probably also envy of their youth and mourning for our own.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does the author describe the rebels within a generation, such as the 1950s beatniks?
options: They are mostly leaders who set new styles.
They are free of their generation's influence.
They are followers who copy their elders.
They are as marked by their generation as anyone, but in reverse.
questions.explain: The young conservatives of the 1960s were just as preachy, fanatic and idealistic as the majority, only with reversed values.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What did the lost generation of the 1920s still show in their later years, even after dropping some pleasures?
options: They remained tough, cynical, materialistic and brazen in expressing opinions.
They gave up all cynicism.
They became cautious and conformist.
They became idealistic and moralizing.
questions.explain: A generation's personality changes with age, but something remains intact; the lost generation stayed hard-boiled and cynical.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these is the author's definition of the zeitgeist?
options: The spirit of the youngest generation alone.
The blending, tension and clashing of the roughly four generations alive at the same time.
A list of the dominant fashions of a decade.
The values inherited unchanged from the past.
questions.explain: The overall spirit of the times arises from the interplay of the generations, as in the 1960s when youth culture and older antagonism interacted.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the author say we can best associate with a generational spirit?
options: The statistics of its economy.
The speeches of its political leaders.
Its dominant music style, artistic imagery, or the mood of its literature and films.
The laws passed by its legislators.
questions.explain: The spirit is a mood, not easily put into words, so jazz and the saxophone best capture the 1920s.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says that most of the change that comes from tension between two generations comes from the older one.
questions.explain: He says the greater part comes from the young, who are more restless, in search of identity and attuned to the group.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says we cannot step outside the historical moment we are born into, even if we react against it.
questions.explain: The generational mind-set dominates everyone from within, including rebels.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: The author says young people in their teens become attuned to styles and fashions because they are struggling to form an identity separate from their parents.
questions.explain: They want to show they belong to their generational tribe, with its own look and manner.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The overall spirit of the times is commonly known as the ____.
questions.explain: It arises from the clash and blending of generations alive at once.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The author calls a generation's collective personality its ____.
questions.explain: It is the sense of what is moving in the present, as opposed to what is inherited.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Older people judge the young because of an illusion of ____.
questions.explain: The author adds that hidden envy may also play a part.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The author says nothing better captures the wild spirit of the 1920s than jazz and the brassy sound of the ____.
questions.explain: Music and similar trends capture the unspoken mood of a generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The time period we live through generally comprises ____ generations alive at the same time.
questions.explain: Their blend and tension create the overall spirit of the times.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does the author list as decisive events in youth that shape a generational personality?
options: A financial crisis or economic boom
A major war
A political scandal
A change in school curriculum
questions.explain: He also names new technology with a profound impact on social relations. School curriculum is not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these describe what happens in our twenties and thirties?
options: We clash with the older generation that holds power
We are in a position to assume some power
We absorb our parents' ideas like sponges
We begin to influence the culture and its politics
questions.explain: Absorbing ideas as sponges belongs to the first years of life.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these three kinds of people does the author distinguish within any generation?
options: Elders who refuse any influence
Rebels who go against the grain of their generation
A larger group of followers who keep up with trends
Aggressive individuals who lead and express trends first
questions.explain: Danton is the author's example of the aggressive type.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does the author say about the generational spirit?
options: It can be stated precisely in a list of beliefs
It is more a mood or emotional tone than a set of ideas
It is a collective personality
It is the sense of what is moving in the present
questions.explain: The author says it is not easily put into words, which is why music and imagery capture it best.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these periods or groups does the author mention as examples of generations?
options: The lost generation of the 1920s
The young conservatives of the 1990s
The baby boomers of the 1960s
The beatniks of the 1950s
questions.explain: The 1990s are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the phases of life in which a generation forms and acts, in order.
items: First years: absorbing parents' and teachers' ideas
Awareness of peers
Teens: rebellion and attunement to styles
Twenties and thirties: assuming power and clashing with elders
Forties: taking leadership and judging youth
questions.explain: The author follows the person from sponge-like early years to leadership in midlife.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these generational examples in chronological order.
items: Young royalists of the 1780s
The lost generation of the 1920s
The beatniks of the 1950s
The baby boomers of the 1960s
questions.explain: The author uses these in turn to illustrate rebels and the persistence of a generation's personality.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the stages of how generational change works in order.
items: The young bond with peers over a shared view
They clash with the older generation
They gain power in their thirties and forties
They shape the world with a look and feel distinct from their parents
questions.explain: The greater part of change comes from the young as they move into positions of power.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each phase of life to its description.
pairs: Rebellion and strong attunement to styles
Assuming power and clashing with the older generation
Taking leadership and judging the young
questions.explain: Each phase involves a different relation to the older and younger generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each generation to its characteristic traits.
pairs: Flappers, wild jazz and a cynical, hard-boiled attitude
Intense idealism and a propensity to judge and moralize
Defying their own generation by going against the grain
Preachy and fanatic in reversed values
questions.explain: These show both the majority and the reverse versions of a generation's spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each group within a generation to its description.
pairs: Leaders who express trends first and fear breaking with the past less
A larger group who find it exciting to keep up with trends
Those who define themselves by going against the grain
questions.explain: The author describes three types, with Danton as the example of the first.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A generation's collective personality or mood
The overall spirit of the times from clashing generations
The collective mind-set formed from the angle of childhood and youth
Judging the young as if objectively while following a pattern
questions.explain: These are terms the author coins or uses in this section.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each item by whether it belongs to the formation of the generational perspective or to the exercise of power in the twenties and thirties.

items.t: Absorbing parents' and teachers' ideas
Bonding with peers over humor and ideals of coolness
Rebelling to find an identity
Altering the world according to one's own values
Influencing culture and politics
Clashing with the older generation in power

questions.explain: The first phase shapes the perspective unconsciously; the next puts it into action.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each event by whether it tends to make a generation cautious or hungry for adventure.

items.t: A major war
A crash in the economy
An event that sparks prosperity
An event that brings stability

questions.explain: The author ties war or crash to caution and prosperity or stability to adventure.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each item by whether it is the collective spirit or what is inherited from the past.

items.t: What is moving and evolving in the present
A restless, searching nature
A mood or emotional tone
Key values that remain unquestioned
Ways of looking at the world passed down by parents

questions.explain: The spirit is what is altering in the present, as opposed to what is inherited.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each trait by whether it belongs to the lost generation of the 1920s or the baby boomers of the 1960s.

items.t: Wild parties and alcohol
A hard-boiled, cynical attitude
Intense idealism
A propensity to judge and moralize

questions.explain: Each generation's core trait persisted into its later years.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Describe the first phase of life in which a person's generational perspective forms, and why people are ignorant of it.
questions.a: In our early years we are sponges absorbing the energy, style and ideas of parents and teachers, with open minds and intense experiences. We become aware of peers, see the adult world from a child's angle, and in the teens bond over a shared view and rebel against our parents. We are too young to understand or analyze this perspective, so we are generally ignorant of how it forms and influences what we see.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How do the tensions between generations play out through life, and who generates most of the change?
questions.a: In our twenties and thirties we assume power and clash with the older generation, who think us immature and unready. In our forties we hold leadership positions and judge the next generation in turn, a pattern at least three thousand years old. The greater part of the change comes from the young, who are more restless, in search of identity and attuned to the group.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What are the three types of people within a generation, and how are rebels still marked by their generation?
questions.a: There are aggressive individuals who lead and express the trends first, like Danton, a larger group of followers who enjoy keeping up with trends, and rebels who define themselves by going against the grain. Rebels are just as marked by their generation as anyone, but in reverse. The young conservatives of the 1960s were as preachy, fanatic and idealistic as the majority.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Distinguish the spirit of a generation from the spirit of the times.
questions.a: The spirit of a generation is its collective personality, the sense of what is moving and evolving in the present as opposed to what is inherited, felt as a mood or emotional tone. The spirit of the times, or zeitgeist, is the overall spirit created by the blending, tension and clashing of the roughly four generations alive at once, as when the 1960s youth culture and the dismay of older people interacted.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does a generation's personality change and stay the same as it ages? Use an example.
questions.a: Circumstances, historical events and aging modify the spirit, so the generation relates to the world differently in its fifties than in its twenties. Something in the personality remains intact, however. The lost generation of the 1920s dropped some of its pleasures and manias but stayed tough, cynical, materialistic and brazen, and the boomers kept their idealism and moralizing while changing what they moralize about.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Chapter 17 is titled Seize the Historical Moment. What does the title signal about the chapter's aim?
options: Using awareness of your generation and times to exploit the spirit of the times rather than be constrained by it.
Predicting exact historical events.
Withdrawing from the pressures of the group.
Preserving the traditions of the past against the present.
questions.explain: The law of generational myopia says understanding your generation's influence lets you anticipate and set trends and free your mind from its constraints.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Chapter 17's third section, The Generational Phenomenon, is followed by Generational Patterns. What does the Keys section say these two sections must supply?
options: First the larger patterns in history, then predictions for the future.
First the study of Danton, then the study of Robespierre.
First the effect our own generation has on our view, then the larger generational patterns in history.
First fashion trends, then economic cycles.
questions.explain: In Keys to Human Nature, the author says generational awareness has two parts: our generation's profound effect on us, and the larger patterns and where our time fits.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: In the book's order, chapter 17 comes after the chapter on aggression and before the chapter on mortality.
questions.explain: Chapter 16 is the Law of Aggression, and chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality, follows chapter 17.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The chapter that follows chapter 17 concerns the Law of ____ Denial.
questions.explain: Chapter 18 turns from historical time to mortality.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these sections come after The Generational Phenomenon in chapter 17?
options: Generational Patterns
Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
The Human Beyond Time and Death
The Rising Tide
questions.explain: The Rising Tide opens the chapter. The later sections cover patterns, strategies and the human beyond time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the sections of chapter 17 in order.
items: The Rising Tide
Keys to Human Nature
The Generational Phenomenon
Generational Patterns
Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.explain: The chapter moves from a story, to the key puzzle, to the generational phenomenon, to patterns and then strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each chapter to its law.
questions.explain: These are the laws as titled in the table of contents.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort each section by whether it comes before or after The Generational Phenomenon in chapter 17.

items.t: The Rising Tide
Keys to Human Nature
Generational Patterns
Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
The Human Beyond Time and Death

questions.explain: The generational phenomenon is the third section of six.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the story of Louis XVI and Danton in The Rising Tide contribute before the chapter explains the generational phenomenon?
options: A concrete case of one person blinded by the past and another attuned to the changing spirit of the times.
A list of rules for becoming a revolutionary.
A comparison of two economic systems.
A proof that generations last twenty-two years.
questions.explain: The author uses the interpretation to set up the theme: the king saw the past, while Danton felt the tide, which the later sections explain through generations.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why was France perpetually short of money under Louis XVI, and how did this feed the unrest?
questions.a: France's financial structure was antiquated: onerous feudal-era taxes fell on the lower and middle classes while the clergy and nobility were largely exempt. Revenue could never match the court's lavish spending, especially Marie Antoinette's parties. As money ran short and the price of bread rose, riots broke out, and the king was forced to call the Estates General.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How did Danton exemplify the Romantic spirit of his generation, according to the author?
questions.a: Danton's generation tired of empty formality and wanted freer, spontaneous expression, looser clothes and open mingling of the classes. The author calls this the first real explosion of Romanticism, valuing emotions and sensations over the intellect. Danton wore his heart on his sleeve, his speeches felt like spontaneous outpourings, and his disinterment of his wife was an expression of emotion unimaginable ten years earlier.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the Babylonian tablet show about how older people view youth, and why does the author say the judgment is flawed?
questions.a: The tablet from around 1000 BC complains that youth is rotten and will never preserve the culture, and similar complaints appear in all cultures and periods. The author says older people are reacting according to a pattern at least three thousand years old and succumbing to an illusion of perspective. There is probably also hidden envy of the young and mourning for their own lost youth.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the author raise the example of changes in how arguments in books are constructed?
questions.a: He uses it to show that the shifts in style apply to thinking and theorizing too: fifty years ago arguments rested on psychoanalysis and sociology in a loose, speculative style, whereas now they rest on genetics, the brain, studies and statistics. A similar back-and-forth has occurred since the eighteenth century, showing the limited range, recurrence and increasing speed of such shifts.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Danton was a member of the secret society of ____, whose lodges were hotbeds of discontent.
questions.explain: The author lists the Freemasons as the supreme example of the secret societies sprouting up everywhere.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Danton's rival ____ packed the Committee of Public Safety with his sympathizers.
questions.explain: Danton did not receive enough votes, and Robespierre spread the rumor that he had lost his revolutionary fervor.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Fifty years ago, many arguments in books were rooted in psychoanalysis and ____.
questions.explain: Arguments then saw the environment as the primary influence on behavior; now they revolve around genetics and the brain.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The Babylonian clay tablet complaining about youth dates from around ____ BC.
questions.explain: The author cites it to show the pattern of judging the young has lasted at least three thousand years.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each place to what happened there.
pairs: The boarding school where Danton wrote the prize essay
Where the royal family was housed in Paris until the crowd invaded it
The medieval priory that served as the royal family's prison
questions.explain: Each place marks a stage in the story of the king and Danton.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which thinker does Greene credit as perhaps the first to formulate history as a pattern of four acts corresponding to four generations?
options: Lionel Casson, the historian of ancient Rome
Ibn Khaldun, the fourteenth-century Islamic scholar
Johan Huizinga, the historian of the late Middle Ages
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, the scientist and novelist
questions.explain: Greene names the great fourteenth-century Islamic scholar Ibn Khaldun as perhaps the first to frame history this way. Huizinga and Casson appear later as authors who help bring past eras to life, and Goethe as a figure who lived outside his time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: In the four-generation pattern, what marks the second generation?
options: It still feels the heat of the revolution but craves order, conventions and dogma
It turns pragmatic and drains the spirit out of the revolution
It questions inherited values and drifts into cynicism
It makes a radical break with the past and creates chaos doing so
questions.explain: Having lived through the revolution at a very early age, the second generation wants to stabilize the world. Breaking with the past belongs to the first generation, pragmatism to the third, and cynicism to the fourth.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does the third generation tend to drain the spirit out of the original revolution?
options: It has little direct connection to the founders, so it focuses on solving problems, comfort and building things
It deliberately rejects the revolution out of loyalty to the old order
It spends its energy hunting for scapegoats for social problems
It is too fearful of chaos to put the founders' ideas into practice
questions.explain: Greene describes the third generation as pragmatists who care less about ideas than about building things and making life comfortable, so material concerns predominate. Scapegoat-hunting is a feature of the later crisis period.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: According to Greene, why is the fourth generation's crisis of values often the most painful period to live through?
options: Older generations forcibly suppress all questioning of inherited values
Material comforts disappear and the economy collapses
Revolutionary violence always breaks out in the streets during this period
People have a deep need to believe in something, and doubt about the old order leaves a vacuum that makes them a little mad
questions.explain: Greene stresses the human need for belief: when old values are doubted and nothing replaces them, people latch onto charlatans, scapegoats and tribal groups. The pain is psychological rather than a matter of economic collapse or repression.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: In a crisis period, which subgroup does Greene say tends to form, and why?
options: Formerly privileged people anxious about losing what they took for granted, who want to return to a golden age
Elders who have accepted the change and try to mentor the young
Young idealists who want to speed up the coming revolution at any cost
Pragmatic builders who hope to profit from the chaos
questions.explain: The subgroup consists of those who felt somewhat privileged in the past and are threatened by the coming change; Greene calls them doomed, because the cycle cannot be stopped and the past cannot be revived.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does Greene describe the silent generation, shaped by the Great Depression and World War II?
options: Security-craving and averse to conflict, valuing teamwork
Idealistic and adventurous, valuing personal expression
Cautious and conservative, valuing stability and material comfort and fitting tightly into the group
Pragmatic and confrontational, valuing self-reliance
questions.explain: Marked by the Depression and the war, the silent generation sought stability and conformity. The other descriptions fit the baby boomers, Generation X and the millennials respectively.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Against what did the baby boomers react, and what did they come to value?
options: They found their parents' conformity stifling and valued personal expression, adventure and idealism
They found their parents' recklessness frightening and valued stability
They found their parents' idealism hypocritical and valued individualism
They found their parents' individualism cold and valued teamwork
questions.explain: Not haunted by their parents' financial fears, the boomers pushed against conformity in the 1960s. Reacting against idealism is what Greene says Generation X did.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which pair correctly states what Generation X valued and what it reacted against?
options: Individualism and self-reliance, in reaction to the hypocrisies and impracticalities of the boomers' idealism
Teamwork and security, in reaction to the boomers' individualism
Personal expression, in reaction to the silent generation's conformity
Stability and comfort, in reaction to the boomers' wildness
questions.explain: Marked by the chaos and scandals of the 1960s and after, Generation X became pragmatic and confrontational. Teamwork and security are the millennial reaction to Generation X.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Greene says generations seem capable only of reacting against the previous one. What reason does he offer?
options: Young people are naturally less intelligent than their elders
Social media forces each generation into extremes
A generational outlook forms in youth, when we are insecure and prone to black-and-white thinking
Older generations refuse to share any of their values with the young
questions.explain: Greene suggests that because the perspective is formed in youth, a balanced middle way that picks the good and bad in the previous generation's values seems contrary to our collective nature.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does Greene call the back-and-forth generational rhythm salutary?
options: It prevents any generation from ever feeling anxious
If each generation simply carried on the last one's tendencies, we would suffocate through too much self-expression or stagnation
It guarantees that every revolution produces lasting progress
It keeps the older generation in permanent control of society
questions.explain: He imagines generations continuing the wildness of the 1920s or the conformity of the 1950s and concludes we would have destroyed ourselves. He adds that some revolutions are trivial, so progress is not guaranteed.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: A man from a fearful, cautious generation avoids buying a house or car and tells friends it is because he values freedom and wants to help the environment. How would Greene read this?
options: As a genuinely independent choice unaffected by his generation
As a generational flaw reinterpreted as a virtue, hiding the fears underneath
As a sign that he belongs to the revolutionary generation
As proof that his generation is wiser than older ones
questions.explain: Greene uses almost exactly this example: when it comes to the flaws of our own generation, we tend to see them as virtues and avoid confronting the fears that are really beneath them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: When mapping the decisive events behind your generation, which event does Greene say influences you more?
options: The one closest to your retirement years
The one closer to the formative years between ten and eighteen
The one that happened earliest in your parents' lives
The one that received the most newspaper coverage
questions.explain: Greene says both events matter, but the one nearer to ages ten to eighteen, when we gain awareness of the wider world and develop core values, counts for more.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What do the millennials, traumatized by terrorism and a financial crisis, crave and dislike?
options: They crave adventure and dislike authority of any kind
They crave individualism and dislike group projects
They crave stability and dislike material comfort
They crave security and teamwork and dislike conflict and confrontation
questions.explain: Greene says the millennials reacted against the individualism of Generation X by valuing security and teamwork.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does Greene say a generation's particular style of humor can reveal?
options: Its level of formal education
Its official political beliefs and voting habits
Its loyalty to the values of the previous generation
Its unconscious shadow side, where frustrations and inhibitions are released
questions.explain: Through humor people release frustrations and express inhibitions; a generation that looks prudish may have raunchy, irreverent humor, which is the shadow side leaking out.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Ibn Khaldun theorized that history seems to move in four acts, corresponding to four ____.
questions.explain: The four acts are tied to four successive generations, from revolutionary to crisis and back to revolution.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The third generation is made up of ____ who want to solve problems and make life as comfortable as possible.
questions.explain: Having little direct connection to the founders, this generation prefers building things to debating ideas.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Without a unifying belief to anchor us in a crisis period, we become ____, relying on some small affinity group for a sense of belonging.
questions.explain: Greene links the lack of shared belief to retreat into small groups, alongside scapegoating and charlatans.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The subgroup that forms in a crisis period wants to return to some ____ it can vaguely remember.
questions.explain: These anxious, formerly privileged people try to restore a vaguely remembered past, but the cycle cannot be stopped.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The silent generation valued stability, material comforts and fitting tightly into the ____.
questions.explain: Shaped by the Depression and war, they were cautious and conservative and prized conformity.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Greene notes that generations seem capable only of ____ and moving in an opposing direction to the previous generation.
questions.explain: Each generation defines itself against the imbalances of the one before.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Greene says to approach your own generation like an ____, digging into your own past for artifacts that reveal its underlying spirit.
questions.explain: This image stresses patient, objective, judgment-free excavation of memories.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Greene suggests looking at the decisive events in about ____ years before entering the work world to profile your generation.
questions.explain: He says that if this period is roughly twenty-two years, there is often more than one decisive event in it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Greene warns that each generation's outlook creates a particular kind of ____, closing the mind to other possibilities.
questions.explain: This is the myopia from which the chapter's law takes its name.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say people tend to do in the crisis of values that comes with the fourth generation?
options: Look for scapegoats for their dissatisfaction
Rely on small affinity groups for a feeling of belonging
Quickly agree on a single unifying belief
Latch onto belief systems peddled by charlatans and demagogues
Place new trust in the institutions they inherited
questions.explain: Without a unifying belief people grow tribal and susceptible to demagogues. Trust in inherited institutions and quick agreement are the opposite of the vacuum Greene describes.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does Greene suggest examining to build a personality profile of your generation?
options: Which political party was in power when you were born
The parenting styles of those who raised you
The decisive events before you entered the work world
The stock market record of your birth year
The heroes and icons of the generation
questions.explain: Events, parenting styles and icons are all on his list; he also names fads, humor and gender relations. Stock markets and party control are not.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise for examining your own generation objectively?
options: Treat it like a scientific fact about an organism
Piece together artifacts from your memories like an archaeologist
Avoid judgments and moralizing about it
View even emotional memories with some distance
Defend it against criticism from older and younger people
questions.explain: Greene warns that we cannot understand our generation as we would a scientific fact, and that we get defensive when criticized; the advice is distance and no moralizing.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as benefits of understanding the generational pattern and the zeitgeist?
options: You can anticipate what is around the corner
You can permanently stop the cycle of generations
You will never feel out of harmony with your time
You do not overreact to the outrage of the day
You feel connected to an unbroken chain of history
questions.explain: Awareness brings foresight and calm. Greene says the cycle cannot be stopped (and we would be doomed if it did), and that if you feel out of harmony you know the bad days will end.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these are reasons Greene gives for why generational knowledge is more critical now than ever?
options: Technology and social media have made the zeitgeist more globalized
Older generations now hold far more cultural power
People of one generation have less in common across countries
The quickening pace of change creates more crises and dizziness
questions.explain: Greene says people now share more with their own generation abroad than with older compatriots, and the pace of change tends to make us lose perspective. The other two options reverse his claims.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the fourth generation knows exactly what should replace the lost vitality of society.
questions.explain: The fourth generation feels society has lost vitality but is not sure what should replace it, so it questions inherited values and some become cynical.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the revolution that ends the cycle can be extreme and violent or can simply be the emergence of new and different values.
questions.explain: He allows that the revolution can be violent or less intense, and he adds that the pattern has variations and is not a science.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Greene says generations usually pick the good and discard the bad from their predecessors' values, finding a balanced middle way.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: a balanced middle way seems contrary to our collective nature, and generations tend to move in an opposing direction.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that feeling your generation is superior to others is simply an illusion.
questions.explain: He says each generation's myopia makes it judge everything by certain values, and that thinking it is superior is an illusion that awareness frees you from.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: Greene says children who were overprotected generally grow up to become helicopter parents themselves.
questions.explain: He notes that parenting styles come in waves: the overprotected do not generally become helicopter parents.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the four acts of Ibn Khaldun's generational pattern in order.
items: Revolutionaries make a radical break with the past
A second generation craves order and conventions
Pragmatic third generation drains the revolution's spirit
Fourth generation questions values and a crisis emerges
questions.explain: The cycle runs from revolution to stabilization to pragmatism to doubt and crisis, after which a new revolutionary generation arrives.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the four modern generations Greene discusses in the order they came of age.
items: Silent generation
Baby boomers
Generation X
Millennials
questions.explain: Each reacted against the one before: the boomers against conformity, Generation X against idealism, and the millennials against individualism.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put Greene's three tasks for a student of human nature in order.
items: Alter your attitude toward your own generation
Create a personality profile of your generation
Piece together the wider zeitgeist and the historical pattern
questions.explain: Greene calls the attitude change first and foremost, then the profile of your generation, then the broader zeitgeist involving the two dominant adult generations.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put these items from Greene's list for profiling your generation in the order he presents them.
items: Decisive events and inventions
Socializing style of peers
Views of success, money and failure
Parenting styles of those who raised you
Heroes, icons and fads
Humor as the shadow side
questions.explain: He moves from events to their effect on socialization and values, then to parenting, icons and trends, and finally the unconscious shadow, with humor as a sign.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each generation to its trait as Greene describes it.
pairs: Cautious and conservative, valuing stability and fitting in
Valued personal expression, adventure and idealism
Craved security and teamwork, disliking confrontation
questions.explain: Each trait is a reaction to the imbalance of the preceding generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each stage of the four-act cycle to what Greene says about it.
pairs: Radical break with the past, with some chaos
Feels vitality has been lost and questions inherited values
questions.explain: The stages move from revolution through stabilization and pragmatism to crisis.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each generation to the decisive events Greene links to it.
pairs: The Depression and then World War II
The Vietnam War, then Watergate and political scandals
The sexual revolution and the era of latchkey kids
9/11 and then the financial meltdown of 2008
questions.explain: Greene lists these as examples of decisive events that shaped each generation's personality.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each parenting style to the generation it tended to produce, according to Greene.
pairs: A wild, carefree lost generation in the 1920s
Self-absorbed, somewhat neglectful parents shaped by the 1960s
Children who felt alienated and even angry
A generation that fears leaving its comfort zone
questions.explain: He argues parenting styles come in waves and leave a personality stamp on a generation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort these traits by the generation Greene associates them with.

items.t: Valuing personal expression
Having adventures
Being idealistic
Valuing teamwork
Craving security
Disliking conflict and confrontation

questions.explain: The boomers reacted against conformity with expression and adventure, while the millennials, traumatized by terrorism and a financial crisis, reacted against individualism.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort these features by the generation of the four-act cycle they belong to.

items.t: Pragmatists who want to build things
Material concerns predominate
Drains the spirit of the revolution
Questions inherited values
Some become quite cynical
Nobody knows what to believe in

questions.explain: The third generation is practical and comfort-seeking; the fourth senses lost vitality and falls into doubt, which leads to crisis.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort these socializing effects by the kind of period that produces them, according to Greene.

items.t: Banding together for comfort and security
Valuing the team and feelings of love
Allergy to confrontation
Seeking adventure in groups
Group experimentation
Behavior sometimes bordering on the reckless

questions.explain: A crisis pushes peers together for security, while a long stagnant period makes the restless young seek excitement.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Describe the four acts of Ibn Khaldun's generational pattern as Greene presents it.
questions.a: The first generation makes a radical break with the past and creates some chaos. The second craves order and sets conventions and dogma, the third is pragmatic and builds comfort while draining the revolution's spirit, and the fourth feels vitality is lost and questions inherited values. A crisis follows, until a new revolutionary generation unified around a belief tears down the old order.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why is the fourth generation's crisis of values so painful, and how do people behave during it?
questions.a: People have a deep need to believe in something, and when old values are doubted and nothing replaces them, they can go a little mad. They latch onto charlatans and demagogues, look for scapegoats, and become tribal, relying on small affinity groups. A subgroup of formerly privileged people tries to hold on to a golden age, though the cycle cannot be stopped.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What two lessons does Greene draw from the back-and-forth sequence of the silent generation, boomers, Generation X and millennials?
questions.a: First, our values depend on where we fall in the pattern and on how our generation reacts against the imbalances of the previous one; we would not be the same person if born in another era. Second, generations seem capable only of reacting and moving in an opposing direction, perhaps because the perspective forms in youth when we think in black and white.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What is the first of Greene's three tasks, and why is it hard?
questions.a: The first task is to alter your attitude toward your own generation and understand how deeply it has shaped how you see the world. It is hard because the perspective formed in childhood, our bond to peers is early, and we become defensive and see our generation's flaws as virtues. Greene says to act like an archaeologist, free from judgment and moralizing.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What should you look at to build the personality profile of your generation, and what does it tell you about socializing style?
questions.a: Look at the decisive events in the roughly twenty-two years before entering the work world, along with inventions that changed interaction. A major crisis makes peers band together, valuing the team and love and avoiding confrontation, while stability and nonevents push peers toward adventure, group experimentation and sometimes recklessness. Also examine views of success, money and failure, and parenting styles.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How do heroes, fads and humor help reveal a generation's spirit and its shadow side?
questions.a: Heroes and icons act out qualities others secretly wish they had and show emerging values, while fads reveal an unconscious attraction beneath the surface. A generation's humor shows its shadow, releasing frustrations and inhibitions. Its extreme tendency also hides an attraction to the opposite, as the 1960s generation's spiritual stance hid a taste for the best material goods that emerged in the yuppie years.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What is Greene's third task, and what benefits does it bring?
questions.a: The third task is to understand the zeitgeist by looking at the tension between the two dominant adult generations and where your generation fits in the historical pattern. This frees you from the myopia of thinking your generation is superior, lets you anticipate what is coming, and gives a calm that stops you overreacting. You feel connected to the unbroken chain of history.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does Greene say generational knowledge is more critical now than ever?
questions.a: Technology and social media have unified generations across cultures, so the zeitgeist is more globalized and people share more with their own generation abroad than with older compatriots. And the pace of change has quickened, creating a self-fulfilling dynamic of more crises. This makes us dizzy and apt to mistake trivial shifts for real change, which only calm historical perspective prevents.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Why does Greene consider the back-and-forth generational pattern beneficial despite its imbalances?
questions.a: If each generation simply continued the last one's tendencies, we would suffocate through too much self-expression or stagnation and probably have destroyed ourselves. The pattern ensures that we revitalize ourselves. Sometimes a strong crisis produces a revolution that lasts centuries and moves toward more rational and empathetic values, which suggests a human spirit that keeps us evolving.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What simple premise does Greene say you must begin with to exploit the zeitgeist?
options: You are mostly independent of the times if you work hard enough
You are a product of the times, so frustrations you feel are probably shared by others of your generation
Older generations hold the secret to what the young want
Your generation's tastes are less important than your own
questions.explain: Greene says that if you act on a frustration or a sense that something is missing in the culture, your work will resonate with your generation and help shape the zeitgeist.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Why does Greene tell you to push against the past with great force rather than gently?
options: Internalized parental values pull on you, so your defiance tends to come out tepid
A gentle break would be too slow to matter
Pushing hard is the only way to avoid being copied
Older people only respond to loud, angry protest
questions.explain: Because you are fearful and conflicted, you may hesitate to go full throttle; Greene says to use the past as something to push against, even using your anger.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Why did Josephine Baker come to exemplify the new spirit of the lost generation in the 1920s?
options: She disguised her new style within familiar fashions
She became a mentor to older performers
She made her performances as unfettered and shocking as possible, embodying spontaneity
She revived the dances of ancient Rome
questions.explain: Greene cites Baker, along with Danton and Jacqueline Kennedy, as someone who gained force by making a sharp, audacious break with the past.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What does associating your innovation with a mythic figure or period of the past accomplish?
options: It hides the fact that your idea is new
It lets you avoid breaking with the older generation
It gives added weight and suggests your effort is a more perfect, progressive version of what happened before
It proves that history never changes
questions.explain: Danton's link to Cicero and Kennedy's New Frontier are examples where emotionally loaded symbols from the past lent a present mission authority.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What condition does Greene attach to the strategy of resurrecting the spirit of childhood?
options: Use it only if you feel a particularly powerful connection to your childhood, or it will seem flat and contrived
Re-create the period literally, with every detail accurate
Avoid linking it to any present-day issue
Use it only with an audience older than yourself
questions.explain: He wants the spirit, not a literal re-creation, tied to a present issue so it is not mindless nostalgia.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: A young filmmaker dislikes her generation's cynical mood but does not want to lecture anyone about it. Following Greene, what should she do?
options: Make a film with the look and feel of the times, while inserting a somewhat different spirit through its content
Make an openly moralizing film condemning the era
Remake a film from her parents' era frame by frame
Wait until the mood changes before releasing anything
questions.explain: Greene's subversion strategy says preaching or condemning only marginalizes you; work within the zeitgeist and loosen the generational framework through the content.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: How did Coco Chanel gain power to alter American tastes after World War II?
options: She partnered with other European designers against American culture
