She copied the wild styles of the younger generation
She embraced American women's new power and their desire for less fussy, more athletic clothing, earning their trust
She refused to design for the American market in order to stay exclusive
questions.explain: Unlike other designers who disdained American culture, Chanel used the women's own language and then subtly brought in her elegance.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: In the strategy of creating a new social configuration, what does eliminating the middlemen achieve?
options: It guarantees the group will last for centuries
It hands control of the group to older members
It makes the group secret and impossible to join
It removes barriers that kept people from freer association
questions.explain: Greene advises forging a new way for like-minded people to interact, removing intermediaries, adding rituals and symbols, and offering a thrill of breaking past taboos.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What did Alfred Hitchcock do that Greene says other aging directors failed to do?
options: He imitated younger directors' styles as closely as he could
He stopped adapting once he reached mass popularity
He abandoned his silent-era methods completely
He kept his obsession with visual language while adapting it to new styles, creating a hybrid of past and present
questions.explain: Other aging directors fell out of fashion or mimicked the current style; Hitchcock layered adaptations on top of his 1920s-formed craft, which gives his work an effect of seeming beyond time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Danton associated himself with the Roman orator ____, whose speeches favored the Republic and opposed tyranny.
questions.explain: The link gave Danton's mission the added weight of the ancient past.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: John F. Kennedy called the programs he would initiate the New ____, tying them to the American pioneer spirit.
questions.explain: The imagery of the pioneer spirit became a powerful part of his appeal.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: If the spirit of the times is like a tide, Greene says it is better to gently ____ it than to fight its direction.
questions.explain: Greene's point is to work within the zeitgeist and subvert it rather than preach against it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Hitchcock mastered camera angles and movement as part of perfecting a visual ____ for telling a story.
questions.explain: This silent-era obsession stayed with him through six decades of directing.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: As you age without adapting, Greene says you become a ____ of the past to those who are younger.
questions.explain: Locked in the values and styles of your youth, you narrow your audience and stop evolving.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Which of these people does Greene cite as breaking sharply with the past to epitomize their generation's new spirit?
options: Coco Chanel
Danton
Jacqueline Kennedy
Josephine Baker
Alfred Hitchcock
questions.explain: Danton, Baker and Jacqueline Kennedy illustrate pushing against the past; Chanel illustrates subverting the spirit, and Hitchcock illustrates continuing to adapt.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Which of these does Greene list as past examples of new social configurations?
options: The salons of seventeenth-century France
The fashion houses of postwar Paris
The court of King Louis XV
The speakeasies and jazz clubs of the 1920s
The lodges of the Freemasons in eighteenth-century Europe
questions.explain: Greene's examples are places where people met in new, freer ways. A royal court and fashion houses are not among them.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say about the strategy of resurrecting the spirit of childhood?
options: Aim to capture the spirit rather than a literal re-creation
Use it regardless of your feelings, since nostalgia always works
Use it only if you feel a strong connection to your early years
Connect it to some issue or problem in the present
Re-create the period as exactly as possible
questions.explain: Greene wants adult reflection on a vivid childhood spirit tied to the present, not mindless nostalgia or a literal copy.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: True or false: Greene advises keeping your defiance of the older generation tepid so that you do not alienate people.
questions.explain: He says to make your break with the past as sharp and clear as possible, expressing the taboo and shattering conventions.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the strategy of resurrecting the spirit of childhood works equally well whether or not you feel a strong connection to your childhood.
questions.explain: Without a powerful connection, he says, your attempt to re-create the spirit will seem flat and contrived.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Coco Chanel succeeded after World War II by embracing the new power of American women rather than disdaining American culture.
questions.explain: She catered to their wish for less fussy clothing, gained their trust, and then subtly altered their tastes.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Hitchcock never abandoned his obsession with visual language even as he adapted to new styles.
questions.explain: He adapted to color spectacles in the 1950s and to thrillers and horror in the sixties and seventies while keeping his core craft.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Put Greene's six strategies in the order he presents them.
items: Push against the past
Adapt the past to the present spirit
Resurrect the spirit of childhood
Create the new social configuration
Subvert the spirit
Keep adapting
questions.explain: The list moves from breaking with the past, to borrowing from it, to childhood, to social forms, to subverting the times, and finally to staying fresh as you age.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Put the steps of Coco Chanel's rise as an influence on American fashion in order.
items: Other European designers disdained the American market
Chanel embraced American women's new power
She catered to their wish for less fussy, more athletic clothing
She gained their trust and used their language
She subtly brought elegance into American tastes
questions.explain: Her power to redirect the zeitgeist came from first working with the American spirit rather than against it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Match each strategy to the person Greene uses to illustrate it.
pairs: Jacqueline Kennedy, breaking with demure first ladies
Adapt the past to the present spirit
Akira Kurosawa, reviving the samurai world
Coco Chanel, working with American tastes
Alfred Hitchcock, a hybrid of past and present
questions.explain: Each person shows a different way of working with the generational spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Match each new social configuration to what Greene says about it.
pairs: Men and women could talk freely and openly
Secret rituals and an air of subversion
Speakeasies and jazz clubs of the 1920s
questions.explain: Each offered a new way of interacting that let a generation shake off repressive elements of the past.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Match each figure to the past association or symbol they used or evoked.
pairs: The New Frontier and the pioneer spirit
The samurai world commenting on postwar Japan
questions.explain: These examples show adapting the past to the present spirit, thinking in grand, mythic terms.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Sort these pieces of advice by the strategy they belong to.

items.t: Express what is taboo
Use your anger as fuel
Make your break as sharp and clear as possible
Never preach or moralize about the times
Make something with the look and feel of the times
Insert a different spirit through the content

questions.explain: Pushing against the past is bold and open; subversion hides a different message inside the style of the times.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Sort these examples by the strategy they illustrate.
groups: Adapt the past to the present spirit

items.t: Danton linking himself to Cicero
Kennedy's New Frontier
Kurosawa's samurai films
Seventeenth-century salons
Freemason lodges
Speakeasies and jazz clubs

questions.explain: The first set borrows symbols from history; the second forges new ways for like-minded people to gather.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene advises them or warns against them for those who are aging.

items.t: Modernizing your spirit
Adopting some values of the younger generation
Becoming an unusual hybrid of old and new
Aping the styles of the young
Staying locked in the values of your youth
Becoming a caricature of the past

questions.explain: Greene wants a blend of your own experience with change, not imitation or stagnation.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Explain Greene's strategy of pushing against the past and why it requires force.
questions.a: The past exerts a pull through the values of your parents that you absorbed early, so your defiance tends to be tepid. Greene says to use the past as something to push against with great force, express what is taboo, and make the break sharp, as Danton, Josephine Baker and Jacqueline Kennedy did. This shock of the new attracts followers and sparks desires waiting to come out.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What does it mean to adapt the past to the present spirit, and how did Danton, Kurosawa and Kennedy do it?
questions.a: You find an analogous moment in history and borrow its loaded symbols, giving the impression that your effort is a more perfect and progressive version of the past. Danton linked himself to Cicero, Kurosawa revived the samurai world to comment on postwar Japan, and Kennedy's New Frontier tied his program to the pioneer spirit. Greene says to think in grand, mythic terms.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: How should the strategy of resurrecting the spirit of childhood be used?
questions.a: You bring to life the humor, events, styles and feeling of your early years through an adult's eyes, which will reach everyone who experienced that period similarly. It works only if you feel a powerful connection to your childhood, or it will seem flat and contrived. It should capture the spirit, not copy it literally, and connect to a present issue rather than be mindless nostalgia.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: What does Greene mean by creating a new social configuration, and what should the group include?
questions.a: People crave interaction with those they feel an affinity for, so you gain power by forging a new way of interacting that appeals to your generation, perhaps through new ideas or technology, while eliminating middlemen. Introduce rituals and symbols that bond members, and think about the repressive elements of the past people want to shake free of. Salons, Freemason lodges and speakeasies are examples.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Why does Greene advise subverting the spirit of the times rather than condemning it, and how did Chanel do this?
questions.a: Preaching or moralizing against the spirit of the times only marginalizes you, so it is better to redirect it like a tide. You make something that has the look and feel of the times but insert a different spirit through its content. Chanel embraced American women's wish for less fussy, more athletic clothing, gained their trust, and then subtly brought elegance into American tastes.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
questions.q: Why does Greene say to keep adapting as you age, and how did Hitchcock exemplify it?
questions.a: As we age we tend to remain locked in the values and styles of our youth, becoming a caricature to the young and narrowing our audience. Aping the young looks ludicrous, so the answer is to modernize your spirit and become a hybrid. Hitchcock kept his obsession with visual language while adapting to color spectacles and the thrillers and horror films of later decades.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: According to Greene, what is the source of much of our anxiety and bouts of depression in relation to time?
options: The speed at which technology changes
Our inability to remember the past accurately
Our active, transformational nature is neutralized, leaving us helpless before time's course
The pressure to compete with younger generations at work
questions.explain: Humans transform nearly everything but cannot stop linear time, aging or death, and Greene says this helplessness, though not consciously registered, feeds anxiety and depression.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: What does the changing way we experience the passing of hours and days lead Greene to conclude about time?
options: Time is a human creation whose experience is subjective and malleable
Time is a fixed, objective force that experience cannot touch
Time moves faster for older people because it is physically speeding up
Time can be reversed by sufficiently strong willpower
questions.explain: Boredom, excitement and calm all alter the passage of time, which Greene takes to show it is an artificial measure we can consciously slow or speed.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: What does Greene say we cannot do about time, and what can we do?
options: We can defy death, but not our generation's perspective
We cannot change our experience of time, but we can stop aging
We cannot alter anything, so we must accept helplessness
We cannot stop aging or defy death, but we can alter our experience of them
questions.explain: Greene says we can make time feel more cyclical or step outside the stream into timelessness, transforming what is painful into something different.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which historical figures does Greene give as examples of people who consciously transcended their era and described their changed experience of time?
options: Leonardo da Vinci and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Benjamin Franklin and Mary Wollstonecraft
Danton and the Earl of Essex
Alfred Hitchcock and Coco Chanel
questions.explain: Leonardo and Goethe are named as examples. Franklin and Wollstonecraft are cited later under other aspects of time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: How does Greene describe the typical shift from youth to later phases of life?
options: Youth is wise and detached; later years are foolish and gregarious
Nothing important changes across the phases of life
Youth is calm and inward; later years are intense and outward
Youth is intense, emotional and outwardly focused; later years bring less intensity, tighter conventional ideas and more inward direction
questions.explain: In youth we worry about fitting in; later we care less what others think, gain distance and self-control, but our minds tighten around conventions.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: A twenty-year-old wants to build the premature wisdom Greene describes. What should he do?
options: Lessen the group's influence on him and become more inwardly directed
Dismiss older people's experience as outdated
Avoid emotions so he becomes less vulnerable
Join as many groups as possible to learn what others think
questions.explain: Greene says the young can drop the outward fixation on others and cultivate the inner distance and reflection that come naturally with age.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Why does Greene say aging can become a self-fulfilling prophecy?
options: Our bodies are programmed to follow our expectations exactly
Telling ourselves we are slowing down leads us to act on it, which speeds aging and deepens depression
Younger people treat us as if we are old
Medical science confirms we cannot do as much
questions.explain: The psychological component loops: we say we are slowing, do less, intensify the aging, and become more depressed.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: If you are older, how does Greene tell you to relate to people of a younger generation?
options: As a peer rather than a parent or authority figure, believing they have something to teach you
As a mentor who corrects their mistaken values
As a rival you must keep up with by copying their style
As an observer who stays emotionally neutral
questions.explain: Interacting with other generations as peers widens your perspective and builds a bond of people alive at the same time in history.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Why do we tend to turn the past into a dead and spiritless caricature, according to Greene?
options: Historians deliberately exaggerate how backward past people were
The records of the past have been mostly lost
We feel smug and superior, project present values onto it, or ignore it as irrelevant
We feel intimidated by the achievements of earlier eras
questions.explain: Greene points to filmed history where people talk and act like us in costumes, and says the past is not dead because we are shaped by earlier generations' struggles.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which of Leonardo da Vinci's actions does Greene cite as evidence of his living in the future through imagination?
options: Writing letters to the future signed with a false name
Founding a school based on the troubadour tradition
Refusing to take commissions from the powerful
Drawing future inventions such as flying machines and freeing caged birds because he believed animals have souls
questions.explain: Leonardo imagined future technologies and future values, such as seeing all nature as one, to the point of becoming a vegetarian.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Greene says that time is a human ____, a way for us to measure its passage for our own purposes.
questions.explain: Our experience of this measure is subjective and changeable, which makes our relationship to time malleable.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Leonardo da Vinci and Johann Wolfgang von ____ are two historical figures who consciously transcended their era.
questions.explain: Both described their transformed experience of time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Whenever we idealize the beloved in love, Greene says we relive an emotion introduced by the ____ of the twelfth century.
questions.explain: It was a sentiment that had never existed before in the Western world.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Greene recommends Everyday Life in Ancient ____ by Lionel Casson as a book to help gain a feel for a period.
questions.explain: He pairs it with Huizinga's The Waning of the Middle Ages as examples of books that capture daily life.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Greene says the novels of F. Scott Fitzgerald give a livelier connection to the ____ Age than any scholarly book.
questions.explain: Literature of a time lets you detect its prevailing spirit.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Benjamin ____ kept challenging his mind and body as he aged and kept a jovial, childlike disposition into his seventies and eighties.
questions.explain: He is Greene's icon of going in the opposite direction from the self-fulfilling prophecy of aging.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which of these does Greene say we can do as we age to regain youthful qualities?
options: Learn a new skill or study a new field
Accept that slowing down is simply inevitable
Meditate on intense experiences from our youth
Drop the smugness and know-it-all attitude to regain curiosity
Avoid younger people to keep our minds settled
questions.explain: These steps restore the joy of learning and youthful intensity. Avoiding the young and resigning ourselves to slowing down work against Greene's active approach.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which of these historical figures does Greene cite in connection with imagining or living in the future?
options: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
Mary Wollstonecraft
Alfred Hitchcock
Leonardo da Vinci
Benjamin Franklin
questions.explain: Leonardo envisioned inventions and values, Wollstonecraft imagined equal rights for women, and Goethe sought universal knowledge to commune with the future.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as ways we render the past dead?
options: Studying the literature of the period
Reading histories of daily life
Feeling smug and superior to past eras
Ignoring history as irrelevant
Projecting present ideas and values onto the past
questions.explain: The last two are, in fact, the ways he recommends for bringing the past back to life.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Which of these does Greene advise in dealing with people of other generations?
options: If you are younger, treat other older people as peers while attending to their values
If you are younger, cultivate some older people as mentors and role models
If you are younger, dismiss older generations' views
If you are older, interact with the young as a peer, not as an authority figure
If you are older, guide the young as a parent would
questions.explain: The aim is to widen your perspective by active association, not by dominating or dismissing.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that time is a human creation and that our experience of it is subjective and changeable.
questions.explain: He draws this from how the passage of time feels different when bored, excited, calm, or when a child versus an adult.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that changing our mindset lets us stop the aging process altogether.
questions.explain: He says we cannot stop aging or defy death, but we can alter our experience of them and mitigate the negative qualities of life phases.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: True or false: Greene says the past is by no means dead, because our thoughts and beliefs are shaped by the struggles of past generations.
questions.explain: He cites the early Christians, troubadours and Romantics as sources of ways we still think and feel.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Goethe foresaw the eventual unification of Europe after World War I.
questions.explain: Greene says Goethe foresaw the eventual unification of Europe after World War II, along with an early theory of evolution.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Put Greene's four elemental aspects of time in the order he presents them.
items: The phases of life
Present generations
Past generations
The future
questions.explain: He moves from our own life stages, to those alive with us, to the past, and finally to the future.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Put the phases of life Greene lists in order.
items: Youth
Emerging adult
Middle age
Old age
questions.explain: Greene lists these four phases when describing common changes as we age.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Put these shifts in human thinking, which Greene says we still relive, in chronological order.
items: Early Christians devote life to an ideal (first century)
Troubadours introduce idealized love (twelfth century)
Romantic movements extol emotion over intellect (eighteenth century)
questions.explain: Greene uses these three as examples of how past changes in psychology live on in us.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Put Greene's steps for bringing a past era back to life in order.
items: Pick an era that excites you
Use active imagination to get inside the experience of the actors
Read books on the daily life of the period
Read the period's literature to detect its spirit
Drop tendencies to judge or moralize
questions.explain: He moves from choosing an era to reconstructing its subjective experience, then drawing on books and literature, while avoiding judgment.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Match each aspect of time to what Greene advises.
pairs: Drop or mitigate the negative qualities of each phase
Actively associate with people of different generations
Use imagination to bring history back to life within you
Communicate with and influence those who come after you
questions.explain: Each aspect gets an active approach rather than passive acceptance.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Match each figure to how Greene uses him or her.
pairs: Imagined future inventions and values, freeing caged birds
Imagined a future of equal rights for women
Anticipated a theory of evolution decades before Darwin
Kept a childlike, jovial disposition into his seventies and eighties
questions.explain: These figures illustrate the phases-of-life and future strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Match each state of mind to how Greene says time feels.
pairs: Time feels empty and grinds to a crawl
Time may pass slowly but feels full and satisfying
questions.explain: Greene uses these differences to show that our experience of time is subjective.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene says they are typical of youth or of later phases of life.

items.t: More intense and emotional
Concerned with what people think
Gregarious but prone to foolish behavior
Minds tighten around conventional ideas
More inwardly directed
Some distance, self-control and wisdom

questions.explain: Greene says each phase has gains and losses that we can partly choose to keep or drop.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Sort these by whether they make the past dead or bring it to life.

items.t: Seeing it as a spiritless caricature
Projecting present values onto it
Ignoring it as irrelevant
Imagining the subjective experience of its people
Reading the literature of the time
Dropping the tendency to judge or moralize

questions.explain: The first set drains the past of its own perspective, while the second recovers it from the inside out.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Sort these by whether Greene says we can change them or not.

items.t: Time's linear forward course
The aging process itself
The ultimate reality of death
Whether time feels linear or cyclical
The experience of aging and death
Stepping outside the stream into timelessness

questions.explain: Greene says we cannot stop aging or defy death, but our experience of them is malleable.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Why does time defeat our transformational nature, and how does Greene say we can respond?
questions.a: Humans transform almost everything but cannot stop time's linear advance, aging or death, and this helplessness is a source of much anxiety and depression. Yet our experience of time changes with mood and circumstance, which shows time is a human creation and malleable. We cannot stop aging or death, but we can alter our experience, make time feel more cyclical, or step outside the stream.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: How does Greene's approach to the phases of life let us defy aging?
questions.a: Youth is intense, emotional and outwardly focused, while later phases bring distance, self-control and wisdom but also tight conventional ideas. We can drop negative qualities of each phase: the young can reduce the group's influence and become inwardly directed, while the old can regain curiosity, learn new skills, meditate on youthful experiences and accept people's quirks. Aging can be a self-fulfilling prophecy.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: What does Greene advise about relating to present generations in order to be less a product of the times?
questions.a: Actively associate with people of different generations. If you are younger, interact with older people, cultivating some as mentors and role models and treating others as peers, paying attention to their values. If you are older, interact with the young as a peer, not a parent or authority, with the idea that they can teach you. This creates a bond of people alive at the same time and enhances your grasp of the zeitgeist.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: Why does Greene say we make the past into a dead caricature, and why is that mistaken?
questions.a: We feel smug and superior, project present values onto the past, or ignore it, so past people talk and act just like us in costumes. But past eras could be superior in participatory democracy or psychological realism, and their values reflected their circumstances. The past is alive in us, since early Christians, troubadours and Romantics shaped how we still think, so denying it makes us rootless.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: How does Greene tell us to bring history back to life within ourselves?
questions.a: Choose an era that excites you, then use active imagination to re-create its spirit and get inside the subjective experience of its people. Use books on daily life, such as Casson's or Huizinga's, and the literature of the time, like Fitzgerald's novels for the Jazz Age. Drop any judging or moralizing, and you will see yourself as part of an unbroken chain of history.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: How do Leonardo, Wollstonecraft and Goethe illustrate relating to the future?
questions.a: Leonardo tried to live in the future through imagination, drawing possible inventions like flying machines and holding values like seeing animals as having souls. Wollstonecraft believed we create the future by imagining it and pictured equal rights and reasoning powers for women. Goethe aspired to universal knowledge, anticipated evolution decades before Darwin, and foresaw European unification.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.section: The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.q: How can the strategy of immortality help someone who feels born into the wrong period?
questions.a: If you feel out of harmony with the times, you are locked into the moment but can look to the future, knowing the pendulum will swing, perhaps after you are gone. You can reach out to future people and make them part of your audience, since some day they will read your words. The connection goes in both directions and shows the human ability to surmount one's time and the finality of death.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: The chapter that follows Chapter 17 in the book is about our common ____.
questions.explain: The table of contents titles Chapter 18 Meditate on Our Common Mortality.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: What does the name of the Law of Generational Myopia refer to?
options: The inability of old people to see clearly in their later years
The tendency to ignore events that happened before one was born
The way young people overestimate how fast technology will change
The way a generation's outlook, formed in reaction to the previous one, closes the mind to other points of view
questions.explain: Greene says each generation tends toward an imbalance as it reacts against the previous one, and judges everything by its own favored values, which makes it myopic.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does the opening statement of the law connect understanding your generation to seizing the historical moment?
options: Understanding your generation lets you avoid all contact with older people
It shows you which generation is destined to dominate history
Knowing your generation guarantees that you will become its leader
Knowing the spirit of your generation lets you exploit the zeitgeist, anticipate trends and free your mind
questions.explain: The law promises that by understanding your generation's spirit you will anticipate and set the trends it hungers for and escape its mental constraints, which sets up the chapter's three-part progression.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which chapter follows Chapter 17 in the book, and which theme from the end of Chapter 17 does it pick up?
options: Chapter 13, on purpose, picking up the theme of the inner voice
Chapter 18, on our common mortality, picking up the theme of surmounting death
Chapter 16, on aggression, picking up the theme of hostility
Chapter 15, on authority, picking up the theme of followers
questions.explain: The final section of Chapter 17 ends on the human ability to surmount time and the finality of death, and the next chapter in the table of contents is about meditating on our common mortality.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these chapters does Greene point to in the second half of Chapter 17?
options: Chapter 12, on gender
Chapter 15, on authority
Chapter 5, on desire
Chapter 3, on role-playing
Chapter 13, on purpose
questions.explain: He cites chapter 12 on the split between the genders, chapter 13 on being more inwardly directed and in harmony with one's uniqueness, and chapter 15 on the Earl of Essex.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Which of these earlier chapters' topics does Greene list as reasons we are not so superior to past eras?
options: Repression
Irrationality
Covetousness
Grandiosity
Aggression
questions.explain: Greene's list is irrationality, shortsightedness, envy, grandiosity, conformity and aggression. Covetousness and repression are not in it.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: True or false: In the book's order, Chapter 17 comes directly before the chapter on mortality, which fits its closing section about the human ability to surmount time and death.
questions.explain: The table of contents places Chapter 18, on meditating on our common mortality, right after Chapter 17.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Put the three sections of the second half of Chapter 17 in order.
items: Generational Patterns
Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times
The Human Beyond Time and Death
questions.explain: The chapter moves from understanding the pattern and your place in it, to using the zeitgeist, to transcending time itself.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Match each chapter cross-referenced in Chapter 17 to the point it is cited for.
pairs: The sudden split between the genders in the 1950s
Being more inwardly directed and in harmony with one's uniqueness
The Earl of Essex becoming the darling of his generation
questions.explain: These cross-references link the generational material to other laws in the book.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: Sort these items by the section of Chapter 17 in which they appear.
groups: The Human Beyond Time and Death

items.t: Ibn Khaldun's four generations
Humor as a generation's shadow side
Millennials craving security
Early Christians devoting life to an ideal
Leonardo freeing caged birds
Wollstonecraft imagining women's rights

questions.explain: The first section maps the generational cycle and profile; the last explores transcending time.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How do the three sections of the second half of Chapter 17 build on each other and fit the title Seize the Historical Moment?
questions.a: Generational Patterns teaches you to see the cycle of generations and your own generation's spirit, which Greene says is the basis for exploiting the zeitgeist. Strategies for Exploiting the Spirit of the Times turns that understanding into six ways to shape the times. The Human Beyond Time and Death goes further, showing how to transcend your era and feel part of an unbroken chain.

questions.unitTitle: Seize the Historical Moment
questions.q: How does the end of Chapter 17 prepare for the chapter that follows it?
questions.a: The last section deals with our helplessness before time and shows we can alter our experience of aging and death and feel a strange intimation of immortality. This leads naturally into Chapter 18, which according to the table of contents is about the Law of Death Denial and meditating on our common mortality.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the opening statement of the Law of Death Denial, how does Greene say the inevitability of death should figure in our minds?
options: It should be considered once, deeply, early in adult life
It should be continually on our minds
It should be a private religious matter, apart from daily goals
It should be saved for moments of illness or loss
questions.explain: The opening says most of us avoid the thought of death, whereas it should be continually on our minds. Treating it as an occasional or purely religious topic is the avoidance he criticizes.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to the opening of the Law of Death Denial, what does understanding the shortness of life give us?
options: A stronger drive to outdo the people around us
A calm detachment from our goals and ambitions
A readiness to lower our expectations of ourselves
A sense of purpose and urgency to realize our goals
questions.explain: Greene says awareness of life's brevity fills us with purpose and urgency. It does not make us detached, competitive, or resigned.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: In the opening of the Law of Death Denial, Greene says we should find ways to separate ourselves from others and feel superior.
questions.explain: He says the opposite: most people look for ways to feel superior, but we should instead see the mortality in everyone, which equalizes and connects us.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the opening statement of the Law of Death Denial, understanding the shortness of life fills us with a sense of purpose and ____ to realize our goals.
questions.explain: The opening links awareness of limited time to purpose and urgency about what we want to achieve.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these does the opening of the Law of Death Denial say follows from training ourselves to accept the reality of death?
options: We learn to withdraw from other people's company
We gain a sense of proportion about what really matters
It is easier to manage setbacks, separations, and crises
We see how mortality equalizes and connects everyone
questions.explain: Greene lists easier handling of setbacks, a sense of proportion, and seeing mortality as a connection among all people. Withdrawal is not part of it; the stress is on connection.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the opening statement of the Law of Death Denial, what does Greene say we should do about death, and what does it do to our experience of life?
questions.a: Greene says that instead of avoiding the thought of death, we should keep its inevitability continually in mind. Seeing the shortness of life gives us purpose and urgency, helps us handle setbacks, and shows us the mortality we share with everyone. By becoming deeply aware of mortality we intensify our experience of every aspect of life.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the story of Flannery O’Connor, what made her feel so strongly connected to her father, Edward?
options: They both disliked schooling and avoided study
They shared a devout Catholic practice that her mother did not
Their way of thinking and feeling seemed in sync, and they could communicate without words
They both aspired to a place in local society
questions.explain: Beyond a physical resemblance, Mary felt their thinking and feeling matched, as in the games she invented. Her mother, not her father, cared about social standing.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Flannery O’Connor’s father died on February 1, 1941, at the age of ____ , of lupus erythematosus.
questions.explain: The text gives his age at death as forty-five. Mary only learned months later that the illness was lupus.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Lupus is a disease that makes the body create ____ that attack and weaken its own healthy tissues.
questions.explain: Greene describes lupus erythematosus as a condition in which the body's antibodies attack its own tissues, the disease that killed her father and later struck her.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What did Mary write in her private notebook after her father's death, according to the story?
options: That the reality of death had broken their complacency like a bullet in the side
That grief had shown her she must leave Georgia
That death had made her doubt the plan of God
That she was now free of her mother's expectations
questions.explain: Her notebook says death broke their complacency “like a bullet in the side,” filling her with grief but above all wonder. It was not a loss of faith.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: After her father's death, how did Mary O’Connor change in the months that followed?
options: She grew more playful and began mocking her teachers
She became unusually serious about her schoolwork and began writing longer, more ambitious stories
She withdrew from school and turned to caring for her mother
She gave up writing and turned to her faith alone
questions.explain: Her father's early death could not be meaningless to her, so she took his belief in her as her destiny and worked seriously at writing.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to the story, what inspired Flannery to call her first novel Wise Blood?
options: The family she inherited from her father's side
The many blood transfusions she underwent as part of her treatment
The blood she saw on a hospital visit to her father
A phrase from her mother's religious reading
questions.explain: While hospitalized and treated with frequent transfusions, she finished the novel and named it for them. Its hero, Hazel Motes, thinks he has wise blood and needs no spiritual guidance.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: The hero of Flannery O’Connor’s novel Wise Blood is a young man named Hazel ____ .
questions.explain: Hazel Motes is determined to spread the gospel of atheism, and the book follows his descent into murder and madness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: In the story of Flannery O’Connor, she gave her novel's main character blindness only after she felt herself growing blind during her hospital fevers.
questions.explain: She had decided to make him blind months before she was ill. Greene notes the odd coincidence and wonders whether she had foreseen her fate or whether the disease was already making her think such thoughts.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these were effects of the cortisone given to Flannery O’Connor?
options: It completely cured the lupus and ended her hospital stays
It made her hair fall out and bloated her face
It greatly alleviated the pain and inflammation in her joints
It gave her bursts of energy that made her mind race
questions.explain: The text lists pain relief, restless bursts of energy, and the hair loss and bloated face. Later it also softened her hip and jawbone. It never cured the disease.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the story, who finally told Flannery that she had lupus, and what had been kept from her?
options: Erik told her; her father had asked him to wait
Her uncle told her; the hospital had lost her records
Sally Fitzgerald told her; her mother, in league with the doctors, had hidden it
A New York doctor told her; her friends had hidden it
questions.explain: Sally Fitzgerald said, “Flannery, you don’t have arthritis, you have lupus.” Her overprotective mother and the doctors had kept the truth from her.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How did Flannery O’Connor react when she learned she had lupus, and why did Greene call it a second bullet in her side?
questions.a: She replied calmly that it was not good news, but thanked Sally and said she had thought she had lupus and was going crazy, adding that she would rather be sick than crazy. Greene calls it a second bullet because the original sensation of her father's death returned with double the impact. She now knew she had inherited the disease and might not live long.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: A woman learns she has a serious illness and says she can with one eye squinted take it all as a blessing. Which reason from the story of Flannery O’Connor would best support such a view?
options: Illness releases people from any duty to work or care for others
Illness makes it easy to ignore other people's views
Knowing early, she has time to get used to dying young, and every experience will mean something
Serious illness proves that a person's life has been lived correctly
questions.explain: Flannery counted the advantage of early knowledge: the blow would be lessened, she would relish every minute, and she could not expect much so everything she got would mean something.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these did Flannery O’Connor count among the blessings of knowing she was dying young?
options: She would be spared the need to write any more stories
She would have time to get used to the idea of dying
She would find it easier not to take petty concerns seriously
She would relish every minute and experience
questions.explain: She counted time to get used to dying, relishing each moment, and not taking petty worries seriously. Writing became more urgent, not less.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How did Flannery O’Connor's thinking about death shape the way she planned to spend her remaining time at Andalusia?
questions.a: As she faced death she decided that what mattered most to her was her writing, more than friends, where she lived, or even her health. She set aside two or more sacred morning hours for writing, welcomed the lack of distractions, and told herself she had no time to waste. Writing also let her forget herself and inhabit her characters, which eased anxiety about the illness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these did Flannery O’Connor see in the people of 1950s America?
options: They were disconnected from the past and religion
They were preoccupied with death to the point of despair
They felt superior to any kind of outsider
They were obsessed with material things
questions.explain: She saw superficiality, loss of roots and faith, coldness, and feelings of superiority. Their problem was avoiding the thought of death, not dwelling on it.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In her story “The Enduring Chill,” a young man returns home to Georgia ____ ill, and wants his mother to see death in his face at once.
questions.explain: The young man hopes the sight will introduce his sixty-year-old mother to reality and help her grow up, which mirrors Flannery's own view of readers.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What did Flannery O’Connor decide her readers needed, and how would she deliver it?
options: Their own bullet in the side, by portraying the selfishness and brutality below the surface of pleasant characters
A gentle consolation, by portraying a world in which suffering is rewarded
A moral lecture, by portraying villains who are plainly evil
A distraction from grief, by portraying comic lives of southern gentry
questions.explain: She wanted to shake readers out of complacency by showing raw selfishness and brutality in characters who seemed outwardly pleasant and banal.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why did Flannery O’Connor prefer to keep up friendships through letters rather than close contact?
options: Her illness made it impossible for her to speak with visitors
She thought letters showed more of her wit than speech did
Her mother forbade visitors to the farm
Letters kept physical distance, and she feared intimacy with people she would soon have to say good-bye to
questions.explain: She needed company but feared attachment, because getting close meant losing people. Letters let her build what Greene calls the perfect social world for her purposes.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How did Flannery O’Connor use the story “Good Country People” in connection with Erik Langkjaier?
options: She wrote it as an apology for refusing his kiss
She wrote it to ask him to return from Denmark
She wrote it as her way of coping with his extended stay in Europe, casting them as the salesman and the cynical crippled woman
She wrote it to mock his fiancée in Denmark
questions.explain: In the story a Bible salesman runs off with a woman's wooden leg after she lowers her guard. Flannery caricatured herself and Erik that way: Erik had taken her wooden leg.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: In the story of Flannery O’Connor, Erik Langkjaier was a traveling textbook salesman from Denmark whom she met in the spring of 1953.
questions.explain: He was twenty-six and sold textbooks across the South. She inscribed a copy of Wise Blood to him, writing that he had wise blood too.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put these events in the Erik Langkjaier episode of Flannery O’Connor's story in order.
items: Erik visits in the spring of 1953
A good-bye car ride and a kiss in May 1954
She writes Good Country People in January 1955
She receives his letter announcing his engagement
questions.explain: The visit came first, then the kiss before he went to Denmark, then the story, and finally the engagement news that came the day after she mailed him a letter.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why had Flannery O’Connor tried to protect herself from deep feelings of parting and separation?
options: They had once cost her a place at the university
They had made her break off friendships in Connecticut
They had embarrassed her badly in her family's social circle
They were small reminders of the death that would take her away while others went on living and loving
questions.explain: Separation was unbearable because it echoed her own death. Erik's engagement let those feelings pour in, but she chose to face them as she had faced death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What did Flannery O’Connor decide to do with the pain of losing Erik?
options: Withdraw from letter-writing and avoid visitors
Transmute it into stories and her second novel as a way to enrich her knowledge of people
Stop writing about love and turn to religious subjects
Move away from Georgia to put distance between them
questions.explain: She reasoned that having looked death in the eye, she should not recoil from this latest suffering, and she used it to deepen her understanding of people and their vulnerabilities.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Flannery O’Connor named her returning lupus after an animal; lupus is the Latin word for ____ .
questions.explain: She imagined the disease raging inside her, tearing things up, after surgery for a benign tumor.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the events of Flannery O’Connor's final illness in order.
items: She faints before Christmas of 1963 and is treated for anemia
A benign tumor is found and surgically removed
Her lupus comes roaring back by mid-March
She is allowed home on June 21
She loses consciousness on July 31 and dies on August 3
questions.explain: The text moves from the anemia and transfusions to the tumor surgery, the lupus return, the discharge home, and her death at thirty-nine.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: At the end of her life, Flannery O’Connor stopped writing once the doctors prohibited her from working.
questions.explain: She kept going: she concocted stories in her head and memorized them, hid notebooks under her pillow, and tried to get in two hours, or even one, every day.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: According to Greene, Flannery O’Connor was buried next to her father, in accordance with her last wishes.
questions.explain: The story closes with her death at thirty-nine and her burial beside Edward, mirroring the bond that began the account.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In Greene's interpretation, what difference between Flannery O’Connor and the people who sought her advice does he stress?
options: She was more religious than they were
She was luckier in her doctors and her friends
She had spent years looking death squarely in the eye without flinching
She was less troubled by the loss of her health
questions.explain: Greene says she was solid because she faced death for years, whereas the others dabbled, felt empty, and fell apart under adversity or loneliness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these did Flannery O’Connor refuse to do when facing her early death, according to Greene?
options: Accept the early death sentence imposed on her
Indulge vague hopes for the future
Drown her sorrows in alcohol or addiction
Put her trust in medicine
questions.explain: Greene says she did not indulge vague hopes, trust in medicine, or drown her sorrows. She did accept the sentence and used it for her own ends.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these did Flannery O’Connor's closeness to death serve as a call to, according to Greene?
options: To deepen her religious faith
To spark her sense of wonder at life's mysteries
To stir herself to action and feel a sense of urgency
To avoid close contact with other people
questions.explain: Greene lists urgency, deeper faith, and wonder. He says it also deepened her empathy, the opposite of avoiding people.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In Greene's interpretation, how did Flannery O’Connor use the closeness of death to handle ordinary life and pain?
questions.a: She used it to learn what really matters and to steer clear of the petty squabbles that plagued others. It anchored her in the present, made her appreciate every moment and encounter, and removed any need for self-pity. By confronting her illness straight on she toughened herself, managed the pain, and kept writing.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Greene says many people around Flannery O’Connor suffered from a ____ deficit, avoiding the thought of their mortality and other unpleasant aspects of life.
questions.explain: In contrast to her being at home with the ultimate reality represented by death, most people avoid unpleasant truths. Greene calls this a “reality deficit.”

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to Greene, what effect did Flannery O’Connor's focus on her mortality have on her relationship to other people?
options: It made her more critical of their weakness
It made her place her faith above their company
It made her prefer solitude to company
It deepened her empathy and her sense of connection to them
questions.explain: Greene says she saw that we are all connected and made equal by our common mortality. Her fate was tied to her father's, and she extended that tie to everyone.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does Greene connect Flannery O’Connor's sense of common mortality to the change in her racial attitudes?
questions.a: Her feeling of unity with others, shown by her wish to communicate with all kinds of people, led her to let go of the racist sentiments she had absorbed from her mother and many others in the South. She saw them in herself and struggled against them in her work. By the early 1960s she embraced the civil rights movement and in later stories imagined the races converging as equals.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: Greene says Flannery O’Connor’s religious faith alone explains why she faced death so well, since religious people are free of illusions about mortality.
questions.explain: He says her faith helped, but many religious people are just as full of illusions and evasions about their own mortality. Her choice to use the disease for the most intense life possible mattered.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Greene says that for over thirteen years Flannery O’Connor stared down the barrel of the ____ pointed at her, refusing to look away.
questions.explain: The image extends the bullet metaphor: she kept facing the threat of death for over thirteen years.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the Understand section, what grave mistake does Greene say we make when reading stories like Flannery O’Connor’s?
options: We assume her illness was unusually painful
We read them with distance and relief, forgetting that her fate is our fate
We admire her more for her faith than for her writing
We blame her doctors for the way her illness developed
questions.explain: We feel relieved to be more comfortable, but we are all dying and facing the same uncertainties. The mistake is treating her mortality as hers alone.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In Greene's argument, what advantage did Flannery O’Connor have over the rest of us?
options: She had more time to reflect than healthy people have
She had a gift for suffering that most people lack
She had a mother who could look after her
Her mortality was so present that she was compelled to confront and use her awareness of it
questions.explain: Greene says we can dance around the thought of death and imagine endless time, while she could not. The advantage was the forced awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these does Greene give as examples of the “bullet in the side” that might strike us?
options: The death of someone close
An unexpected crisis in our career
A slow rise in our social standing
A painful breakup in a relationship
questions.explain: Greene names a career crisis, a painful breakup, the death of someone close, or a life-threatening illness. A rising social standing is not a shock of that kind.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to Greene, how does our avoidance of the thought of death shape the way we handle crises and adversity?
questions.a: He says our avoidance of death sets our pattern for handling every unpleasant reality. When a crisis hits we are unprepared, so we become hysterical and lose our balance, blame others, feel angry and sorry for ourselves, or reach for distractions to dull the pain. This becomes a habit we cannot shake, leaving a generalized anxiety and emptiness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: Greene says that a fleeting, abstract meditation on death is enough to change our approach to life.
questions.explain: He warns against fooling ourselves with a fleeting, abstract meditation. We must look at our mortality without flinching and focus hard on the uncertainty it represents.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put these steps of Greene's prescription for facing mortality in the order he gives them.
items: Shake ourselves out of the dreamlike state
Look at our mortality without flinching
Focus hard on the uncertainty death represents
Stop postponing our awareness
Stop feeling superior and special
questions.explain: Greene moves from waking up, to looking without flinching, to facing uncertainty, ending postponement, and giving up the feeling of superiority.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Greene says that seeing death as a fate shared by all should bind us in an empathetic way, as part of the brotherhood and sisterhood of ____ .
questions.explain: The phrase “brotherhood and sisterhood of death” sums up the equalizing, connecting effect of mortality.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to the end of the Understand section, how does our life change once we make death a familiar presence?
questions.a: We understand how short life is and what should matter to us, so we feel urgency and deeper commitment to our work and relationships. In a crisis, separation, or illness we are not so terrified and do not slide into avoidance, and we use suffering to strengthen ourselves and learn. As with Flannery, awareness of mortality cleanses us of silly illusions and intensifies every aspect of our experience.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: A man in his thirties has a parent die suddenly and spends the next months working late and drinking to avoid thinking about it. Using Greene's reading of the O’Connor story, how would you describe his response and what would a better response look like?
questions.a: His response is the avoidance pattern Greene describes: opting for distractions and quick ways to dull the pain, a habit that breeds anxiety and emptiness. This is his bullet in the side, and a better response would be to look at his own mortality without flinching, see that death is a fate shared by all, and use the loss to feel urgency about what truly matters, as Flannery did after her father's death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: A man dismisses a stranger's illness with relief that his own life is comfortable and secure. According to Greene, what is wrong with that attitude?
options: It forgets that we are all in the process of dying and that his fate is the same
It treats suffering as more common than it is
It shows a lack of faith in his own doctors
It ignores how much money he has saved for old age
questions.explain: Greene says that reading others' stories at a distance is a grave mistake: her fate is our fate. Feeling superior or separate is just what common mortality should dissolve.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: A student keeps telling herself she will start her real work someday and pictures endless years ahead. Which problem from the Understand section does this show?
options: Seeking out hardship in the hope of meaning
Feeling too much grief for people who have died
Being too focused on her physical health
Dancing around the thought of death and dabbling through life by envisioning endless vistas of time
questions.explain: Greene says we are able to dance around the thought of death and dabble our way through life. He urges us to stop postponing awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each person in Flannery O’Connor's story to what he or she did.
pairs: Showed visitors the little book of her caricatures
Wanted to mold her into a southern lady
Told Flannery she had lupus, not arthritis
Young woman from Georgia who confided in Flannery
Danish textbook salesman she came to love
questions.explain: Each person plays a distinct role in the story: father as admirer, mother as shaper, Sally as truth-teller, Betty as correspondent, and Erik as the lost love.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each of Flannery O’Connor’s writings to its description in the story.
pairs: Caricatures of her family written at age ten
Novel about Hazel Motes, finished in the hospital
Story of a deathly ill young man returning home
Story of a woman with a wooden leg and a Bible salesman
questions.explain: The four works span her childhood sketches, first novel, and two stories drawn from her illness and her loss of Erik.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each place in Flannery O’Connor's story to its role.
pairs: Where she grew up as a child
Where she lived with her mother in central Georgia
Where she studied at the Writers’ Workshop
Where she worked in the Fitzgeralds’ country house
Her mother’s farm where she spent her last years
questions.explain: These places mark the stages from childhood, to study, to independence, and finally the return home that shaped her last years.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each year to the event in Flannery O’Connor's life.
pairs: She began at the University of Iowa
questions.explain: These dates run from her father's death to her schooling, her first novel, and the story she wrote while Erik stayed abroad.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each term from the chapter's O’Connor story to its meaning.
pairs: A shock that breaks our complacency about death
The lupus news, returning the first sensation doubled
Avoiding the thought of mortality and other hard facts
The shared mortality that should bind us
questions.explain: These terms capture Greene's key images: the shock, its repetitions, the avoidance that breeds weakness, and the connection mortality creates.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each treatment or event in Flannery O’Connor’s illness to its effect.
pairs: Relieved joint pain but caused bodily side effects
Inspired the title of her first novel
Feared as a trigger for the return of lupus
questions.explain: Each treatment or condition had both a medical effect and a place in the story of how she lived with the disease.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each group of people to Greene's description of them in the O’Connor interpretation.
pairs: Used the closeness of death to anchor herself in the present
Turned to her for the truth about themselves and direction
Dabbled in new pleasures and distractions while feeling empty
Needed their own bullet in the side to be shaken
questions.explain: Greene contrasts her solid, death-aware life with the emptiness of those around her and the shock she wanted her stories to deliver.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these into Flannery O’Connor's response to death and the avoidance Greene says is typical of the rest of us.

items.t: Feeling urgency about her work
Appreciating every moment and encounter
Looking death squarely in the eye
Not taking petty concerns seriously
Dancing around the thought of death
Picturing endless vistas of time
Postponing awareness of mortality
Losing balance when a crisis hits

questions.explain: Greene presents her as using death to focus and calm herself, while the rest of us delay and are unprepared when reality strikes.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these actions into those of Flannery O’Connor's father and those of her mother.

items.t: Collected her caricatures into a little book
Slipped easily into her invented games
Foresaw a great future for her as a writer
Wanted to turn her into a southern lady
Begged her not to go to Iowa
Kept the lupus diagnosis from her

questions.explain: The father cherished her eccentric gifts while the mother tried to shape and protect her.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these places from Flannery O’Connor’s story into those in Georgia and those outside Georgia.

items.t: Savannah
Milledgeville
Andalusia farm
University of Iowa
Fitzgeralds’ house in Connecticut
Doctors’ offices in New York

questions.explain: She grew up and ended her life in Georgia, with Iowa, Connecticut, and New York marking her time away.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these into effects of the cortisone treatment and symptoms of the illness itself in Flannery O’Connor’s story.

items.t: Hair falling out
A bloated face
Softening of the hip and jawbone
Bursts of energy and racing thoughts
Painful, inflamed joints
High fevers
Rashes triggered by sunlight

questions.explain: The text ties the first group to the drug and the second to the lupus and its flare-ups.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these into what Greene says facing mortality brings and what avoiding it brings.

items.t: Urgency and deeper commitment to work
Not being overwhelmed by crises
Every aspect of life intensified
Using pain to strengthen and learn
Generalized anxiety and emptiness
Blaming others for our fate
Seeking quick ways to dull the pain
Feeling angry and sorry for ourselves

questions.explain: Greene contrasts the strength and richness of facing death with the anxiety and self-pity of avoiding it.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort these into titles of Flannery O’Connor’s works and characters in those works.

items.t: Wise Blood
The Enduring Chill
Good Country People
Hazel Motes
A deathly ill young man returning to Georgia
A cynical young woman with a wooden leg
A traveling Bible salesman

questions.explain: The first group are titles the story names; the second are characters drawn from them.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the story of Flannery O’Connor, what did her father do with her ten-year-old caricatures of the family?
options: He collected them into a little book that he showed to visitors
He had them printed to send to her relatives
He used them to teach her how to write plays
He kept them hidden to protect her from her mother
questions.explain: Her father found the caricatures called My Relitives delightful, while her mother and relatives were shocked.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: After her father's death, how did Mary O’Connor change, and what led her to leave Georgia for the University of Iowa?
questions.a: She became unusually serious about school and began writing longer, more ambitious stories, deciding her father had guessed her destiny as a writer. Growing confident in her creative powers, she felt that her success depended on leaving Georgia and found living with her mother in Milledgeville claustrophobic. She won a full scholarship to Iowa and simplified her name to Flannery.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What did Flannery O’Connor see wrong with American life in the 1950s, and what did she want her fiction to do about it?
questions.a: She saw people as superficial, obsessed with material things, bored like children, and cut off from the past and from religion, and she thought the core problem was their inability to face mortality. She wanted her readers to receive their own bullet in the side to shake them out of complacency. She did this by showing as rawly as possible the selfishness and brutality below the surface of seemingly pleasant characters.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why did Flannery O’Connor rely on letters for company, and how did she handle the loss of Erik Langkjaier?
questions.a: Letters gave her people to talk to while keeping physical distance, because she feared intimacy with those she would soon have to say good-bye to. When Erik announced his engagement, the feelings of separation she had avoided came pouring in. Having trained herself to look death in the eye, she did not recoil but turned the pain into stories and a second novel.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What mistake does Greene say we make when we read stories like Flannery O’Connor's, and what advantage did she have over us?
questions.a: We read with distance and relief at our more comfortable position, forgetting that her fate is our fate and that we are all dying. She had her mortality so present that she was compelled to confront it and use it, while we can dance around the thought and imagine endless time ahead.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Told she had lupus, Flannery O’Connor replied that she would a lot rather be sick than ____ .
questions.explain: She said she had suspected lupus and thought she was going crazy, so the diagnosis came as a relief of sorts, although it stunned her.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Flannery O’Connor’s mother managed the family farm just outside Milledgeville, called ____ .
questions.explain: Andalusia is where Flannery lived for the rest of her life, writing in her room.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Flannery O’Connor’s traveling salesman friend Erik Langkjaier sold ____ for a major publisher.
questions.explain: He was a Danish textbook salesman whose territory included most of the South.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these are true of Erik Langkjaier in the story of Flannery O’Connor?
options: He grew up in Milledgeville and stayed there
He was a traveling textbook salesman
He came from Denmark
His father had died when he was young, as hers had
questions.explain: He visited in 1953 and shared the loss of a father with her. He was a worldly outsider, not a local.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: According to the story, the doctors thought Flannery O’Connor could live a normal length of life thanks to cortisone, but she did not share their confidence.
questions.explain: She had experienced the adverse side effects firsthand and wondered how long her body could endure them.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the diagnoses Flannery O’Connor was given in the order she received them.
items: A floating kidney
Rheumatoid arthritis
Lupus, as told by Sally Fitzgerald
questions.explain: She was first treated for a floating kidney at Christmas 1949, then told she had rheumatoid arthritis, and learned the truth about lupus from Sally.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the stages of her father's decline in the order they happened.
items: Rashes and afternoon weariness appear in 1937
He lets his real estate business go
He takes a poorly paid government job in Atlanta
By 1940 he is too weak to keep working
He dies on February 1, 1941
