questions.explain: The decline runs from subtle symptoms and the end of his business to a job in Atlanta, total weakness, and death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put these stages of Flannery O’Connor's life in order.
items: Her father dies of lupus
She studies at the University of Iowa
She works on her first novel in Connecticut
She falls ill on a train home and enters the hospital
She settles at Andalusia and learns of the lupus
questions.explain: Her father died in 1941, she went to Iowa in 1945, wrote in Connecticut, fell ill in December and later settled at Andalusia.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the Understand section, what does Greene say we must do to shake ourselves out of our dreamlike state about death?
questions.a: We must look at our own mortality without flinching and without fooling ourselves with a fleeting, abstract meditation. We must focus hard on the uncertainty death represents, since it could come tomorrow, stop postponing our awareness, and stop feeling superior and special. Seeing death as a fate shared by all should bind us in an empathetic way.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Where does the chapter on the Law of Death Denial sit in the book's sequence of laws?
options: It is the final law, following the chapter on seizing the historical moment
It is a middle law, following the chapter on envy
It is the first law, opening the survey of human irrationality
It is an appendix that comes after the laws
questions.explain: Chapter 18 is the last of the eighteen laws and follows the chapter whose last section is The Human Beyond Time and Death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: Chapter 18 opens with the story of Flannery O’Connor, titled The Bullet in the Side, before it presents the Keys to Human Nature.
questions.explain: The table of contents lists The Bullet in the Side first, then Keys to Human Nature, then A Philosophy of Life Through Death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: The law of Chapter 18, Meditate on Our Common Mortality, is called the Law of ____ Denial.
questions.explain: The title urges meditation on mortality, and the law names the opposite habit: denial of death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these are section titles of Chapter 18?
options: The Bullet in the Side
A Philosophy of Life Through Death
The Human Beyond Time and Death
Keys to Human Nature
questions.explain: The last of these is a section of the previous chapter, about generations. Chapter 18's own sections are the first three.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the sections of Chapter 18 in the order they appear.
items: The Bullet in the Side
Keys to Human Nature
A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.explain: The story opens the chapter, the keys explain the law, and the philosophy section draws a lesson for life.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why does Greene open Chapter 18 with the story of Flannery O’Connor, and how does her story set up the rest of the chapter?
questions.a: Her story shows a person who confronts death directly and turns it into purpose, empathy, and a rich life, while those around her avoid it. It illustrates the law's claim that awareness of mortality gives urgency and connects us, before the Keys to Human Nature explain the idea and the closing section turns it into a philosophy of life.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does the first half of Chapter 18 lead into the Keys to Human Nature, in terms of what Greene asks the reader to do?
questions.a: The Bullet in the Side shows both the model of facing death and the cost of avoiding it, and ends with Greene urging us to stop postponing awareness and see our common mortality. This sets up the Keys to Human Nature, where the law is treated as a principle about people, and then the final section on a philosophy of life through death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What does the author call the effect by which brushes with death and loss leave people feeling more awake and alive?
options: The amor fati effect
The paradoxical death effect
The mortality mirror effect
The Sublime effect
questions.explain: The author names the paradoxical death effect for moments that, oddly, make us feel more alive. The other labels belong to other ideas or are not in the chapter.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: According to the author, why is death a source of awkwardness for humans specifically?
options: We have lost the rituals that once made dying a public event, so we feel unprepared
We are the only animal truly conscious of our impending mortality, and our thinking brings only misery here
We reason well about most things but cannot calculate when our death will arrive
We are the only animal that buries its dead, which forces us to face the subject
questions.explain: The author says we alone are truly conscious of mortality, and here our thinking only brings misery. The other options are not what the author gives as the cause.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What did the earliest humans do to soften their awareness of death?
options: They created spirits, gods and a concept of the afterlife
They moved their settlements away from burial grounds
They built monuments meant to outlast their own lives
They avoided speaking about the dead for a season
questions.explain: The author says our earliest ancestors created a world of spirits, gods and an afterlife to soften the blow. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why, in the author's view, have growing reasoning powers and science made our awkwardness about death worse?
options: Science has removed the rituals that once surrounded dying
Many can no longer believe in an afterlife but are left without any compensation for the stark reality
Reasoning makes us dwell on death more often than our ancestors did
Science has proven that death is more painful than earlier generations believed
questions.explain: We can no longer believe in the afterlife with conviction yet are left with no compensation, so the stark reality confronts us. The author does not say science shows dying to be more painful.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What does the author say about how death is experienced in many parts of the world today, compared with the past?
options: It occurs earlier in life, so most people witness it as children
It is now discussed openly in schools and families, which lessens the fear
It has been made largely invisible, occurring mostly in hospitals, so many people never witness it
It has become more visible through constant news coverage of disasters
questions.explain: The author notes death occurs mainly in hospitals and that we can pass through life without ever witnessing it, which makes it feel unreal.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What does the author conclude from the cartoonish way death is shown in entertainment?
options: It proves that people prefer violent stories to realistic ones
It reveals how deep the need is to repress the awareness of death and desensitize ourselves to the fear
It shows that audiences have become comfortable with the idea of dying
It reflects a healthy curiosity about mortality that needs no change
questions.explain: Dozens of people die violent deaths with only excitement at the imagery, which the author reads as a sign of the deep need to repress and desensitize.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why does the author say we avoid old objects and films from the past and surround ourselves with what is new and trending?
options: They unconsciously remind us of the shortness of life and the fate awaiting us
They remind us that technology is advancing too quickly
They are usually of lower quality than modern things
They make us feel nostalgic for people who have died
questions.explain: Aged objects and past films unconsciously remind us of life's shortness, so we surround ourselves with the new and fresh.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What happens to the anxiety about death that we repress as adults, according to the author?
options: It turns into curiosity about the unknown over the years
It stays the same size but is hidden behind our daily routines
It fades gradually, because the mind forgets what it does not face
It is made stronger by not confronting its source, and the slightest uncertainty can stir it up and make it chronic
questions.explain: Not confronting the source makes the anxiety stronger, and any uncertainty about the future can make it chronic. It does not fade through forgetting.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does the author contrast death and life?
options: Death is certain; life is uncertain and therefore unpredictable
Death is a single event; life is a long series of events
Death is an ending that we fear; life is a beginning we welcome
Death is absolute stillness and separation; life is movement, connection and diversity
questions.explain: The author sets death as absolute stillness and separation against life as movement, connection and diversity.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What does the author say the story of Flannery O'Connor illustrates?
options: That denying death can be a source of courage
That illness can lead to creative work
That closeness with death and the ability to confront it makes us feel more alive
That writers are more aware of mortality than other people
questions.explain: The author says closeness with death has the paradoxical effect of making us feel more alive, as the story of Flannery O’Connor illustrates.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: The author says that humans are the only animal truly conscious of their impending mortality.
questions.explain: The author makes this point to explain why death is a source of awkwardness for us as well as fear.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: According to the author, belief in the afterlife removed the pain of dying and the anxiety of separating from loved ones.
questions.explain: The author says belief in an afterlife could not eliminate the anxiety of separation or lessen the physical pain; it offered a psychological compensation instead.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: The author argues that the belief that technology can overcome death shows we have become stronger than our primitive ancestors.
questions.explain: The author calls this the ultimate in human denial and says we are no stronger than our most primitive ancestors, having simply found new ways to delude ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: True or false: The author says that repressing the thought of death makes the anxiety stronger.
questions.explain: Because we do not confront the source, the anxiety grows stronger.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: The author calls the effect in which moments of loss or danger make us feel more alive the ____ death effect.
questions.explain: The effect is paradoxical because contact with death makes us feel more alive.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In many parts of the world today, death has been made largely invisible, occurring mostly in ____.
questions.explain: The author says death has been moved out of daily view into hospitals.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: The author says we have come to venerate ____, creating a virtual cult around it, partly to avoid reminders of death.
questions.explain: The cult of youth is one of the author's examples of denial.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: In the author's contrast, death is absolute ____, without movement or change except decay.
questions.explain: Stillness is set against life as movement and connection.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Having lost belief in an afterlife, we now rely on ____, repressing the awareness of death as much as possible.
questions.explain: Denial is the modern substitute for older belief systems.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: The author says we became aware of our mortality quite early in ____, producing an anxiety we cannot remember.
questions.explain: This early anxiety remains latent in adults.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these does the author give as ways modern people repress awareness of death?
options: Making death invisible by keeping it in hospitals
Venerating youth and surrounding ourselves with the new
Requiring long periods of mourning
Holding public festivals for the dying
Showing death as cartoonish in entertainment
questions.explain: The author lists hidden death, cartoonish entertainment and the cult of youth. Festivals and long mourning are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these does the author describe as intimations of our own death in smaller doses?
options: Traveling in a strange land
Clearly entering a new phase of life
Separating from people we know
Buying a home
Winning a competition
questions.explain: All three involve changes that make us look back as if a part of us has died. Winning and buying are not offered as examples.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these does the author say can result when we repress the thought of death?
options: Turning to addictions that dull the anxiety
Narrowing our thoughts and activities to stay in our comfort zone
Becoming more curious about strangers
Becoming more self-absorbed and less dependent on people
questions.explain: Repression leads to a narrower, more self-enclosed life, not greater curiosity.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the author's account of how denial of death leads to a more deathlike life in order.
items: We become aware of mortality in childhood and feel anxiety
We repress the thought rather than confront it
The anxiety grows stronger and can become chronic
We narrow our thoughts and activities to feel safe
We become more separated, habitual and deathlike from within
questions.explain: Each step follows from the one before it in the author's argument.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Put the author's account of humanity's changing response to death in order.
items: Awareness of mortality brings fear and awkwardness
Early humans create spirits, gods and an afterlife
Reason and science erode belief in the afterlife
Without compensation, we rely on denial
Denial turns the paradoxical effect negative
questions.explain: The author moves from the origin of the awkwardness, through the old compensation and its loss, to the modern pattern of denial.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each idea to the author's description of it.
pairs: Encounters with death leave us feeling more awake and alive
A psychological compensation for the anxiety of death
A way of avoiding reminders of the shortness of life
Repressing the awareness of death as much as possible
questions.explain: Each pairing restates the author's definition or role for the idea.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Match each way of relating to death with the author's description.
pairs: Death was a daily, visceral presence in cities and towns
Death is largely invisible, occurring in hospitals
Death is cartoonish, met with excitement rather than emotion
A feeling of godlike powers that lets us ignore reality
questions.explain: The author contrasts the past with several modern ways of making death unreal.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort each feature into the author's picture of death or of life.

items.t: Absolute stillness
Separation from others, completely alone
Nothing but decay
Movement
Connection to other living things
Diversity of life forms

questions.explain: The author sets death as stillness and isolation against life as movement and connection.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Sort each item into how our early ancestors coped with death or how people cope today.

items.t: Believing in spirits and gods
Elaborate rituals around the passage to death
Belief in an afterlife
Hiding death away in hospitals
Cartoonish death in entertainment
Hoping technology can overcome death

questions.explain: Ancestors built belief systems; modern people mostly rely on denial.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What is the paradoxical death effect, and what examples does the author give of it?
questions.a: It is the paradox that moments and encounters that bring us near death, such as a loved one dying, leaving people behind, traveling in a strange land or surviving a brush with death, make us feel more awake and alive. Our senses sharpen, our emotions deepen and we pay closer attention. The effect is strongest if we ourselves survive a brush with death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why is death a source of awkwardness for humans, and how did our ancestors cope with it?
questions.a: We are the only animal truly conscious of our mortality, and here our power to think brings us only misery: pain, separation and uncertainty. Our earliest ancestors created spirits, gods and an afterlife as a psychological compensation. Rituals around dying strengthened the effect.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Why does the author say modern denial of death leaves us no better off than our ancestors?
questions.a: Science has weakened belief in the afterlife, so we lack the old compensation, but we cannot erase our elemental fear of death. We therefore repress it by hiding death in hospitals, making it cartoonish and venerating youth. Technology gives a feeling of godlike powers, but this is just a new way to delude ourselves.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does repressing the thought of death make us more deathlike, according to the author?
questions.a: The childhood anxiety about mortality stays latent, and repression makes it stronger, so small uncertainties can make it chronic. We respond by narrowing our thoughts and activities, using addictions to dull it and becoming self-absorbed and less connected to people. We end up more separated, habitual and unchanging, which resembles the stillness of death.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What does the author mean by saying the paradoxical effect can take hold in the negative direction?
questions.a: When we go so far in denying death, the paradoxical effect works in reverse: instead of feeling more alive, we make life more constrained and deathlike. Connecting to death connects us to the fullness of life; separating the two does the opposite.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: What goal does the author set at the end of the Keys section for the modern world?
questions.a: The author says we need a way to create the positive paradoxical effect for ourselves. This means forging a practical philosophy that turns the consciousness of our mortality into something productive and life enhancing.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: According to the author, why do we convert death into an abstraction?
options: Because abstract thinking is the best route to wisdom
Because death cannot be observed directly by anyone
Because we are taught that it is impolite to dwell on it
Out of fear, so that we can entertain it now and then or repress it
questions.explain: Out of fear we turn death into a thought we can entertain or repress, but the author insists life and death are both flesh-and-blood realities.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What happened to Dostoyevsky in December 1849, according to the author?
options: He witnessed a public execution that changed his view of crime
He faced what he thought was imminent execution, was reprieved at the last moment and felt reborn
He was released from prison and wrote about his freedom
He survived a serious illness during his exile in Siberia
questions.explain: Dostoyevsky was told he would be executed, was reprieved in the last moment and felt reborn, gaining empathy and observation. Releasing him, a later illness or witnessing someone else die would change the events.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Why, according to the author, does the proximity of death sharpen our attention?
options: It makes us believe that we have little time left to waste
Our body responds to the threat with adrenaline and extra blood to the brain, focusing the mind
It stops us from thinking about our private concerns
It frightens us into a state of constant worry
questions.explain: Adrenaline and blood pumping to the brain focus the mind, so we notice details and see people in a new light. The author does not describe it as worry.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What does the author say happens to our sense of time when we disconnect from the awareness of death?
options: It becomes loose and distended, so we imagine we have more time than we do and keep postponing
It speeds up, so we feel constantly rushed
It stops, so we live entirely in the present
It becomes rigid, so we cannot adapt our plans
questions.explain: We imagine we always have more time than is real, so commitment is hard and we postpone. A forced deadline shatters that dreamlike sense of time.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the author suggest we think of our mortality, to gain the focusing effect of a deadline?
options: As a signal to reduce our commitments
As a reason to pursue pleasures while we can
As a distant date to prepare for in later life
As a kind of continual deadline that applies to all our actions
questions.explain: A deadline imposes focus and energy, and the author wants mortality to work as a continual deadline on all our actions.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the author treat the thought, Why bother to try, since we just die, so live for pleasure?
options: As another form of evasion that avoids the thought of death by drowning it out
As a justification for a simpler life
As a stage on the way to wisdom
As a realistic assessment that must be accepted
questions.explain: The author says this is not a realistic assessment but another form of evasion, since devoting ourselves to pleasures tries to fool death by drowning out the thought.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: In Defoe's account of the plague year, why did people feel greater empathy toward one another?
options: Religious leaders brought them together in common worship
Everyone was equally at risk, so differences and privilege melted away
Rich citizens used their wealth to help the poor
The danger was shared only by those in the same neighborhood
questions.explain: With the plague no one was spared, so everyone felt personally vulnerable and saw the vulnerability of others, and the normal sense of difference melted away.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the author explain why mass slaughter in war does not stimulate empathy, unlike the plague?
options: The slaughterers see their victims as separate, less than human and under their power
The slaughterers do not know what death looks like
War deaths are too far away to be noticed
People are used to death in wartime
questions.explain: In such cases the killers feel separate from their victims, whom they see as less than human and under their power, unlike in the plague where all were at risk.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What does the author mean by the Sublime?
options: Any experience of great beauty in art or nature
The feeling of satisfaction after finishing demanding work
A religious state in which fear of death is removed
Anything that exceeds our capacity for words or concepts by being too large, too vast, too dark and mysterious
questions.explain: The Sublime is whatever exceeds our capacity for words or concepts by being too large, too vast, too dark and mysterious. It is not simply beauty or satisfaction.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What link does the author draw between death and love?
options: Love grows only after a close relative dies
The specter of death impels us toward our fellow humans and makes us avid for love
Love becomes stronger when we are certain that it will last
Love is the best way to forget that we will die
questions.explain: The author says death and love are inextricably interconnected: the ultimate separation that death represents drives us to unite with others.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: True or false: Dostoyevsky noticed the rays of light on a cathedral dome in the few minutes before his expected execution.
questions.explain: He saw that all life was as fleeting as those rays, and everything seemed more vibrant to him.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: True or false: The author says the heightened awareness that comes from proximity to death fades within days.
questions.explain: The author says the effect can linger for years, even decades.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: True or false: The author says seeing the mortality of a nasty person means we should drop our guard against dangerous people.
questions.explain: Seeing the mortality and vulnerability of even the nastiest individual helps us deal with them from a neutral, strategic space, while staying alert.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: True or false: The author says we can train our minds to feel the Sublime through thoughts other than death, such as the night sky.
questions.explain: Death is the model, but the author offers other routes, including contemplating space and the origin of life.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Nietzsche's formula for greatness, amor fati, means love of ____.
questions.explain: Amor fati means wanting nothing to be other than it is, and loving it.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: For Japanese samurai, the center of our connection to life and death was in the gut, the ____.
questions.explain: The samurai meditated on this sensation to create physical death awareness.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Hazlitt observed that our repugnance to death increases in proportion to our consciousness of having lived in ____.
questions.explain: The author uses it to show that a life of pleasures and distractions leaves us haunted by wasted potential.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Defoe's book about the 1665 epidemic is titled A Journal of the ____ Year.
questions.explain: Defoe re-created the events decades later from memory, research and his uncle's journal.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: The Latin root of the word Sublime means up to the ____.
questions.explain: Death is a threshold we all must cross, and the Sublime is what lies at the edge of our understanding.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Montaigne's closing passage says that he who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a ____.
questions.explain: Knowing how to die frees us from subjection and constraint.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Which of these are among the author's five strategies?
options: Delay thinking about death until old age
See the mortality in everyone
Make the awareness visceral
Distract ourselves from pain with pleasures
questions.explain: Making death visceral and seeing mortality in everyone are strategies; delaying the thought and distracting ourselves are the evasions the author warns against.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Which of these does the author suggest as ways to experience the Sublime?
options: Reflecting on how unlikely the origin of life was
Reading celebrity news
Memorizing historical dates
Looking at the night sky and the infinity of space
Thinking about how bats perceive the world through echolocation
questions.explain: These examples confront us with what exceeds our ordinary conceptions. The others are not mentioned.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Which of these does the author list as ways people avoid pain and adversity?
options: Breaking off relationships early
Taking drugs or engaging in addictive behavior
Welcoming failure as a lesson
Lowering ambitions so as not to risk failure
questions.explain: Welcoming failure as a lesson is the opposite of avoidance, the stance the author recommends.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Which of these exercises does the author suggest for making the awareness of death visceral?
options: Envisioning the day our death arrives
Looking at the world as if for the last time
Risking our lives in dangerous activities
Imagining everyday sights and sounds going on without us
questions.explain: The author notes that we cannot reproduce a brush with death without risking our lives, so we use smaller doses instead.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Put the events of Dostoyevsky's story in order.
items: He is imprisoned for an alleged conspiracy
He and the other prisoners are taken to a square and told they will be executed
In a few minutes he notices the light on a cathedral dome and his fellow prisoners' faces
A representative of the czar announces the sentences are commuted
He feels reborn and keeps the experience for life
questions.explain: The story moves from arrest to a mock execution and a last-minute reprieve, with lasting results.

A forced deadline shatters the dreamlike sense of time
Adrenaline brings focus and creativity
We treat mortality as a continual deadline
questions.explain: The author derives the practice of treating mortality as a continual deadline from the effect of real deadlines.

questions.explain: Meditating on bodily sensations helps us feel mortality in the body; space, origins and vast landscapes confront us with what exceeds our grasp.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the Dostoyevsky story illustrate the first strategy, and why does a brush with death have this effect?
questions.a: Dostoyevsky expected to be shot, and in those minutes he noticed light, faces and the terror behind brave facades. The reprieve left him feeling reborn, with deeper empathy and sharper observation for life. The author says the threat of death brings adrenaline and blood to the brain, which snaps us out of our distracted, dreamlike state.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the author want us to use mortality as a continual deadline, and why is the Why bother reaction mistaken?
questions.a: Real deadlines focus us with adrenaline and make us creative, so we should treat mortality as a continual deadline that gives urgency and clarity to our actions. Thinking Why bother and living for pleasure is another evasion, because it drowns out the thought of death and leaves us bitter and haunted by wasted potential.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: Why did the plague bring out empathy in Defoe's narrator, and how can we reproduce this effect?
questions.a: Because the plague spared no one, people felt their own vulnerability and saw everyone else's, and differences and privilege melted away. We can produce a milder version by imagining the deaths of those around us, picturing the pedestrians in a city and the billions who have come and gone, and seeing each person's uniqueness. This also helps us handle even nasty people from a neutral space.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: How does the author connect death and love?
questions.a: The specter of death, with its ultimate separation and disintegration, drives us to unite with others. Our unique consciousness of death has created our particular form of love. Deepening our awareness of death should strengthen this impulse and rid us of lifeless divisions.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What is amor fati and how does the author want us to apply it?
questions.a: It is Nietzsche's love of fate: wanting nothing to be other than it is, and loving what happens rather than merely enduring it. Death is the ultimate thing we cannot control, so we accept it and the illness, failures and separations of life as chances to learn and strengthen ourselves. The conversion into a lesson takes time, but becomes easier with practice.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.section: A Philosophy of Life Through Death
questions.q: What is the Sublime, why does the author value it, and what freedom does the whole philosophy promise?
questions.a: The Sublime is anything that exceeds our capacity for words or concepts, such as death, which brings fear mixed with awe. It reminds us of our smallness and shakes us out of complacency and the grip of habit. More broadly, awareness of mortality frees us from restricting our lives to be predictable, so we can be daring and commit fully to our work and relationships.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does the Philosophy section relate to the Keys section?
options: The Keys section gives the exercises and the Philosophy section gives the examples
The Philosophy section repeats the history of belief that the Keys section covers
The Philosophy section argues against the paradoxical death effect described earlier
The Keys section diagnoses death denial, and the Philosophy section offers five strategies to turn awareness into something life enhancing
questions.explain: The Keys section lays out the problem of denial and ends by promising a practical philosophy, which the final section provides as five strategies.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How does the end of the Keys section prepare the reader for the Philosophy section?
questions.a: The Keys section ends by saying we need a way to create the positive paradoxical effect and promises a practical philosophy for turning the consciousness of death into something productive. The next section delivers it, with five strategies and exercises.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: How do the words of the chapter title, Meditate on Our Common Mortality, point to the two halves of the chapter?
questions.a: The Keys section shows why we avoid death and how denial makes life deathlike, while the Philosophy section prescribes meditating on it. The word common is echoed by the strategy of seeing the mortality in everyone, which links us through shared vulnerability.

questions.unitTitle: Meditate on Our Common Mortality
questions.q: Which of these are true of how this half of the chapter is organized?
options: It then gives five strategies with exercises
It begins with the five strategies and ends with the history of belief
It first describes how denial of death works and what it costs
It ends with a closing passage on freedom from Montaigne
questions.explain: The Keys section is the diagnosis and the Philosophy section the prescription, ending on freedom. Starting with the strategies and ending with the history of belief reverses the real order.
